The Knesset election and the prospect of meaningful Palestinian political participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

Could this election usher in a new era of meaningful Palestinian political participation?
Tuesday’s election took place amid deep polarisation in Israeli society between those seeking to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in power and those determined to remove him. This divide may make little difference to Palestinians on fundamental issues concerning the future of their cause, but it could bring immediate changes to their living conditions, both within the Green Line – the 1949 armistice line separating Israel from the territories it occupied in 1967 – and beyond it. These changes chiefly concern a reduction in the current escalation, which Netanyahu’s government has fuelled since taking office in 2022, particularly following the events of 7 October the following year.
What could mark the beginning of a more profound change, however, is the scale of Palestinian participation in this election. Preliminary estimates put Palestinian turnout at around 80 per cent; between 1999 and 2022, it ranged from a high of approximately 75 per cent in 1999 to a low of 44.6 per cent in 2021. What prompted Palestinian citizens of Israel to turn out in such large numbers? Did elites play a role in the success of this mobilisation? More importantly, what role might the Palestinian vote play in future decision-making within a state where Palestinians constitute roughly one-fifth of the population, yet which makes no attempt to conceal its drive to entrench religious purity?
A study examining Palestinian towns within the Green Line suggests that Palestinian voter turnout in Knesset elections is closely linked to political considerations. It found a substantial decline in turnout in the elections following the Al-Aqsa Intifada at the beginning of this century, attributing the decline to political exclusion and the repercussions of the events of October 2000, when Israeli police killed 13 Palestinian protesters, for relations between Palestinians and the state.
By contrast, Arab turnout rose markedly in the first election after the Oslo Accords, held on 29 May, 1996, reaching approximately 77 per cent, compared with 69.7 per cent in 1992, an increase of 7.3 percentage points. Palestinian participation in the current Knesset election is being described as historic, with preliminary turnout figures reaching 80 per cent.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced worsening challenges under Netanyahu’s current government compared with previous periods, including personal security, civil liberties, development budgets and housing. These problems did not begin with this government. Long-standing social and economic disparities between Arab and Jewish communities were already evident in educational and employment opportunities, infrastructure and public services, alongside an intractable and escalating crisis of violence and crime within Palestinian society.
Personal security has become the most pressing of these challenges. Figures documented by The Abraham Initiatives, an Arab-Jewish civil society organisation, show that the number of Palestinian victims of violence and crime rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2023, followed by 230 in 2024 and 252 in 2025, more than double the figure recorded before the current government took office. This escalation has not been accompanied by effective accountability. The Times of Israel reported that Israeli police solved only around 10 per cent of murders within the Palestinian community in 2025. A 2024 opinion poll identified violence and crime as the greatest challenge facing Palestinian society within the Green Line.
Alongside the deterioration in personal security, Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced increasing restrictions on freedom of opinion, expression and protest under Netanyahu’s current government, particularly since 7 October, 2023. Adalah – The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel has documented investigations, arrests and legal proceedings arising from social media posts and online protest activities, including statements falling within the scope of freedom of expression, such as opposition to the targeting of civilians and solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. These restrictions have extended beyond the online sphere to include sweeping limitations on organising anti-war demonstrations and the use of measures to silence Palestinian criticism.
These challenges extend to education, employment, infrastructure and the capacity of local authorities to provide services in Palestinian communities. A report published by the Knesset Research and Information Center in March 2026 documented a decline in both funding allocations and the implementation of development programmes for Palestinian towns between 2022 and 2024. Press reports revealed that in December 2025 the government approved the transfer of approximately 220 million shekels ($68 million) from a civilian development plan to the police and the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, diverting resources partly earmarked for building classrooms and supporting cultural institutions and youth centres in Palestinian towns. Human rights organisations and the National Committee of Heads of Arab Local Authorities also filed a petition with the High Court challenging the government’s decision in July to reallocate 496.9 million shekels ($162 million) from the five-year development plan (Government Resolution 550) to the police and the Shin Bet.
These pressures also extend to escalating demolitions and displacement in the Negev, where the Negev Coexistence Forum for Civil Equality, an Arab-Jewish rights group, documented 5,187 demolitions of buildings and structures in 2024, an increase of 58 per cent over the previous year. Among the most prominent cases was the demolition of dozens of homes in the village of Wadi Al-Khalil, leaving hundreds of Palestinians homeless. These policies pursued by Netanyahu’s government against Palestinians within the Green Line intersect with even harsher and more complex policies targeting Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, which explains the anxiety and mounting fears surrounding the government’s intentions.
These factors, together with Palestinian party elites’ awareness of them, may have played a significant role in guiding, mobilising and encouraging the public to vote in this election. The two Palestinian electoral lists, the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am), conducted campaigns relatively free of mutual attacks compared with previous campaigns. They emphasised that strengthening the lists’ electoral position would make it harder to form a new government including extremist ministers.
Activists and community leaders also played a role in encouraging different segments of society to vote and avoid provocations that could obstruct access to polling stations. The electoral messaging of some of these elites reflected a political evolution that had unfolded over the years and matured in response to the Netanyahu government’s policies targeting Palestinians.
The significance of Palestinian participation in Knesset elections lies in its ability to tip the political balance, as Palestinian seats in the Knesset can help determine whether a government is formed or remains in power. Following the withdrawal of the ultra-Orthodox Shas party from Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s government in 1993, the government remained in office despite its parliamentary support falling to 56 seats, relying on outside backing from five Knesset members belonging to factions representing Palestinian society.
In 2021, the participation of Ra’am in the coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid helped form the government that replaced Netanyahu’s. The influence of Palestinian parliamentary factions also extends to the passage of legislation and budgets benefiting Palestinian communities within the Green Line. Palestinian parties, working alongside local authority leaders and civil society organisations, have helped advance government plans to narrow disparities between Jewish and Palestinian communities. Palestinian representation in the Knesset has also enabled issues affecting Palestinians to be placed on the parliamentary agenda and referred to its committees, including the demolition of homes in Qalansawe, which was brought before the Interior Committee, and the issue of Palestinian workers’ wages, which was raised before the Labour Committee.
Broader Palestinian representation could place Palestinian parties among the larger forces in the Knesset and enable them to influence decision-making to a limited extent. As past experience suggests, however, an increase in seats does not automatically translate into substantive influence over decisions or a change in political direction. Such influence remains confined to the avenues outlined above, particularly when it comes to decisions affecting the fate of Palestinians. It is therefore necessary not only to sustain and organise greater Palestinian electoral participation, but also to draw on left-wing and centrist voices within the Green Line, particularly those sympathetic to Palestinian rights and the justice of their cause, both in the Knesset and on the streets. These voices should be supported, both to strengthen their standing and to invest in partnership with them.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Haze-fueled protests engulf Jakarta – RT reports (VIDEO)
A wave of protests fueled by toxic haze from massive wildfires continues in Indonesia, with thousands of demonstrators rallying in central Jakarta last week.
Anti-government demonstrations began earlier this month, around the second anniversary of President Prabowo Subianto’s inauguration.
Anger over the government’s handling of the wildfire crisis, described as the worst in more than a decade and linked to widespread respiratory illnesses, has compounded discontent over the rising cost of living, perceived corruption and other grievances.
Protesters are demanding that the government declare a national emergency, a step officials have argued is unnecessary because sufficient resources have already been allocated to tackle the situation. The administration says it has deployed an additional 70,000 firefighting personnel. Combined with improving weather conditions, the effort has helped reduce air pollution in affected parts of Indonesia and neighboring Malaysia and Singapore, according to officials.
Scientists say extreme heat and an intensifying El Nino phenomenon in the Pacific have made Indonesia’s forests and peatlands particularly vulnerable to fires this year. The government has also alleged that some of the fires may have been deliberately started and has launched investigations.

Poland may reconsider transferring additional MiG-29s to Ukraine if Bulgaria deal falls through – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Poland may reconsider transferring additional MiG-29s to Ukraine if Bulgaria deal falls through – expert
Polish expert and former Minister of National Defence Janusz Onyszkiewicz expressed this opinion in a comment to Ukrinform.
According to him, Poland has more than two MiG-29 fighter jets, so the transfer of two aircraft to Ukraine does not mean that the issue of the remaining jets is “definitively closed.”
“We are transferring two aircraft to Ukraine, while regarding the remaining few, as I understand it, talks with Bulgaria are ongoing,” Onyszkiewicz said.
He suggested that if Poland and Bulgaria fail to reach a final agreement, the issue of transferring these aircraft to Kyiv could return to the agenda.
“Since there is no final agreement signed, the matter could come back if the talks with Bulgaria ended in failure,” the former minister said.
The expert noted that the transfer of two MiG-29s to Ukraine would be part of a broader military aid package that would also include, in particular, air defense equipment.
Commenting on reports that Poland had allegedly considered suspending the transfer of a military aid package to Ukraine following the Lviv Regional Council’s decision to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and Roman Shukhevych, Onyszkiewicz noted that the regional council’s proposal has not yet been formally approved.
“The Polish side took note of this and regarded it as a positive fact,” said the former Polish defense minister.
At the same time, he stressed that military cooperation between Poland and Ukraine is well established.
“I think military assistance is working quite well. I hope it will continue to do so and that cooperation will be strengthened even further,” he said.
According to Onyszkiewicz, Ukraine’s need for support may increase due to intensified Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, particularly energy networks. He stressed that the purpose of such strikes is to break the spirit of resistance of the Ukrainian people, but expressed confidence that Russia would fail to achieve this.
Commenting on the possible contents of Poland’s next military aid packages for Ukraine, Onyszkiewicz declined to speculate, noting that the list of weapons and equipment transferred cannot always be made public. At the same time, he stressed that Ukraine is constantly in need of air defense systems.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 29, Poland said it would soon transfer two more MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million. The package will also include ammunition and air defense equipment.

TAIEX falls 5.69% in worst October on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:19:32 UTC
22:19:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The benchmark stock index on Friday ended the month under heavy selling pressure, as investors weighed returns on AI capital spending.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, fell as much as 1,652.07 points during the session, reaching a low of 44,726.26. Although buying emerged, the index remained under pressure and closed down 1,156.5 points, or 2.49%, at 45,211.83, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
For October, the TAIEX fell 2,728.3 points, or 5.69%, marking its worst performance for the month on record. Senior analyst Chien Po-yi (簡伯儀) said the decline was largely driven by a correction in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a key indicator of global chip stocks, rather than a deterioration in domestic market fundamentals, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Turnover totaled NT$877.7 billion (US$26.9 billion) on Friday. The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$148.03 trillion, compared with NT$156.81 trillion at the beginning of the month, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
All of the market’s most heavily weighted stocks ended lower. TSMC fell 1.86% to NT$2,370.
MediaTek lost 3.21% to NT$3,915 ahead of its earnings conference after market close. Investors were looking for updates on its fourth-quarter outlook, application-specific chip development, and profitability.
Foxconn declined 1.01% to NT$245.5. Delta Electronics hit its daily limit-down at NT$1,335, while ASE lost 2.2% to NT$668, according to Yahoo Stocks.
All 46 companies trading above NT$1,000 per share ended lower. Aspeed Technology and King Slide Works, the market's two most expensive stocks, fell 5.95% and 2.33%, respectively, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Selling extended beyond heavyweights to the broader AI supply chain. Semiconductor packaging and testing companies, including Greatek Electronics, King Yuan Electronics, Ardentec, and Powertech Technology, lost more than 5%.
Optical communications stocks also came under pressure, with Truelight Electronics hitting limit-down. LandMark Optoelectronics, Visual Photonics Epitaxy, Apac Opto Electronics, and Global Communication Semiconductors each lost more than 7%.
Profit-taking weighed on panel stocks despite earlier interest in their expansion into advanced chip packaging and glass substrates. AUO hit the daily limit, Innolux lost 7.5%, and Hannstar Display declined 4.32%, according to Sinotrade.
Passive component stocks retreated after earlier gains on expectations of higher specifications in AI servers and reported price increases. Industry leader Yageo lost 7.55% to NT$502.
Walsin Technology fell to its limit-down, while Prosperity Dielectrics lost 9.23%, Honey Hope Honesty 8.73%, and Holy Stone Enterprise 8.82%. Nichidenbo, Ta-I Technology, Kaimei Electronic, and Lelon Electronics each recorded losses of between 6% and 7%.
The silicon wafer sector weakened after analysts lowered their fourth-quarter forecasts for foundry utilization and pricing, citing weaker demand for long-term contract shipments and a sluggish recovery in mature-node production. Winstek Semiconductor fell to its daily limit, while Phoenix Silicon International lost 7.63% and Episil-Precision declined 7.38%.
Cybersecurity stocks bucked the broader decline as domestic institutional investors moved funds into companies with lower shareholdings and policy support. Changing Information Technology hit its daily limit-up, Provision Information gained 7.42%, and Baas Innovation added 2.75%.
Traditional industries outperformed. Shipping stocks gained on stable spot freight rates, Red Sea disruptions, and expectations of year-end restocking in Europe and the US.
Evergreen Marine and Wan Hai Lines each gained more than 4%. U-Ming Marine Transport and Yang Ming Marine Transport rose more than 2%.
Food stocks also posted gains, led by Wei Chuan Foods, which reached the daily limit. Ve Wong, DaChan Great Wall, Uni-President Enterprises, and Hunya Foods ended higher.
Analyst Tsai Ming-han (蔡明翰) said the market was experiencing a correction similar to July's. He noted that investor sentiment tends to become more cautious and sensitive at the start of earnings seasons, which typically fall in the first month of each quarter, including October.
Analysts said month-end portfolio adjustments by institutional investors and shifts in foreign investors' positions in the spot and futures markets may have added to volatility. They said the market may need more time for selling pressure to ease, according to CTEE.
Continued weakness in US tech equities could keep Taiwan shares in a consolidation pattern. Analysts said the TAIEX's ability to regain its six-month moving average and a return of buying interest in key sectors such as AI, semiconductors, and printed circuit boards would be key indicators of market direction next month.

Rescue workers in Kenya's capital Nairobi recovered a woman's body Friday from the rubble of a collapsed 16-story building, as emergency teams continued searching for 16 people still missing eight days after the disaster.
Nairobi North County Commissioner Simon Osumba confirmed the recovery, saying the woman had been crushed beneath a concrete wall.
"We recovered the body of a woman who had been crushed by a collapsing wall, leaving her body split in two. We are saddened to report this loss of life, but we are not giving up," Osumba told reporters at the scene.
He said her remains had been transferred to Nairobi City Mortuary.
The building, still under construction, collapsed Oct. 23 in the densely populated Eastleigh neighborhood, trapping people beneath concrete and steel.
Businesses had already begun operating from ground-floor shops, exposing workers and customers to the collapse during a busy Friday.
Authorities said rescue teams had cleared approximately 85% of the debris, while six people had been pulled out alive over the past five days.
Osumba said a joint verification exercise by the Kenya Red Cross and the Directorate of Criminal Investigations had confirmed the number of people still unaccounted for.
National Disaster Management Unit Director Duncan Ochieng said emergency personnel were focusing on sections of the wreckage where possible signs of life had been detected.
Rescuers continued working through unstable concrete slabs and twisted metal to reach those believed to be trapped.
The disaster has renewed concerns about construction safety and enforcement of building regulations in Nairobi, where rapid urban development has increased pressure on oversight authorities.

Binance’s $6.3 billion hack: What happens to users’ money?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:17:54 UTC
22:17:54 KST

Binance’s $6.3 billion hack: What happens to users’ money?
Binance has pledged to cover all losses after a security breach affected an estimated $6.3 billion in assets, raising questions about access to funds and how much can be recovered. According to the exchange’s official statement, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Around $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen through cooperation with blockchain partners, Binance said. The company plans to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and its own funds.
Can users access their funds?
In a subsequent service update, Binance said deposits were operating normally, while withdrawals remained paused as its team overhauled the withdrawal service and related addresses. The exchange said it expected withdrawals to resume within 48 hours, although that remained an estimate.
For customers, the distinction matters: Binance’s assurance that funds are safe does not mean they can immediately transfer those funds out of the platform. Access to withdrawals depends on the completion of security work.
How could an attacker get in?
The initial investigation pointed to a potentially compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. Binance said this may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
The exchange said it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys. Its findings remain preliminary, with a detailed technical report promised once the investigation is complete and the facts have been verified.
Does $6.3 billion mean that amount is lost for good?
Not necessarily. Binance described the figure as the estimated total impact of the incident, rather than a final tally of unrecoverable losses.
The exchange said approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain. That figure could increase as investigators trace additional assets, according to its subsequent update. Frozen assets, however, should not be confused with funds already returned to users.
What should customers watch for next?
The next key updates will concern the restoration of withdrawals, further asset recovery and the investigation’s findings. Binance also said it would publish updated proof of reserves after completing remediation.
The company urged users to rely only on its official channels for updates. Its commitment to cover losses is clear; the final extent of the damage and the full explanation of how the breach occurred remain under investigation.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that hackers had stolen approximately $88.6 million worth of Bitcoin from thousands of addresses generated using vulnerable firmware on Coldcard hardware wallets.

Estonia's Russia expertise is respected by the US, says foreign minister
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said the United States has not made any proposals to Estonia to change its tone when discussing the Russian threat. He said Estonia is respected in America because the country is an expert on Russia.
On Friday, Reuters news agency, citing anonymous sources, reported that Pentagon officials had urged several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their public rhetoric on the threat posed by Russia.
Tsahkna and outgoing Ministry of Foreign Affairs Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov pushed back on the media reports on Friday afternoon.
"The United States has not made any official proposal to us that we should in any way change our foreign policy or our communication," Tsahkna told ERR.
"These are anonymous sources. I cannot comment on them, and I do not want to comment on them. However, Estonia is highly respected in the eyes of the United States and more broadly within NATO, because we are, after all, experts when it comes to Russia. Likewise, we can see very far into Russia, and our expert assessments and intelligence are highly valued," the minister said.
He pointed out that Russia is "organizing terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage" against Europe and that Estonia has not been afraid to point this out, publicly.
"Estonia has always been very clear and honest when it comes to the Russian threat and Russia's aggression against Ukraine. Also about the fact that we do not currently see Russia preparing for large-scale aggression against NATO, because we do not see any major movements of Russian troops or increases in their capabilities beyond our borders. At the same time, however, we see Russia increasingly organizing terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage against Europe. And here, too, we have been very clear in publicly attributing these acts and punishing the perpetrators. However, what Russia is doing is trying to undermine Western unity. It is trying to play on that same fear of escalation, which Russia has constantly done, while continually accusing NATO and the Western world of preparing some kind of aggression against Russia, which is absolutely not true," Tsahkna said.
'Russia is provoking us'
One source told Reuters that Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon's top policy official, recently told an official from one of the Baltic states that Russia should not be provoked.
Tsahkna denied that Estonia is provoking Russia.
"We are in constant contact with the United States on security policy, on the deployment of their troops here and on NATO defense plans. And it is certainly not in our interests to provoke Russia in any way; rather, Russia is provoking us. So we are not under any pressure one way or the other. We discuss these matters together. The United States is a NATO ally and Article 5 works, so this communication takes place daily," Tsahkna said.
Tsahkna stressed that neither the Baltic states nor Estonia have been aggressive in their messages in any way. "This entire narrative is connected to Putin's desire to undermine the political unity of our Western world," he said.
Ministry of Defense spokesperson Ines Edur told ERR that the ministry does not comment on a story based on anonymous sources and that no such request has been received by the ministry through official channels.

Two men dead, baby critically ill after migrant boat reaches Spain's El Hierro island
MADRID, Oct 30 - Two men were found dead aboard a migrant boat that reached Spain's Canary Islands early on Friday after departing from Gambia, and a baby was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition, Spanish rescue services said.
The vessel, carrying 113 people, was located about 37 nautical miles south of the tiny island of El Hierro after emergency services received distress calls late on Thursday. Rescuers brought 110 survivors ashore, including eight women and eight minors.
The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.
Arrivals typically pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings.
Migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with 2025, but crossings increased sharply this month, putting additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less populated ones.
Migrant arrivals in the archipelago fell 18% year-on-year to 11,527 people to date, according to the office of the Spanish government's representative in the Canary Islands. REUTERS

Russia set to return to international hockey tournaments after top sports court's ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:16:29 UTC
22:16:29 KST

Controversial court ruling paves way for Russia's return to world ice hockey. European nations push back
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled the International Ice Hockey Federation's exclusion of Russian athletes from its tournaments unlawful, in a ruling announced on Oct. 30.
Russia is increasingly returning to international sporting and cultural events, using them to whitewash its reputation on the world stage and distract from its war against Ukraine.
"The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) expresses its disappointment with the decision of the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to allow the Russian Ice Hockey Federation to enter a Russian Team in all IIHF Championships with immediate effect," reads a press statement from the IIHF.
"While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments," reads the statement.
In a press release, the CAS says that the IIHF cited safety and security concerns for barring Russian participation, but that for them "the evidence was insufficient."
"The Panel unanimously concluded that... only substantiated security concerns could outweigh athletes of a particular nationality to participate in competitions," reads the CAS statement.
The CAS ruling means that Russia will be able to participate in a sweep of forthcoming ice hockey tournaments in Canada, Czechia, the U.S., and Germany.
The Czech, German, and Austrian hockey associations criticized the court's decision, saying their position on Russia's participation remains unchanged and that they would evaluate their next steps.
The Finnish association called the CAS's ruling "incomprehensible" and groundless.
"As a member of the IIHF, the Finnish Ice Hockey Association is committed to abiding by its decisions," the association said, adding that Finnish athletes "have the right" to participate in competitions with Russia and Belarus, but are not "under any obligation" to do so either.
The EU is mulling ideas on how to restrict Russia's access to sporting events, and even a Russian visa ban to the bloc for anything other than necessary travel.
However, Lithuania's recent refusal to issue visas to Russian and Belarusian athletes led to it being stripped of the right to host a world pentathlon tournament.
The European Commission has expressed "regret" over decisions to allow Russia to return to world sports events, but has said it would respect the "autonomy" of sporting organizations.
With CAS serving as the supreme decision-maker in disputes between sports organizations, the Oct. 30 ruling raises the question of whether it sets a broader precedent that Europe will be unable to stop.
But CAS's own press release also mentions an Oct. 13 decision to maintain a ban on Russian participation in World Curling events, and it reads that all cases are assessed "on their individual merits."
In March, the CAS ordered the Russian Chess Federation to halt all activities in the occupied territories of Ukraine or risk a three-year ban — a ban was subsequently put in place until June 2029. Yet, Russia’s Ice Hockey Federation also operates in the occupied territories, raising questions about how such cases are being handled.

'They killed us' – Pressure from Russian authorities forces closure of Novaya Gazeta
Novaya Gazeta will shut down on Nov. 9 after Russian authorities made it impossible to continue its more than three decades of work, the independent news outlet reported on Oct. 30.
"(The Russian authorities) claim they are defending the constitutional order. No, this is an anti-constitutional order. Because the Constitution has been raped, beaten, and left gagged in prison for a long sentence," the Novaya Gazeta staff wrote.
"In this country, human rights and freedoms have been abolished, and defending them is now equated with a crime. Elections and elected bodies have been effectively eliminated. Public institutions have been dismantled. Freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled. Private life has been turned inside out by dirty hands."
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 and was known for its investigative coverage. Six of its journalists died under suspicious circumstances over the course of the newspaper's run, including the murder of Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on Russian military abuses during the Chechen wars.
Increased censorship in Russia following the start of the full-scale war against Ukraine made it almost impossible for independent outlets like Novaya Gazeta to continue to operate within the country.
Several staff members went into exile, and after Russian authorities made collaboration with printing houses impossible, the publication was forced to switch to an online-only format. Russian authorities subsequently revoked its media license and blocked access to the website from within Russia.
Novaya Gazeta Europe was founded abroad in 2022, but it exists as a separate publication.
A number of Novaya Gazeta's journalists who remained in Russia were targeted, with reporter Elena Milashina severely beaten in 2023 while working on the ground in Chechnya, and reporter Oleg Roldugin arrested in April 2026 on alleged illegal use of personal data.
Russian authorities forced the news outlet to vacate its office on Oct. 28, and its donation system was subsequently cut off, making it impossible to continue working.
"This is not just our personal story. This is the story of a country and a society that are being crushed in exactly the same way," the Novaya Gazeta staff wrote. "They killed us."

The Russian Federation refused to disclose data to the WHO about the mysterious death of an employee of a plague institute
Kyiv • UNN
Russia refused five times to provide the WHO with details of Daria Shipilova’s death. The institute had safety problems for years and cooperated with the Russian Defense Ministry.
The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Russia, where employee Darya Shipilova became infected and later died, received warnings from oversight bodies for years because of deficiencies in its safety system. At the same time, the institution cooperated with Russia’s Ministry of Defense, while the Russian authorities did not provide the WHO with additional information about the circumstances of the employee’s death. The Wall Street Journal reports this, UNN writes.
Details
The World Health Organization (WHO) appealed to Russia five times with a request to provide additional information about what had happened in order to determine the level of danger associated with Shipilova’s death, the publication writes. However, Russian officials merely repeated their public statement: the woman died of pneumonia of unknown origin.
At the same time, it emerged that the research institute cooperated with Russia’s Ministry of Defense.
"Russian health authorities are very actively hiding from the WHO what is actually happening," microbiologist Alisa Lytovka, who worked in laboratories across Russia but left the country for political reasons, told the WSJ.
For reference
The Irkutsk Research Institute was founded in 1934, when the USSR was forced to actively develop means of combating plague. During the Cold War, one of its directors became the founder of the Soviet program to develop means of protection against Western biochemical weapons. Western scientists claim that the program later became a cover for the development of offensive biological weapons, in which plague transmitted through aerosols played a significant role.
The ties between the institute and the Ministry of Defense remain, the publication writes, after analyzing government procurement data. Last year, they jointly worked on modernizing a laboratory: the ministry’s funds were used to equip it with new equipment.

22:15:13 KST

Following last month’s Jerusalem Post Magazine story on blocked access to the Saint George Monastery lookout in the Judean Desert, the Tourism Ministry this week announced a new procedure that once again opens up the breathtaking view to Israelis and tourists alike.
Licensed tour guides received a document saying that the ministry and the Mitzpe Yeriho settlement adjacent to the site have prepared a new paved driving route to the lookout that follows the community’s perimeter security road while completely avoiding travel through residential neighborhoods.
For the past three years, ever since the October 7 massacre, the road leading to the monastery has been blocked by a labyrinth of electronic arm barriers, and codes - some erected by Mitzpe Yeriho and some by the IDF.
Before then, the lookout for the fifth-century complex, where a handful of Greek Orthodox monks live, was a “must” stop for tour buses heading to or from the Dead Sea. Since the post-October 7 road closure, however, it has become a desolate and rarely visited destination.
Visitors must pass through three electronic gates
According to the new instructions, travelers must stop at the guard post at the entrance to Mitzpe Yeriho, present an identification document, and leave it with the guard. The guard will then provide access codes for the two electronic gates, which were erected by the settlement along the driving route. When drivers get to a third gate, administered by the IDF and the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, they must press the intercom to request that the gate be opened.
From there, it’s an easy four-kilometer drive to the entrance to the lookout. There, visitors can descend a steep, paved path heading down to the monastery, which is theoretically open daily from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. for visitors.
If it sounds convoluted or complicated, rest assured that the bureaucracy is well worth it for the astounding view of the fortress-like series of structures built into the severe rock formations of the Judean Desert.

Time capsule of Pompeii: Ancient cupboard provides glimpse into life before Vesuvius erupted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:14:46 UTC
22:14:46 KST

A cupboard sealed for almost 2,000 years in Pompeii has yielded an intimate snapshot of one resident's life before Mount Vesuvius destroyed the ancient Roman city, from make-up utensils and perfume to coins, cooking pots and childhood amulets.
The once-thriving city of Pompeii, near Naples, was buried by a volcanic eruption in 79 CE, preserving buildings, objects and graffiti under meters of ash.
Archaeologists pieced together bits of the wooden cupboard from traces uncovered in a house on Via dell'Abbondanza, one of the busiest streets of ancient Pompeii, the site said in a statement.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of whoever lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily life," said site director Gabriel Zuchtriegel.
Among the objects stored inside was a necklace comprising at least 24 tiny objects made of bone, glass paste, earthenware and rock crystal, including images of the gods Bes and Mercury, as well as miniature hands, feet, pine cones and bunches of grapes.
Such necklaces, known as crepundia, were traditionally given to Roman children both as protective amulets and as rattles whose sounds helped adults keep track of them.
They were sometimes kept into adulthood as mementos of childhood, offering a particularly personal connection to the unknown inhabitant of the house.
Perfume, money, mice
Other finds tell a more prosaic story of daily life.
There were tweezers, a small glass perfume or ointment bottle and an incense burner, alongside bronze, glass and ceramic vessels and cooking pots. Lead weights in a wooden box suggested that someone in the house was involved in trade.
A small woven container held 38 bronze coins.
The fact that both money and objects with apparent sentimental value remained behind suggests the owners had no time to retrieve them after Vesuvius erupted.
"Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art. It is also a place where the most ordinary objects restore the human dimension of the past," Zuchtriegel said.
"The value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces of a life: personal habits, work and memories."
The house, in a central area of Pompeii, is tentatively associated with a man named Cornelius Maximus because of inscriptions discovered there. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but archaeologists have only now investigated some of the rooms behind it as part of a wider restoration project.
The excavation also provided evidence that some problems of urban living have changed remarkably little in two millennia, with archaeologists finding the fragmented skeletons of two young mice inside an amphora kept on a raised storage area.

Italy tightens security as students, unions launch nationwide protests
Rallies across the country target living costs, investment in education, and the wars in the Middle East.
Italy has tightened security as tens of thousands of students and unions took to the streets across the country.
Marches were held in dozens of cities nationwide on Friday. Rome, Milan and Naples were among those affected by the protests, which targeted soaring living costs, demanded investment in education and called for an end to the wars in the Middle East.
A large police presence was on hand, as the hard-right government tightened security measures in a bid to control potential unrest seen in Italy and other European states in recent weeks.
In Rome, security was stepped up around the Colosseum, Italy’s most visited tourist attraction, while Milan’s cathedral also received special protection.
A few skirmishes between protesters and riot police occurred at the start of a protest in Turin, with other rallies in Bologna and Genoa.
The USB trade union called for a general strike that attracted large numbers of demonstrators, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers. Rallies in recent weeks have demanded an end to higher fuel prices and rising defence spending.
Unions have also issued a joint call with peers in France, Greece, Spain, Turkiye and Morocco to demand an end to the wars in the Middle East, including the war in Gaza and “an end to the militarisation of ports”.
“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” the statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”
The government last week agreed on a 175 million euro ($195 million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
The prices paid in Italy for food, energy, transport and bills have risen by 68 percent since 2000, while the average wage fell by almost 5 percent.
Measures to support young people and families – such as an annual bonus of 2,500 euros for workers under 30 – have also been inserted into the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general… who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said at a news conference on Wednesday, stressing that the measures were “not for those who smash windows”.
Following clashes over the weekend of October 17-18 between youth and police in Milan, in which groups of mainly young people looted shops and smashed windows, Meloni toughened laws on public gatherings and eased restrictions on the detention of minors.

Finland's endangered Saimaa ringed seal population ticks up to nearly 550
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:13:53 EET
22:13:53 KST

Populations of Finland's highly endangered Saimaa ringed seals grew slightly this year, according to estimates by Metsähallitus.
The state-owned natural resource management outfit said there are around 545 of the seals, reflecting an increase of 15 individuals over last year. The animals are one of the rarest and most endangered seals in the world.
An estimated 116 pups were born, a couple more than in 2025. This year, as many as 90 percent of observed pups were born in snow banks and artificial nests created in efforts to boost their numbers. An estimated 13 percent of the newborn pups died in their nests.
Nest mortality was likely even higher, as low snow cover levels left many pups without shelter — which protects them against predators, among other things — soon after birth.
The Saimaa seal population's recovery has been hampered by poor breeding conditions and deaths from fishing nets.
The population estimate is based on the number and location of nests detected during nest counts, along with pup numbers. As winters grow milder, experts have had to adopt new methods.
Last winter's nest counts no longer involved systematically surveying shorelines. Instead, experts mainly inspected artificial snow banks and nests.
The seals' population has grown steadily since the 2010s, something WWF Finland programme director Petteri Tolvanen credits to extensive and varied conservation efforts.
"Although the result is good given last winter's conditions, it's largely a consequence of conservation measures such as artificial snow banks and fishing restrictions. We cannot assume the Saimaa seal's future is secure without active conservation and action against climate change," Tolvanen said.
The endangered seals can now be found swimming in nearly every part of Lake Saimaa.

A 30-year-old Czech diplomat who arrived in Israel in recent weeks was killed Thursday when a minibus mounted a sidewalk and struck her near Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda Market.
Klára Schneiderová, head of the Czech Embassy's Jerusalem office, was critically injured when the driver of the minibus lost control on Agrippas Street, a busy thoroughfare near the popular market. The vehicle veered onto the sidewalk, struck Schneiderová and crashed into a storefront.
She was taken to Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem, where doctors pronounced her dead.
Security cameras along the street captured the moment of the collision.
Police detained the minibus driver for questioning and said they were continuing to investigate the circumstances of the crash.
Schneiderová's death came just weeks after she arrived in Israel to take up her diplomatic posting, a return that held particular personal significance.
Her father served as the Czech Republic's ambassador to Israel in the late 1990s, and Schneiderová spent part of her childhood in the country, developing a lasting affection for Israel.
Just two days before her death, she was introduced to guests at a reception marking Czech Statehood Day at Jerusalem's King David Hotel.
During the event, Schneiderová spoke about the personal significance of returning to Israel as a diplomat, following in her father's footsteps and serving in the country where he had once represented the Czech Republic.
A day later, she was killed in the crash.
The Czech Embassy in Israel announced her death, expressing "deep sadness" over the loss of a colleague and friend.
In its statement, the embassy described Schneiderová as a "bright, warm and outstanding diplomat" and extended condolences to her family and loved ones.
Her remains will be flown to the Czech Republic for burial.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, who had met Schneiderová at the diplomatic reception just a day before her death, expressed his condolences.
"We received the horrible news of the tragic passing of Klára Schneiderová with deep sorrow," Sa'ar said in a statement. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to her family, her loved ones, and the entire Czech diplomatic community."
"Klára was a dedicated senior diplomat and a true friend to Israel. May her memory be a blessing," he added.
Adam Čurgo, a spokesperson for the Czech Foreign Ministry, described her death as a "painful loss."
As a mark of respect, a black flag will be flown Friday and Saturday at the Czernin Palace in Prague, which houses the Czech Foreign Ministry.

New York City’s most iconic address is getting a 1,800-key hotel, bringing with it plenty more reasons to visit.
Times Square in New York City might just be the world’s most iconic address, known for its dazzling billboards, its proximity to Broadway, and, of course, its New Year’s Eve celebrations.
And in the next few years, there’s going to be a new address to know about here: The StandardX Times Square.
The newly announced hotel, set to open in the second half of 2028, will offer a new perspective on the locale, with an enclosed free-fall thrill ride on its upper floors, an observation deck more than 1,000 feet above Manhattan, and a rooftop pool.
The 1,800-key hotel will also bring with it new restaurants, bars and nightlife spots.
“The Standard brand has always been about being part of the city,” Amar Lalvani, chief creative officer at Hyatt, which owns the brand, said.
“With StandardX hotels, we’ve taken that same idea and made it simpler and more accessible.
“Usually, that means putting people in the middle of an interesting neighborhood, with everything happening right outside the door. In Times Square, a lot of it will be happening right inside the building. I love that. It’s energetic, theatrical and completely over the top.”
The Standard already has two properties in New York: The Standard, East Village and The Standard, Highline.
For those looking to experience the hotel brand here in Europe, there are hotels in London’s King’s Cross, Ibiza and Brussels, while a new property will be opening in Lisbon soon.
So far, there is only one The StandardX in the world, in Melbourne.
Other upcoming hotels in New York City
Iconic British restaurant The Wolseley is set to open its flagship hotel in New York early next year.
Found within what was once the clubhouse for The Lambs Club, the property is on 130 West 44th Street in Midtown Manhattan.
The Rockefeller Center will be getting its first ever hotel in 2027 when The Nell New York opens next autumn.
Created by Aspen Hospitality, which is known for The Little Nell, the hotel is taking over former office space and will have 130 rooms.
While not a new opening, The Plaza is set to close early next year for renovation works for at least four years.

China successfully tests stealth drone takeoff, landing from warship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:12:04 UTC
22:12:04 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
China said Friday it had successfully conducted the first takeoff and landing of a stealth drone from a warship fitted with an electromagnetic catapult, state media reported.
The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), Gongji-21 (GJ-21), “capable of both reconnaissance and strike recently made its first successful take-off and landing on the Sichuan, the country's first Type 076 amphibious assault ship,” Xinhua News reported.
It is the Chinese military’s first carrier-borne stealth drone with reconnaissance and strike capabilities.
The Sichuan warship was launched in 2024 and was recently on a sea voyage when the tests were conducted.
“This marks another breakthrough in the development of my country's amphibious assault ships, signifying that the Chinese Navy possesses the capability to launch and land fixed-wing stealth UAVs on large maritime combat platforms,” it added.
The domestically built warship uses a fully automated landing guidance system, a new integrated power system, an electromagnetic catapult and arresting gear.
“It can carry fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles, helicopters, and amphibious equipment,” the report added.
This is the first Chinese warship fitted with an electromagnetic catapult.
The GJ-21 drone is a large, tailless subsonic aircraft powered by a turbofan engine.
According to open sources, the launch bar allows the GJ-21 drone to be accelerated by the electromagnetic catapult, while its arresting hook allows it to be recovered using the warship’s arresting wires.
The drone’s folding wings also make it easier to store and move around the carrier deck.

From France to Italy: Europe swept by a wave of protests over the rising cost of living
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:11:49 EET
22:11:49 KST

From France to Italy: Europe swept by a wave of protests over the rising cost of living
Kyiv • UNN
European countries have been swept by a wave of protests over the rising cost of living, the housing crisis, and a lack of funding for public services. Trade unions have announced new strikes.
Mass protests have erupted in a number of European countries over the rising cost of living, high energy prices, unaffordable housing, and insufficient funding for public services. Demonstrations have taken place in France, Italy, Spain, Belgium, Portugal, and other countries. Some rallies escalated into clashes with police, while trade unions have already announced new strikes for November. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg, Reuters, Le Monde, and ANSA.
Details
A wave of public discontent is spreading across Europe amid accelerating inflation, rising energy prices, and worsening housing affordability. Although the causes of the protests vary from country to country, their participants are united by demands for higher wages, affordable basic services, and stronger social protection for the population. Young people, in particular, are taking an active part in the demonstrations, complaining about deteriorating educational conditions, a lack of jobs, and the absence of prospects for buying their own homes.
France: Hundreds of thousands of protesters and preparations for new unrest
The largest-scale rallies are taking place in France, where student protests over problems in the education system have gradually evolved into nationwide demonstrations over the rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with government policy.
On October 17, demonstrations in a number of French cities were accompanied by large-scale unrest. Participants in the riots set cars on fire, damaged administrative buildings, ransacked shops, and clashed with law enforcement officers. In particular, a fire broke out in the city hall building in Limoges, protesters entered the municipal administration building in Marseille, and a tourist office was set on fire in Lyon.
On October 24, a new wave of demonstrations swept across France. According to the Ministry of the Interior, about 410,000 people took part. Not only students but also teachers, healthcare workers, firefighters, trade union representatives, and other groups of the population joined the protest movement.
Against the backdrop of public pressure, the government of President Emmanuel Macron presented a package of measures on October 26 aimed at improving educational conditions. These include limiting the number of students in some classes, funding repairs to educational institutions, and reforming the university admissions system. The proposed measures are estimated to cost €5 billion. However, representatives of student organizations consider these steps insufficient.
Despite this, the French authorities are preparing for a new wave of demonstrations on October 31. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has already warned of an extremely high risk of public-order disturbances. About 70,000 police officers and gendarmes are planned to be deployed to ensure security. In addition, French trade unions have announced a nationwide strike for November 5, demanding higher wages and increased funding for public services.
Italy: Nationwide strike against the high cost of living and government policy
A nationwide strike organized by the USB trade union federation began in Italy on October 30. Thousands of workers, students, and activists took to the streets of Rome, Milan, Naples, Turin, Venice, Palermo, and other cities. Demonstrators are demanding higher wages, lower energy costs, more affordable housing, and increased government spending on education and healthcare.
The rise in military spending has become a separate source of discontent. Some protesters oppose the priorities of the budget policy pursued by the government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
The current strike was preceded by unrest in Milan on October 17–18, as well as clashes in Turin, Rome, and Bologna. Therefore amid fears of further violence, the Italian authorities have increased the presence of law enforcement officers in the cities where demonstrations are taking place.
Spain and Portugal: Housing crisis drives people into the streets
In Spain, the protests are largely linked to the sharp rise in housing costs and insufficient tenant protections. A new wave of outrage was sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from an apartment in Madrid on September 23 following a substantial increase in the rent.
As early as September 26, protesters set up a tent camp in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square. Similar actions subsequently spread to other cities. The protesters are demanding limits on rent increases, stronger protection against evictions, and the expansion of affordable housing programs.
It is estimated that Spain’s housing deficit amounts to around 750,000 units. The problem particularly affects young people and citizens with low incomes.
A similar situation is being observed in Portugal, where mass demonstrations took place in Lisbon, Porto, and Coimbra on October 17. Participants in the protests demanded higher wages and pensions, as well as state intervention in the real estate market. According to Le Monde, housing prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017.
Government proposals to speed up the eviction of tenants with outstanding debts also provoked discontent.
Belgium and Germany: The protest movement is spreading among young people
In Belgium, the demonstrations brought together students, teachers, and opponents of budget cuts.
On October 9, tens of thousands of people took part in a protest in Brussels against the federal government’s austerity policies. On October 17, new demonstrations in Brussels and Liège were accompanied by clashes with police, arson, and property damage. Law enforcement officials reported nearly 200 arrests, including more than 25 minors.
Against the backdrop of the unrest, the European Commission condemned cases of looting while emphasizing the need to protect citizens’ right to peaceful protest.
Meanwhile, student and youth organizations became more active in Germany.
Demonstrations are planned for October 31 in dozens of cities, including Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Frankfurt, and Cologne. The main demands include increased education funding, more affordable living conditions, and a review of government priorities in the social sphere.
Why Europeans are taking to the streets
One of the main reasons for growing public discontent is the rising cost of living. According to Eurostat, annual inflation in the European Union accelerated to 3.8% in September 2026, compared with 3.2% in August. At the same time, energy prices in the euro area rose by 18.9% over the year.
The prolonged rise in food prices remains particularly burdensome for households. According to Euronews calculations based on Eurostat statistics, between August 2021 and August 2026, food and non-alcoholic beverages in the EU became approximately 34% more expensive. At the same time, even a slowdown in inflation does not mean that prices will return to their previous level. Citizens’ expenses on food, utilities, and housing remain high.
Additional discontent is being caused by problems with public services, including a shortage of teachers, the poor condition of schools, and insufficient funding for medical institutions. According to an EU survey published in 2025, 40% of Europeans aged 16 to 30 cited prices and the cost of living among the issues that concern them.
What the wave of protests could lead to
Mass demonstrations are already creating additional economic and political risks for European governments.
They have been most pronounced in France, where the unrest caused significant damage to retail businesses, infrastructure facilities, and local enterprises. According to one estimate by French analysts, the damage and economic losses from the unrest on October 17–18 could have reached approximately €1.1 billion.
At the same time, European governments’ ability to increase social spending remains limited by budget deficits and high public debt. In particular, France’s public debt amounted to approximately 119% of GDP at the end of June 2026.
The wave of protests is unfolding ahead of important election campaigns. In Spain, early parliamentary elections are scheduled for November 29, 2026, while presidential elections are to be held in France in spring 2027. Analysts believe that public discontent could intensify political polarization and complicate the adoption of budgetary decisions.
As a reminder
On October 25, large-scale protests against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama took place in Albania's capital, Tirana. People took to the streets despite the fines imposed by the authorities for participating in the demonstrations.

In recent weeks, the Pentagon has urged several NATO allies, among them Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, to tone down their public warnings about the threat from Russia, four people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Pentagon officials argued that some European statements undermined Europe's security, the sources said. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby recently advised a Baltic official against any "poking" of the Russians, one of the people said.
Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine is in its fifth year, and Moscow has spread a deniable arson and sabotage campaign across Europe. As Washington offers Moscow sanctions relief and presses Kyiv to stop hitting Russian energy, the restraint it seeks appears to fall on those Russia threatens, first Ukraine and now NATO's eastern flank.
An Estonian delegation was told to be "measured"
As an example of unhelpful rhetoric, Colby cited Europeans' public suggestions that Russia was "cornered like a rat," the person said. Reuters could not determine whose words he meant. In late September, Estonia said Russia had ordered the arson at Milrem Robotics, a Tallinn company supplying ground robots to Ukraine, and Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened Putin to a "rat in the corner." Michal said Putin was stepping up activity in Europe to erode the West's backing for Kyiv, and that the surest deterrent was to "back Ukraine."
At another meeting, Pentagon officials asked an Estonian delegation to keep its communications "measured," a person briefed on the encounter said. Another European official described the Pentagon's private messaging this way:
"We are helping you. The Americans are there… Just don't be loud. Don't make noise."
One European official called the advice cordial but baffling, since the Baltic states' own intelligence services have repeatedly judged it unlikely in recent months that Russia would test NATO's mutual defense provisions.
Deals with dictators lead to hell: Estonia’s PM urges Europe to help Ukraine destroy Russia’s refineries after Washington eased sanctions on diesel
The Pentagon refused to discuss "private conversations among allies," and the Baltic defense ministries did not reply.
One messenger is a key figure in the review of US troops in Europe
Colby is a key figure in the Pentagon's ongoing review of US force posture in Europe, which could lead to a sharp troop drawdown. In September, the Pentagon was weighing pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe.
Russia has lately stepped up its deniable attacks on NATO members, Western intelligence officials say. Its suspected arson campaign against Starlink sites serving Ukraine has reached Lithuania, and on 28 October German prosecutors announced the arrest of two Belarusians suspected of plotting arson near Nuremberg. Russia denies running a sabotage campaign. Meanwhile, US officials have discussed business deals with Russia, which many European officials oppose.

MP pushes for regulation of AI in healthcare, medical education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:11:07 UTC
22:11:07 KST

NEW DELHI: India must adopt a robust legal framework to ensure the safe, ethical and accountable use of artificial intelligence in healthcare, clinical research and medical education, where errors can have serious consequences for patients and medical professionals.With the objective to establish a science-based, patient-centric statutory framework that keeps AI under meaningful human control while safeguarding patient safety, informed consent and data governance, Rajya Sabha MP Ajeet Gopchade has urged govt to take up the Artificial Intelligence (Human Health and Medical Education) Regulation Bill, 2026.The objective of this private member Bill is to facilitate responsible and trustworthy innovation, aligned with India’s national priorities, by providing legal clarity, regulatory and confidence in the deployment of artificial intelligence in sectors where human life and dignity are paramount, Gopchade told TOI.The Bill provides for the establishment of an independent regulator, National Authority for Artificial Intelligence in Human Health and Medical Education, with powers to register, scrutinise and approve AI systems, classify risks, establish standards, monitor performance and take enforcement action.``When an AI system causes harm, responsibility must not disappear between hospitals, developers and technology providers.
A regulatory authority is needed to oversee system approval, audits, compliance, liability and appropriate compensation’’, Gopchade said.The Bill, a copy of which is available with TOI, empowers the Authority to identify high-risk AI systems based on potential harm, complexity, autonomy and impact on human safety, ethics and rights. Those systems capable of causing death, serious bodily injury, psychological harm, unethical experimentation or other grave consequences would face heightened regulatory scrutiny, it adds.
It requires AI systems covered by the Bill to undergo scientific validation in clinical, research or educational settings in India, followed by continuous post-deployment monitoring, bias assessment and performance review.At present, there are existing guidelines covering certain aspects of AI in healthcare, but they may not be legally binding. Earlier, the Indian Council of Medical Research released ethical guidelines to address issues including patient safety, informed consent, transparency and ethical review of AI-based biomedical research and healthcare applications. While the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, cover AI-enabled software that qualifies as a medical device, including safety and performance requirements.

A Palestinian man was wounded and two others were arrested on Friday amid attacks by Israeli forces and illegal Israeli settlers targeting olive pickers and agricultural communities across the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian sources.
In the northern occupied West Bank, a 36-year-old Palestinian man sustained bruises and other injuries after being beaten by illegal Israeli settlers in Burqa, northwest of Nablus.
The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its medical teams treated him after he fell from a height during the attack.
In Beit Dajan, east of Nablus, illegal settlers attacked farmers harvesting olives in the northern part of the town, prevented them from continuing their work and forced them to leave their fields, local sources told Anadolu.
Israeli soldiers also pursued olive pickers in the southern and eastern parts of Al-Lubban Al-Sharqiya, south of Nablus, and fired sound grenades at them.
More than 30 Palestinians were forced to leave agricultural land located just dozens of metres from homes in the village, according to local sources.
Homes and agricultural property targeted
In the Al-Masoudiya area northwest of Nablus, illegal settlers reportedly broke into a house, damaged its door and belongings, and cut electricity lines.
In the Jenin governorate, settlers entered the eastern part of Jaba early Friday and stole equipment from a vehicle repair workshop. They also damaged three vehicles by smashing windows and slashing tyres, and stole a car radio, other equipment and two sheep from outside Palestinian homes.
Jaba Mayor Mohammad Al-Baddad told the official Palestinian news agency Wafa that the settlers arrived in a vehicle before carrying out the thefts and vandalism.
In the central occupied West Bank, settlers attacked olive pickers and a foreign solidarity activist in Kafr Malik, northeast of Ramallah, according to local sources. The activist was assaulted while accompanying Palestinian farmers, while Israeli forces arrested two Palestinians harvesting olives east of the town.
In Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, illegal settlers attacked olive pickers near homes belonging to the Jabr family and opened fire towards Palestinian houses, local sources said.
Palestinian commission documents hundreds of attacks
The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said on October 22 that it had documented 409 attacks targeting olive farmers, trees, agricultural land and equipment across the occupied West Bank between October 1 and 21.
According to the commission, 317 of the incidents were attributed to illegal Israeli settlers and 92 to Israeli forces.
The reported attacks included preventing farmers from reaching their fields, forcing them off their land, stealing crops and damaging olive trees and agricultural equipment.
Israeli military raids and settler attacks have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, since October 2023.
Palestinians have reported killings, arrests, home demolitions, arson, land bulldozing and the displacement of communities during this period.

Swiss foreign minister completes North Korea diplomatic trip
Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis has concluded a two-day visit to Pyongyang, the first by a government minister to North Korea since 2003.
The diplomatic visit was aimed at re-establishing political dialogue with Kim Jong Un’s regime.
“I am delighted to mark the official reopening of the Swiss diplomatic mission” in Pyongyang, Cassis said on the social media platform X. According to him, this is a concrete step aimed at strengthening direct dialogue with the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea (DPRK).
In Pyongyang, Cassis met with his counterpart Choe Son Hui and Jo Yong Won, Secretary of the Central Committee of the DPRK. Meetings focused on the normalisation of political relations and the resumption of political dialogue. The discussions also covered the security situation on the Korean Peninsula.
The diplomatic office in the North Korean capital has been operational again since October 19. It reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, which remains responsible for diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. It had been closed in March 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Cassis has crossed the border into South Korea for the second leg of his visit to the Korean Peninsula. Switzerland’s involvement in the region dates back more than 70 years, from the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission to its mediation efforts.
Also in South Korea, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of German reunification 36 years ago during a visit to the inter-Korean border. “Let us hope that Korea, too, will one day have the chance to regain its national unity,” he said.
“Here, too, we can see just how much such a country suffers from division and how strong the desire for reunification is, at least in this part of the Korean peninsula,” Merz added.
He also noted that, during his talks in Seoul, the German experience of reunification had been raised on several occasions.

US economy, soaring living costs dominate voter concerns ahead of November midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:07:31 UTC
22:07:31 KST

Economic pressures from high inflation, rising energy prices, cooling job growth and affordability issues take center stage for voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the US, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Soaring living costs dominate voter preferences, public opinion polls ahead of the elections show.
Some 84% of registered voters consider the state of the economy very important to their vote, including 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats, a survey by the Pew Research Center on Oct. 8 found.
Accelerating inflation, weakening consumer confidence and persistently high borrowing costs just days before the elections underscore these concerns.
Energy costs continue to strain households amid tensions in the Middle East that began with the joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran at the end of February.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) reported that the average price of gasoline stood at $4.23 a gallon as of Oct. 29, marking a surge of more than 39% from the $3.04 average recorded during the same period last year.
Diesel prices remain at record highs of around $6.33 per gallon, up 72%. Since diesel is used in the transportation and agriculture sectors, soaring prices drive up costs throughout the supply chain.
The US is paying the heaviest toll of the Middle East conflict and the oil shock in the Strait of Hormuz, shouldering around $160 billion of the $468 billion in additional costs added to the global fuel bill, according to the nonprofit Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Inflation remains well above the US Federal Reserve’s 2% target as the country’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% month-on-month and 3.7% year-on-year in September, pushing monthly and annual inflation to five-month and four-month highs, respectively.
The core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% year-on-year in September.
The producer price index (PPI) surged 1.3% month-on-month and 6.3% year-on-year in the same month, marking multiyear highs.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh recently said Americans have been facing inflation that has remained above the bank’s target for nearly six years.
The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, hiking them by 25 basis points before maintaining rates at a range of 3.75%-4% this month. The bank had cut rates by a total of 75 basis points last year and maintained them at its first five meetings of this year.
The labor market also started to cool, with nonfarm payrolls rising by only 29,000 in September, well below estimates, while the figures for July and August were revised downward by a combined 60,000 jobs.
The number of initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 in the week ending Oct. 24, the lowest level since mid-July.
While the unemployment rate rose slightly by 0.1 percentage points to 4.2%, representing 7.1 million people, the US economy showed resilience in the third quarter, growing at an annual rate of 3.4%, driven by private consumption and massive tech investments.
This performance failed to positively influence consumer sentiment, as the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index dropped to a five-month low of 48 in October amid a rise in short-term inflation expectations to 4.7%.
Consumer confidence declined by 10% year-on-year and 15% compared with February, before tensions with Iran escalated.
Meanwhile, inflationary pressures and expectations of tighter monetary policy kept bond markets under selling pressure, with the US 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hitting 24-year highs earlier in October before retreating somewhat, although they remained elevated.
At the same time, the housing market came under pressure from high financing costs as 30-year fixed mortgage rates hovered around 7.37%, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA).
Pending home sales dropped 11.3% year-on-year and 7.3% month-on-month in September, data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR) showed.
The US federal budget ran a deficit of $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, marking the highest level since the COVID-19 pandemic, while total public debt hit $40.4 trillion.
Net interest payments on the massive debt exceeded $1 trillion as debt servicing became the federal government’s third-largest spending item, surpassing defense and overall health care, while ranking behind Social Security and Medicare.
Trade protectionism also drove up domestic cost pressures. Although the Supreme Court struck down initial tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), Washington imposed new tariffs of 10%-12.5% on the EU and other countries under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
Some 69% of registered voters disapproved of US President Donald Trump’s tariff policies, according to a poll by Fox News in mid-October.
Some 81% of participants in an Ipsos poll conducted in September think tariffs directly drove up prices.
A recent poll by The New York Times/Siena College showed that 64% of registered voters disapprove of the current administration’s handling of the US economy.
Some 69% of voters disapproved of Trump’s stance on the cost of living, while 65% disapproved of his approach to the war in Iran.
Some 73% expressed dissatisfaction with the policy Trump has pursued regarding gasoline prices, the survey showed.
Economic pressures will decide the outcome of the elections, given that key races for seats in the House of Representatives and the Senate are neck and neck.
