AFP: The Swiss President Guy Parmelin will meet with President Xi Jinping today. Following the meeting, both countries will sign an optimized bilateral free trade agreement. Can China share the expectations you have for this upgraded agreement?
Guo Jiakun: We’ve shared information on President Parmelin’s visit to China. There will be timely updates on the visit. Please stay tuned.
Reuters: We had a story out of Washington that U.S. telecom regulator is voting next month to ban Chinese telecom companies from direct access to U.S. telephone numbers. And also the same U.S. regulator has decided to ban all Chinese labs from testing U.S. electronics like smartphones. Any comment regarding those matters?
Guo Jiakun: The U.S. is overstretching the concept of national security and abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses. China firmly opposes and deplores this. The U.S. move severely hinders normal economic and trade cooperation between Chinese and American businesses and is not in the interest of any party including US companies and consumers. China will do what is necessary to firmly defend its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.

'The state failed to do its duty': the man rebuilding Israel's war-battered north and south
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:03:36 UTC
21:03:36 KST

The odometer in Aviad Friedman's car tells the whole story. Every month, he drives more than 8,000 kilometers (5,000 miles) across Israel, traveling between two regions scarred by war. His wife, Hannah, sometimes asks how much longer he can keep running a marathon at a sprinter's pace. But Friedman, who wakes up every morning at 4:30 and begins his day with a run before plunging into mountains of bureaucracy, refuses to slow down.
For the past two years, he has led the Tekuma Administration, responsible for rebuilding the communities surrounding the Gaza Strip. About nine months ago, in January 2026, he took on the equally daunting and complicated challenge of rehabilitating northern Israel when he was appointed chairman of the unified Tekuma-Tnufa reconstruction administration.
It turns out that his decision to assume responsibility for rebuilding the northern border communities went directly against the advice of those closest to him.
"No normal person would take this job," Friedman admits, recalling the moment his father pulled him aside for a private conversation. "It was the first time in my life my father ever asked me, 'Aviad, I'm asking you not to do this.' He told me I'd been very successful in business, successful in my previous positions and successful in the south. He asked why I wanted to fail and why I wanted to be associated with this after five people before me had failed. He practically begged me."
Our journey together through the communities surrounding Gaza in the south and along the northern border takes place at a particularly charged moment. Three years have passed since that dark morning during the Jewish holiday of Simchat Torah, and the gulf between the two regions is evident on every road, in every landscape and in every conversation with residents.
Standing on an observation hill in Sderot, the reconstruction chief points toward Beit Hanoun and Beit Lahia on the outskirts of the Gaza Strip, but asks us to shift our gaze from the destruction to what is rising around us.
"What's the most beautiful view in the world? A construction crane!" he declares with the enthusiasm of someone who once served as director-general of the Housing Ministry. "Because it means construction, because it means growth. That's what excites me. Forget Gaza for a second. Look at what's happening here and see how many cranes there are, and then look over there. Do you understand the difference?"
Sderot's success is reflected in striking demographic figures. The city entered the war with approximately 36,000 residents and has since grown to 42,000. Of the 12,000 families evacuated from the city in October 2023, only about 250 have chosen not to return.
Yet Mayor Alon Davidi is far from complacent. "If anyone in the government thinks that when the Tekuma Law and its funding end in 2028 the post-traumatic suffering here will also end, they're living in a fantasy," he tells us.
The Tekuma region, the official designation for the area surrounding Gaza, is now home to approximately 66,000 residents, an increase of about 10% compared with the prewar period and a growth rate 2.5 times the national average.
But as we head north toward the Galilee, the picture changes dramatically. There, facing Hezbollah and Lebanon, no forest of construction cranes fills the skyline. In Moshav Shomera, in the Ma'ale Yosef Regional Council, children heading to school in October 2026 still wait each morning for their bus beside a shelter riddled with shrapnel holes.
This contrast defines Friedman's daily struggle in his dual role: trying to bring hope and optimism to a region where the state removed obstacles and allocated resources generously, while confronting another where rigid bureaucracy, endless delays and a profound crisis of trust have prevailed, in an area that received little government attention even before the war.
Six months of hell
The disparity begins with the powers and resources granted to the two reconstruction administrations.
In the south, the Tekuma Administration was established immediately in October 2023, backed by dedicated legislation designed to remove bureaucratic obstacles and provide exemptions from tender requirements. It received independent implementation budgets, allowing it to manage infrastructure, education, health care and municipal funding without having to plead with individual ministers.
Of the 17.2 billion shekels (about $5.7 billion) approved for rebuilding the south, approximately 11.6 billion shekels (about $3.8 billion) had been committed and spent by the end of 2025, including more than 1.5 billion shekels (about $496 million) for physical reconstruction and temporary housing.
At Kibbutz Nirim, for example, the burned-out young adults' neighborhood was rebuilt by a contractor employing Chinese workers in double shifts. More than 90% of the kibbutz's community has now returned. At Kfar Aza, one of the communities devastated most severely in the October 7 attacks, the state invested 300 million shekels (about $99.2 million), and the first families began moving back into their homes this past summer.
In the north, however, the process unfolded in almost exactly the opposite way.
The implementation headquarters established for the region had no executive authority. Maj. Gen. (res.) Eliezer "Chiney" Marom resigned after six months of unsuccessful efforts, while five different project directors were replaced or blocked for political reasons. The Joint Distribution Committee, a Jewish humanitarian organization, found itself drafting government resolutions instead of the state.
When Ze'ev Elkin was appointed a minister within the Finance Ministry, responsible for rehabilitation in both the north and south, he stabilized the system but failed to formalize the status of the understaffed northern administration or provide it with the authority and resources it needed.
Only in December 2025 was a decision made to merge it with its southern counterpart. The government's 13.4 billion-shekel (about $4.4 billion) reconstruction plan for the north was not finalized until June 2026, following Elkin's decision to approve it in stages, a process that took longer than expected.
Of the 6.1 billion shekels (about $2 billion) spent in the north so far, approximately 2 billion shekels went toward evacuation grants, compensation for abandoned properties and temporary arrangements rather than infrastructure reconstruction.
"It wasn't right. The government resolutions should have been approved long before I arrived," Friedman acknowledges candidly. "I came in December, and it was miserable. How can you get anything moving with eight or nine employees? The Joint had to draft a government resolution? Where does something like that happen? It's not normal. The State of Israel failed to do its duty."
Friedman also had to contend with a six-month period without a permanent director-general when he began his tenure at Tekuma, a leadership vacuum that delayed legislation and created difficulties that ultimately reduced the administration's original budget by nearly 10%, from 19 billion to 17.5 billion shekels.
"I felt like I was running up a downward-moving escalator. You're trying to climb, but the stairs are moving down beneath your feet," he recalls. "We went through six months of hell, fighting with every ministry. Here you have to get past the Finance Ministry, there the Budget Department, somewhere else the Justice Ministry. And the local authority heads are supposed to trust you when their basic level of trust isn't zero, it's minus 200."
The starting point was a race against the clock, with the approaching elections setting a hard deadline.
"It was clear we didn't have unlimited time, and there were two options," Friedman recalls. "Either continue as things were, in which case there would be no government resolutions and we wouldn't finish before the elections, or go all in, build an administration from scratch, recruit 40 employees and get all the government resolutions approved for 13.5 billion shekels in the north and another billion or so for the Golan Heights.
"Can you imagine what would have happened if we hadn't managed to approve those resolutions before the elections were called? Trust was so low that people would simply have left."
Friedman knows the enormous disparity between the two administrations from every possible angle.
"At Tekuma, we control the money. We make the decisions and implement them together with government ministries and organizations such as Netivei Israel. I insist on working closely with the ministries' directors-general, but I'm not dependent on their goodwill," he explains.
"By contrast, Tnufa had no implementation capabilities from the outset, and most of the budgets remained with the government ministries. Only now have we established our own accounting and legal departments within Tnufa, and we're implementing projects worth nearly 1.5 billion shekels ourselves over the next five years."
Despite the grueling work and the long wait before tangible results emerge, Friedman refuses to give up.
"We have a moral obligation to the citizens of the State of Israel, especially those in the north, to believe this is possible," he says passionately. "If we, as a professional team, don't believe things can change, we've already lost.
"We were brought into the game in the second half, trailing 3-0. In a soccer match, you can sit on the sidelines and say it's over, curse the referee's mother or offer commentary on television. But in real life, this is our country. What's the alternative? The State of Israel has no choice but to win this game."
'Not allowed, not allowed, not allowed'
For meaningful change to take place, Friedman knows the reconstruction system must be insulated from the political interference that has accompanied it.
For more than a year, Kiryat Shmona Mayor Avichai Stern was boycotted by ministers and political figures, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who sought to help Stern's Likud-backed rival in the municipal elections. Although Stern published a video this week supporting Netanyahu and thanking him for the resources that will finally be invested in the city, the underlying hostility has not disappeared.
Later, allegations emerged that Likud activists and politically connected figures had been appointed as project directors in the north during Elkin's Likud primary campaign. Even delays in releasing reconstruction funds through the Knesset Finance Committee in August were linked to attempts by committee chairman Knesset lawmaker Hanoch Milwidsky to exert political pressure amid the rehabilitation crisis.
"It's always good when the primaries are over, because they're a constant source of background noise," Friedman admits. "I have no idea whom the administration's employees vote for, and compared with government ministries, Tekuma and Tnufa are remarkably nonpolitical.
"When Milwidsky tried to make political capital at my expense, presenting himself as someone who was 'saving the north,' he approached 18 local authority heads and asked them to join a video he was making. Not one agreed to cooperate with him.
"Unfortunately, the government system rewards whoever shouts the loudest, leaving the weakest behind. But ultimately, residents of Kiryat Shmona or anywhere else shouldn't suffer because of politics involving their mayor.
"We're in the middle of a long war that will continue for a long time, even if there are no sirens or rocket impacts. We have to rise above left and right, above one party or another, and above individual ministers. I'm glad all the unnecessary disputes with Avichai Stern at the beginning have ended."
Then, almost casually, the man who has spent 30 years at the highest levels of public administration offers a pointed observation about the government's attitude toward Israel's periphery: "For starters, the Israeli government doesn't have a single government ministry director-general who lives in the north or the south."
Looking ahead to the next government, which will take office after the elections, and to the remaining years of the administrations' mandates, ending in 2028 in the south and 2030 in the north, Friedman sets out three critical demands. Without them, he warns, the entire reconstruction effort could collapse.
His first demand directly concerns northern residents' finances: the immediate approval of an income tax benefits package for communities along the confrontation line, which remains stalled in the Knesset Finance Committee.
"Ask me what hurts me the most. It's that they haven't finished the income tax issue," he says in frustration. "We allocated 300 million shekels to increase tax benefits, but the work in the Finance Committee and the Knesset simply hasn't been done.
"We have to finish this. Otherwise, the loss of trust will be enormous. If every resident in the north could feel that extra disposable income in their pocket right now, the entire atmosphere would be different. Do residents of the northern confrontation line deserve more than residents of Ashkelon or Samaria? Yes, absolutely, and we'll fight for it," he said.
His second demand from the next government and Knesset is the passage of a Tnufa Law for the north, modeled on the Tekuma Law enacted for the south.
"Why? Because once you have a law defining this as a region requiring special treatment, I don't have to beg the accountant general and government lawyers for a tender exemption with every decision," he explains.
"What could kill all our work in the north is the planning committees. If I have to stand in line at a planning committee to build a conservatory in Beit Jann, waiting behind a woman in Ma'alot who wants to enclose her balcony, you won't see results in the north even in two years," he says. "I don't care who the next prime minister is. We've been through a war. Give us two years without all these obstacles."
His third demand, and the one keeping him awake at night more than anything else, is an absolute prohibition on across-the-board cuts to reconstruction budgets in the north and south. For Friedman, this is not a theoretical concern but a fear rooted in past experience.
"In 2015, they announced a major 15 billion-shekel plan for the north, and then they cut it. In 2018, they launched a 5 billion-shekel fortification plan for the north, and then they cut that, too. I'm afraid the next government will say, 'What a wonderful plan,' and then start cutting it bit by bit. Not allowed, not allowed, not allowed. Not a single shekel can be cut from the budgets for the north and south. They have to be exempt.
"There will always be health problems and children who have been harmed, but a genuine plan for the growth of the north comes along once every 50 years," he said.
Friedman's worst nightmare materialized sooner than he imagined. Just this week, during a contentious Cabinet meeting on Sunday, ministers approved an across-the-board cut of approximately 4% to government budgets, citing urgent security needs. The decision will remove 114 million shekels from the northern Tnufa programs and approximately 130 million shekels from the southern Tekuma programs.
Although the finance minister and his ministry's director-general quickly made public commitments to restore the funds later, Friedman sees the move as playing with fire, threatening to destroy what little trust remains among residents.
"One very effective way to destroy the trust that's left is to tell people, 'Here's what you're getting,' and then turn around and say, 'Actually, you're getting less,'" Friedman warns. "Anyone who wants to bring about change has to give people a sense of stability. The message must be that the budgets for the north and south are untouchable."
He believes the prospect of future cuts could distort decisions on the ground and damage long-term reconstruction.
"As an economist, I know that when someone senses a shortage, they tend to say, 'Let's invest in something quick, because if I invest in infrastructure, which is long and complicated, the money might no longer be available when I need it.' A mayor shouldn't have to live with that feeling, and we mustn't put ourselves in that position."
The security situation in the north remains a constant reminder of how fragile the recovery is. Just last week, the Galilee was shaken by a tragedy in which an unexploded cluster munition detonated during an outing by students from a religious high school in the Upper Galilee.
The incident has left Friedman deeply concerned about further damage to the northern tourism industry, already struggling after years of conflict. Here, too, assistance aimed at recovery and growth remains slow, with few tangible results.
"This tragedy worries me enormously," he says. "The relevant authorities have to locate and remove every unexploded munition, and people must be warned again and again not to touch them. But the solution absolutely cannot be to tell people to stop hiking or vacationing in the north. We took our family vacation in the north this year. We visited all 12 Druze communities. We have to bring tourists back to the north."
'What breaks my heart'
At a progress meeting in the Beit Jann Local Council, the gulf between government decisions and ordinary citizens becomes painfully clear. Friedman holds meetings of this kind every few weeks in each of the 25 local authorities covered by the Tnufa Administration.
Council officials and project directors from JDC's ELKA division, which supports the community, describe the cultural and practical difficulties of making government programs accessible to residents. Druze farmers do not know how to navigate digital tenders and are reluctant to apply for government assistance, while efforts to encourage women's employment encounter additional barriers.
Friedman listens, takes notes and presses his staff to simplify the procedures. For him, the government's decision to subsidize daycare in northern border communities illustrates both the potential to transform families' lives and the intolerable difficulty of actually getting public funds released.
"The crisis of trust is insane, and I understand the people. They're absolutely right after three years in which they felt the region had been abandoned and nobody cared," he says with visible pain.
"It breaks my heart to see residents waiting for a few crumbs and getting no answers because of legal obstacles and bureaucracy. Look at Beit Jann. There's a government decision here affecting 198 children, whose families are now paying 2,000 shekels less every month for daycare.
"For a young couple here, 2,000 shekels a month is half a mortgage payment! You have no idea what we went through fighting the bureaucracy and the lawyers to get that money released."
As we drive away from Beit Jann, I confront Friedman with what local authority heads have been telling me behind closed doors: The government may finally have approved a resolution, but in practice, it amounts to a cumbersome 900-page document with an endless maze of provisions that nobody knows how to navigate.
Worse still, the administrative structure in the north remains an anomaly. Friedman is responsible for the entire region, but within it are whole areas over which he has no control. The Ministry for the Development of the Negev and Galilee oversees certain activities in the cities; the Settlement Division operates in moshavim and kibbutzim; the Interior Ministry pursues its own priorities. And on top of everything else, his administration must also oversee the government resolution concerning the Golan Heights.
Friedman chooses his words carefully. "From the outset, on October 8, they should have established two separate administrations with all the necessary departments, including people and community, construction and economics, and legislated the Tnufa Law as a second part of the Tekuma Law," he says.
"In practice, that didn't happen. So when I came in, I had two choices in dealing with the existing situation: either get into territorial fights over authority or sit down with the directors-general of the Ministry for the Development of the Negev and Galilee and the Settlement Ministry, who are excellent professionals, and build a system in which people support one another rather than put obstacles in each other's way. None of us is running in party primaries, and none of us is seeking elected office."
But what about the claim that the administration itself, which controls the flow of approvals, sometimes becomes another obstacle, making life miserable for local authority heads?
"I told the mayors that nothing sits on my desk for more than 72 hours, one way or the other," he replies. "I can say yes and I can say no, because we have an obligation to make sure the money goes toward growth rather than plugging budget holes or serving political interests.
"Sometimes it's actually useful for a mayor facing political pressures to have someone who tells him no. But he'll get an answer within 72 hours. In the south, no request sits with us for more than 24 hours.
"We constantly remind ourselves that an administration that doesn't work quickly has no right to exist. The excellent people who came to work in our administrations, some of whom gave up permanent positions elsewhere, have no career ladder here. They're not going to retire from the administration. They came because they believe in the mission, and they're giving everything they have for the region, where most of them live."
Friedman asks that he and his team in the north be judged in a matter of weeks, when the money begins flowing and government resolutions are translated into actual projects and construction cranes start changing the Galilee's landscape. But he says the real bottleneck lies with the gatekeepers in Jerusalem, particularly the Finance Ministry's Budget Department and the Justice Ministry.
"Do you know when things really started changing on the legal side in the north?" Friedman asks. "The day we brought Gil Limon, the deputy attorney general, and his team on a tour. He stood out there with drones overhead, and afterward I took him to meet Stern in Kiryat Shmona. His entire perspective changed that day."
Reality is measured by results
But the shift in attitudes in Jerusalem has yet to translate into priorities on the ground. The gap between the north and south is particularly glaring when it comes to transportation and infrastructure.
I present Friedman with figures that would drive any northern resident to despair. In the south, road reconstruction and improvement projects worth more than 700 million shekels have already been completed. In the north, by contrast, a government resolution allocating 600 million shekels for transportation was approved only in early June 2026.
By mid-October, the state had released a first, pitiful installment of just 37 million shekels, which arrived last week. Another 40 million shekels is expected to be transferred soon, with a promise of 156 million shekels by the end of December.
Why does everything happen quickly and professionally in the south while reconstruction in the north drags on?
"If you're asking me what happened over the past three years, why none of this happened earlier and why it's all taking so long, I have nothing to say," Friedman replies. "And I'm not going to give you excuses, because reality is measured by results."
Forget grand visions for a moment. The shrapnel-riddled bus shelter we saw in Shomera is the face of the reconstruction effort. The Ma'ale Yosef Regional Council approved a record budget of approximately 290 million shekels this year, yet infrastructure damaged during the recent wars has still not been repaired. 
Why don't you pick up the phone and make sure that shelter gets replaced?
"How much does a bus shelter cost? The council head has money now, and he has a substantial municipal budget. Let him replace it!" Friedman responds.
"On my next tour there, I'll say to council head Shimon Guetta, 'Shimon, what's going on? Why does it look like this?' And then he'll fix it. But the administration cannot and must not replace the local authority heads. Elected officials have responsibilities. The local authority has to function, and our job is to push it forward and strengthen it.
"If local authority heads tell you they don't have engineers, and a project to build a community center is stuck waiting for a quarter-time engineer at the planning and building committee, behind a neighbor's request for a pergola permit, that's exactly why we allocated money to strengthen local authorities, so they can hire engineers.
"Just as 180 new families have arrived in Kiryat Shmona, engineers who are drawn to the Zionist challenge will come, too."
Friedman distinguishes between different parts of the north following the prolonged rounds of fighting.
"I separate Kiryat Shmona and Metula from the other local authorities," he says. "In Shlomi, Nahariya, Ma'alot, Mevo'ot Hermon and the Upper Galilee, this isn't a tragedy with a predetermined ending. That's not the situation there. But I agree that the atmosphere is difficult. Still, residents will begin seeing results within weeks.
"I prioritized funding for the hospital in Nahariya at the expense of other things, because when a western Galilee resident sees in 2027 that the hospital has another operating room and an MRI machine, and that the hospital itself looks different, they'll feel that something has changed.
"When Kiryat Shmona residents have a 24/7 medical center, when millions are invested in schools through the GEFEN education programs, and when the municipal funding reaches local authority accounts in a month or two, people will sound different.
"That won't undo the failures of the past, and I've told the local authority heads that I'm not a magician. But in another year, at least, you'll be able to judge me by what we've achieved in the north."
As our journey draws to a close and darkness settles over the roads of the Galilee, the odometer in Friedman's car continues to climb. We return to the biggest question of all: How does he balance residents' pain and despair with the strategic planning needed for long-term growth, including a target of attracting 100,000 new residents to the north and doubling the population of the Gaza border region over the next decade?
"Once, when I was trying to explain how I envisioned the administration, I said it had to be like Jacob's ladder, a ladder standing on the ground with its top reaching heaven," Friedman says. "That means, on the one hand, staying firmly grounded, always down there in the field, close to people's pain, making them feel comfortable calling me even at 2 a.m., and never lying to them, because as a country, we've already lied to them a hundred times.
"On the other hand, our minds have to be focused on the future. We have to believe that Tel-Hai in Kiryat Shmona, where we've invested a billion shekels in the institution and higher education in the north, and the half-billion shekels invested in Sapir College in the south, are the keys to attracting young people.
"As long as the Swiss aren't living in Gaza and the Australians aren't living in Lebanon, we'll be living alongside enemies. And in a place that lives alongside enemies, the State of Israel has to reach into its pocket and give its residents security and hope."

EXPLAINER - What are the possible outcomes of US midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:03:16 UTC
21:03:16 KST

- Democrats could take control of one or both chambers of Congress, challenging Trump’s agenda and intensifying scrutiny of his administration
- Senate control will shape presidential appointments, while House results could determine investigations, impeachment efforts and federal spending battles
Americans will head to the polls Tuesday in midterm elections that could reshape Washington and determine how much room President Donald Trump has to pursue his agenda during his final two years in office.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats, including two special elections, are on the ballot.
Republicans currently control both chambers, holding 53 Senate seats against 45 Democrats and two independents aligned with them, as well as a narrow House majority.
Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to secure a majority, while 218 seats are required to control the House.
Election forecasts generally favor Democratic gains in the House, while the Senate race remains more competitive. An Oct. 29 forecast by Decision Desk HQ identifies Democratic control of both chambers and a divided Congress with a Democratic House and Republican Senate as the two leading scenarios.
Whatever the outcome, Trump will retain his presidential veto power and broad executive authority, limiting the extent to which a Democratic-controlled Congress could reverse his policies.
Here are the four possible outcomes of the US mid-term elections and what they could mean. 
Democrats win both the House and Senate
A Democratic victory in both chambers would represent the biggest change in Washington’s political balance, giving the opposition control of Congress for the remainder of Trump’s presidency.
Democrats would gain leadership of congressional committees, allowing them to launch investigations, hold hearings, issue subpoenas and demand testimony from senior administration officials.
Their oversight efforts could focus on Trump’s immigration enforcement policies, the administration’s handling of the Iran conflict, tariffs, government spending and other actions by the executive branch.
Control of both chambers would also allow Democrats to block much of Trump’s legislative agenda, including efforts to enact further immigration restrictions, expand tax cuts and overhaul health care.
Democrats could advance their own legislation on health care, voting rights and other priorities, although Trump could veto such measures. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, a threshold Democrats would be unlikely to reach.
Perhaps the most significant difference would be control of the Senate, which has the power to confirm presidential nominees.
A Democratic majority could reject or delay Trump’s appointments to federal courts, senior administration positions and potentially the Supreme Court, limiting his ability to shape the federal government.
Democrats would also have greater leverage in negotiations over government funding and the national debt, potentially forcing the White House to accept concessions to avoid shutdowns or other disruptions.
However, even with control of both chambers, Democrats would face the Senate’s filibuster rules, which generally require 60 votes to advance most legislation. 
Democrats win the House, Republicans retain the Senate
A divided Congress would create a different set of challenges for Trump, with Democrats able to block legislation in the House but Republicans retaining control over Senate proceedings and presidential confirmations.
House Democrats could use their committee leadership and subpoena powers to investigate the administration, summon officials for questioning and examine government policies and spending.
They could also pass legislation challenging Trump’s policies on immigration, health care and foreign affairs, although Republican control of the Senate would make it difficult for such measures to become law.
A Democratic-controlled House could initiate impeachment proceedings against Trump or other administration officials. However, conviction in the Senate would require a two-thirds vote, making it unlikely without substantial Republican support.
Separately, Senate Republicans could continue confirming Trump’s judicial and executive nominees, preserving an important avenue for the administration to advance its priorities.
The House would also have considerable influence over federal spending, since funding legislation must pass both chambers.
This could lead to prolonged negotiations over government funding, the debt ceiling and the administration’s priorities, raising the risk of legislative gridlock and government shutdowns.
Trump could continue implementing policies through executive orders and federal agencies, although his administration would face more aggressive congressional scrutiny and potentially tighter constraints on funding. 
Republicans retain both the House and Senate
If Republicans maintain control of both chambers, Trump would have a clearer path to pursue his remaining legislative priorities.
These could include additional immigration restrictions, tax measures, changes to health care and legislation supporting other administration policies.
Republican control of the Senate would also allow the party to continue advancing Trump’s judicial and executive nominations.
However, narrow majorities, disagreements within the Republican Party and Senate procedural rules could still complicate efforts to pass major legislation.
Republicans retain the House, Democrats win the Senate
The fourth outcome would leave Republicans in charge of the House while Democrats take control of the Senate.
Republicans could continue advancing Trump’s legislative priorities through the House, but Democrats would have the power to block them in the Senate.
Democratic senators could also slow or reject presidential appointments and launch investigations through Senate committees.
Both parties would need to negotiate on government funding and other legislation, while Trump’s ability to secure new laws would be substantially constrained.
Regardless of which party controls Congress, the newly elected lawmakers will take office in January 2027, setting the stage for the final two years of Trump’s presidency and the run-up to the 2028 presidential election.

My Word: Negative political thinking - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:01:13 UTC
21:01:13 KST

Talk about a split vote. Ask the average Israeli how they voted this week, and the answer is likely to be 50:50 – half in favor of a particular politician, and half against someone else. And the negativity continues long after the ballots are counted and a coalition somehow formed.
The question became less a matter of “Whom am I voting for?” and more “Whom am I voting against?” Above it hovered the political joker: “Whom am I likely to end up with?”
Voter turnout at 77.7% was high, particularly in the Arab sector. In my Jerusalem neighborhood, Election Day had a buzz to it. The streets felt festive, and a local “social cafe” held election-themed activities for families with young kids.
There were fewer political banners hanging from windows and balconies. Some (mis)interpreted it as a sign of apathy; others saw it as a reflection of the way the battle for voters had moved from the streets to social media. Perhaps it’s also because so many parties kept merging and changing their names.
It is not yet clear who will ultimately lead the next government; it ain’t over until it’s over. The Israeli system is built on blocs. The prime minister is not automatically the leader of the party that gains the largest number of votes, but the person who can present to the president the likelihood of the most stable coalition – usually a collection of parties amounting to at least 61 seats out of the 120-member Knesset.
Hence, the myriad small parties are a sign of a vigorous democracy but also detract from it, placing an inordinate amount of power in their hands. Remember how Naftali Bennett became prime minister in 2021 for a short-lived term with just seven mandates? Here is where the Arab parties’ gains can have an impact.
Netanyahu’s outgoing government lasted its full four-year term is why he’s earned the title “The Magician.” To have survived the chaos of the backlash to the proposed judicial reform and then the horrors of the October 7, 2023 Hamas invasion and mega-atrocity and resulting war on seven fronts is remarkable.
Ultimately, however, this election also came down to the same question that has shadowed Israeli politics for three decades: To vote “Only Bibi” or “Anyone but Bibi.”
While both Left and Right agree on the need to topple the Iranian regime, too many politicians are more concerned with bringing down a perceived enemy closer to home – a rival party leader.
There will always be political wheeling and dealing in coalition bargaining – either before or after the elections, or both. The question is whether politicians are held accountable for promises made, paid for, and broken.
Expect “a fighting opposition”: infighting among the various parties that compose it. Even worse, there could be paralysis in a coalition because of the disparate nature of its numerous components.
Among the challenges are the splits within different parties and the so-called “change bloc” itself. Tellingly, ahead of the election this week, the parties led by Bennett (B’Yachad), Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar), and Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu), among others, could not even agree on who would head the bloc – who potentially would be prime minister or official leader of the opposition.
Road map to forming a government
Election campaigns included promises about which lists each party would not sit with, but it is hard to see how a government can be formed without either the ultra-Orthodox (haredi) or the Arab parties.
The coalition will be its own opposition. Neither the haredim nor the Arab parties are likely to support a law on mass conscription, despite this being a hot topic in the wake of the massive burden on reservists (and their families) during the three years of war.
The public needs to consider the price of these constant changes. When ministers believe they might not have long in office, they do not plan ahead. They want to cut as many red ribbons as possible even if it means cutting corners.
The judicial reform launched by the outgoing government as soon as members had sat in the leather seats around the Cabinet table is a product of this phenomenon: the ministers and MKs involved had not hidden their desire for a judicial overhaul – the need for a reform was acknowledged across the political spectrum – but the speed and intensity took some by surprise. But following five elections in four years, the new government did not want to risk losing time.
The protests against the judicial reform were accompanied by calls to stop serving in the military, to emigrate and create a brain drain, and to transfer businesses and finances abroad. In effect, to boycott Israel under the Netanyahu government.
Even some of those demanding a commission of inquiry into the events of October 7 acknowledge that the rifts – verging at some points on a call for a military coup by veterans – weakened the country and contributed to the timing and scope of the Hamas-led attack.
Headlines social media posts warned of post-election clashes that would mimic the storming of the Capitol in January 2021 after Donald Trump’s loss to Joe Biden. The warnings could be considered part of some campaigns.
Israel’s ballot system makes mass voter fraud difficult (but not impossible), but the greater threat lies in delegitimization – that one side won’t accept the other’s victory. This can happen from either side, Left or Right.
News stories leading up to the election noted the Shin Bet security given to Yashar’s Eisenkot, Democrats leader Yair Golan, and Amcha Yisrael head Ofer Winter (who didn’t pass the threshold) – who were all assumed to be under threat from the Right.
There is a missing story: what happened to anti-government activist Tamar Gershuni who was arrested in July 2025 for plotting to assassinate Netanyahu and released to house arrest? The assassination threat seems to have fallen off the mainstream media’s radar. Or, more likely, it was deliberately dropped.
The left and center-left parties boycotted Netanyahu’s government after the November 2022 elections, citing his criminal trials. Four years later, the trials are ongoing, although the central case involving bribery charges appears to have collapsed, with even the judges twice telling the prosecution they should be dropped. Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit on the witness stand admitted serious irregularities concerning the investigation and prosecution.
Among the scenarios that cannot be discounted is that the new Knesset, which is sworn in before the government is formed, could appoint a Speaker from the current opposition, who could then help promote legislation regardless of whomever ultimately is appointed prime minister.
Liberman last week began promoting the “Defendant Law,” under which an indicted politician would be prevented from forming a government. The theory sounds noble. The intent, less so.
It is obviously an attempt at blocking Netanyahu from becoming prime minister. If passed, it is likely to lead to a flurry of charges against politicians of different political persuasions – and to hell with the right to be presumed innocent.
Ultimately, it will place even more power in the hands of the judiciary – to decide whom to prosecute and when – at the expense of the democratic voice of voters and parliament’s right to rule.
No matter who wins, the world will be watching. If Netanyahu forms a government, Israel can expect more of the same or even a worsening of sanctions; but don’t expect a lovefest if someone else takes the reins.
The global wave of antisemitic sentiment and actions are about the existence of the State of Israel itself, not who its citizens have elected, or ended up with, as their leader. On Election Day itself, the Netherlands, for example, announced it would boycott the Eurovision Song Contest again this year over Israel’s participation.
Few imagined that Israel’s first peace treaty would have been signed by Menachem Begin’s Likud government with Egypt. And the Abraham Accords, drawn up under US President Donald Trump and Netanyahu, have proven their worth during the years of war, particularly due to the shared threats from Iran.
Not only will the results of the Israeli elections have an impact, but also next week’s US midterms.
Meanwhile, I’ll let Winston Churchill have the last word. As he said in November 1947, “No one pretends that democracy is perfect or all-wise. Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of government, except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time…”

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu survived Israel's election - but a political reckoning may only be beginning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:01:03 UTC
21:01:03 KST

Oops, he did it again.
For seemingly the umpteenth time, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defied the polls, the odds, and conventional wisdom, emerging from Tuesday’s election with the upper hand.
In the final weeks of the campaign, Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot repeated one refrain: he would not allow Netanyahu to win by not losing.
In the end, that is precisely what happened.
True, Netanyahu does not have a clear path to a 61-seat coalition. But he is firmly in the driver’s seat.
With a majority among the country’s Jewish parties, he will likely call for some kind of unity government, trying to bring in Eisenkot’s party, or part of it, along with the parties of Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman.
Eisenkot's path to 61 is harder than Netanyahu's
Eisenkot’s path to 61 is much harder because it would require support from the Arab parties, whether inside or outside the coalition. Some of their leaders have declined to call Hamas a terrorist organization, and some of the parties reject the definition of Israel as a Jewish state.
If Netanyahu’s efforts fail, he can wait for another round of elections. If the coalition-building process runs its full course, that could mean nearly another half year in office. Throughout that period, he would remain caretaker prime minister, making life-and-death decisions for the country.
Another election, while hardly good for Israel, would not necessarily be bad for him. The stars were pretty well aligned for Eisenkot and the change bloc this time: no small parties siphoned off many of its votes, and tens of thousands of people reportedly flew in to vote for it. It is hard to imagine those conditions repeating themselves next time around.
The parties will enter coalition negotiations with one eye already on the next campaign.
That could constrain Eisenkot’s bloc as it weighs whether to try to form a minority government with outside support from the Arab parties. Such an arrangement might offer a way to replace Netanyahu now, but it would also hand the prime minister a potent campaign weapon if the government proved short-lived and the country quickly returned to the polls.
That Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as the largest party despite October 7, having shed “only” six seats since the 32 of the previous election, depending on the final count, is nothing less than astounding.
Perhaps even more astounding was Netanyahu’s ability to remain in power after October 7.
Anyone in the country at the time remembers the palpable anger at the government. The country was seething. Few outside Netanyahu’s family and inner circle thought he could survive politically.
Yet he did. And under his leadership, Israel turned the tide of the war, going from being bruised and battered on October 7 to delivering devastating blows to its enemies over the next three years.
In the five previous elections fought against Netanyahu, the opposition harped on his legal cases. They called him “the accused,” “corrupt,” and headed for jail. This time, those cases barely figured in the campaign.
It didn’t help the opposition that former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit spent the final two weeks of the campaign on the witness stand in Netanyahu’s trial, giving Netanyahu’s supporters fresh ammunition to question how the investigations were conducted and whether they should have been launched in the first place.
So instead of focusing again on Netanyahu’s legal woes, the change bloc focused on October 7: what Netanyahu allegedly knew beforehand, what warnings he missed, and why he was asleep at the wheel – literally asleep when Hamas attacked at 6:29 a.m.
The campaign made the election about October 7. And it did not work.
Why? Because after October 7 came October 8, and the three years that followed. For many of Netanyahu’s voters, the reckoning also included the way Israel, against considerable odds, turned the tide against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran, emerging as the strongest player in the Middle East.
If Netanyahu bears responsibility for what happened on October 7, then he also bears responsibility for what came afterward. Enough voters gave him credit for that to leave him with the upper hand.
About three hours after the polls closed Tuesday night, Eisenkot took the stage in Tel Aviv and declared: “The Israeli public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu’s term as prime minister.”
On the seat count, he had a point. Netanyahu’s coalition won 53, meaning 67 went to parties opposing him.
But a majority against Netanyahu is not necessarily a majority for an Eisenkot government. Those 67 seats include 19 held by Arab parties, leaving the change bloc itself with just 48.
The parties may agree that Netanyahu should go. That does not mean they can agree to sit together in a government to replace him. How can a Zionist party find common ground with a party that rejects a central premise of Zionism: Israel’s existence as a Jewish state?
That the change bloc failed to secure a majority of its own – despite October 7, despite Netanyahu’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the massacre, despite anger over the haredi conscription issue, despite the judicial reform, despite hundreds of protests over the last four years, and despite the sympathetic treatment it received from an often adoring media – should set its alarm bells ringing.
Something is not working.
Perhaps it is the message. Perhaps it is the messengers – the leadership. Perhaps it is both. But something is not connecting with enough of the public.
The failure to unseat Netanyahu now, after all that has happened, should force the change bloc to rethink its message, its leadership, and how it hopes to win. Because if it could not defeat him under these favorable circumstances, it needs to ask itself: under what circumstances will it ever be able to do so?
Yet the opposition’s failure to unseat Netanyahu does not mean the political consequences of October 7 have run their course.
Look more closely, and you see the beginnings of processes that could significantly alter the political landscape.
How Israel's 2026 vote resembles post-Yom Kippur war election
Here, a historical precedent is worth considering: the 1973 Yom Kippur War. Then, as on October 7, Israel was caught by surprise by an enemy attacking on one of its holiest days. The attack exposed colossal failures at the political, intelligence, and military levels.
And then, too, a badly wounded nation emerged seething. The first election after the Yom Kippur War took place less than three months later. The Labor-led Alignment, whose dominant party and its predecessors had governed Israel since its founding 25 years earlier, lost ground but retained power. Golda Meir’s list fell from 56 to 51 seats.
The upheaval came in 1977. Menachem Begin’s Likud rode a wave of anger and frustration to a historic victory, ending Labor’s long hold on power; the Alignment dropped from 51 to 32 seats, ushering in a fundamental political realignment. The war was not the only factor – corruption scandals also played a major role – but its political consequences took time to fully emerge.
The timing differs: Tuesday’s election came three years after October 7, rather than three months. Nor does the comparison mean another 1977 is waiting around the corner. It does mean, however, that the first election after a national catastrophe does not necessarily deliver the final political verdict.
Tuesday’s vote may be sowing the seeds of changes whose significance will become clear only later.
First, Netanyahu’s bloc recorded its weakest showing in the nine elections since he returned to power in 2009. October 7 exacted an electoral price, even if it did not produce the change of government the opposition had hoped for.
Second, this election will send nearly 50 people to the Knesset who have never served there before, one of the largest freshman classes in the country’s history. At least 12 – roughly a quarter – have a direct personal connection to October 7 through bereavement, a relative’s captivity, or their own participation in the fighting that day.
Some may rise through the ranks before the next election. Others may eventually lead. They represent the beginnings of a political generation shaped directly by the trauma of October 7.
Finally, a new phenomenon appeared on the scene: the haredi list headed by Moti Leitner, which raised the banner of greater haredi integration into Israeli society – if not through military service, then through workforce participation and teaching core subjects in schools.
Before the double-envelope ballots were counted, it had won fewer than 10,000 votes – less than 2% of the combined total for Shas and United Torah Judaism. Another haredi challenger, the Tzeva Shachor party, drew a few hundred more votes than Leitner’s party, while taking an even harder line against conscription than the established parties.
In other words, the integrationist vote was a drop in the bucket. But at least now there is a bucket.
The significance lies in its willingness to establish an explicitly haredi alternative that advocates greater integration. Even a small number of voters crossing that barrier deserves attention.
Whether the party grows or disappears remains to be seen. But the pressures it sought to address – over military service, employment, education, and the haredi community’s relationship with the state – will remain.
These elections may not have closed the chapter many Israelis wanted closed. They may, however, have begun political processes whose full significance will be felt only down the line.
But if the longer-term significance of this election will take time to emerge, one immediate casualty is already apparent: the credibility of some of the country’s leading pollsters.
Black Tuesday: Why Israeli election results demand an explanation
As for preelection polling, October 27 was Black Tuesday.
Polls are snapshots, not prophecies. They measure public opinion at a particular moment, and voters can change their minds. Fair enough. They identify trends. But this time, several of the most closely watched polls did more than miss the precise seat distribution. They got the order of the blocs wrong. They badly missed the trend.
The average of the final polls from Channels 11, 12, and 13 gave the opposition more than 55 seats and Netanyahu’s bloc 50. Maariv put the opposition at 58 and Netanyahu’s bloc at 48. Those polls predicted a fundamentally different political landscape than what emerged on election night.
Two polls stood apart: Channel 14 and i24. Both correctly put Netanyahu’s bloc ahead of the opposition, though neither captured the full picture.
Critics easily dismissed Channel 14’s numbers: the station is unabashedly pro-Netanyahu, and its pollster, Shlomo Filber, is a former Netanyahu confidant. Yet it correctly identified which bloc would finish ahead, even as it predicted a 62-seat majority that did not materialize. i24 put Netanyahu’s bloc at 55 and the opposition at 47, but underestimated the Arab parties by five seats and put Ofer Winter’s party above the threshold.
The lesson is not that an outlier must be right. It is that agreement among pollsters does not necessarily make them right, either.
And the damage goes beyond the pollsters’ professional reputations. Such misses feed an existing suspicion that media polls do more than measure public opinion: they shape it.
Results do not prove deliberate manipulation, but they do demand an explanation. Did the pollsters misjudge turnout? Miss particular groups of voters? Make similar assumptions that produced similar mistakes?
“Polls are only snapshots” will not suffice as a response to discrepancies of this size. The country’s pollsters need to look inward and publicly explain what went wrong. Otherwise, they risk further erosion of the one thing their work depends on: trust.

People who favor science over religious dogma are surprisingly open to believing in ghosts and magic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:00:47 UTC
21:00:47 KST

As traditional religious affiliations decline in the United States, supernatural beliefs are not necessarily vanishing but rather transforming into individualized forms of magic. A recent survey reveals that people who favor secular reasoning and science over religious authority often hold magical or superstitious beliefs, provided they maintain some residual connection to a religious tradition. These findings, published in the journal Social Forces, suggest that the modern shift toward rationality does not eliminate enchantment but redirects it away from organized institutions.
Sociologists track the process of secularization across post-industrial countries. This concept generally refers to the declining social authority of religious institutions, rather than the complete disappearance of individual faith. As churches and religious leaders lose their ability to monopolize moral meaning and regulate behavior, alternative spiritual practices often emerge to fill the void.
Historically, magic and religion have operated side by side, yet they function quite differently in practice. Religion typically requires belief in a god or gods, offers overarching explanations for existence, and binds adherents together in a shared moral community. Magic, by contrast, relies on transactional efforts to manipulate supernatural forces for worldly rewards. It does not require a formal theology or a centralized institution.
In many ways, magic shares a structural similarity with early scientific thought. Both frameworks assume the universe operates via mechanical forces that humans can uncover and manipulate for their own ends. Magic promises tangible, worldly results without demanding total devotion to a religious doctrine. This shared mechanical outlook makes magic an appealing alternative for individuals who value scientific discovery but still desire a sense of mystery.
During the scientific revolution, early natural philosophers often dabbled in alchemy and astrology. They viewed the universe as a hidden puzzle that could be decoded through rigorous observation and secret knowledge. While modern science eventually discarded supernatural explanations in favor of strict empirical verification, the psychological appeal of manipulating unseen forces remains. A magical mindset can provide a sense of existential agency, enhancing personal optimism in a chaotic world.
Paul Froese, a sociologist at Baylor University, led the new study alongside Isaiah King of Carson-Newman University and Ruiqian Li of American University. The researchers wanted to understand the supernatural beliefs of people who prioritize science and individuality over organized religion. They proposed that a scientific worldview might actually foster an environment where ancient superstitions and magical thinking can flourish outside of religious boundaries.
The researchers analyzed data from the 2025 Baylor Religion Survey, a nationally representative poll of 1,812 American adults. The survey asked respondents a wide range of questions regarding their spiritual practices, religious attendance, and philosophical views. Using these responses, the team constructed a scale to measure a concept they called secular rationalism.
This secular rationalism scale identified individuals who rely on science as the sole way to understand the world. It also captured those who believe moral decisions should be based on human experience rather than religious teachings. High scorers on this scale preferred to interpret spiritual matters on their own and expressed a general disinterest in official religious doctrines.
To categorize supernatural beliefs, the researchers created three distinct scales based on clusters of survey responses. The first scale measured belief in traditional miracles, such as the idea that miracles happen in modern times and are created by God. The second scale measured belief in magic, which included concepts like ghosts, curses, predicting the future, talking to the dead, and the idea that inanimate objects have spirits.
The third scale captured everyday superstitions. This included performing minor rituals to avoid bad outcomes, avoiding jinxes, or feeling uncomfortable buying a house where a murder occurred. The researchers then ran statistical models to see how a person’s level of secular rationalism predicted their scores on the miracle, magic, and superstition scales.
The initial analysis revealed a stark divide between traditional religious beliefs and individualized supernaturalism. As expected, respondents who scored high in secular rationalism were much less likely to believe in traditional miracles. Valuing science and human reason predicted a strong rejection of divine, institutionalized interventions.
The opposite was true for alternative forms of enchantment. Higher levels of secular rationalism predicted stronger belief in both magic and superstition. Rather than erasing all supernatural beliefs, a rationalist worldview was associated with a shift toward individualized, mechanistic forms of the supernatural.
The researchers also accounted for demographic factors like age, gender, education, and income. Income showed a slight negative association with belief in magic, meaning wealthier individuals were slightly less likely to hold these views. Education levels lacked a statistically significant relationship with any of the three supernatural belief categories.
To uncover more nuance, the research team tested how religious participation interacted with secular rationalism. They divided respondents based on their belief in God, their religious affiliation, and their church attendance. This allowed the researchers to see if the link between rationalism and magic applied equally to strict atheists and those who kept one foot in the church.
The results showed that strict nonbelievers and individuals who never attended religious services did not experience a boost in magical thinking from their rationalist views. For fully secular individuals, the link between secular rationalism and magical or superstitious belief largely disappeared, consistent with traditional secularization narratives. In other words, among these individuals, a rationalist outlook no longer translated into greater belief in magic or superstition.
Magic flourished most robustly among people who combined secular rationalism with residual religious habits. The positive association between rationalism and magical belief was strongest for individuals who still believed in God, claimed a religious affiliation, or attended church services. These individuals seem to inhabit a hybrid cultural space where secular reasoning and spiritual openness coexist.
This phenomenon aligns with a concept sociologists call bounded affinity. This theory suggests that moderate levels of religious commitment create a prime environment for alternative beliefs. A person must be open enough to the supernatural to accept unseen forces, but detached enough from strict religious dogma to explore unorthodox ideas. Secular rationalism appears to provide that necessary detachment.
The researchers interpret this as evidence that traditional religious institutions actively police supernatural boundaries. When people remain attached to a faith but adopt secular rationalism, they begin to step outside those institutional doctrines. This creates a fertile mental environment for exploring unsanctioned supernatural ideas like ghosts, curses, and fortune-telling.
The study provides a detailed look at how modern belief systems evolve, but it relies on observational survey data. Because the data captures a single moment in time, the researchers cannot prove that adopting a rationalist worldview directly leads a person to adopt magical beliefs. The findings only show a mathematical association between these specific mindsets.
The broad definition of magic used in the study also bundles together a wide variety of spiritual concepts. Practices like ghost hunting, fortune-telling, psychics, and preternatural healings all fall under the same conceptual umbrella here. While this helps identify general trends, it might gloss over distinctions between a casual superstition and a deeply held belief in psychic phenomena.
Future studies could explore how these individualized magical beliefs spread in the modern era, particularly through social media. Online platforms host a massive market of wellness gurus and spiritual entrepreneurs who operate without traditional institutional constraints. This digital landscape might be the perfect catalyst for blending scientific language with ancient magical concepts.
The study, “The magic of secularization,” was authored by Paul Froese, Isaiah King, and Ruiqian Li.

Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
Guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme for veterans who served under, and were impacted by, the Ban on LGBT personnel in HM Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
Documents
Details
LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Data detailing scheme progress which will be shared on a monthly basis.
Data as of 26/10/26:
Total individual applicants*: 1,877
*Applicants may have more than one case due to there being two payment types.
Total decisions made on cases: 2,540
Value of total payments made: £61,916,000
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme was recommended by the LGBT Veterans Independent Review which was published in July 2023.
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme is a payment scheme open to those who served under and were directly impacted by the Ban on LGBT personnel serving in the Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
This page provides information and guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, including eligibility and how to apply.
Types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments
There are two types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments:
1. LGBT Dismissed or Discharged Payment. This payment is for those who were dismissed or administratively discharged because of the Ban, including officers who were ordered or instructed to resign or retire by their respective Service Board.
2. LGBT Impact Payment. A payment to recognise other experiences of those who served under the Ban, as outlined in the Financial Recognition Payment Types and Tariff Table. (LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme Rules, Annex B).
Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above before starting an application.
How to Apply
Online applications
The Ministry of Defence encourages all eligible applicants to submit their applications online.
An app for the scheme can be accessed on Defence Gateway from 13 December 2024.
This platform will ensure that your data and any uploaded documents are secure. The app dashboard will keep you updated about the status of your application.
The online application process has two steps:
Step 1: Register for a Defence Gateway Account so you can access the online Financial Recognition Scheme application form.
Step 2: Sign in to your Defence Gateway account and submit your Financial Recognition Scheme application form via the Financial Recognition Scheme app.
Hard copy applications
If you would prefer to submit a hard copy (paper) application form, read scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above.
Hard copy application forms can also be obtained from Veterans UK.
Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Help with applying to the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion have partnered with the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme to provide support to veterans who are applying to the scheme.
These charities can assist with completing the application form, provide guidance on writing the necessary evidence and answer any questions applicants may have.
Royal British Legion
- Email: info@britishlegion.org.uk
- Phone: 0808 802 8080
For more information on the support the Royal British Legion can offer, visit Royal British Legion - Applying for restorative measures for LGBTQIA+ Veterans.
Fighting with Pride
For more information on the support Fighting with Pride can offer, visit Fighting with Pride LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme.
Veterans Welfare Service
Additional support is also available from the Veterans Welfare Service (VWS) who provide information, guidance and support to veterans and their families, as well as supporting veterans through a network of case managers across the UK and Republic of Ireland.
To find out more, visit Veterans Welfare Service or contact the Veterans’ Helpline using the details below.
- Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
- Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
- Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Other restorative measures
For information on non-financial restorative measures visit LGBT veterans: support and next steps.

UN rights office warns of deepening displacement ‘nightmare’ in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

UN rights office warns of deepening displacement ‘nightmare’ in Gaza
Israeli forces continue to push Palestinians into ever-smaller areas of the Gaza Strip while destroying civilian infrastructure and attacking displacement sites, the UN human rights office, OHCHR, warned on Friday amid concerns of ethnic cleansing.
OHCHR said that Israel has stated that it aims to increase the area of military deployment to 70 per cent of Gaza’s territory.
The relentless contraction of space has caused new displacement in areas adjacent to the “yellow line” demarcation boundary.
Military expansion, reported attacks
Over the past two weeks, OHCHR documented the westward expansion of Israeli military deployment areas in Al Shujaiyeh, Gaza City, and in three locations in Middle Gaza – eastern Al Bureij, eastern Deir Al-Balah and eastern Al Maghazi.
In Al Shujaiyeh, at least two Israeli attacks were reported on displacement camps, while forces reportedly used explosive robots to detonate the few buildings left standing in the area.
OHCHR said that it received reports that on 25 October, an Israeli drone dropped munitions on tents sheltering displaced families at Al Shujaiyeh junction near the yellow line and the resulting fire burned for five hours.
As a result, 200 families comprising 800 people – mostly women, children and older persons - were displaced, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Public Works and Housing.
Little hope of return
“The nightmare of displacement in Gaza is both acute and chronic,” said Ajith Sunghay, Head of UN Human Rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).
“Those displaced before the announcement of a ceasefire have little to no prospect of return to the areas they fled, most of which are inaccessible because they fall beyond the so-called yellow line. And they continue to be displaced again and again.”
OHCHR said that as an occupying power, Israel must cease the forcible transfer of Palestinians within the Gaza Strip, noting that this is a war crime that may also amount to a crime against humanity.
Israel also must facilitate Palestinians’ safe and dignified return to their homes and the areas they fled.
Instead, its military operations have displaced nearly the entire population multiple times in addition to damaging and destroying buildings, structures and civilian infrastructure,
Shelter materials restricted
OHCHR said that Israeli forces appear to treat the yellow line as a kill zone, preventing Palestinians from returning to what is left of their homes on the other side.
Furthermore, the displacement crisis is worsened by the restrictions Israel has imposed on the entry of shelter-related humanitarian assistance.
“There must be an end to this suffering. This is the fourth year of displacement for most Palestinians in Gaza, the fourth winter in tents too flimsy to withstand the rain, and they are still under fire through it all,” said Mr. Sunghay. “Let this be the last.”

Yemen war makes reaching assistance too dangerous for many
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Yemen war makes reaching assistance too dangerous for many
More than 280,000 people have now been displaced by fighting in Yemen and many vulnerable people are unable to access lifesaving relief because it is too dangerous to do so, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said on Friday.
In an alert, the agency said that tens of thousands of refugees and asylum seekers were struggling to survive.
It described a rapidly worsening humanitarian crisis for more than 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen, as “escalating insecurity, economic collapse, depleting resources and severe humanitarian access constraints leave tens of thousands with nowhere to turn”.
Despite intensifying conflict between Houthi opposition fighters and Government forces which escalated last month and ended a four-year ceasefire, thousands of people continue to risk dangerous sea crossings from the Horn of Africa to Yemen, said UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh.
Access heavily restricted
Aid teams are particularly worried about the situation in Kharaz refugee camp in the southwestern governorate of Lahj, close to the front line.
The camp shelters around 9,500 refugees from Somalia and Ethiopia in a Government-controlled area. Although no refugee casualties have been verified so far, “nearby shelling has disrupted services and led to movement restrictions for those in the camps…who have already previously fled conflict”, Mr. Saltmarsh noted.
UNHCR partners have distributed food inside the camp in coordination with local authorities, and health assistance and water provision continue, with significant difficulty. But most other services are on hold, with schools suspended, legal and documentation services interrupted and the rising prices of fuel and staple foods making it increasingly difficult for refugees to cover their basic needs.
“When access allows, we do move in that assistance, but it has been challenging,” Mr. Saltmarsh said. “We’ve been hearing a lot that a number of displaced people have been unable to get to places where we have our supplies and our assistance… in many cases, it’s been too dangerous for us to get to them.”
According to UNHCR, more than 280,000 people in Yemen have been displaced by the fighting. The significant increase in humanitarian needs has coincided with severe supply chain shocks in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab El-Mandeb Strait, linked to the US-Iran war, while resources available to help them are falling short. Today, the agency’s appeal for Yemen only 19 per cent funded.
Relief supplies on the way
In a positive development, the agency announced that it has secured pro bono transport support for 11 containers of emergency relief items from Dubai to Yemen, “although shifting security conditions and logistical constraints are challenging those delivery efforts”, Mr. Saltmarsh noted.
“Those 11 containers should arrive tomorrow, bringing 3,000 relief kits to over 20,000 people in Yemen,” he added, before warning that the agency’s operations in Sudan, Djibouti and Ethiopia are among the most exposed to disrupted trade and shipping in the Red Sea.

DR Congo: Hunger deepens for millions amid conflict, Ebola and climate shocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

DR Congo: Hunger deepens for millions amid conflict, Ebola and climate shocks
More than 28 million people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) are not getting enough to eat and the number is expected to tick up in the coming months, according to the latest alert from the IPC global food security monitor.
The DRC continues to confront a severe food security crisis due to persistent conflict in the east, widespread displacement, an expanding Ebola outbreak, economic shocks and the potential impacts of the El Niño weather pattern.
The IPC is a UN-backed platform that uses a five-phase scale to classify the severity of food insecurity, with level 5 being famine.
Read our UN News explainer here
High levels of hunger
Roughly 28.8 million people, or 23 per cent of the population analysed, are forecast to experience high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) through December.
More than 3.6 million people, three per cent, are facing emergency conditions or IPC Phase 4.
The alert covers the period from September 2026 through next June and was published against the backdrop of the record Ebola outbreak that is about to enter a six month, with more than 10,000 cases as of this week.
The crisis first emerged in Ituri province in the volatile eastern region – where armed groups have terrorised the population for decades - and has now spread to eight provinces nationwide.
Deterioration in the east
“While the national proportion of the population in Phase 3 or above is only marginally higher than in the previous analysis, conditions have deteriorated more markedly in the northeastern and eastern provinces,” the alert said.
North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri remain the hardest-hit provinces, with 10.4 million people in Phase 3 or above, while four territories within them - Djugu, Fizi, Shabunda and Walungu - are classified in Phase 4.
Among those most affected are displaced persons, returnees, refugees and poor households.
“In eastern DRC, conflict and violence continue to drive displacement, disrupt livelihoods and restrict access to food and markets,” the alert said.
“A rapidly expanding Ebola outbreak, recurrent disease epidemics, rising food and fuel prices, and the impacts of floods and other climate shocks are compounding vulnerabilities,” leaving millions of people with only limited means to guard against hunger.
Conditions set to worsen
The IPC expects food security to worsen slightly from January to June. Some 30.3 million people are projected to face Phase 3 or above, including 4.2 million who are likely to face Phase 4.
The increase will be driven by continued conflict and displacement, the spread of Ebola, and the anticipated impacts of El Niño, including flooding that could disrupt agricultural production and market access.
Other factors include rising food, fuel and agricultural input prices, along with declining humanitarian assistance.
