Crypto platform Binance confirms 'complex' $6.3 billion hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:38:42 UTC
20:38:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Crypto platform Binance confirms 'complex' $6.3 billion hack
Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around $6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist.
The company—the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes—said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach", contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote on X.
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said it had "high confidence" that the attack was orchestrated by a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group -- which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview," a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Binance confirmed on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion."
That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.
That heist was attributed at the time to North Korea-backed TraderTraitor.
Binance warned the $6.3 billion figure "may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets."
It said around $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses.
Fund freeze
At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended".
"Deposits remain unaffected," it said.
The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorized party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
But it said later that "subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether -- a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT -- said his firm froze about $1.6 billion "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins," or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Crypto prices tumble
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly five percent and nearly six percent respectively on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

Taiwan passes death penalty for repeat drugged-driving fatalities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:37:53 UTC
20:37:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The legislature on Friday passed amendments to the Criminal Code that increase penalties for driving under the influence of drugs, allowing the death penalty for repeat offenders who cause fatalities within 10 years.
Lawmakers passed the amendments to Article 185-3 after the KMT and TPP joined forces to approve their version of the bill, per FTV News. Under the revised law, drug-impaired driving carries a prison sentence of six months to five years and a fine of up to NT$500,000 (US$15,800).
If the offense causes death, the penalty increases to at least seven years in prison, with a possible fine of up to NT$7 million. Causing serious injury carries five to 12 years in prison and a fine of up to NT$5 million.
Those who reoffend within 10 years and cause a death face the death penalty, life imprisonment, or at least 10 years in prison, along with a possible fine of up to NT$10 million, according to FTV News. Repeat offenders who cause serious injuries face at least seven years in prison and a possible fine of up to NT$7 million.
The amendments follow several high-profile drugged-driving incidents that have fueled public calls for tougher penalties, per TVBS. In December 2025, a driver in Keelung who had allegedly used etomidate and amphetamines struck and killed a man in his 70s, injuring three other people.
Keelung District Court sentenced the driver to seven years and eight months in prison for drug-impaired driving resulting in death and other offenses. The victim's daughter questioned whether her father's life was worth just seven years and eight months in prison, prompting public debate over sentencing.
Another high-profile case involved Chen Chia-ying (陳嘉瑩), who killed New Taipei police station chief Liu Tsung-hsin (劉宗鑫) while fleeing a drug-related traffic stop on Sept. 30, 2024. Chen was sentenced to death for murder, obstruction of official duties, and drug-impaired driving in February this year, but appealed the verdict. The next hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, per TaiSounds.
The Cabinet approved its own proposed amendments to Article 185-3 on June 11, calling for a prison sentence of five to 12 years for drug-impaired driving resulting in death, per TVBS. Under its proposal, repeat offenders who cause a fatality within 10 years could face life imprisonment, but not the death penalty.
The Cabinet's version was rejected Friday by a vote of 57-41, with 98 lawmakers present. The KMT and TPP version subsequently passed 57-1, with one abstention, among 59 lawmakers present.
Most DPP lawmakers did not participate in the final vote, citing insufficient substantive discussion of the legislation, TVBS reported. DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) was the only party member to vote against the measure.

The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:36:52 UTC
20:36:52 KST

Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.
Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.
Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”
The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.
“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.
The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.
Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.
Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.
Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.
“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”
“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”
TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.
“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”
While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”
Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

====================================================================================================

The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:34:16 UTC
20:34:16 KST

The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University College London
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.
- Share:
Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions.
Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics.
Published in Science Advances, the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years.
The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges.
Why Crocodiles Survived the Dinosaur Extinction
The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover.
Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact.
Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group.
"Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out."
The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions.
Ancient Crocodiles Were Far More Diverse
Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles.
The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton.
Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus, a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus, was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four.
Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug.
"Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate."
Fossils Reveal 245 Million Years of Climate History
To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today.
The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history.
A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled.
About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica.
Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions.
Two Surprising Exceptions
Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions.
During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times.
A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments.
These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions.
What Happened After the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid?
The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs.
They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions.
When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption.
However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely.
Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles.
Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs.
The Survival Strategy That Could Now Become a Weakness
The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction.
Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat.
The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change.
For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move.
Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder."
The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC).

Environmental rangers honored for protecting natural heritage

Environmental rangers honored for protecting natural heritage
TEHRAN – A ceremony was held on Thursday to mark National Environmental Ranger Day and honor the dedication, sacrifices, and vital role of environmental rangers in protecting the country’s environment and natural resources.
President Masoud Pezeshkian and Head of the Department of Environment (DOE) Shina Ansari addressed the event.
Emphasizing the need to reform environmental management approaches, Pezeshkian said protecting natural resources requires balancing available resources with consumption, preventing environmental degradation, strengthening continuous monitoring, revising regulations, and encouraging public participation. He added that the government is responsible for safeguarding the country’s natural assets and preventing their destruction.
The president described environmental rangers as being on the front lines of protecting the country’s natural heritage, stressing that they should receive greater attention and support in recognition of their responsibilities, challenging working conditions, and services.
Pezeshkian also warned that wars, misguided actions, and destructive decisions are damaging the planet and threatening human life. He described environmental protection as an intergenerational responsibility, emphasizing that education is the first step toward preserving natural resources for future generations. He cautioned that once the Earth’s natural resources are destroyed, restoring them to their original condition is far from easy.
Criticizing the benefits some developed countries derive from environmental degradation in developing nations, he said the consequences of such practices are increasingly threatening the planet.
For her part, Ansari said more than 13 protected areas across the country had been damaged during recent wars, with ranger stations, equipment, vehicles, and wildlife also suffering losses.
She noted that, alongside their conservation duties, environmental rangers had worked during the wartime period in coordination with military and provincial authorities to defend the country’s territorial integrity and continue protecting its natural assets.
Ansari also paid tribute to 154 environmental rangers who have lost their lives in the line of duty over the years, adding that 374 others had been injured or sustained disabilities while carrying out conservation missions.
In September, Pezeshkian described environmental protection as a key pillar of the country’s national and social security, stressing that the preservation of natural resources must be addressed within this framework.
Speaking at a meeting with environmental experts, Pezeshkian said the government was prepared to create the necessary conditions for using the plans, ideas and initiatives put forward by environmental activists and specialists.
He added that the government would support scientific and practical solutions for addressing the country’s real environmental challenges, IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian emphasized that tackling environmental problems requires close cooperation among the government, universities, the private sector, civil society organizations and the public.
“This shared capacity must be used to move toward sustainable governance, balanced development and the protection of the country’s resources for future generations,” he said.
The president also identified education and public awareness as key elements in reforming consumption patterns and protecting the environment.
“If we invest in properly educating the next generation, we are in fact investing in the future of the country,” Pezeshkian said.
He warned that without educating children and teenagers from an early age about environmental protection, efficient use of water and electricity, energy management and social responsibility toward natural resources, future generations could repeat patterns of environmental degradation, even if significant resources are spent on environmental protection today.
Pezeshkian stressed that environmental awareness should begin at school, saying that teaching students how to use water, electricity, gas, and other natural resources responsibly should be incorporated into the educational and developmental process.
The Department of Environment has taken different steps to promote public participation in environmental protection.
Encouraging eco-friendly students, teaching environmental awareness courses in universities, developing a plan titled “skilled ranger soldier”, and preparing guidelines for environmental protection are among the most important measures.
Over the past Iranian year, which ended on March 21, DOE mainly focused on enhancing formal and informal environmental education, developing public participation, utilizing the potential of new technologies, and promoting the culture of environmental protection, IRNA reported.
In the education sector, the DOE designed a ‘national environmental curriculum’, and the first scientific-educational event based on a book titled ‘Humans and the Environment’ was held for teachers and eleventh-grade students at the national level. During the event, the provincial and national winners were honored.
A national plan for environmental helpers has also been implemented. About 20 percent of the elementary students are health ambassadors. Some 25 percent of them will join the national plan over five years. Currently, there are 11,000 environmental helpers at schools across the country. The plan has also empowered 7,258 elementary school principals and 6,051 elementary school health care providers so far.
Another initiative of the DOE is to offer environmental courses in all universities in the country. It was previously implemented on a pilot basis in 10 selected universities. In addition, the Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) major for the MA degree has been revised.
The DOE has developed two other plans. The first, titled ‘skilled ranger soldier’, aims to employ students in environmental protection stations, and the second one intends to train and empower local communities with the participation of environmental protection students.
In an effort to strengthen the participation of local communities in conserving nature, the DOE has approved seven natural areas to be protected by the public.
The initiative showcases national determination to conserve the country’s environment and also opens a new prospect for people’s contribution and the development of participatory governance in protecting the country’s biodiversity.

King Charles' sorrow over slavery faces test as reparations movement gains ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:31:28 UTC
20:31:28 KST

King Charles' sorrow over slavery faces test as reparations movement gains ground
LONDON, Oct 30 - King Charles has since 2022 expressed sorrow for the suffering caused by slavery without crossing a line that Britain has long resisted: an apology.
That balancing act is likely to be tested at next week's Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, where Caribbean leaders who back a reparations campaign through the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) are expected to press their case.
Buckingham Palace has indicated Charles would not apologise on behalf of Britain, which has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over its role in the transatlantic slave trade.
Speaking in the Bahamas on Tuesday ahead of a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting that begins on Sunday, Charles said it was "only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past," and said leaders from affected countries would discuss the issue at the summit.
But Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas' National Reparations Committee, said that did not go far enough. "We do not need more carefully crafted words about healing," she said in a statement. "We need action equal with the scale of the harm inflicted."
ROYAL LINKS TO SLAVERY UNDER SCRUTINY
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database.
Alan Lester, a University of Sussex historian whose research spans the legacies of slavery and empire, said opponents of the reparations movement had "successfully weaponised" the idea that reparations simply meant writing a cheque, an idea that few Western governments will countenance.
Instead, Caribbean leaders often frame their demands in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare and climate resilience, measures they say would address inequalities rooted in slavery and colonialism.
"I think King Charles III is in a difficult position because you can express sorrow about something, but an apology goes much further," royal commentator Afua Hagan said.
Buckingham Palace said in 2023 that Charles had given his support to research that was examining the monarchy's links to slavery after the Guardian newspaper reported on a document showing a historical connection.
In a more recent finding, independent researcher Desiree Baptiste told Reuters her forthcoming book, "George IV, Empire, and Objects of Prestige," would cite House of Lords papers and other British government records showing that profits derived from enslaved labour helped fund furniture and decorative work commissioned by George IV at royal residences.
In a response, the Royal Collection Trust, a charity that maintains and displays artworks and historic objects held in trust by the king, said constant research helped it to keep its records "continually under review in order to improve the information presented on an object or subject". REUTERS

Türkiye rejects Greek claims over Libya deal at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:30:23 UTC
20:30:23 KST

Greece and Türkiye clashed over the maritime agreement between Ankara and Libya during a United Nations Security Council debate on maritime security on Oct. 29, with both sides defending their positions on the legality of the 2019 memorandum.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis used a map during the open debate to criticize the Türkiye-Libya memorandum, arguing that it disregarded the sovereign rights of Greek islands and violated fundamental principles of international law.
Libya’s House of Representatives unanimously approved the maritime boundary agreement with Türkiye on Oct. 20, reversing its previous rejection of the deal and a decision to sever political ties with Ankara, according to a statement from the Libyan parliament.
The deal has long been a source of regional tensions, with Greece, Egypt and Greek Cyprus opposing it.
“The agreement completely disregards geography. It ignores the very existence of the Greek islands. It is as though these islands simply disappear from the way Türkiye and Libya view the region,” the Greek premier told the council.
Responding to Mitsotakis, Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Ahmet Yıldız rejected Athens’ characterization of the agreement, arguing that the Security Council was not a judicial body mandated to delimit maritime zones.
He said maps could illustrate competing claims but could not establish their legal validity.
Yıldız defended the memorandum and pointed to its recent ratification by Libya’s House of Representatives as evidence of domestic support for the agreement.
He also rejected claims that the deal prejudged the maritime rights of third countries, stressing that it neither determined nor infringed upon the rights of states that were not parties to it.
Türkiye did not dispute the existence, population or sovereignty of Greek islands, Yıldız said, but argued that the legal issue was how much weight islands should be given when maritime zones are delimited in areas where claims overlap.

Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with “lantern-like” glass-block facade
In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.
Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.
It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.
The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.
Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.
Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.
“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.
“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.
Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.
“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.
“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”
On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.
The glass-block facade brings in soft morning light while offering privacy to the first-floor interior and, viewed from the garden and house, transforms the studio into a “glowing lantern” at night, Olaver said.
The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.
“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”
The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.
“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”
More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.

Star’s Tech Starcrush (which until late 2026, was called Eco-St) promises to de-ice much more effectively than traditional road salt with almost none of the corrosive effect on steel. Its secret sauce? The porous bones of an invasive starfish breed that has devastated shellfish and seaweed farms, says Star’s Tech founder Seungchan Yang. Iranian, Greek universities seek to beef up scientific ties
TEHRAN – A delegation from Greek universities has visited Shahid Beheshti University to explore ways to expand academic ties between the two countries.
The delegation visited the university on Wednesday and attended a scientific roundtable at the Faculty of Economics and Political Sciences, where Shahid Beheshti University Chancellor Mahmoud-Reza Aqamiri and Greek academic officials emphasized the importance of strengthening scientific, research, and educational cooperation.
During the meeting, the two sides explored areas for collaboration, including exchanges of professors and researchers, sharing expertise, conducting joint research and educational projects, and attracting students.
Underscoring the need to address human and legal dimensions of the war against Iran, the Greek delegation called for the expansion of scientific, interdisciplinary, and international cooperation to strengthen social justice and confront shared challenges.
Iranian academic officials, for their part, emphasized the historical interactions between the two nations and stressed the need to address challenges, such as financial constraints, difficulties with travel, bank transactions, visa-related issues, and administrative obstacles, prior to developing joint scientific efforts.
Also, they suggested holding online meetings, publishing joint articles, promoting library cooperation, and implementing ongoing research projects as practical measures for the enhancement of academic ties between the two countries.
According to Aqamiri, Shahid Beheshti University would follow up on the implementation of the reached agreements and lay the basis for sustainable scientific interactions between the two sides.
Iran ranks first in key scientific output among Islamic countries
Iran ranks first among Islamic nations in key fields of scientific output such as quantum science, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced materials, the head of the Presidential Affairs Office at the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) announced in August.
The country is in close competition with Turkey and Saudi Arabia in these fields, IRNA quoted Saeed Bakhtiari as saying.
He made the remarks in a press briefing on August 17, noting that the development of science in these fields has also been emphasized in national development plans.
Based on the reputable Web of Science database, Iran ranks first among Islamic countries in scientific output in some of these fields, while placing second or third in others. Overall, however, Iran holds the top position, he said.
Bakhtiari noted that in advanced materials—a multidisciplinary field spanning physics, chemistry, mechanics and materials science—Iran ranks second among Islamic countries and ninth worldwide.
He added that Iran ranks third in artificial intelligence, behind Saudi Arabia and Turkey, while in quantum science it ranks second, after Saudi Arabia.
The ISC official further said that Iran holds the top position among Islamic countries in scientific output in cognitive sciences and ranks first overall.
According to Web of Science (WoS) data, over a five-year period (from 2021 to 2025), Iran (with 32 documents) ranks first in cognitive sciences among Islamic countries.
Turkey, with 23 documents, and Saudi Arabia, with 22 documents, are placed second and third, respectively, IRNA reported.
From 2014 to 2023, Iran ranked either first or second in most fields of cognitive sciences among Islamic countries. Over the course of the decade, the country ranked first in cognitive neuroscience, cognitive rehabilitation, and cognitive linguistics with 387, 156, and 30 documents, respectively.
The country is placed second in quantum (with 216 documents) and advanced materials (with 5975 documents), after Saudi Arabia, with 283 and 6160 documents in quantum and advanced materials. Malaysia (with 154 documents) and Egypt (with 3151 documents) are placed third in quantum and advanced materials, respectively.
Despite illegal sanctions, Iran secures first place in cognitive sciences among Islamic nations and ranks ninth globally in advanced materials. Numerous prestigious Iranian universities and institutions are included in international rankings. These accomplishments underscore the country’s scientific capabilities, IRIB quoted Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf as saying, addressing the 7th Turkey Educational Technologies Summit (known as TETZ 2026), held in Istanbul from June 26 to 28.
Iran serves as a great opportunity to invest in higher education and modern technologies. The country has one of the largest higher education systems in the region, with more than three million students and over seventy thousand faculty members and researchers.
Highlighting that the rapid development of emerging technologies, including AI, is fundamentally transforming human relationships and higher education systems around the world at an unprecedented pace, Simaei-Sarraf said that effective use of smart technologies requires the establishment of a system based on algorithmic transparency, educational justice, accountability, protection of learners’ rights, and responsible data governance.

Russia is waging its war on Ukraine's cities around the clock as winter approaches, striking homes, transport, and the power grid that keeps them running. On 29 October, including the late attack on Kyiv, Russian strikes killed at least 27 civilians and injured more than 140 across six regions, by EP's tally of regional authorities' reports. It was one of the deadliest days of the autumn. Most died in daylight, on a train platform in Dnipro, in an apartment block in Kremenchuk, in central Chernihiv, and under guided bombs in Izium.

In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian drones destroyed the house of culture in Mena late on 29 October, and in the morning a drone hit a house in Bobrovytsia and injured a woman, the regional administration said. In Chernihiv itself, 37 people sought medical help after the 29 October strike on the city center that killed two 15-year-old girls, Yana and Mariia.

Poltava Oblast also mourns three people killed when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in Kremenchuk on 29 October. Another 32 were injured, six of them children, the regional administration said.
Russian jet drone hits Dnipro railway platform, killing 14 people next to a Zaporizhzhia-bound train
In Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, Russian guided bombs hit a five-story building on 29 October, killing four people and injuring 14, police reported. In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people in Bilenke and injured 23 across the region, 13 of them when Russia sent seven FPV drones at vehicles and public transport in Zaporizhzhia city, police said. Former US ambassadors: America must stand with Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:28:44 UTC
20:28:44 KST

Flags for the United States and Ukraine billow in the wind off an activist's bicycle on April 23, 2024 in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
The United States cannot credibly defend freedom around the world while treating the survival of a democracy under attack as a bargaining chip.
Russia’s war against Ukraine is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a test of whether democratic nations will defend the principles that sustain their freedom — or allow an authoritarian aggressor to destroy these principles through military force, terror and economic coercion.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was unlawful. Its conduct has included attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and in March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. All grave allegations that demand accountability.
Advertisement
As Ukraine continues to fight for its survival, current U.S. policy raises a fundamental question: Does Washington understand what is at stake?
If Moscow succeeds in subjugating Ukraine, other authoritarian leaders will also ask whether military conquest can succeed. Can U.S. commitments be trusted? Will democratic nations stand together when the price becomes politically inconvenient?
Ukraine’s defense is not charity. It is a strategic investment in American and European security, Washington’s credibility and the deterrence of future conflicts.
The U.S. emerged from World War II understanding that an international order based on sovereignty, freedom and rule of law serves its interests. And successive Republican and Democratic administrations recognized that unchecked authoritarian expansion threatens both American security and the independence of its allies.
That understanding must guide U.S. policy toward Russia today.
Diplomacy is essential. Negotiations to end the war should be pursued seriously. But peace cannot mean rewarding aggression, compelling Ukraine to surrender its sovereignty or giving Moscow time to rearm for another invasion.
Advertisement
Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it.
Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion.
On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided.
The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained.
The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law.
This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives.
Advertisement
If Washington weakens its own pressure without obtaining meaningful concessions, it risks surrendering leverage while leaving Russia’s aggression unresolved. Every source of revenue helping Moscow sustain its military campaign has consequences for Ukrainian civilians, who bear them in destroyed homes, shattered families and lost lives.
U.S. policy should not make it easier for Russia to finance a war Washington says it wants to end.
American history has a bipartisan tradition of leadership that combines the defense of freedom with strategic judgment.
Harry Truman understood U.S. security depended on resisting authoritarian expansion. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, John F. Kennedy demonstrated that strength and diplomacy are not opposites. Ronald Reagan understood freedom must be defended against those who seek to suppress it. And George H. W. Bush knew sovereignty and alliances are essential to an international order where nations cannot redraw borders by force.
Though from different eras, the leadership of these presidents reflected a common principle: American security is strengthened when the U.S. combines military strength, alliances, diplomacy and a commitment to the independence of free nations.
A policy that pressures Ukraine more than Russia, offers Moscow economic relief without substantial concessions or asks Ukrainians to accept an insecure future is not a strategy for lasting peace. It risks rewarding aggression and inviting further conflict.
Advertisement
And above all, Ukraine’s future should not be decided over the heads of Ukrainians.
Democratic institutions can be attacked and dismantled far faster than they can be rebuilt. Ukraine’s struggle is therefore about more than one war. It is about whether the democratic world will remain a community of nations bound by common principles or become a collection of states left to negotiate individually with authoritarian regimes.
History will not judge U.S. policy solely by the immediate cost of weapons, energy or sanctions. It will judge whether America stood by a nation fighting for survival, upheld the principles it asks others to respect and helped prevent future wars by demonstrating that aggression does not pay.
Adrian Zuckerman is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2019-2021); Mark Gitenstein is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2009-2012) and to the EU (2022-2025); Ron Gidwitz is a former U.S. ambassador to Belgium (2018-2021) and acting U.S. ambassador to the EU (2020-2021); Jim Gilmore is a former U.S. ambassador to the OSCE (2019-2021); Kathleen Kavalec is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2023-2025); Jim Rosapepe is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (1998-2001).
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Oct. 30 for talks with Iranian officials, state media has reported, as mediators press efforts to revive peace talks with the United States.

Senior officials from several countries have flown to Tehran in recent days as fears rise of a return to hostilities in the Middle East war, which started eight months ago.

The Middle East war began on Feb. 28 with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran that killed former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and senior military commanders in Tehran.

Iran attends World Young Scientist Summit 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:27:28 UTC
20:27:28 KST

Iran attends World Young Scientist Summit 2026
TEHRAN – The head of the National Institute for Oceanography and Atmospheric Sciences has represented Iran at the World Young Scientist Summit (WYSS) 2026.
The event took place on October 24 and 25 in Wenzhou, China, ISNA reported.
Attending the WYSS Deep-Sea Resources and Environment Forum, Ali Mahdinia delivered a talk on ‘Deep-Sea Natural Resources Survey in the Oman Sea: Experiences and Evidence’, presenting Iran’s scientific findings and research experiences in studying natural resources in the deep waters of the Sea of Oman. The official also elaborated on the country’s research capacities in marine science.
The forum was held under the theme “Marching to the Deep and Distant Sea — Marine Resources Empowering the Blue Economy Future”, bringing together young scientific and technological talents in the deep-sea field from more than 20 countries and regions to exchange views on key topics such as green development of deep-sea resources and ecological synergy.
Nearly 800 representatives, including scientists, educators, and entrepreneurs from more than 60 countries and regions, attended the World Association of Young Scientists.
With the theme “Gathering Talents Worldwide to Create a Better Future,” the summit’s annual agenda was “Global Youth Action in the AI Era: Building a Sustainable Future.” It aimed to draw on the insights of young people around the world, deepen international sci-tech cooperation, and jointly address questions about young people, science, the world and the future.
This year’s summit placed greater emphasis on the growth needs of young scientists, with young talents under the age of 45 accounting for 88 percent of participants.
It aimed to build a cluster of international journals, bring together young scientific talent, facilitate a batch of international collaborative projects and advance the application and commercialization of scientific and technological achievements.
Iran deepens scientific ties with China through new ocean research pact
In November 2025, Iran’s National Institute of Oceanography and Atmospheric Science signed a cooperation agreement with the Second Institute of Oceanography of China’s Ministry of Natural Resources, aiming to expand joint research in deep-sea studies under the framework of Iran’s BRICS membership.
According to Mahdinia, the memorandum was designed to strengthen scientific and technological collaboration between the two sides as part of Iran’s active participation in the BRICS “Working Group on Ocean and Polar Science and Technology.”
He said the agreement included joint deep-sea research projects, scientific and technological events, exchange of professors, researchers and students, shared access to research facilities, and the exchange of scientific data, books and journals.
“The agreement builds on Iran’s integration into the expanded BRICS group, whose members include Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Arab Emirates, Iran, Indonesia, Bolivia and Nigeria,” he added.
Iranian scholars dispatched to Chinese scientific centers via TYSP
The Iran-China Talented Young Scientist Program (TYSP) has so far facilitated the dispatch of 71 Iranian scholars to the top Chinese scientific center to conduct research, laying the groundwork for expanding scientific and research cooperation between the two countries.
The TYSP is an international mobility scheme funded by the Chinese government aimed at cultivating future leading scientists, together with other countries.
According to the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy, the two countries started the young scientists exchange program in 2017, IRNA reported.
The program, which includes scholarships and financial support from Chinese universities, as well as educational and research institutes, came to a halt following the Covid-19 pandemic. The program restarted in October 2024.
The new edition of the Iran-China TYSP, announced in January 2025, opened up 53 opportunities for young scientists from the two countries.
The majority of Iranian applicants are associate professors or those with higher degrees, and the rest are selected among faculty members and researchers.
TYSP offers sponsorship for talented young scientists from other countries to work in China on a full-time basis for 6 or 12 months together with China’s team; the Ministry of Science and Technology of China has allocated 12,500 yuan per month to support the implementation of research activities of the young talented scientists in China.
Iranian scholars are primarily working with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Tongji University, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and China Agricultural University.
Agricultural sciences and plant protection, earth sciences and natural hazard management, physics and optics, mathematics and computer science, materials science and engineering, energy, and bioinformatics are among the most important scientific fields in the TYSP program.
TYSP promotes cross-border exchanges of excellent young scientists, scholars, and researchers. The program also enhances cooperation among research institutes, universities, and enterprises.
When the program is over, participant will receive a TYSP Certificate based on their performance evaluation.

Indian exports to cross $1 trillion in current financial year – top Modi aide
Indian exports are set to cross $1 trillion in the 2026-27 financial year, government Chief Economic Adviser V Anantha Nageswaran has said.
The South Asian nation’s cumulative exports, including goods and services, totaled $476.20 billion in the April-September period, government data showed.
“We are on track to exceed or even achieve $1 trillion exports this year,” he said, pointing to the 13.84% growth recorded in the first half of the fiscal, from the year-ago period.
India’s total exports in the financial year ended March was 863.1 billion, with merchandize exports reaching 441.8 billion, and services exports at $421.3 billion.
To compare, China’s goods exports alone stood at $3.77 trillion in 2025, while overall US exports, including services, came in at $3.43 trillion.
Achieving the ambitious export targets would, however, require New Delhi to strengthen its manufacturing amid geopolitical tensions and supply-chain disruptions.
Sectors that received robust federal government backing should help deliver strong export numbers and provide the country with the ability to compete on import prices, the government’s chief economist said.
India is on course to exceed $1 trillion in exports in 2026-27, according to Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran. He described 2025-26 as a critical economic inflection point for India — comparable to 1991 in significance, not in crisis terms — after years of global supply-side shocks from the pandemic, the Ukrainian conflict, and tensions in the Gulf. https://t.co/hpFV5iIYKE
— Sputnik India (@Sputnik_India) October 29, 2026
“We have to insist on quid pro quo from the industry in terms of export competitiveness, and/or import parity,” he said.
Nageswaran also advocated setting up reservoirs of essential commodities as a way to deal with supply chain issues.
India’s Niti Aayog pointed out in its executive summary for the Jan-March quarter that challenging global trade conditions, along with continued uncertainty surrounding trade policies, investment flows, and supply chains were weighing on economic activity.
The South Asian nation clocked real GDP growth of 7.8% in the first quarter of 2026-27, making it one of the fastest-growing major economies in the world.
The US remained India’s largest export destination in the first-half of the fiscal year, with exports of $50.81 billion, up from $45.82 billion a year ago despite the tariff uncertainties and continuing negotiations over a trade deal.

Serbian election winners plan gas talks with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:27:15 UTC
20:27:15 KST

Serbian election winners plan gas talks with Russia
Serbia’s incoming leadership plans to hold talks with Russia to negotiate a long-term natural gas supply agreement, prominent Student List candidate Radomir Saicic has said.
The student-backed movement, which defeated the coalition of longtime Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic in a parliamentary election this month, previously indicated that Belgrade would not join Western sanctions against Moscow.
Vucic himself, however, has warned that the Student List would renege on its position, while some high-profile members of the movement have suggested that Serbia’s relations with Russia could be reconsidered.
The Student List secured around 52.5% of the vote in Sunday’s snap election. The movement emerged from mass protests triggered by the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people and sparked widespread accusations of government corruption.
While the authorities launched an investigation into the tragedy and made several major concessions, the protests continued. Vucic eventually called snap parliamentary elections and resigned the presidency in September to seek a return to power as prime minister. The Serbian leader denounced the protests as an attempted Western-backed ‘color revolution’, but pledged to respect the election results and avoid bloodshed, ultimately conceding defeat.
Moscow, which had shared Vucic’s concerns about possible foreign interference, acknowledged the election results. Earlier this week, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic’s contribution to bilateral ties, expressing hope that the incoming leadership would continue developing constructive relations with Russia. He stressed that cooperation with Moscow was in Serbia’s interests, adding that “it takes two to tango.”
Speaking to Serbian weekly NIN in an interview published on Wednesday, Saicic, a founding signatory of the Student List who is reportedly viewed as a possible prime minister, outlined ties with Russia as one of the incoming government’s priorities.
“In the first 30 days… energy supply, which includes oil, gas and the functioning of the Electric Power Company of Serbia, will be ensured. To this end, our delegations will hold talks in Washington (expiration of OFAC’s decision on the temporary suspension of NIS sanctions) and in Moscow (gas arrangement), in order to conclude longer-term arrangements,” he said.
Saicic also previously reaffirmed the movement’s opposition to sanctions against Russia over Ukraine despite pressure from the EU, stressing that “problems should be resolved through dialogue, negotiations, and agreements, not sanctions.”
Another Student List representative, university professor Jovo Bakic, gave similar assurances in an interview with RT Balkan on Monday, saying that “we respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector.”
At the same time, Ilija Srdanovic, another prominent member of the movement, delivered a different message, signaling in an interview with US-funded RFE/RL that all options remain on the table, saying that “there will certainly be a dialogue within our society.”
Russia is Serbia’s dominant natural gas supplier, accounting for up to 90% of its imports in 2025, with most deliveries arriving through the TurkStream pipeline via Türkiye and Bulgaria. However, the two countries have yet to negotiate a new long-term gas contract since their previous three-year agreement expired in May 2025, relying instead on successive short-term extensions. The current gas agreement is valid until December 31.
The overall talks have been complicated by the uncertainty over the fate of NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery and faces US sanctions over its majority Russian ownership. Hungarian energy company MOL has been negotiating to acquire the Russian stake, while Washington has issued temporary waivers to keep the company operating.
Moscow said that long-term contracts were complicated by EU energy policies, Serbia’s European integration ambitions, and uncertainty over gas transit through Bulgaria. Nevertheless, Russia has repeatedly stressed it is open to supplying gas to any interested European customers.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Vucic discussed energy cooperation and NIS in late September before the elections, with the Serbian leader saying at the time he was confident that Russian gas deliveries would continue at favorable prices – €318 ($356) per 1,000 cubic meters, compared with a European market benchmark of more than €800.

$6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:26:55 UTC
20:26:55 KST

$6.3 billion Binance hack was likely work of North Korea, blockchain intel firms say
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.
What is TraderTraitor?
In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.
Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.
The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.
Working "around the clock"
Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:26:00 UTC
20:26:00 KST

Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
October 30, 2026
Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead Israel's new government.
Although the right-wing bloc, including religious hardliners, led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset.
Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.
Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin.
But he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.
Alabali Radovan: 'Winter in Gaza will be difficult'
One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.
"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.
In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
"The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end," she said.
All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.
More distanced from Netanyahu's government
Relations between Germany and Israel are traditionally close, in part because of Germany's historical responsibility for Nazi Germany's murder of millions of Jews during the Holocaust.
Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.
Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.
In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after Israel's 2026 election.
So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.
CDU hoping for a centrist government
At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremists, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people, and above all the elected politicians, will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."
The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made large gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. The historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.
However, Netanyahu’s bloc have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties.
Eisenkot's opposition bloc has not yet said whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List/Ra'am, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.
Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable.
"The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority."
The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW: "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."
This article was originally published in German.

WHO: Yemen escalation leaves over 9,000 dead or injured, displaces 276,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:25:58 UTC
20:25:58 KST

The World Health Organisation (WHO) says the death and injury toll from the latest military escalation in Yemen has reached 9,072, warning that health services are deteriorating and medical supplies, fuel and water are in short supply, particularly in Taiz governorate.
In a report released on Thursday, the WHO said 1,677 people had been killed and 7,395 injured as of 25 October, with 559 casualties recorded over six days.
The average number of casualties during the reporting period stands at 93 a day, almost half the daily average of 168 recorded in the previous report. However, deaths and injuries continue to be reported across several governorates.
Marib has recorded the highest number of deaths among the governorates covered by the data, with 45 deaths out of 143 casualties. Taiz follows with 34 deaths out of 237 casualties, while Lahj has recorded 21 deaths out of 158 casualties.
The WHO says 276,301 people are displaced across Yemen as of 24 October, including more than 46,000 families. Taiz hosts around 46 per cent of all registered displaced people.
The report says restrictions on access from Aden to Taiz and the western coast are delaying the delivery of supplies. Severe shortages of medicines, fuel and water, alongside disruptions to waste management services, are increasing the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
It adds that only six of the 31 hospitals in Marib remain operational.
The developments come amid continued military escalation in Yemen, following the resumption of clashes between government forces and the Houthi movement in late June.

Trump pressures Lithuania to open its ports for Belarusian potash exports despite EU sanctions

The United States seeks to reduce its dependence on Canada for supplies of this key fertilizer component and help lower costs for American farmers. Politico reports this, citing four European officials and sources familiar with the negotiations, UNN writes.
Details

One of the journalists’ sources said that Trump’s team had stepped up contacts with the Lithuanian side. Two Eastern European officials reported that Coale has been raising the issue of transiting Belarusian potash at various levels of the Lithuanian government for more than a year.
They are applying pressure politely, but we are responding absolutely clearly: no
The U.S. State Department declined to comment on specific commercial arrangements. At the same time, a department representative said that Washington regularly considers with its partners opportunities that align with the economic interests of the United States. He also emphasized that purchasing Belarusian potash would help lower prices for American farmers.
US lifts sanctions on Belarusian potash - media19.03.26, 18:53 • 5720 views
As the publication notes, the United States is almost entirely dependent on imports of potash fertilizers, with about 80% of supplies coming from Canada. The search for alternative sources intensified after trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down and both sides raised tariffs. Belarus controls about 20% of the global potash market.
Last month, Trump said he was working on a major deal with Minsk to purchase Belarusian fertilizer at lower prices. Before sanctions were imposed, about 90% of Belarusian potash fertilizer exports passed through the Lithuanian port of Klaipėda.
At the same time, U.S. initiatives are meeting resistance in the Baltic countries. European officials fear that easing the restrictions would strengthen Alexander Lukashenko’s position and provide his regime with additional resources. EU sanctions against Belarus require regular renewal, with the next renewal expected in February 2027.
