By Tuvan Gumrukcu
ANKARA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev skipped a summit of Turkic states on Friday despite a personal invitation from his Turkish counterpart, highlighting growing tensions between the historic allies over domestic and regional policies.
Ties between Turkey and Azerbaijan have become strained in recent weeks over some Turkish officials’ criticism of Baku’s decision to impose restrictions on the use of headscarves under new secular school uniform regulations.
Aliyev and other Azeri officials warned against interference in Baku’s affairs, without mentioning Turkey — a rare crack in an alliance of nations at the heart of a fractured region. Any worse break could hurt Turkey’s ambitions of increasing its influence in an area where Russia traditionally holds sway.
HEADSCARF DISPUTE IS ‘SYMPTOM OF A DEEPER RIFT’
The two countries are also at odds over Israel. Ankara is a fierce critic of Israel over the war in Gaza, while Azerbaijan has strong ties with it.
Turkish officials have sought to downplay tensions and Erdogan delivered a message of unity at the opening of Friday’s summit of countries united by language, culture and roots.
“There is no place for separation, division, or conflict in our family picture. We are all one, together and, God willing, we are brothers forever,” he said at the meeting in Ankara, without naming Azerbaijan.
Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov represented Azerbaijan at the summit. Speaking after Erdogan, he did not mention the tensions, thanking Turkey for its hospitality.
The tensions are unusual. The two countries describe their relationship as “two states, one nation”. Ties deepened after Turkey backed Azerbaijan during the 2023 Nagorno-Karabakh war and they have built strong ties in defence and energy. Ankara is a major buyer of Azeri natural gas.
Erdogan this week removed one of his advisers, Oktay Saral, after his public criticism of the headscarf decision. He also personally invited Aliyev to the Organisation of Turkic States summit during a phone call last week, according to his office.
The Azeri-Press Agency said, without citing sources, that Aliyev skipped the summit arranged months ago due to “previously planned events and the tightness of his work schedule”, including a ceremony and festival at the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku.
There has been no official comment from Azerbaijan, while Turkey’s presidency and foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
Gonul Tol, director of the Washington-based Middle East Institute’s Turkish programme, said that Aliyev skipping the summit was the latest sign of growing tensions between the allies.
“Beneath the ‘two states, one nation’ rhetoric, tensions have long simmered over a number of issues including Azerbaijan’s sovereignty, Ankara’s influence in Baku, diverging policies toward Israel, and Turkey’s rapprochement with Armenia. The hijab dispute is a symptom of a deeper rift,” she said on X.
Turkey has been working to normalise relations with Armenia but has said that this would depend on peace efforts between Azerbaijan and Armenia. Turkish officials have said Ankara has been looking for progress there so it can take concrete steps like opening borders with Armenia.
Amid the tacit warnings against Turkey, Azerbaijan’s foreign ministry this month declared 31 Turkish nationals persona non grata over social media posts criticising Baku.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this month after meeting Aliyev at a Baku summit that disinformation was being spread on social media about Turkey-Azerbaijan ties.
He said that while the countries may not agree on everything, they could “sit and discuss our own problems” in a civil way that befits their close ties.
“Can there be different perspectives, different views on certain issues? There can be. Brothers then sit amongst themselves and discuss it in line with their brotherly ties,” he said.
(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu; Editing by Daren Butler and Andrew Heavens)

Hong Kong fire exposes entrenched triad networks in building renovation industry
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:24:28 CET
20:24:28 KST

By Clare Jim
HONG KONG, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A deadly fire at a Hong Kong housing estate has exposed how bid-rigging networks linked to criminal gangs exploited weaknesses in the city’s lucrative building renovation industry to influence contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Organised crime groups known as triads were mentioned more than 40 times in the report on the government-subsidised Wang Fuk Court inferno, which killed 168 people and displaced thousands of residents.
In response to the report’s findings, the government proposed to make bid-rigging in building renovation a criminal offence, punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a HK$10 million ($1.3 million) fine. Laws against triads will also be tightened.
“After all these years, the syndicates are so sophisticated that they make use of all the legal loopholes,” said Chiu Yan Loy, founder and spokesperson of the All-Hong Kong Owners’ Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bid-Rigging Alliance.
Some networks delay distributing profits for months and use channels including cryptocurrencies, making money flows difficult to trace, he added.
Lawyers and law enforcement officers say the new offence will only work if it helps investigators gather hard evidence.
“We’re talking about offences that exist in a kind of twilight world. There aren’t always transactions between offenders, bribery or a paper trail to prove collusive behaviour or a cartel,” said one law enforcement officer, who declined to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue.
LOOSE REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
Triad gangs — fraternal brotherhoods whose members swear blood oaths of loyalty and secrecy — have for decades been linked to extortion, prostitution, drug trafficking and loan-sharking.
Less prominent than in the 1980s and 1990s, they remain active and operate more complex white-collar scams, police and academics say.
The report explained that loose regulation and lax enforcement around vetting and hiring contractors let them enter the construction ecosystem.
Industry experts say bid rigging worsened when the government introduced hundreds of millions in subsidies in 2012 alongside a scheme requiring owners to repair buildings more than 30 years old, creating a lucrative market for contractors.
Tommy Leung, an associate professor at Wake Forest University, said his research showed renovation prices rose about 40% after the scheme began.
BID-RIGGING AT PLAY
The Wang Fuk Court renovation, whose cost rose from an initial HK$152 million estimate to more than HK$330 million, provides a window into alleged methods used to manipulate projects.
According to the report, the alleged scheme began with gaining influence over the consultant who helps owners select contractors.
Will Power Architects secured that role with a HK$220,000 ($28,000) bid, well below an estimated HK$500,000 market rate, then issued misleading tender assessments, including giving main contractor Prestige Construction full marks for safety compliance despite previous convictions.
Authorities have brought at least 25 criminal charges related to Wang Fuk Court, which housed more than 5,000 people in eight 31-storey towers, against Prestige, Will Power and seven individuals. The report did not say whether the firms had triad links.
Prestige and Will Power could not be reached for comment.
Security Secretary Chris Tang, the former police chief, said on Friday the government would “dismantle the criminal networks behind such activities.”
Hong Kong now plans to give law enforcement greater investigative powers, create a joint task force involving police, the Independent Commission Against Corruption and Competition Commission, and a new bureau overseeing renovation work.
Some former Wang Fuk Court residents were unconvinced.
“It’s just a slogan. They’ll say, ‘we’ll crack down on bid-rigging,’ but ultimately, nothing gets done,” said Betty, who declined to give her full name.
(Reporting By Clare Jim in Hong Kong, additional reporting by Greg Torode and Carol Mang; Editing by Anne Marie Roantree and Saad Sayeed)

Exclusive-Japan pushes to remove Myanmar from global financial watchdog’s blacklist
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:24:13 CET
20:24:13 KST

By Tamiyuki Kihara and Poppy McPherson
TOKYO/BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Japan is pushing a global financial crimes watchdog to remove Myanmar from its blacklist to make it easier to do business there, the latest sign that some major countries are looking to bring the pariah state’s military-backed government in from the cold.
Japan wants the Financial Action Task Force to drop requirements that its members apply enhanced screening to financial transactions with Myanmar to avoid money laundering and terrorist financing, said a senior Japanese government official and another person familiar with the matter.
Removing Myanmar from the list would ease checks on business with a country whose military seized power in a 2021 coup and which remains under scrutiny over scam centres and illicit finance.
The only other countries currently on FATF’s blacklist are Iran and North Korea. The 40-member body will conclude its third and last plenary meeting of the year in Paris on Friday.
It was not immediately clear whether a change is imminent, though the second source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said at least one other major Asian country was pushing for Myanmar’s removal.
A spokesperson for the FATF Secretariat said meetings were ongoing, discussions were confidential, and any changes to the blacklist would be announced after their conclusion on Friday. A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment.
Myanmar was added to the blacklist in 2022 as the country plunged into turmoil and widespread civil war after the coup.
The chaos has fuelled illicit drug production, trafficking and the growth of industrial-scale scam centres in the Golden Triangle, some of them run by militia aligned to the military-backed government.
Myanmar’s government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres. It has also said it has been making efforts to seize narcotics and that drug production and trafficking is carried out by armed groups.
On Monday, Reuters reported Myanmar imported sanctioned jet fuel from Iran, used for deadly bombing campaigns, in shipments disguised with sham paperwork. Myanmar government officials did not return requests for comment.
DIPLOMATIC ENGAGEMENT
The push to remove Myanmar from the blacklist is the latest effort by some nations including Japan to re-engage with Myanmar after a period of international isolation that followed the ousting of leader Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021.
The coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and the crushing of a popular uprising that followed.
The United States last month held direct talks with Myanmar’s military-backed government in Naypyidaw, the highest-level contact since the coup. Those talks, which focused on shutting down scam centres but could pave the way for negotiations on access to Myanmar’s abundant rare earth deposits, were quickly followed by more secretive talks in Tokyo earlier this month.
Japan, whose companies have maintained a large corporate presence in Myanmar even as other firms fled following the coup, believes that getting Myanmar off FATF’s blacklist will make it easier for countries to do business there and help its economy recover, the Japanese government official said.
Myanmar was added to FATF’s blacklist, formally known as the High-Risk Jurisdictions Subject to a Call for Action list, in October 2022 after missing a deadline to address deficiencies.
The global watchdog said at the time that its members must apply enhanced due diligence to business relations and transactions with Myanmar, while ensuring that funds for humanitarian purposes, legitimate non-profit activity and remittances were not disrupted.
In a June assessment, FATF said Myanmar had demonstrated some progress but urgently needed to address deficiencies including ensuring money laundering was investigated and prosecuted, while illicit finance from cyberfraud remained a concern.
(Reporting by Tamiyuki Kihara in Tokyo and Poppy McPherson in Bangkok; Writing by John Geddie; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

IRGC says two tankers stopped south of Strait of Hormuz after ignoring radio warnings from Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:24:06 UTC
20:24:06 KST

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Friday that two oil tankers that switched off their navigation systems were involved in an incident and stopped in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz, after ignoring radio warnings and attempting to use what it described as an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway.
Iran also said on Friday that it destroyed a US unmanned vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the US military.
In a separate incident, a small boat attached two limpet mines to the hull of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz causing a fire in its engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel, in the first successful use of such explosives in the waterway since the US war with Iran began in February, maritime sources said on Friday.
The crew was safe, there was no environmental impact and the fire had been extinguished, British navy agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in an advisory note, adding that the vessel, which it did not name, was continuing to its next port of call.
The incident occurred on Thursday, 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Oman's Khasab, UKMTO said.
IRGC claims responsibility for both tanker attacks
"Early this morning, an enemy vessel operating within the operational zone east of the Strait of Hormuz was struck and destroyed by the brave personnel of the Army Navy," a spokesperson for the IRGC's Navy said in a statement.
"Furthermore, two enemy oil tankers - which had violated regulations by disabling their tracking systems and navigating through prohibited and unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz, despite receiving warnings - sustained damage and caught fire after striking naval mines.
"The owners of the oil tankers shall bear full responsibility for all consequences resulting from this unauthorized transit and the disregard for safety and maritime warnings," the statement added.
"We warn the enemy that any movement, infiltration, or provocative action within areas under the surveillance of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran will be met with a decisive and proportionate response."
Iran has repeatedly attacked commercial tankers transiting Hormuz
The incident comes amid repeated attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil export routes, since the outbreak of the conflict between the US and Iran in February.
Iran has hit vessels it says have violated its restrictions on passage through the strategic waterway, as it seeks to assert control over the strait and exert pressure on Washington.
The tanker - the Panama-flagged Louise 1 - was targeted with limpet mines, according to assessments from three maritime security sources.
This is the first known successful strike using limpet mines in the area since the beginning of the US war with Iran and followed a separate attempt in September using such devices which did not detonate, two of the sources said.
"The apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait's congested shipping lanes," Greece-based maritime risk management group Marisks said in a note on Friday.
Limpet mines have been deployed in Hormuz since 2017
Marisks said limpet mines were first deployed in the region in 2017 and used against tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in subsequent years, adding that "limpet mines are cheap and easily available."
"The methodology of a small craft attaching these mines on the hulls of vessels in transit is cheap, low-tech and very efficient," it said.
Ukrainian forces also hit the Louise 1 in July with naval drones in the Black Sea over what Ukraine’s SBU security service said was its role in transporting Russian oil and being part of the so-called shadow fleet of tankers deployed by Moscow to keep oil exports flowing.
The vessel's Panama-based operator, listed in shipping databases as Aquarius Maritime Ventures, could not be immediately reached for comment.

Preliminary results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation have been summed up

On October 30, 2026, the results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation were summed up as part of the implementation of the 2026 Plan of Key Activities of the Coordinating Council of Heads of Competent Drug Control Authorities of CSTO Member States (CCHCDCA).
From October 18 to 23 this year, in accordance with the 2026 Plan for the Joint Training of Command and Control Bodies and Formations of Forces and Assets of the Collective Security System of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the “Cobalt-2026” special exercise was held at the Magob training range of the Special Purpose Units Training Center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan.
	 An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Greater Eurasia: Institutions, Development, Cooperation” was held at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, jointly organized with the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences (ICCA RAS). CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov took part in the conference.

	 An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Transformation of the Global Security System and the Shaping of a Eurasian Security Framework” was held at Moscow State Linguistic University (MSLU).
Preliminary results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation have been summed up
30.10.2026
On October 30, 2026, as part of the implementation of the 2026 Plan of Key Activities of the Coordinating Council of Heads of Competent Drug Control Authorities of CSTO Member States (CCHCDCA), the preliminary results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation were summed up by CSTO CCHCDCA Secretary, Deputy Head of the Main Directorate for Drug Control of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Russia, Police Major General Boris Yakovchenko, together with Chairman of the Committee for Combating Drug-Related Crime of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Police Colonel Abay Zhusupov, a representative of the CSTO Secretariat, heads of anti-drug agencies of Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan, and experts from relevant international organizations who participated in the operation.
The operation was conducted from October 26 to 30 this year across the territories of CSTO member states. Participants included law enforcement agencies, border and customs services, state security agencies, and financial intelligence units of CSTO member states. Observers included officers from the law enforcement agencies of Iran and China, representatives of the Eurasian Group on Combating Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism, the Committee of Heads of Law Enforcement Units of the Council of Heads of Customs Services of CIS Member States, the Central Asian Regional Information and Coordination Centre (CARICC), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.
The operation aimed to block drug supply routes into the CSTO area of responsibility, enhance efforts to counter drug trafficking along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, neutralize international transnational drug-trafficking groups, dismantle clandestine drug laboratories, and undermine the economic foundations of the drug trade.
Nearly 9,000 personnel from Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan, as well as more than 2,000 personnel from China and Iran, were involved in the operation. Joint measures resulted in the detection of 790 drug-related crimes (445 by CSTO member states), including 81 cases of smuggling, and the exposure of 101 drug-trafficking groups (12 and 61, respectively, by CSTO member states).
In addition, through coordinated efforts by CSTO member states and observer countries, more than 11.4 tonnes of prohibited substances were seized from illicit circulation in the territories of CSTO member states, China and Iran (1.7 tonnes by CSTO member states). These included approximately 11 tonnes of narcotic drugs, 9.4 kg of psychotropic substances, 23 kg of potent substances and 8 tonnes of precursors. Approximately 200,000 drug-containing plants, more than 153,000 tablets containing prohibited substances, 213 firearms and 1,722 rounds of ammunition of various calibers were also seized.
A total of 376 people were detained for drug-related offences, including 135 citizens of countries outside the CSTO. Another 59 wanted individuals were apprehended.
A total of 674 websites disseminating prohibited drug-related information were identified.
According to preliminary data, more than 1 tonne and 260 kg of marijuana, over 232 kg of hashish, 47 kg of alpha-PVP, more than 68 kg of mephedrone, 31 kg of heroin and approximately 3 kg of precursors were seized from illicit circulation in CSTO member states.
To prevent the smuggling of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances and their precursors, the Main Directorate for Drug Control of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, together with the Main Directorate for Combating Smuggling of the Federal Customs Service of Russia and the competent authorities of Kazakhstan, organized and is conducting a dedicated anti-drug operation in the Chelyabinsk Region targeting individuals and vehicles crossing the Russian-Kazakh border.
A joint delegation of financial intelligence units of the Eurasian Group reported that, during the active phase of the operation, more than 80,000 financial transactions had been identified. A significant proportion involved transfers to individuals’ accounts, including those of drug couriers used to receive and move illicit funds, the accumulation of assets in such accounts followed by cash withdrawals, and cryptocurrency conversions. The total value of these transactions exceeded 1 billion rubles.
Information provided by financial intelligence units to law enforcement agencies contributed to the initiation of six criminal cases involving money laundering.
During the operation, participants exchanged best practices for combating cross-border drug trafficking.
The “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” operation helped address practical challenges related to stabilizing the drug situation in the CSTO area of responsibility. New joint measures to ensure anti-drug security have been outlined.
Joint efforts to combat illicit drug trafficking within the CSTO framework will continue.

Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:23:06 GMT
20:23:06 KST

Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
- Published
For the last three decades, Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia.
Now it's shutting down - and it has accused the Russian authorities of the "murder" of a newspaper.
"They've killed us," reads a statement on the Novaya Gazeta website.
"The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction order. Crucially, at the same time, the system that had allowed the paper to receive donations from readers was disabled.
That leaves no way to fund the publication.
Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.
In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said.
"The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.
The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.
Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form.
Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.
One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov, external. In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.
At the offices of Novaya Gazeta, they've already started packing.
The end of this newspaper is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

Atlantic bonito abundance delights Turkish consumers but worries fishermen
An abundance of Atlantic bonito in Turkish waters of the Black Sea, unprecedented in 40 years, is delighting market customers with low prices but also raising concerns about the ecological balance, the Nefes newspaper's website (nefes.com.tr) reports.
Selling at affordable prices of between 30 and 50 lira per fish (EUR 0.54–EUR 0.90), Atlantic bonito are being snapped up by customers in large quantities. However, fishermen warn that Atlantic bonito, being one of the most voracious species, prey on numerous other marine creatures, including crustaceans. They say the fish must be caught quickly to protect marine biodiversity.
Towards the end of spring, Atlantic bonito migrate to the Black Sea to spawn, where they lay their eggs, grow in size and build up fat reserves. From October onwards, as the waters begin to cool, the shoals migrate back through the straits towards the Sea of Marmara and the Mediterranean.

"We've been killed by secret services": Independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta to close after 30 years
Novaya Gazeta, an independent Russian newspaper, has announced its permanent closure after more than 30 years, blaming pressure from the authorities, law enforcement agencies and secret services.
Source: Novaya Gazeta
Quote: "We have been killed. On 9 November, we will turn off the lights in our home, where we lived for 30 years, shut down the servers and leave. The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian intelligence services have forced the editorial board to stop working...
We managed to work for almost five years completely surrounded by intelligence services... This is being done by the FSB, the Ministry of Justice, the prosecutor's office, and others who have appropriated the state and usurped power. This is not merely nostalgia for the Soviet past and bitterness over its loss. Behind that façade, a military dictatorship has all but been established."
Details: Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction notice for its office in central Moscow, where its journalists had worked for 29 years. Its system for accepting reader donations has been disabled. Novaya Gazeta says it has now been stripped of everything it needs to keep operating.
The newspaper also recalled that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the authorities had blocked all its online resources and seized its printing house. Intelligence officers and censors had also intervened to stop other printers from producing the paper.
Many of Novaya Gazeta's employees were forced to leave the country. Its editor-in-chief was the target of an assassination attempt. The authorities later revoked the newspaper's media registration and began designating its journalists as "foreign agents", starting with the editor-in-chief. The designation carries strict reporting requirements and other restrictions and is widely used to target independent media and Kremlin critics.
In September, the authorities designated Novaya Gazeta's entire editorial board as a "foreign agent" and added more than 100 journalists and contributors to the register.
For reference: Founded in 1993, Novaya Gazeta became a platform for some of the most outspoken critics of Vladimir Putin and his inner circle in the early 2000s. Among them was human rights activist Anna Politkovskaya, who was murdered in 2006.
Background:
- In 2021, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, received the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts to protect freedom of speech. On 22 March 2022, Muratov announced that he would sell his Nobel Committee medal and donate the proceeds to support Ukrainian refugees affected by Russia's war.
- After the Kremlin adopted the so-called "law on fakes about the Russian army" in early 2022, Novaya Gazeta changed the phrase "Russia's war against Ukraine" to "special military operation" to be able to continue publishing materials in Russia.

"One of the key challenges the Strategy takes into account is the rapid development of AI. So the document must provide for developing the state's capacity to detect and neutralize new threats in good time," he said after a meeting of the National Cybersecurity Coordination Center at the Council on Friday.
Klymenko said participants also discussed strengthening the state's cyber resilience, protecting energy infrastructure, military systems and defense industry enterprises, and countering cybercrime and fraud.
He said Russia is increasing the number of cyberattacks, makes growing use of artificial intelligence tools and synchronizes attacks in cyberspace with missile and drone strikes.
At the same time, despite the overall rise in the number of cyberattacks since 2022, the number of critical incidents has fallen by more than 98%, he said. Ukraine currently ranks 19th in the National Cyber Security Index (NCSI).
Representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine, the Defense Ministry, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Digital Transformation Ministry, the State Special Communications Service, the National Police, the Foreign Ministry, the Energy Ministry, intelligence bodies and the National Bank took part in the center's work.
"Specific measures were determined for each area, including training of specialists, development of the necessary infrastructure and solutions for early detection and neutralization of threats in cyberspace," the statement posted on Telegram said.
Officials responsible for overseeing the tasks have also been named in government bodies.
The proposals will form the basis for further consideration at a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief. "We must build the cybersecurity system taking into account not only current risks but also challenges that may face Ukraine in the future," Klymenko said.

North Korean Hackers Suspected in Record $6.36 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:19:00 UTC
20:19:00 KST

- Category
- World
North Korean Hackers Suspected in Record $6.36 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
North Korean hackers are believed to be responsible for a cyberattack on the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Binance that resulted in the theft of approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets, making it the largest cryptocurrency heist on record, according to Reuters on October 30.
US blockchain analytics company TRM Labs identified TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit, as the group behind the attack, citing evidence gathered from blockchain activity and other intelligence sources.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“An attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM Labs said in a statement.
According to CNN, the attack took place on October 29 with hackers gaining unauthorized access to digital wallets belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said its preliminary investigation indicated that hackers gained access through an employee engineer’s laptop, enabling them to infiltrate a service container and initiate unauthorized cryptocurrency withdrawals.
In response to the breach, Binance halted deposits and withdrawals pending security reviews, withdrew authorization for the compromised address, and began working with law enforcement and blockchain analysis companies to track down and recover the stolen cryptocurrency.
The exchange also assured customers that their assets remained safe, promising to cover any losses through company resources and its emergency reserve fund.
At the same time, cryptocurrency firms launched efforts to prevent the hackers from accessing the stolen funds. According to CNN, approximately $3 billion worth of digital assets had been frozen by October 29 night in the United States through a joint effort involving several companies.
“It’s the biggest hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan, head of systematic over-the-counter trading at cryptocurrency market maker GSR, said, as reported by CNN.
Other blockchain intelligence companies also identified North Korean hackers as the likely perpetrators, supporting the findings published by TRM Labs.
Among them was Singapore-based Pangolin Intelligence, which told CNN that its conclusions were drawn from examining blockchain transactions associated with the theft and comparing them with patterns observed in earlier cyberattacks linked to North Korean groups.
One of the company's analysts, who requested anonymity, suggested that the hackers could rely on established money laundering networks to transfer and eventually convert the stolen cryptocurrency into accessible funds.
“I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the analyst told CNN.
Meanwhile, blockchain tracking firm Chainalysis said it was monitoring the movement of stolen assets across several cryptocurrency networks, including Bitcoin and Ethereum. A company representative told CNN that the firm was highly confident North Korean hackers were responsible for the operation.
If North Korea’s involvement is conclusively established, the incident would mark a significant increase in the scale of cryptocurrency theft attributed to the country’s hacking operations.
The attack also comes amid previous scrutiny of Binance over its handling of cryptocurrency transactions involving Russia.
In August, Reuters reported that Binance had provided Russian authorities with information about cryptocurrency donations to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns. The data was subsequently used as evidence in a terrorism financing case against a Russian IT specialist.
According to the outlet, the disclosure occurred despite Binance announcing in 2023 that it had fully withdrawn from the Russian market. Although cryptocurrency exchanges generally comply with legitimate law enforcement requests for customer information in countries where they operate, Binance had already exited Russia when it shared the data.

Russia’s most powerful warship, the nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Veliky, deemed too worn out to repair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:18:18 UTC
20:18:18 KST

Russia’s most powerful warship, the nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Veliky, deemed too worn out to repair
A special commission has concluded that repairing and modernizing the heavy nuclear-powered missile cruiser Pyotr Veliky is not practical, said Vladimir Maltsev, head of the All-Russian Movement in Support of the Navy.
“The cruiser cannot be restored. The ship has a certain degree of wear,” he said. Maltsev stressed that this is a preliminary conclusion, and a final decision has not yet been announced.
A source in the naval sector told the Russian state news agency TASS as early as 2023 about plans to retire the Pyotr Veliky from service. According to the source, the idea of decommissioning it emerged because of the prolonged repair of the cruiser Admiral Nakhimov.
A source who spoke to the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti claimed the same year that there were no plans to decommission the Pyotr Veliky or remove it from the Navy’s active service.
The Pyotr Veliky is the flagship of Russia’s Northern Fleet and the only active nuclear-powered cruiser of the Project 1144 Orlan class. Aside from aircraft carriers, it ranks among the largest warships in the world and is one of the most powerful surface ships in the Russian navy.
Four such ships were built under the project between 1977 and 1996. The Admiral Ushakov and Admiral Lazarev have already been decommissioned, while the heavy nuclear-powered cruiser Admiral Nakhimov went to sea this year for the first time after 28 years of repairs. Plans called for returning it to the Navy by the end of the year.
The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk, which handles the cruisers’ modernization, can take on only one ship of the series at a time. Repairs on the Pyotr Veliky were initially planned to begin after work on the Admiral Nakhimov was completed in 2018. However, the repairs dragged on, and the cost doubled over that time, exceeding 200 billion rubles.

Indonesia: nine orangutans rescued from wildfires return to the forest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:17:45 UTC
20:17:45 KST

Deep in the protected Batu Nyambu forest, conservationists opened the transport cages on Thursday, 29 October, allowing the animals to scramble up nearby trees and vanish into the canopy. The group included four mothers accompanied by their young, three of whom had also been found to be pregnant during their final veterinary examinations.
The orangutans had been rescued in August and September from an oil palm plantation in Ketapang, where fires had swept through their habitat. Some suffered burns to their hands and feet, while others were severely underweight and malnourished, according to Karmele Llano Sanchez, head of the YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation.
After spending four to eight weeks recovering at a rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, the orangutans faced a difficult journey to their new home. Conservationists transported them by vehicle, boat and on foot, carrying heavy cages through steep, slippery forest terrain to reach Batu Nyambu, a 23,000-hectare protected area chosen for its largely undisturbed habitat and abundant food.
The release comes amid growing concern over the survival of Borneo's critically endangered orangutans. Indonesia's forestry ministry says at least 51 have been rescued from burning forests in West Kalimantan since early August, while monitoring group Nusantara Atlas estimates that fires consumed more than 1.9 million hectares of land across Indonesia in the first nine months of 2026.

UP finds that Odesa businessman may have sheltered fugitive prosecutor general Kravchenko in Vienna
Odesa businessman Volodymyr Halanternyk may have helped former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko settle in Vienna. People who are believed to work for the businessman gave statements to Austrian police against Ukrainska Pravda journalists who were searching for Kravchenko.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda's investigation CarthageProsecutor: Why Ukrainska Pravda journalists were really detained in Vienna (English subtitles coming soon)
Details: Sources in political and business circles told Ukrainska Pravda that Halanternyk is close to Kravchenko. The sources say he may have helped the former prosecutor general settle in Austria after leaving Ukraine.
Halanternyk himself has been living abroad in hiding for many years and is implicated in two cases investigated by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). Investigators suspect him of involvement in a criminal group that caused losses to the Odesa hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories .
Ukrainska Pravda's sources in anti-corruption agencies do not rule out the possibility that Halanternyk was one of the behind-the-scenes organisers of the attack on NABU and SAPO in July 2025. Sources in law enforcement agencies also suggest that the businessman may have given evidence against the anti-corruption bodies, including in the case involving MP Fedir Khrystenko.
The UP investigation says that after journalists appeared outside the building believed to be Kravchenko's home, people likely linked to Halanternyk contacted Austrian police.
Quote from Ukrainska Pravda journalist Mykhailo Tkach: "The investigation materials available to our editorial team suggest that the statements against our film crew, the Ukrainska Pravda crew, may have been given by representatives of the staff working for Halanternyk himself: an assistant to the manager of the property and, presumably, Halanternyk's own driver."
Details: One witness told police that his car had been followed. Ukrainska Pravda journalists did indeed follow him and filmed him bringing a man resembling Halanternyk to central Vienna. The driver did not mention the passenger in his statement.
Another witness reported filming from a car used by Tkach and Bondarenko and said that the driver resembled one of the "suspicious men". According to Tkach, one of the servicemen from Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) detained in Vienna does indeed look similar to Bondarenko.
Ukrainska Pravda contacted Halanternyk for comment, but he ignored its messages and calls.
According to one report, between 14 and 18 September, the Austrian security service was dealing with a "Ukrainian national who was in danger". This person said they had seen Artan commander Viktor Torkotiuk at the Park Hyatt hotel in Vienna. Law enforcement officers checked his identity. Torkotiuk explained to them that he had arrived as a tourist.
On 6 October, two of his subordinates were detained in Austria. They had military ID cards, concealed cameras and trackers with them. They said they were there on holiday. Torkotiuk confirmed to the security service that they were his subordinates. Bondarenko, an Ukrainska Pravda cameraman, was also mentioned in the report on Torkotiuk's contact with the service.
Quote from the report, as cited in the investigation: "He [Torkotiuk] had a photo of a Polish passenger car used by the two DIU servicemen and Bondarenko during surveillance. The photograph had also been taken in Vienna."
Details: In another report, Austrian law enforcement officers claimed that Bondarenko and one of the detained servicemen had left a car park together. They cited CCTV footage and data from the car rental company.
However, Ukrainska Pravda stresses that the footage attached to the case shows Tkach sitting next to Bondarenko, not a DIU serviceman.
According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources in DIU, the two intelligence officers noticed at one point that they were being followed but were instructed to continue their work. The editorial team contacted Torkotiuk for comment.
After their detention on 8 October, Tkach and Bondarenko explained during questioning that they were carrying out an editorial assignment and looking for Kravchenko. Austrian law enforcement officers checked the Central Register of Residents to establish whether he was registered at the building where the journalists had been working.
Official records made by a prosecutor on the night of 8-9 October state that the journalists' explanations appeared credible and that no connection between Bondarenko and DIU servicemen had been established.
Quote from the official records, as cited in the investigation: "A query to the ZMR [Central Register of Residents] showed that the target individual was registered there. According to the caller, the accounts are generally consistent and entirely credible. Order for immediate release from custody."
Details: The investigation's authors say the results of the check confirm that the journalists had managed to establish Kravchenko's address in Vienna. Ukrainska Pravda also suggests that the former prosecutor general was the "Ukrainian national in danger" being protected by the Austrian security services.
Ukrainska Pravda also offered Kravchenko an opportunity to comment or give an interview.
Instead, on 28 October, Kravchenko claimed that the heads of NABU and SAPO had asked for a team to be sent to Austria to carry out "violent actions" against him, and that the orders had supposedly come from the President's Office.
He also linked Ukrainska Pravda journalists to DIU servicemen but did not explain why he had not returned to Ukraine.
NABU rejected the allegations, describing Kravchenko's statement as an attempt to secure protection for himself abroad.
Background:
- Kravchenko left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September. Under an order he had signed himself, he was due to spend five days in Paris, allegedly attending hearings on Ukrainian children under the auspices of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. However, his name did not appear on the list of participants in the discussion.
- His business trip ended on 18 September. According to Mariana Haiovska, spokesperson for the Prosecutor General's Office, Kravchenko had not returned to work by 21 September.
- Ukrainska Pravda journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko were detained in Vienna on 8 October while searching for the former prosecutor general. Tkach said that armed masked men smashed the windows of their car and dragged both journalists onto the road. Bondarenko was injured.
- Tkach said that after their detention, they were accused of espionage on behalf of Ukrainian military intelligence, participation in a criminal organisation and causing harm to Austria. According to the Austrian Interior Ministry, the suspicion of espionage was subsequently not substantiated.
- The Vienna Prosecutor's Office said the detention had been based on eyewitness statements. Ukrainska Pravda believes that law enforcement officers exceeded their authority.

UK bars Swedish academic ahead of London conference with Palestine Action co-founder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:16:00 UTC
20:16:00 KST

Swedish climate scholar Andreas Malm has been barred from entering the UK ahead of a planned appearance at a London conference, with immigration officials saying his presence "may not be considered to be conducive to the public good," The Guardian reported on Friday.
Malm was scheduled to speak alongside Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, a pro-Palestine group banned under UK law, at a conference organised by Tribune magazine next week.
The event was set to discuss the impact of Palestine Action's proscription and coincide with a Supreme Court challenge to the group's designation.
Malm, an associate professor of human ecology at Lund University in Sweden, was notified of the decision before travelling to the UK.
He described the decision to deny him entry as "scandalous" and urged the government to reverse it, saying he had travelled to the country for decades for academic research, lectures and conferences.
In comments reported by The Guardian, Malm said Britain had been a central part of his academic life. He conducted archival research in the country for his PhD dissertation, lectured at dozens of universities and participated in numerous conferences. His previous engagements included institutions such as Oxford, Cambridge and King's College London.
"I have always considered the UK a centre of the world of ideas, where differences in opinions and scientific approaches can be aired freely," Malm said, describing his longstanding relationship with the country.
He also expressed dismay at the decision, saying he had expected greater respect for freedom of expression and other democratic rights. He appealed to the government to reverse the ban.
Malm was also scheduled to appear on BBC Radio 4's ‘Radical with Gabriel Gatehouse’ during his visit. His planned appearance would have provided an opportunity for public discussion of the issues surrounding Palestine Action's proscription.
Tribune editor Oliver Eagleton said Malm had been due to speak about attacks on freedom of speech, including the implications of Palestine Action's proscription, but had now himself been prevented from entering the country.
“He is being censored for speaking out about censorship, in truly Orwellian fashion,” Eagleton said in comments to the Guardian.
Author Sally Rooney criticised the decision as "a sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm", describing Malm as one of Europe's influential intellectuals.
Malm has won international awards for his books, and his writings have inspired many to take action for Palestinian rights and environmental justice, according to the Guardian.
The Home Office declined to comment on individual cases, according to the report.

Swiss supermarket chain plays down job loss rumours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:14:15 UTC
20:14:15 KST

Swiss supermarket chain plays down job loss rumours
A planned merger of the regional co-operatives at Swiss supermarket chain Migros will not cost thousands of jobs, according to chair Mario Irminger.
“Incorrect figures are circulating in the media,” he told the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ). “It is certainly not a matter of thousands of jobs. These estimates are probably based on an analysis of the merger with Coop that took place 25 years ago, but the situation at Migros is different.”
More
Scandals and losses force revamp of Swiss supermarket chain Migros
The SonntagsZeitung has suggested potential annual savings of between CHF300 million and CHF400 million, resulting from 3,000 job cuts. Based on its own calculations, the NZZ estimates that 400 to 600 administrative jobs could be shed.
“At the moment, I don’t wish to comment on a figure like that,” Irminger said. “One thing is certain: at management and administrative level, we will be phasing out parallel structures over time. At Migros Supermarkets, we employ 55,000 staff, and if we take staff turnover within the group into account, we’re talking about 10,000 vacancies that we need to fill every year.”
“Our concern is that we may not have enough specialists to manage our business.”
Irminger will be leaving the company next summer. “The last few months have been very intense. The transformation will continue beyond my retirement,” he said.
For the merger proposal to be approved, the consent of all ten regional co-operatives is required with a two-thirds majority and a 25% turnout.

It was the only transport serving a village where more than 1,600 people still live: Russian forces strike a social bus with a drone in Bilenke, killing a woman and injuring other passengers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:13:46 UTC
20:13:46 KST

A Russian FPV drone struck a social bus operated by the Proliska Humanitarian Mission in the frontline village of Bilenke, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, while it was carrying 23 passengers and a driver. The mission’s head, Yevhen Kaplin, reported the attack on Facebook on 29 October. In a comment to Ukrainska Pravda, he later gave slightly different details: 20 passengers and around 14:50.
Earlier that day, Russian attacks on Bilenke killed a 49-year-old man and wounded three other men, acting Zaporizhzhia Oblast head Mykhailo Semikin said. The village of Bilenke is likely to face the most difficult conditions in Zaporizhzhia Oblast this winter, then-head of the oblast Ivan Fedorov said in an interview with Ukrinform on 15 August. Russian forces use the village as a testing ground because the front line runs roughly across the river, he said.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, this marks the 121st attack on the mission’s staff and volunteers while they were providing aid, as well as on its vehicles, offices, and warehouse infrastructure, Kaplin said.
The drone was reportedly lying in wait
The attack killed a female passenger born in 1952. The bus driver sustained serious injuries and was evacuated to a medical facility, Kaplin said. Another passenger, a man born in 1947, sustained multiple shrapnel wounds, while another woman suffered injuries from flying glass. The remaining passengers suffered acoustic barotrauma. Most of the people on board were elderly.
According to preliminary information, this was a drone that was lying in wait, Kaplin said. The attack took place at around 14:30 in the center of the village, on a section of road protected by an anti-drone net.
The bus was clearly marked with the humanitarian mission’s logo on the hood and roof, as well as the words “social bus,” Kaplin said.
National Police special units and military personnel evacuated the wounded, accompanied by aerial cover teams, due to the threat of further drone attacks.
It was the only transport serving the village, Kaplin said
Commercial transport operators no longer serve the village of Bilenke, but more than 1,600 people still live there.
As a result, residents had no way to reach the Oblast center to access essential services, or to buy food and medicine, Kaplin said. They also could not collect their pensions or winter aid payments from the state and humanitarian organizations.
The Proliska team launched the social bus at the request of regional and local authorities.
Russians attack public transport in Zaporizhzhia with drones
Russian drones also hit civilian transport in the Oblast capital several times on 29 October. The city came under a record number of FPV drone attacks that day, Semikin said, adding that Russia had changed its tactics and modified its drones.
- In the morning, a Russian FPV drone struck a municipal bus in the city, Semikin said on 29 October. He first said the strike injured a woman and a man, then said four people were injured.
- Russia launched two strikes on Zaporizhzhia, Semikin reported the same day. Two men, aged 66 and 41, were injured. The strikes damaged 15 vehicles, a warehouse building, a power line, and a nearby apartment block. A fire broke out at the site, he added.
- Later, a Russian drone struck a minibus in central Zaporizhzhia, Semikin reported. According to preliminary information, one person was injured.
- A Russian FPV drone struck a municipal trolleybus in Zaporizhzhia again, Semikin said. He initially reported one woman injured, then said the number rose to three. They included a 56-year-old woman in serious condition and two other women, aged 71 and 66, who sustained minor shrapnel wounds to their legs, he said.

Iraq sentences 3 French nationals to 20 years in prison for Islamic State membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:12:25 UTC
20:12:25 KST

An Iraqi court on Thursday sentenced three French nationals to life imprisonment, equivalent to 20 years in prison, for membership of the Islamic State group in Syria and Iraq.
The ruling by the Third Karkh Criminal Court in Baghdad applies to Amir Abdelkader, known as Abu Baraa al-Faransi, who was born in the French city of Lille in 1989 and is of Algerian origin; Kamal Habib Ahmed, 42, a French national of Tunisian origin known as Abu Sumayya al-Muhajir; and Charlie Saint-Raymond, 32, who was born in Paris and is of Vietnamese origin and known as Abu Sufyan.
On Tuesday, the same court sentenced six other French members of Islamic State to 20 years in prison and another to 15 years.
The court also heard statements from three other defendants — Ibrahim al-Khalil, Noureddine Abdelkader al-Mansouri and Majid Fatimi Abdelkader — about how they joined the group and the roles and positions they held while operating in Syria.
Two of the defendants are French nationals and the third is Moroccan. The court has set 18 November for the verdict in their cases.
The court began proceedings on 20 September against 47 French nationals accused of belonging to Islamic State, scheduling hearings in stages.
Iraqi lawyers have been appointed to defend the defendants after French lawyers requested by them were unable to attend.

Bilbao, Wrocław and Bordeaux top the best-value destinations list for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:12:18 UTC
20:12:18 KST

You could save up to two-thirds on flight prices and hotel stays by selecting the right city for your next holiday.
Despite the cost of living crisis, travel remains a top priority for many Europeans.
People aren’t, for the most part, cutting down on the number of holidays they take, but they are being far savvier about the places they visit in a bid to save some serious cash.
If you’re looking to do the same, we have good news, as Skyscanner has unveiled its list of the best-value destinations for 2027.
Compiled based on the percentage price drop for economy class return flights booked in the first half of the year for travel throughout 2026, compared to the same period last year, you could save as much as two-thirds on your flights. The pricing of accommodation in each of the places selected was also considered.
“As people become more intentional about how they spend their time and money, they're making different choices about where they go, how they book and what creates lasting value,” Skyscanner CEO Bryan Batista said.
“They're prioritising meaningful experiences over material possessions, seeking confidence in every booking decision, and, in some cases, using AI during the planning process.”
The best-value destinations for 2027
After all that number crunching, there was one clear winner: Bilbao in Spain.
With airfares down 66% and hotel stays down 63% compared to 2025, there’s never been a better time to explore Basque Country.
The world-famous Guggenheim Museum Bilbao is an obvious first port of call on any visit, but the city is also known for its fantastic foodie offering, so why not make your way through its bars trying various pintxos along the way?
Next up is Wrocław in Poland, where flights are down 47%, and hotel stays are cheaper than other major cities in the country.
With a history spanning more than 1,000 years, Wrocław has plenty to see and do, from Cathedral Island, which is still lit up by gas lanterns at night, to the UNESCO-listed Centennial Hall, an icon of reinforced concrete architecture.
In fantastic news for wine lovers, third place went to Bordeaux, where flights to the French city are down by a third and hotel rates by 9%.
Zürich in Switzerland might be a place you typically associate with high prices, but according to Skyscanner’s analysis, flight prices are down by a third, and hotels by 13%.
Rounding out the top five is Ancona in Italy, where flights are down 31% and hotel prices are down 13%.
Top 10 destinations where airfares have fallen the most
- 1. Bilbao, Spain (-66%)
- 2. Wrocław, Poland (-47%)
- 3. Bordeaux, France (-34%)
- 4. Zürich, Switzerland (-33%)
- 5. Ancona, Italy (-31%)

Public polling suggests Democrats are likely to take control of the House of Representatives, and analysts who parse what politics means for investors are in overdrive to tell their clients how to prepare for what Congress will look like after the Tuesday election.
Concern about the spending plans and priorities of a Democratic-controlled Congress permeates analyst reports reviewed by CNBC. But because Trump has another two years of his presidency, a divided government would likely create gridlock that would prevent congressional leadership in opposition to the president from getting much done, analysts are advising their clients.
Most analysts believe Democrats are also within striking distance of a Senate majority, though that outcome is significantly less likely than a House flip according to the polls. Next Tuesday's elections will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress for the remainder of Trump's presidency, after two years of full Republican control.
Divided government typically makes must-pass legislation, like government funding and raising the debt ceiling, harder to enact. A debt ceiling standoff — or first-ever default on federal debt — could be particularly damaging.
Wall Street watchers are also expecting Democrats to try to advance an ambitious and expensive agenda should they gain control of Congress. An Oct. 29 report from Piper Sandler analyzing Congressional Budget Office data projected that policy proposals from Democrats "would add $5 trillion to the deficit over the coming decade." The analysis assumes repeals of Trump's tariffs and reversing cuts to Medicaid, nutrition programs and Affordable Care Act subsidies.
Major policy swings — and big spending packages — become less likely as a divided government is unlikely to agree on issues. That's a dynamic the market typically enjoys. Trump's veto power would effectively block major Democratic policies from becoming law.
"A blue House is the obvious consensus base case," Wolfe Research said in an Oct. 27 report. The firm surveyed 138 investors and found 96% of those polled believed Democrats would prevail in House control.
"The scale of polling error that would be required for Republicans to retain House control would be unprecedented in modern history, well above the polling error in the famously bad 2020 cycle," Wolfe wrote.
Wolfe is less bullish on a Democratic Senate, though investors clearly see a possibility that Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.
Fifty-eight percent of investors the firm surveyed believed Democrats would gain control of the Senate, while 42% believed Republicans would retain control of the chamber. The investors surveyed were more bullish than Wolfe itself, which puts the chances of a Democratic Senate at 49%.
Other analysts are largely coalescing around the potential for a good night for Democrats.
"A blue wave scenario has become our base case," an Oct. 20 report from TD Securities reads. An Oct. 23 Raymond James report says "Democrats are in a solid position to win a majority in the House of Representatives and are increasingly likely to win enough seats to capture a Senate majority."
Even if Democrats sweep both chambers, protracted battles could still play out as Republicans maintain the White House and the Senate must still surpass the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
Democrats winning control of the Senate could allay concerns about the Federal Reserve's independence from Trump, TD predicted.
That's because any new Fed members would need to be confirmed by the Senate, which would be unlikely to support a nominee who wouldn't support the central bank charting its own course.
Democrats are also expected to investigate companies that have done business with the Trump administration should they win control of a chamber. The majority party in Congress holds subpoena power on committees. Some Democrats have already telegraphed their investigative priorities ahead of the election.
The debt ceiling is likely the most critical sticking point for the economy that lawmakers will need to address during the next Congress, unless Republicans raise it during the lame-duck session between the election and the start of the next Congress in January. The Bipartisan Policy Center expects the U.S. will reach the so-called X-date — the point at which Treasury runs out of cash under the debt ceiling — between late-winter and mid-summer 2027.
"While negotiations around the debt ceiling may come down to the wire, a Democratic Congress would make it slightly more likely that a bill is passed than a divided Congress," TD said.
If Congress does not raise the debt ceiling by the X-date, the U.S. could default on its debt, causing catastrophic economic consequences.
Democrats, should they control one slice of government, are expected to demand concessions from Republicans in exchange for their votes to raise the debt ceiling. That sets up a potential standoff, which analysts note Republicans could avoid if they lose next week and raise the debt ceiling during the lame duck.
"[R]aising the debt limit before January could substantially reduce leverage Democrats have over healthcare, Medicaid, SNAP, and broader domestic spending priorities in the next Congress," Raymond James told its clients.

Police launch criminal investigation into Google data centre works
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:08:48 EET
20:08:48 KST

Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into preparatory work at Google's planned data centre in Muhos, northern Finland, over suspected environmental damage. The investigation follows concerns about drainage and water management at the site, where the company cleared hundreds of hectares of forest before completing environmental assessments.
The Oulu Police Department announced on Thursday that it had begun investigating activities carried out by Tuike Finland, Google's Finnish subsidiary, following a request from the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV).
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Police have received five requests for an investigation concerning the Muhos project. All five will form part of the same criminal inquiry.
According to the police statement, preliminary findings indicate irregularities and shortcomings in drainage arrangements and water management at the construction site. Investigators will examine these activities to establish whether environmental offences have occurred.
Police said the investigation also covers potential lesser offences.
The case follows weeks of scrutiny over Google's preparations for data centres in Muhos and Kajaani, where extensive forest clearance and earthworks began before the completion of environmental impact assessments.
Tuike Finland cleared approximately 330 hectares of forest in Muhos. Finnish legislation requires the assessments when permanent forest removal exceeds 200 hectares in a continuous area.
The Finnish Supervisory Agency intervened in early October, instructing Tuike Finland to suspend work affecting the environment at both locations. The restrictions covered logging, excavation, drainage, soil removal and the construction of roads and storage areas.
Google confirmed on 14 October that preparatory activities had stopped at both sites.
The agency had raised concerns that the scale of the work risked changing the environment before the assessment process established its potential consequences.
Google has maintained that it acted in accordance with Finnish legislation and understood from discussions with municipal authorities that preparatory work was permitted.
In an earlier statement, Google communications manager Sondre Ronander acknowledged concerns about the company's handling of the projects.
“We understand the concern caused by the situation. In this case, we did not meet the high standards we set ourselves,” Ronander said.
Google previously claimed it had conducted nature surveys and taken measures to protect environmentally sensitive areas. It also announced plans to plant trees across 130 hectares in Muhos.
The projects form part of Google's announced €13 billion investment programme in Finnish data centre infrastructure.
The Oulu Police Department aims to complete the preliminary inquiry during 2027 and plans to release further information in December 2026.

Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
A symbol of independent journalism, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a ‘foreign agent’ by Moscow.
Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it will shut down, citing pressure from the authorities.
The independent outlet’s editorial board said in a statement released on Friday that the newspaper has been forced to end its operations.
The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. The authorities recently searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s senior editor and arrested the editor-in-chief.
“The newspaper is gone. The Russian authorities and … intelligence services forced the editorial staff to cease operations,” the editorial board said in the statement, which was entitled: “We were killed.”
Viewed as a relative bastion of independent journalism in Russia, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement published on YouTube. “On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
Earlier this month, Sokolov was taken in for questioning as Russian authorities searched his home due, they said, to a link to a criminal case involving his colleague Oleg Roldugin.
Roldugin was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”.
“How far will the Kremlin’s relentless campaign against Novaya Gazeta go?” asked media watchdog Reporters Without Borders in a statement after Sokolov was arrested on October 15.
“Six of its journalists and staff members have been murdered, its newsroom has been raided, its journalists have been prosecuted, and the publication has been designated a ‘foreign agent’,” the press freedom organisation noted.
The forced closure of Novaya Gazeta marks another escalation in Russia’s crackdown on press freedom, with few independent media outlets or journalists left in the country, as censorship levels and arrests of regime critics have skyrocketed since it launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The newspaper had already trimmed production inside Russia after Moscow invaded Ukraine, as authorities revoked its media licence.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

BP's net profit quadrupled between July and September as the Iran war sent refining margins and oil prices soaring, with the British energy giant beating forecasts and cutting its net debt by $8.4 billion (€7.5bn) ahead of a strategy update in December.
BP's profit attributable to shareholders rose to $4.7 billion (€4.2bn) for the July to September period, four times the $1.16 billion (€1.04bn) of a year earlier, it said on Friday, as disruption from the Iran war boosted its refining and trading earnings.
The British oil and gas major also beat analysts' forecasts and cut its net debt by $8.4 billion (€7.5bn), weeks before its new CEO sets out her strategy in December.
Its underlying replacement cost profit, the figure investors judge BP on, nearly quadrupled to $8.5 billion (€7.6bn) from $2.2 billion (€1.96bn), well above the $6.2 billion (€5.55bn) expected.
It strips out swings in the value of BP's oil and fuel stocks and one-off items, such as $4 billion (€3.58bn) of writedowns this quarter, mostly on what it called "transition businesses".
Like its rivals, BP cashed in on refining margins, the difference between what refiners pay for crude and what they earn from fuels such as diesel. With the war choking off fuel exports from the Middle East, refineries elsewhere are profiting from tight global supplies.
CEO Meg O'Neill, who took over in April, described "a strong set of results, supported by the higher-price, higher-margin environment".
Net debt also fell to $13.9 billion (€12.4bn) from $22.3 billion (€19.9bn) three months earlier, helped by BP suspending share buybacks in February to put spare cash towards its balance sheet. The company said it had now met its targets for cutting debt and costs, and kept its quarterly dividend at 8.66 cents a share.
BP also said it intends to prioritise using spare cash to settle its remaining liabilities from Deepwater Horizon, the 2010 explosion and oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico that killed 11 workers, after agreeing last week to speed up payments of the $16 billion (€14.3bn) settlement to the US state of Louisiana.
O'Neill unveils her strategy on 15 December as BP, long seen as lagging its peers, had already cut back clean energy spending to refocus on more lucrative oil and gas. Rivals Shell and TotalEnergies also posted bumper profits on Thursday.
BP shares were up 0.3% in early trading on Friday.
Where oil stands
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded at around $113.6 a barrel on Friday morning, up roughly 2.5% on the week, after falling more than 6% on Monday as diplomacy over the Iran war seemingly gathered pace.
That is still far above the roughly $72 per barrel that Brent fetched before the Iran war began in late February.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate stood at around $104.2 a barrel, up roughly 1.5% on the week.
BP has also raised the oil price it uses to value its assets, and now assumes Brent will average $87 a barrel this year, up from $70, both adjusted for inflation to 2024 prices.
It expects supply disruptions in the Middle East to last into 2027, and refining margins to "remain elevated" in the final quarter of this year.

Slovak prosecutor reopens probe into fighter jet donation to Ukraine
Oct 30 - Slovakia's top prosecutor ordered on Friday a new probe into the donation of MiG-29 fighter jets and air defence systems to Ukraine by the country's previous government, restarting an investigation ended earlier this year.
The current government of Prime Minister Robert Fico, which pursues a more pro-Russian foreign policy and ended military aid for Ukraine, has repeatedly attacked the donation made in 2023.
The decision reopens a criminal case at the centre of a dispute between Fico's government and its predecessors over military support for Ukraine.
Fico has said the donations left the country dependent on allied air patrolling, and a senior official in his party called it sabotage.
The country's chief prosecutor, Maros Zilinka, said on Facebook on Friday he had ordered a new investigation as the previous one ended prematurely.
"In the preparatory proceedings, facts were not established in an extent necessary for a decision," he said.
A Bratislava regional prosecutor, Rastislav Remeta, said in ending the previous probe in February this year that the dozen Soviet-era MiG-29 jets and the KUB air defence systems were outdated, not fully operational and lacked pilots and missiles. He said their donation was no crime.
The defence minister at the time, Jaroslav Nad, has denied any wrongdoing.
The case is an illustration of the highly polarised Slovak political scene, where Fico has repeatedly accused his predecessors of pursuing criminal prosecutions against his party when he was in opposition. REUTERS

Pranksters fake US$10 theft from struggling Minnesota dad – viewers raise over US$250,000 for him

- Viewers raised more than US$250,000 on GoFundMe for Walt. Red Baron said it had spoken to the employee involved and was supporting him after the August incident.
AI generated
It was a simple prank, but the two trolls behind it picked the wrong mark: a Michigan father of four with bills to pay, shelves to stock and a whole universe of frustrations to unload.
So, in a two-minute video that has been watched more than 2.2 million times on social media platform X, he let the pranksters have it.
He berated them and angrily told them why they should not be making fun of someone like him who was nearly at the end of his rope, just so they could entertain their Instagram followers.
Viewers responded to that raw emotion with more than just sympathy. They chipped in, raising more than US$250,000 (S$319,000) as at Oct 29 for the man, publicly identified only as Walt Z.
The encounter began when two men approached Walt, who was wearing a Red Baron pizza shirt, as he stocked a grocery store freezer, and asked for the time.
When Walt took out his phone to check the time, one of the men held another phone near it and set off a fake Apply Pay sound and a simulated money transfer.

“My life is hard enough as it is, okay? I don’t need this crap,” he told the two men.
“Bro, bro, it’s just a joke! It’s just a prank,” the man recording the video replied, trying to pacify Walt.

“I got kids at home that went to bed without me right now! I was supposed to be off an hour ago! I gotta wake up at five in the morning and do 10 more stores!” he told them.
One of the men then said: “I’m sorry, bro, chill. We’re just filming a video, it was just a joke.”
