Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:50:22 UTC
19:50:22 KST

Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Michigan
- Summary:
- A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.
- Share:
A surprising discovery made with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from darkness. The findings suggest that powerful explosions from dying stars may have actually interfered with a process scientists once believed they helped drive.
An international research team, including astronomers from the University of Michigan, found that powerful winds produced by exploding stars can prevent ultraviolet radiation from escaping galaxies. This is the opposite of what a widely accepted theory had predicted, and it could change how scientists understand one of the most important transformations in cosmic history.
The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, offers new clues about how the universe became transparent to ultraviolet light roughly 13 billion years ago.
How the Early Universe Emerged From Its Cosmic Fog
During the first billion years after the Big Bang, vast amounts of neutral hydrogen filled the space between galaxies. This hydrogen formed a kind of cosmic fog that absorbed ultraviolet radiation, preventing that light from traveling freely across the universe.
That changed during a period known as reionization, which began approximately 13 billion years ago. Intense radiation from early galaxies gradually transformed the hydrogen by stripping electrons from its atoms, leaving behind positively charged protons and free electrons.
As more hydrogen became ionized, ultraviolet light could travel much farther through intergalactic space. This transformation helped establish the relatively transparent universe that astronomers observe today.
"Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today," said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe."
Despite its enormous importance, astronomers still do not fully understand which objects supplied the radiation responsible for reionization or how enough of that radiation managed to escape from early galaxies.
"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," said Carr, who conducted and led the research while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China, before joining the University of Michigan. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."
Hubble Challenges a Leading Theory About Exploding Stars
For years, one prominent explanation centered on supernovae, the powerful explosions that occur when certain stars reach the ends of their lives. These explosions can generate enormous winds that sweep through galaxies, pushing gas and other material outward.
Scientists proposed that these winds cleared pathways through the gas surrounding young stars, allowing ultraviolet radiation to escape into the space between galaxies. Once outside, that radiation could help break apart the neutral hydrogen responsible for the universe's ancient fog.
However, new observations from Hubble suggest that this explanation may have the process backward.
Rather than opening routes for radiation to escape, the researchers found that stronger galactic winds were associated with less escaping ionizing radiation. The observations indicate that the winds generated by supernovae can actually make it harder for the radiation to leave a galaxy.
"Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn't what we thought," Carr said.
The results lend support to a different possibility. Radiation from young, massive stars may escape their galaxies before those stars explode as supernovae and generate large winds that reshape the surrounding environment.
"Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form," Carr said.
Photons are individual packets of light energy. In this case, the researchers are interested in ultraviolet photons energetic enough to ionize hydrogen, making them essential to understanding how the early universe became transparent.
What Hubble Discovered in Nearby Starburst Galaxies
To investigate how radiation escapes, the international team used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby starburst galaxies. These are galaxies experiencing exceptionally intense periods of star formation, making them useful modern examples of the kinds of galaxies believed to have contributed to reionization.
Hubble, a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency, allowed researchers to study the light coming from these galaxies in detail.
The team examined their spectra, which reveal how much light is present at different wavelengths. By studying the patterns in those spectra, astronomers can learn about the gas surrounding stars and determine how quickly it is moving.
Gas absorbs particular wavelengths of light, creating recognizable dips in a galaxy's spectrum. The locations and shapes of these dips provide clues about the speed and movement of galactic winds.
When the researchers compared wind speeds with the amount of ionizing radiation escaping from each galaxy, they uncovered a surprising relationship. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.
That result directly challenges the expectation that stronger winds should clear away more gas and make it easier for radiation to reach intergalactic space.
"It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape," said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.
In other words, instead of clearing a path for ultraviolet light, energy from exploding stars appears to redistribute gas and dust in ways that can block more of it.
Young Stars May Hold the Key to Cosmic Reionization
Although large galactic winds appear to suppress escaping radiation, smaller winds and other activity around young stars could still help create openings in the surrounding gas.
These processes may occur before the first supernova explosions, giving radiation a chance to escape while conditions are more favorable.
The findings suggest that astronomers may need to pay greater attention to what happens during the earliest stages of star formation, rather than focusing primarily on the effects of exploding stars.
Carr and his colleagues are seeking additional observing time with Hubble to examine more galaxies and investigate whether the same patterns appear elsewhere. More observations could help establish how important the activity of young stars is in allowing ionizing radiation to escape.
The results also have implications for computer simulations of the early universe. These simulations attempt to recreate how galaxies formed, how gas moved through them, and how radiation eventually transformed the hydrogen filling intergalactic space.
"Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies," said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. "Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode."
By accounting more accurately for these early interactions between stars, radiation, and gas, researchers may be able to build better models of how reionization unfolded.
The discovery does not yet settle the question of what caused the universe's last major phase transition. However, it provides an important new clue, suggesting that the radiation that helped lift the universe's ancient fog may have escaped galaxies before powerful stellar explosions began to alter their surroundings.
International Research Collaboration and Funding
The research brought together nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions around the world. Sally Oey, a professor of astronomy at the University of Michigan, also contributed to the study.
The project received additional financial support from Zhejiang University, the Zhejiang Provincial Top-Level Research Support Program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities in Spain, the European Regional Development Fund, and the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program.
The research was also supported in part by federal funding from NASA and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Additional support for the Hubble Space Telescope observations came through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

How can Israel break its election deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:50:21 UTC
19:50:21 KST

How can Israel break its election deadlock?
No political party has achieved the 61-seat majority required in the Knesset to form a government in Israel.
No clear winner has emerged from Israel’s election, raising speculation over which party could form the next government.
Early on Friday, the Central Elections Committee (CEC) published the final results of the October 27 vote, which had a high voter turnout of 77.9 percent.
Neither Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot has secured the majority necessary to form a government. Both leaders have also ruled out working with the two main electoral lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List.
So how can Israel break its political deadlock?
Here’s what we know:
Have all votes been counted?
Yes. On Thursday, at least 500,000 “double envelope” votes which came in from soldiers and diplomats were counted. These voters use two envelopes: the first contains their ballot without any identifying information, while the second bears their personal details. The anonymous envelope is placed inside the second envelope, allowing officials to check that voters have not cast ballots elsewhere, without compromising the secrecy of their choice.
What was the final result?
Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48 seats.
The United Arab List, or Ra’am, and the Joint List secured a combined 19 seats.
To form a government, a political party must hold at least 61 seats. No single party has ever won that majority and alliances have led to governing coalitions, with a prime minister at the helm.
What happens next?
Political consultations to form a coalition are reported to be under way.
If the process fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog could choose which candidate has the best chance to form a government. That candidate is then given about 28 days to do so – a period that could be extended.
If the candidate fails, the president can then choose another. If that candidate is unable to form a government, then a 21-day window opens in which 61 members of the Knesset can submit a request to Herzog to assign the task to a Knesset member.
Is a second election possible?
Yes, because if all the processes listed above fail, Israelis will have to return to the polls.
Are Arab parties being considered for coalitions?
Many Israeli leaders have rejected the idea of partnering with Arab-led parties.
Netanyahu has ruled out working alongside them and demonised them following their strong showing.
“It is forbidden to form a government with them,” Netanyahu posted on X on Friday.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has accused the Arab-led parties of “stealing” the election, after his own coalition lost its majority.
According to a Times of Israel report this week, Eisenkot has said he would only consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service.
He has not said whether the Arab-led parties would meet those criteria.
On Thursday, another opposition figure, Avigdor Lieberman, the hard-right leader of Yisrael Beytenu, also ruled out certain coalitions. “Neither Bibi nor Tibi”, he said, using Netanyahu’s nickname and invoking Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al party – part of the Joint List.
Where do the Arab parties stand?
The Arab parties have shown interest in partnering with anti-Netanyahu factions.
Yousef Jabareen from the Joint List said that his party was ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”, which he called one of “bloodshed”.
“Against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative. The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Political analyst Ahmed Najar said the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel have shown considerably more pragmatism than Eisenkot and most of his allies.
“Ra’am has indicated that it is open to participating in an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has left open the possibility of supporting a minority government from outside the coalition, provided that such support delivers meaningful commitments on equality, violent crime in Palestinian communities, home demolitions and a political pathway for the wider Palestinian question,” he said.
Can Arab parties break the political deadlock?
It is still too soon to say, according to analysts.
“The numbers don’t add up for any side,” Roi Zur, a lecturer at Essex University and specialist in Israeli voting behaviour and election strategies, told Al Jazeera. “However, there are rumours that Eisenkot will ask for the support of the Arab parties in a government investiture vote in return for financial investment in their communities. Yet, this is unlikely on both sides, and even if both sides go forward with this idea, it might fall due to Lieberman objecting to the idea.”
Zur said that if the four parties in Eisenkot’s “change bloc” were closer to a majority, outside support would have been more likely because Ra’am is perceived as a more “moderate” Arab party.
“Then a European-style confidence-and-supply agreement would be more probable,” he added.
Nimrod Flaschenberg, a Berlin-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is still unclear whether Eisenkot is willing to rely on Ra‘am and the Joint List.
“If Eisenkot will be willing to go for such cooperation, then there are three options: The first is the Israeli-Arab parties could be part of the government. This is what Ra‘am wants; the Joint List does not want this at this stage. The second option is they could be a coalition member but without any government seats. This is what Ra‘am was in the Bennet government from 2021-2022,” he said.
“The third option is they could support from the outside as a preventive bloc that does not vote down the government. Most predict that if there is such a government, it will include Ra‘am in the coalition and will rely on the Joint List from the outside,” he added.
Palestinian political analyst Najar said that the real obstacle at this stage is not a lack of pragmatism from Arab parties, but rather “the refusal of Eisenkot and several of his partners to recognise Palestinian citizens of Israel – and the 19 representatives they elected – as legitimate political partners”.
“The election produced 67 seats outside Netanyahu’s bloc, but Israel’s political system continues to behave as though 19 of those seats do not fully count. Eisenkot wants Palestinian votes to remove Netanyahu while insisting on a ‘Zionist government’ that excludes the representatives of those same voters,” he noted.
“That is not merely coalition arithmetic; it exposes a profound democratic contradiction. Palestinian citizens are permitted to vote, but when their votes become decisive, their political legitimacy is immediately questioned,” he added.
What options does Netanyahu have?
To keep power, the prime minister could yet form a coalition, according to Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House.
“He can try and persuade Eisenkot and others to form a coalition with him and in the meantime he can delegitimise the Arab parties to make it difficult to form an alternative government,” he told Al Jazeera.
Flaschenberg said Netanyahu will likely push for another round of elections.
“In his calculation – the Arabs will not turn out as before and the opposition would be discouraged and stagnant. He believes that in another round of elections his bloc could get to 61,” he said.
“The other option that [Netanyahu] is working on is getting one or two parties from the Change bloc to join his government. Most likely Bennet and Liberman. But at the moment it doesn’t look like they are going to join him,” he added.
How do Palestinians view the deadlock?
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, called the election “an existential moment for Palestinian Israelis”.
Palestinian analyst Najar said that for Palestinian citizens of Israel, the result represents both an achievement and a test.
“They turned out in large numbers, secured unprecedented representation and may now have the power to prevent another Netanyahu government. Yet they are again being told that their votes are acceptable only if they do not translate into real political power,” he said.
“For Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, however, there is little reason to see this as a contest between occupation and peace, or between oppression and equality. It is principally a struggle over who will govern Israel and how Israel will present itself — not whether Palestinians will continue to live under military occupation, settlement expansion, dispossession and systemic inequality,” he added.
“But Palestinians will judge any successor by policy, not personality – whether it ends the genocide in Gaza, stops settlement expansion and settler violence, and recognises Palestinian freedom and self-determination,” he said.

Apple takes “monumental step forward” with first touchscreen MacBook
Apple has revealed its latest MacBook Pro model, which features the technology brand’s first laptop touchscreen and what it claims is “the world’s best laptop display”.
Sixteen years after Steve Jobs described touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible”, Apple has ventured into the market with its new MacBook Pro, which is available from 6 November at prices ranging from £2,899 to £14,549.
As well as being touchscreen, the laptop features a PROLED XDR display, which Apple said is “the world’s best laptop display”, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, 128 gigabytes of memory, 16 terabytes of storage, up to 24 hours of battery life and a thinner, lighter design compared to previous models.
It comes in 14- and 16-inch models, weighing three and four pounds respectively. The laptop was designed to be both portable and a powerful tool for professional creatives on the go, whether they’re working on 3D models or playing musical instruments onscreen.
“The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is a monumental step forward for the Mac,” said Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.
“PROLED XDR is the world’s best laptop display,” he continued. “And with the magic of Touch coming to MacBook Pro, combined with the game-changing performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, we’ve created a whole new way for pros to interact with their content, taking their workflows to a completely new level.”
“The new MacBook Pro is the result of the deep integration between Apple silicon, hardware, and software, and there’s simply nothing else like it.”
Aiming to provide an intuitive experience, the Touch technology allows users to scroll through a webpage by swiping, zoom in on a photo by pinching, drag and drop slides in presentations and double-tap a window to fill the screen.
The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than layered over it, to give the feel of touching the displayed content itself.
To support the Touch feature, Apple redesigned the laptop hinge for better stability and created real-time video stabilisation to smooth the camera feed when using the touchscreen on a video call.
Apple said that the macOS operating system automatically translates touches into clicks, meaning multiple existing apps will work with Touch right away. These include Adobe Lightroom, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.
“Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing,” said Apple.
“Musicians can play software instruments right onscreen, and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.”
Apple said the new PROLED XDR display offers “true-to-life colour and unparalleled brightness and contrast”, made possible by combining OLED technology with algorithms that control light across the display.
“The PROLED XDR display offers tandem OLED technology unlike any other, with deep innovations in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display, while minimising internal reflections common in traditional OLED designs,” said Apple.
“It’s all backed by advanced algorithms in the display engine that precisely control each pixel in real time, plus a meticulous manufacturing process and precise calibration of every panel for consistency from display to display.”
The MacBook Pro also has a six-speaker sound system, designed for deeper bass and improved sound clarity compared to previous models, and the Dynamic Island search and notification feature currently used in iPhones.
Other recent releases from Apple include its first folding smartphone, the HomeView dashboard for home controls and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

UK and Ukrainian industry unite to accelerate drone innovation
UK and Ukrainian defence companies have come together at Larkhill Garrison on Salisbury Plain to showcase the latest innovations in battle-proven drone technology.
- 12 Ukrainian drone manufacturers showcased combat-ready uncrewed systems to UK industry, investors and military officials.
- The event connected Ukrainian innovators with British companies and investors to accelerate collaboration, investment and capability development to enhance the UK’s readiness for future threats.
- UK support to Ukraine is unwavering and Ukrainian defence companies are expanding in the UK, strengthening both nations’ industrial bases.
The event explored opportunities for collaboration, co-development and investment in uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) and related technologies, building ties between British and Ukrainian stakeholders.
Demonstrations gave attendees the opportunity to see technologies shaped by frontline experience, while dedicated networking and engagement sessions helped build new commercial and industrial partnerships between the UK and Ukraine.
The event also provided UK industry, investors, and defence stakeholders with the opportunity to learn directly from the Ukrainian operational experience and successes, recognising that the rapid evolution of uncrewed systems on the battlefield is helping to shape the future of warfare and how we can collectively safeguard European security.
The showcase puts into practice the UK-Ukraine 100 Year Partnership, opening up MOD support to Ukraine’s defence sector. As the war continues to evolve at pace, Ukraine’s success will depend on its ability to innovate faster than Russia and rapidly field new capabilities. By bringing together industry, military users and technology developers, events such as this help ensure Ukraine remains ahead of emerging battlefield challenges, strengthening its ability to fight, adapt and ultimately prevail, while boosting defence capability and industrial resilience in both Ukraine and the UK.
Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, said:
  Ukraine’s security is Europe’s security.
That’s why the UK Government is backing British and Ukrainian collaboration, across our armed forces and industry.
We want businesses and innovators from both countries to build together, invest together and succeed together.
Brigadier Stu Nasse, Head of the Drone Capability Coalition and Deputy Head of the Uncrewed Systems Centre, said:
  This showcase is about turning innovation into action. By connecting Ukrainian companies with UK manufacturers, investors, and defence stakeholders, we can accelerate the development and delivery of technologies that strengthen both nations’ security.
The UK offers a strong environment for growth, investment, and international collaboration, and we are actively encouraging UK-Ukraine partnerships that can help deliver the next generation of defence technology breakthroughs.
One of the most important lessons from Ukraine is that government, industry, and the military must work together earlier and more closely to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats.
The event featured Ukrainian companies demonstrating technologies across intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, autonomous systems, and other emerging UAS capabilities.
It also builds on wider UK–Ukraine cooperation in defence technology and industrial development, including initiatives such as the Kyiv Business Centre, which is helping companies explore opportunities in Ukraine while supporting deeper collaboration between both nations. Together, these efforts are creating opportunities in both the UK and Ukraine for future investment, innovation, and economic growth.
The attendance of senior UK and Ukrainian representatives highlighted a shared commitment to delivering practical outcomes that strengthen capability, support industry, and reinforce the enduring partnership between the two nations.

Jonathan Reynolds says UK needs to know more about where EU heading before it opts for much closer relationship
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.
He made the comment in an interview with the Sun, a day after John Healey, the chancellor, also hinted that he might have reservations about Andy Burnham’s ambitions for a new relationship with the EU undoing the damage done by Brexit.
Burnham is attending a summit with the EU next month where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. There is strong support for all these initiatives in cabinet.
But Burnham also wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election, when – if it wants – Labour will be able to dump the 2024 manifesto pledges ruling out joining the single market or the customs union.
Burnham has not said what he wants to propose in Labour’s next manifesto, and he insists ultimately the public will decide, but he has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime and he seems open to trying to rejoin the single market in the next parliament.
Asked by the Sun if he shared Burnham’s dream of rejoining the EU, Reynolds replied:
I genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is – because [of] some of the very strong political currents in member states.
For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?
In a bid to stop ministers disagreeing in public about the EU, Burnham sent them a letter earlier this week telling them to stay “disciplined” and not to “advocate for specific options” as the debate on the future UK-EU relationship gets under way.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship. (See 1.28pm.)

Ap Iorwerth claims Burnham has now accepted in principle that Welsh government should get more borowing powers
Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, has released his readout from his meeting with Andy Burnham. Breaking with convention (these readouts are normally rather bland), he has included some news in his.
Ap Iorwerth claims Burnham has now accepted that Wales should greater borrowing powers. Under the current rules, the Welsh government’s borrowing powers are extremely limited. “This has led to the bizarre situation where it has been forced to rely on local authorities to do its borrowing for it (such as a school-building programme),” Will Hayward said in a recent Guardian column.Ap Iorwerth said:
There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency. I welcome the prime minister’s comments that this is now a matter of how and when.
He said he told Burnham that “further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd” – which sounded like a rather blunt ‘stay in your lane” response to Burnham’s “regional empowerment” proposals.
Ap Iorwerth said he asked Burnham to lean on the Treasury “to enable the Welsh government to press ahead with our Cynnal weekly child payment pilot to support the poorest families”.
Ap Iorwerth urged him to back rejoining the EU single market and customs union “as a priority”.
The Downing Street readout did not mention any of these issues. It just repeated some of what was in the Swinney one about the NEC meeting (see 3.28pm), and said Cardiff would host the next NEC meeting in spring 2027.
Burnham and Swinney agree 'Westminster doesn't work' - but remain divided over what sort of devolution offers solution
John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, has now issued a statement about today’s national economic council [NEC] in Glasgow, and Downing Street has issued a readout about Andy Burnham’s bilateral meeting with Swinney. Reading them together, three points emerge.
Swinney and Burnham were both positive about the meeting, and sounded keen to be constructive not confrontational. No 10 said both leaders agreed the NEC meeting had been “extremely positive”, and Swinney said it was “a welcome start of work to develop the UK government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’”.
But there is still a problem because, although they both want devolution, it’s not the same devolution.Swinney’s statement is all about the devolution of power from Westminster to Scotland. No 10’s is mostly about “regional empowerment” (devolution within Scotland), although it does say the PM agreed to “review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister”.
They agreed to differ on independence. The No 10 statement restates Burnham’s position that a second independence referendum is off the table. Swinney could have chosen to have a row about this, but he didn’t. While not at all resiling from his pro-independence position, he politely said: “While the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland.”
For the record, here is the full readout from the No 10 spokesperson.
The prime minister met with the first minister of Scotland in Glasgow following a meeting of the National Economic Council today.
The prime minister and first minister agreed the meeting at the NEC had been extremely positive. They said it had been a valuable exercise in starting the process of exploring how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode.
They agreed that now there would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from both governments, to take this agenda forward.
Outside that process, the prime minister said the UK government would review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister.
This would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland, which the prime minister has repeatedly made clear is off the table.
While the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland. And when the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will come about.
To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with him to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland – as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living.
Today’s meeting of the national economic council was a welcome start of work to develop the UK Government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’ and the prime minister has been clear that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour.
I welcome that commitment, and look forward to our governments jointly developing a plan to consider further devolution to Scotland that will boost economic growth.
Rise in rough sleeping numbers for London 'stark reminder' of challenge facing Burnham, campaigners say
A rise in rough sleeping in London is a “stark reminder of the huge challenge” Andy Burnham faces in his pledge to get people off the streets, campaigners have said. As the Press Association reports, data shows there were 4,678 people recorded as sleeping rough in the capital in July to September this year. PA says:
While this is a slight drop of 1% on the same three-month period in 2025, the figure has risen by almost a fifth (18%) on the previous quarter this year.
The Combined Homelessness and Information Network (Chain) figures, published today, showed that there were 819 people classed as living on the streets (a separate category) – a rise of 8% on the same time last year and up by a fifth (20%) on the previous quarter.
Rick Henderson, chief executive of Homeless Link, the national membership body for frontline homelessness services, said: “The increase in rough sleeping across London, and particularly of those spending longer on our streets, is a stark reminder of the huge challenge London and the wider country face in turning the prime minister’s ambition to end rough sleeping into action.”
Burnham says he does not want Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to be 'left behind' as England embraces fiscal devolution

The agenda is moving quickly in England. There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind. I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.
So it’s really important that we all move at the same pace together. And I won’t allow anything to delay that. Growth can’t wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK.
Referring to the absence of Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister, he said:
It’s disappointing that the first minister and deputy first minister of Northern Ireland weren’t here. There was some representation, but we will continue the discussions too with Stormont about how do we take forward the same ideas.
Burnham says UK government to consider further devolution of employment support to Scotland and Wales

We had a good discussion today on two fronts.
One around reindustrialisation, and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level. It’s about creating those structures at a regional level, and that’s a matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries.
It’s not for me to impose or try to interfere there. But once there is a vehicle, that can be backed by the Scottish government, it can be backed by the UK government …
Secondly, we had a conversation about employment support, and particularly young people. There are too many young people out of work here in Scotland, in Wales, and in England too.
It’s a very big agenda that’s coming towards us. We need to localise as much as we can support for young people, employment support to help them back to work.
Now, as part of those discussions that will follow this meeting of the national economic council, we need to look at what are [the] arrangements for further devolution of employment support, particularly for young people in both Scotland and Wales.

Patrick Stewart 'one of the very best', says No 10 in tribute

Burnham wrong to think Manchester-style regional devolution would work for Wales, says former Welsh Labour minister
Lee Waters, a former Labour minister in the Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until May this year, thinks it is a mistake for Andy Burnham to think Manchester-style devolution (greater powers for mayors) will help in Wales. Referring to posts earlier summarising Burnham’s thinking (see 9.11am, 9.33am and 12.05pm), Waters sent me this note.
Just a reminder that when it comes to Wales, we are not comparing like with like. The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas. The Swansea Bay city region captures some 700,000 people, and similarly North Wales around 690,000 people. In Mid-Wales sheep outnumber people by 7:1. Only the Cardiff city region is comparable to English tiers, and even then at the lower end: around 1.5 million people.
Transposing an English mayoral worldview onto a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.
Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government. Powers over skills, employment support, economic development, housing investment and major spending programmes sit at an all-Wales strategic level (covering a similar population size to Greater Manchester.)
His argument for England is that powers should flow from Westminster to city regions because they operate at an economically meaningful scale. Yet when the PM turns to Wales, he seems to suggest that powers already devolved to Cardiff Bay should be dispersed further down the system.
But notably he is not calling on his successor as the mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, to fragment the powers of the Greater Manchester combined authority and redistribute them amongst its ten constituent councils. On the contrary, the whole logic of the Greater Manchester model rests on concentrating strategic authority at a regional level.
Yet the implication of his comments is that Wales should move in the opposite direction.
Burnham tells devolved governments he wants to 'draw a line', leading to better relationship
Andy Burnham delivered his opening remarks at the national economic council meeting in Glasgow on camera. Here are the key points.
Burnham stressed that he wanted to be cooperative. He said:
What I want to do is set the tone which is one of positive offer to work with both the Scottish and Welsh governments, in terms of looking at a model of deeper devolution in Scotland and Wales.
Referring to John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth using their first names, not their titles, Burnham also said that he hoped they had seen enough of him as PM to know that he was serious about wanting “problem solving rather than point scoring”. He also said he wanted to “draw a line”, implying previous relations with the devolved governments weren’t ideal.
He said that, while he wanted “deeper devolution” (see 9.11am), “obviously, it’s for the devolved governments to determine the shape and the structure of that”.
He suggested his experience as mayor of Greater Manchester had made him more inclined to see Westminster the way Scotland and Wales did. He said:
Obviously, speaking as a former mayor, I saw how Greater Manchester was able to go on a very different track to the one that we’d been on pre the arrival of devolved powers in Greater Manchester.
I’ll be honest, I looked at the world differently, and perhaps more from Scotland and Wales’ point of view, when we were making that case for a greater level of power.
He said, using devolved powers, as mayor he was able to set “high ambitions” for Manchester – “and a decade on the results are there to see.”
He said he wanted Westminster to work “in a more collaborative way” with the devolved governments.
He said that Britain in the past had not been particularly good at handling “industrial transition” and that he wanted to change this. He recalled visiting the site of the Ravenscraig steelworks near Motherwell recently, saying:
I was on the site of Ravenscraig and … I used to hear that word in the news when I was growing up. I only then, when I was there, understood the scale of what that industry once was, and how the country didn’t help those communities through industrial transition.
You could say the same of Port Talbot in south Wales, he said. He said what was happening in Port Talbot was a model of industrial transition.
He expressed regret that Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister weren’t at the meeting.
John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, arrived together for the national economic council meeting in Glasgow. The SNP and Plaid Cymru are sister parties, and recently Swinney, ap Iorwerth and the Sinn Féin leaders Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill held a meeting in Cardiff that was characterised by opponents as a summit to dismantle the UK.
Voters regard Healey's budget as one of fairest for years, poll suggests
Yesterday the Institute for Fiscal Studies (see here) and the Resolution Foundation (see here) delivered fairly negative assessments of the budget. But mostly the gloom was triggered by the thinktanks said about the overall state of the economy and the public finances; they were critical of John Healey for deferring difficult choices, but less hostile about the decisions he did actually announce.
However, according to YouGov, voters are quite positive. They regard it as one of the fairest budgets for years.
The public’s initial reaction to John Healey’s first budget is in some key respects broadly positive, with nearly half of Britons (45%) regarding the budget as being fair, relative to just 20% seeing the measures announced as not fair.
This is a notable improvement on last year, when Rachel Reeves’ second budget was declared ‘not fair’ by a near-inverse margin of 48% to 21%. In fact, on this measure, this is one of the most positively received budgets in recent times. In data going back to 2010, only George Osborne’s first budget in 2010 and Rishi Sunak’s Covid budgets of 2020 and March 2021 have been judged ‘fair’ by a greater proportion of Britons (50-55%).
The Covid budgets were both giveaway, rescue budgets, and so it is not surprising they polled well. Osborne’s first budget was an austerity budget, and it is not a model popular with Labour MPs, but it probably polled well on fairness because the pain was spread across all groups in society.
The YouGov figures also show that only 15% of people think their family finances will improve as a result of the budget. That may not sound much but, as Difford says, “this is a sharp and favourable contrast with last November’s budget, which 50% of Britons believed would leave them and their family worse off, compared to a mere 3% feeling they’d be better off.”
In fact, Healey and his first budget outperform Rachel Reeves and her budget last year on every measure assessed in the polling.
Yesterday one of the criticisms of the budget from the Resolution Foundation was that the energy cost of living support package helped the rich almost as much as the poor. That meant it was “poorly targeted”, said the RF, applying a progressive, social justice definition of fairness. What the YouGov poll suggests is that voters as a whole judge fairness differently; it is probably precisely because most households get the £100 energy payment that people regard it as fair.
In their London Playbook briefing for Politico yesterday, Sam Blewett and Megan McElroy said Healey used focus groups extensively before finalising his measures.
Government officials say they focus-grouped all this relentlessly. Playbook was told these sessions helped convince ministers to go for wider support payments for council tax bands A-D rather than the initial plans to go with something more targeted. It was the supposedly better-off voters who were complaining about the pinch as well.
MoD says under new offset policy foreign firms will only get big defence contracts if they spend equivalent amount in UK
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, was on the interview round this morning, announcing a new aspect of defence procurement policy. The Ministry of Defence is now saying that, if overseas suppliers win UK defence contracts, they will be required to spend the equivalent amount in the UK.
British workers, businesses and apprentices will benefit from major changes which will see more defence work carried out in the UK thanks to the launch of a world-leading Offsets policy.
Under the new rules, overseas companies that win significant UK defence contracts will be required to invest back into Britain, through new British jobs and apprenticeships, opening UK factories, investing in domestic suppliers, transferring technology and innovation know-how.
This means contracts worth over £50m will be considered for offsets. The contractors will be required to deliver such benefits to the UK that could reach the same value as the contract, for example a £100m contract could see new jobs, facilities, or skills training up to the same £100m value in the UK.
The government is prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible. Where it must buy defence equipment from overseas, this new approach will ensure British workers and businesses still benefit.
John Healey, the chancellor, and Streeting are formally announcing this on a visit to BAE Systems Scotstoun in Glasgow today.
The MoD says countries like Poland, Norway and the Netherlands use similar offset policies. Further details of how this will work are set out in an offset policy paper published today.
Streeting said:
Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. That’s why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can.
Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry.
In the past, the conventional globalist, free market approach to defence procurement operated on the basis that cost and quality were all that mattered and that, if a foreign firm could supply kit better and more cheaply than anyone else, that was enough. But the US is not the only country that has become protectionist in recent years, and this is a good example of Europe prioritising local employment in government procurement.
John Swinney urges Burnham to devolve more powers to Scottish government
In his statement ahead of the devolution summit in Glasgow today, Andy Burnham made it clear that he is interested in transferring more power from Edinburgh to Glasgow. (See 9.11am.) But John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, would rather talk about devolving further powers from London to Edinburgh. He issued this statement ahead of the meeting.
The prime minister has made devolution a central focus for his government. However the UK government must ensure that any devolution proposals respect devolution in Scotland. That means working with the Scottish government.
The Scottish government has put forward substantive proposals to the UK government on areas where further devolution would help grow Scotland’s economy and I will press the prime minister, and his government, to work with us to deliver those proposals.
The SNP wants Scotland to be fully independent (the ultimate version of devolution). But, pending that, it is also calling for the Scottish parliament to have power over policy areas currently reserved to London. Greater control over taxation, immigration, employment law and energy policy are particular priorities.
Burnham admits he would have liked more radical first budget
Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country, Kiran Stacey reports.
Burnham says he wants to offer more ‘regional empowerment’ ahead of devolution summit with Scottish and Welsh leaders
Good morning. Andy Burnham is in Glasgow today for a meeting with the leaders from Scotland and Wales and he says he wants to use it to talk about “the next stage of devolution”. According to the overnight briefing from No 10, he is less interested in giving more powers to the devolved parliaments and more interested in promoting “regional empowerment” in their countries.
In his pre-summit statement, Burnham says:
Through No 10 North, we are rewiring the state. I want to make sure every city and region in the United Kingdom is part of that.
Today I’ll be making an offer to the governments of each nation. Put politics aside and work in partnership with the UK government to develop models of regional empowerment that ensure communities can use their own strengths to unlock their potential.
This is the next stage of devolution. Together, there is no limit to what we can achieve.
Burnham is speaking at a time when Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have since the May elections (when Plaid Cymru won in Wales) for the first time had first ministers from nationalist parties that want to break away from the UK. John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, will be at the meeting today. But Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister from Northern Ireland won’t be there. She holds power jointly with a DUP deputy, and both of them have to stay away because the DUP has vetoed their attendance due to an ongoing row about Drumcree. Some officials will attend instead.
Downing Street says at today’s meeting Burnham “will say that devolution by default shouldn’t be about the transfer of powers from one parliament to another but should go deeper within nations to empower all places and communities who know best what they need to grow and access opportunities.”

High inflation, stagnant wages eroding people's standard of living - Mattarella

standard of living through inflation and stagnant wages," said

Production of Ruta Cruise Missiles Used by Ukraine Reaches Nearly 300 per Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:49:12 UTC
19:49:12 KST

Destinus has ramped up production of Ruta cruise missiles to nearly 300 units per month — more than the whole of Europe produced in a year before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Destinus made this announcement on the official website.
The total number of Ruta B1 missiles produced has exceeded 1,750.
To sustain this production rate, the company has established in-house manufacturing of engines, airframes, avionics and guidance systems. This allows it to independently control the key stages of the production process.
For example, the company is mass-producing T150 turbojet engines with a thrust of approximately 1.5 kN. They are used in the Ruta Block 1 and are also supplied to other weapons manufacturers.
Destinus is expected to be able to meet European market demand for propulsion systems of this class as early as 2027, including orders for Ukraine.
At the same time, no Chinese components are used in production. Although cooperation with Chinese suppliers could reduce costs and speed up missile manufacturing, the supply chain has been organised without their involvement.
Destinus CEO Mykhailo Kokorych noted that as missile production increases, the main challenge for European armed forces is their practical deployment. In particular, it is necessary to establish dedicated units and develop infrastructure for storage, maintenance and target designation. In particular, it is necessary to establish appropriate units and develop infrastructure for storage, maintenance, and targeting.
In addition to ramping up production of the base version, Destinus announced the start of production of the larger Ruta Block 2 cruise missile. According to updated company data, it is designed to carry a 250 kg payload and has a range of more than 700 km.
Unlike Block 1, the new variant can be stored, transported and launched from a single container. This simplifies logistics and deployment, particularly when large missile stockpiles need to be built up.
Militarnyi previously reported on the design changes introduced in the Ruta Block 2. The new variant features a box-shaped fuselage and an integrated wing-folding mechanism, allowing the missile to be housed in a canister.
The Ruta Block 2 is also equipped with a solid-fuel booster that provides initial acceleration during launch. This allows the missile to be launched directly from the canister without the need for a separate launch rail.
Ukraine is already using Ruta cruise missiles to strike Russian targets. In particular, in July, reports emerged that Russian forces had found debris from these missiles, providing one of the first public confirmations of their combat use.

MADRID, October 30. /TASS/. A powerful explosion rocked an ammunition factory in the Spanish city of Granada (autonomous community of Andalusia), the 20minutos newspaper reported.
National police, civil guard, local police, firefighters, and medical personnel, including two mobile intensive care units, have been deployed to the scene at the Granada Ammunition Factory (Fabrica de Municiones de Granada, FMG), according to the publication.
The blast, which was felt in several municipalities in the metropolitan area, affected three workers who required medical attention for hearing problems. According to the publication, initial reports indicate that the explosion occurred in the factory’s incineration area. The detonation may have occurred during one of the routine tests carried out at the facility, in which something malfunctioned.
FMG is one of the world’s oldest ammunition factories. According to the Granada Hoy newspaper, the enterprise’s contracts with the EU, primarily in the interests of Ukraine, have led to an increase in the factory’s activity of late. The factory produces various types of ammunition and employs about 300 people.

Putin may evade accountability for war crimes, and Russia may avoid paying reparations to Ukraine – The Economist
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:49:00 EET
19:49:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin may not face an international court for war crimes, and Russia is unlikely to pay reparations to Ukraine for the damage caused by the war despite demands for accountability for the aggression, reports The Economist.
The publication notes that, notwithstanding Russia’s responsibility for the full-scale invasion and numerous crimes committed against Ukraine, the prospects for holding the Russian leadership accountable remain uncertain. In particular, participants at the Helsinki Security Forum, held this month in Finland, expressed skepticism regarding the feasibility of securing reparations from Russia or successfully prosecuting Putin.
A former U.S. official, who recently returned from meetings with high-ranking Russian representatives in Moscow, stated at the forum that any peace settlement is unlikely to align with the principles of justice.
He said that peace wouldn’t be fair, predicting that Russia would ultimately retain a portion of Ukrainian territory and that Putin would never face trial in The Hague for war crimes.
Other forum participants with extensive connections have indicated that the Russian elite has no intention of paying reparations to Ukraine for the damage caused by the war. Furthermore, dozens of military veterans who fought against Ukraine have recently been elected to the Russian parliament—a development that, according to the publication, sets the stage for individuals involved in the war to remain part of Russia’s political elite for a long time to come.
The Economist notes that for the past four years, the strategy of Ukraine’s allies has been to prevent a Russian victory and ensure that Ukraine can continue the fight. To this end, Western nations have provided Kyiv with financial and military aid while maintaining sanctions against Moscow, operating on the assumption that economic pressure and domestic discontent would eventually force Putin to change his policies or step down from power.
However, the war has reached a stalemate, and an increasing number of influential European states, notably Great Britain, France, and Germany, are considering a shift in their approach toward Russia. Specifically, there is talk of offering a potential path forward to those Russians who stand outside the current regime.
At the same time, the publication emphasizes that Putin remains a danger to both Ukraine and Europe. Russian missiles and drones continue to strike Ukrainian cities and ports, while Moscow has stepped up acts of sabotage across European countries and issued nuclear threats against the West.

Parashat Vayera: What a vote cannot decide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:46:42 UTC
19:46:42 KST

God is different. He is unlike anything in the world He created. No physical description captures His essence. Whenever we describe Him, we rely on approximations, using language and images that the human mind can comprehend. God exists beyond human experience and understanding.
We, too, are different. He gifted us with traits that distinguish us from the rest of creation: self-awareness, complex emotions, cognitive speech, creativity, imagination, dreams, and political instincts.
Chief among these qualities is our free will. We can choose between right and wrong. God implanted within us a moral instinct to distinguish good from evil. He also revealed His will to help us navigate a complex world.
The gift of free will lends consequence to our actions. Since our moral choices are not predetermined, we alone bear responsibility for them. We suffer our failures just as we celebrate our achievements. Our freedom gives our lives moral significance.
Free will also lends us dignity. Our choices aren’t merely products of hormones or instincts. We consider different possibilities, weigh their merits, and determine our course. We shape our lives through decisions rather than surrendering to forces beyond our control. This ability to choose makes us similar to God, the ultimate Free Being.
The need to belong
However, alongside our freedom, we also desire belonging. Absolute and unrestricted freedom is lonely. We crave interaction with other human beings. We desire love, friendship, family, community, and, of course, a covenant with a Higher Being. Our lives feel more meaningful when we stretch beyond our solitary and free existence and enter into relationships.
Our communities also convey and reinforce values. We choose relationships with people who share our core values. They lend our lives meaning and purpose.
Throughout our lives, we balance freedom with belonging to a larger framework – demanding we surrender some autonomy. Relationships carry expectations. Societies demand basic behavioral norms. Nations impose laws. Covenants make us summoned human beings.
Six centuries of freedom
About 700 years ago, this balance began to shift. In antiquity and throughout the Middle Ages, human freedom was severely limited. Society was largely static, and people occupied the social position into which they were born. For security and order, people were beholden to monarchs or noblemen who dictated their lives but offered protection. Human freedom and dignity were compromised for survival.
With the advent of the 14th-century Renaissance, we began a grand journey toward greater freedom and, with it, the potential for greater human dignity. The Renaissance emphasized human beings as the masterpiece of Divine creation, atop nature’s hierarchy.
The Scientific Revolution took freedom one step further by democratizing truth. Truth was no longer dictated by a select few who claimed a monopoly over it. It could be discovered through universal methods of inquiry, available, at least in theory, to everyone.
Taking this journey toward greater freedom one step further, the 18th-century Enlightenment emphasized the natural rights with which every person is born and which no government could seize, even for the sake of broader goals of security and stability.
Eventually, the defense of natural rights led to democratic systems which enshrined these rights in law. Individual freedom and human dignity now enjoyed legal protection against the arbitrary exercise of power.
Alongside political freedom came financial freedom through capitalism and free-market economies. No longer was economic potential limited by social station or rank. People could chart their own financial destinies and pursue opportunities made possible by economic independence.
Having achieved political and financial freedom, man was still bound by established patterns of thought and religion. During the 19th century, these constraints began to loosen. Secularization allowed greater freedom of worship, including the freedom not to worship at all. Morality was increasingly shaped by individual conscience rather than absolute religious dogma, allowing moral judgments to differ from person to person.
This growing freedom to think and believe independently also extended to the world of emotions. Romantic art and literature brought emotional freedom. People were no longer expected to express emotions in conventional forms or about prescribed subjects. The Romantics taught us that beauty and meaning discovered in ordinary experiences can produce emotions just as valid and profound.
The next century brought two additional forms of freedom. The sexual revolution challenged traditional norms of marriage and reproduction, allowing people to express their sexuality outside marriage and without necessarily facing the responsibilities of childbearing. Finally, the digital revolution provided unprecedented access to information. No longer do we receive information exclusively through institutions that select and filter what we may know.
Across six centuries of revolutions, humanity achieved unprecedented freedom. The individual, once confined by inherited structures and established authority, now enjoys extraordinary power to determine the course and meaning of his own life.
The price of individualism
The rise of individualism has come at great cost. Greater freedom liberated individuals, but also weakened the shared covenants, families, communities, religious traditions, and moral values that once anchored human identity. As these larger frameworks erode, people increasingly struggle with questions of identity and belonging. Without structures to reinforce common values, moral convictions become fragile and personal choices are increasingly guided by individual preference.
As people increasingly define their own identities and values, personal satisfaction becomes the measure of their commitments. Relationships and obligations are judged by what they offer the individual, making them easier to abandon when they demand sacrifice.
Greater freedom has expanded our ability to define ourselves, but weakened the bonds that once gave our lives stability, direction, and purpose.
Freedom and Jewish destiny
In Israel, we are blessed to live inside a living narrative. Our lives are anchored in shared history, strong communities, enduring commitments, and a covenant binding us to God and one another. While much of the Western world increasingly emphasizes individual identity and personal choice, Israel remains a society in which shared identity and national belonging retain enormous power.
Despite our differences, we still view our lives as part of a larger common historical story. Much of the hostility directed at Israel from liberal Western Europe stems from discomfort with a people that unabashedly champions a national story and shared historical destiny.
After the vote
I am writing these thoughts on the eve of elections in Israel.
Every vote is an expression of the individual freedom and dignity that humanity has struggled for centuries to achieve. We celebrate democracy as the best form of government humanity has developed.
That we have sustained a democracy despite military threats and internal dissent, an achievement especially remarkable in our largely undemocratic region, affirms the Zionist dream.
As we celebrate democracy, we must also recognize the dangers of unrestricted personal freedom. The rise of individualism has brought with it a crisis of identity. Our shared Jewish identity provides an anchor against this growing crisis.
We are part of a community of Jews who returned to our homeland to undertake one of history’s most ambitious projects. We are part of a long heritage of Jews who dreamed of returning to this land. We are also responsible to future generations of Jews who will judge how we navigated one of the most challenging periods in Jewish history.
We have inherited more than a country. We have inherited the dreams of generations who never lived to see Jewish sovereignty restored. They dreamed of freedom, but they also dreamed of the Jewish future that freedom would make possible.
We owe them more than a free society. We owe them a Jewish future worthy of their dreams.■
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, at mtaraginbooks.com.

Parashat Vayera: Bridging heaven and earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:46:41 UTC
19:46:41 KST

The purpose of Jewish life is to unite the spiritual and the physical, the world of the soul and the world of the body, and our spiritual aspirations with the realities of everyday life. When the body becomes a vehicle for fulfilling our spiritual obligations, the material world itself is sanctified, and all of creation is elevated.
This is the central mission of humanity, as expressed in the famous saying of the Kotzker Rebbe: “‘The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, but the earth He has given to mankind’ (Psalms 115:16) – to make it into heaven.”
The heavens represent the spiritual realm, while the earth was entrusted to humanity to cultivate and shape. Our task is not to leave the world as it is, but to elevate it, infuse it with spiritual values, and make our everyday lives part of our service of the Creator.
Abraham's way of life embodied the integration of the spiritual and the material
WE LEARN this principle from Abraham, the founding Patriarch of our people, whose way of life embodied the integration of the spiritual and the material.
One example is the story of his hospitality, from which our sages derive a special connection between Abraham and the Cave of the Patriarchs.
Commenting on the verse “And Abraham ran to the cattle” (Gen. 18:7), our sages describe how the young calf Abraham pursued led him to a place of extraordinary significance. The midrash relates:
“That calf ran ahead of him all the way to Hebron and entered the Cave of Machpela. Our forefather Abraham entered after it and saw Adam and Eve lying there, with candles burning before them and a pleasant fragrance surrounding them, like the fragrance of a sweet offering. Abraham said, ‘This cave is well suited for burial,’ and he acquired it at great expense” (Midrash Aggadah on Genesis 18:7; Yalkut Shimoni, Vayera).
In the holy Zohar, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai reveals that the Cave of Machpela is the entrance to the Garden of Eden. After Adam was expelled from the Garden because of his sin, he sought to return. When he passed near the cave, he smelled the fragrance of the Garden of Eden and asked to be buried there with his wife, Eve.
The runaway calf led Abraham to discover this special place as well. He therefore sought to purchase it from the Hittites and establish it as the burial place of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs of our nation.
The name “Machpela” also reflects this theme, as it comes from the root meaning duality.
Our sages and commentators offer various explanations for the name, one of which is that the cave became the burial place of couples: Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, and Jacob and Leah.
Beyond this physical duality lies a deeper idea: the spiritual and material realms exist side by side, not as disconnected worlds, but as complementary dimensions of a single reality that human beings can bring together.
It is fitting that the cave lies in Hebron, a city whose Hebrew name is associated with connection.
The Cave of Machpela is therefore more than the burial place of our nation’s Patriarchs and Matriarchs. It symbolizes the mission they passed down to us: to bring spirituality into our physical lives and make faith tangible through our actions.
We see Abraham fulfilling this mission through his hospitality. When he sees three men standing nearby, he immediately sets about preparing an elaborate meal for them. At first glance, this is simply an act of generosity. Yet our sages teach that these deeds had an immense spiritual effect, extending far beyond that day and place. The midrash states:
“Everything that our forefather Abraham personally did for the ministering angels, the Holy One, blessed be He, later did for his children in the wilderness.... Rabbi Yehuda Halevi son of Rabbi Shalom said in the name of Rabbi Yona... The manna descended for them during 42 journeys. And where did it first descend? In Alush. And why in Alush? In the merit of Abraham’s words, ‘Knead [lushi] and make cakes.’ Thus the Holy One, blessed be He, repaid his children, as it is said: ‘Behold, I will rain down bread for you from heaven’” (Exodus Rabbah, Beshalah, 25:5).
Abraham and Sarah elevated the material through their actions
When Abraham tells Sarah, “Knead and make cakes,” he demonstrates how an ordinary human act can draw heavenly blessing into the world. In the merit of preparing food for the angels, the people of Israel were later rewarded with manna, the “bread of the mighty” that descended from heaven.
Abraham and Sarah elevated the material through their actions and gave it spiritual significance. In return, a heavenly blessing became physical sustenance for the Children of Israel.
This teaches us that spirituality is not an abstract ideal, but a way of life expressed through the simplest deeds: preparing food, caring for others, performing acts of kindness, and directing our daily efforts toward a higher purpose. Through these actions, we invite blessing into the world.
This is the deeper significance of the Cave of Machpela: it represents the possibility of uniting the earthly and the heavenly, like “a ladder set on the earth, with its top reaching heavenward.” Those who bring spiritual purpose into their everyday lives fulfill their true calling.
WE MUST remember that the purpose of physical life is not to escape it, but to live it fully. This world was given to us by the Creator, with all it contains: family, work, relationships, responsibilities, joys, and challenges. These are not necessarily obstacles to a spiritual life. They can instead become the very means through which spirituality finds expression.
When we seek the higher values behind our everyday actions, we elevate our surroundings and give our lives meaning and purpose. In this way, daily life itself becomes a form of sacred service, allowing us to glimpse the light of a higher reality and experience something of the Garden of Eden here on earth.■
The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.

Israel&#8217;s election committee rejects claims of systematic breaches of electoral integrity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:46:33 UTC

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said on Thursday there was no basis for claims of systematic breaches of electoral integrity.
Israel’s Channel 12 reported the committee as saying in a letter that the integrity of the election had been maintained and that claims of systematic breaches were unfounded.
“The numerous media reports are unfounded,” the committee said, adding that it had received confidential and sensitive information that raised suspicions requiring further examination to determine whether there was evidence to support the allegations.
Meanwhile, Israel’s domestic security agency, Shin Bet, said a limited investigation should not be used to discredit an entire community that had voted democratically and legally, referring to Arab citizens.
“Action will be taken only against those who break the law,” the agency said.
The Shin Bet said the information about suspected foreign interference came from intelligence-gathering operations conducted as part of its legal duties, not from any political party or entity.
It stressed that the investigation was still ongoing and that any statements about the content or nature of the suspicions did not represent its position.
The agency also revealed that its chief, David Zini, had briefed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and opposition leader Yair Lapid on the main suspicions.
The Israeli right wing, led by Netanyahu’s Likud party, has campaigned against Arab voting in the election, alleging that Qatar had funded efforts to increase turnout among Arab voters. Doha has denied the allegations, describing them as “another disinformation campaign”.

Kazakhstan ready to share AI expertise with Turkic states, Tokayev says
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has expressed Kazakhstan's readiness to share its experience in digitalization and artificial intelligence with brotherly Turkic countries if needed, Qazinform News Agency reports via Akorda.
Speaking at the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Ankara, Tokayev described the development of digital technologies and artificial intelligence as a necessity in today's world, highlighting Kazakhstan's ambition to become a fully digital nation.
"Our countries are actively pursuing large-scale digital transformation. Kazakhstan has set itself the goal of becoming a digital state, and significant work is underway in this direction. This year has been declared the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence in our country," Tokayev said.
The President also highlighted Kazakhstan's progress in digitalization and artificial intelligence, noting that the Alem.ai Artificial Intelligence Center had been established in Astana and Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU) had opened to train AI specialists.
He said the country was developing a data center valley with a total capacity of 1 gigawatt and had already launched two supercomputers, with a third, significantly more powerful one expected to become operational soon.
Tokayev also pointed to the adoption of the Digital Code and a dedicated law on artificial intelligence, reaffirming Kazakhstan's readiness to share its experience in these areas with fellow Turkic countries if needed.
The Head of State recalled that the prospects for AI and digital development had been discussed at a meeting in Turkistan in May, leading to the implementation of several important initiatives.
He also highlighted the launch of the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic communications line connecting Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, noting that other Turkic countries would also be able to benefit from the project.
“Other Turkic states will also be able to benefit from this unique project. At the same time, much remains to be done, and we must act swiftly. In particular, we need to accelerate efforts to establish a Cybersecurity Council, as well as digital monitoring and innovation centers. These initiatives will undoubtedly contribute to further strengthening cooperation among our countries in the digital sphere,” the President emphasized.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev had expressed support for Russia's potential participation in the OTS through the OTS Plus format or as an observer.
