North Korea shows kamikaze drone blowing up a mock U.S. Abrams tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:11:15 UTC
19:11:15 KST

- North Korean photos show a loitering munition destroying a mock U.S. Army M1 Abrams tank during an Oct. 29 demonstration watched by Kim Jong Un.
- The drone’s tandem cross-shaped wings and rear propeller closely resemble the Hero-400 made by Israel’s UVision.
North Korea has released images of a loitering munition diving onto and destroying a mock-up of a U.S. Army M1 Abrams tank, part of a firepower demonstration Kim Jong Un watched on Oct. 29, and the drone in the photos closely resembles the Hero-400 built by Israeli company UVision.
The photos, published by state news agency KCNA on Oct. 30, show a slender drone with two sets of cross-shaped wings, one near the nose and one near the tail, descending at a steep angle toward a sand-colored tank target built to look like an Abrams, with its distinctive angular turret and gun.
A second frame shows a large fireball where the target stood. KCNA did not name the drone, give its range or warhead size, or say how many were used.
The demonstration followed North Korea’s “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026” exhibition, where Kim called for the country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology, Reuters reported, citing KCNA. Tactical suicide drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and a battalion of 600 mm multiple rocket launchers took part. Other targets in the drill were built to resemble South Korean Army guard posts along the Demilitarized Zone and K9 self-propelled howitzers, the open-source account Korea Defense Blog noted in a post.
Exhibition photos show Kim leaning in to inspect a row of the same type of drone, mounted on stands with serial numbers on their fuselages, which suggests the system has moved beyond a single prototype.
The layout matches UVision’s Hero family: a long tube-shaped body, tandem cruciform wings and a propeller at the rear, a design that lets the munition fold into a launch canister and loiter before diving onto a target. The Hero-400EC, the larger long-range version, weighs about 40 kg (88 pounds) at takeoff, carries a 10 kg (22-pound) warhead and can stay airborne for up to two hours, according to the company. Photos alone cannot show whether North Korea’s drone matches that size or performance, or how it is guided onto its target.
North Korea has shown similar designs before. When Kim toured drone factories in September, state media photos revealed a one-way attack drone resembling Israeli loitering munitions on an assembly line, alongside airframes matching the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9 reconnaissance and strike drones, which copy the look of the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-9 Reaper.
The choice of target stands out because the design North Korea appears to have copied is in American service. The U.S. Marine Corps has used the Hero-400, and in 2025 the U.S. Army awarded UVision’s U.S. partner Mistral a $982 million contract for loitering munitions. U.S. Army armored units rotating through South Korea operate the M1 Abrams.
Loitering munitions attack from above, where tank armor is thinnest, and both Russia and Ukraine have used them in large numbers against armored vehicles. South Korea’s military said North Korea fired around 10 projectiles on Oct. 29, including short-range ballistic missiles, from the Wonsan area during the same demonstration.

Agricultural drones make first flights in Estonia as rules start to ease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:11:00 UTC
19:11:00 KST

Agricultural drones make first flights in Estonia as rules start to ease
Agricultural drones capable of crop-spraying and seeding are making their first flights in Estonia, though strict safety rules still limit wider use.
Simpler survey drones have been in use by Estonian farmers for several years already, to gather field data. From this week, the law permits the aerial spraying of plant protection products, though under strict conditions.
Farmers have been trained at a Rural Knowledge Center (METK) open day at the Nurmsi drone center in Järva County on Thursday, learning to use drones for field monitoring as well as for sowing and weed control.
"Weed infestation, sowing errors, drainage system failures — a great deal of different information. Together with the Rural Knowledge Center, we are currently learning spectral analysis, how to analyze the light reflected from plants by spectral bands," said Madis Pruus, agronomist at Järva County-based agricultural concern Väätsa Agro.
That analysis reveals the health of a given crop. Väätsa Agro has been using simpler and lower-cost drones for six years now, to gather information from fields. This helps in making production decisions.
METK estimates that drones are still not a regularly used tool in day-to-day Estonian agriculture, even as they can perform about a dozen different tasks.
"A drone allows precision farming techniques, variable-rate work cards or spot treatments only," said Ainar Härm, drone technology engineer at METK. For example, if there is a patch of thistles in the middle of a field, only that patch can be treated. "We don't have to go and treat the whole field," he added.
Drones have other advantages too, for instance being lightweight or, since they are airborne, not leaving much of a footprint at all, unlike heavy agricultural plant.
"Since an agricultural drone is light and doesn't flatten down the field, you can work field edges in spring when the fields are soft. You can fertilize and spread seeds," said Anti Konsap, senior engineer at METK.
The main obstacle so far to wider use has been strict restrictions on drone flying, though the situation is gradually improving, experts say.
"From yesterday the law permits the use of plant protection products for aerial spraying, but according to special conditions. It is very important to remember that the product itself must also be approved for aerial use. To my knowledge that list is still extremely short," said Taavi Võsa, researcher in agro-technology at METK.
Farmers who attended the open day said that although drones may turn into an efficient aid, they will fully replace neither the tractor nor the farmer at any time soon.

Ukrainian forces ‘hunt down’ and kill Russian nuclear plant worker
A Ukrainian drone strike has killed a worker while he was traveling to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, the Russian facility’s management reported on Friday morning.
The statement described Thursday’s attack as “barbarism” and part of a “hunt” targeting plant personnel.
“Strikes such as this one not only affect particular people. They are designed to intimidate plant workers, seed panic and tensions among those who ensure the atomic site operates safely every day,” it said.
Russia’s nuclear energy agency Rosatom mourned the death of the worker, who was employed as a welder and was traveling to work on an e-scooter when he was targeted.
The incident was first reported on Thursday by Maksim Pukhov, the mayor of the city of Energodar, near which the Zaporozhye NPP is located. He identified the victim as a man in his early 40s but did not mention his connection to the plant.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) condemned the incident, saying any attack on the facility is “completely unacceptable” and urging “maximum military restraint” around the Zaporozhye plant.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the UN nuclear watchdog for failing to explicitly blame Ukraine for attacks on Europe’s largest nuclear power plant, including strikes targeting its personnel.
Rosatom head Aleksey Likhachev told an IAEA conference in September that 20 people, including nine plant employees, had been killed since Ukrainian forces intensified drone and artillery strikes against the facility in late April.
Among the victims were chief engineer Aleksandr Yakovlev and driver Dmitry Filippov, who were killed in July when a drone struck a car carrying the senior employee.
Russian management took control of the Zaporozhye NPP in 2022. Residents of Zaporozhye Region voted to join Russia in a referendum later that year, which Kiev rejected as a “sham” vote. The IAEA established a permanent on-site observer mission at the plant in September 2022.

Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Likud of attempting to undermine the legitimacy of Israel's election results, while Yair Lapid urged the public to remain patient as negotiations to form the next government continued behind the scenes.
The statements came amid uncertainty over the composition of the next government following Tuesday's election, with neither political bloc securing a clear majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Meanwhile, leaders of the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu held meetings on Thursday in several configurations, some involving the Ra'am party. Democrats chairman Yair Golan met separately with Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas, Eisenkot, and Lapid, while B'Yachad party chairman Naftali Bennett held meetings with Eisenkot and Golan.
Meetings also took place within Netanyahu's bloc. Otzma Yehudit said party chairman and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir held a lengthy meeting with Netanyahu on Thursday, during which the two discussed "how to preserve the right-wing government and prevent the establishment of a left-wing government supported by supporters of terrorism."
Netanyahu also met with Religious Zionist Party chairman Bezalel Smotrich on Thursday for what was described as "coordination of steps."
Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of undermining election results
Eisenkot also addressed suspicions of foreign interference in the elections following meetings with the head of the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and the chairman of the Central Elections Committee.
He said it was too early to determine whether such interference had occurred and stressed that the relevant professional authorities must be allowed to complete their investigations without political involvement.
At the same time, he accused Netanyahu and Likud of conducting a coordinated campaign to delegitimize the election results and said he would not allow any deviation from the planned timetable for the swearing-in of the Knesset.
Eisenkot also announced that his teams were preparing several bills to be submitted when the Knesset convenes, including legislation establishing military recruitment and national service requirements for all Israeli citizens, the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre, and changes to the budget allocation mechanism.
He pledged to continue acting with determination while calling on the public to show restraint and patience.
Lapid urges patience as coalition negotiations continue
Meanwhile, Lapid issued a statement addressing the disappointment that neither political bloc had secured a clear majority of 61 Knesset seats.
He argued that although the election had not produced a decisive outcome, the results nevertheless represented a victory for Netanyahu's opponents.
Lapid pointed to the high voter turnout, which he said reached 77.7%, and argued that Netanyahu had no way to form a government based on the election results.
However, he acknowledged that forming an alternative government would also be a complicated task, with no guarantee of success.
In his statement, Lapid urged the public not to expect constant updates about the political negotiations, explaining that forming a government requires prolonged, discreet work.
He compared the negotiations to the work of a watchmaker, carefully assembling gears until the mechanism begins to function.
Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas reaches out to Joint List leaders
Ra'am chairman Dr. Mansour Abbas initiated phone calls with his counterparts Yousef Jabareen, head of the Joint List and Hadash, Ahmad Tibi, head of the Joint List and Ta'al, and Sami Abu Shehadeh, head of the Balad party.
Abbas congratulated the party leaders and Knesset members of the Joint List on the election results, emphasizing the significant responsibility placed upon all Arab MKs in the upcoming period. The three leaders, for their part, congratulated the United Arab List and its MKs, expressing their appreciation for the immense public trust they received.
Abbas called for strengthening cooperation, coordination, and the integration of roles between the United Arab List and the Joint List in order to serve the interests of the Arab community and the aspirations of both slates' voters, in light of the high voter turnout and the unprecedented number of votes they garnered.
The discussions also addressed the election results, the political landscape in the incoming Knesset, and opportunities for forming an alternative government to the Netanyahu–Ben-Gvir–Smotrich coalition. Both sides agreed to maintain direct communication and coordination in the coming period.

Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

Democrats have long known heartbreak in Texas. Could this finally be their year?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:06:43 UTC
19:06:43 KST

Democrats have long known heartbreak in Texas. Could this finally be their year?
FORT WORTH, Texas, Oct 30 - Texas has been the Democratic Party’s great, unrealized hope for three decades: a vast and fast-changing state that often seems within reach, only to slip away.
On the eve of a midterm election that could decide control of the US Senate, Democrats are dreaming again about breaking the Republican stranglehold on the Lone Star State, even as they brace for heartbreak.
Most polls show Democrat James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative, seminarian and former schoolteacher, narrowly ahead of Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. In the governor's race, Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa is trailing three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott by just a few points.
No Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, the longest drought in the nation. Ending it would reverberate far beyond this state of 31 million people, redrawing America’s political map ahead of a wide-open contest for the presidency in 2028.
“This is the most competitive election between the parties that we have seen here since the early stages of Republican hegemony,” said James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin (UT). “If Talarico or Hinojosa win, it’s a political earthquake.”
For the first time since 1972, Democrats are contesting every state and federal race, testament to a party that says it is investing in its future rather than just individual candidates.
Interviews with more than 40 voters, activists and organizers on both sides of the partisan divide revealed three potential cracks in the Republican coalition -- Latinos jolted by President Donald Trump’s immigration raids; conservative women uneasy about Paxton’s alleged marital infidelity and, to a lesser degree, Republican men squeezed by rising prices and the war with Iran.
Tyson Jex, 33, a suburban father of three, has always voted a straight Republican ticket. This year he’s undecided.
“We have conservative people in power, but it doesn’t seem like anything changes,” he said.
TWO PLAYBOOKS
Many Texas Republicans remain confident in their chances on November 3, believing the political fundamentals are still in their favor.
About 49% of Texas voters identify with or lean toward the Republican Party, compared with 40% for Democrats, according to UT polling.
Then there's the money: Republicans have spent over $300 million on ads supporting Paxton, dwarfing the $102 million spent for Talarico, according to FEC data.
Dave Carney, Abbott’s chief strategist and a veteran of Republican campaigns in Texas, added that the party’s ground game is peaking late by design. “We’re going to win, absolutely," he said, referring to both Republican candidates.
For their part, Talarico and Hinojosa have focused relentlessly on the cost of living and the outsize political influence of billionaires like Elon Musk, who poured nearly $160 million into Texas to buoy Paxton.
“We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” Talarico said at a rally in the city of Temple last week to thunderous applause.
Republicans, meanwhile, have leaned into culture-war issues. In ads, Paxton has hammered Talarico over his support for transgender rights and branded him a heretic for his progressive Christianity.
Rallying for Paxton last week at a brewery in the small town of Sanger, just north of Dallas, speakers riled up a raucous crowd by painting Talarico as a radical leftist and describing the election stakes as existential.
“If we lose one race this cycle, Texas will be a battleground state for the rest of our natural lives,” warned state Representative Andy Hopper.
Neither the Paxton nor the Talarico campaign made its candidates available for an interview.
LATINO BACKLASH
Tarrant County, home to the city of Fort Worth, is the most conservative of Texas’ big urban counties and is seen as a bellwether. In the 2020 presidential race, Joe Biden was the first Democrat to carry it since Lyndon Johnson in 1964, winning by less than 2,000 votes; Trump easily won it back in 2024.
The challenges facing Republicans among Latinos and women voters come into focus here.
Latinos helped deliver Texas to Trump in 2024, giving him 55% of their votes in a dramatic swing away from Democrats, according to exit polling.
Now, their enthusiasm is surging in the opposite direction. Among likely Latino voters, Talarico leads 54% to 41% and Hinojosa 56% to 42%, UT polling shows.
About 1.56 million Latinos had cast ballots as of Wednesday, nearly double the number who had voted at the same point in 2022's midterms, according to TargetSmart, a data firm that works mainly with Democrats.
Latinos make up roughly 28% of early voters, up from 20% at the same time four years ago, the data shows, while white, rural turnout is lagging significantly behind 2022 levels.
“Higher Latino turnout is almost certainly going to be good for the Democratic candidates,” said Tom Bonier, a senior adviser at the firm.
While Hispanics account for nearly a third of Texas’ eligible voters, their 2024 turnout trailed that of non-Latino whites by more than 20 points, according to the Census Bureau.
This year feels different for people like Rick Arredondo, a 52-year-old welder in Fort Worth’s heavily Latino northside. He rolled up to a polling station on his bike last week, eager to vote for the first time in his life.
He said he would cast his ballot for Democrats after immigration agents detained and deported his neighbor.
“Anybody that’s my skin color is fair game,” said Arredondo, a US-born citizen who now carries his passport for fear of being swept up in a raid. “Politics finally reached me in my little corner of the world.”
Down the street, Vanessa Dalay, 23, said she had skipped past elections but wouldn’t make the same mistake again.
“The deportations have radicalized me,” she said.
For Carlos Ronquillo, a 35-year-old house painter who voted for Trump in 2024, his anger over the raids has been compounded by economic struggle.
“I’ve got a diesel truck and I’m spending over $200 to fill it up,” Ronquillo said while getting a tire fixed at a Fort Worth shop. “That’s bad enough. But then you have ICE taking everybody, not just the criminals they said they would.”
Chuck Rocha, a Democratic strategist advising the Talarico and Hinojosa campaigns, said that in focus groups that many Latinos still back closing the border and deporting lawbreakers.
“But none of us signed up for (ICE) to be in our community, picking up our cousins and our aunts and uncles,” he said.
TROUBLE AT HOME
Republican organizers say a different issue is troubling women voters, one particular to Paxton, who beat incumbent John Cornyn in the party primary with Trump’s backing.
Paxton’s wife, state Senator Angela Paxton, filed for divorce last year on “biblical grounds,” accusing him of adultery. Paxton has declined to discuss the matter publicly.
Jill Tate is president of the Texas Federation of Republican Women, a grassroots group with more than 10,000 members in 160 clubs. She estimates about 40% of the conservative women her members are talking to have doubts about Paxton because of his marital problems.
“I’ve never seen us have to work quite so hard to win in my 30 years,” Tate said while canvassing in Allen, a deeply conservative suburb of Dallas.
Lauren Stewart, a 25-year-old Republican in Temple, said her religious upbringing made it hard to overcome her reservations about Paxton.
“I might skip voting in that race,” Stewart said. "I’ve heard that from a lot of my friends, too.”
Among likely Republican voters, 71% of men view Paxton favorably, compared with just 59% of Republican women, UT polling shows.
That might not matter in a typical year. But with polls showing Democrats more energized, it could be crucial.
“This is an election where small increments of voters matter,” Henson said. REUTERS

Toxic online subcultures fuelling Asia’s school attacks
Security experts urge vigilance as teenagers across Southeast Asia turn to radical online networks that celebrate notorious mass murderers
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Recent school attacks across Malaysia have shone a light on a troubling trend of teenagers joining an online subculture that glamorises real-life killers, according to a prominent security analyst.
Three violent incidents in Malaysian schools – in Kuching on October 21, Banting in July and Bandar Utama in October last year – could be linked to the True Crime Community (TCC), said Munira Mustaffa, founder of Kuala Lumpur-based security consulting firm Chasseur Group.
In the Kuching case, the suspect live-streamed an axe attack on a teacher, while a female student who stabbed her schoolmate in Banting flashed an “OK” hand gesture in a TikTok video posted before the assault.
The TCC subculture typically glorifies serial killers and mass murderers – such as the 1999 Columbine High School massacre in the United States – while instilling a narrative among members that the world is cruel towards them. Adam Lanza, who murdered 26 people at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, had reportedly taken part in similar online communities before the killings.

Seven governor races to watch as voters weigh Trump, economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:06:27 UTC
19:06:27 KST

Seven governor races to watch as voters weigh Trump, economy
NEW YORK, Oct 30 - Three dozen governors' races will be decided in the November 3 elections, with President Donald Trump's unpopularity and the cost of living at the top of voters' minds, alongside local concerns ranging from water rights and data centers to cancer rates.
Some races have turned ugly, including an Ohio contest between Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton that features the Democrat's estranged mother in an attack ad. Others could be history-making, such as Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms' bid to become the country's first Black woman elected governor.
Democrats now hold 24 governorships and Republicans 26. If Democrats can manage a net gain of at least two seats they will lead a majority of states for the first time since 2010.
Here are seven key governor races to watch:
ARIZONA
Water has become a key campaign issue in drought-hit Arizona, where Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs is seeking reelection against Republican US Representative Andy Biggs. Other top issues are cost of living and immigration, with Hobbs seeking to position herself as tougher on border security than many national Democrats.
Biggs is a former head of the right-wing US House Freedom Caucus, which has pushed for deep cuts in federal spending.
Abortion rights have featured prominently in the race, with Hobbs a supporter while Biggs has a long record as an opponent. Arizona voters approved a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights in 2024.
MICHIGAN
Michigan's race is one of the most competitive gubernatorial contests, pitting Democrat Jocelyn Benson, the state's top election official, against Republican US Representative John James. The candidates are battling to succeed term-limited Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer, making it one of 19 open-seat races this cycle.
Michigan is a closely divided swing state that Trump won in 2016 and 2024, while Democrat Joe Biden carried it in 2020. Neither party has elected back-to-back governors in the state since the 1960s.
GEORGIA
Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, is running against Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, to succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp. A Bottoms win would make her the first Black woman elected governor in the US and the first Democrat elected governor of Georgia in more than a quarter century.
Because Georgia will likely be a key presidential battleground in 2028, both parties view the gubernatorial race as an early test of voter sentiment.
Jackson, who has spent more than $100 million of his own money on the race, has generally aligned himself with Trump's agenda, while Bottoms has sought to mobilize the diverse Democratic coalition that helped Biden win the state in 2020.
Bottoms rose to national prominence in 2020 as she guided Georgia's largest city through protests, civil unrest and the COVID pandemic. Her base is in the Atlanta metro area, whose rapid growth has reshaped Georgia politics.
OHIO
The race between Republican entrepreneur Ramaswamy and Democrat Acton, a physician, drew national attention over an explosive attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother. In a video run by the Ramaswamy campaign, Donna Arthur disputes Acton's account of a childhood marked by homelessness and sexual abuse and urges Ohioans not to vote for her.
Acton, a former director of the Ohio Department of Health who led the state’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, has said she was sexually abused by her stepfather. The stepfather, who died in 2004, fled the state after he was charged with raping his stepdaughter and never stood trial.
The state's reputation as a perennial swing state faded after 2016 when Trump won it with strong support from working-class voters, who helped to turn it into a reliably Republican state. The race is being watched as a test of whether Democrats can turn economic dissatisfaction into votes. Democrats have won just one of the state’s last nine gubernatorial elections.
IOWA
Iowa is holding its first open governor's race since 2006, after Republican Governor Kim Reynolds said she would not seek reelection. State Auditor Rob Sand, the only Iowa Democrat currently holding statewide elected office, faces Republican businessman Zach Lahn.
The state's incidence of cancer, at the second-highest rate in the country behind Kentucky, has emerged as a major campaign topic alongside kitchen-table issues such as the cost of living. Interest has been fueled by worries that exposure to nitrates, pesticides and other environmental contaminants may be contributing to the high cancer rate.
The race has also focused on education and government accountability. Sand has campaigned as an independent watchdog critical of Republican fiscal management and the state's private-school voucher program.
Lahn has embraced lower taxes, school choice and a more conservative approach to social issues.
NEVADA
In a contest centered on affordability, Republican Governor Joe Lombardo is in a neck-and-neck race with Democratic challenger Aaron Ford, the state’s attorney general.
Nevada residents have voiced concerns over tariffs, a tourism slowdown and high gas prices, giving Ford an opening to defeat Lombardo despite the incumbent's 2-1 fundraising advantage.
Data centers have also emerged as a central campaign issue. Ford has proposed a halt to new data-center tax abatements and wants to require that developers shield residents from higher energy costs. He has also called for strong regulations to protect jobs from AI.
Lombardo, while imposing new restrictions on some of the tax incentives that lured the industry to the state, has generally championed data centers as an economic driver.
WISCONSIN
A central question in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race is whether voters, who backed Trump in 2024 and Biden in 2020, want a governor aligned with the Republican president. Republican Tom Tiffany, a three-term US Representative endorsed by Trump, has played down that connection. His Democratic opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, has sought to link Tiffany to Trump's agenda.
In Congress, Tiffany has supported conservative causes such as gun rights and lower taxes, and co-sponsored federal legislation that would have banned most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy. Crowley supports abortion rights and has framed reproductive rights as a key campaign issue. Wisconsin bans abortion after 20 weeks and requires a 24-hour waiting period as well as parental consent for minors. REUTERS

Seven Rotterdam police officers to face trial over arrest death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Seven Rotterdam police officers to face trial over arrest death
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Seven police officers will go on trial in January next year over the death of a 32-year-old man who was held in a “prone position” on the ground for a long time after being tasered during an arrest in Rotterdam in 2023, the public prosecution department (OM) said on Thursday.
Two officers chased the man on June 9 that year, first in a police van and then on foot, after reports that he had crashed his bicycle into a car and then cycled on.
When he ignored their instructions, one officer used a taser, but it did not incapacitate him or stop him from further resisting. More officers arrived and several of them pinned him down. Soon after he became unwell and was given CPR but died in hospital.
In February 2024 the OM said it would prosecute eight officers after an investigation by the Rijksrecherche, which investigates the police. A pathologist concluded the man’s death could have been caused by the way he was restrained.
The officers are accused of breaching the rules on the use of force with fatal consequences, which has been a criminal offence in its own right since July 2022.
The OM said on Thursday it had dropped a case against an eighth officer, as he was still in training and was following instructions.
The case will be heard on January 19 and from February 15 to 18 by the Blauwe Kamer, a special court in Utrecht that handles cases against police officers. The court will rule on all seven cases at the same time.
In September another Rotterdam man, Alfredo Goeloe (51), died during an arrest after collapsing while officers held him on the ground. That incident led to protests in the city. The Rijksrecherche is investigating his death as well.

Five compulsory board papers, optional skill subject as safety net: CBSE clarifies Class X scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:05:47 UTC
19:05:47 KST

NEW DELHI: Students currently in Class IX will have five compulsory papers in their CBSE Class X board examinations in 2028, with the option of taking an additional skill paper that can help them clear the examination even if they fail in mathematics, science or social science. Clarifying the examination structure well in advance, CBSE on Thursday outlined two pathways for vocational education, allowing students to choose between school-based assessment and a board examination leading to a nationally recognised skill certification.The clarification applies specifically to students studying in Class IX in 2026-27, who will appear for their Class X board examinations in 2028. It does not affect the current Class X batch."The circular is intended to provide clarity to the current batch of Class IX students as they progress to Class X. Our foremost priority is to safeguard students’ interests by clearly communicating the academic and examination-related provisions well in advance. The emphasis is on encouraging students to focus on meaningful learning rather than solely the examinations," CBSE sources said.Under the scheme, the five compulsory board-exam subjects will be two languages, mathematics, science and social science.
Students will, however, study nine compulsory curricular subjects, including a third language, art education, physical education and well-being, and vocational education.While vocational education remains compulsory, students can choose between Kaushal Vikas and any one of 22 notified skill subjects.Those opting for Kaushal Vikas will undergo school-based internal assessment and receive a school certificate on securing at least 33% marks. They will not be required to appear for a board examination in the subject.Alternatively, students can opt for any of the 22 skill subjects, including artificial intelligence, data science, information technology, financial markets, healthcare and design thinking. These will require a Class X board examination, with successful students receiving certification under the National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF).
The distinction assumes significance because students opting for a board-examined skill subject will have an additional safeguard. If they fail in any one of mathematics, science or social science but pass their skill subject, the latter can replace the failed subject while computing their Class X result. This benefit will not be available to those choosing Kaushal Vikas.The circular also clarifies that the specified interdisciplinary components and CT&AI modules will not form part of the prescribed scheme for this particular batch, in keeping with the implementation schedule. This does not amount to discontinuation of CBSE's broader AI education initiative.Students will continue to have options for advanced mathematics, advanced science and other additional subjects under the prescribed examination provisions.

What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:04:35 UTC
19:04:35 KST

What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza?
More than 25 dockworkers’ trade unions in at least 110 ports in 22 countries are going on strike on October 30.
Dock and port workers have long had a tradition of solidarity with the oppressed, upheld by strong labour unions and workers’ rights.
In February 2025, nearly a year and a half into Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, dockworkers’ unions from Mediterranean countries came together to disrupt weapons shipments to Israel and Western countries’ military support of the onslaught.
“Weapons need transport, infrastructure, and workers’ hands to reach their destination,” Markos Bekris, leader of Greece’s dockworkers’ union, ENEDEP, at the Port of Piraeus in Athens, told Al Jazeera. “That is where our power lies.”
Now, dock and port workers in 22 countries across five continents are holding a strike on Friday, which workers and researchers told Al Jazeera is expected to be “historic” in scale. The International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers – also called “Dockworkers do not work for war” – involves 110 ports and 25 trade unions.
“Every union will do what they choose, but be connected to the same principles and struggle,” Francesco Staccioli, the national secretary of transport and ports in Italy’s USB trade union, told Al Jazeera.
The unions’ main demand is “an immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and all imperialist wars”.
Mohammed al-Attar, a dockworker who left Gaza in 2015 and is now based in Hamburg, Germany, said the workers “are the power”.
“We can save thousands of lives if we stop working just for two days,” he said.
Al-Attar feels hopeful about the global strike, but is “deeply disappointed” in his trade union Ver.di in Germany, which he accused of “incomprehensible silence” over Gaza.
What is the International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers?
In early 2025, dockworkers in the Mediterranean area came together to discuss how to concretely act “against privatisation, and against the genocide in Palestine”.
The original meeting included five unions organising in 20 ports across five countries, but continued to grow. The unions met several times, first in Athens, then in Genoa, and later in Istanbul. That was where unions from more than 35 ports published the Istanbul Declaration in May this year, and declared October 30 as their day of action.
In a statement, the unions called for the “recognition of an independent Palestinian state, recognised by the international community, within the 1967 borders and with East Jerusalem as its capital”, and “an end to the US-Israeli wars of aggression in the Middle East and against Iran, and full solidarity with the peoples of Cuba, Venezuela and Sudan”.
“Refusing the war is giving humanity a chance to live better. This is what I’m really convinced about,” the USB’s Staccioli told Al Jazeera.
How many ports and unions are taking part?
More than 25 dockworkers’ trade unions, representing more than 110 ports in 22 countries and regions across five continents, are taking part. Most of the strikes will happen at regular working hours, but in France, Italy, India, Greece and Turkiye, 24-hour strikes have been called.
Strikes of up to two hours have also been announced in Morocco, Cyprus and other ports.
Organisers told Al Jazeera that workers and trade unions from other sectors have been called on to join with port workers, notably in Greece, while in Italy the USB has called for a general strike.
“It’s bigger than we thought,” Staccioli said. “This has spread all over the world.”
No Harbour for Genocide (NHG), a campaigning collective that researches weapon supply chains, supports the action. A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that maritime infrastructure was important in “facilitating military trade within the context of the genocide in Palestine”.
Dockworker unions in India, Sweden, Denmark, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Uruguay and the west coast of the United States have all pledged to take part, the spokesperson added.
The Palestinian labour movement endorsed the strike and called on more to join, urging unions to “escalate Boycott, Divest, Sanctions (BDS) pressure to end all state, corporate and institutional complicity in Israel’s illegal occupation, apartheid and genocide.”
How are these ports involved in wars?
Of the ports participating, Genoa, Livorno and Gioia Tauro in Italy, Marseille in France, Piraeus in Greece, and Tangier in Morocco all have proven links to weapons shipments to Israel, according to No Harbour for Genocide.
The group said that between August 2025 and September 2026 it tracked 315 shipments of components for Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, moving through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries. All these 56 ports are expected to be on strike on October 30 , representing a major disruption, even if only for a day.
NHG said it expects that more than $2bn worth of cargo will sit idle on October 30 .
“Up to 95 percent of Israel’s imports and exports travel by sea, relying on port infrastructure across the Mediterranean,” the campaign’s spokesperson said. “Tangier, Piraeus, Gioia Tauro and Genoa, where the largest vessels unload containers onto smaller ships for the rest of the sea, are a few of the Mediterranean’s most frequently used transshipment hubs. All four are taking part on Friday.”
“The participating Mediterranean ports handle 63 percent of all container activity in the sea,” the spokesperson added, noting that “between southern France and Piraeus, the striking ports hold 74 percent of container activity. Worldwide, the ports taking part [in the strike] handle 13.5 percent of global shipping.”
Linda Maggiore, an Italian journalist and activist, said that she has discovered several examples of increasing weapons shipments from Italy’s major ports to Israel since the start of the war on Gaza.
“In Europe, a regulation on military mobility is about to be approved, which will make it even easier for arms to be transferred without scrutiny,” Maggiore told Al Jazeera. “Blockades are essential actions, because they make it clear that civil society does not wish to be complicit.”
From the Vietnam war to Iraq, the USB’s Staccioli said that “dockworkers have a long tradition of rallying against any imperialist war or aggression in the world.”
Are protest actions prosecuted?
In Greece, union leader Bekris is facing prosecution for a protest in which he and other workers blocked the loading of a container holding 21 tonnes of ammunition destined for Israel in October 2024.
“We carry forward the tradition of workers who refuse to load weapons against other people,” Bekris told Al Jazeera on the eve of the global strike. “Our hands get covered in grease and sweat every day. We refuse to let them be stained with the blood of other people.”

The administration of US President Donald Trump is pressing Lithuania to allow Belarusian potash fertiliser exports through the port of Klaipeda despite European Union sanctions, Politico reported, citing European officials.
US special envoy to Belarus John Coale has in recent weeks asked Lithuanian diplomats about ways to ease restrictions on the shipment of goods from Belarus, according to four European officials familiar with the discussions.
The restrictions are part of EU sanctions against the government of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko. EU ports are prohibited from handling Belarusian goods, and the sanctions must be renewed annually.
Trump said last month that he was working on a “big deal” with Minsk to buy potash fertiliser at prices significantly lower than those currently paid by farmers to Canadian suppliers. Such an arrangement would require a route through Klaipėda, Lithuania’s main Baltic Sea port, or other regional ports.
“There has been intensified outreach to the Lithuanians by Donald Trump’s team in the last weeks,” a source familiar with the discussions told Politico.
The US State Department did not respond to a request for comment.
The administration’s interest in Belarusian potash, which accounts for about 20% of the global market, has grown following the collapse of US-Canadian trade negotiations in August and subsequent tariff increases, Politico reported.
The push is part of Trump’s broader efforts to ease sanctions on Russia and its allies in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine. However, the approach has faced strong opposition in Europe.
“They are pressing politely, but we say very clearly ‘fuck no’,” one Eastern European official told Politico.
Two Eastern European officials said Coale had been lobbying Lithuanian authorities at various levels for more than a year. Washington has also explored the possibility of shipping Belarusian potash through Latvia’s Riga port, which could offer a simpler route than transportation through Russia.
Lithuania has repeatedly rejected the possibility of resuming transit.
Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has said EU sanctions prohibit not only imports of Belarusian potash but also its transit through EU territory, regardless of the ownership of the fertiliser or the country in which the exporting company is registered.
The Lithuanian president’s national security adviser Deividas Matulionis has also warned that violating the sanctions would carry legal, financial and moral consequences.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in September that Lithuania had received no US request to allow Belarusian fertiliser transit. Former Prime Minister and opposition politician Ingrida Šimonytė has likewise argued that such shipments would be incompatible with EU sanctions and pose national security risks.

herzog & de meuron to convert former birkenstock warehouse into the eames institute museum

herzog & de meuron to convert former birkenstock warehouse into the eames institute museum
beneath a sculptural concrete roof, a mid-century campus in novato, california, will house exhibitions, workshops, and public gardens, with a museum opening targeted for 2030.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
HERZOG & DE MEURON REVEALS EAMES INSTITUTE MUSEUM PLANS
A warehouse with a roof this expressive already has something to exhibit. In Novato, California, Herzog & de Meuron is reworking the former Birkenstock campus into the future museum of the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity, preserving its sculptural concrete silhouette while changing what happens beneath it. Newly released renderings show the proposal taking shape with San Francisco practice EHDD as executive architect and Field Operations designing the landscape. Across an approximately 88-acre site, the project brings exhibition spaces, workshops, a theater, and gardens into a cultural destination whose ambitions extend beyond the work of Charles and Ray Eames.
The existing campus was designed for publisher McGraw-Hill by Jan Lubicz-Nycz for the office of John Savage Bolles, before becoming associated with Birkenstock. Its most recognizable element is a roof assembled from repeated hyperbolic paraboloid shells, developed with structural engineer Raj Desai. These curved surfaces use geometry to span large distances with remarkably little material, producing a sequence of pointed edges that gives the industrial building its unexpected drama. Retaining this structure makes the museum itself an example of design ingenuity: visitors will encounter an experiment in construction before reaching the first exhibition.
A REFLECTIVE BRIDGE REFRAMES THE CONCRETE WAREHOUSE
Herzog & de Meuron organizes the interior around a generous central hall, keeping the roof’s geometry visible overhead. An entrance court cut into an existing earth berm establishes the approach, while a steel-clad bridge introduces an elevated route through the building. Its reflective finish will catch fragments of the surrounding space, setting a visually shifting surface against the weight of the concrete canopy. Below, circulation routes connect exhibitions with places to gather and work. Building services and lighting will be integrated into the ceiling to reduce the visual clutter beneath its peaks.
The museum’s program gives visitors opportunities to see how things are made alongside the finished works. Studios and workshops for wood and ceramics sit within an arrangement of flexible exhibition spaces, allowing creative activity to become part of the visit. This approach also informs the broader collecting strategy, which encompasses industrial design, painting, sculpture, and other disciplines. The Eames legacy provides a point of departure for a museum interested in experimentation across generations, with space for the practical, occasionally messy business that precedes an object’s arrival on a pedestal.
FIELD OPERATIONS BRINGS THE EAMES MUSEUM INTO THE LANDSCAPE
At the building’s northern and southern edges, recessed glass façades create deep covered areas between the interiors and gardens. These sheltered thresholds extend the possibilities for exhibitions and everyday use, while former loading zones become places to spend time outdoors. Field Operations connects ten gardens through paths, introducing native species including oak, manzanita, and California poppy. Planting draws on the region’s different habitats, from woodland to coastal prairie, giving the grounds a character rooted in Marin County rather than treating them as a uniform backdrop.
Outdoor sculpture, places to play, and areas for communal events will share this landscape with quieter spaces for sitting and walking. The proposal allows a museum visit to unfold across different settings and at different speeds, from a workshop or performance to an afternoon outside. Following the Institute’s acquisition of the property in 2025, the masterplan has been submitted to the City of Novato. Major construction is intended to begin in 2028, with 2030 set as the target opening year.

Location: Novato, Marin County, California, USA

Naples Airport to close for the whole of November for €30m revamp – here’s what passengers need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:03:26 UTC
19:03:26 KST

The Italian airport will shut for the entire month of November for major runway upgrades, with flights diverted to nearby Salerno and extra bus and taxi services planned to limit disruption.
One of Italy’s busiest airports is set to close to air traffic for the entire month of November.
Naples Airport will shut its doors to allow for extensive renovation work on its runway and connecting taxiways, which will shore up the long-term safety, reliability and operational continuity of the existing infrastructure.
It will also include the replacement and modernisation of the airport’s visual aids lighting (AVL) systems, which include the runway and taxiway lighting and illuminated signalling systems, essential for guiding aircraft during take-off, landing and taxiing, especially in poor visibility.
The project, which will cost around €30 million, is being carried out at a time which typically sees fewer flights than in peak season. To minimise disruption further, the work will be done continuously, for 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
Workaround plans in place to avoid major disruption
For travellers needing to get to the region, some airlines plan to transfer their aircraft to – relatively – nearby Salerno Costa d’Amalfi and Cilento airports.
Flights here are operated by the likes of Ryanair, easyJet and Vueling, and fly to and from Bergamo, Milan Malpensa and Milan Linate, Genoa, Turin and Trieste in Italy.
Further afield, flights will run between the airports and Amsterdam, Barcelona, Casablanca, Dubai, Dusseldorf, Madrid, Paris, Sharm el-Sheikh and Stuttgart.
To handle the strain of Naples Airport’s closure, additional bus services between Naples Piazza Garibaldi and Salerno Airport will operate throughout November.
Services to Salerno railway station are also set to be increased, while existing routes to Potenza, Eboli, Battipaglia and the Amalfi Coast will continue to run as usual.
For those not keen to rely on public transport, a shared taxi service with fixed fares has also been introduced on a trial basis. It will cover two routes, one from Salerno Airport to Naples Central railway station, and the other from Salerno Airport to Salerno Central railway station.

Loss

Human error or system failure? Spain probes deadly train crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:01:23 UTC
19:01:23 KST

Spain’s second major train collision this year has reignited questions over whether human error or systemic failures in its once-praised high-speed rail network are to blame.
The causes remain disputed.
Spain’s transport minister has pointed to a traffic controller’s alleged poor judgment as a key factor in Wednesday’s crash in Toledo province, which claimed 69 lives.
Railway unions, however, reject the focus on individual responsibility, arguing that worsening working conditions have left the network increasingly vulnerable. They cite a shortage of traffic controllers, heavier workloads and mounting pressure on staff responsible for the safety of some 45 million passengers each year.
A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly collision, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has pledged a thorough inquiry to establish what caused the disaster.
"This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened," Spain’s King Felipe VI said Thursday after visiting injured passengers at a hospital in Toledo. "We will have to take measures so this never happens again."
The chain of events that led to the disaster began at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday, when the communication system essential to the line’s safety operations went down. Known as LZB, the system monitors train positions and can automatically activate a train’s brakes to prevent collisions.
The malfunction forced human controllers at a control center in Madrid to assume full responsibility for monitoring train movements and safety along a 63-kilometer (39-mile) stretch between Madrid and Seville. Authorities believe six trains were on the affected section at the time.
At 8:36 a.m., a controller told a train operated by state-owned RENFE that it could resume normal-speed operations. Another train, operated by privately owned IRYO and located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) farther down the line, also attempted to restart, but its engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and notified the controller.
At 8:53 a.m., the trains collided, derailing carriages and leaving parts of the wreckage torn apart.
It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente, who is facing calls to resign, described the controller’s decision to allow one train to resume at full speed while the other remained stopped as "inexplicable" and "erroneous."
Puente said the RENFE train should never have been authorized to move because a stop signal was still active on the line.
"An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision," Puente told reporters. The decision "was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light," he said.
Railway unions, however, argue that the circumstances surrounding the decision cannot be ignored.
Raquel Ayllon, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that workloads regularly exceed what existing staff can safely manage. She said controllers have been calling for additional personnel for years while safety systems continue to fail.
"We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions," she said. "Human error isn't incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing."
SEMAF, Spain’s train engineers union, said the three-decade-old LZB safety system, which remains in use on the Madrid-Seville line as it is gradually phased out, has failed before, leaving human operators to manage train movements without its protection.
"The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago," said Diego Martin, a SEMAF spokesperson. "It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past."
Railway workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand that the government honor its commitments to improve safety conditions following the January crash.
Representatives of several unions also condemned what they described as the "irresponsible" leak of audio recordings of conversations between the control center and train engineers to Spanish media outlets.
Spain’s railways were exclusively operated by state-owned companies until the country opened its high-speed passenger network to private operators in 2021.
Both major crashes this year involved trains operated by RENFE and IRYO.
Rail traffic has increased since the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for example, the average number of daily services rose from 56 in 2019 to 89 in 2024, according to the SCF union.
Joan Rodriguez, a spokesperson for a Spanish railway workers union, said the increase in traffic following privatization had placed additional pressure on the network.
"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodriguez told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Wednesday. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

The world needs the United Nations more than ever. It needs a new lease on life | Alex Rondos and Mark Medish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:52 UTC
19:00:52 KST

To save the United Nations from the irrelevance in which it now wallows, the next secretary general will require the concerted backing of the few powers that govern the security council.
The paradox is that the great powers who created the institution in the 1940s and recently treat it with a cavalier cynicism are now the ones who need it most, as does the rest of the world.
This is not about nostalgia for what was created after the second world war. That world has changed. We are no longer in the cold war. But it is carelessness of high order to assume that some mystical process will create a world while, in the meantime, the most powerful give license to some dangerous pathologies that have brought us to ruin in the past.
The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again. Restraint has given way to calculated recklessness. Changing facts on the ground before talking now creates leverage, and that is why we see an unprecedented multiplication of centers of violence. Militias and mercenaries abound.
Collective security to which all commit to be effective is now supplanted by a petulant isolationism. Revolutionary new technologies have spurred a rush to secure minerals and supply routes upending traditional notions of sovereignty. Drone warfare has made violence much more affordable. Frontiers are now up for grabs.
The permanent members of the security council, anachronistically still composed of the victors of the second world war, have a tall order. Quarrels that are as old as tribes, communities and nations now have new, more lethal weapons.
Civil wars, border wars and the return of imperial ambition are not relics. They drive the war in Ukraine, the drift toward conflict in the Horn of Africa, the instability around the Gulf and the Red Sea, and the standoff over Taiwan.
These conflicts are now multiplying at a scale and speed in a time when global regulatory arrangements over existential threats are denigrated. Proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, pandemics, climate change will either be fueled or managed by artificial intelligence.
As AI is woven into military planning, early warning and command systems, it compresses the time leaders have to think before they act, and it multiplies the tools of deception and destabilization. A world that learned, slowly and at great risk, to live with nuclear weapons must now learn to live with machines that may shape decisions about using them.
These dangers can only be contained if we dispense with some misplaced assumptions.
The first is that the UN is a club of the like-minded. It was never meant to be. The UN exists so that states that distrust or even detest one another have somewhere to meet – a place that offers hospitality to adversaries.
If the hard conversations about war and technology do not happen there, where else will they happen in a way that protects the rest of humanity? It is about co-existence, not convergence.
The second assumption is that power can be evenly distributed. It cannot. Pretending otherwise is idealism to the point of fault. A handful of states possess the disproportionate capacity to contain these dangers or to unleash them. In practice, today this means the United States, China and Russia.
But there is no reason to exclude India or a better-integrated European Union. Even if they do not trust one another, they need only recognize a shared interest in a world that remains manageable.
This harsh reality should temper the fashionable faith in “middle powers”. Their activism is understandable, even admirable: they see the great powers changing character and are trying to respond. But they are called middle powers for a reason. They cannot, on their own, end a major war or govern a technology developed mostly elsewhere.
This does not mean that might makes right. Neither does it mean that complicated times need simple answers which would be a repudiation of politics at the international level. Power checked by reasonable deliberation, negotiation and diplomacy is a core principle that inspired the charter of the United Nations. This moment calls for a rededication to principled pragmatism.
History has much to teach. When the plague swept Europe in the 14th century, the city states of Italy established the practice of quarantines and an early form of health certification. The science may have been wrong and the system imperfect. But it worked well enough, and it rested on self-interest, not virtue.
Since the mid-20th century, in a radically different technological era, nuclear proliferation and the risk of nuclear war have been contained, so far, through a lengthy process of negotiation and agreements.
Imagine a renewed UN that is a problem-solver rather than a bystander, a credible forum rather than a costly talking shop, and the prime instrument for collective action.
None of this happens unless the great powers want it to. Choosing a secretary general is one of the few moments when they must agree on a qualified person and a timely agenda. The superpowers, middle powers and emerging powers of the global south may each have reasons for skepticism. But they share a stronger reason to make this effort.
We need neither “peace in our time” nor “perpetual peace” – but enough peace to keep civilization.
- Alex Rondos is a former envoy of the European Union. Mark Medish is a former senior US national security and treasury official

One casualty of the cuts is the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined.
Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda.
Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that a Labour government will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.”
Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.
Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned.
“It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.”
The cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband.
Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system.
One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”
Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.
“This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.”
Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.”
But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.
One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”
A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.
“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”

- North Korea displayed a new flying-wing stealth drone, FPV quadcopters and loitering munitions at an Oct. 29 exhibition attended by Kim Jong Un.
- Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology, and a firepower demonstration followed using suicide drones, cruise missiles and 600 mm rocket launchers.
North Korea has shown off what appears to be a new large flying-wing stealth drone, along with first-person-view attack quadcopters and loitering munitions, at an exhibition on Oct. 29 where leader Kim Jong Un called for the country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology, state news agency KCNA reported on Oct. 30.
The exhibition, titled “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026,” displayed strategic and tactical multipurpose drones, suicide attack drones and other combat systems, KCNA said. Photos showed drones carrying the emblem of the North Korean Air Force, and Kim attended with his daughter, Ju Ae. North Korea did not release specifications for any of the systems on display or say whether the new aircraft has flown.
The most striking new design was a tailless flying-wing aircraft that North Korean state media showed for the first time, NK News reported. Analysts have compared its overall size to the U.S. Navy’s X-47B demonstrator and Russia’s S-70 Okhotnik, both large jet-powered stealth drones built to fly into defended airspace. A flying-wing shape with no vertical tail is used to reduce an aircraft’s radar signature, but photos alone cannot show what engine, sensors or radar-absorbing materials the North Korean drone uses, or whether it is a working aircraft or a mockup.
The exhibition also featured small FPV quadcopters, the cheap camera-guided attack drones that have become a defining weapon of the war in Ukraine, alongside several drone models North Korea has displayed before. In September, state media showed Kim touring production lines for at least three drone types, including a one-way attack drone resembling Israeli loitering munitions and airframes matching the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9 reconnaissance and strike drones, which resemble the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-9 Reaper.
Kim said pursuing drone superiority was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare, and that putting high-level artificial intelligence into unmanned weapons should be a top priority for the country’s military, KCNA reported. He laid out a defense development plan aimed at rapidly expanding North Korea’s unmanned aviation forces, without giving numbers or a timeline.
A firepower demonstration followed, using tactical suicide drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and a battalion of 600 mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said. South Korea’s military said North Korea fired around 10 projectiles that day, including short-range ballistic missiles, from the Wonsan area on its east coast.
Targets in the demonstration appeared to represent South Korean and U.S. forces. Strike drones and loitering munitions resembling Russia’s Lancet hit practice targets built to look like South Korean Army guard posts in the Demilitarized Zone, K9 self-propelled howitzers and U.S. Army M1 Abrams tanks, the open-source analysis account Korea Defense Blog said in a post, along with fortified defensive positions and a mockup of a counter-battery radar, the kind used to locate enemy artillery. South Korea’s Yonhap-sourced reports likewise described strikes on mock South Korean forward posts and U.S. ground equipment. The same account noted that South Korea’s forward air defense along the DMZ, including the K30 Biho self-propelled anti-aircraft gun, has limited ability to stop small drones.
North Korea has expanded its drone program since its troops fought alongside Russian forces against Ukraine, and South Korean intelligence has said North Korean units may have received training in Russian drone tactics. Kim oversaw tests of AI-equipped suicide and reconnaissance drones in March 2025 and has repeatedly called for mass production.
