Foreign arms firms to pay benefits back into Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:57:58 GMT
18:57:58 KST

Overseas companies winning British defence contracts worth more than £50 million will be required to put benefits back into the country that could match the full value of the contract, through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers and transfers of technology, under an offsets policy published today, according to the government.
A contract worth £100 million could carry an obligation to deliver up to £100 million of new jobs, facilities or skills training in Britain, and a new central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor what each supplier owes through dedicated Offset Agreements.
The policy was announced by the Chancellor and the Defence Secretary on a visit to BAE Systems at Scotstoun in Glasgow, and forms part of the Back British approach set out in the Budget.
John Healey, Chancellor of the Exchequer, said: “We are putting British jobs and British businesses at the heart of how Government spends taxpayers’ money.
“When a big contract goes overseas, these changes will ensure 100% of the value creates new opportunities for workers and businesses here at home, strengthening our industrial base and supporting growth across Britain.”
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. That’s why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can.
“Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry.”
The money at stake is the eleven per cent of departmental spending with industry that goes abroad. More than £35.2 billion has been spent on defence contracts and services with overseas industry since 2016, measured against total direct expenditure with industry and commerce between 2016-17 and 2025-26, while 85 per cent of spending already goes to British firms. Last year defence investment supported 274,000 jobs in British industry, up ten per cent on the year before, with £34.1 billion going to businesses based in Britain.
Companies holding qualifying contracts will be able to meet the obligation by creating British jobs and apprenticeships, opening or expanding factories here, investing in British suppliers, transferring technology and know-how to British firms, or using more British-made components.
Offsets of this kind are standard practice among allies, and the government named Poland, Norway and the Netherlands as countries already running similar schemes. Britain abandoned its own industrial participation requirements more than a decade ago in favour of open competition, so the policy reverses a position held across several governments.
Scotland was chosen for the announcement because the defence economy there is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, with the £10 billion Norwegian order for Type 26 frigates supporting 2,000 local jobs and a £453 million Typhoon radar contract supporting 300 roles in Edinburgh.
The policy delivers commitments from the Defence Investment Plan and the Defence Industrial Strategy, and follows the Chancellor’s confirmation on Wednesday that the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over four years into defence, dual use and other sectors supporting national security, alongside the start of treaty negotiations with the Netherlands, Poland and Finland on a Multilateral Defence Mechanism to procure and stockpile equipment at scale.

Iran’s most decorated para swimmer Izadyar calls time on career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:56:33 UTC
18:56:33 KST

Iran’s most decorated para swimmer Izadyar calls time on career
TEHRAN – Shahin Izadyar, Iran’s most decorated Paralympic swimmer, has announced his retirement from competitive swimming after an illustrious career that saw him claim 28 medals across five editions of the Asian Para Games.
Despite bringing down the curtain on his remarkable career, Izadyar insists his journey in the pool is far from over, revealing plans to return to the sport as a coach in the near future.
In an exclusive interview with the Tehran Times, Izadyar reflected on his achievements, memorable performances and the milestones that shaped his career.
“My first Asian Para Games were in Guangzhou, China, in 2010. I was just 17 years old and managed to win two gold, one silver and three bronze medals, becoming the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation. I also broke the Asian record in both events in which I won gold,” he said.
“In 2012, I competed at the London Paralympics as Iran’s first and only representative in swimming. For the first time in history, an Iranian Para swimmer reached the final of the men’s 100m breaststroke. It was a huge achievement for our sport.”
Izadyar continued his medal-winning run at the 2014 Asian Para Games in Incheon, South Korea, where he collected five silver medals and one bronze.
“Although I delivered some strong performances in Incheon, I couldn't win gold. However, with five silvers and one bronze, I once again became the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation,” he recalled.
Two years later, Izadyar made his second Paralympic appearance at Rio 2016, again carrying Iran’s hopes as the country’s sole representative in Para swimming.
“I reached the 100m breaststroke final once again and clocked an impressive 1:09.63. I also recorded 25.32 seconds in the 50m freestyle, a record that still stands,” he said.
The highlight of Izadyar’s career came at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, where he delivered a sensational performance, capturing six gold medals and one silver.
“Jakarta was my third Asian Para Games, and it was an unforgettable experience. With six gold medals and one silver, I became the most decorated athlete among approximately 3,700 competitors at the Games,” he said.
Although Izadyar missed the Tokyo Paralympics, he returned to the continental stage at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games in 2023, competing at the age of 30.
“In Hangzhou, I won two silver and three bronze medals and once again finished as the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation,” he explained.
Izadyar also represented Iran at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games alongside fellow swimmer Sina Zeighaminejad, but an injury prevented him from reaching the final.
His final competitive appearance came at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya, where he added three silver medals and one bronze to his impressive collection.
“Competing in Nagoya marked my fifth appearance at the Asian Para Games. I won three silver medals and one bronze and once again shared the distinction of being the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation,” Izadyar said.
“That was my final competition, and I decided to say goodbye to competitive swimming. But I hope it won't be long before I return to the pool, this time as a coach, to continue serving the sport I love.”
With 28 Asian Para Games medals and a career spanning multiple Paralympic appearances, Izadyar leaves behind an extraordinary legacy as one of the most successful figures in Iranian Para swimming.

French presidential candidate Édouard Philippe designated 'assisted witness' in embezzlement case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:54:09 UTC
18:54:09 KST

Through his lawyer, Philippe welcomed the decision to have been given assisted witness status, which is less serious than being formally investigated. "This confirms that there is nothing to reproach him for in this case," his lawyer told the AFP news agency.
Former French Prime Minister Édouard Philippe has been placed under the status of assisted witness in an investigation into the alleged misuse of public funds at the Le Havre metropolitan authority.
Philippe, a 2027 presidential candidate for the Horizons party and mayor of Le Havre, appeared before two investigating financial judges on Thursday to answer questions relating to the case.
Following the hearings, Philippe released a statement through his lawyer, Emmanuel Marsigny, welcoming the decision to have been given assisted witness status, which is less serious than being formally investigated.
"This confirms that there is nothing to reproach him for in this case," his lawyer told the AFP news agency.
The case dates back to 2020 following allegations raised by Cornelia Findeisen, a former deputy director general of the Le Havre metropolitan authority.
She subsequently filed two complaints, one in 2023 that led to the opening of a preliminary investigation and searches carried out by the National Financial Prosecutor's Office.
A second complaint, filed two years later, included a request to join the proceedings as a civil party and resulted in the case being referred to financial investigating judges in Paris.
Philippe became president of the Le Havre Seine Métropole authority in July 2020. He later signed a multi-year agreement with Stéphanie de Bazelaire, voluntary president of the LH French Tech association, for running the Cité Numérique innovation hub in Le Havre.
LH French Tech was the only organisation to respond to calls from the authority for expressions of interest. The association was to receive €2.154 million in public funding to carry out various projects.
Investigators are now working to establish whether Philippe and de Bazelaire struck a deal involving "political, financial and networking support in return for the management of the Cité Numérique."
Findeisen said she was sidelined and subjected to harassment after exposing the alleged arrangement. In January last year, she was granted whistleblower status.
Philippe's questioning "shows that my alert deserved to be examined," she has said.
Assisted witness status
The Picovschi law firm says that an assisted witness is an individual "involved in a criminal case whose situation sits between that of a witness and that of a person under formal investigation."
This status can change as a case progresses and as new evidence emerges.
"A person is granted the status of 'assisted witness' when the investigating judge’s case file contains evidence suggesting alleged guilt in relation to an offence," the firm says on its website.
"The assisted witness is implicated in a judicial investigation; however, they are not directly charged with the offence in question."

Irish government to scope out possibility of unity with Northern Ireland for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Irish government to scope out possibility of unity with Northern Ireland for first time
DUBLIN, Oct 30 - Ireland will set up a government body that would for the first time undertake research and preparations for the possibility of future unity with British-run Northern Ireland, Prime Minister Micheal Martin was quoted as saying on Friday.
Martin told the Irish Times that the new body would be tasked with scoping out the models and challenges for different potential outcomes, including Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom or maintaining its devolved entity but as part of a united Ireland.
He was fleshing out an idea first referenced in a speech this week, when he said a new approach was required to carefully address the need for an "independent and dispassionate base of knowledge on which you can have a credible discussion about constitutional futures."
"What has concerned me about this push for a border poll since Brexit is that it's partisan, it's a one-sided advocacy approach," Martin told the Irish Times.
"It's sort of putting forward the idea that this would be easy and that it's inevitable and our time has come. And it's almost that this would be a victory for nationalism, as opposed to an approach which genuinely seeks to hear all voices."
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement, the British government is obliged to call a referendum on Irish unity if it appears likely that a majority of Northern Irish voters would back it.
While opinion polls consistently show a majority in favour of remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed since the UK voted to leave the European Union a decade ago and Irish nationalist parties like Sinn Fein stepped up calls for a referendum.
Martin's proposal, the first steps of which he said he would bring to cabinet before the end of the year, is the latest gradual move by the dominant government parties south of the border to consider what a united Ireland might look like.
His government partner Fine Gael will publish what it has described as a blueprint for a unified island at its annual conference next week. REUTERS

Why is India's dam project near China border facing local opposition?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:58 UTC
18:50:58 KST

India has deployed paramilitary troops in parts of its northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh amid protests against a proposed mega hydropower project near the Chinese border.
The deployment follows a protest last week in the Siang Valley, which borders Tibet, during which four women were injured during a clash with police, according to reports. At least 21 arrests were also made.
The protesters were opposing the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), a proposed 11,200-megawatt project, saying the dam would submerge ancestral villages, destroy farmlands, displace large populations and disrupt livelihoods
Police claimed protesters vandalised police vehicles and pelted stones at security personnel.
What is the project?
First proposed as a national project by the Congress-led government in 2008, the Siang River project has since emerged as one of Arunachal Pradesh’s most contentious infrastructure proposals. The Congress party is now the main opposition party.
The project is considered strategically significant for India, particularly in light of China's plans for a major hydropower project upstream on the same river.
India views the proposed dam as a major water storage facility to regulate river flows and strengthen the country's water and energy security.
In December 2024, China announced plans to construct the world's largest hydropower dam upstream, officially known as the Medog Hydropower Station.
The proposed Chinese project has raised concerns in Arunachal Pradesh, where the state government has described it as an "existential threat."
China and India both claim Arunachal Pradesh, which China refers to as Zangnan and considers part of southern Tibet.
The Siang River flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Zangbo.
Why the protests?
The proposed project, to be developed by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, is located in the Siang Valley, where opposition has largely come from local communities, particularly members of the Adi tribe.
Residents fear the proposed dam could submerge ancestral villages, displace communities and disrupt their way of life.
The Adi Bane Kebang Youth (ABKU), a local grassroots movement, has warned that the dam could submerge several villages and cause extensive losses.
This week, it demanded the immediate release of its workers detained or arrested in connection with the protests.
Former Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Gegong Apang has called for the immediate cancellation of the proposed dam.
In New Delhi, the Congress has linked the protests to a wider movement among young people to protect the "environment and local communities'" rights.
"Gen Z across the country is taking to the streets. In Delhi, it is for education. In Arunachal Pradesh, it is to protect the forests, rivers and ecosystems that the Adi people have depended on for centuries," Congress leader Pawan Khera wrote on X.
Government response
Apart from strengthening security to counter the protests, the Arunachal Pradesh government has attributed growing apprehensions about the project to what it described as "misinformation and misconceptions."
Chief Minister Pema Khandu this week held a meeting with various groups to discuss the project and strengthen efforts to spread awareness across the state.
"Our people deserve accurate information to understand the project, its strategic importance and the concerns associated with it," he said.
At a separate meeting with legislators from different political parties, Khandu said discussions covered national security, environmental concerns and the apprehensions of local residents.
"Our priority is to protect national interests while respecting the rights and aspirations of the people of Siang Valley," he said.
Arunachal Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Chowna Mein recently took to X to explain how India's proposed dam could help address concerns arising from China's planned 60,000-MW hydropower project upstream.
"The answer lies in understanding that MW measures power, not water. The proposed Medog Dam in China is primarily designed for hydropower generation, with an estimated height of around 2,000 metres (2 km) and storage capacity of 5.5 billion cubic metres," he said.
Mein said India's proposed dam, with a height of around 280-300 metres and live storage capacity of approximately 9.2 billion cubic metres, was primarily intended to store, regulate and manage water, alongside generating electricity.
"In the event of sudden releases or extreme flows upstream, this storage can help regulate downstream discharge and reduce the risk of flooding in the Siang basin and downstream areas of Arunachal Pradesh and Assam," he said.

The letters that gave five human rights activists hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:31 UTC
18:50:31 KST

For the past 25 years, Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign has been bringing people together to fight for justice and dignity. Millions of people have changed the lives of those whose human rights had been stripped from them, giving them hope in times of darkness.
Amnesty’s brilliant supporters have written letters both to those whose rights are being violated, and the people in authority who can make change happen.
For many, a simple letter made so much difference, letting them know that there were people out there rooting for them.
Here, five people who were part of Amnesty’s Write for Rights campaign share a letter that meant the most to them…
Wendy Galarza
Wendy Galarza was shot after attending a protest in Cancún, Mexico. She almost lost her life speaking out for women’s rights in her country. She lodged a complaint against the police, though it took months for the State Prosecutor to accept her additional evidence, which included clothing showing bullet holes from the day of the protest. While the case continues, Wendy has set up a collective with other persons who were assaulted that day.
People across the world came together to demand justice and support Wendy in Write for Rights 2021.
“These letters are among my favourites, though it was difficult to choose them from the vast number I received.
“One key reason is the hope I felt knowing my case had reached as far as Taiwan – a place that sent some of the most creative letters, most of which were written by teenagers.
“This particular letter inspired me with its clear message reminding us that ‘no one should face gender-based violence.’ It led me to reflect on the main reason I attended the march on 9 November 2020: to raise my voice and demand justice for the femicide of Bianca Alejandrina Lorenzana Alvarado in Cancún in the State of Quintana Roo.
“I would also like to thank everyone who wrote a letter to show their support; though it may sound like a cliché, those words provided me with emotional strength and became a beacon of hope on a dark path toward justice.”
Germain Rukuki
On 30 June 2021, Burundian human rights defender Germain Rukuki was released from prison four years into a 32-year sentence. He had been found guilty on a number of sham charges relating to his human rights work. He was jailed before getting a chance to hold his youngest child, born just weeks after he was arrested in July 2017.
Through Write for Rights 2020, hundreds of thousands of people around the world demanded Germain’s release.
“I chose this pink letter with the drawing of an elephant, balloons and a little purple heart. But more than the drawings, it was the words that touched me and spoke to me. The phrase ‘you are strong’ immediately takes me back to the moment I was arrested. It was a very difficult moment. I was trying to hold myself together. To leave the house without alarming my family and those around me. Deep down, it felt like a farewell, like I would never see them again. But I did not want to show that, and I did not.
“In that moment, I felt truly strong and perhaps a bit extraordinary. What stays with me are the words ‘strong and extraordinary’, which take me back to everything I went through that day and during my detention.
“It wasn’t easy to choose one letter. Each letter is important to me. I received them after my release. In prison, we were not allowed to receive letters or cards, but I was well aware of Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign, and the authorities saw the wave of international solidarity.
“One day, I would like to create a work of art from all these letters, cards and messages. Each letter has a place in my heart.”
Magai Matiop Ngong
Magai Matiop Ngong was a 15-year-old schoolboy in South Sudan when he was sentenced to death in 2017 for murder. Magai told the judge the death was an accident and that he was only a child; despite this, Magai faced trial for capital murder without any access to a lawyer. More than 700,000 actions were taken for Magai during Write for Rights 2019, and in March 2022 the High Court agreed that given his age at the time of the conviction, he should be released.
“Out of all the letters I received during the Write for Rights campaign, this one stayed with me the most. Joy was only 19, yet she chose to believe in my future when I was struggling to believe in it myself. She didn’t pretend to understand everything I had been through; she simply reminded me that I was not alone.
“She was a stranger who knew nothing about the person I would become, yet she believed in my future when my own future felt uncertain. Today, her words remind me that sometimes a little hope from one person can keep another person alive inside.
“Today, having survived that chapter of my life and being able to live the future she believed in, her words feel even more powerful. She believed in a future she could not see. I am living that future today.”
Bernardo Caal Xol
Bernardo Caal Xol, a Guatemalan teacher and environmental activist, worked tirelessly to defend communities affected by hydroelectric projects on the Cahabón river, in northern Guatemala. In November 2018, he was sentenced to more than seven years in prison on bogus charges aimed at preventing his human rights work. During Write for Rights 2021 more than half a million actions were taken for Bernardo and in March 2022 he was released.
“The student tells me that in Canada, they have many rivers and lakes. I love knowing that they take care of and protect them there. Being in prison is painful; it’s torture. But the student tells me that I’m a strong and intelligent man and that I deserve all the rivers in the world. I no longer feel the pain of prison because she tells me I’m strong and gives me an award: ‘I deserve the rivers of the world.’
“She inspires me – she wants to be a lawyer in the future ‘because she feels the injustices after learning about my case.’ She is outraged by the Guatemalan government’s criminalization of me; she writes a very profound letter.”
Panusaya “Rung” Sithijirawattanakul
Rung – which means “rainbow” in Thai – became politically active while studying sociology and anthropology at university in the capital, Bangkok. She bravely took part in protests for social and political change throughout 2020. By August, she had become a protest leader. Accused of provoking unrest, she was arrested in March 2021 and imprisoned for 60 days. The authorities denied her bail six times. In defiance, she went on a 38-day hunger strike and was released on 30 April 2021. Rung faces dozens of charges and, if found guilty, life imprisonment. She now lives in exile, outside of Thailand.
Rung featured in Write for Rights 2021, with people around the world calling for her freedom and sending her cards and letters of solidarity.
“Every letter that was written and sent to me while I was imprisoned meant so much to me. Every handwritten message, every drawing, every colour painted across those poster-sized sheets of paper gave me a sense of hope. They reminded me that I was not alone in the movement I was part of.
“When you are in prison, it is incredibly difficult to imagine hope. Everywhere I looked, there was only gray, white, and a sense of bleakness, inside a small, square cell crowded with strangers. Your letters brought some colour from the outside world into my life and brought a little brightness back into my heart. They reminded me that beyond those prison walls, there were still people who saw me, people who knew what I was going through, and people who stood with me.
“With so many letters arriving, they did more than simply give me strength. They also sent a powerful message to those in power that people around the world were watching what was happening in Thailand. “They were watching what was being done to me and to the students who had taken to the streets to demand change. I believe that this international attention and pressure was one of the factors that eventually led to me being granted bail, a right we should have had from the beginning.
“Today, even though I had to leave Thailand and live in exile, I still think about and feel deeply grateful to everyone who helped me, to everyone who wrote a letter, drew a picture, added colour to a page, and sent those pieces of hope across the prison walls to reach me.
“Perhaps to the person who wrote it, it was just one letter. But to me, receiving it on a day when hope was almost impossible to see, that letter meant more than you could ever imagine. I also just found out that, even today, people are still sending letters to me at Amnesty International Thailand’s office. I honestly cannot put into words how that makes me feel.”

Merz seeks swift end to Iran war amid mounting pressure on Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:28 UTC
18:50:28 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called for an end to the war involving Iran as quickly as possible, warning that the conflict is placing a growing economic and security burden on Europe, while using his Asian tour to strengthen trade and defense partnerships and address concerns over European protectionism.
Speaking Friday during the final stop of a weeklong visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea, Merz said the war's consequences for Europe remained severe and that diplomatic efforts to end the fighting were a priority.
The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies, has driven up energy prices and intensified pressure on European economies. Germany, with its energy-intensive industrial sector, has been particularly exposed to the economic fallout.
Merz has repeatedly warned against allowing the conflict to become a prolonged war, arguing that the collapse of the Iranian state or uncontrolled instability across the region would have serious consequences for European security, energy supplies and migration.
While acknowledging concerns over Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programs and its support for regional armed groups, the German leader has stressed the need for a negotiated settlement that prevents further escalation.
Berlin has been working with European and regional partners, including France, Britain and Gulf states, to support diplomatic efforts and establish conditions for a lasting agreement.
Merz has also linked the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz directly to easing pressure on global energy markets, describing the reopening of the waterway as essential to stabilizing fuel and gas prices.
Germany has indicated that it could contribute to securing the strategic waterway after a cease-fire, potentially deploying minehunters and other military assets. However, Merz has made clear that any such involvement would require a cease-fire, an international mandate, preferably from the United Nations, and approval from the Bundestag.
The conflict has also tested relations between Europe and the United States, with European leaders increasingly concerned about the economic costs of a prolonged military campaign.
Merz has maintained that his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump remains functional despite differences over the war's direction and how it should end.
Against this backdrop, Merz has sought to strengthen Germany's economic relationships across Asia, a region increasingly important to European trade and industrial supply chains.
Speaking Friday at the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul, he pledged to raise concerns expressed by Asian trading partners about the European Union's proposed "Made in Europe" initiatives with officials in Brussels.
The initiatives, intended to strengthen European industrial production and competitiveness, have raised concerns among some trading partners that the bloc could turn toward protectionism and restrict access to its markets.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism, that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Merz said the European Union should take the lead in defending international trade and the rules-based global economic system at a time when free trade faces growing pressure.
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements," he said, adding that Germany was prepared to work with like-minded partners in Europe and elsewhere to protect and further develop the international economic order.
He noted that international trade had contributed significantly to the prosperity of many countries and that governments were reluctant to abandon the benefits of an interconnected global economy.
His remarks came amid concerns over U.S. tariffs and China's state-backed industrial expansion, which have prompted European countries to reconsider their economic dependencies and strengthen domestic industries.
During his Asian tour, Merz sought to deepen Germany's economic and defense relationships with countries facing similar challenges in an increasingly uncertain international environment.
In South Korea, he met President Lee Jae-myung on Thursday, with the two leaders agreeing to establish an enhanced security partnership.
Merz also pointed to similarities between German and South Korean industries, saying they offered opportunities for closer cooperation.
South Korea's Industry Ministry said nine memorandums of understanding had been signed by companies and organizations from the two countries. The agreements cover cooperation in electricity, energy and biohealth, alongside support for startups and efforts to facilitate access to each other's markets.
The South Korean visit followed earlier stops in Japan and Singapore, where Merz also sought to strengthen economic and strategic cooperation.

Viet Nam and Kazakhstan bring friendship closer to everyday life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:05 UTC
18:50:05 KST

Viet Nam and Kazakhstan bring friendship closer to everyday life
On 10 October 2026, Vietjet launched Ha Noi-Almaty services, expanding travel options between Viet Nam, Kazakhstan and Europe.
The new October routes offer two return flights a week on each route, helping people meet and businesses find partners. New flights, rising trade and investment in green transport are bringing Viet Nam and Kazakhstan closer. The Strategic Partnership relation is opening new opportunities for businesses and travellers.
Having presented my credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on 19 August 2026, I see these connections as a practical way to turn our countries’ mutual trust into benefits for their people.
A friendship looking forward
Our ties reach back to President Ho Chi Minh’s visit to Kazakhstan in 1959. During his August 2023 visit to Viet Nam, President Tokayev presented General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong with an album commemorating that journey, a reminder of our shared history.
Diplomatic relations followed on 29 June 1992. General Secretary To Lam’s state visit in May 2025 brought a new milestone: a Strategic Partnership. Both countries value peace, independence, sovereignty, the UN Charter and peaceful dispute settlement. Cooperation in international forums and exchanges on reform and integration reinforce that foundation.
Trade gathers pace
Bilateral goods trade reached about USD 564.8 million in the first nine months of 2026, up 44.7 per cent year on year, according to Viet Nam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade. Vietnamese exports rose 35.8 per cent to USD 463.7 million, while imports from Kazakhstan grew 106.5 per cent to USD 101.1 million.
Electronics lead Viet Nam’s exports, with room for agricultural products, processed foods and consumer goods to grow. Viet Nam offers Kazakhstan access to Southeast Asia; Kazakhstan helps connect Viet Nam with Central Asia.
Wheat shows how these strengths can complement each other. Citing Kazakhstan’s Government, Kazinform reported exports of more than 15,000 tonnes to Viet Nam in 2025, following an eight-year pause. Multimodal transport helps cut costs and delivery times, pointing to wider prospects in food and logistics.
The Viet Nam–Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement, in force since October 2016, provides a platform for growth. Making full use of it requires support on tariff preferences, rules of origin and quality standards, and closer coordination on sanitary and phytosanitary measures, payments and transport.
Investment takes new forms
Six projects involving Vietnamese companies are under way, with Vingroup, Sovico Group, Crystal Bay Tourism Group and Mareven Food Central among the participants. ROX Group is also interested in exploring investment opportunities in Kazakhstan’s energy, infrastructure and real estate sectors. Kusto Group’s operations in Viet Nam add to this two-way investment relationship.
Following a 2025 agreement, the Vietjet Qazaqstan brand is being developed from Qazaq Air. The airline unveiled its new livery and introduced services in Astana in February 2026, opening opportunities for staff training, management exchanges and improved passenger services.
On 23 June 2026, Green SM launched its green mobility service in Almaty. Such projects show what Vietnamese technology-enabled services can offer. Their lasting value depends on meeting local needs, creating jobs and contributing to communities.
Finance offers another avenue. The two countries regularly exchange delegations to share experience in finance, banking, innovation and entrepreneurship via connection with the Astana International Financial Centre, the central bank, Astana Hub and Samruk-Kazyna Fund.
Closer ties between people
In 2025, Viet Nam had welcomed nearly 200,000 Kazakh visitors. Visa exemptions and more convenient flights support further growth. Nha Trang, Phu Quoc, Da Nang and heritage destinations await Kazakh visitors, while Kazakhstan’s landscapes, culture and hospitality offer much for Vietnamese travellers to discover.
Tourism businesses can encourage travel in both directions through familiarisation visits, suitable products and destination promotion. Scholarships, student exchanges and business internships build skills and lasting friendships.
The Vietnamese community in Kazakhstan and Kazakh friends with ties to Viet Nam help sustain these links. The Embassy will work with them, local authorities and educational institutions to support exchanges and cultural preservation, while helping businesses find information and partners.
As the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations approaches in 2027, my priority is to listen and turn shared ambitions into practical cooperation. The success of our Strategic Partnership will be felt in the opportunities it brings to people’s work, studies and daily lives.
H.E. Mr. Nguyen Thanh Le,
Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam to the Republic of Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with OTS countries rises 40% to nearly $10bn, says Tokayev
Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with member states of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) has increased by 40 percent compared to last year, reaching nearly 10 billion US dollars, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the 13th OTS Summit, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Akorda press service.
Speaking at the summit, Tokayev highlighted the significance of the Alley of the Turkic World, inaugurated at the initiative of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, expressing confidence that it would become a symbol of the countries’ enduring brotherhood.
The Kazakh President also commented on the deteriorating geopolitical situation, particularly tensions in the Middle East and the confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz.
The geopolitical situation in the world continues to deteriorate. The situation in the Middle East, particularly the confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz, is becoming increasingly tense. All this is having a negative impact on global trade and economic relations, as well as transport and logistics chains, including those connecting neighboring Turkic states, said Tokayev.
He added that Kazakhstan strongly condemned attacks by the Houthi armed movement against Saudi Arabia.
Kazakhstan strongly condemns the unjustified attacks by the Houthi armed movement against brotherly Saudi Arabia. We support calls for an end to such unlawful actions, the President stated.
Turning to economic cooperation, Tokayev said Kazakhstan placed particular importance on strengthening economic ties within the OTS framework.
This year, our country's trade turnover with the member states of the Organization has approached 10 billion US dollars. Compared to last year, this figure has increased by 40 percent, he said.
To maintain this growth, Tokayev called for effective implementation of the Turkic World Vision 2040 program and faster adoption of the OTS Strategy for 2027-2031.
To maintain this momentum, we need to take a number of steps. First and foremost, we must ensure the effective implementation of the Turkic World Vision 2040 program. In this regard, it is important to accelerate the adoption of the Organization of Turkic States Strategy for 2027-2031, he said.

It is fundamentally important that the five-year strategy being adopted focuses on the implementation of specific projects, Tokayev stressed.
He also called for making fuller use of the Turkic Investment Fund, noting that the institution had considerable potential.
This institution has enormous potential, and all the necessary conditions must be created to ensure its full realization, he said.
In addition, Tokayev highlighted the role of the Turkic Chamber of Commerce and Industry in deepening economic integration. He proposed holding a business forum in Kazakhstan in 2027 to give further impetus to cooperation.
We believe that the activities of the OTS Council of Elders are also highly significant. We need to provide this body with financial and other comprehensive support, said the President.

Italian military chopper spirals into deadly crash in Bosnia (VIDEO)
An Italian military helicopter has crashed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, killing four people and injuring 11, the Italian Defense Ministry has confirmed. Dramatic footage shows the aircraft spinning out of control before plunging to the ground.
The CH-47 Chinook, operated by NATO member Italy, crashed on Thursday near the town of Brcko in northern Bosnia. The aircraft was deployed as part of the European Union Force (EUFOR) in the country.
Videos filmed by witnesses show the twin-rotor helicopter spiraling downward while flying at low altitude before crashing into a field.
The accident occurred shortly after takeoff from Brcko airport, according to Italian Ambassador Sarah Castellani. Weather conditions were reportedly favorable.
HELICOPTER CRASH IN BOSNIA KILLS FOUR ON EU PEACEKEEPING MISSION An Italian military helicopter operating under the EU’s Operation Althea crashed in Bosnia, killing 4 people & injuring 11 others. Italy’s Defence Ministry says the cause of the crash is under investigation.
— Subodh Kumar (@kumarsubodh_) October 30, 2026
Investigators are examining several possible causes, including a collision with high-voltage power lines, ANSA reports.
All 15 people aboard were Italian nationals. Two Italian Army personnel and two members of the Italian Red Cross Military Corps are among the dead. The 11 survivors were hospitalized, with none reportedly facing life-threatening injuries.
The helicopter crashed in an uninhabited area near the village of Gorica, narrowly avoiding nearby homes, according to local officials.
The EU-led military mission traces its origins to NATO’s intervention in Bosnia following the 1992-1995 war between Bosnian Serbs, Bosniaks, and Croats. Around 50,000 NATO troops were deployed in 1996 to enforce the peace agreement, before the EU took over the mission in 2004. Beyza Binnur Donmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
EU member states will accelerate the release of 42.6 million barrels from their strategic oil reserves over the coming months to help contain rising energy prices, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen announced Friday.
The commitment was reaffirmed during talks among European energy ministers in Luxembourg, Belgian news agency Belga reported.
Jorgensen said about half of the planned release would consist of diesel.
The move is part of a broader G7 initiative announced earlier this month to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, with the International Energy Agency coordinating the operation.
However, the EU's contribution amounts to only about four days of consumption across the bloc, raising questions about its potential impact on prices.
"We will monitor the effects," Jorgensen said.
The commissioner warned that the war in the Middle East could keep gas and diesel prices elevated throughout the winter.
"We do not expect a problem with supply itself, but that is little comfort to people who are struggling to pay their bills," he said.
Jorgensen acknowledged that governments may need to provide relief to vulnerable households and sectors dependent on fossil fuels, but stressed that such measures should remain "temporary" and "targeted."
He emphasized that accelerating the green transition and reducing reliance on oil and gas would offer a more sustainable response to high energy costs.
The commissioner also met representatives of European refineries Wednesday to discuss ways to increase production.

‘They killed us’: Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announces its closure after decades of repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:45:46 UTC
18:45:46 KST

‘They killed us’: Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announces its closure after decades of repression
Novaya Gazeta, the best-known independent news outlet still operating inside Russia, has announced that it is closing. The day before, it became known that the editorial staff was being evicted from its office in Potapovsky Lane in central Moscow, where journalists had worked for 29 years. As a result, the Anna Politkovskaya museum, located in her former office, will also close. After the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian authorities blocked the outlet’s websites and stripped the newspaper of its registration, and in September 2026 designated Novaya a foreign agent. According to The Economist, the newspaper’s editorial staff held a meeting on October 26 at which the decision was made to close the outlet. On the morning of October 30, Novaya officially announced that it was ceasing operations. Meduza is publishing a translation of the Novaya Gazeta editorial staff’s statement.
They killed us.
On November 9, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave. The newspaper no longer exists. Russian authorities and Russian security services forced the editorial staff to stop working.
More than 30 years of living alongside the country and its citizens will end for us out on the street, without means of subsistence, under the constant threat of repression.
Our years were happy: filled with creativity and hope, readers, friends, texts, films. At times, those years were desperately bitter.
Bitter, because it was during the rule of this regime — not during the lawless 1990s — that our colleagues were killed for political reasons, for carrying out their professional and civic duty: Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, Stas Markelov, Anastasia Baburova, and Natalia Estemirova.
At the same time as the eviction notice, our donation system, which allowed us to receive contributions from our readers, was shut off. In other words, we were stripped of funds. Entirely.
This is a coordinated action. The banks’ excuses — that they are simply following internal corporate rules — will convince no one. The state’s repressive apparatus, officers of Russia’s Federal Security Service who have embedded themselves inside every organization, set these rules instead. They consider the country their own property.
After military action began, Russian authorities stripped us, like all other journalists, of the ability to talk about the most important and tragic events of our time. They passed laws that brought censorship back into the country, and that censorship then spread to nearly every sphere of human life.
Authorities blocked all of our online resources. The state seized our printing house, and security service officers and censors entrenched elsewhere refused to let us publish the newspaper. Many of our staff were forced to leave the country.
The state then stripped us of our media registration, taking away our right to earn a living through our own work.
Attackers assaulted editor-in-chief and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov, who nearly lost his eyesight as a result. No criminal case was opened, even though the perpetrators are known.
Then Russian authorities began designating our journalists as foreign agents, starting with the editor-in-chief.
Then Russian authorities brought administrative cases against the editorial leadership.
In Chechnya, our columnist Elena Milashina was abducted and beaten half to death.
Our executive editor Oleg Roldugin was taken hostage, accused of having worked as a journalist. His trial is coming soon.
Authorities searched Novaya Gazeta’s editorial office for hours and also searched the editor-in-chief’s apartment.
In September of this year, Russian authorities designated the entire editorial staff as foreign agents, placing more than 100 journalists and contributors on the registry.
For nearly five years of the war, we managed to keep working, surrounded on all sides by the security services.
And now, that’s it. We have ended up in a “kill zone.”
This is not just our private story. It is the story of a country and a society being finished off the same way.
The FSB, the Justice Ministry, the prosecutor’s office, and others who have privatized the state and usurped power are doing this. This is not Soviet resentment. Behind that label, a military dictatorship has nearly been built.
They say they are defending the constitutional order. No, this is an anti-constitutional order. The Constitution has been raped, beaten, and thrown into prison for an enormous term with its mouth taped shut, just like thousands of the country’s citizens who simply followed its articles, and tens of thousands of other citizens who were forced to become refugees, leaving their homes and heading into the unknown.
Stop saying that this isn’t Stalin’s 1937, and that the repression has some sort of “digital character.” This is state repression. And people, not numbers, are dying in cells. Period.
Human life has lost its meaning and been devalued.
The word “Constitution” provokes sarcasm and laughter. From everyone. Even from judges. Especially from judges. No one believes that it is the country’s basic law, the one the president swore an oath on. Notice that official propaganda has long since stopped calling the president the guarantor of the Constitution.
Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country, and defending them has been equated with a crime. Elections and elected bodies of government have been de facto eliminated. Public institutions have been eliminated. Freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled. Private life has been turned inside out by dirty hands.
Doesn’t Article 29 of the Constitution — “censorship is prohibited” — sound like mockery today? The courts have been destroyed along with law and justice. Having convictions is now treason.
But treason is when the state betrays its own Constitution. This treason is an ongoing crime, unfolding right now before the eyes of the world.
The killing of Novaya Gazeta is further proof of that.
All these years, we wrote about exactly this, for as long as we could. That is exactly why we were killed.
Thank you to everyone who heard us.
The Editorial Staff

It is therefore extremely important to continue strengthening the cyber resilience of Ukraine’s civilian sector and to support the protection and development of the country’s critical digital infrastructure,” Popp said.
The meeting also formally approved Spain’s accession to the Tallinn Mechanism as its 15th member state. Japan was also officially granted observer status. At the invitation of Italy, the Mechanism’s current chair, eight countries attended a Tallinn Mechanism meeting for the first time and expressed interest in becoming members in the future. “Spain’s accession confirms the Mechanism’s international significance and central role in the multifaceted cooperation to support Ukraine. The discussions focused on the need to make the Tallinn Mechanism’s work more consistent, efficient and effective, particularly in implementing projects. The importance of public-private cooperation was also emphasised, and several companies and other project implementers shared their experiences, lessons learnt and expectations for future cooperation. “The private sector’s contribution to the joint efforts of the Mechanism is critically important for rebuilding Ukraine and creating a better future for Ukrainians,” the Special Envoy for Digital and Cyber Diplomacy stressed.
One discussion, for example, looked at the challenges faced by Ukrainian public sector institutions in restoring the operation of information and communications technology infrastructure damaged by cyberattacks, drawing on projects implemented in Ternopil and Odesa. Member states and observer countries were encouraged to support similar projects at regional level.
This year, more than €32 million has been allocated to cyber support for Ukraine through Tallinn Mechanism projects, of which approximately €700,000 has been contributed by Estonia. Estonia plans to provide a larger amount in 2027.
On 1 July, Italy took over the rotating chairmanship of the Tallinn Mechanism, also known as the lead country role, from the United Kingdom. Italy will lead the Cyber Support Working Group until the end of December this year. The meeting announced that Finland and Norway will become the Mechanism’s lead countries in the first quarter of next year.
The Tallinn Mechanism is a framework established by Estonia and its Allies to amplify the cyber support of donor countries for Ukraine’s civilian sector.

Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta says it is shutting down after 'coordinated campaign'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russian independent paper Novaya Gazeta finally forced to close its doors
MOSCOW, Oct 30 - The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta said on Friday that it was winding up its remaining operations after a campaign of state pressure in which a senior editor has been prosecuted and its financial support and premises have been taken away.
"We have been killed," the publication, set up with money from the Nobel Peace Prize of the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, said in a statement.
The paper halted its print edition inside Russia in 2022, but had continued to produce online content and operate from its office in central Moscow.
"On November 9, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave," it said. "The newspaper no longer exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations."
NOVAYA GAZETA A THORN IN RUSSIAN AUTHORITIES' SIDE
There was no immediate comment from the authorities, which had designated the publication a "foreign agent".
But the Kremlin - which accuses foreign intelligence services of trying to stir up discontent inside Russian society - has said in the past that some censorship is necessary at a time when Russia is locked in what it describes as an existential struggle with the West over Ukraine.
The prominent war blogger Rybar offered a taste of how the publication is seen in some official circles, reposting a diatribe that accused Novaya Gazeta of systematically promoting an anti-Russian narrative and of relishing the difficulties faced by the Russian state.
Founded in 1993 in line with Gorbachev's vision of 'glasnost' or openness, Novaya Gazeta ("New Newspaper") became one of Russia's most influential newspapers and defenders of democracy with its investigations into corruption and critical coverage of Russian politics.
Dmitry Muratov, its co-founder and long-time editor-in-chief, shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, dedicating it to six colleagues who had been killed because of their work, including the investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, who wrote about Moscow's wars in the restive Chechnya region.
PRESSURE FROM FALLOUT OF UKRAINE WAR
Like other media outlets not run by the state but critical of it, Novaya Gazeta came under increasing pressure after Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022. Sweeping censorship rules were introduced that mandated long jail terms for "discrediting" the Russian army or disseminating what the authorities deem to be fake news.
"Since the start of the 'special military operation' in Ukraine and the introduction of criminal charges for 'discrediting the Russian army', we cannot report on the most critical and tragic events of our time," the newspaper said. "Censorship applies to virtually every sphere of civic life."
Many of its own journalists and those from other outlets had fled Russia in 2022, it added. Some of its former employees began a separate Latvian-based print and online publication called Novaya Gazeta Europe, which the Moscow authorities designated an "undesirable organisation", effectively banning it within Russia. It will continue to operate.
Inside Russia, Novaya Gazeta noted that its website had been blocked, its print licence revoked and its presses seized, and that one of its editors, Oleg Roldugin, was under house arrest awaiting trial on allegations that he misused personal data, an offence that carries a prison term of up to 10 years.
Its offices in central Moscow - from which it is now being evicted - have also been searched by the authorities, and the home of Sergei Sokolov, its editor-in-chief, was also searched this month.
"We carried on as long as we could," Novaya Gazeta said in its farewell statement. REUTERS

Divorce: what needs to be taken into account before applying to court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:41:05 EET
18:41:05 KST

Divorce: what needs to be taken into account before applying to court
Kyiv • UNN
Divorce does not automatically determine the fate of children, property, or loans. A lawyer explained when court proceedings are necessary and why disputes should be separated.
At first glance, divorce appears to be a simple legal procedure. In practice, however, the termination of family relations is often accompanied by a whole range of disputes that go far beyond the divorce itself: determining the children's place of residence, the procedure for parents' participation in their upbringing, child support, division of marital property, use of housing, fulfillment of credit obligations, and other issues that have accumulated during the time the couple lived together. Family law attorney Alina Parkhuta of the Legal Company "Logic" told UNN about the legal nuances in a comment.
When a client seeks advice on divorce, it is important to clarify not only their desire to end the marriage, but also the actual state of the family and property relations between the parties.
"The most common mistake is to perceive divorce as a single process within which the fate of the children, property, and financial obligations will automatically be resolved. In reality, the termination of a marriage is merely one of the possible elements of a family dispute," the attorney explains.
Alina Parkhuta, family law attorney of the Legal Company "LOGIC"
What determines the procedure for divorce
"The procedure for divorce depends on the specific circumstances. If the spouses have no minor children together and both agree to end the marriage, the law allows the marriage to be dissolved out of court. If the spouses have minor children together or one of the spouses does not consent, the matter is decided by a court," Parkhuta says.
Sometimes one of the spouses believes that their refusal can block the divorce process. As the attorney explains, this is not the case: marital relations are based on free will, and a person cannot be forced to remain married simply because the other spouse does not want a divorce.
Lack of consent to divorce is not grounds for preserving the marriage
When considering a claim, Alina Parkhuta explains, the court establishes the parties' actual relationship, the reasons for the termination of family life, and other circumstances relevant to the case.
"The key question is whether continuing to live together and preserving the marriage would conflict with the substantial interests of one of the spouses or their children. The defendant's refusal to consent to the divorce is not, in itself, grounds for preserving the marriage," the attorney emphasizes.
There are cases when one of the spouses does not appear in court, does not receive court correspondence, lives abroad, or otherwise delays the consideration of the case. However, according to the attorney, the defendant's failure to appear does not, by itself, prevent the divorce: if the defendant was duly notified of the date, time, and place of the hearing, the court may, where the grounds provided by law exist, consider the case in their absence.
Having children changes the situation
"Having children significantly expands the range of issues that need to be assessed before or simultaneously with the divorce, since the divorce itself does not automatically determine whom the child will live with. If there is no dispute between the parents, they can independently agree on whom the child will live with, how the child will communicate with the other parent, and in what form each parent will participate in the child's support and upbringing," Alina Parkhuta notes.
If no agreement can be reached, the dispute over the child's place of residence is considered separately. The law, the attorney emphasizes, does not presume an unconditional preference for either the mother or the father: what matters is each parent's attitude toward their responsibilities, their actual involvement in the child's life, the child's age and health, the child's attachment to each parent, living conditions, and other circumstances that make it possible to determine the option that best serves the child's interests.
The termination of a marriage does not deprive the parent who will live separately from the child of parental rights and does not release that parent from the corresponding duties. Divorce is not grounds for one parent to unjustifiably restrict the child's communication with the other parent. If there is a conflict between the parties, the specific arrangements for communication and participation in the child's upbringing often require separate legal regulation.
How is marital property divided
"The widespread belief that after a marriage is dissolved, all property is automatically divided between the husband and wife is mistaken. Dissolution of the marriage does not terminate the regime of joint marital ownership with respect to property acquired during the marriage. If the parties have not divided the property by agreement, the right of joint ownership continues to exist even after the marriage is dissolved," explains a lawyer at Logic.
Importantly, the same applies to joint debts: dissolution of the marriage does not terminate obligations under loan agreements or change the terms agreed with a bank or other creditor.
"A dispute may arise between the spouses themselves over whose interests the loan was taken out for, how the funds were spent, and whether a particular obligation can be considered connected with the needs of the family, but this dispute does not concern the bank and does not release the formal debtor from performing the agreement," emphasizes Parkhuta.
As the lawyer explains, it is not always advisable to combine in one case a claim for dissolution of the marriage, division of property, determination of the child's place of residence, and other claims. If there is a complex property dispute between the parties requiring a real estate valuation, examination of banking transactions, determination of the sources used to acquire the property, or the consideration of a large amount of evidence, combining the claims may substantially prolong the proceedings.
"In such situations, it is often justified to separate the disputes: resolve the issue of terminating the marriage separately, and resolve the dispute over property, alimony, or children in separate proceedings. There is no universal rule here: the procedural strategy depends on the amount of property, the nature of the conflict, and the available evidentiary basis in the particular case," the lawyer says.
According to her, before applying to court, it is worth doing more than filing a standard claim for dissolution of the marriage; a full analysis of the family and property situation should be conducted. It is at this stage that it is determined which claims should be filed together and which separately, what evidence should be collected in advance, and what risks may arise after the marriage ends.
"This approach makes it possible to resolve key issues in advance and minimize the risk of additional disputes arising in the future," the lawyer emphasized.

SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Friday he would relay to Brussels concerns voiced by key Asian trading partners that the EU’s “Made in Europe” initiatives risk becoming a new form of protectionism.
“There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism — that we are closing ourselves off from other nations,” said Merz in South Korea, the last stop on a week-long trip that also took him to Japan and Singapore.
Merz said he had heard similar concerns at all three stops about the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which is intended to strengthen the bloc’s industrial base by encouraging more manufacturing and sourcing within Europe.
The proposal is part of broader EU efforts to help local industries compete with overseas rivals that do not face Europe’s stringent regulations and higher energy costs, while also reducing reliance on China.
However, the plans have fuelled concerns among non-European countries about the potential emergence of new trade barriers.
EU governments and the European Parliament must still agree on a final text, with approval expected next year.
“I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here,” Merz said.
He added German and European products could succeed in Asian markets only if the bloc remained open to trade.
The chancellor used the trip to promote closer cooperation among “like-minded” middle powers as a counterweight to the trade and economic policies of the US and China.
“The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, its foreign economic policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same,” he said.
The same applied to defence policy, Merz added, as he seeks to deepen security cooperation with regional partners.

Spanish train was travelling at 160 kph when it smashed into second one, report finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:40:40 CET
18:40:40 KST

By Mireia Merino and Charlie Devereux
MADRID, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Spain’s transport minister on Friday rejected calls for his resignation over the second train accident on his watch to cause mass casualties this year, as authorities worked to identify the victims from a crash that killed at least 69 people.
Lawmakers from across the political spectrum this week condemned Transport Minister Oscar Puente for attributing Wednesday’s crash to a break in protocol by control centre operators rather than accepting responsibility, with rail workers’ unions calling for his immediate dismissal.
The crash, which happened near the town of Urda in central Spain, followed another accident involving the same rail companies on the same line that killed 46 people in January.
It has reopened a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe, as the country prepares for an election that left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called for November 29.
“My duty now is not to focus on discussing whether I will remain in office, but on solving the problem, determining exactly what happened and providing clear explanations,” Puente said at a press conference on Friday.
At the scene of the crash, large cranes were lifting the mangled wreckage as the Civil Guard listed 64 people as missing in what is already Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013. It was unclear if all those missing were accounted for in the death toll.
Authorities have carried out 49 autopsies so far and formally identified five people, three women and two men, Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on state television network TVE.
AUTHORITIES CAN’T RULE OUT MORE FATALITIES
No additional bodies were found when rescue teams overturned a train carriage on Thursday, Castilla-La Mancha regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said on TVE.
Identifying the bodies was proving difficult because many were in pieces, he said. On Thursday, rescue teams had placed partial remains in 31 bags.
“We cannot rule out the possibility of more fatalities,” Garcia-Page said.
The collision occurred after several trains were automatically stopped due to the failure of a signalling system, after which the central control centre in Madrid took over. A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorised to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Puente.
Audio of communications between the control centre and the train drivers obtained by El Pais showed how a controller authorised the Renfe train to continue on its journey at a normal speed, which Puente said disregarded a protocol to travel at no more than 40 kph in such circumstances.
CONTROLLERS SAY FOCUS SHOULD BE ON FAILED SIGNAL SYSTEM
The debate about who was at fault intensified, with unions saying it was unfair to lay the blame on human error.
Raquel Ayllon, a union leader at state-owned infrastructure operator Adif, said controllers were having to operate under difficult working conditions.
“Human error is being criticized and questioned very quickly, while people are not really focusing on the central issue: the failure of the safety system,” Ayllon said on TVE.
Puente said the number of staff working at the control centre in Madrid had almost doubled since 2012 and that the controller who made the call had been working for two hours when the crash occurred.
“I have never used the term ‘human error’, although that is not to say that there was no human error,” he said.
He said the LZB train control system that failed on Wednesday had an average of 170 failures per year, which was about the same as the rest of Europe.
The system was behind schedule for an upgrade, public documents show.
The European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) has been installed across most of Spanish high-speed rail, according to a factsheet by European rail association UNIFE, which developed the new standard.
Thales España, the Spanish arm of the French equipment maker, won a 2021 contract to install the ERTMS on the Madrid-Seville line, site of the two fatal crashes, by early 2026, but the work fell behind and passed to Hitachi Rail in 2024, according to Thales.
Thales declined to comment on the delay of the rollout.
Puente said the ERTMS system on the Madrid-Seville line was expected to begin working in early 2027, adding that the delay was due to the complexity of installing the system while keeping the line in operation.
($1 = 0.8930 euros)

Oleshky evacuation begins but volunteer claims Russia already moved people outside of agreed terms

Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction, said the Ukrainian delegation and evacuated residents of Oleshky were heading to Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai on Oct. 30.
They were expected to fly from there to Belarus before continuing by bus to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Arakhamia added, without specifying when the transfers would take place.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XIV, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
Twenty-five buses with a combined capacity of 750 passengers, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility, had been prepared to evacuate residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on the morning of Oct. 30.
Lubinets's statement came amid reports that Russia had begun evacuating residents ahead of the agreed date.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Lubinets said.
Lubinets and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova held a joint press briefing in Armiansk, Russian-occupied Crimea, ahead of the evacuation from Oleshky.
Lubinets said the Ukrainian and Russian delegations were accompanied by media representatives from three countries. However, photos published by Ukraine's Ombudsman's Office show predominantly Russian media outlets.
Around 11:30 a.m. Kyiv time, the Ukrainian delegation had safely reached Oleshky, and the ceasefire had been in effect for 80 hours and was still holding, Lubinets said.
Lubinets added that he was speaking with local residents to hear about their needs and understand what kind of assistance they required most.
Arakhamia said around noon that humanitarian aid had been delivered to Oleshky and that "technical support" was being provided to those wishing to evacuate.
Lantratova also confirmed on social media that the evacuation from Oleshky had begun, with people gradually boarding buses. She added that some residents wanted to travel to Russia, while others wished to go to Ukrainian-controlled territory, without specifying how many people were in each group.
Later on Oct. 30, Lantratova said that the humanitarian mission in Oleshky was nearing completion and that buses carrying evacuees had reached Armiansk in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they would split into convoys heading to Ukraine and Russia.
Lubinets subsequently said he was continuing to personally coordinate the mission, confirming that the convoys had separated and that he was heading back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Earlier, Lubinets told TSN on national television that a convoy was traveling from Oleshky to Crimea. According to him, people who had not previously registered for evacuation were also given the opportunity to leave.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi initially said during a public government Q&A session on Oct. 30 that 527 residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky were planning to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory. He later clarified on Telegram that he had shared the figure "by mistake" and that "no exact numbers" were available at the time.
Koretskyi also said during the Q&A session that preliminary medical examinations of residents preparing to leave were expected to be completed by 2 p.m. local time on Oct. 30. He added that the evacuees would then travel to Belarus before crossing into Ukraine.
Under the original evacuation plan, residents wishing to leave Oleshky were expected to depart by 2 p.m. local time on Oct. 30, with security measures arranged for their evacuation. Humanitarian aid distribution was scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., according to the ombudsman.
On Oct. 29, Lubinets announced that demining of designated routes had been completed and that a humanitarian convoy was ready to depart. Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported that one person had been injured by the explosion of a Russian mine that day.
Russian state news agency TASS, citing Lantratova, also reported that buses had been prepared for Oleshky residents, including ambulances and a special bus for people traveling with pets.
Kseniia Arkhipova, an evacuation volunteer from Oleshky who is now based in Ukrainian-controlled territory, said that Russia had violated the terms of the agreement by starting the evacuation early.
Footage broadcast by TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30. TASS also showed interviews with people it claimed were evacuated from Oleshky on Oct. 29.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents will have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
But a source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 29 accused Ukraine of "creating a humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky, despite the fact that Russian forces have been in control of the city since 2022.

European air traffic expected to shrink by 110,000 flights amid Middle East tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:38:06 UTC
18:38:06 KST

Gokhan Yildiz and Emir Yildirim
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East are expected to slow European air traffic growth, leading to a loss of around 110,000 flights in 2026, according to forecasts from aviation agency Eurocontrol.
The European aviation sector performed below growth expectations despite strong passenger demand in the summer.
The number of flights in the European Civil Aviation Conference (ECAC) region is expected to grow by 1.7% this year to 11.2 million, below the previously projected 2.7% growth, marking a 1-percentage-point downward revision.
Developments in the region that prompted changes in flight routes and sent jet fuel prices soaring affected the growth outlook for European aviation, but Eurocontrol expects growth to regain momentum next year, with a projected 3.2% increase to 11.6 million flights in 2027.
The downward revision to this year's growth forecast fueled expectations that the number of flights next year may also fall short of estimates.
Eurocontrol assumes the situation in the Middle East will stabilize by the end of the first quarter of 2027, but a more pessimistic scenario forecasts tensions persisting until the end of the first quarter of 2028, with high fuel costs and weak economic growth limiting air travel demand.
The recovery in air traffic is expected to become more pronounced next year, but the organization noted that the recovery could be stronger in Türkiye and some Eastern Mediterranean countries.
The number of flights across Europe is expected to rise by an average of 2.1% per year from 2026 to 2032, while the total number of flights in the region is estimated to reach around 12.8 million by 2032, according to Eurocontrol.
While the organization expects the medium-term growth outlook to remain largely the same, the number of flights may fall slightly short of previous expectations due to geopolitical developments.
Eurocontrol's network management report recorded an average of 35,679 flights per day in European airspace last month, up 2.5% month-on-month.
The busiest day was Sept. 4, when 37,548 flights were recorded in European airspace. Total delays due to air traffic flow management reached a little over 2.4 million minutes, according to the report.
Capacity constraints, adverse weather and air traffic management issues affected operational performance despite the rise in air traffic.
Geopolitical developments, airspace restrictions, energy prices and air travel demand will determine trends in the coming period, the organization said.
