Marju Kõivupuu: Halloween won't displace Estonia's mardi and kadri traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:41:00 UTC
17:41:00 KST

Marju Kõivupuu: Halloween won't displace Estonia's mardi and kadri traditions
No holiday pushes another out of the calendar automatically — people themselves can make the choice about which rituals live on, folklorist Marju Kõivupuu finds.
In the same way, Halloween, which in its present-day form is an import from North America, will not in and of itself destroy Estonians' twin mardi- and kadrisants festivals, held on November 10 and November 25 respectively.
"I have said time and again that no holiday displaces anything on its own, these are choices made by people. For me as a researcher it is interesting to look at what basis we make these choices on," Kõivupuu found in an interview given to R2 hommik.
The folklorist noted that representatives of various faiths tend to label each others' rituals. "That false notion derives precisely from the fact that this or that faith or religion starts to consider itself 'higher' and via that terming belittles others. Christianity took over the holidays connected with marking the old souls' day and honoring the dead, worked them into something more amenable to itself and took them into use," Kõivupuu offered by way of an example.
The same logic holds for Halloween, she said. "Halloween's roots too are indeed in pre-Christian Celtic customs, from which the Christianized Germanic peoples took over that tradition. We now know it as a commercial, entertaining children's holiday that arrived in Europe from America via a circuitous route," the folklorist went on.
Kõivupuu recalled that the Irish carved lanterns which are now characteristic of Halloween from turnips and swedes, but on the European side of the pond. In America, the Europeans found new types of crops, and swapped out the older root vegetables for the pumpkins we now associate with the holiday, just for convenience's sake.
As a theme running through many cultures, the darkening autumn-winter nights serves to bring ancestors' souls back to earth. "If we compare it with our souls' time, then that cloaking is the result of the fact that, according to old beliefs, there is a certain time of the year when the spirits or souls of dead ancestors — whatever we term them — return to earth but want to take the living with them from here," the expert continued.
Kõivupuu added that customs need to be able to breathe, to be dynamic, to stay alive: "A tradition lives when people develop it further. If we give something up, then it stays behind us, but presumably this Halloween was so important that it was adapted according to circumstances."
Equallly, an intentional support and international attention have their place too. "Very few people also know that the Estonian folklore council is currently working in the direction of getting our mardi and kadri day tradition onto UNESCO's representative list of intangible heritage," said Kõivupuu.
Holidays' campaigns on the store shelves
Clever marketing also adds spice to these red-letter days. As a result, international corporations create convenient ready-made solutions so people can celebrate holidays. In the same way, domestic candy producers try to offer children special kadrisants sweets, with the major difference from Halloween being, as Estonian traditions, their lack of a global reach.
As a wider trend, traditional calendar holidays are pushing ever earlier into the commercial sphere, sometimes not even in the most obvious areas. "I went to a building supplies shop at the start of September; I needed a few screws there, and the first thing you could see, in September was already the Christmas trees and elves. I'm sorry, but we still have very plenty of holidays in between; but we can't wait for the holidays any more, they push in from every side," Kõivupuu shared as an anecdote.
The folklorist noted at the same time that more domestic holidays tend to fall below those red-letter days with a bigger commercial footprint, even when children learn the traditional ways thoroughly and wait for sweets at the door when they go "santing" (specifically "mardisandid" on St. Martin's Day (Mardipäev) and "kadrisandid" on St. Catherine's Day (Kadripäev) and originally more akin to carol singing than trick or treating). "Let's be frank, it still stays very, very much in the shadow of that pumpkin holiday, or Halloween," Kõivupuu conceded.

Can the US Defense Industry Keep Pace with China’s Military Machine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:39:00 UTC
17:39:00 KST

As modern warfare continues to evolve in its complexity, the sheer quantity of weapons a country possesses is no longer the only decisive factor in an armed conflict. If, for example, a Taiwan crisis were to escalate into a protracted conflict, the central dilemma would be: Is the United States capable of replenishing its weapons and munitions at a pace adequate to sustain the war effort? Would the strategic gain China would obtain from invading Taiwan outweigh the operational costs of the invasion?
The average military planner is busy counting ships, aircraft and missile stockpiles, as well as calculating defense spending. But these figures illuminate only part of what a geopolitical and military power such as the United States needs in order to be combat-ready. Maintaining a sustained combat posture also depends heavily on the companies that produce munitions, components, spare parts and replacement equipment.
Understanding defense readiness requires looking beyond national military preparedness and keeping track of the production capabilities of industrial manufacturers. According to a CSIS assessment, China’s defense industrial base is built to operate under wartime conditions, while the U.S. base remains largely geared toward peacetime production. Being able to assess readiness at the manufacturer level and close any existing gaps will give the United States the strategic wartime advantage it seeks.
China considers wartime industrial readiness a strategic priority. China’s manufacturing scale could make the difference in a protracted conflict in the Asia-Pacific. A Taiwan contingency could include a blockade, sustained maritime operations, missile strikes and loitering munitions, as well as attacks on supporting infrastructure. In this scenario, the United States and its allied forces would need to sustain their aircraft fleets, replenish missile stockpiles, repair ships and maintain a logistics chain across a vast theater of operations. It is in this context that China’s shipbuilding capacity, and its ability to produce, maintain and repair military equipment at scale and in real time, pose a serious industrial challenge for Washington. In 2024, CSIS estimated China’s shipbuilding capacity at roughly 230 times that of the United States, with China acquiring specific high-end weapons systems at five to six times the U.S. rate.
In response to a potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific, in June 2025 the Department of War requested a 13 percent increase in the 2026 defense budget. This increase therefore signals a U.S. industrial-military outlook aimed at deterring China’s ambitions. The increase prioritizes not only the growth and strengthening of U.S. naval power, but also investment in other areas of defense, such as the production of higher-performance fighter jets; at the same time, an increase in stealth units capable of operating from existing aircraft carriers; in turn, initial investments in the “Golden Dome” for Taiwan, which points to increased air defense capability against enemy missiles and aircraft; and finally, investments focused on upgrading nuclear technology.
It is crucial that U.S. lawmakers understand that defense spending is only one part of the equation. The fact that a company holds a defense contract does not mean it has the capacity to accelerate delivery times. Optimizing production often requires new facilities, specialized tooling, skilled workers and an increase in raw-material suppliers. Financing alone does not guarantee a manufacturer’s ability to meet increased demand. A 2025 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that none of the seven major U.S. shipbuilders it examined was in a position to meet the U.S. Navy’s ship delivery targets at the time. Key issues cited included infrastructure and workforce constraints. The key takeaway here is that national budgets and procurement totals alone cannot reveal the delivery times or capacity constraints of individual defense companies.
New ways of evaluating the companies that drive U.S. military power are emerging. As a practical response to the existing gap in manufacturing measurement, DefenseWatch.org has introduced an index. It currently scores 27 companies on a scale of 0 to 100, offering a more structured way to evaluate and rank U.S.-based defense manufacturers. Prime contractors, as well as other companies, are weighted differently according to the index’s unique methodology. The score is calibrated based on quarterly datasets fed into the algorithm from the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS), SEC filings and notices from the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS).
Rather than analyzing the U.S. defense industrial base as a monolithic entity, the index provides a company-level framework that makes it easier to compare manufacturers’ wartime readiness. The index is not a definitive prediction of wartime performance, but rather a tool that helps structure comparisons and expose potential vulnerabilities in the defense manufacturing industry.
The ability to surge defense production matters as much as, or more than, existing output. In a Taiwan conflict scenario in which the U.S. fires the first military salvo, weapons could be expended faster than peacetime production schedules can replenish them. In this scenario, it is worth being able to identify which manufacturers have the right facilities, workforce and supply arrangements to increase production at any moment. The key metric to watch is not necessarily a company’s current manufacturing capacity, but how quickly it could respond to an extraordinary surge in demand, as well as the cost reductions in manufacturing new technologies; in other words, the use of loitering munitions reduces the operational costs of achieving military objectives and, at the same time, has transformed the modern battlefield, partially replacing the use of conventional weapons and platforms with higher acquisition costs.
CSIS wargames of the Taiwan Strait illustrate the magnitude of the challenge. Across nearly two dozen iterations, U.S. forces typically expended more than 5,000 long-range missiles in three weeks. Replenishment, however, operates on a very different timeline: CSIS reported that producing a Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) took nearly two years, while the U.S. budget for fiscal year 2023 proposed buying only 88. The figures measure different things—simulated consumption, production lead time and planned procurement—but together they expose the core problem: the U.S. industrial base is not prepared for a potential conflict with China. The Taiwan Strait wargames highlight that, in such a scenario, the U.S. military would likely expend critical weapons far faster than its industrial base can currently replace them.
Key components for helping assess a manufacturer’s viability during a conflict include “Investment Quality,” “Domestic Contribution” and “Adversary Exposure.” “Investment Quality” refers to the ability to assess how much of the capital flowing into a given company is actually used to resolve production bottlenecks and meet reliable delivery schedules. “Domestic Contribution” refers to the extent to which a manufacturer can rely on locally sourced components and labor to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers. This also includes exposure to international imports of components and raw materials, as well as dependence on foreign labor. In a scenario in which U.S. strategic readiness will depend on its ability to operate a self-sufficient industrial base, this may be a crucial metric to assess. “Adversary Exposure” refers to how exposed a manufacturer’s supply chains are to foreign inputs. These risks include partial or full ownership of a defense production entity by a foreign government, as well as international cyber vulnerabilities.
The Defense Watch index methodology takes all of these criteria into account, allowing decision-makers to categorically assess replenishment capacity by manufacturer or across manufacturers. Being able to evaluate a company on the basis of individual information pillars is crucial. Two manufacturers may look equally strong on paper, but in practice one may turn out to underperform in a wartime scenario because of one or more exposed vulnerabilities. Returning to a potential Taiwan crisis, index rankings of this kind can help improve policymakers’ decisions, thereby strengthening deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.
Image caption: Defensewatch.org defense contractor tracking index
At the government level, manufacturer readiness analysis can shed light on where additional industrial investment or supplier diversification deserves attention. Defense planners could leverage the data to examine whether multiple programs depend on the same manufacturer or limited industrial input. Meanwhile, allies such as Japan and Australia could benefit from a clearer understanding of the industrial dependencies and resilience of their defense supply chains.
Industrial readiness is a key component of military power. The key question to keep in mind is this: “If a Taiwan crisis escalated into sustained combat, would Washington know which manufacturers could keep delivering, and would it pinpoint where the industrial base might struggle?” Beyond that, weapons inventories, as well as defense budgets/contracts, are an important, though insufficient, metric to monitor. Being able to readily assess a manufacturer’s surge capacity, investment quality, domestic contribution and adversary exposure adds another lens for understanding the industrial resilience of defense manufacturing. Deterrence depends not only on the military capabilities available to the United States at the outset of a conflict, but on the industrial capacity to sustain them. Measuring that capacity before a crisis arises is a strategic necessity.
Luis Márquez is a lawyer who graduated from the Universidad de los Andes in Venezuela. He holds a diploma in Strategic Intelligence Management, with a specialisation in Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), from the National Technological University of Argentina. He is currently studying Urban and Port Security at the same institution, further developing his expertise in intelligence, security analysis, and the protection of critical infrastructure.

Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:38:00 UTC
17:38:00 KST

65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty
October 30, 2026
Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.
At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.
By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."
Some upward mobility among migrants, but discrimination a big problem
According to integration expert Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that.
Even 65 years later, he told DW, people of Turkish descent still suffer a great deal of discrimination in Germany.
But he believes that the German Turkish labor recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story.
"We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.
Uslucan himself is one such a success story. His father came to Berlin from Turkey and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, his father brought his wife and two sons to join him in Germany.
Haci-Halil Uslucan subsequently earned his Ph.D. in psychology and a professor of contemporary Turkish studies at the University of Duiburg-Essen.
One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement. He is examining loneliness, an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called "guest workers."
But poverty is also increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.
With a rate of between 25-30%, poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants in Germany than among Germans, which is about 12-14%, he says, adding that the disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor.
They are also twice as likely to become unemployed 10 years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan.
"In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."
Pensions €360 lower among Turkish citizens in Germany
An analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, uncovered some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €890 ($997) in pension benefits per month. That is €360 less than German pensioners, who receive €1,250 per month on average.
Even more troubling is that in June 2026, more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).
One reason for this is that many of the Turkish workers who came to Germany were already in the middle of their working lives and consequently has less years to contribute to their pension fund, social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW.
"But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.
With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many Turkish workers in Germany also lost their jobs.
"There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."
Few chances for migrant workers to train
Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants in Germany.
It's a major problem in Germany that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty, she said.
"This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, it would be an even sorrier situation."
Older Turkish migrants in Germany also often have limited opportunities to earn extra euros during retirement.
This is because either because they are poorly qualified or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit.
According to figures from Germany's Federal Employment Agency, the employment rate of for retired Turkish people living in Germany is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%).
"Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training," Söhn said.
The Turkish workers in Germany didn't get similar chances.
"The people who did these tough jobs, which are always necessary for any economy, paid for it with their health," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

Mexico: world's tallest Catrina unveiled for Día de Muertos in Mexico City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:37:59 UTC
17:37:59 KST

The monumental female skeleton, roughly the height of an 11-storey building, surpasses the previous record of 28.15 metres set in Puerto Vallarta in 2023.
Created by around 140 artists and technicians from Taller Xibalbá, the figure wears a purple dress stretching more than 27 metres. Visitors gathered beneath the installation to take photographs as workers put the finishing touches to the display. Facing the Metropolitan Cathedral, the Catrina stands at the centre of an enormous ofrenda, a traditional altar honouring the dead, surrounded by a carpet of some 70,000 marigold plants grown in Xochimilco.
The installation pays tribute to Mexican artist José Guadalupe Posada, whose 1913 illustration of a skeletal woman became the inspiration for La Catrina, now one of the most recognisable symbols of Day of the Dead.
The elaborate display also features coloured sawdust carpets and figures inspired by axolotls and alebrijes, Mexico's fantastical folk-art creatures. Celebrated on 1 and 2 November, Day of the Dead brings families together to remember deceased loved ones through photographs, food, flowers and offerings. Marigolds, known as cempasúchil, are traditionally believed to guide spirits home through their colour and scent.
The record-breaking Catrina and its illuminated altar will remain on display until 2 November.

Oil flows are up as Iran war turmoil eases. Why do prices keep rising?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:36:11 UTC
17:36:11 KST

Oil flows are up as Iran war turmoil eases. Why do prices keep rising?
Brent crude prices are up more than 60 percent compared with pre-war levels, despite rebound in supply.
Oil flows out of the Gulf have increased substantially, easing the huge supply disruption caused by the United States/Israel war on Iran.
Crude exports from the Gulf averaged 24.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week to October 18, exceeding the pre-war average, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
Yet, oil prices continue to rise.
Brent crude, the global benchmark, is trading at its highest prices since April, up more than 60 percent compared with before the war.
On Friday, Brent crude front-month futures – contracts for oil deliveries in December – rose more than 2 percent to briefly top $117 a barrel.
The climbing prices reflect anxiety about the possibility of renewed hostilities in the US war on Iran, dwindling oil stocks, and the increased costs of transporting supplies out of the region, according to market analysts.
“The market is doing exactly what it is supposed to do: It is telling us there is plenty of prompt oil, but there is no end to this war in sight – in fact … escalation is very likely,” Adi Imsirovic, a lecturer in energy systems at the University of Oxford, told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore, futures markets reflect that expectation,” Imsirovic, a veteran oil trader, said.
Oil producers have become increasingly adept at responding to the volatile climate in the Middle East to keep supplies flowing.
Facing the threat of Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, shipping lines have established a shuttle system involving ship-to-ship transfers off Oman and the United Arab Emirates to reduce the distance any one vessel must travel in perilous waters.
Shuttle boats carry the oil through the strait and load it onto waiting tankers once they are out of the danger zone.
In August, more than 70 percent of the crude that crossed the strait did so via ship-to-ship transfers, according to Kpler.
Oil producers have also ramped up exports that bypass the strait altogether via Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which carries oil supplies from its eastern oil fields to its Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, and the United Arab Emirates’ Habshan-Fujairah pipeline.
As of September, 40 percent of exports from the Gulf were bypassing the strait, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies during peacetime, compared with 17 percent before the war, according to Kpler data.
The soaring cost of delivery
Such workarounds have nonetheless come at a cost.
Freight costs have reached as much as $40 per barrel in recent weeks, about 10 times the usual rate, according to data from the London Stock Exchange Group, the surge driven by elevated insurance premiums in addition to logistical challenges.
October has been the deadliest month for attacks on commercial vessels since the start of the war, with 32 incidents logged by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) as of Friday.
“So barrels are moving, but neither smoothly nor reliably. That should not be read as a sign of normalisation,” Isabel Figuerola-Ferretti, an expert in oil markets at Comillas Pontifical University in Madrid, Spain, told Al Jazeera.
“Delivering a barrel has become far more expensive,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.
While market intelligence data has shown exports reaching pre-war levels at various points in recent weeks, the longer-term supply trend is less clear.
Pavel Molchanov, an investment strategist at Raymond James & Associates, expressed scepticism that supply has returned to the pre-conflict trend.
“The IEA’s most recent production data – for September – shows OPEC Gulf production at 15.8 million bpd, which equates to 75 percent of the pre-war baseline,” Molchanov told Al Jazeera, referring to the International Energy Agency’s latest energy outlook.
“That slightly surpassed July’s 74 percent to reach the highest level since the start of the war, but it’s still a considerable distance from 100 percent.”
Meanwhile, oil stockpiles, a buffer during supply disruptions, are waning.
Observed inventories fell by 10 million barrels in September, taking the global stockpile to 509 million barrels below its pre-war level, according to the IEA.
“The market has moved to a chronic squeeze, driven by concrete supply risks: Hormuz transit, shipping and depleted inventories,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.
No reprieve anytime soon
With no permanent end to the Iran war in sight, few analysts see prices returning to normal anytime soon.
Brent futures for delivery in October 2027 stood at more than $90 a barrel on Friday, in a sign that markets see normality as a long way off, still.
“When could prices return to $70? Not soon,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.
“It would need durable de-escalation, a return to normal transit and shipping conditions through Hormuz, rebuilt inventories and freight costs back to normal,” she added.
Molchanov, the investment strategist, said he did not believe supply could realistically exceed 85 percent of pre-war levels without a permanent diplomatic solution to the war.
“Once the political groundwork is in place, the next steps will be logistical: Demining Hormuz, bringing shipping crews back to work, and resuming production at currently shut-in oilfields,” he said.

27 Ugandans recruited by Russia killed or presumed dead in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:35:33 UTC
17:35:33 KST

Twenty-seven Ugandans recruited into Russia’s military have been killed or are presumed dead while fighting in Ukraine, according to diplomatic correspondence that highlights growing concerns over the recruitment of African nationals into Moscow’s war effort.
A letter dated Oct. 17 from Uganda’s embassy in Moscow to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Kampala listed 11 citizens whose deaths had been confirmed and 16 others whose bodies could not be located, including through searches of prisoner-of-war records.
Reuters obtained the letter Thursday, Oct. 29, and an official at Uganda’s foreign ministry confirmed its authenticity.
The document, signed by Uganda’s ambassador to Russia, Moses K. Kizige, said the information had been provided by Russia’s Foreign Ministry through a diplomatic communication known as a note verbale, following an earlier inquiry by the Ugandan embassy.
The embassy had sought information in August about approximately 35 Ugandans believed to be serving in Russia’s so-called special military operation in Ukraine.
Of the 27 men now listed as dead or missing, Russian authorities confirmed the deaths of 11, while the remaining 16 have not been accounted for. Their remains have not been recovered, and their names do not appear on available prisoner-of-war lists.
The embassy effectively considers the missing men dead, although their individual circumstances and the locations where they disappeared remain unclear.
The correspondence also identified five Ugandans who remain under contract with the Russian military. They are expected to leave service when their contracts expire.
Another citizen, Robert Tumwebaze, was reportedly dismissed from military service after receiving treatment at a military hospital in Nizhny Novgorod. He subsequently left embassy personnel at a railway station, according to the letter.
Ambassador Kizige urged Uganda’s foreign ministry to inform the families of the deceased as soon as possible so they could pursue compensation and other benefits potentially available under their relatives' Russian military contracts.
Russia's embassy in Kampala did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The deaths add to mounting concerns across Africa over the recruitment of citizens into Russia's military, with increasing reports of men travelling to the country after being promised civilian employment before finding themselves deployed to the front lines in Ukraine.
Investigations and accounts from relatives have described recruitment offers involving well-paid jobs as drivers, security guards, construction workers and cooks. Some recruits reportedly discovered only after arriving in Russia that they were expected to sign military contracts and participate in combat operations.
In several cases, families have struggled to establish contact with relatives after they travelled to Russia, while others have reported that recruits had their passports and mobile phones confiscated, leaving them with little ability to seek help or return home.
Ukraine has repeatedly raised concerns about the involvement of African nationals in Russia's military campaign. Ukrainian officials said last year that more than 1,400 citizens from approximately three dozen African countries were fighting alongside Russian forces, with some allegedly recruited through deception.
An investigation by Journalists For Justice identified at least 3,034 Africans from 40 countries who had enlisted in Russia's military since October 2022. At least 502 deaths had been documented by the end of June 2026.
Kenya, Ghana and South Africa have been among the countries most vocal about the recruitment of their citizens, with governments raising the issue through diplomatic channels and warning people against accepting suspicious employment offers in Russia.
Kenya has reported hundreds of its citizens becoming involved in the conflict, with dozens killed or missing. Nairobi has also pursued diplomatic engagement with Moscow over the recruitment of Kenyans and efforts to secure the return of those caught up in the war.
The concerns have spread beyond East Africa, with families and authorities in countries including Uganda, Cameroon, Nigeria and Ghana seeking information about citizens believed to have joined Russian forces.
The Ugandan embassy's correspondence does not establish how each of the 27 men was recruited, whether they knowingly signed up for combat service or which battles they may have fought in. However, relatives of some Ugandans involved have previously said their family members travelled to Russia after receiving offers of civilian employment before losing contact with them.
The latest diplomatic disclosures also come amid reports that recruitment networks are increasingly targeting other African countries as governments step up efforts to discourage their citizens from joining Russia's military.
Russia has repeatedly denied illegally recruiting African nationals to fight in Ukraine, maintaining that foreign citizens serving in its armed forces do so voluntarily under formal military contracts.
Moscow has also argued that it has sufficient manpower for its military operations and does not need to resort to coercive recruitment.
However, investigations into recruitment networks have raised questions about the role of intermediaries who allegedly use misleading job advertisements to attract foreign workers before directing them toward military service.
Some investigations and United Nations-related findings have also highlighted possible trafficking and exploitation involving recruitment brokers.

MPs call for ban on generative AI in primary schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

MPs call for ban on generative AI in primary schools
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
MPs are calling for a ban on AI tools in Dutch primary schools, saying they threaten children’s ability to develop basic reading, writing and critical thinking skills.
A motion put forward by pan-European progressive party Volt and centrist Christian Democrat CDA asks the cabinet to arrange a formal rule disallowing tools like ChatGPT for primary school pupils. So far the motion has the backing of 10 parties with 88 of parliament’s 150 seats, according to broadcaster NOS.
Volt leader Laurens Dassen said in a statement: “I believe in the opportunities AI offers us, but at the same time generative AI is widening learning gaps.”
New learning goals for primary schools, due to take effect in 2027, will require pupils to explore AI and learn to “interact responsibly with an AI system”. In secondary school, students will start experimenting with training AI systems.
The motion tabled by Volt and CDA acknowledges these plans, and doesn’t rule out teaching children about AI, even if they wouldn’t be allowed to use it themselves.
Barend Last, an education specialist who teaches the final year of primary school, told NOS he agreed children should not have unlimited access to AI. However, he also said it can be a useful teaching tool if used in the right way, and that ruling it out altogether risks children learning too little about it.
The PO-Raad, the umbrella body for primary schools, said early research shows pupils learn less when they use generative AI heavily, and that it understood MPs’ concerns. But it said a total ban would come “out of the blue”, and that it would rather reach agreement with the education ministry.

Experts urge Cappadocia closures after heavy rain

AA photo.
Experts called for temporary visitor closures after heavy rain in Türkiye’s central Cappadocia region, where a fairy chimney collapsed near Göreme Open Air Museum in Nevşehir on Oct. 29, killing three people and injuring five.
Istanbul Technical University’s Geological Engineering Department Head Şenel Özdamar said access should be suspended until conditions stabilize. Whether human intervention contributed was unknown; natural erosion continues to shape the formations, he said.
Mining technology and earth sciences expert Serkan İçelli said he had filmed a warning there two months earlier and identified similar hazards. Cavities carved as dwellings should be individually assessed and restored in keeping with nature, he said.
Governor Hüseyin Kök attributed the collapse near the museum entrance parking lot to a rain-induced landslide. Only the immediate area was cordoned off; no problems were reported with other formations.
Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), National Medical Rescue Team (UMKE) and health and rescue crews searched the debris as officials established a crisis desk. Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said a deputy chief prosecutor and two prosecutors were assigned to investigate. The injured were in good condition in hospitals, Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu said.
The dead were journalist Fatih Eray Tuna and his wife Begüm Çetinkaya Tuna, both 31, who married in July, and French tourist Cynthia Francine Marie Madeleine Houpert, 37. Tuna worked in northwestern Sakarya.
Cappadocia Area Head Cem Aslanbay previously identified old carved spaces at the base of a collapsed formation. The authority inspects risky formations and carries out reinforcement and restoration where needed; regular assessments, barriers and compliance with warnings help protect visitors.
Volcanic ash from Erciyes, Hasandağı and Göllüdağ hardened into tuff millions of years ago. Wind and water eroded the soft rock beneath harder caps into fairy chimneys. Loss of a cap or weakening of the body can accelerate erosion. Rain, snow and temperature changes weaken them, while water freezing in cracks expands and breaks rock apart.
Nonfatal collapses occurred in Uçhisar’s Tekeli neighborhood in December 2024, after snowmelt and Göreme’s Gaferli neighborhood in September 2025. Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia have been on UNESCO’s World Heritage List since 1985.

Türkiye’s economic confidence index fell 3.9 percent month-on-month in October, declining to 97.3 from 101.3 in September, the Turkish Statisticial Institute (TÜİK) said on Oct. 30.
Readings above 100 indicate optimism about the general economic outlook, while values below 100 point to a pessimistic assessment.
Consumer confidence, which advanced 1.3 percent in September, recorded the sharpest drop among the main indicators, falling 7.7 percent from the previous month to 84.8.
The real sector (manufacturing industry) confidence index decreased 1.4 percent to 101.1, after edging up 0.1 percent month-on-month in September. The services confidence index fell 2.4 percent to 109.2 in October, after remaining unchanged in the previous month.
In contrast, the retail trade confidence index rose 1.1 percent month-on-month to 112.5, and the construction confidence index, which fell 0.2 percent in September increased 0.4 percent to 83.3 in October.

Türkiye’s tourism income increased 5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, reaching $25.53 billion, according to data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 30.
In the first 9 months of 2026, Türkiye’s tourism income rose by 2.4 percent annually to $51.28 billion.
Of the total, tourism income from visitors amounted to $25.29 billion in the third quarter, while income from transfer passengers stood at $232 million. Turkish citizens residing abroad accounted for 14.4 percent of tourism income generated by visitors.
Visitors either organized their trips individually or through package tours. Individual travel expenditures totaled $17.11 billion, while package tour spending reached $8.18 billion in the third quarter.
The number of departing visitors fell 1.6 percent year-on-year to 23.26 million. Turkish citizens residing abroad made up 13.6 percent of all visitors, totaling 3.16 million people.
The number of visitors fell 2.2 percent year-on-year to 48.09 million in the January-September period.
Average spending per night by visitors was $107 in the third quarter, rising 6.7 percent from a year ago, while Turkish citizens residing abroad spent an average of $68 per night.
Average spending per capita by visitors also increased by 6.7 percent compared to the third quarter of 2025 to $1,088, showed TÜİK data.
Package tour expenditures accounted for 32.3 percent of total tourism income, followed by food and beverage spending at 20.5 percent and accommodation expenditures at 12.5 percent.
Compared with the same quarter a year earlier, health expenditures increased 23.6 percent, accommodation expenditures rose 19 percent, and domestic transport expenditures advanced 12.1 percent.
Visitors primarily traveled to Türkiye for travel, entertainment, sports and cultural activities, which accounted for 74.5 percent of visits. Visiting relatives and friends ranked second with 16.9 percent, followed by shopping with 3.7 percent.
Among Turkish citizens residing abroad, the main purpose of travel was visiting relatives and friends, representing 63.9 percent of visits.
Meanwhile, tourism expenditure by Turkish citizens residing in Türkiye who traveled abroad increased 22.6 percent year-on-year to $3.04 billion.
Of the total outbound tourism expenditure, $2.57 billion was spent on individual travel, while package tour expenditures amounted to $468 million.
The number of Turkish citizens traveling abroad rose 24.2 percent year-on-year to 4.2 million, with average spending reaching $723 per person.

"Over the past day, Russia continued attacking energy infrastructure facilities. As of this morning, we have new power outages affecting consumers in Kyiv, Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv regions," the statement said.
Restoration work is ongoing everywhere that the security situation allows.
Schedules and emergency outages
"Due to the ongoing Russian attacks, measures to restrict electricity consumption are being implemented today in some regions of Ukraine," the Ministry of Energy said.
As noted, these measures are necessary to balance the energy system and preserve its stable operation.

Netanyahu left on shaky ground after losing election majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:22:00 UTC
17:22:00 KST

Israel's final election results have left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu without a parliamentary majority, setting the stage for difficult coalition negotiations in which Arab-led parties could determine who forms the next government.
Results released early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the main opposition bloc secured 48. Arab-led parties captured the remaining 19 seats, their strongest showing to date, putting them in a potentially decisive position as rival camps seek the 61 seats required to govern.
Neither Netanyahu nor his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has an obvious path to a majority. Both must negotiate with parties whose ideological differences and competing demands could make an agreement difficult.
"Now comes the truly hard part," centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging Israelis to remain patient.
The biggest question is whether Eisenkot and other opposition leaders will cooperate with Arab-led parties to remove Netanyahu or abandon their campaign promises and consider joining a government led by the prime minister.
One potential route to an anti-Netanyahu government would involve Eisenkot's bloc joining forces with Arab-led parties, potentially creating a 67-seat majority. Even without formally joining the coalition, the Arab parties could provide the support needed for a minority government.
However, such an arrangement would carry considerable political risks for Eisenkot and his Jewish allies.
Arab citizens make up about 20% of Israel's population. Many are Palestinians whose families remained within the country's borders after the 1948 Nakba.
They maintain close ties with Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza, contributing to longstanding suspicion among many Jewish Israelis.
An Arab party joined an Israeli governing coalition for the first time in 2021, when the United Arab List became part of a government that lasted approximately 18 months.
Netanyahu has portrayed renewed cooperation as a betrayal of Israel's Jewish identity and a national security threat, increasing pressure on right-leaning opposition lawmakers to reject such an alliance.
Hundreds of Israelis have meanwhile demonstrated, urging Eisenkot and his allies to work with Arab-led parties rather than allow Netanyahu to remain in power. Strong Arab turnout also reflected opposition to Netanyahu's far-right allies, particularly National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose party lost seats.
Another possibility would involve Netanyahu persuading Eisenkot or some of his right-leaning allies to abandon their opposition and join a unity government.
Such an arrangement could potentially secure a 67-seat majority but would require significant compromises.
Eisenkot and his allies have repeatedly ruled out serving under Netanyahu, blaming him for the security failures surrounding Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, incursion and accusing him of undermining democratic institutions. They have also cited his ongoing corruption trial as a reason he should leave office.
Joining a Netanyahu-led government would risk alienating voters who supported the opposition to secure a change in leadership. One of their central demands is an official inquiry into the failures preceding Oct. 7.
Netanyahu could also seek to exploit divisions within the opposition by approaching right-wing politicians Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman. Both support settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank but have longstanding disputes with Netanyahu and oppose military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, a major demand of his religious allies.
The negotiations are unfolding amid controversy over unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties manipulated the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
Before the final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified claims that Arab-led parties had stolen the election.
Opposition figures accused the prime minister of undermining the legitimacy of Arab voters and inflaming tensions against a population representing about one-fifth of Israel's citizens.
In his first public response Friday, Netanyahu posted on X that forming a coalition with Arab parties was forbidden.
Noam Sohlberg, head of Israel's election committee and a Supreme Court justice, said serious suspicions of foreign interference had been brought to his attention. Although he could not verify the claims, he requested an investigation by the Shin Bet security agency.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party had accused Qatar of involvement. The Gulf country rejected the allegations as "ridiculous and dangerous."
The election committee said the investigation was based on classified intelligence but stressed that it would not affect the final results or target any particular section of the population. Acting Director General Dean Livne also warned against unfounded reports surrounding the inquiry.
The Shin Bet said its investigation was not intended to cast suspicion on an entire community that had exercised its democratic right to vote lawfully. The election committee described allegations of systematic electoral violations as baseless and requested the agency's findings within a week.
If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot secures a majority, Israel could face another election early next year, with Netanyahu's government remaining in a caretaker capacity.
A fresh vote could hurt the opposition, which entered the latest contest with considerable momentum but failed to secure an outright majority. Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad reportedly travelled home to vote, raising questions about whether they would make the same journey again.
Netanyahu could use the additional time to strengthen his position. Several smaller parties aligned with him failed to cross the electoral threshold required to enter parliament, leaving some pro-Netanyahu votes without representation. Their supporters could shift toward larger right-wing parties in another election.
Israel previously endured five elections in three and a half years following a similar political deadlock in 2019.
Losing office would also expose Netanyahu to increased pressure over his corruption allegations and calls for an official investigation into the security failures surrounding the Oct. 7 incursion.
The results must be certified and submitted to President Isaac Herzog next Wednesday. He will then select a candidate to attempt to form a government. The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10.
Herzog has pledged to do everything possible to prevent another election, but Israel's political future remains uncertain as party leaders prepare for negotiations that could reshape the country's government.

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. The price of gas in Europe has already exceeded the $1,200 per 1,000 cubic meters mark, and it could even climb to $2,500 if winter temperatures are low, Gazprom chief executive Alexey Miller said.
"Gas prices in Europe have exceeded $1,200 per 1,000 cubic meters already in October, although Western experts forecasted that this price level would not be reached before autumn/winter peak demand. With the streak of all-time lows set by Europe in terms of gas injection into UGS (underground gas storage - TASS) facilities - for example, the fill level at the gas storages of Germany, which is the largest gas consumer in the EU, is just 61.6 per cent - one can expect that, if this winter is cold, the gas price in Europe will reach $2,500 per 1,000 cubic meters at its peaks," he was quoted as saying by the holding’s press service.
The spot price of gas at the TTF hub in Europe exceeded $1,200 per 1,000 cubic meters during Friday trading for the first time since December 2022. Prices have also surpassed the 100 euro per MWh mark for the first time in four years. Gas prices in Europe have been climbing amid historically low storage levels ahead of the upcoming winter and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has not ruled out the possibility that gas prices in Europe could rise to $1,500 per 1,000 cubic meters.

Tehran hosting international industry exhibition

Sudan investigation maps commanders linked to wartime rape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:20:40 UTC
17:20:40 KST

Sudan investigation maps commanders linked to wartime rape
Investigative unit CIR identifies 25 commanders present at five sites during periods of reported sexual violence.
On the day the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) entered el-Fasher in October 2025, a video posted on TikTok showed one of the paramilitary group’s commanders addressing fighters. She appeared to be encouraging fighters to rape women in Sudan’s Northern State, hundreds of kilometres from el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur.
“The Northern State? You’ll just go for its women, so you cleanse their lineage and bring [brave] sons just like you.”
The speaker was Khademallah Khashmin Herika, also known as Shiraz Khalid, a major commanding the RSF’s female contingent, according to the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR).
The British open-source investigative organisation describes her words as an explicit incitement to rape. It could not establish exactly where the video, posted on October 26, 2025, was filmed. Separate footage placed Herika in el-Fasher and in Garni, where survivors described girls being detained and raped.
Herika is among 25 commanders identified in a CIR investigation into sexual violence in Sudan’s war. Published on Monday, a year after her video was posted, it examines five locations and periods of reported abuse, linking commanders’ appearances and roles to evidence gathered by the United Nations, rights groups and Sudanese organisations.
The findings cover both the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces, which have been fighting a three-year-long war, as well as their allied forces. They identify commanders who exercised authority where atrocities were reported, but do not establish that each personally committed or ordered acts of rape.
Investigators checked identities, locations and, where possible, filming dates, with commander sightings independently verified by two analysts. They compared that record with survivor accounts, reported incidents, threatening rhetoric, and indicators of heightened risk, including forced separation of men and women.
The UN fact-finding mission documented mass and gang rape during the RSF takeover of el-Fasher, including at the Saudi Hospital and el-Fasher University. Women and girls were also attacked along escape routes out of the city.
CIR’s report cites a survivor who described being held with other girls at soldiers’ quarters near Garni and raped over two nights. Her family’s detention for ransom further delayed her access to specialist medical care.
The chain of command
The most senior RSF officer identified around el-Fasher was Abdul Rahim Hamdan Dagalo, deputy commander and brother of RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.
CIR verified him at the army’s former 6th Infantry Division base on October 26, 2025, and at the Saudi Hospital on November 4.
In separate drone footage from October 27, a voice instructs artillery commander Hussein Abu Jalak to pursue vehicles fleeing an earth embankment outside the city, associated with civilian detention and executions. CIR matched the voice to Dagalo by manually comparing it with other verified recordings of him speaking.
RSF sector commander Gedo Hamdan Ahmed, known as Ibn Shouk, also appears across the investigation: at Zamzam displacement camp during the RSF’s April 2025 assault, then around el-Fasher during its takeover six months later.
His appearances connect two offensives under the same regional command, but they do not establish his responsibility for a specific sexual assault.
A commander on both sides
Another officer appears on opposing sides of the war.
Abuaqla Mohamed Ahmed Alwakil, known as Kaykal, was appointed commander of an RSF division in Wad Madani on December 19, 2023, according to an RSF announcement cited by CIR.
Investigators verified him at a former army base there on December 24. The same day, the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa documented the rape of seven women at the city’s Industrial School.
The following day, RSF captain Samar Ibrahim Tirab appeared about 750 metres from the school, dismissing reports of rape and looting as lies.
In October 2024, Kaykal defected to the army’s side. When army and allied forces recaptured Wad Madani in January 2025, CIR verified him in the city and nearby Wad al-Mehidi, now commanding the Sudan Shield Forces.
The United Nations human rights office reported that Sudan Shield fighters abducted 13 women and a man from Tayba camp on January 10. Human Rights Watch separately recorded witnesses identifying attackers as Kaykal’s forces. Radio Dabanga reported allegations of rape by the group in Tayba and other settlements.
The army’s allies
In Gezira, southeast of Khartoum, CIR also examined abuses against Kanabi communities, historically marginalised settlements made up of descendants of migrant agricultural workers. These communities faced attacks amid accusations of supporting the RSF.
Verified footage from Hantoub Bridge shows fighters beating and sexually degrading a detained man before pushing him off the bridge. CIR identified insignia associated with the army-allied Baraa Bin Malik Brigade, General Intelligence Service and Special Mission Forces.
The most senior army officer CIR placed in Wad Madani during the recapture was Major-General Abdelmoneim Abdelbasit Mohamed, commander of the Sennar axis, identified on January 12, 2025.
His presence is part of CIR’s assessment of command structures, but it does not establish that he directed the filmed attack.
Al Jazeera contacted the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces to ask for a response to the findings laid out in this article, but received no response.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces have previously denied allegations of sexual violence by their personnel.
UK sanctions
On October 26, Britain imposed sanctions on 15 senior commanders from Sudan’s rival forces over suspected atrocities, including conflict-related sexual violence.
The measures include asset freezes and travel bans. Among those named were Abu Jalak and Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as al-Qubba, whom the UK Foreign Office linked to the siege and assault on el-Fasher.
The UK government said the announcement followed CIR reporting on sexual violence and starvation. It also pledged 5 million pounds ($6.7m) for survivors, including healthcare and psychosocial support, and a further 10 million pounds ($13.4m) for humanitarian assistance.
The 15 sanctions designations are a separate list from the 25 commanders cited in CIR’s report, and sanctions do not equate to criminal convictions.
What the evidence can establish
CIR says it has reasonable grounds to believe the commanders identified were directly or indirectly responsible for sexual violence. It also explicitly states that data limitations prevent it from attributing individual responsibility for specific incidents.
Presence, rank and repeated appearances can guide further investigation; but they cannot alone establish criminal guilt. A command-responsibility case would also require evidence about effective control, knowledge and failures to take necessary measures to prevent, repress or report crimes.
For survivors, stigma, insecurity and inaccessible services still obstruct both treatment and testimony. The investigation preserves another source of evidence: the images fighters recorded themselves.

Smoke from wildfires killed 3,500 people in Indonesia in September: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:20:30 KST

Smoke from wildfires killed 3,500 people in Indonesia in September: Report
Persistent wildfires sparked by drought have enveloped the region in smog.
Toxic smoke from wildfires killed 3,560 people in Indonesia last month, according to a new report.
The study, released by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) on Thursday, found that air pollution-related deaths in Indonesia surged by 42 percent in September, rising from an estimated 3,740 people killed in August to 5,310.
Toxic smoke from forest and land fires caused 3,560 deaths last month, the report said. “Chronic, non-fire emissions from urban and industrial air pollution sources” caused another 1,750 deaths, the Helsinki-based think tank found.
Toxic fire smoke accounted for 94-99 percent of air pollution-related deaths in Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, and more than 80 percent on Sumatra, the regions worst affected by the fires, the report notes.
Deaths on the southern island of Java, meanwhile, remained largely tied to urban and industrial sources, the study found.
It added that the number of citizens exposed to “unhealthy” to “hazardous” air quality reached a record peak of 58 million in September.
“Citizens inhaling hazardous-level air in Kalimantan alone nearly tripled from 2.8 million to 6.4 million during the worst days of the month,” it found.
Amid an El Nino weather pattern, Indonesia has been dealing with devastating wildfires sparked by severe drought, which have led to deforestation and sent toxic smog across the Southeast Asian archipelago.
It has also raised pollution levels in neighbouring countries, including Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor.
The government in Jakarta is facing increasing criticism for its response to the fires. On Wednesday, it defended its approach, noting it has deployed more than 72,000 people to carry out cloud-seeding and firefighting operations, activated more than 2,100 doctors and health workers in hard-hit areas, and distributed 5.3 million masks.

Former FIDE presidential candidate Rosenstein responded to accusations of circumventing sanctions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Former FIDE presidential candidate Rosenstein responded to accusations of circumventing sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
Vadim Rosenstein denied ties to the russian federation and claimed there was pressure during the FIDE elections. He challenged Timur Turlov’s victory.
German businessman Vadim Rosenstein, who ran for president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), denied allegations of ties to the Russian authorities and sanctions evasion, and also revealed details of the dirty election campaign and scandalous election for the federation's president, in which Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, "appeared" on the team of newly elected FIDE President Timur Turlov, reports Apostrophe.
On allegations of ties to Russia and pressure during the election
According to the businessman, he was threatened and pressured to withdraw his candidacy throughout the election campaign. He called it one of the dirtiest campaigns in FIDE's history and emphasized that his sole main goal was and remains the popularization of chess.
"Throughout the election period, I was blackmailed and threatened with the imposition of Ukrainian sanctions, with demands that I withdraw my candidacy. I am not a politician. I am a businessman and a person wholly devoted to chess. There is only one thing that interests me in this entire process—the popularization of chess!" Rosenstein said.
He also drew attention to the dirty campaign against him in the Ukrainian media, where accusations were made against him. According to him, journalists did not contact him for comment before publishing the materials, and later similar claims appeared in paid publications in English-language outlets.
The businessman categorically denied allegations of sanctions evasion and the supply of military-use products. He maintains that the publications cite no specific deals, goods, or entries on sanctions lists that could confirm such claims.
"Not a single publication names any specific deal, product, or sanctions-list entry. […] This is primitive manipulation and a substitution of facts," he emphasized.
Rosenstein separately denied claims that he was allegedly an agent of Russian influence. He said that he had never received or carried out instructions from the Russian authorities, and that his candidacy in the election was supported by the German Chess Federation.
The businessman also recalled that he had publicly advocated the immediate implementation of the decisions of the Court of Arbitration for Sport concerning the Chess Federation of Russia. At the same time, the Russian federation did not participate in the voting in the FIDE presidential election because its membership had been suspended.
Rosenstein also denied allegations related to the Russian company "VR Rus." According to him, he does not participate in its management and does not receive dividends. The company is managed by an external administrator, while, as the businessman claims, withdrawing from it requires permission from a government commission of the Russian Federation.
He also stated that WR Group had banned doing business with Russia, and that the group's companies do not enter into contracts with Russian counterparties. Previously signed agreements, he said, were fulfilled in accordance with EU legislation.
Commenting on information about the import of Italian footwear into Russia, Rosenstein called it an independent commercial operation by the Russian company, to which the German entities of WR Group have no connection.
He also denied reports of alleged supplies to the Russian company "NOVATEK."
"All orders received by the group's companies came from European partners, and they provided logistics services to those partners; I have already published evidence of this. And most importantly, all of this concerns events from 2019–2021, yet it is presented as if it were happening right now. At that time, these supplies complied with the applicable legislation, and they were discontinued in 2021. I am not personally acquainted with the owners of these companies," he added.
Rosenstein emphasized that his business operates in more than 70 markets worldwide, but, in his view, the publications focused exclusively on the Russian direction.
On refusing to recognize the results of the FIDE election
Commenting on the results of the FIDE presidential election, held on September 26 in Samarkand (Timur Turlov defeated Rosenstein in the second round by a score of 110 to 85), and the composition of the federation's new leadership, Rosenstein said that he did not recognize them.
"I do not recognize the election results, as I believe that Turlov and Payne violated Article 9.7 of the FIDE electoral regulations, which clearly prohibits candidates from actions, cooperation, or collusion with the intent to deceive or manipulate the outcome of the vote. I filed complaints with the Ethics Commission. Moreover, regardless of the outcome of the consideration of my complaints, I am certain that American and European sanctions will soon be imposed on Turlov," he says. "Therefore, I am convinced that new elections for the FIDE presidency will be held in the near future."
According to Rosenstein, he filed the relevant complaints with the Ethics Commission, and American and European sanctions could be imposed on Turlov. The entrepreneur also expressed his conviction that the federation would soon face new presidential elections.
The dispute surrounding Mykhailo Podolyak and Ukraine's representation in FIDE
Rosenstein separately commented on the scandal that erupted over the participation of Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, in the team of FIDE President-elect Timur Turlov.
As is known, in September, Podolyak accepted an invitation to join his team, which prompted objections from the Chess Federation of Ukraine (CFU). The Ukrainian federation stated that it had not authorized Podolyak to represent its interests in FIDE. In addition, the CFU challenged the federation's decision to assign Podolyak an identification code under the Ukrainian flag, claiming that this had been done despite its objections.
On October 23, the board of the European Chess Union (ECU), at a meeting in Budva, unanimously supported the position of the CFU. The European and Ukrainian federations stated their intention to submit a joint protest against the decision of the FIDE General Assembly and seek its annulment.
"It is a disgrace that FIDE is now run by Turlov and Podolyak, who have absolutely no ability to play chess. I am ready to sit down at the board with either of them at any moment and show who they really are," Rosenstein said.
Against the backdrop of this dispute, Rosenstein criticized FIDE's new leadership, saying that Turlov had retained the influence of the team of the federation's former president, Arkady Dvorkovich. He drew attention to the fact that Viswanathan Anand, who had previously held a similar position under Dvorkovich, became the federation's vice president.
"Today, after the elections, we can clearly see: Turlov has fully retained Dvorkovich's team and influence," Rosenstein says.
As for the attacks and pressure against him, Rosenstein called them a commissioned campaign carried out by a well-known Ukrainian media figure, who had also undertaken, for money, to have the sanctions against Turlov lifted.
"I was born in Ukraine, in the Zhytomyr region, into a Jewish family; I am a citizen of Germany," he says. "And for reasons incomprehensible to me, it is precisely in Ukraine that I am being smeared, while some people, on the contrary, praise Turlov, who was born in Moscow and continues to actively conduct business there, despite the fact that Ukraine itself imposed sanctions against him."
What caused the scandal
On September 26, the election for the president of the International Chess Federation took place in Samarkand. In the second round, Timur Turlov defeated Vadym Rosenstein by a vote of 110 to 85.
Before the vote, a public discussion arose around Rosenstein's candidacy because of media reports that raised questions about his possible business ties to Russia and compliance with sanctions restrictions. The entrepreneur himself denies these allegations.
Another part of the dispute concerns FIDE's new leadership and Mykhailo Podolyak's participation in Turlov's team. In September, Podolyak, an adviser to the Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, accepted an invitation to join the team of the federation's new president. The Chess Federation of Ukraine opposed this step and stated that it had not authorized Podolyak to represent its interests in FIDE.
On October 23, the board of the European Chess Union, at a meeting in Budva, unanimously supported the Chess Federation of Ukraine in the dispute over Podolyak's status. According to the position of the Ukrainian federation, FIDE assigned him an identification code under the Ukrainian flag despite the CFU's objections.
The European Chess Union and the Chess Federation of Ukraine announced their intention to file a joint protest against the decision of the FIDE General Assembly and seek its reversal.

Unity in action means turning our words into deeds, our determination into achievements and our decisions into results," he said.
Erdogan also announced that Türkiye had taken over the rotating chairmanship of the organization from Azerbaijan, thanking Baku for its efforts during its tenure.
He pledged to build on the organization's institutional achievements and promote greater cooperation in cultural activities, language, and travel among member states.
Emphasizing the importance of unity, Erdogan said there was “no room for division or discord in the Turkic world.”
"We are united, we stand together, and we will remain brothers forever," he added.
Erdogan also expressed confidence that the organization's Family and Women's Council would strengthen its ties with the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, while voicing hope that Turkmenistan would soon become a full member of the organization.
Regional peace, Gaza reconstruction
Turning to regional developments, Erdogan said a peaceful and stable South Caucasus would offer significant opportunities for regional countries and the entire Turkic world.
He expressed support for Azerbaijan's ongoing talks with Armenia, reaffirming Türkiye's commitment to contributing to lasting peace.
On Iran, Erdogan said Ankara hoped renewed tensions would be resolved through diplomacy rather than military confrontation.
Addressing the situation in Palestine, Erdogan urged Turkic states to step up efforts toward a just solution to the Palestinian issue.
He called for greater contributions to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza and the swift launch of reconstruction efforts.
The Turkish president also reiterated support for establishing an independent, sovereign Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Digital cooperation, cybersecurity
Erdogan also highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, digital trade, and space technologies.
Describing cybersecurity as vital as land, air, and maritime security, he called for the swift signing and implementation of a memorandum on cybersecurity cooperation.
He said member states could bring their markets together through a common digital trade platform, while accelerating work on a joint satellite project.
Erdogan also called on member countries to contribute to the development of a large Turkic language model covering the Oghuz, Kipchak, and Karluk language groups.
He said Türkiye's chairmanship would prioritize implementing an artificial intelligence and digital development action plan focused on concrete results.
The Turkish president also invited fellow leaders to attend the COP31 Leaders' Summit, scheduled for Nov. 11-12 in the southern Turkish city of Antalya.
Concluding his remarks, Erdogan thanked outgoing Secretary General Kubanychbek Omuraliev for his service since 2022 and wished incoming Secretary General Mirvahid Azimov success.
He described Türkiye's assumption of the organization's chairmanship as a "significant responsibility," pledging to fulfill its duties.
Following his opening remarks at the summit, Erdogan gave the floor to the visiting heads of state and officials.
After the speeches, Erdogan announced the conclusion of the summit.
"With the Ankara Declaration adopted and the decisions taken today, we have outlined concrete steps guided by our motto, 'Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.' I thank each of you for your valuable contributions, constructive approaches, and the spirit of brotherhood you have demonstrated," Erdogan concluded.

‘Godspeed, Captain’: Heartfelt tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:16:56 UTC
17:16:56 KST

Tributes have poured in following the death of British actor Patrick Stewart, celebrated for his decades-long Shakespearean stage career and iconic roles in the Star Trek and X-Men franchises.
Tributes from across Hollywood and beyond are pouring in following the news of the death of legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86.
The celebrated actor, a two-time Olivier Award winner and multiple-time Tony, Golden Globes, and SAG Awards nominee, died following a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”.
Stewart was a commanding and charismatic performer who brought gravitas to all his roles – be it Shakespeare or a starship captain on Star Trek: The Next Generation and a mutant telepath in the X-Men series.
He will be remembered for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Professor Charles Xavier, Enobarbus in "Antony and Cleopatra", Claudius opposite David Tennant's Hamlet, as well as his memorable turns in John Boorman’s Excalibur, David Lynch’s Dune, Mel Brooks’ Robin Hood: Men in Tights, and as the soft-spoken neo-Nazi leader in Jeremy Saulnier's Green Room.
The official Star Trek social media account thanked Patrick Stewart.
"A voice. A presence. A captain unlike any other," the account says, adding: "Sir Patrick Stewart gave generations of fans an icon who inspired us to look toward the stars. Today, we celebrate an extraordinary life and an enduring legacy."
His fellow USS Enterprise captain William Shatner wrote: “What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”
George Takei, who starred in Star Trek: The Original Series with Shatner, wrote on Bluesky: "Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before. He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”
Alex Kurtzman, who co-created “Star Trek: Picard”, wrote: “It’s hard, impossible really, to express how grateful I am to have shared this moment with him. Grateful in a ‘once in a career’ kind of way. Right from our first meeting, he made it known that the only reason to play Picard again was to break new ground. His challenge was clear: Picard needed to be the man we knew and loved, but also entirely different, just as Patrick himself was 30 years after last wearing the uniform. The world of the Federation had to feel fresh and mirror many of the big issues the world faces today, issues that he wanted to face as a human and an artist, which meant interrogating an ideal to expose something more honest. He demanded truth. And in perhaps the trickiest high wire act, he wanted to reward fans with the nostalgia they would rightly demand, while subverting their expectations."
Stewart’s Next Generation cast members also paid tribute, with Wil Wheaton (Wesley Crusher) posting a photograph of the two with the caption: “Godspeed, Captain.”
Elsewhere, Will Riker actor Jonathan Frakes released a statement that read: “There’s no one on this planet that I have acted with or directed more often than my late great friend Patrick Stewart. He will be with me forever. May he rest in Peace.”
Marvel Studios also paid tribute to Stewart, saying he brought Charles Xavier to life with "extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday."
“He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”
Actor Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside Stewart in the X-Men films as Logan/Wolverine, described him as a "tremendous friend and man". In a post on Instagram, he wrote: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."
"I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
Rebecca Romijn, who played Mystique in X-Men said: "I feel so grateful to have known him for the last 25 years, and to have been in his orbit."
"He was positively delicious, hilarious, naughty, incredible sense of humour," Romijn added, "and that booming vice of his that always spoke to the back of the room..."
A particularly heartfelt tribute came from Sir Ian McKellen, with whom Stewart shared a longtime friendship, the screen in the X-Men films, and the stage with performances in "Waiting for Godot" and "No Man's Land."
McKellen described Stewart as the "most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic".
In a statement shared on social media, McKellen described him as “a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love”.
The two frequently expressed their affection for each other, with McKellen officiating Stewart's wedding in 2013.
“Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end,” McKellen wrote. “You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues.”
McKellen remembered trying to talk Stewart out of accepting the role of Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, asking: “But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?”
Stewart took the part anyway. “Thank goodness for us all that he did,” McKellen said, going on to praise his friend who used his “international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes”, as well as classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Harold Pinter and Samuel Beckett.
McKellen wrote that despite the US becoming his “adopted home”, the actor “never forsook his origins”.
“And the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University in Yorkshire,” he wrote.
McKellen will share the screen with Stewart one last time for his the actor's final performance as Professor Charles Xavier in Avengers: Doomsday, which will be released on 18 December.
RIP Sir Patrick. As he said as Picard: “Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.”
