Over 75 hours of ceasefire: Ukraine's human rights commissioner arrives in Armiansk, 25 buses ready for evacuation from Oleshky
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 EET
17:00:00 KST

Over 75 hours of ceasefire: Ukraine's human rights commissioner arrives in Armiansk, 25 buses ready for evacuation from Oleshky
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has reported that the ceasefire for the humanitarian mission to Oleshky has been holding for over 75 hours. The Ukrainian team is in Armiansk, where 25 buses with a total capacity of at least 750 passengers have been prepared to evacuate residents.
Source: Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Lubinets on X (Twitter); Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova
Quote from Lubinets: "We have now had a ceasefire between Ukraine and the Russian Federation for more than 75 hours. Special thanks to the people overseeing and monitoring the ceasefire process. Neither side has violated the ceasefire even once."
Details: The Ukrainian official noted that this is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established over such a large section of the front and has lasted this long.
Lubinets said the humanitarian mission was effectively launched on 23 October. Since then, he and Lantratova have been coordinating technical issues on a daily basis. Following his arrival the day before, the parties held another meeting and plan to travel together to Oleshky on 30 October.
The mission aims to deliver humanitarian aid to the city's residents and facilitate the departure of those who wish to leave. Lubinets noted that assistance will be provided both to people who want to leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory and to those who wish to go to the Russian Federation. Residents who decide to remain in Oleshky will receive humanitarian support.
Quote from Lantratova: "The humanitarian aid was put together according to the needs reported to us by the people. This includes food, hygiene products, everything essential, medical supplies, fuel – everything people need."
Details: According to the Russian representative, 25 buses with a total capacity of 750 passengers, special transport for about 30 bedridden individuals, and nine ambulances have been prepared for the evacuation. She stated that over 50 medical staff are working with the convoy.
Lantratova also reported that the buses are stocked with water and dry rations. A separate bus with cages has been allocated for transporting pets, and another bus has been designated for luggage.
Quote from Lantratova: "People who have made the decision to leave will have the opportunity to register and board the buses until 14:00. The distribution of humanitarian aid will take place after 14:00."
Details: She explained that boarding the buses and distributing aid were scheduled at different times to avoid crowding.
Lantratova also stated that two people had been killed whilst the mission was being prepared, including a bomb-disposal expert during demining operations. She did not specify the circumstances of the second person's death.
Journalists from Ukraine, the US and Russia have joined in covering the mission. Lubinets expressed hope that the experience of assisting Oleshky residents could be applied to humanitarian missions in other towns and villages.
Both officials thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her mediation. According to Lubinets, her team has been facilitating the mission since 20 October.
Background:
- Davyd Arakhamiia, the head of the Servant of the People faction who is involved in organising the operation, reported on 29 October that a delegation of representatives from Ukraine, the US and Russia had arrived at the location from which aid was to be delivered to temporarily occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast the following day.
- Under the agreements between the Russian and Ukrainian sides, the evacuation route for residents of Oleshky will run via Russia and Belarus to Ukraine.
- Earlier, US television channel Fox News published a document signed by Russian commissioner Yana Lantratova which stated that Oleshky residents who wish to evacuate to Ukraine will initially be taken to Anapa airport in Russia's Krasnodar Krai. From Anapa, the Ukrainian delegation and Oleshky residents will be taken to Homiel (Gomel) airport in Belarus on a Russian Defence Ministry military transport plane. This is likely to take place on Saturday 31 October.

Why Switzerland is missing from the debate over trust in government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Why Switzerland is missing from the debate over trust in government
How can governments regain the public’s trust? The OECD brought politicians, officials and civil society representatives together in Paris for a discussion. But Switzerland was absent, and the potential of direct democracy to rebuild that trust went unexplored. An analysis.
Hundreds of government and civil society representatives gathered at the heavily guarded Paris conference centre of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to confront a growing problem: public trust in government institutions is crumbling.
While participants debated among themselves inside the OECD headquarters, tens of thousands of school pupilsExternal link and university students were protesting on the streets of Paris. Later that week, over the weekend of October 17, there was looting and riots.
The scale of the problem is evident in the OECD’s Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions, published in summer 2026. It found that many people lack confidence in their governments’ ability to deal with major challenges such as global warming, migration and geopolitical tensions.
Across the 38 countries surveyed, an average of just 40% of people say they have at least a moderate level of trust in their government.
‘Growing expectations’ of a greater say in political decisions
According to the survey, fewer than one in three people feel that “people like them” have a say in government decisions, despite a large majority believing that elections can bring about change. This contradiction suggests voters want more ways to participate between elections. The report describes “growing and unmet citizens’ expectations about having a say in decision-making beyond elections”.
Switzerland is a clear outlier, where 62% of people trust the government, and 65% feel that those who have a say in political decisions are “people like them”.
For Switzerland, the findings could be seen as international validation of its political system. Regular nationwide votes help people feel heard, and a consensus government brings together almost all major political forces. This means nearly all voters have someone in the government who represents their part of the political spectrum.
On the face of it, Switzerland would seem an obvious case study for countries looking for ways out of the trust crisis. Yet the OECD report does not present it as an example, and its political model played no role in the conference discussions.
Participation models go largely unchallenged
Rather than endorsing a particular model, the study offers broader recommendations on what governments can do to build trust. These include giving citizens more opportunities to participate in decision-making and ensuring that the civil service is politically neutral.
Read our analysis of the OECD Trust Survey:
More
High Swiss trust in government sparks little interest abroad
Participation also featured prominently in discussions at the OECD conference. But speakers largely focused on what their countries were already doing. Costa Rica cited its social dialogue as a success story, and Andorra is making efforts to increase transparency in public administration.
Art O’Leary of Ireland’s Electoral Commission was particularly proud of his country’s citizens’ assemblies, where members are chosen by lottery. Their recommendations on same-sex marriage and abortion were put to referendums and approved by voters. The unexpectedly decisive results attracted considerable attention at the time.
O’Leary explained in detail how citizens’ assemblies work and how Ireland has used them. But he did not mention that Ireland’s last such assembly was three years ago, and that no more have been announced. No one pressed him on whether these assemblies, successful though they have been, are becoming a permanent feature of Irish democracy.
Read our article on the cancellation of a citizens’ assembly in Geneva and international developments in this field:
More
Are citizens’ assemblies on the decline in an era of eroding democracy?
When other politicians and civil servants at the OECD conference discussed what greater participation might look like, they often sounded as though their countries already had it largely under control. They showcased their petition systems, dialogues with citizens, and citizens’ assemblies. They seemed to suggest that others might follow their lead.
Yet these examples were rarely scrutinised. No one pointed out, for example, that the much-cited petition systems do not actually shift political power from politicians to citizens.
Plenty of concern, little talk of change
Calls are growing louder for participation that would genuinely shift political power to the people. The protests in Paris and elsewhere are only the latest sign of this, and speakers at the conference referred to them repeatedly.
“We have kids demonstrating right this morning in Paris,” Elsa Pilichowski, the OECD’s director for public governance, said as the conference opened. They have no say in decision-making, she added. Later, a Portuguese minister came close to shouting, as though he wanted to take to the streets himself: “People are angry, they are upset. They feel that governments are not solving their problems.”
No one denied the absurdity that inside, officials discussed public trust without the public, while outside, protesters encountered riot police and water cannons. Others saw the authorities failing to prevent the destruction of private property. Neither image does much to restore public trust.
Also, no one discussed what changes France might make to its political system in response to the protests. O’Leary presented Ireland’s experience with citizens’ assemblies but stopped short of suggesting that other countries adopt them. No one asked whether decisionmakers were genuinely prepared to surrender meaningful political power to citizens. In an international organisation, one does not interfere in another country’s affairs.
Still, many speakers seemed genuinely concerned. They appeared to recognise that technological and social change has fundamentally altered the relationship between citizens and the state. Governments and public institutions can no longer rely on the trust they once enjoyed. This is partly because people can now theoretically access vast amounts of information – and misinformation – on their own.
Those who ask must act
“All OECD countries are trying to improve trust. In a rapidly changing world, they are ready to take action. Hopefully, this will help stabilise public trust,” Pilichowski told Swissinfo. “In the past, people went to the polls every few years—and today, analysis shows that this isn’t enough.” That is why many countries are now developing forms of “participatory democracy”, she said.
Pilichowski said the data pointed to one clear conclusion: governments must react after consultations. “If you consult a representative group of citizens, decisions must follow,” she said.
Of course, it is unclear exactly how introducing more social dialogue would strengthen trust in society. Will angry citizens want to participate if they know they are only being listened to? The more consequential forms of “participatory democracy”, as Pilichowski calls it, require governments to relinquish some power. Under direct democracy, for example, the government must repeatedly win majority support from voters if it wants to get its proposals through.
During the two-day conference in Paris, direct democracy was largely absent from discussion. When referendums came up, Brexit was the main example, and was framed as a negative, populist exception.
Brexit is still a major issue in the UK:
More
Ten years after Brexit, the ‘Swiss model’ just keeps popping up
But the Brexit vote was fundamentally different from Switzerland’s instruments of direct democracy, which allow citizens to initiate nationwide votes from the bottom up. Brexit was initiated by the British government. Despite the slogan “take back control”, the UK had, and still has, no mechanism for citizens to bring their own proposals onto the nationwide ballot.
Can Switzerland be an example for others?
Pilichowski says the Swiss model received little attention because Switzerland is a special case. Its mechanisms of direct democracy are “so deeply rooted in society”. They are the “most direct and obvious means” of giving citizens greater power, she says, but countries do have other options. “There are different ways, and countries can choose different paths.”
For its approach to feature more prominently, Switzerland would probably need to take a more active role in the international debate over trust. But whether it wants to is another question. The country often likes to see itself as a special exception.
The next debate at the OECD will be about an issue that Switzerland has not yet solved: the gap in trust between people with and without an advanced education. While 80% of highly educated people in Switzerland trust the government, the figure is only 45% among those with lower levels of education.
How confident are you in the state and society? Tell us:

Greece arrests three over explosion that killed six people in Athens
Italy

16:59:26 KST

ATHENS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Greece has arrested two Greek men and an Albanian national suspected of stealing copper gas pipes from a building, causing a leak that led to a deadly explosion in central Athens last month, authorities said.
Six people were killed during the September 25 blast in the tourist district of Plaka, four Americans among them.
Following an investigation, experts with the fire brigade’s crime investigation unit concluded that hours before the blast the suspects damaged the two-storey building’s main natural gas supply infrastructure as they removed the copper pipe parts, fire brigade officials said late on Thursday.
The explosion occurred early in the morning when one of the residents turned the light on.
The suspects are expected to appear before a prosecutor on Friday.

French centrists’ feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:59:25 CET
16:59:25 KST

By Michel Rose
PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Infighting has broken out among centrist candidates for France’s presidential race, splitting the mainstream vote and making a runoff between far-right Marine Le Pen and hard-left Jean-Luc Melenchon more likely.
Opinion polls before next April’s presidential election show Le Penis nearly certain to qualify for a second-round runoff in May and that Melenchon is consistently nudging ahead of mainstream candidates.
Centre-right Edouard Philippe, President Emmanuel Macron’s former prime minister, has so far been the centre’s torchbearer.
But Philippe’s lacklustre campaign, voter weariness near the end of Macron’s two terms, an explosive social and security context and the challenges he faces from within his own camp have hurt his polling, people in Macron’s camp and political analysts say.
“There’s panic on board because there was no scenario planned for this. They hadn’t anticipated the cataclysm under way,” said Philippe Moreau-Chevrolet, a political communications specialist at Sciences Po.
Philippe has also faced criticism over several awkward interventions — including suggesting in a podcast that ideally a newly elected president should have three months to rest before taking office — and political analysts say he is struggling to connect with voters at a time of rising political tensions.
“The terrible thing is that he isn’t cutting through,” Moreau-Chevrolet told Reuters. “They didn’t understand that you have to campaign. There’s a kind of dilettantism.”
The anxiety has sharpened tensions between Philippe and his main rival, Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister. They are locked in a battle over who should step aside for the centrist ticket.
Philippe fell to 15% support in an IFOP-Fiducial poll for Le Figaro newspaper, a six-point drop since September. That is below the 16.5% for Melenchon, who would have enough to qualify for a runoff against Le Pen.
Attal stood at 13%, behind Melenchon and Raphael Glucksmann, a mainstream centre-left candidate.
Under pressure from lawmakers in his camp to abandon his presidential ambitions and rally to Philippe, Attal irritated many Macron allies this week by reviving the idea of a broad centrist primary, a proposal critics say risks fuelling division at a time when moderates can least afford it.
Still, Attal has leverage. As leader of Macron’s Renaissance party, he controls the purse strings of the party machine.
CENTRIST VOTE FRAGMENTS
“It’s catastrophic,” said Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp.
“They are attacking one another in the media and they are both collapsing in the polls. We’re heading straight towards an RN-LFI second round,” he said of Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) and Melenchon’s France Unbowed (LFI). “In the current state of opinion, I don’t see how we avoid it.”
The fragmentation stretches beyond the Philippe-Attal feud.
On the centre-left, Glucksmann has gained ground after winning the Socialist primary. On the right, Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister, and David Lisnard, the free-market mayor of Cannes, are targeting the same moderate electorate.
Philippe’s supporters say reports of his demise are premature. Laurent Marcangeli, a member of Philippe’s party Horizons, acknowledged recent polling setbacks but said the former prime minister remained the only centrist candidate with a realistic path to the runoff.
“He’s still in the race for the second round and to prevent a Le Pen-Melenchon duel,” said Marcangeli, adding that in some polls Attal scored as low as single digits.
Some Macron allies, however, are openly questioning whether either man should carry on. They say any association with Macron, who is finishing his second term at record-low popularity, will weigh on a centrist candidate.
“The two of them are collapsing,” said Perrine Goulet, a lawmaker from Macron ally MoDem. “Any candidate who has been in a Macron government is going to be struggling.”
With Le Pen and Melenchon consolidating support at opposite ends of the spectrum, she said moderates needed to put aside personal ambitions and rally behind a single contender able to unite supporters of Glucksmann through to Retailleau.
“We’re calling on everyone to put their egos aside and find the best candidate,” Goulet said.
“If we keep Glucksmann on one side, Retailleau on the other, Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, we’ll end up with an LFI-RN second round. The danger is simply too great.”
(Editing by Mark John and Timothy Heritage)

Nigerian families and survivors seek justice over miners’ deaths
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:58:35 CET
16:58:35 KST

By Ibrahim and Ndiamitso
MINNA, Nigeria, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Families of 37 artisinal miners who died in custody in Nigeria want swift justice and the return of property seized during their arrest, saying no financial compensation will make up for their loss.
A presidential panel on Tuesday found that the detainees, who were suspected of being illegal miners, had died from overcrowding, extreme heat, dehydration and neglect while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger state last month.
Nigeria’s government welcomed the panel’s findings, and Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said the panel’s report had been sent to the attorney-general for immediate judicial action. He did not respond to requests for comment on when victims’ families and survivors would receive compensation.
The deaths, including of teenagers, triggered protests in Nigeria, raising new concerns about conditions in detention facilities and the treatment of suspects awaiting trial.
“What we wanted was for our children to be alive and return to us,” said Zainab Salihu, whose son was among the dead.
She said the deaths in detention had led to the deterioration of the health of her husband, who later died. Reuters was unable to verify the circumstances of her husband’s death.
“No matter how much money they give us, it will never bring our children back,” Salihu said.
Dantala Tanko, whose 25-year-old son Suleiman died in detention, is struggling to come to terms with his loss.
“Now he is gone, and this is deeply painful for me. I know he will never return,” he said after praying at his son’s grave.
Some survivors said they appreciated the investigation’s findings, but wanted accountability.
“Officers who demonstrate such disregard for human life should not remain in positions of authority. They must be held accountable, and appropriate disciplinary action should be taken,” said said 25-year-old Dauda Shehu.
Abdulsalam Yakubu, 23, said government action had been slow. He said he wanted the government to return motocycles, phones, mining equipment and gold which he said had been seized during the victims’ arrest.
“We have suffered enough. We are asking for justice, the promised support, and the return of our property so that we can begin to rebuild our lives,” he told Reuters.
(Reporting by Ibrahim Ndiamitso in Minna, Writing by Ben Ezeamalu, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

People wishing to leave Oleshky would be given an opportunity to evacuate by 2 p.m. on Friday, while humanitarian aid distribution was scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., he added.

Arakhamia later reported that the Ukrainian delegation, accompanied by evacuated residents of Oleshky, was heading to Anapa. From there, they were expected to fly to Belarus before continuing home by bus.
A total of 25 buses with capacity for 750 passengers had been prepared for the evacuation, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Cyberattack on Refrigerators: Pentagon Investigates Series of Malfunctions at Military Bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:56:54 UTC
16:56:54 KST

The Pentagon is investigating a series of freezer malfunctions at US military bases in August as a suspected cyberattack.
Reuters reported this, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
US military investigators have already contacted their French counterparts to exchange information about a similar cyberattack targeting commercial refrigeration units in Europe.
The Pentagon confirmed that a unit of the U.S. Cyber Command is working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners.
In August, the malfunctions affected at least six military stores at US bases where service members buy groceries.
In some cases, the refrigerators did not simply shut down but switched to defrost mode on their own, causing the temperature inside to rise and food to spoil.
A similar incident occurred in France, where hackers hijacked temperature controllers at more than 350 establishments and stores.
In some cases in France, the temperature in commercial refrigerators was raised so high that the equipment caught fire, with losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
Cybersecurity experts say these vulnerabilities stem from outdated controllers, which were originally designed for standalone operation, being connected to the internet.
Earlier, the Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI) called for strengthening the security of refrigeration systems, warning that a hacked cooling system can be just as dangerous as a malfunctioning one.
It was previously reported that the Pentagon suffered a data breach affecting more than three million people connected to the US military.
The exposed information includes Social Security numbers and details of the positions held by military personnel and civilian employees.

Bolsonaro's self-exile, ChatGPT blunder cloud political ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:55:00 UTC
16:55:00 KST

Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has faced widespread ridicule and mounting political isolation after fleeing to the United States and declaring himself Brazil's rightful leader following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
The 45-year-old's claims sparked a wave of mockery on Brazilian social media, where pop star Anitta jokingly declared herself free of cellulite, one influencer proclaimed himself the "true president" of Twitter, and another announced he had won the next lottery.
The eldest son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro stunned Brazil's political establishment Wednesday when he published a statement challenging the election outcome and presenting himself as the country's legitimate leader. The declaration, however, quickly became an embarrassment after a series of confusing revisions and failed to win support from influential figures within his own political camp.
Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday after leaving Brazil through Argentina and Ecuador, despite a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports as part of ongoing investigations, including a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Hours after arriving in the United States, he published a statement on social media proclaiming himself Brazil's "true president-elect." About an hour later, he deleted the document and replaced it with a revised version describing himself as the country's "leader."
The abrupt change prompted questions about the original statement, which also featured an outdated version of Brazil's coat of arms, abandoned in the 1960s.
A close Bolsonaro ally, right-wing influencer and podcast host Paulo Figueiredo, later blamed the errors on ChatGPT, saying the chatbot had been used to help prepare the document.
Figueiredo, who acts as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States and initially circulated the statement to journalists, said the document had passed through several drafts involving multiple contributors.
According to Figueiredo, Flavio's younger brother, former Congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, sought ChatGPT's assistance in finalizing the letter. The chatbot allegedly inserted an earlier version of the text and an outdated national emblem.
"When generating the document, AI ended up including an earlier version of the text, in which Flavio presented himself as the true 'president-elect'," Figueiredo wrote on X, adding that the mistakes were discovered only after the document had been distributed to the press.
He said Flavio eventually chose the word "leader" for legal and moral reasons, describing the changes as minor and claiming those involved found the mistake amusing.
OpenAI and Flavio Bolsonaro's press officers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Despite the revised wording, Figueiredo maintained that the senator considered Sunday's election illegitimate and intended to continue challenging the result.
The declaration drew widespread condemnation in Brazilian media, with several outlets describing its language as an attempt to undermine democratic institutions.
O Globo newspaper likened Flavio Bolsonaro to a "lunatic asylum Napoleon," while Folha de S.Paulo dismissed the statement as "pathetic."
Politicians across the political spectrum called for the election results to be respected, further exposing the senator's isolation.
Among the most significant rebukes came from Sao Paulo Gov. Tarcisio de Freitas, a former minister under Jair Bolsonaro who had been considered a leading contender to represent the right in the next presidential race before the former president backed his son.
"We are democrats. The election result is sovereign. What we have seen is the will of the majority of the population, which must be respected," De Freitas told Estadao newspaper.
With Flavio now outside Brazil and his political standing weakened, attention has quickly shifted to who might emerge as the conservative movement's leading figure.
De Freitas, who enjoys strong support in business circles, acknowledged that a presidential bid in 2030 was a possibility.
Other prominent Bolsonaro allies have also rejected claims that the election was stolen.
Rogerio Marinho, who coordinated Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign, said there was no evidence of electoral fraud. Supreme Court Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, also issued a statement defending the security and integrity of Brazil's electoral process.
The election authority and international observers have recognized the result, while leaders around the world have acknowledged Lula's victory.
Despite his defeat, Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to lead the opposition from the United States, seeking to maintain his influence over Brazil's conservative movement while remaining outside the country.
His departure has not, however, translated into an immediate loss of political strength for the right. Conservatives secured substantial representation in Congress, and Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) is expected to hold the largest number of seats when the new legislature begins its term in February.
But political analyst Geraldo Monteiro of the State University of Rio de Janeiro said Flavio's attempt to establish himself as a leader in exile was unlikely to command the loyalty he expected.
Rather than a political misstep, Monteiro described the declaration as a calculated effort to preserve his authority over the conservative camp.
"I do not believe he has the means to lead the opposition from afar, as the newly elected officials have already secured their seats and no longer need him," Monteiro told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
He said the statement had drawn a dividing line within the right between politicians willing to demonstrate unwavering loyalty to the Bolsonaro family and those unwilling to become involved in another attempt to undermine democratic institutions.
Monteiro also drew parallels between Flavio's conduct and that of his father, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.
The backlash has extended to the leadership of Bolsonaro's own party.
On Thursday, PL leader Valdemar Costa Neto visited Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving his sentence under house arrest. Asked about Flavio's statement afterward, Costa Neto made clear that the party was not endorsing the declaration.
"No one approves" of the letter, he said, adding that the party needed to "move forward."

Health workers and local residents danced and sang outside an Ebola treatment centre in Mongbwalu, in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri province, to celebrate the discharge of its last remaining patients. In footage published by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) on 28 October, staff and members of the community gather outside the facility, moving to the rhythm of the celebrations.
According to the medical charity, it is the first time since May that the centre has had no confirmed Ebola patients under treatment. The joyful scenes mark a welcome moment for healthcare workers and residents in a region that has been grappling with the deadly virus for months.
The celebrations come despite the continuing Ebola epidemic in the region. On 27 October, Congolese health authorities reported that Africa's latest outbreak had surpassed 10,000 confirmed cases, the vast majority recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause life-threatening illness and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people. Although the discharge of the final patients represents an important milestone for the MSF facility in Mongbwalu, it does not mean the outbreak has ended or that new cases cannot emerge. The charity's announcement concerns patients being treated at this particular centre, rather than the wider situation across Ituri province or the country.

The Swiss National Bank (SNB) posted a profit of CHF44,2 billion in the first nine months of 2026. The third quarter alone was also very positive.
Following a profit of 25.2 billion in the first half of the year, the third quarter period resulted in a profit of around CHF19 billion.
+ Should the SNB give more to the government and cantons?
The SNB recorded a gain of CHF43.3 billion on its foreign currency positions in the first three quarters and a small valuation gain of CHF1.2 billion on its gold holdings, the volume of which remained unchanged. There was also a minimal gain of CHF100 million on its Swiss franc positions.
The SNB said its results depend predominantly on developments in the gold, foreign exchange and capital markets. Significant fluctuations are therefore the norm, and it is only possible to a limited extent to draw conclusions about the full-year result from the interim figures.

‘My life is buried here’: Iranian man whose 12 family members were killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:51:08 UTC
16:51:08 KST

‘My life is buried here’: Iranian man whose 12 family members were killed
Hamed Mirzaei lost his wife, parents and many others in a devastating US-Israeli attack on Tehran.
Hamed Mirzaei lost 12 members of his family in an attack on a residential building in Tehran. Among those killed was his wife, 26-year-old Mohadeseh. The young couple had been planning to start a family.
He describes how the United States-Israeli attack on his home on March 9, 2026, changed his life in this first-person account, shared with Al Jazeera:
“Seven months have passed since the bombing. Even now, on many days, when I come to my senses, I find myself back at my destroyed home, searching for my loved ones.
“My grandfather and my father’s uncle built the house that was hit. They divided its apartments among their children. A year ago, when I got married, my wife and I moved into one of the apartments in the same building. We were just beginning to prepare for a child. We were young, with our whole lives ahead of us. Then the bombing happened.
“March 9 was a Monday. At about 1:00 in the afternoon, I left home to check in at work. At 2:30 pm, my wife messaged me, asking me to buy her some headache medicine on my way back. I called her to ask which medicine she wanted, but her phone was busy. We were expecting guests at home, so I called our guest’s phone. That line was busy, too. I hung up, intending to call my wife again.
“I was five minutes from home when I suddenly heard a whistling sound. The first missile had just struck.
“The ground shook beneath my feet from the force of the explosion. With my phone still in my hand, I called my wife again, but her phone was unreachable. I began calling my family members, my grandfather, my father, my mother. All their phones were unreachable.
“Even so, I thought our home had not been hit. I kept telling myself it was impossible that they had struck our house. I thought perhaps a missile had hit somewhere else in our neighbourhood. In those moments, all I wanted was to get home and see that the house was still standing.
“In those same minutes, five more missiles struck our home.
“When I arrived, I saw that everyone in the neighbourhood had come out of their homes, but I still couldn’t bring myself to step into the street. It never even crossed my mind that those missiles could have hit our house. But they had. Even from a distance, it was clear that all that remained of the house was its skeleton.
“When I reached it, everything was burning. All I could think about was getting to the second floor and finding my wife, but the staircase was gone. Several neighbours from the first floor were trapped beneath the rubble. The Red Crescent helped rescue them.
“I thought that if they kept searching, perhaps they would find my family alive somewhere beneath the debris, too. But they didn’t. No one was found that hour. Nor in the hours that followed. By nightfall, no one else had been found in the building. Twelve members of my family were missing, and I still couldn’t bring myself to leave.
“That night, the next day, the day after that, and every day following the attack, I returned to my home. For 20 days, I searched through the rubble and the remnants of the missiles and explosions for my loved ones. There was nothing left.
“My wife was killed. My sister-in-law, who had been a guest in our home, was killed. My father and mother, my grandfather and grandmother, my aunt’s husband and her daughter, my uncle, my father’s cousin, his wife and their child were all killed. Twelve members of my family died in the attack, and people ask me how I am.
“I miss them. I miss them more with every passing day. At first, I thought that perhaps, with time, our grief would ease and we would find some peace. But we haven’t. As each day passes, I feel worse.
“I was an only child, and I always thought that, although I had no brothers or sisters, I had a large family with whom I would grow old. All my life, the members of our extended family had lived together, side by side. Now all those people, and all the love that flowed through our family, have vanished.
“I am the only one left. There is no one else from my family. I am utterly alone.
“I am living proof for anyone who still believes that war can lead to a good outcome. Anyone who thinks war is good should look at what has happened to me and ask themselves: ‘What, in any of this, is good?’
“The building where I was born, the building where my father was born, the building where I had hoped my child would be born, all of it was destroyed in a fraction of a second. My home and my family were wiped out together. And when I miss them, I truly don’t know where to turn or what to look at.
“Seven months have passed since the day they destroyed our home, and every day, when I wake up, I come here to look at the ruins. I cannot bring myself to leave this place. I feel as though my life is buried here, and I return every day, hoping I might find some piece of it. But there is nothing left.
“When someone asks me what I am thinking or how I feel, I cannot answer. Everything I have ever done in my life was for the happiness of my family. Now I no longer have a family for whom I can do anything.
“Every day, I ask myself: ‘Why do I keep going?’ I have no answer.
“The difference between me and my family, who were killed, is that they were buried beneath the rubble, while I am still walking around. Other than that, I am just as dead as they are. The only difference is that my name is not included among the dead.”

How cleaning affects the energy of the home
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:51:00 EET
16:51:00 KST

How cleaning affects the energy of the home
Kyiv • UNN
Folk traditions associate cleanliness with prosperity, while cleaning is advised to begin from the top. The practical benefit is less dust and clutter.
Cleaning can be not only a household chore but also a way to change the atmosphere at home and your own well-being. In folk beliefs, a clean space is associated with prosperity, good luck, and new opportunities. More details about how to tidy up your home, which traditions are associated with cleaning, and what can help make your home more comfortable will be provided by UNN.
Details
In different cultures, cleaning has not only practical but also symbolic significance. It is associated with cleansing from negativity, renewing one's living space, and attracting prosperity. Such beliefs are particularly common in feng shui traditions and folk omens.
Why clutter is associated with negative energy
According to Eastern beliefs, the energy of Qi plays an important role in a person's life. Dust, cluttered corners, and accumulated unnecessary items are believed to hinder its free flow. That is why feng shui followers recommend regularly clearing the home of clutter and not neglecting hard-to-reach places. Particular attention is paid to broken objects, old clothes that are no longer used, and damaged dishes. In folk beliefs, such things symbolize stagnation and tie people to the past, while getting rid of them is perceived as an opportunity to make room for new changes in life. There is also a wholly practical side to this tradition. In particular, when there are fewer unnecessary things at home, it is easier to find what is needed, maintain cleanliness, and organize household life. And the feeling of an orderly space can contribute to calm and comfort.
Where to start when cleansing the home
It is important not to try to do everything at once. First, you can sort through items that have not been used for a long time, clear surfaces, and pay attention to places where dust accumulates. This approach allows you to gradually organize the space and prevents cleaning from becoming an exhausting task.
How to clean properly so that there is more space in the home
In traditions of cleansing the home, not only the result but also the sequence of actions is important. In particular, followers of energy practices advise starting with upper surfaces and gradually moving to lower ones. First, dust is wiped from ceilings, lighting fixtures, and the tops of cabinets. Then they move on to shelves, tables, and other furniture. After that, carpets are cleaned and the floor is washed. This sequence also has a practical advantage: dust and debris that fall while the upper surfaces are being cleaned can be removed at the end.
To remove dust, a dry cloth is used first, and then, if necessary, the surface is wiped with a damp cloth. According to folk beliefs, the floor—and especially the threshold of the home—is best washed with salt, ordinary or sea salt, in order to cleanse the house energetically. Do not forget about corners and remote areas of rooms. In folk beliefs, these are supposedly the places where negative energy accumulates. From the perspective of ordinary cleaning, these areas also require attention, since dust that is not always immediately visible can collect there.
Why it is important to get rid of unnecessary things
If broken or unnecessary items are found during cleaning, it is worth deciding whether there is any reason to keep them at home. Things that are no longer used take up space and make it more difficult to maintain order. In a symbolic sense, letting go of excess is associated with readiness for a new stage of life. Therefore, sorting through a closet, shelves, or a storage room can become a kind of renewal ritual. It is only important not to throw things away thoughtlessly; items that are still suitable for use can, in particular, be given to those who need them.
Which day of the week is best for cleaning
Folk omens attribute special significance to each day of the week. According to these beliefs, the time when order is restored can symbolically influence prosperity, good luck, and the atmosphere in the home.
In some beliefs, Monday is considered an unfavorable day for cleaning, as it is associated with the risk of financial losses.
Tuesday is called a favorable day for tidying up and symbolically attracting monetary energy.
Wednesday is associated with prosperity in affairs and business.
In folk beliefs, Thursday symbolizes cleansing the space and opening up new opportunities.
Friday is advised not to be overloaded with heavy housework, especially if fatigue has accumulated by the end of the week.
Saturday is traditionally considered a convenient time for a thorough cleaning, when one can devote attention to the entire home.
Sunday is often reserved for rest rather than extensive household chores.
How to Finish Cleaning and Refresh the Atmosphere
After tidying up, it is worth airing out the rooms. Fresh air will help refresh the atmosphere in the home, while open windows are symbolically associated with the movement of energy and the release of stagnation. Another important element is one’s own mood. If cleaning is perceived not as an endless obligation but as an opportunity to take care of yourself and your space, the process can become more enjoyable. You can play your favorite music or, after finishing your tasks, create a cozy atmosphere with pleasant lighting or a favorite fragrance.
Some traditions also recommend wiping surfaces with water containing a small amount of salt, considering this a way of symbolically cleansing them. However, this practice has no proven ability to eliminate negative energy. When caring for surfaces, one should follow the manufacturer’s recommendations, as salt water may damage certain materials.
Ideas about the energy of the home, favorable days for cleaning, and money-related omens remain part of cultural traditions. For some, they are important rituals that help them tune in to positive changes. Others view them as interesting customs without literal meaning. At the same time, regular cleaning has clear practical benefits: it helps get rid of dust, organize belongings, and maintain comfort in the home. Getting rid of unnecessary items can also be an opportunity to reconsider habits and arrange everyday life more conveniently. Therefore, the best approach, of course, is to maintain cleanliness at a pace that is comfortable for you, without turning folk omens into strict prohibitions.

Aid is being delivered to Oleshky, with 25 buses and ambulances for people with limited mobility prepared. Civilians are being offered safe evacuation or support.
Humanitarian aid is being taken to the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region as part of a humanitarian mission. Twenty-five buses and ambulances have been prepared for departure. Representatives of the Ukrainian and Russian sides are currently in Armyansk. This was reported by Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, who is coordinating the process, on social media on October 30, UNN writes.
"Humanitarian mission in Oleshky: aid must reach every person. We are in Armyansk. Here, we are working with Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova and coordinating further actions as part of this mission. Journalists from three countries have also joined the coverage," Lubinets wrote.
According to him, "everything has now been prepared at a high level."
We are bringing humanitarian aid for the local residents of the city of Oleshky. Our main task is to ensure that this aid reaches every person who needs it. We are paying particular attention to the elderly, people with disabilities, and everyone who, due to their health or other circumstances, cannot care for themselves independently. Twenty-five buses with 750 seats have been prepared, as well as ambulances for people with limited mobility
He added:
A separate and no less important area of our work is ensuring the possibility for civilians to leave. Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to depart safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay may remain and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support
"It is now no less important for both sides to observe the ceasefire. Special thanks to Ukraine’s Defense Forces. We continue to work," Lubinets emphasized.
"I thank Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova for her cooperation in conducting this mission," he added. " Special thanks to U.S. First Lady Melania Trump for her mediation and coordination. The work continues".
What is known about the humanitarian mission in Oleshky
Ukraine announced that, starting at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on October 27, a ceasefire would be in effect in a designated area of the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region. This is necessary to conduct a humanitarian operation, deliver aid to the city’s residents, and prepare for the safe evacuation of civilians.
Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov announced the start of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky on the morning of October 27. Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets went to the site and would be responsible for coordinating the process. On the night of October 27, Lubinets stated: "Oleshky: the ceasefire has begun, and the Ukrainian side is fulfilling its commitments."
The ceasefire will last from October 27 until 10:59 p.m. on November 1, said People’s Deputy Davyd Arakhamia, one of Ukraine’s negotiators in the peace talks.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump is personally devoting time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky.

Turkish president stresses solidarity among Turkic states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:44:34 UTC
16:44:34 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan underlined the importance of solidarity among the Turkic states, calling it a “strategic necessity.”
“World politics is undergoing a profound transformation. At a time when the international system is struggling to establish justice and trust, and wars and crises are affecting vast geographical regions, solidarity among Turkic states has become a strategic necessity,” Erdogan said in an article published in leading media outlets across the member and observer countries of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) ahead of its 13th summit.
Unity among the Turkic states is “the strongest expression” of the long-standing legacy inherited from the shared history, Erdogan said.
“The unity of the Turkic world is the strongest expression of the deep-rooted legacy inherited from our shared history and our determination to shape our common future,” Erdogan added.
He noted that the bonds connecting Turkic peoples across different regions and centuries now form the foundations of political, social, economic, and cultural cooperation under the Organization of Turkic States.
Erdogan underlined that mobilizing the vast potential of the Turkic world toward common goals, strengthening unity through tangible achievements, and leaving a stronger Turkic world to future generations constitute a historic responsibility for all member states.
“I regard the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, which we will hold in Ankara under the theme ‘The Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed,’ as an important gathering that will further strengthen this shared determination,” Erdogan further noted.
He added that Türkiye considers assuming the chairmanship from Azerbaijan a historic responsibility in achieving common objectives and enhancing the organization's institutional capacity.
Referring to remarks by influential Turkologist Ismail Gasprinski on the importance of unity, Erdogan said that his vision continues to inspire the organization's activities.
He noted that the organization, established on the foundations laid in Nakhchivan, is becoming increasingly influential through its shared historical and cultural heritage.
“Turkic states, united around a common will, have the strength to overcome the most difficult challenges and determine their own future. The foundation of unity in the Turkic world is respect for the sovereignty, independence and national will of each brotherly country. This unity will be built not only on shared values but also on mutual trust and common interests,” he added.
Addressing economic integration, Erdogan highlighted the opportunities offered by the Trans-Caspian East-West Middle Corridor.
“Economic integration of the Turkic world is among the foremost priorities that our organization must carefully address in the coming period. The Trans-Caspian East-West Middle Corridor offers a historic opportunity in this regard.
“At a time when trade between Asia and Europe is being reshaped, the Turkic geography has the potential to become one of the major hubs of global transportation and logistics networks,” he added.
Erdogan said that railway networks, ports, road connections, and customs systems were being developed as complementary elements.
He underlined that every investment connecting the two shores of the Caspian Sea would increase trade between brotherly countries and contribute to shared prosperity.
He added that Türkiye and other Turkic states would make more effective use of the Turkic Investment Fund, remove barriers to trade between member countries, strengthen their production and investment capabilities, better utilize energy resources and renewable energy potential, improve communications infrastructure, and expand cooperation in production, trade, and technology.
Erdogan stated that solidarity established in the economic sphere would also be maintained in security cooperation.
He said member states would strengthen their ability to act together against terrorism, cross-border crime, cyber threats, and natural disasters by pooling their resources.
He also highlighted cooperation in the defense industry, emphasizing the importance of sharing experience, developing domestic and national technologies, and increasing joint production capacity.
“The most valuable foundation of our unity is our shared civilizational consciousness. The wisdom of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, the words of Ali-Shir Nava'i, the knowledge of Nizami Ganjavi, the verses of Magtymguly Pyragy, the language of the heart of Yunus Emre and the writings of Chinghiz Aitmatov are all landmarks illuminating the future of the richness of one great civilization that transcends geographical boundaries.”
Erdogan described the consensus reached on a common Turkic alphabet as a historic step toward greater cultural rapprochement.
He said cooperation in education, science, publishing, and digital technologies would further advance this initiative.
He also emphasized encouraging young people to study in fellow Turkic countries, bringing universities and scientists together, and ensuring that Turkic languages receive their rightful place in the age of artificial intelligence.
In his article, Erdogan also addressed the protection of the rights of the Turkish Cypriot people and the strengthening of their relations with the Organization of Turkic States.
“Our responsibility, entrusted to us by this deep-rooted civilization, is to protect our brotherhood under all circumstances and safeguard one another's rights and interests. We continue our solidarity with the Turkish Cypriot people, who are an inseparable part of the Turkic world, in accordance with this understanding,” he noted.
Erdogan stressed the importance of expanding the opportunities provided by the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' observer status within the organization and strengthening its ties with other Turkic states.
He added that Türkiye would maintain its firm position in seeking an end to what it describes as unjust isolation imposed on Turkish Cypriots, as well as recognition of their sovereign equality and equal international status.
He further stated that strengthening the OTS would contribute to peace and mutual trust across the region and support regional and global stability.
The organization's main responsibility is to transform shared political will into lasting achievements in the economic, political, cultural, and technological fields, Erdogan said.
Concluding his article, Erdogan expressed his confidence in the future of cooperation among Turkic nations.
“I sincerely believe that the 21st century will be the ‘Century of the Turkic World.’
“The Ankara Summit will open new horizons toward this goal, increase our organization's international influence and further strengthen solidarity among our brotherly countries.
“Our greatest responsibility is to crown the ideal of unity, which we have kept alive in our hearts for centuries, with lasting achievements and leave future generations a Turkic world that is stronger in every respect.”

sabine marcelis turns light and color into immersive spaces at zurich’s museum für gestaltung

sabine marcelis turns light and color into immersive spaces at zurich’s museum für gestaltung
from mathmos lava columns and a glowing walk-through tunnel to a collaboration with boris acket, the exhibition explores how light, color, and materials transform objects into immersive spaces.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
SABINE MARCELIS EXPLORES LIGHT AND COLOR IN ZURICH
Mathmos lava lamps stretch into an apparently endless landscape, familiar IKEA lights form a walk-through tunnel, and moving reflections bring the rhythms of sunlight and water indoors. At Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis brings these encounters together in Light and Color, her first museum exhibition. Running from October 30, 2026, to April 4, 2027, at the museum’s Toni-Areal venue, the show combines key works from recent years with installations developed specifically for its galleries. Across furniture, lighting, mirrors, and spatial interventions, the Dutch designer explores how glass, resin, stone, and other materials capture and transform light, giving even substantial objects an unexpectedly elusive presence.
The exhibition moves between individual objects and environments that surround the visitor, with material samples and studies offering a closer look at the experiments behind the finished works. ‘What I wanted to create was not a retrospective in the traditional sense but a series of spatial experiences that show how light and colour behave across different scales and materials,’ Marcelis explains. A restrained exhibition design gives those effects room to unfold, allowing shifts in transparency, reflection, and color to guide the experience. ‘Some works are presented individually so you can really focus on their material and optical properties. Others are arranged as full room-sized installations where light and colour permeate the entire space.’
MATHMOS LAVA COLUMNS MULTIPLY IN A MIRRORED LANDSCAPE
Developed through Marcelis’s ongoing collaboration with British manufacturer Mathmos, Mathmos Lava Columns gives the lava lamp considerably more room to perform. Eight columns, each standing 2.56 meters high, occupy a mirrored environment conceived for the exhibition. Their reflections extend the installation into an apparently infinite field, while pastel Bubblegum pink lava rises, merges, and falls inside frosted glass bottles. White aluminum bases and caps keep the surrounding structure visually quiet, directing attention toward the softly diffused movement. ‘I always wanted to design a giant lava lamp, that was the thought I had in my very first meeting with Mathmos,’ Marcelis says.
The collaboration builds on a shared interest in light, color, and translucency, drawing on Mathmos’s manufacturing expertise at its factory in Poole, Dorset, where Marcelis visited to approve the final prototypes. ‘The lava lamp is one of the only objects that has light, colour and translucency all in one. It does what I try to do with resin and glass, but it adds the dimension of time and movement,’ she explains. In Zürich, that movement expands from an object’s interior to the surrounding room through the mirrored walls. The installation’s Bubblegum palette also carries into a new limited-edition Astro lamp launching in November, translating the collaboration back to a domestic scale.
IKEA’S VARMBLIXT TUNNEL MEETS SUNBEAM CAPTURED
Elsewhere, Marcelis gives another recognizable lighting design an architectural role. Developed with IKEA, the VARMBLIXT collection comprises around twenty objects, with the circle emerging as a recurring motif and its ring-shaped lamp becoming particularly recognizable. For the exhibition, 125 lamps combine with a gradient mirror wall to create an eleven-meter-long, walk-through light tunnel. Repetition transforms a mass-produced object into an environment with its own depth and rhythm. As with the Mathmos columns, the mirror actively reshapes the perceived space, allowing a familiar product to exceed the dimensions of its everyday setting.
Created with Boris Acket, Sunbeam Captured turns to the fleeting interaction between sunlight and water. Mechanically generated waves ripple across a thin layer of water while a moving light source traces the passage of the sun. Colored reflections fill the space, amplified by a mirror that shifts from blue to orange in a gradient inspired by light’s changing color temperatures. Alongside the glowing tunnel and flowing lava, the installation gives movement a central role in Marcelis’s exploration of materials. Visitors encounter objects whose appearance keeps changing, making time as much a part of the exhibition as glass, color, or light.

brand: Mathmos | @mathmos_originals
location: Museum für Gestaltung Zürich | @museumgestaltung
dates: October 30, 2026 – April 4, 2027

Africa battles Ebola surge as ministers reject border closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:44:07 UTC
16:44:07 KST

African health ministers have agreed to keep their countries' borders open while strengthening surveillance and cross-border cooperation as an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to spread, with more than 10,000 confirmed cases and nearly 5,000 deaths.
The decision followed an emergency virtual meeting convened by the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), attended by more than 40 health ministers who discussed ways to contain the outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus.
The meeting agreed that countries should prepare their health systems for potential infections, coordinate their responses and closely monitor cross-border movements rather than impose widespread border closures.
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warned that the continent was falling behind in its efforts to contain the outbreak, which has a case fatality rate of 48.5%, according to the agency.
"I stood before more than 40 African ministers and said what the data tells us: We are not winning so far," Kaseya said.
"Together, we agreed to prepare every country, coordinate across our borders and keep those borders open while watching them closely. Our partners are standing behind Africa's plan."
Kaseya said the outbreak had evolved over five months from a national emergency into a continental health security challenge, with insecurity, humanitarian crises and limited funding complicating containment efforts.
Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said his country's experience showed that early detection and decisive action could interrupt transmission.
Uganda was declared free of Ebola by the World Health Organization (WHO) in August after reporting 20 confirmed cases following the outbreak's declaration in May.
The Africa CDC has identified 10 other countries at risk, including Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, Angola, Burundi, the Central African Republic, the Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, South Sudan and Zambia.
The outbreak has surpassed 10,170 confirmed cases, making it the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record. Some experts fear it could eventually overtake the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected about 28,000 people and killed more than 11,000.
Although researchers disagree over whether the current epidemic will reach that scale, they warn that the risk of further international spread will increase unless transmission in the DRC is brought under control.
The country is reporting between 400 and 500 new confirmed infections each week, with numbers remaining relatively stable.
Dr. Boghuma Titanji, an infectious disease specialist at Emory University, said the figures offered limited encouragement because infections were neither rising exponentially nor declining.
One major obstacle is the difficulty of tracing contacts and securing cooperation from affected communities. Health workers have sometimes spent more time persuading residents to cooperate than providing medical assistance.
Fewer than a quarter of new cases involve people already identified as contacts of infected individuals, suggesting that numerous transmission chains remain undetected.
France, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have also reported cases linked to the outbreak, with approximately 30 confirmed infections recorded outside the DRC.
Justin Lessler, a University of North Carolina researcher who studies infectious disease outbreaks, said the direct threat to the United States remained extremely low but warned that countries with fragile health systems could face greater difficulties.
South Sudan, particularly vulnerable because of conflict and humanitarian challenges, is among the countries of concern.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, including blood, vomit and semen. Controlling transmission therefore requires effective isolation, contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The current outbreak has been particularly difficult to contain because it is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a strain related to but distinct from the Ebola virus responsible for most previous epidemics.
Initial diagnostic testing was primarily designed to detect the more familiar Ebola virus, delaying recognition of the strain behind the current infections. Although the outbreak was declared in May, medical evidence suggests transmission had begun months earlier.
Armed conflict, weaknesses in health systems, community mistrust, misinformation and reductions in international aid have further complicated the response.
Katie Thomas-Canfield, the International Rescue Committee's Ebola response director, said working directly with affected communities was essential to breaking transmission chains.
Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, warned that the outbreak remained far from being controlled and could deteriorate further.
Experts expect transmission to continue through the end of the year, although vaccine development offers hope for 2027. Several candidates are being tested against the Bundibugyo strain, and Titanji said she was optimistic an effective vaccine could become available within the next 12 months.
Meanwhile, researchers are updating projections to assess how the epidemic could develop.
In May, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published computer-generated scenarios estimating that infections could reach between 10,000 and more than 20,000 over three months. The agency is updating its projections but declined to make scientists available to The Associated Press (AP) to discuss the latest trends.
Alessandro Vespignani, a disease modeler at Northeastern University, said weekly infections had yet to decline enough to signal meaningful progress.
He said there had not been the kind of "decay in the number of cases weekly that we need to see the light at the end of the tunnel."

He added that Türkiye and other Turkic states would make more effective use of the Turkic Investment Fund, remove barriers to trade between member countries, strengthen their production and investment capabilities and better utilize energy resources and renewable energy potential.
Erdoğan said solidarity established in the economic sphere would also be maintained in security cooperation.
He said member states would strengthen their ability to act together against terrorism, cross-border crime, cyber threats and natural disasters by pooling their resources.
In his article, Erdoğan described the consensus reached on a common Turkic alphabet as a historic step toward greater cultural rapprochement.
He said cooperation in education, science, publishing and digital technologies would further advance this initiative.
Erdoğan also addressed the protection of the rights of the Turkish Cypriot people and the strengthening of their relations with the OTS.
“Our responsibility, entrusted to us by this deep-rooted civilization, is to protect our brotherhood under all circumstances and safeguard one another’s rights and interests. We continue our solidarity with the Turkish Cypriot people, who are an inseparable part of the Turkic world, in accordance with this understanding,” he noted.

Australian ‘mushroom murderer’ Erin Patterson loses appeal bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:38:20 UTC
16:38:20 KST

Australian court rejects ‘mushroom murderer’ Erin Patterson’s appeal
Court rules Patterson will spend the rest of her life behind bars after denying parole.
An Australian court has dismissed an appeal by “mushroom murderer” Erin Patterson against her conviction and ruled that she should spend the rest of her life behind bars.
A three-judge panel at the Supreme Court of Victoria delivered its ruling on Friday. The justices said that Patterson, who was convicted last year of murdering three of her estranged husband’s relatives with a meal laced with deadly mushrooms, should not have the chance of parole.
“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” Justice Stephen McLeish, speaking on behalf of the panel, told the Melbourne court.
“In all the circumstances, after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period.”
Patterson, then 51, was convicted for the murder of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, Gail and Donald Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, by serving them a lunch of beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, Heather’s husband, who survived the meal.
Her crimes involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including falsely claiming a cancer diagnosis to explain the absence of her two children from the lunch, the judge noted.
The survivor testified that Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice about what to tell the children about her diagnosis.
Patterson was sentenced to life in prison with a 33-year non-parole period, among the longest terms ever handed to a woman in Australia. She has always denied wrongdoing, saying the deaths were accidental.
Her lawyers had argued that certain evidence should have been kept from the trial, that her cross-examination was unfair, and that placing the jury in the same hotel as other parties to the case compromised the result. Judges found these grounds for an appeal to be insufficient.
She can apply to Australia’s High Court to overturn the verdicts on her sentence and her convictions. The High Court is her last appeal option.
Patterson is only the second woman in Australia to be imprisoned for life without possibility of parole. The first is meatworker Katherine Knight, who was sentenced in New South Wales state in 2001 for the murder a year earlier of her partner John Price, whom she’d stabbed at least 37 times.

Europe struggles to reach 75% gas storage capacity despite increased LNG imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:38:10 UTC
16:38:10 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. European countries increased liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports to record levels for this time of year in late October, but still cannot fill their underground gas storage facilities (UGS) to even 75% of capacity ahead of winter, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Since the start of the summer injection season in April 2026, Europe has managed to inject only 75.5% of the gas volumes required to meet the winter storage target, or 51 bln cubic meters, into its UGS facilities.
Meanwhile, several countries have been recording net withdrawals (with withdrawal volumes exceeding injections) from European underground gas storage facilities for the second consecutive week, signaling the gradual start of the heating season in the region.
As of October 28, European UGS facilities were 74.89% full (14.79 percentage points below the five-year average for that date), compared with 82.8% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level recorded for that date since monitoring began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold approximately 82 bln cubic meters of gas, 9.4 bln cubic meters less than a year earlier and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that European UGS inventories might not even reach 75%, warning that the region faces a difficult fall-winter season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas reserves. By the traditional start of the fall-winter period, EU countries may have filled their storage facilities to just 70-75%, which would mark the lowest level ever recorded at the beginning of a heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10-percentage-point flexibility margin is permitted in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. Accordingly, net injections into European storage facilities ahead of the 2026-2027 fall-winter period must total at least 68 bln cubic meters to meet the required storage target. However, the European Commission, hoping for an exceptionally warm winter, is prepared to lower the target to 80% this year.

The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine stated: "Several attack drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing! ... We are holding the skies!"

Russian barrage kills 20 across Ukraine despite hopes for truce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:36:00 UTC
16:36:00 KST

A Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people at a crowded railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, while separate daytime attacks killed five more people in two other Ukrainian cities.
A late-night missile strike on the capital, Kyiv, killed another person, officials said.
The wave of attacks rocked Ukrainian cities as a local cease-fire in the southern Kherson region raised cautious hopes for a possible resumption of diplomatic efforts.
"Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings," Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
"There is no justification for this terror, and there never can be."
Another Russian missile attack struck several districts of Kyiv shortly before 11:00 p.m. (9:00 p.m. GMT), killing one person, the city's military administration said. The attack set warehouses ablaze, while falling debris damaged a building on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River.
A few hours earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had described the attacks as "very cruel" and "deliberate when everyone expects de-escalation steps."
Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine had intelligence "about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. We need the means to take out all this Russian evil. We are expecting relevant decisions."
The six-day truce, brokered with U.S. help, applied only to the southern Kherson region, where a humanitarian mission was underway to deliver aid to the Russian-held town of Oleshky, which has been isolated in a war zone since the start of Moscow's 2022 invasion.
Both sides issued virtually identical statements saying demining operations had been completed and the mission could proceed, allowing aid to reach the town and giving residents the opportunity to leave if they wished.
Elsewhere, Russian drone and missile attacks on critical infrastructure, including the rail network, have disrupted civilian life and ravaged the economy. The strikes have been compounded by an acute shortage of air defense missiles.
Bodies scattered across platform
In Dnipro, state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said a jet-powered drone had struck a platform at the city's main railway station, where a commuter train was preparing to depart.
Mangled bodies lay scattered across the pavement, which was marked by shrapnel, as pools of bright red blood collected nearby. Police placed bodies in black bags amid the wail of an air-raid siren.
"And for what? What goal are they (Russians) trying to achieve?" said Svitlana Shcherbak, 67, as she sheltered underground at the station. "I don't understand it at all."
Another attack on Dnipro struck a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. He added that a day of attacks had cut power to 350,000 households in the city.
Russia's escalating bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities has repeatedly killed civilians. Moscow has denied targeting civilians.
Two teenage girls were killed on a central street in Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, while three people died in strikes on residential buildings in the central city of Kremenchuk.
In Chernihiv, 23 people, including four children, were wounded in a drone attack on a busy downtown street, in addition to the two teenagers killed.
"Ordinary, peaceful people were attacked who were just going to work, going about their daily business, making plans for the day," said Dmytro Bryzhynskyi, head of the city's military administration.
In Kremenchuk, strikes on a residential block and private buildings killed three people and wounded 32, the regional governor said. Russian drones also struck city buses in three separate attacks in Zaporizhzhia in southeastern Ukraine, wounding six people, officials said.
Thursday's strikes came amid renewed efforts to revive U.S.-backed peace talks to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.
New three-way talks are expected to take place next month, with Ukrainian officials, including top presidential adviser Kyrylo Budanov, urging Kyiv's partners to increase pressure on Moscow.

‘A living hell’: The occupied town of Oleshky captures the world’s attention — including Melania Trump’s

Unknown Publisher
