Hello, and happy Friday. My name is Angela Skujins. On today’s agenda: the horrors of a Russian-captured community, EU-Canada affairs throw up more questions than answers, and hefty fines for angry Albanian protesters. Let’s go.
But first some news: Former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatseniuk just told Europe Today that “there is no way to trust Russians” over an ongoing temporary ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia focussed on one small town.
“What is happening right now in Oleshky is a humanitarian disaster and it's actually a living hell,” he said of the Russian-occupied community on the morning programme. Watch.
As Sasha Vakulina writes, a rare humanitarian mission is expected to reach the Russian-occupied Oleshky, the town Yatseniuk is referring to, on Friday to change this. It would mark the first operation of its kind in years, with evacuations of residents and aid distribution ready to start and scheduled to last until the afternoon. An accompanying ceasefire for the town to make this operation possible lasts until Sunday.
But for around 2,000 residents, the deadline presents a frightening choice: risk leaving through Russia or occupied Crimea, without assurances they can reach Ukrainian-controlled territory, or remain in a town where basic necessities are increasingly scarce.
Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky city military administration, previously painted a frightening picture to Euronews of the situation on-the-ground. “People have been forced to eat weeds,” she said. “The city is practically destroyed.”
Help from Washington? The humanitarian mission was agreed to with the involvement of US First Lady Melania Trump. Despite the good tidings, however, the former Ukrainian prime minister has accused Moscow of using civilians as "hostages" and staging the humanitarian operation to portray itself as their rescuer.
All eyes will be on Oleshky to see if the operation goes off without a hitch.
Another bloody conflict: "We're not leaving. We're going to stay. We will resist," said Mustafa Barghouti, General Secretary of the Palestinian National Initiative, speaking about Palestinians living under the immense weight of far-right Israeli sentiment. The United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry found Israel committed genocide in the Gaza Strip.
Barghouti was speaking on Europe Today in the wake of the Israeli legislative elections on Tuesday, which, among other things, showed Arab parties making immense gains. But does this win forebode any future for the two-state solution, and hope for peace?
"The only way to save the two-state solution is to remove the illegal Israeli settlements from the West Bank," he said. This has been made more challenging due to the the "lack of response" from the international community to apply sanctions on Israel for these actions, Barghouti said. Watch.
Meet me in Montréal: The second day of the EU-Canada summit kicks off Friday with a meeting between European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
The love-in is expected to expand cooperation across multiple areas, including trade, investment, supply chains, AI, quantum, and other topics, most notably support for Ukraine.
Context matters: Much of the meeting will occur in the long shadow of US President Donald Trump, whose abrasive “America First” policies and turbulent policies towards Kyiv have brought the two sides closer, making this summit possible, Jorge Liboreiro writes in a curtain-raiser.
What's noticeable, however, is that von der Leyen dug her heels in and renewed her push to make Canada the bloc’s first-ever “associate member”. This is despite a forceful push by Germany that killed the wording from the joint declaration. Speaking at an event in Montréal, the Commission president described her pitch as a “new frontier together”. “Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession,” von der Leyen said.
Try to keep up: In the hours following, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz published a cryptic tweet endorsing the “alliance for the future” concept instead.
But then Carney threw a spanner in the works by declaring that “we’re in the process of forging a new alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member”. So, is the idea of “associate membership” dead, and should it be resuscitated? Luca Bertuzzi explores.
The summit’s concluding press conference is scheduled for 5:25pm CET, which should hopefully answer these questions.
Did the EU just get its own ICE? The EU's border and coastguard agency, Frontex, is set to gain unprecedented powers to deport irregular migrants, monitor social media and respond to mass arrivals at EU borders under a sweeping reform proposed by the European Commission.
According to reporting by Vincenco Genovese, the overhaul would significantly expand Frontex's mandate, triple its workforce and give it a much greater role in deportations beyond EU territory. How’s that for a Halloween scare?
But the proposal has already sparked controversy, with critics warning that the agency's expanded powers and budget could lead to further fundamental rights violations and intrusive surveillance. For Member of the European Parliament Cecilia Strada, it inches closer towards resembling Trump’s controversial ICE operation.
Trouble in Albania: Albania introduced heavy fines on Wednesday for people present at demonstrations that turn violent. It comes as officials in Tirana try to manage daily protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama in the capital.
The fines — which can go as high as 500,000 leks (€5,500) — are not limited to people directly engaged in violence and will be imposed on "anyone who chooses to remain in a crowd" that is carrying out acts of violence or looting in a public space, or that is "concealing their identity". Important to note: The average monthly salary before tax in Albania stands at €930.
Albania has seen months of anti-government protests, with demonstrations in recent days escalating into clashes between protesters and security forces on the streets of Tirana. It follows trends of similar public demonstrations gripping France, Spain and Belgium.
Taking a leaf out of Paris’ note: Rama said he had drawn inspiration from a French bill passed by the upper house of parliament on Wednesday, which would hold protesters financially responsible for damage caused during demonstrations.
In France, the proposed legislation would require protesters to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused during demonstrations.
This is important because: Next week the Commission will deliver scorecards for each EU accession country, such as Albania. Will the elephantine fines factor into the report, and is the bloc’s enlargement boss, Marta Kos, taking stock? Time will tell.
Brussels hopes unspent defence loans may help plug Ukraine’s budget hole
The European Commission has opened a new round of low-interest defence loans and is urging member states to spend them on joint ventures with Ukraine, as Kyiv faces a €70 billion budget gap.
On Thursday, €21.3 billion of unspent funding under the Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s financing programme for strategic defence investment, was made available, with the Commission hoping to steer some of it towards Ukraine.
“Using the remaining funds from SAFE, we will be setting up a new programme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament last month.
Is this hot air, or will Kyiv actually get the defensive capabilities it has been promised? Luca unpacks it all in this story.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:33:08 UTC
16:33:08 KST

Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has lost at least 9,000 officers.
The KIU research group, which monitors losses among the Russian military command, reported this.
The figure represents the minimum confirmed number, as the statistics include only individuals whose identities have been established.
The information is collected from publicly available Russian sources, including obituaries, funeral announcements and memorial plaques.
Over the 1,708 days of the full-scale war, the average number of Russian officers eliminated has remained stable.
On average, around five names are added to the list of confirmed Russian command personnel losses every day.
Journalists previously identified at least 20 Russian army officers eliminated in a missile strike on Donetsk on August 26.
18 of them died on the day of the strike, while two others later died of their injuries.
The officers served at the headquarters of the Center military group: the headquarters of the Central Military District and the headquarters of the 41st Guards Combined Arms Army.
The Russian Knights aerobatic demonstration team also acknowledged the deaths of two of its pilots.
They were Colonel Oleg Yerofeyev, an honoured military pilot and sniper, and Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Kochetov, a senior pilot.
The pilots died on October 21 during a training flight in a Su-30SM fighter jet.

airBaltic to reduce Vilnius-based fleet to two aircraft as job cuts loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:32:00 UTC
16:32:00 KST

The Latvian airline airBaltic will reduce the number of aircraft based in Vilnius from three to two for the winter season, as the carrier restructures its operations across the Baltic states and plans to cut hundreds of jobs.
The airline has not yet confirmed how many employees in Lithuania will be affected by the planned cuts, airBaltic told BNS.
Edvardas Dalderis, a spokesman for the company, said it would have two Airbus A220-300 aircraft based in the Lithuanian capital, one fewer than during the summer season.
“During this year’s summer season, the airline had three aircraft based in Vilnius. From this winter season, airBaltic will have two aircraft in Lithuania’s capital,” Dalderis told BNS.
He said the reduction followed adjustments to aircraft allocation among the airline’s bases in the Baltic capitals under a new business plan announced in August.
Lithuanian Airports confirmed to BNS that airBaltic had informed it in August about plans to reduce the number of aircraft based in Vilnius.
In early October, airBaltic announced that it could cut 500 to 700 jobs across the Baltic states as part of its restructuring plan.
The airline previously told BNS that it employed nearly 90 people in Lithuania but did not disclose how many could lose their jobs. The airline now says it has 81 employees in Vilnius, adding that the difference reflects routine workforce changes rather than layoffs.
“Employee numbers naturally fluctuate. The difference reflects normal changes, such as crew members moving between airBaltic’s operating bases and regular staff turnover. This is not related to layoffs,” Dalderis said.
He declined to disclose how many employees in Lithuania could be affected, saying the figure would be available once the restructuring process was completed.
“Efforts are currently being made to mitigate the impact of the planned workforce reduction, and the final number of affected employees has not yet been confirmed. However, it is expected to be lower than initially planned,” Dalderis said.
Hundreds of crew members could lose their jobs
The Latvian aviation trade union said Thursday that airBaltic planned to lay off about 100 pilots and approximately 200 flight attendants.
According to the union, employees were informed October 27 that, following a reduction of the airline’s fleet to 36 aircraft, about four in five pilots and three in four flight attendants would retain their jobs.
airBaltic spokesman Augusts Zilberts confirmed to Latvian news agency LETA that the workforce reduction was linked to the volume of flights planned for next year.
The planned reduction in the number of pilots will affect all three of the airline’s bases, in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn, he said.
The airline has more cabin crew members than needed at its Riga base, while its Vilnius and Tallinn bases face staff shortages. Employees in Riga will therefore be offered the opportunity to continue working at the other bases where vacancies are available, according to previous reports.
Under its new business plan, airBaltic will offer 10 direct routes from Lithuania next summer, half the number available during the summer of this year, when it operated 22 routes.

Netanyahu bloc emerges ahead in Israeli election but fails to secure majority

The result means Israel is now set to face a lengthy and likely tricky period of negotiations as party leaders work to form a government.
Final results from Israel's pivotal legislative election this week showed there was no clear winner, with both of the two main blocs well short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc finished on 53 seats, while the opposition camp, led by the centrist Yashar party of rival Gadi Eisenkot, ended on 48.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party remained the largest party, with 27 seats, while the Arab parties secured a record 19 seats between them.
The result means Israel is now set to face a lengthy and likely tricky period of negotiations as party leaders work to form a government. Failure to do so would see Israelis head back to the polls.
‘Ra’am-gate’
Netanyahu has accused Arab parties of "stealing" the election, calling on police and Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet to carry out a "thorough investigation into election fraud."
The Likud party also pushed claims that foreign funding had been used to influence voters in the election. The allegations focused on claims that the Ra'am party had received money from Qatar.
"The ‘Ra’am-gate’ scandal is an earthquake. The Israeli elections have been stolen," Likud said in a statement on Thursday.
Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas reportedly denied any wrongdoing and said he would welcome an investigation.
In a post on social media, Eisenkot said foreign interference was "unacceptable and extremely serious" and called on Shin Bet to investigate the allegations "fully and immediately, without bias."
Next steps
Moving forward, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with leaders of the parties elected to the Knesset before assigning the task of trying to form a government to the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing sufficient support to do so.
Under Israeli law, that individual will have 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.
Should that fail, the president can give a second leader the chance to form a government, this time with a maximum deadline of 28 days. If this second round were also to fail, then the Knesset can request a third candidate be given a go. They would have 14 days to complete the task.
If all attempts fail, another election is called.

'Mushroom killer' Patterson's appeal fails as court locks in life sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:30:16 UTC
16:30:16 KST

An Australian appeals court on Friday ruled that triple murderer Erin Patterson must spend the rest of her life in prison, citing the “shocking criminality” of her poisoning four relatives of her estranged husband with deadly death cap mushrooms.
A three-judge panel of Victoria state’s Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson’s challenge to her convictions and upheld prosecutors’ appeal against the leniency of her original sentence. The ruling set aside her 33-year non-parole period, which would have made her eligible for parole consideration at age 82.
“The offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of the three judges.
“After anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a nonparole period,” McLeish added.
Patterson is among the very few women in Australian history to receive a life sentence without the possibility of parole.
The first woman to receive such a sentence was Katherine Knight, a meatworker sentenced in New South Wales in 2001 for murdering her partner, John Price, the previous year. Knight stabbed Price at least 37 times.
Patterson’s convictions stemmed from a family lunch she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023, where she served four relatives beef Wellington dishes laced with poisonous death cap mushrooms.
She was found guilty of murdering her former parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson. Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, survived after spending weeks in the hospital but was also the victim of an attempted murder for which Patterson was convicted.
Patterson was sentenced in September 2025 to three life terms for murder and 25 years in prison for the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson. The sentences included a 33-year nonparole period.
She may still seek special leave to appeal to Australia’s High Court, the country’s highest judicial authority, although doing so would require meeting a high legal threshold.
Patterson has maintained her innocence and denied deliberately poisoning her relatives.
The deaths of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson within days of the lunch attracted widespread international media attention, turning the case into one of Australia’s most closely followed criminal trials.
The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations.
Emmy-nominated actor Melanie Lynskey announced this week that she will portray Erin Patterson in a six-episode series for Paramount+, a subscription video-on-demand streaming service.
Lynskey will also serve as an executive producer on the series, which will dramatize the 97 days between the fatal lunch and Patterson’s arrest.
Prosecutors argued during an appeal hearing in August that Patterson should never become eligible for parole, saying her original sentence failed to reflect the calculated nature of the crimes.
McLeish said Patterson’s intention to murder all four lunch guests had been sustained for nearly three weeks, from the time she invited them to the meal through the preparation and serving of the poisoned food.
The judge also pointed to what he described as an “elaborate series of deceptions,” including Patterson’s false claims about having cancer, which she used to explain why her two children would not attend the lunch.
The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice on what to tell the children about her supposed diagnosis.
McLeish also noted that Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from.
“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust,” McLeish said.
Patterson chose not to attend Friday’s hearing in person and watched the proceedings via video link from prison.
Because of her notoriety, she is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne’s Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, a women’s prison where inmates considered at high risk from other prisoners are housed for their protection.
During her sentencing in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Beale said there was a “substantial chance” Patterson could remain in solitary confinement for years.
Patterson’s estranged husband, Simon Patterson, had also been invited to the lunch but declined the invitation the day before.
Evidence presented before the trial revealed that Simon Patterson had previously expressed suspicions that his estranged wife might have tried to kill him.
He testified during a pretrial hearing that he declined the lunch invitation because he feared for his safety.

From Coastal Reclamation to Data Centers: How India's Architecture Grows Around Water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Architecture has treated water either as a backdrop or a problem: a view to be framed, a hazard to be drained, or a utility to be connected. In contemporary India, a more consequential relationship takes shape. Water remains a shared ecological resource, yet the land and infrastructure around it are increasingly financed and defended as economic assets. Coastlines are extended to carry traffic and lake edges become lucrative development zones. The decision to do so passes through multiple institutions with different vocabularies, thereby challenging who determines how water and its surroundings are used, and who faces the consequences.
Manufacturing Land: Mumbai's Coastal Road
Mumbai has historically been built by displacing water, and the Coastal Road continues that tradition at infrastructural scale. According to the municipal corporation (BMC), the 10.6-kilometer southern section has created approximately 111 hectares of reclaimed land, which contains roads, bridges, interchanges, and lots reserved for public amenities. The BMC's case rests on mobility and public benefit. The road was expected to cut travel time in the city, and the open space sought to bring in roughly 1.24 square meters per person in one of the densest and most populous megacities in the world.
In 2019 the Bombay (Mumbai) High Court cancelled the coastal clearances, citing a lack of proper scientific study. However, it upheld the rule change allowing land reclamation for roads, and the Supreme Court stayed the order, allowing work to continue. Whether the reclamation damages coastal ecosystems, and how the sea wall will perform, remain debated rather than settled.
To local architect Alan Abraham, who later petitioned the court for design changes to the section on reclaimed land, the real problem is the priorities. "Roads are needed for the city, not the coast," he has argued, proposing that the road be pulled inland so that open space meets the water. The BMC's response was that the design rested on expert studies and that, with almost all of the work complete, changes were not feasible.
Erasing Boundaries: Bengaluru's Lakes and Drains
Bengaluru's lakes were originally conceived as a connected system of man-made stormwater drains known as rajakaluves. Their protection depends less on the existence of rules than on where a boundary is drawn. City authorities set a uniform 30-meter buffer around lakes in which construction is restricted. In 2025, however, the state advanced an amendment replacing it with size-based buffers - no buffer for the smallest water bodies and three meters for those up to an acre. Legal commentary notes that the earlier norms were treated as unscientific and that the bill would permit certain public-utility structures, such as roads and pump houses, within buffers.
The bill returned in late 2025, noting that neither the state's expert committee nor the public had been consulted. Lakes that once absorbed monsoon runoff and recharged the aquifer now push that water into drains that have been narrowed themselves. Building within these buffers can reduce the space available for water to spread and soak into the ground during heavy rainfall, increasing runoff and pressure on already constrained drainage networks.
An analysis of flood-hit neighborhoods confirms significant encroachment on or misuse of the drains linking the lake network. One locality saw the water table fall from roughly 100 feet to 600 feet within six years of a lake being removed. In Bengaluru, a buffer is no longer a natural feature but is a legal figure, and changing it alters what classifies as buildable land.
Concealing Demand: Data Centers and Water Stress
Data centers present a different problem, since their water demand is largely invisible in a building's form and site. WRI India reported that more than half of India's data centers are in water-stressed regions, with the majority concentrated in five states: Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, and Uttar Pradesh. Uttar Pradesh's draft 2026 policy, in fact, promises uninterrupted water supply to data centers while India currently has no established disclosure requirement.
Cutting on-site water use can raise electricity demand, and because power plants also draw on water, the shortage may be relocated to the grid rather than removed. In India, recycled municipal wastewater is a supply that other users in a stressed city may need as well. In India's water-stressed regions, the location and design of a data center can affect how much water remains available for households, agriculture, and other local uses. A highly efficient facility in an over-allocated basin still draws on a shared supply, which makes site selection really a decision about who gets water.
Together, the three cases describe water as a resource: displaced, constrained, and allocated to infrastructure. In each, and in most projects, the decision precedes design. Architects always inherit conditions rather than shape them.
Individual practitioners can still push earlier in the process. They can question briefs that assume a site, request water balances and hydrological assessments before accepting or proposing a location, and suggest alternatives to a fixed alignment, as Abraham's collective did. Mumbai's architects have tried this more than once. The Mumbai Architects Collective, a group of about 120 firms, proposed reimaginations of the Coastal Road. In Chennai, design teams in the 2019 Water as Leverage program drew up closed-loop neighborhood water systems.
Sustainability cannot be assessed solely through how an individual building performs, because that performance depends on the territory the building occupies and the shared resources it draws on. If the claim on water were declared at the outset as a condition of the site, some of the buildings now defended as inevitable might never be proposed where they stand. Whether the profession, and the institutions that commission it, are willing to begin from that point remains open.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

A one-story commercial building, probably hit by falling debris, was significantly damaged. Part of it had no tenant, and part houses Rozetka.
There is no fire at the scene now, and rescuers are working. There is no information on casualties.
As of 11:55 p.m., owners of housing and affected businesses were clearing up the damage. A repeat ballistic missile threat was announced at that time.
This is at least the fourth case of buildings in the complex being damaged by Russian shelling. Debris of an enemy drone first fell on the roof of one of the buildings in May 2023.
Debris of a drone also hit one of the buildings in the complex overnight on November 29, 2025. The Academy of Modern Education A+ in the complex was also slightly damaged at that time.
Overnight on January 9, 2026, a hit landed on the roof of the five-story part of a building and the neighboring facade of a 13-story one, and several floors were damaged. The facade was also damaged and glass was blown out in neighboring buildings.
On April 15, the Academy of Modern Education A+ in the complex burned after shelling. A nine-story building opposite was also damaged, with windows blown out and the facade damaged, and several cars burned.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,586,500 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:28:23 UTC
16:28:23 KST

Ukrainian service members walk along a road toward Druzhkivka, with smoke rising from an airstrike, in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 24, 2026 (Alex Nikitenko/Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images)
Russia has lost 1,586,500 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 30.
The number includes 1,590 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,450 tanks, 25,617 armored combat vehicles, 168,274 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,720 artillery systems, 2,246 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,728 air defense systems, 452 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,039 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky toldFrance TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

French economy contracts 0.1% in 3rd quarter as investment, exports fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:27:59 UTC
16:27:59 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
By Seyma Erkul Dayanc
ISTANBUL (AA) - France's economy contracted 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, following stagnation in the previous three months, the country's statistics agency INSEE said Friday.
The decline marked the second quarterly contraction this year, after gross domestic product (GDP) fell 0.2% in the first quarter.
Household consumption rose 0.4%, accelerating from 0.2% in the second quarter, while public consumption increased 0.3%.
Investment, however, fell 0.6%, following a 0.5% decline in the previous quarter.
Foreign trade also weighed on economic activity, with exports dropping 1.7% while imports remained largely unchanged.
Net foreign trade subtracted 0.6 percentage points from GDP growth.

Foreign minister announces interim secretary general
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) on Thursday announced that an interim secretary general has been appointed to the ministry and will take over the role until the position has been filled.
Last week, the long-serving secretary general Jonatan Vseviov announced that he would resign to enter politics.
Tsahkna said Undersecretary for Administrative Affairs Rasmus Lumi will temporarily take over the running of the ministry from the start of November.
Lumi has served as the ministry's undersecretary for administrative affairs since November last year and has worked at the ministry for over 30 years.
Lumi graduated from the University of Tartu's Faculty of Law. He began working at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1995 as a junior desk officer in the legal department and has since held several senior positions.
He has served as director general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' personnel department, Estonia's ambassador to Spain and Estonia's permanent representative to the Council of Europe.
Vseviov hopes to be the Social Democratic Party's candidate for prime minister at the upcoming national election in March 2027.

Stewart played Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films. He also spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company and was knighted in 2010.

SIR PATRICK STEWART (1940-2026) Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love. We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago but we weren’t in the same productions. My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in 'Star Trek'. “But Patrick think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?”. Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences, who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes ('X-Men' of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway. America was his adopted home, where he met his adored Sunny who has cared for him through sickness and health, through thick and thin. But he never forsook his origins: and the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as Chancellor of Huddersfield University in Yorkshire. His farewell performance in 'Avengers: Doomsday' is yet to be seen. Ian McKellen 29 October 2026 Photo: University of Huddersfield
— Ian McKellen (@IanMcKellen) October 30, 2026

“Even the greatest heroes could be uncertain,” the Academy wrote, adding that “strength could exist alongside vulnerability, and that compassion was never a weakness.”
There was something extraordinary about the way Sir Patrick Stewart could make even the most powerful characters feel profoundly human. Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them. Behind that unmistakable voice was an actor who understood that even the greatest heroes could be uncertain, that strength could exist alongside vulnerability, and that compassion was never a weakness. Over a career spanning more than six decades, his performances became woven into the lives of generations who grew up watching him. Deal or war? US sees Iran's hardline power broker as 'greatest hope for peace'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:21:48 UTC
16:21:48 KST

The United States is making a potentially final diplomatic push to reach an agreement with Iran, with Vice President JD Vance offering to meet personally with one of Tehran's most powerful hard-line figures as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military action against the Islamic Republic.
Vance sent a message last week to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, expressing his willingness to hold direct talks on an agreement to end the war. The message described Rezaei as the greatest hope for peace, according to reports.
The diplomatic overture comes as Washington considers resuming large-scale military operations against Iran. Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, presented Trump with military options for action against Iran on Wednesday during an unusual personal visit to the White House, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The disclosure of Vance's letter to Rezaei first emerged earlier this week. On Thursday, a U.S. official familiar with the negotiations told The Washington Post that the message sought to emphasize the central importance of both countries' national interests in reaching an agreement.
American officials close to the negotiations believe the confrontation with Iran is approaching a decisive moment and have sought to convince Tehran's hard-line leadership that Vance's diplomatic initiative is serious.
According to one official, Vance identified Washington's overriding objective as ensuring that Iran does not acquire nuclear weapons.
He described Iran's principal interests as rebuilding an economy severely damaged by war and sanctions while preserving its national sovereignty.
Vance also stressed that Iran must send representatives authorized to negotiate nuclear issues, the official said.
The White House believes the window for reaching an agreement without returning to war may be closing. Vance's outreach reflects the Trump administration's assessment that Rezaei has become the central power broker in Tehran and may be the only figure capable of assembling sufficient political support for an agreement to halt Iran's nuclear program.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Rezaei maintains regular contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and that the two have spoken in recent days, following the arrival of Vance's letter.
Should a meeting take place, Istanbul or Doha, Qatar, would be the most likely venues, the American official said.
Washington turns to Rezaei after earlier talks collapse
Vance has been leading the administration's diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict with Iran.
In April, he traveled to Islamabad, Pakistan, where he met Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and proposed lifting U.S. economic sanctions in exchange for a binding nuclear agreement.
The proposal also envisioned extensive economic cooperation, which Trump's negotiating team described as a "golden bridge" toward a more stable relationship between Washington and Tehran.
Ghalibaf, however, was unable to secure support for the proposed agreement among Iran's leadership.
A narrower memorandum of understanding was subsequently signed, but it quickly unraveled when hostilities resumed in the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically vital waterway through which a substantial share of the world's oil supplies passes.
Since the Islamabad meeting, U.S. intelligence agencies have increasingly concluded that Rezaei occupies a pivotal position within Iran's political and security establishment.
The former Revolutionary Guards commander retains considerable influence among his former colleagues in the military organization, which plays a central role in Iran's security apparatus and political system.
He has also consolidated his authority by reorganizing the Supreme National Security Council and appointing loyalists to influential positions within the body.
The council is one of Iran's most important decision-making institutions, coordinating national security and defense policy across the country's political and military leadership.
Rezaei's influence extends beyond security matters. He works closely with officials responsible for overseeing Iran's economy, which has been severely weakened by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and increasingly stringent international sanctions.
American officials believe his familiarity with both the security establishment and the country's economic difficulties could make him particularly influential in determining whether Tehran accepts a negotiated settlement.
One U.S. official said Rezaei "understands the gravity of the situation."
Qatar maintains contact with Iranian leadership
Qatar has emerged as the principal mediator in the conflict, with its envoys maintaining regular communication with Rezaei and other senior Iranian officials.
The Gulf state has played a central role in facilitating indirect contacts between Washington and Tehran, making Doha a possible location for direct negotiations if both sides agree to meet.
According to reports, Iranian leaders interpreted Vance's decision to approach Rezaei personally as a gesture of respect, suggesting Washington recognizes his standing within the country's leadership.
However, there has been no indication that Tehran has softened its position on the nuclear issue.
The lack of movement underscores the uncertainty surrounding the latest diplomatic initiative, even as the United States attempts to identify an Iranian official capable of delivering a deal that the country's leadership would accept.
For the Trump administration, the immediate challenge is determining whether Rezaei can translate his political influence into meaningful concessions before Washington concludes that diplomacy has run its course.
With military options once again under consideration at the White House, the outreach to Rezaei represents an effort to test whether an agreement remains possible before the confrontation enters another phase of fighting.

Taiwan’s Realtek steps up 3 nm efforts for AI server connectivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:21:22 UTC
16:21:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Realtek Semiconductor Corp. is advancing development of high-speed interconnect chips using 3-nanometer manufacturing technology, targeting growing demand for faster data transmission, CTEE reported Friday.
The company aims to increase revenue from high-performance computing and edge AI applications, including automotive and robotics. These currently account for a high-single-digit percentage of total revenue, a figure it aims to raise to more than 30% by 2030.
As Taiwan’s third-largest chip designer, Realtek is developing 3 nm technology as part of a broader effort to move beyond its traditional networking and audio chip businesses into higher-value AI infrastructure components. The company leads the global market in ultra-high-speed Ethernet shipments and holds more than 70% of the market for audio codec chips used in computers, according to Sinotrade.
Realtek is focusing its development on high-speed server interconnect products, including components that facilitate data transmission between processors, memory, and other system components. Its roadmap draws on existing interface silicon intellectual property and covers PCIe retimers, redrivers, and switches, as well as optical communication products.
In optical communications, Realtek’s 100G physical-layer chips are undergoing customer validation, with shipments expected to increase more significantly next year. The company is also developing 400G and 800G solutions, scheduled for release in the second half of next year.
Separately, Realtek said discussions on application-specific chips remain at an early stage. The company cited confidentiality requirements in withholding details about the number of projects, their applications, and the customers involved.
Realtek reported third-quarter revenue of NT$37.7 billion (US$1.2 billion), up 27.9% year-on-year. It maintained a cautious outlook for the fourth quarter due to higher foundry, packaging, and testing costs.

Apple cuts Taiwan App Store commission to 26%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:20:59 UTC
16:20:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Apple will cut its standard App Store commission in Taiwan from 30% to 26% on Saturday following an investigation by the Fair Trade Commission, CNA reported Friday.
The commission said Friday that it had accepted Apple’s proposal after reviewing its App Store business practices. The investigation examined whether Apple’s restrictions on app developers violated competition law.
Apple confirmed Thursday that the lower rate would apply to paid apps and in-app purchases through Taiwan’s App Store on iPhones and iPads. Developers will receive the reduced rate automatically without having to sign updated terms by Oct. 31, per Tai Sounds.
The change will allow developers to keep more revenue from app sales and purchases. For every NT$1,000 (US$32) in sales subject to the standard commission, Apple will collect NT$260 instead of NT$300, leaving developers with an additional NT$40.
The investigation focused on Apple’s restrictions on developers and the fees it charges for sales through its App Store. Apple proposed lowering its commission under Article 28 of the Fair Trade Act, which allows regulators to suspend investigations when companies agree to take corrective action.
The commission said it would monitor Apple to ensure the company meets its commitments. The regulator may reopen the investigation if Apple fails to comply, circumstances change significantly, or the decision was based on incomplete or misleading information, per Economic Daily News.
The commission also said it could launch separate investigations into other potentially unfair business practices by Apple.

Taiwan plans disaster coordination centers for vulnerable areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:20:56 UTC
16:20:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of the Interior said Thursday it plans to assign advisors and substitute service personnel to help with disaster prevention in indigenous communities and areas at risk of becoming isolated during disasters.
The ministry said in a press release that it held a meeting Thursday afternoon on training for disaster prevention advisors. Deputy Interior Minister Sawyer Mars (馬士元) delivered a status report at a press conference on behalf of Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳).
Mars said the ministry plans to set up disaster coordination centers at township and district offices, including those serving indigenous areas. Substitute service personnel could assist the centers with disaster relief and administrative work.
Starting in 2027, the ministry plans to assign one advisor and 10 to 15 substitute service members to each of 65 offices in indigenous areas and places vulnerable to isolation during disasters, Mars said. Advisors will receive refresher training each year before the flood season.
Ministry of the Interior Department of Conscription Administration Director-General Shen Che-fang (沈哲芳) said advisors would be recruited from disaster prevention professionals, retired military officers, police officers, firefighters, and teachers with Emergency Medical Technician 1 or disaster prevention specialist certification.
The ministry said advisors would receive initial training in interpreting disaster risk maps, operating disaster coordination centers, responding on-site, and leading substitute service personnel to help local offices prepare.

Drone firm Align executives detained over alleged use of Chinese chips

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Prosecutors have detained Align Corp. Chair Tu Ta-sen (杜大森), his wife, and Deputy General Manager Huang Wen-li (黃文麗) over allegations that the company supplied the military with drones containing Chinese-made components.
Align has long participated in government drone procurement contracts, supplying equipment to the military, emergency services, and other government agencies, per UDN. During a recent military acceptance inspection, personnel discovered Chinese-made chips inside its drones.
After discovering another batch of Align drones containing Chinese components, prosecutors searched the company and questioned Tu and five others. They said the contracts explicitly prohibited components originating from China, Hong Kong, and Macau.
Prosecutors subsequently sought to detain Tu and his wife on suspicion of fraud and violating the National Security Act. They identified two military contracts involving Align drones containing Chinese-made chips. The contracts were worth a combined total of more than NT$8 million (US$245,300).
Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said the military was reviewing its inventory, per Liberty Times. He asked prosecutors to provide more concrete evidence to assist the military in its investigation.
Align began as a contract manufacturer for international brands, becoming an original equipment manufacturer for Toshiba and Hitachi, per NOWNews. When Taiwan’s manufacturing industry increasingly shifted production to China, Align remained in Taiwan and invested in remote-controlled helicopters and drones. At its peak, the company held 70% of the global market for remote-controlled helicopters.
As that market became saturated, Align expanded into other applications, including search-and-rescue and military drones. During Taichung’s National Day celebrations this year, an Align drone carried flags into the ceremony grounds ahead of the flag-raising ceremony.
Tu focused on research and development, while his wife, Huang, handled the company’s business operations. Align owns two flying fields, one in Tainan’s Anping District and another in Taichung’s Shigang District. The company also regularly hosts events and competitions for the model aircraft community.

China triples intelligence satellite fleet, US agency reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:20:30 UTC
16:20:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China has tripled its fleet of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) satellites since 2018, strengthening its ability to track and target Taiwan and other US allies, according to a report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA).
The DIA released a report on Monday reviewing threats the US and its allies face on the ground and at sea. “China employs a robust space-based ISR capability designed to enhance its worldwide situational awareness and enable long-range strikes,” the report said.
The report said China owned more than 510 satellites in orbit as of July. Most are used for commercial and civil missions, but they could still supply data and imagery to the PLA due to the Chinese military-civil fusion policy.
Chinese firms also provide imagery “to state actors banned by Western providers for supporting weapons proliferation,” according to the report. Chang Guang Satellite Technology, China’s first commercial satellite company, was named as one of the “partially state-owned enterprises” focusing on remote sensing, launch, and communication services.
On Sunday, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV released a 42-second video featuring high-resolution imagery of Taiwan’s landmarks captured by Chang Guang’s Jilin-1 satellite constellation. Taiwan was introduced as “China’s Taiwan Province” in the video.
In response, Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) called the footage part of Beijing’s “cognitive warfare,” vowing to take stronger early-warning and response measures.
China’s monitoring capacity has been growing in steps with its space launches. Last year, Beijing set a new record with 93 launches, and is targeting 140 by the end of this year, according to the US Space Force.
China’s fleet continues to expand and modernize, including through low-Earth orbit satellites that can offer images of any location in 30 minutes or less, the report said.
The US, however, may be expanding its fleet faster than China, with 644 operational surveillance and weather satellites this year, according to data from the American Enterprise Institute (AEI).
Todd Harrison, a senior fellow at the AEI, told Breaking Defense the DIA’s data did not make clear which satellites are included in its tally of Chinese systems, adding that the fleet’s growth has leveled off in recent years.

Germany news: Merz in Asia warns against weaponizing trade, calls for 'rules based' order

Germany news: Merz hopes for Korean reunification at DMZ
Published October 30, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea
- Merz draws on Germany's own reunification experience, saying division causes suffering
- Chinese President Xi Jinping lauds 'new chapter' in Germany ties while meeting with President Steinmeier
- Berlin event set to mark the 65th anniversary of West Germany and Turkey's agreement on 'guest workers'
Here are the leading headlines from and about Germany on Friday, October 30:
What did Steinmeier's trip to China achieve?
German President's Frank-Walter Steinmeier latest trip to Asia was intended to provide more clarity. Amid a delicate period, Steinmeier sought a balancing act in China between respect and criticism.
It was a state visit of a kind rarely seen today. For four days, Steinmeier traveled across the country: from Hefei, where the German automaker Volkswagen's China operations are headquartered, through historic villages and the imposing landscapes of the Yellow Mountains. He also visited several points of interest of Chinese history, art, and science, and finally, he headed to Tiananmen Square in the heart of Beijing's political center.
Diplomatic detours
Steinmeier—who is set to leave office in March 2027— spoke as a statesman and diplomat on matters of German and European interest. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Steinmeier have known each other for many years, so in this respect, the president was the right man to address even the most difficult issues as a European.
This political balancing act between respect and criticism did not trigger any visible outrage in Beijing.
When he spoke with Chinese leaders about their subsidies for exports to Europe and the related issue of the trade deficit, Xi replied: "I am ready to work together to open a new chapter in the comprehensive strategic partnership between our two countries and to advance the development of global governance."
Europe's economic crisis also weakens China
Just how much willingness lies behind the push for a strategic partnership will become clear during further negotiations between the EU and China.
Xi Jinping seems to understand that a persistent trade deficit with Europe could also become a problem for his country, as an economic crisis in Europe could further strain China's economy.
As "the world's second- and third-largest economies," China and Germany also bear "an important responsibility for the development of relations between China and Europe, as well as for stable growth in the global economy," Xi Jinping said. While that may not sound like a breakthrough yet, it certainly sounds like an understanding.
China remains silent on the topic of international order
In contrast to his economic arguments, Steinmeier's political appeals for Beijing to assume more responsibility for the international order fell on deaf ears.
The German president addressed global conflicts and wars on several occasions in Beijing, including Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine. But he received no responses in official statements.
That same evening, the news channel of the Chinese TV network CCTV aired a report that merely covered Steinmeier's visit to a well-known astrophysics institute.
There was no mention of the call for China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, to do more to promote world peace.
WATCH: 65 years of Turkish guest workers in Germany – A life between two cultures
Mitat Özdemir is one of more than 870,000 Turkish workers who were recruited to Germany by a government program between 1961 and 1973. He dealt with tough factory work, language barriers and cultural differences.
Six decades later, he and his family still live in Germany. How did the program from back then shape their lives and modern Germany?
Merz at DMZ says he hopes Korea can reunify like Germany did
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.
North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.
In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.
"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.
"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.
North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state."
Munich: Vandals smash Manchester United memorial
A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.
The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.
The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.
The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.
Munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.
"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories."
The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.
The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.
IN DEPTH: Germany takes cautious approach to Israeli election results
German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.
Read the full story here
Carmaker Audi's profits plunge in 3rd quarter
Profits of German luxury car brand Audi for the third quarter came plunged 87% year-on-year to €95 million ($106 million), the Volkswagen subsidiary reported on Friday. This is a drop from €718 million seen in the same quarter last year.
The drop comes amid weak demand in China, and US tariffs.
"Market and competitive conditions have become significantly more difficult in the third quarter," Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger told journalists on a call.
"That all shows that we need to intensify measures and set clear priorities," he added.
Overall in the first nine months of 2026, Audi's profits have dropped 41% to €1.22 billion.
The carmaker trimmed its 2026 profit outlook down to 3 to 5% for the year, down from the previous 5 to 7%.
Audi's sluggish numbers represent more bad news for the 10-brand Volkswagen Group, which on Thursday reported its largest quarterly loss in more than a decade, at nearly €6 billion.
Holocaust 'stumbling stone' ban to remain in Heidenau
A ban on new Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.
Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.
Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.
"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.
The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.
The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.
Chinese President Xi lauds 'new chapter' of Germany-China ties
Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.
"We both bear responsibility for the international order and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.
President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.
"This new paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi said during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.
Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.
The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.
Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.
Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.
Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.
IN DEPTH: 65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty
On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.
Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.
German president in Beijing addresses trade tensions with China
While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.
In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.
Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.
At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."
Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.
Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'
During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.
Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.
"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.
"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."
During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.
In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.
The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.
"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.
"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."
Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."
