Marko Mihkelson: Europe's decisive choice — appease Russia or repel aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:37:00 UTC
15:37:00 KST

Marko Mihkelson: Europe's decisive choice — appease Russia or repel aggression
Europe faces a decisive choice: give in to Russian pressure and accept a situation where aggression forcibly changes Europe's borders and calls into question our entire security order, or defend a united, free and expanding Europe, all at a time when authoritarian regimes around the world are increasing their influence, writes Reform Party MP and Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee chair Marko Mihkelson.
This is not merely a choice between various diplomatic approaches. It is a test of Europe's political will, strategic clarity and leadership. Do we have leaders capable of seeing beyond their own personal political agenda and understanding that peace is not born by giving in to an aggressor, but by creating conditions in which aggression no longer pays?
Europe needs a new strategic clarity: Russia's attempt to change borders by force must be thwarted, Ukraine must be given the military and financial aid it needs to prevail, and stronger economic pressure must be brought to bear on Russia than has been the case so far. A real peace process can start only when the preconditions needed have been created. A position of strength must be built for negotiations, not one's trump cards surrendered before talks have begun.
Another peace plan, same old concessions
Another supposedly Washington-originated peace plan to end Russia's war of aggression is doing the public rounds. Its details have not been officially confirmed, but the proposals outlined in the media again point to the possibility that significant concessions are being offered to Russia. It is possible that elements of the plan were also talked about at President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff's recent meetings in Oslo and St Petersburg.
According to the descriptions that have reached the public, consideration is being given to creating a demilitarized zone in the area of the current contact line, restoring trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the U.S., and Ukraine giving up its aspiration to become a NATO member. In return, Ukraine would be offered investment and continued integration with the European Union. At the same time, sanctions against Russia could be eased, U.S. investment in Russia restored, and even progress made on reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
If these proposals correspond to what has been described publicly, this would be a solution highly amenable to Russia and requiring extensive concessions from Ukraine and from Europe.
The 28-point peace plan that reached the public after President Trump's meeting with Putin in Alaska last year, and which was later amended by European involvement, already contained similar ideas. There is consequently no fundamentally new approach visible in the current discussions. Instead, the question again arises as to whether, in order to end the war, there has been a willingness to sacrifice precisely those principles for whose defense Ukraine and Europe have been fighting for years.
Achieving peace is needed. But peace cannot mean recognizing the consequences of aggression, restricting Ukraine's sovereignty or weakening Europe's security architecture.
Thirty years of the wrong conclusions
A solution to Russia's aggression against Ukraine has been sought via negotiations since 2014. The Minsk agreements and the Normandy process helped, at times, to lessen the intensity of hostilities, but did not end Russia's aggression. Then in February 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
The Istanbul talks that followed brought no agreement, and later diplomatic initiatives have not succeeded in ending the war either. Between 2014 and 2022, ceasefire agreements were concluded repeatedly between Russia and Ukraine, but none brought lasting peace. Even the quietest periods remained short-lived.
Moscow has always blamed someone else for the failure of negotiations — the Ukrainians, the Americans or the Europeans. The Kremlin will not acknowledge its responsibility as the aggressor, but seeks to achieve the same goal via diplomatic and military pressure: to subjugate Ukraine and shape Europe's security order according to Russia's will.
To grasp this, one must look further back than 2014. Russia's imperial wars did not begin with the occupation of Crimea but gained new momentum soon after the collapse of the Soviet Union. An understanding took hold in Russia's leadership that restoring the empire and pushing back Western influence were unavoidable preconditions for restoring the country's great-power status.
Russia's foreign minister at the time, Andrei Kozyrev, who was part of President Boris Yeltsin's cabinet from 1990 to 1996, confirmed to me at our meeting in Miami that, by spring 1992, imperial-minded forces had gained the upper hand in the Kremlin leadership. This observation helps explain why the West's hopes for Russia's rapid democratization proved unfulfilled. The issue was not solely in the personhood of Putin's, but lay much deeper in Russia's political development.
The wars that began in the 1990s, including the Chechen wars, which cost tens of thousands of lives, neither attracted sufficient attention in the West nor led to decisive countermeasures. Nor did the apartment block bombings in Russian cities in the fall of 1999, in which more than 300 people died and which have been suspected of being organized by Russian security services, decisively change the West's attitude. Vladimir Putin's rise to power was greeted in many capitals with a somewhat cautious hope.
President George W. Bush, who met Putin in Slovenia in summer 2001, later summed up his impression in famous words: he looked Putin in the eye and saw in him a straightforward and trustworthy person. History has shown how costly the wish to see an authoritarian leader as that partner he is not can prove to be.
Putin has not hidden his goals. Since his rise to power, Russia has been heading in a direction in which changing borders by force, restricting the sovereignty of neighboring states and weakening NATO and Europe's collective defense have become central planks of Kremlin policy.
The West's mistaken assessments were repeated. After the 2001 terror attacks, Russia offered the U.S. support in the Afghanistan operation, sharing intelligence and allowing the use of Central Asian staging points. Western attention concentrated for a lengthy period of time on Afghanistan and the wider Middle East. The U.S.'s chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 may in turn have reaffirmed in the Kremlin the understanding that Washington's appetite for a long confrontation is limited.
The war Russia fought against Georgia in August 2008 demonstrated Russia was prepared to carry out its geopolitical objectives by military force. After the war Russia continued to occupy a fifth of Georgia's territory, but the Western reaction remained limited. Soon there was talk again of resetting relations. NATO's 2010 strategic concept still saw Russia as a possible strategic partner rather than a growing security threat.
Also in 2014, when Russia occupied and annexed Crimea and began military operations in eastern Ukraine, the Western response initially remained modest. Only the shooting down of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 and the deaths of 298 people forced European countries to react more seriously. Sanctions and support for Ukraine were necessary, but they did not turn into a strategy capable of stopping Russian aggression.
Western disunity, Brexit, domestic political changes in the U.S. and the rise of Donald Trump deepened the uncertainty. By the fall of 2021, the Kremlin had taken the decision to prepare for full-scale war against Ukraine.
Five years later we are in a situation in which Russia has suffered enormous human losses but has retained the military initiative on important sectors of the front. The West's partial awakening and sanctions have so far not been sufficient to force Moscow to abandon its strategic objectives.
What is this stalemate we are talking about?
Lately it has gotten increasingly common to hear that, since no decisive breakthrough has been achieved on the Ukrainian front, diplomacy must again be given a chance. Others have emphasized that Europe must not be left on the sidelines while the U.S. and Russia talk about Ukraine's future. The latter position is in and of itself correct: Europe cannot be discussed without Europe, just as Ukraine's future cannot be decided without Ukraine.
But these arguments do not justify starting talks without a clear objective and a common strategy.
What is the stalemate we are actually talking about? Russia has not stopped its aggression. It continues to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, is boosting its military production capacity and expanding hybrid activity in Europe. Russia is producing ballistic missiles and drones in large quantities, while Western production of air defense systems and interceptors is not growing fast enough. Russia's war machine is being kept running by goods, technology and components from China and other countries.
At the same time, warfare is changing technologically faster than the defense planning and production capacity of many Western countries can adapt. In addition to weaponry, Europe must develop air defense, counter-drone capability, intelligence and surveillance capability, and electronic warfare.
Most important, however, is that Russia has not abandoned its strategic objectives: to change borders by force, restrict Ukraine's sovereignty and shape Europe's security order according to Moscow's interests.
Negotiations are not a problem in themselves. What is dangerous is starting them in a situation where the aggressor retains the military initiative and the West is prepared to make concessions even before talks begin. Such an approach could give Moscow time to restore its military capability, deepen disagreements among Western countries and prepare a new aggression.
Nor must responsibility be forgotten. Negotiations must not mean setting aside the question of accountability for the war of aggression, for war crimes and for other violations of international law. The question of responsibility is not an obstacle to the peace process but part of the preconditions for a just and lasting peace.
Europe cannot permit talk of understanding Russia and of strategic stability to become a pretext for surrendering its interests and values.
A coalition of the willing must not turn into a coalition of the waiting
POLITCO has written about Europe's search for someone who could take on the lead role in engaging with Putin. But the question should not primarily be who sits at the negotiating table. What matters more is with what objectives and from what position of strength they will be going there.
After the strong confrontation between Trump and Zelenskyy at the White House in February 2025, several European countries coalesced into a coalition of the willing, to support Ukraine. That was a required step. But too much of the attention has focused on Ukraine's security guarantees after the war ends, rather than on how to shape the conditions in which Russia could be forced to end its aggression.
So the danger then arose that this coalition of the willing becomes a coalition of the waiting: instead of shaping the conditions for ending the war, it is preparing primarily for the situation after the war.
For Russia, talks often represent an opportunity to buy time, distract the other side and present new conditions. When Europe is first of all looking for a suitable person to engage with Putin but has not agreed on a common strategy, it is showing Moscow a weakness of political will.
Russia's public rhetoric towards European leaders has turned increasingly condescending and threatening. Moscow is trying to convince Europe that resisting its demands is pointless and that the cost of continuing the war is greater than the cost of concessions.
Pressure like this cannot be handled with diplomatic courtesy alone, or with new compromise proposals. Europe must first decide what it is defending and what outcome it considers acceptable.
Russia's strategic clarity — the restoration of empire and the political subjugation of Europe's security — must be met with an equally clear objective: to thwart aggression and prevent borders from being changed by force.
Europe must find strength in its own economy
Europe is economically superior to Russia, but economic superiority does not automatically translate into military capability. Europe is not one single state, and achieving unified political will and strategic clarity requires bold leadership and a readiness to look beyond member states' short-term budgetary interests.
The financial position of Europe's larger states limits their ability to increase defense spending rapidly. The large public debts, budget deficits and growing interest costs of the U.K., France, Spain and Italy mean that increasing defense investment requires some tough political choices.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to need extensive financial and military aid. Without European support, the resilience of Ukraine's state and society would be considerably weaker.
Europe cannot solve this dilemma with borrowed money or new budget targets alone. It also needs a rapid increase in defense industry production capacity, joint procurement, better coordination and decisive investment in technologies that meet the needs of modern warfare.
The increase in defense and security spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035 agreed at NATO's Hague summit provides a framework, but it is not enough if the agreements remain on paper. Europe must turn its economic capability into real deterrent power.
Consistent economic pressure must also be brought to bear on Russia, restricting its access to technology needed for the war industry and strengthening secondary sanctions against those countries and companies that help Russia circumvent restrictions.
Europe must end the situation in which it supports Ukraine with one hand while with the other it enables Russia's war machine to earn money and procure the components it needs.
Europe must answer three questions
Before Europe starts looking for a suitable representative to hold talks with Putin, we will have to answer three basic questions.
Are we ready to accept borders being changed by force and aggression going unpunished? Are we prepared to weaken NATO's collective defense in the hope that Russia will leave us alone?
And do we have enough political will to defend Europe's freedom, unity and a security order based on international law, even when it requires short-term economic and political sacrifices?
These questions cannot be answered by a hope that Putin will change his objectives if he is offered sufficiently favorable conditions. His conduct so far gives no grounds to believe that new concessions would replace the need for credible deterrence.
Russia treats international politics as a zero-sum game in which one side's strengthening means the other's weakening. The Kremlin therefore interprets Western hesitation and internal disagreements as an opportunity to get closer to its objectives.
No diplomatic gesture will alter Putin's strategy if there is no readiness behind it to defend one's interests. Neither a compromise offered by Trump, Stubb nor anyone else can replace credible deterrence.
Finland and Norway's peace efforts must be assessed from the same starting point. Any initiative that contributes to a just and lasting peace deserves attention. But no diplomatic process can succeed if it proceeds from the assumption that Ukraine must give up its sovereignty, or that Europe must give up the principles of NATO membership and collective defense.
Rolling out the diplomatic red carpet to an aggressor without first forcing him to the negotiating table through pressure means weakening one's position before talks have even begun. Europe must not voluntarily surrender its most important trump cards or give Moscow reason to think that sufficient pressure can achieve concessions.
What should Europe's action plan be?
If Europe's objective is to restore a just and lasting peace, concrete steps and their sequence must be agreed.
First, Europe's strategic objective must be to thwart Russia's attempt to change borders by force and break up Europe's security architecture. This means that Ukraine's sovereignty and its right to choose its own future must not become a bargaining chip in negotiations between great powers.
Second, Ukraine must be given every possible military and financial assistance needed to repel Russian aggression. This requires a rapid increase in air defense, ammunition, drones, long-range weapons and defense industry production capacity, and Ukraine's integration into Europe's security and defense space.
Third, Russia's war machine must be weakened via economic measures. Sanctions must be tightened and their enforcement made more effective. Russia must lose the ability to use Western tech and economic ties to achieve its military objectives.
Fourth, Europe must transform its economic and political superiority into real security capability. This requires increased defense spending, defense industry development, joint investment and a greater readiness to take responsibility for Europe's defense.
Fifth, negotiations with Russia can give Europe the desired outcome only when they come from a position of strength. A just and lasting peace must ensure that Russia cannot repeat its aggression or impose its objectives by force. The precondition for this is Ukraine's ability to win its war of freedom and Europe's capacity to defend its own security.
A Ukrainian victory is not only in Ukraine's interest. It is Europe's opportunity to avoid a situation in which a temporary halt to Russian aggression turns into the starting point for a new war. Thwarting Russia's military and political expansion would also give Europe a stronger position in shaping a changing world order.
Europe must choose
In the spring of 2022, many of Europe's friends and allies acknowledged that Estonia and the other Baltic states had been right when we warned about Russia. We did not make a great number of it. We asked only that we be listened to in future.
Today that matters more than ever. Europe again faces a choice whose consequences extend beyond Ukraine's battlefields. The question is whether sovereignty, freedom and the inadmissibility of changing borders by force will remain the foundations of the international order, or whether a world will take shape in which great powers can impose their interests on smaller states at the threat of arms.
Europe cannot afford another concession to Russia that would merely postpone the next conflict and make it harder to avoid. We do not have to choose between war and peace, but between a short-term apparent peace and lasting security.
A just peace is born when the aggressor understands that he will not achieve his objectives by force. For that, Europe must end its hesitations, strengthen Ukraine and turn its common will into credible deterrent power.
Europe's security does not depend on how quickly we can reach an agreement with Russia, but on whether we can stop aggression and prevent its recurrence.
Europe's choice is not between surrender and war. It is a choice between a temporary silence bought with concessions and a just and lasting peace, one that defends freedom.

French investigators on Thursday questioned former prime minister Édouard Philippe, a candidate in next year's presidential election, in a case of alleged embezzlement of public funds. French investigators on Thursday questioned presidential candidate Édouard Philippe, a former prime minister, in a case of alleged embezzlement, sources close to the case told AFP.
Two investigating magistrates handling allegations of misuse of public funds, favouritism and harassment designated Philippe an "assisted witness" in the affair – a less serious status than being placed under formal investigation.

An association called LH French Tech was awarded the contract to run the digital hub in July 2020 after being the sole contender in a call for bids.

US midterms: 4 days to go – What the polls say as Trump cancels two rallies
Trump cancels Kansas and Iowa rallies, opting for telephone events across nearly 20 states ahead of US midterms.
With four days to go before the United States midterm elections, Democrats are leading in national polls as both parties make their final push for votes.
Meanwhile, a legal dispute threatens to delay the Senate result in Alaska, and President Donald Trump has cancelled two weekend rallies in favour of campaigning by phone.
Here’s what you need to know.
What do the latest US midterm polls say?
Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, according to RealClearPolling, with a difference of 8.2 percentage points.
Charles Franklin, professor of law and public policy and director of the Marquette Law School Poll in the US, said Trump’s declining approval ratings and economic concerns are alarming Republicans.
The latest Marquette Law School poll, conducted in Wisconsin from October 14 to October 22 and released on October 28, put Trump’s approval rating at 37 percent and disapproval at 61 percent.
Only 16 percent of respondents said they were better off financially than a year ago, while 42 percent said they were worse off and another 42 percent said things were about the same.
“Democrats are more enthusiastic and more certain they will vote,” Franklin told Al Jazeera.
“That is giving Democrats an important edge, and reflects Republican disappointment in current national conditions,” he added.
In Arizona, where voters are experiencing increasing living expenses, a retiree told Al Jazeera that the cost of groceries had become a major concern.
“We’re retired, and every time we go to the grocery store, it makes me wonder what the heck is going on,” the voter said.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is polling at 49 percent against Republican Ken Paxton’s 43 percent, according to a CNN survey released on Thursday. In Michigan, the same pollster found Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Republican Mike Rogers, 49 percent to 42 percent.
However, Franklin warned: “Polls are not perfect predictions of outcomes.
“We could see those close races go either way, either due to polling errors or due to voters moving just a little more in one direction or the other.”
In Alaska, however, there is also a complication: a legal dispute that could delay the result of a Senate race.
What is happening in Alaska’s Senate race?
The battle for Alaska’s seat could continue in court after ballots close on November 3. The dispute centres on two candidates named Dan Sullivan: the incumbent Republican senator and an independent candidate with the same name, who is also registered as a Republican.
Trump has accused Democrats of recruiting an independent candidate to confuse voters and take support away from the Republican senator.
“It was a scheme. It was an election fraud. Total election fraud,” Trump said.
The Justice Department has taken legal action over the dispute, while Democrat Mary Peltola denied the accusations.
“I feel like this is yet another diversion from the issue that Alaskans want to talk about, which is affordability,” she said.
Al Jazeera’s US correspondent Alan Fisher said the dispute could have consequences beyond Alaska if the Senate’s control depends on the result.
“If this becomes the key seat in the battle for the Senate, we might not actually know who has control there for several days, maybe even weeks after November 3,” Fisher said.
What has happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
Trump travelled to South Carolina to campaign for Republican senator Darline Graham – sister of the late Lindsey Graham – who is running against Annie Andrews in a closely contested race.
In Rock Hill, Trump encouraged voters to cast their ballots and cautioned his supporters not to take the election outcome for granted. About Graham, Trump said that she was in the lead but that he still had to campaign there. “In politics you never know, right? So you got to get out and vote.”
He also addressed his supporters directly and asked the crowd to pretend that he was on the ballot.
“And I am on the ballot because all of these things that we’ve done, all of these incredible successes that we have,” he added.
In Texas, Vice President JD Vance attended a rally in Weatherford, near Dallas, alongside Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, as Republicans called on supporters to vote.
“Texas ain’t surrendering. Texas is not becoming California. It’s going to stay Texas, ain’t that right?” Vance told supporters.
Well-known Democrats have also joined the campaign trail.
On Wednesday, former President Barack Obama gave a speech in Georgia supporting Senator Jon Ossoff, criticising Trump’s management of the economy and his approach to the war with Iran.
When Al Jazeera asked about Obama’s visit, Ossoff’s Republican opponent, Mike Collins, said it showed “the desperation of Jon Ossoff because he knows he’s losing”.
“If he was winning so big, he wouldn’t have brought anybody in,” Collins said.
Democrats also campaigned in Texas and Georgia on Thursday.
In Dallas, Senate candidate James Talarico held a rally as part of his final campaign tour, while former Vice President Kamala Harris joined Ossoff at Clark Atlanta University, urging young people to vote.
Harris also campaigned in Macon, Georgia, where she criticised the Trump administration over rising living costs.
“We have a moment now to turn pain into purpose,” Harris told Democratic volunteers. Harris also urged supporters to participate in local and statewide contests.
Later, at Clark Atlanta University, she asked students to stay engaged.
“Don’t overlook those races, because those are the folks who make decisions about your life every day,” she said.
What happens next on the US midterms campaign trail?
Trump has cancelled weekend scheduled appearances in Kansas and Iowa, replacing them with telephone rallies across nearly 20 states in the final days before Tuesday’s elections.
Trump had been set to appear in Salina, Kansas, on Saturday and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday.
Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters said the change would allow Trump to reach more voters than he could with in-person appearances.
“Voters across the country want to hear from President Trump before Election Day, and this 72-hour sprint will be a huge boost in the closing days,” Gruters said.
Asked about the cancellations on Thursday, Trump questioned the need to travel to Kansas, where Republican Senator Roger Marshall is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton.
“I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said.
When a Reuters reporter asked whether the decision had anything to do with fatigue from travelling, Trump rejected the suggestion. “I feel perfect,” he said, before insulting the reporter.
Trump is still scheduled to hold a rally at the Ocean Center in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday at 23:00 GMT.
At the same time, Harris is due to address the Fulton County Democratic Party’s Fulton Forward dinner in Atlanta, Georgia.
Vance had also planned a news conference with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud in St Cloud, Minnesota, on Friday, but the visit was cancelled on Thursday. No reason was immediately given.

Oil prices rise for the fourth consecutive month amid the war with Iran

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Oil prices rise for the fourth consecutive month amid the war with Iran
Kyiv • UNN
Brent and WTI rose after an attack on a tanker, while Brent is headed for a fourth month of gains. The market fears supply disruptions due to the war.
Oil prices rose on Friday, October 30, and are expected to post a fourth consecutive month of gains after an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz highlighted the continuing supply risks from the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, now in its eighth month. UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Brent crude futures for December delivery, which expire on Friday, rose by $1.20, or 1.04%, to $116.08 per barrel as of 3:23 GMT (5:23 a.m. Kyiv time). The more active January contract rose by $1.39 to $112.19.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures rose by $1.37, or 1.34%, to $103.37.
During the month, Brent crude prices rose by nearly 11%, while WTI prices increased by 14%.
On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz — a key maritime route for oil and fuel supplies from the Persian Gulf — was hit by explosive devices attached from a small vessel, UKMTO reported. The attackers have not yet been identified.
"Ongoing fighting in the Strait of Hormuz area, amid doubts about the viability of a diplomatic path, is keeping oil prices high as markets anticipate an escalation of the conflict in the coming weeks," said Saul Kavonic, head of energy research at MST Marquee.
On Thursday, the Houthis claimed attacks on several facilities in Saudi Arabia, including the largest oil refinery in Ras Tanura, the refinery in Rabigh and a production facility in Abqaiq owned by state-run Saudi Aramco, while the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom's western region.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Thursday, October 29, that Vice President J.D. Vance had asked Iran to help the country obtain medicines after U.S. media reported that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official asking him to resume peace talks.
Iran received a letter from Vance but has not yet responded to it, the country's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported, adding that Tehran wants the United States to meet its conditions and that "any position contrary to these conditions is unacceptable."
Amid concerns about security in the Middle East, ExxonMobil and Chevron canceled plans for their executives to attend the United Arab Emirates' largest oil exhibition next week, two sources familiar with the situation told Reuters.
Price forecast
Oil prices could become even more volatile over the next couple of weeks because of Israel's parliamentary elections and the U.S. midterm congressional elections, Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, said at a media briefing in Singapore on Thursday.
Hansen said that heightened uncertainty makes price forecasting more difficult, but he expects oil to trade in a higher range of $70 to $90 per barrel compared with the prewar level of $60–70, even after the conflict ends, due to the risk of renewed hostilities and the need to replenish inventories.

Humanitarian Mission In Russian-Occupied Oleshky Enters Final Phase, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:30:17 UTC
15:30:17 KST

Moscow and Kyiv said the evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky had been completed "without incident," as buses filled with civilians left the area for the first time in more than four years under a US-brokered truce that is set to remain in effect until November 1.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said in a social media post on October 30 that after arriving in Ukraine's Russia-occupied Crimea, one convoy of buses then headed toward Russia, while a second convoy was bound for Ukraine.
"We are concluding our humanitarian mission in Oleshky. We are currently in the territory of Armyansk (in northern Crimea)," she said in a video posted on Telegram, adding that both sides had praised the high standard of its organization.
Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman David Lubinets confirmed the evacuation saying those residents of Oleshky who wished to travel to Ukraine were on their way to the Russian city of Anapa.
""At this point, those who wished to leave Oleshky for Ukraine have been able to do so and are now on their way. Humanitarian aid has been delivered. The convoys have split up, and I am heading to Ukraine," he wrote.
Hundreds of Oleshky residents were expected to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory via a roundabout route: once in Anapa, in southern Russia, the civilians will head by plane to the Belarusian city of Homel, and from there by bus into Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region.
The circuitous route was needed to avoid roads along frontlines that have been heavily mined and destroyed by the conflict, sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I am currently speaking with local residents to hear their concerns and understand what assistance they need most," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who is leading the Ukrainian delegation, wrote on Telegram on October 30.
He also shared videos of conversations with local Ukrainians who appeared to cheer the long-awaited support and evacuations.
As part of the joint relief operation, aid was distributed to those who stayed behind in the city. Lantratova said that "tens of tons of humanitarian aid" was being distributed.
Since October 27, Ukraine and Russia have observed a localized cease-fire in Oleshky with no violations reported. The arrangement was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, who announced the agreement a week earlier.
Trump said civilians from both countries were expected to visit people in their homes to assess their needs, while those seeking to evacuate would receive coordinated assistance and transportation to their preferred destinations.
Having spent years living under Russian occupation, some Oleshky residents had expressed concern about the evacuation process, fearing "filtration" while traveling through Russian territory, Ukrainian journalist Maria Semenchenko, who grew up in the city, told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service.
The residents, she said, were concerned about potential "coercive screenings and interrogations used by Russia to identify people deemed disloyal," adding that "some have already experienced torture in the past" and that she knew "at least one person who does not want to leave for precisely this reason."
No such incidents were reported so far.
Russian forces captured Oleshky early in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine that Moscow launched in 2022. Later that year, it effectively became a frontline city after Ukraine retook the regional capital, Kherson, less than 10 kilometers away on the other side of the Dnieper River.
Once home to around 24,000 people, Oleshky's population has declined dramatically due to displacement and deaths caused by Russia's war. The destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in June 2023 further compounded the devastation, with an estimated 90 percent of the city's territory flooded.
Fewer than 2,000 people remained in the city by the fall, including around 50 children, according to Melania Trump's office. Most are believed to be elderly residents who have been unable or unwilling to leave.
Remaining in a largely ruined city that is ringed by land mines, Oleshky residents for months were trapped in a war zone that is cut off from the outside world, with little to no food, drinking water, medicine, or electricity.
Kyiv has blamed Russia for the dire situation in the city, accusing Moscow of failing to ensure the safety and well-being of civilians. The Kremlin, in turn, has blamed Ukrainian drone strikes for its inability to do so.
Ukrainian officials and volunteers had previously told RFE/RL that they believed people in Oleshky were essentially being held hostage to Russia's military goals in the region.
While the city has served as an important staging ground for Russian attacks in southern Ukraine, they said its residents were effectively serving as a human shield for Moscow's forces.

World Cities Day 2026 Explores "Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

On October 31, World Cities Day 2026 will be observed under the theme "Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All." Hosted in Fuzhou, China, this year's global observance focuses on how urban regeneration can advance access to adequate housing by improving existing neighborhoods, infrastructure, and public spaces. According to the United Nations, up to 3.4 billion people worldwide lack access to adequate housing, secure tenure, basic services, or affordable living conditions. This challenge points to the need for approaches that consider housing alongside the wider conditions of urban life, including environmental resilience, connectivity, and access to essential services.
Cities are shaped by the relationship between people, their homes, and the environments they share. Housing developments influence the density and character of neighborhoods, transportation networks determine access to jobs and services, and public spaces provide places for recreation and social interaction. These urban systems are also increasingly exposed to environmental pressures, from extreme heat and flooding to storms and other natural hazards. As cities continue to grow and change, providing adequate housing is closely connected to how urban settlements adapt to these challenges while supporting the communities that live in them.
For World Cities Day, we look at these interconnected aspects of urban life through four themes: housing, public space, mobility, and neighborhood livability, bringing together stories that examine the challenges and possibilities shaping cities today.
Housing, Displacement, and Climate Resilience
Adequate housing is about more than having a roof over one's head. Its location, construction, affordability, access to services, and ability to withstand environmental risks all influence the security it provides. As floods, storms, and extreme heat increasingly affect urban settlements, housing strategies must consider how buildings and communities can adapt to changing conditions. For people displaced by environmental pressures, conflict, or economic instability, finding a new home also involves rebuilding access to livelihoods, services, and social networks. These challenges call for approaches that connect housing design with land use, infrastructure, and community participation.
Responding to Displacement: Architectural Strategies Across Latin America
"If You Build Ugly Social Housing, You Will Create Social Problems": An Interview with the OBEL Award 2026 Recipients
UN-Habitat Recognizes Five Approaches to Adequate Housing With 2026 Scroll of Honour
Designing for Density: How Modernist Principles Continue to Shape Social Housing Solutions Today
On Housing, Public Space, and Climate Resilience: In Conversation with the Winners of the 2026 UIA 2030 Award
Urban Landscapes as Infrastructure: Public Space, Water, and Climate Adaptation
Parks, waterfronts, gardens, and open spaces are often understood as amenities that improve the appearance and recreational value of cities. Their role, however, extends into the functioning of urban environments. Landscapes can help absorb rainwater, reduce surface temperatures, support biodiversity, and provide relief during periods of extreme heat. In areas exposed to flooding, the integration of water management into public space and landscape planning can also help reduce pressure on conventional drainage infrastructure. These functions become particularly important as cities expand and natural systems are increasingly affected by urban development.
Lessons from Roberto Burle Marx: Designing Resilient and Evolving Urban Landscapes
Urban Landscape as an "Art of Survival": An interview with Kongjian Yu, the Advocate of the Sponge Cities Concept
Who Owns Public Space? Three Active Models of Shared Management Shaping Urban Commons in Europe and New York
Elevated Infrastructure and Public Space: Reclaiming the Ground Below
From Residual Land to Civic Places: 6 Mexican Public Parks
Moving Through the City: Mobility, Transportation, and Connectivity
How people move through a city directly influences their access to housing, employment, education, healthcare, and public space. Transportation networks connect neighborhoods, but the way streets and infrastructure are planned can also create barriers, particularly for people who rely on walking, cycling, or public transportation. In many cities, car-oriented development has contributed to fragmented urban environments, unsafe streets, and unequal access to essential services. Rethinking mobility involves more than introducing new transportation technologies or expanding road networks. It also requires considering how different modes of travel work together, how infrastructure serves people with different needs, and how connections between urban and rural areas can be improved.
Mobility Justice: Urban Equity in an Era of Innovation
Beyond the Street: Climate, Commerce, and the Evolution of Hong Kong's Elevated Networks
Rural Transportation Hubs: Infrastructure Design, Access, and Regional Mobility
From London to Houston: Four Ongoing Pedestrianisation Initiatives Shaping More Walkable Cities
What Makes a Neighborhood Livable? Health, Green Space, and Community
While citywide strategies establish the conditions for urban development, the experience of living in a city often comes down to the neighborhood scale. Access to parks, healthcare, schools, local services, and safe streets influences how people experience their surroundings and participate in everyday urban life. These qualities are not distributed evenly, and broad indicators or international rankings can sometimes obscure differences between neighborhoods and the needs of their residents. Understanding livability therefore requires looking beyond economic performance or the quantity of green space to consider how people use their environments, interact with one another, and take part in decisions that affect their communities.
The Metrics We Use Decide the Cities We Build: Urban Indicators and Lived Experience
City-Making Through Participation: Lessons from Utopian Hours 2026
Paris as a Living Laboratory: Proximity, Inclusion, and the School as Climate and Social Infrastructure
Building Public Life: How Bogotá and Mexico City Addressed Urban Inequality
The City as a System of Health: Breaking Feedback Loops in Planning

Night polo goesmainstream in Jaipur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:26:59 UTC
15:26:59 KST

A night polo match underway at the Rambagh Polo Club ground in Jaipur
Polo in Jaipur has become easier to catch. Matches at the Rambagh Polo Club ground now begin at 7.30pm, giving office-goers time to get there after work and families a chance to watch once the daytime heat has passed.Over the past couple of months, 10 newly installed floodlights have lit up the ground near the Vidhan Sabha and the high court. In a neighbourhood where lights over the Sawai Man Singh Stadium have long signalled IPL season, there is now another reason to stop for a match.The stands have young spectators watching their first game, taking selfies and discovering a sport whose familiar audience has largely been drawn from royal families, the cavalry and club circles. Broad-brimmed hats, pastel linen jackets and chiffon sarees are still in evidence. The club is hoping to give more people a reason to come.An Evening At The PoloNight polo has been played in Hyderabad and Noida, in smaller arenas with sand surfaces. Jaipur’s matches are on a full-sized grass ground, under lights, as part of the official tournament schedule.For Major Anant Rajpurohit of 61 Cavalry, a veteran player, the advantage is straightforward: more people are free to watch.
“The good point is that people tend to get off from work, office, or day commitments, and the attendance is more,” he says.“Earlier, the matches and all the finals were done during the daytime, so the availability of gentlemen and ladies was very restricted and very confined. The development of any sport comes when the number of people watching it is more. Then, the number of people who intend to get into the sport or invest into the sport increases. So that way it is an added advantage,” he says.
In this bastion of the ‘sport of kings’, horse and rider are routinely taking to the field under floodlights, in the hope of drawing a wider audience, building tourism opportunities — and preserving a bit of the city’s heritage, writes Mandakini Shaly
A Place In The CityFor Padmanabh Singh, 28, India’s polo captain and scion of the erstwhile Jaipur royal family, encouraging people to watch is also part of keeping a city tradition alive.“I have always viewed polo as very intertwined with the culture of Jaipur,” he says. “Jaipur is one of the main hubs of polo across the world and has given a lot to the sport. Some of the most iconic moments have happened here. So when I talk about conservation, restoration, and preservation of our culture and heritage, I mean polo too. It’s part of our tourism.”Rambagh Polo Club is marketing the sport more actively, with support from Rajasthan’s tourism leadership. Padmanabh’s mother, Diya Kumari, is deputy chief minister and tourism minister.Last month, a UAE delegation visited Jaipur to discuss cooperation in polo, horses and tourism. Among its interests was the Marwari, Rajasthan’s indigenous horse breed.“The Marwari is our local breed here in Rajasthan, and the visiting delegation was incredibly keen to see them. We discussed avenues to encourage a vibrant cultural exchange between the UAE, Rajasthan Tourism, and Rambagh Polo Club. They are very eager to support polo further and bring global visibility to this magnificent breed that has served Rajasthan for centuries,” Padmanabh says.Finding Players And SpectatorsElsewhere, access to a convenient ground is a concern. Delhi, Maharashtra and West Bengal have active polo circuits, supported by the Army, professional players and corporate patrons. In Delhi, however, Rajpurohit worries that a change of venue will cost the sport spectators and sponsors.“The finals of all elite tournaments in Delhi used to be at Jaipur Polo Ground, which is in the heart of Delhi,” he says. “Unfortunately, we lost that ground a few months back. Now more matches will be conducted at the Army Polo and Riding Centre. It is a shame that we lost the ground in the heart of Delhi. The number of people who used to attend and sponsor the events were more. Now that number will reduce.”He sees encouraging signs in the number of younger players taking up the sport.“The number of horses that have been shipped in every year is increasing. The number of kids who intend to compete in the sport is increasing. Earlier we used to have around four odd teams in Junior National Championship. Now we have six-seven teams,” he adds.Polo remains expensive to take up, though schools are helping introduce children to it.“There are many schools that are offering the equestrian part and the polo part, like Mayo and Delhi College, and they are coming up very well.”In Jaipur, demand for lessons already exceeds what the Sawai Man Singh Polo School and Academy can offer.“With that spirit in mind, a few years ago we started the Sawai Man Singh Polo School and Academy. It’s the only one of its kind and it’s doing very well. We have 50 students, which is our maximum capacity, and for the last three years, we have had a waiting list,” Padmanabh says.“Unfortunately, we can’t accommodate more because we have a limited number of horses, but it’s in the heart of the city and subsidised by the polo club. I donated some of my horses to the academy and I go there all the time to mentor them. Whenever someone is doing well, I pull them out to play with us,” Padmanabh says.Later Dinners For The HorsesPadmanabh says Jaipur’s experience of playing after dark goes back more than a century. He describes a brass night polo ball, with a small candle inside, used by women who played at night.
At Rambagh, playing under floodlights requires a change in the horses’ routine. Matches fall at what would ordinarily be their dinner time.“I would not say that it changes much. We just have to adjust the feeding time. Now, they have to have dinner a little bit later. So we just have to adapt our schedules,” Padmanabh says.The horses, he says, have settled into the later hours without trouble.“We know that if the horse is not happy, it won’t eat, or it will stop drinking water, or it will stop laying down. None of that happens. In fact, it is better for them because they don’t have the heat of the day.”

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Zhang Laiyuan, a longtime resident in a run-down neighborhood in east China, recalled the days of family reunion dinners in the past: "The living room was so small that half of us had to sit on the bed to eat."
In Shiliu New Village, Nanjing, capital of Jiangsu Province, windows once directly faced those of neighboring homes, roofs leaked frequently, and many residents had no indoor toilets.
This residential compound dates back to the 1950s. Roughly 1,500 residents were once packed onto a 16,000-square-meter plot. Nearly half the units spanned less than 35 square meters, with the smallest measuring a mere seven square meters.
The compound has been rebuilt from the ground up, with the first phase of 282 units completed and handed over last year. Every building now features not only standard amenities -- elevators, independent kitchens, bathrooms and balconies -- but also smart security systems, fire safety equipment and barrier-free ramps, along with underground parking, community commercial space, greenery and recreational plazas.
Last Spring Festival, Zhang's daughter, son-in-law and granddaughter came back for the holiday. The whole family sat together in the new living room, with plenty of space to spare.
UPGRADING AGING HOUSING TO MODERN STANDARDS
The transformation of Shiliu New Village mirrors what is taking place across cities in China.
Following decades of fast-paced urbanization progress, aging housing stock now makes up a substantial portion of China's real estate market. In response, experts say the focus of urban development has shifted away from large-scale expansion to improving the quality of existing housing stock.
Many cities are exploring ways to bring aging housing up to modern living standards, including complete demolition and reconstruction as well as micro-renovation. The goal is to systematically address issues ranging from safety risks and outdated layouts to inadequate accessibility for elderly residents.
In an old courtyard in Beijing's Chaoyang District, workers replaced rotting wooden roof structures with durable steel ones using prefabrication techniques. In Shanghai's Hongkou District, an apartment block was rebuilt with steel frames and prefabricated components, allowing residents to stay in their community throughout construction.
The central government has allocated 97 billion yuan (about 14.45 billion U.S. dollars) in its 2026 budget for urban renewal, mainly for renovating old and dilapidated urban housing, and the funding is expected to benefit around eight million households.
Under the national urban renewal plan (2026-2030) released earlier this year, China aims to launch renovations on 115,000 old urban residential compounds, retrofit or install 575,000 residential elevators, and build or upgrade 50,000 hectares of urban green space.
ECOLOGY, INDUSTRY, CONSUMPTION AS NEW PRIORITIES
The Maozhou River in south China's Guangdong Province was once heavily polluted. Following vigorous pollution control and vegetation restoration by local authorities in Shenzhen, the river has been transformed into a leisure belt with six ecological wetlands and 45.6 kilometers of walking trails. Rowing and dragon boat activities have also been introduced.
Zheng Degao, vice president of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design, said river regulation has gone beyond conventional environmental protection to take on a new meaning -- reshaping urban waterfront spaces to activate the whole city.
According to the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, between 2026 and 2030, China will renovate or upgrade 20,000 hectares of urban parkland, add 15,000 mini-sized "pocket parks" and build or upgrade 20,000 kilometers of urban greenways.
Urban renewal also holds huge potential for investment and consumption. China has set a target of renovating 1,500 old streets and factory compounds from 2026 to 2030, bringing in new industries and business models to inject fresh momentum into urban development.
Experts estimate the total urban renewal market will reach 15 trillion to 20 trillion yuan over the 2026-2030 period.
A renewal project in Shanghai's Xuhui District preserves the industrial heritage of a cement plant, an airport and a railway station while creating media and digital and intelligence industry clusters. More than 4,000 companies covering multiple sectors including artificial intelligence have gathered here, generating over 150,000 new jobs.
"Converting old streets and factory sites into cultural and creative districts drives growth in dining, retail and entertainment, while upgraded parks and sports facilities open new consumption scenarios for families, seniors and leisure seekers," said Yan Yuejin, deputy director of the E-house China R&D Institute.
Urban renewal is injecting lasting momentum into high-quality urban development while opening up broad opportunities for the real economy and capital markets, he said. ■

China calls for efforts to ensure emerging technologies better serve maritime security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:26:07 CST
15:26:07 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Thursday called for efforts to ensure that emerging technologies better serve maritime security and people's well-being.
Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, low-earth-orbit constellations, and unmanned systems are developing rapidly, with broad potential to empower maritime activities, develop the blue economy, and maintain maritime security. At the same time, the misuse and abuse of emerging technologies, together with the growing governance deficit, pose new risks and challenges to maritime security, said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations.
"The international community should strengthen solidarity and cooperation, give equal weight to development and security, and ensure that emerging technologies better serve maritime security and people's well-being," he told a Security Council open debate on emerging technologies and maritime security.
All countries should uphold a people-centered approach and guide emerging technologies to develop for good and to benefit humanity. They need to make comprehensive use of technological tools to enhance maritime situational awareness, early warning, and emergency response capabilities, thereby supporting maritime law enforcement, search-and-rescue operation, and disaster prevention and mitigation, and more effectively combating maritime crimes, he said.
There is also a need to strengthen technical risk assessment and regulatory frameworks to prevent terrorist forces and criminal groups from abusing emerging technologies, to guard against cyberattacks, data breaches, and loss of control over autonomous systems, and to ensure that emerging technologies remain safe, reliable, and controllable at all times, he added.
In recent years, some regional conflicts have triggered tensions in surrounding waters and international waterways, and undermined global shipping security and supply chain stability, said Fu. "The parties concerned should uphold the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, actively engage in dialogue and consultation, resolve disputes through diplomatic channels, and promote the early realization of lasting peace in the region."
There is a need to increase financial, technological, and capacity-building support for developing countries, promote equitable access to emerging technologies for people in all countries, and bridge the digital-intelligence divide and the development divide, he said. "We must jointly foster an open, inclusive, beneficial, and non-discriminatory environment for technological development, avoid overstretching the concept of national security in the field of technology, and oppose efforts to incite bloc confrontation or force countries to take sides."
All countries must interpret and apply the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea fully, accurately and in good faith, and put an end to selective application and double standards. China supports the United Nations in playing an active role in improving global governance in emerging technologies and the oceans, and in fully safeguarding the equal rights of developing countries to participate in the formulation of international rules, he said.
China is a major contributor to global technological progress and a staunch defender of the international rule of law at sea, and is ready to work with the international community to harness emerging technologies to safeguard maritime security, empower and enhance global development, and jointly build a prosperous world with tranquil seas, said Fu. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) has outlined four areas of focus for steadfastly following a distinctive Chinese path to combating corruption in a resolution adopted at a plenary session of the CPC Central Committee, a senior anti-graft official said Friday.
The four areas include maintaining a tough stance against corruption, strengthening checks on and oversight over the exercise of power, fortifying the cultural-ethical foundations for championing integrity and disdaining corruption, and enhancing coordinated efforts to prevent corruption by rooting out audacity, opportunity, and desire.
Zhang Fuhai, deputy secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection of the CPC and deputy head of the National Commission of Supervision, made the remarks at a press conference on the guiding principles from the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC.
The plenum, which concluded on Thursday in Beijing, adopted the Resolution of the Central Committee of the CPC on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance.
Since the 18th National Congress of the CPC in 2012, discipline inspection and supervisory organs across the country have filed 8.105 million cases and punished 7.922 million people, including 963 officials registered at and supervised by the CPC Central Committee, according to Zhang.
Also speaking at the press conference, Xie Chuntao, vice president of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), said the resolution sets specific requirements for "ensuring the enforcement of institutions."
The resolution stresses that mandatory institutional requirements must be executed, with everyone equal before institutions, no one enjoying privileges in observing them, and no exceptions in enforcing them, Xie said.
It also requires that institutions be enforced and overseen throughout the process of Party organizations, Party members and officials performing their duties, ensuring that institutions remain authoritative at all times and effective everywhere, he added.
The resolution also calls for resolutely correcting practices in which directives are ignored and prohibitions are defied, he said. ■

Mayon Volcano in northern Philippines erupts, alert level raised to 3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:25:54 CST
15:25:54 KST

A large plume of smoke and ash is seen after the eruption of Mayon Volcano in Albay Province, the Philippines, on Oct. 30, 2026. The Philippines' Mayon Volcano erupted on Friday, said the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology. (Albay Province Public Information Office/Handout via Xinhua)
MANILA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Philippines' Mayon Volcano erupted on Friday in Albay province in the northern Philippines, said the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS).
According to the institute's statement, a "moderately explosive eruption" occurred at Mayon Volcano at around 11:53 a.m. local time Friday. The eruption lasted for about 6 minutes.
PHIVOLCS said the event generated a plume that rose 3,000 meters above the crater. The ashfall is expected to drift west and southwest.
The institute raised the alert level from 2 to Level 3, with Level 5 being the highest on the scale. This means that Mayon Volcano is in a new phase of magmatic eruption, with increased chances of lava flows and pyroclastic density currents affecting the upper to middle slopes of the volcano in the immediate days to weeks.
The statement said it recommended that people in the 6-km radius Permanent Danger Zone be evacuated and that civil aviation authorities advise pilots to avoid flying close to the volcano's summit.
Mayon, famed for its near-perfect conical shape, is one of the Philippines' most active volcanoes and has a long history of explosive eruptions that have triggered mass evacuations. ■

U.S. eases restrictions on six unapproved peptides despite FDA safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:25:40 UTC
15:25:40 KST

U.S. eases restrictions on six unapproved peptides despite FDA safety concerns
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has issued a draft policy easing restrictions on six unapproved peptides, allowing licensed pharmacies and physicians to prepare them under certain conditions, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The policy, filed with the Federal Register on October 28, covers BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and Epitalon. Under the measure, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) does not intend to take enforcement action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or licensed physicians that compound drugs using these substances, provided specified requirements are met.
Compounding involves combining or modifying drug ingredients to prepare medications tailored to individual patients. Under Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, pharmacies and physicians must meet certain conditions to qualify for exemptions from standard drug approval and manufacturing requirements.
The new policy requires patient-specific prescriptions and ingredients sourced from FDA-registered manufacturers. According to the HHS document, compounders must obtain certificates of analysis verifying the identity, purity and potency of the substances, as well as testing for potentially harmful contaminants, including heavy metals and bacteria.
Compounders must also report serious adverse events and product quality problems to the FDA and relevant state authorities. Products may contain only one active pharmaceutical ingredient to make it easier to identify the substance responsible for any adverse reaction.
The policy also specifies permitted forms of administration for individual peptides. Semax is covered for intranasal use, while KPV is limited to oral and topical formulations. Other substances are subject to different restrictions depending on their characteristics and available safety evidence.
The document was issued by the Health Secretary's office rather than the FDA, which ordinarily oversees drug regulation. It is scheduled for official publication on October 30, after which a two-week public comment period will begin.
HHS describes the measure as an interim enforcement policy while the FDA determines through rulemaking which peptide substances should be permitted for compounding. The Federal Register notice specifies that the policy does not establish legal rights and is not binding on HHS or the public.
Kennedy argued that the policy would provide patients with a more controlled alternative to products obtained through unregulated channels. The HHS document states that the measure "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety."
HHS cited significant demand for the peptides despite the absence of FDA-approved products. The department said its approach is intended to discourage the use of research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers, which it considers a potential safety risk for American patients.
The decision follows a July meeting of the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, which recommended adding six of seven peptides under consideration to the list of substances permitted for compounding. FDA scientific staff had recommended against their inclusion, citing insufficient evidence of safety and effectiveness.
HHS cited additional information, including documented use of the substances and new quality-control records from FDA-registered manufacturers, to support its decision. The department said laboratory testing data addressed some of the deficiencies previously identified by FDA scientists.
In 2023, the FDA placed several peptides, including BPC-157 and TB-500, in a category identifying potential safety risks associated with compounding. The designation was removed on April 22, 2026, although HHS notes that neither the original classification nor its removal changed the substances' legal status under Section 503A.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that perform various biological functions, including cell signaling and hormone regulation. While some peptide-based medications, such as insulin and GLP-1 drugs, are established treatments, the six substances covered by the policy have not received FDA approval.
Interest in experimental peptides has grown within online wellness communities, where they are promoted for muscle recovery, wound healing, weight management and anti-aging. Many of these claimed benefits lack sufficient evidence from human clinical trials.
The consumer advocacy group Public Citizen criticized Kennedy's decision, warning that expanding access to unapproved substances could expose patients to contamination, impurities and unknown adverse effects.
Compounded drugs are not individually reviewed by the FDA for safety, effectiveness or quality before reaching patients. The HHS document also states that the department may reconsider the interim policy if adverse reactions or product quality problems emerge.
The policy does not amount to FDA approval of the six peptides or establish that their claimed health benefits have been demonstrated.

Baltic Defense Line bunkers installed near Estonia's Narva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:25:00 UTC
15:25:00 KST

Baltic Defense Line bunkers installed near Estonia's Narva
The installation of concrete bunkers on Estonia's section of the Baltic Defense Line is continuing in Ida-Viru County, and the first structures have now been completed near Narva.
Estonia plans to place approximately 600 structures along the border with Russia, and the first bunkers were erected in southern Estonia last year.
The Baltic Defense Line is a joint network of defensive structures built by Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, running along the borders with Russia and Belarus. Estonia's section is around 100 kilometers long.
Obstacles installed in northeastern and southeastern Estonia will slow the enemy's movement, while concrete bunkers will protect soldiers from artillery fire, officials say.
The defense line is a peacetime preparation for a wartime plan.
"We know that we will not have much time if the enemy crosses the border. We also do not have land to give up to them to gain time. That is why we are starting right at the border and trying to do as much as possible in peacetime," explained Estonian Defense Forces engineer inspector Ainar Afanasjev.
So far, the most progress in northeastern Estonia has been made with obstacles. Where possible, they have already been constructed. In addition, thousands of "dragon's teeth" have been stockpiled along the border so they can be quickly put in place if necessary.
The most labor-intensive part of constructing the defense line is building the bunkers. So far, only 28 have been completed, as work was slowed down by legal challenges.
"The initial plan was to begin constructing the next strongpoints in the third quarter of this year. Unfortunately, we became embroiled in disputes during the procurement process, which, as of this Monday, have reached a final resolution, and we can proceed with the procurement procedures," said Armin Siilivask, the Baltic Defense Line project manager at the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK).
The completed bunkers will be equipped with electricity and communications systems, while the Defense Forces will dig trenches and firing positions next to the bunkers.
"It is clear that if we receive an early warning, we will mobilize our army, and these positions have been built so that they can come here and begin carrying out their tasks. To fight the battle that we have to fight," Afanasjev added.
Construction of the defense line will cost nearly €60 million, and it is hoped that it will be completed by the end of next year.

Tomb discovered among seating at ancient theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:23:15 UTC
15:23:15 KST

The tomb, featuring a mudbrick sarcophagus and a fired-brick gabled roof, dates to the first century. (AA Photo)
A tomb has been discovered during excavations at the theater of the ancient city of Apollonia ad Rhyndacum in the tourist district of Gölyazı, in the northwestern province of Bursa’s Nilüfer district, in a find expected to shed light on the settlement’s Hellenistic history.
The tomb, featuring a mudbrick sarcophagus and a fired-brick gabled roof, dates to the first century. Archaeologists determined that the deceased had been cremated.
Excavations at the ancient theater began in 2021 with the permission of the Culture and Tourism Ministry and are being conducted on behalf of Bursa Uludağ University under the direction of Derya Şahin, a professor in the university’s Department of Archaeology, with support from Nilüfer Municipality.
Built on the slope of Zambaktepe overlooking Lake Uluabat during the Hellenistic period, the theater is estimated to have held around 5,000 spectators. It also featured areas resembling VIP sections and private boxes. Excavations have uncovered 42 seating steps, which have been returned to their original positions.
The tomb was found in the northern part of the theater’s lower seating section, known as the lower cavea.
“We came across an unusual tomb this year, featuring a mudbrick sarcophagus and a fired-brick roof. The question of why a tomb was located here became a major question mark. At the same time, the discovery excited us,” Şahin told state-run Anadolu Agency.
She said the team was trying to determine the reasons behind the burial’s location and that extensive research would be needed to answer the questions raised by the discovery.
“The most important finding this year was a tomb with a mudbrick sarcophagus in the northern section of the theater’s lower cavea. It dates to the first century,” she said.
Şahin noted that a necropolis was already known to exist at the entrance to the ancient city. Although the newly discovered tomb shares the characteristics of other known graves in the area, its location within the theater is unusual.
“In an ancient city that already has a necropolis, what was a tomb doing in the theater? This excited us greatly. The tomb must have been special, carried some meaning or bore traces of sanctity or heroism,” she said.
The cremation of the deceased has made it difficult to establish how many individuals were buried there, Şahin added. The burning also meant that the tomb yielded few archaeological finds.
Theater may have had two levels
Excavations are also continuing in the theater’s upper seating section, although researchers have found little evidence of its infrastructure. Şahin said the upper seating area may have rested on a vaulted structure, but extensive destruction has made it impossible to establish its original layout.
The team believes the theater may have had two levels, with a passageway approximately 1-meter wide, known as a diazoma, separating the seating sections.
“We envisage a vaulted structure supporting the upper level. The theater originally displayed the characteristics of a classical Hellenistic theater, built into a hillside. Inscriptions indicate that its final phase dates to the early second century A.D. We believe the upper section may have rested on a vaulted structure, similar to those found in Roman theaters,” Şahin said.
The excavation team plans to complete this season’s work at the site by the end of November.
Şahin emphasized that the ancient city had been continuously inhabited, making it difficult to find structures as well preserved as those in abandoned settlements. Nevertheless, the excavations have yielded important findings about the city’s history.
She added that further archaeological work around the theater could reveal structures connected to it, including a temple or an ancient road. Many possibilities about the site’s past remain unexplored, she said.
A tomb has been discovered between the seating rows of an ancient theater in Bursa’s Gölyazı, raising questions about why someone was buried within the theater

Confusion likely as Finland observes Halloween and All Saints on same day
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:22:55 EET
15:22:55 KST

Although Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October, and means 'All Hallows' Eve' — or the night before the Christian feast of All Saints' Day on 1 November — Finnish authorities have this year designated Saturday as the national public holiday.
Following a loosening of the country's alcohol laws earlier this year, outlets of Finland's state-owned alcohol retailer Alko will be permitted to open on a public holiday for the first time ever.
The stores will be open according to their individual Saturday schedules.
Despite the country observing a public holiday on Saturday, shoppers are unlikely to notice any difference in the opening hours of shopping centres and large grocery stores.
There may be some confusion for public transport passengers however, as operators in some cities — such as Helsinki and Tampere — will keep their regular Saturday schedules, while others — for example in Turku and Rovaniemi — will follow a holiday schedule instead. Passengers are advised to check with their local operator.
National rail carrier VR will operate according to its normal Saturday schedules.
People planning a trip to a museum on Saturday are also advised to carefully check the schedules, as many museums are open on All Saints' Day, but the hours may differ from a normal Saturday.
Many libraries will also close their doors on Saturday, while sports facilities in many areas will open according to a Sunday schedule.
Change in the air
There will be much change in the air this weekend, as calendars switch from October to November and Finland's recent spell of unseasonably warm and dry weather comes to an end.
That's because rain showers forecast for southern and central parts of the country on Friday morning are expected to spread to the rest of the country over the coming days, according to Yle meteorologist Henriikka Heikinoja.
In the east, a low-pressure system will move slowly northwards from the southeast throughout the day on Friday, also bringing light rain showers and drizzle.
The air will also feel a bit chillier, as temperatures drop to as low as 3 degrees Celsius during the day in some areas.
On Saturday, temperatures will range between 8 degrees Celsius along the southern coastline to 3 degrees in Finnish Lapland, while scattered rain showers are also expected.
