Grass seeding aims to extend ski season at Ergan Mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:22:45 UTC
15:22:45 KST

The center’s lake and natural trails also attract visitors during the summer. (AA Photo)
Ergan Mountain Winter Sports and Nature Tourism Center in the eastern province of Erzincan is preparing for the new ski season with infrastructure projects, improvements to its slopes and the development of a High-Altitude Training Center.
Located on the foothills of the Munzur Mountains, the center features a summit elevation of 3,258 meters, a vertical drop of 1,300 meters and ski runs stretching more than 30 kilometers in total. Its proximity to Erzincan Airport, just 12 minutes away, and its location 10 kilometers from the city center offer logistical advantages for athletes and holidaymakers.
Having welcomed around 2 million visitors last season, the center aims to exceed that figure this year by promoting year-round tourism, expanding water sports and trekking opportunities and extending the ski season through grass seeding on its slopes.
Mehmet Emre Canpolat, deputy governor of Erzincan and secretary-general of the Provincial Special Administration, told state-run Anadolu Agency that preparations for the coming season began as soon as the previous season ended.
Describing efforts to improve slope quality and increase snow retention, Canpolat said the center was investing in facilities and landscaping to provide better conditions for skiers.
“With our approximately 4,000-square-meter ski lodge, High Altitude Training Center, hotel, day-use facilities and grass seeding work on the slopes, we aim to extend the period snow remains on the ground and offer skiers a more enjoyable environment,” he said.
“When snow comes into contact with soil and mud, it begins to melt much faster. By planting grass, we create a natural cushion between the soil and the snow cover, extending the time the snow stays on the ground. Our aim is to gradually extend this practice all the way to the summit,” he added.
Canpolat said the mountain’s topography offered considerable potential for advanced and professional skiers.
“There is a vertical drop of around 1,300 meters from the summit to where we are. Thanks to this gradient, most of our runs are classified as red and black, making Ergan Mountain a destination particularly appealing to those who practice skiing at an advanced level,” he said.
Canpolat said the administration did not want the center’s operations to be limited to the 100 to 150 days of the winter season, emphasizing that year-round tourism was a priority for new investments.
The center’s lake and natural trails also attract visitors during the summer, he said.
“We are focused on operating our ski center actively throughout all 12 months of the year. While we have investments covering the 100 to 150 days of the winter season, we are placing much greater emphasis on projects that cover the entire year,” Canpolat said.
He added that the lake was used for water sports in summer, while the mountain’s higher elevations offered opportunities for traditional highland grazing, livestock farming, trekking and nature exploration.
“In some seasons, the number of visitors during the summer months can even exceed that of the winter. Ergan Mountain has now become a four-season attraction for Erzincan,” he said.
Targeting international sporting events
Canpolat said interest in the center was growing and new investors were increasingly looking at the region, adding that the administration aimed to raise its ambitions further.
The High-Altitude Training Center, being built under the auspices of the Youth and Sports Ministry, is expected to attract major sports clubs for pre-season training camps once completed, he said.
The administration is also working with the Turkish Ski Federation to plan competition schedules and maintaining contacts with the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) to bring international competitions to Erzincan.
“We welcomed nearly 2 million visitors in previous years, and our target this season is to exceed 2 million. Achieving this figure would provide a strong boost to both our city and the economy of the Eastern Anatolia region,” Canpolat said.
“We are among the few centers in the world where you can reach the ski slopes just 12 minutes after leaving the airport. We welcome all skiing and nature enthusiasts to Erzincan,” he added.

A highliner balances on a suspended line above Murat Canyon during the Diyadin Canyon Walk in Ağrı.
Highline athletes attempted a 120-meter crossing above a 60-meter-deep canyon in Türkiye’s eastern province of Ağrı on Oct. 27, during an annual gathering combining a nature walk, paragliding and local food.
Coordinated by the Ağrı Governor’s Office, the fourth Traditional Diyadin Canyon Walk began at Köprü thermal springs and ended at a recreation area after roughly 8 kilometers. Governor Önder Bozkurt, deputy governors, district governors, institution heads, students and residents attended.
After the walk, Enes Uçar and Sedat Kale gave a brief demonstration at Murat Canyon in Diyadin, walking on a line suspended across the 120-meter-wide gorge. Wind occasionally hampered their progress.

Kale said his team had practiced highlining across Türkiye for 15 years but was performing in Ağrı for the first time.

Highlining is a balance sport in which athletes walk along a narrow line suspended high above the ground.
The canyon follows the Murat River, with cliffs reaching 60 meters in places. Local authorities have organized an October canyon walk annually since 2023. Diyadin is also known for its thermal springs, with hiking trails and camping areas around the canyon offering other outdoor activities.

Nvidia's web of AI bets: smart strategy or bubble risk?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:22:02 UTC
15:22:02 KST

Nvidia's $3 billion investment in Meta's share sale, announced on Oct. 30, is the latest addition to a portfolio of stakes, loans and guarantees that has made the chip giant what some analysts describe as the central bank of the artificial intelligence boom.
The galaxy of deals has helped keep demand running high for Nvidia's processors, which power vast data centers around the world and are the central ingredient of the AI revolution.
That demand has made Nvidia the world's most valuable company by market capitalization and turned chief executive Jensen Huang into AI's kingmaker.
But the investments have raised a nagging question among some doubters on Wall Street: Is Nvidia helping to inflate an AI bubble?
Nvidia has taken stakes in leading AI developers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX.
It has also invested in "neocloud" companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent out computing power built on Nvidia chips.
Its bets extend well beyond the United States. In Europe, Nvidia has backed French AI developer Mistral and British self-driving startup Wayve. In Asia, it has teamed up with South Korea's SK Group to build data centers.
Beyond equity, the company has offered financial backstops, acting as a customer of last resort.
In CoreWeave's case, Nvidia committed to buy up to $6.3 billion of unused computing capacity if no other customer takes it.
Nvidia also has around $36 billion in cloud backstops and a guarantee of up to $105 billion linked to an OpenAI data center, according to U.S. media.
Experts say Nvidia's enormous profits give it few better options.
"They're essentially becoming a bank," said Michael Cusumano, a professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management.
"Channeling it back to infrastructure investment tied to purchases of Nvidia equipment is a smart thing."
He said the alternatives were less attractive.
Running its own data centers would put Nvidia in competition with its biggest customers "and that might also trigger a whole bunch of antitrust complaints," Cusumano added.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia identifies parts of the AI ecosystem that are not investing enough and puts money into them to fill the gaps.
"It's unprecedented, but it appears to be working," he said.
Huang has defended the approach, arguing that frontier AI labs are the first generation of startups that need tens of billions of dollars to get started, not just millions.
Nvidia's investments effectively give those companies more time to succeed.
Critics have compared the deals to the dot-com era, when companies inflated their growth by investing in startups that then bought their products.
"There is nothing intrinsically wrong with Nvidia helping its clients," said Paulo Carvão, a senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School.
"But the closer these relationships are, the harder it is for one to assess true sustainable demand."
Luria said not all demand was equal.
"If Nvidia gives CoreWeave money to turn around and buy Nvidia chips, that's not as good as Microsoft buying Nvidia chips because they have a customer in OpenAI that has a customer in an enterprise technology that's willing to pay for it," he said.
The main concern is concentration. Two direct customers accounted for 22 percent and 14 percent of Nvidia's revenue in its 2026 fiscal year, according to the company's annual report.
Carvão said the web of overlapping investments increases the risk of contagion if a weaker company such as CoreWeave runs into trouble.
"If AI demand disappoints, spending cuts could hit chipmakers, data-center builders and their financiers at once," he said.
Those concerns have grown this month. Shares of several Nvidia-linked neocloud companies, including CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, fell at least 30 percent in October amid worries about tighter credit for AI projects.
Carvão noted that the market for AI chips remains limited by supply. He estimated demand would keep growing for another 12 to 18 months before it begins to level off.
Cusumano said he expected high demand for Nvidia chips to continue for three to five years.

Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery producing jet fuel for the Russian military and a factory supplying food rations to Russian armed forces in separate overnight attacks on Oct. 30, triggering fires at both facilities.
Novokuybyshevsk refinery produces jet fuel for Russian military
The strike on the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Russia’s Samara Oblast marks the first reported attack on a Russian oil refinery in nearly two weeks, potentially signaling a resumption of Kyiv’s campaign against Russia’s oil industry.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Residents of Novokuybyshevsk reported explosions and air defense activity early on Oct. 30. Regional authorities declared a drone threat at around 6 a.m., by which time the attack was already underway, according to the independent Russian outlet ASTRA.
Based on photographs sent in by readers, ASTRA’s OSINT analyst identified the site of the fire as the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery.
The facility has belonged to Russian oil giant Rosneft since 2007 and has an annual processing capacity of approximately 8.8 million tons of crude oil.
It produces more than 20 types of petroleum products, including Euro-5 petrol and diesel, bitumen and petroleum coke, as well as jet fuel used by Russia’s Aerospace Forces.
The refinery has been targeted repeatedly. It was last attacked on Aug. 22, when Ukrainian drones struck the facility and caused a fire. Following Ukrainian strikes on April 18, the plant suspended operations at both of its primary crude distillation units, AVT-11 and AVT-9.
Ukrainian Soldier Suspected of Passing Troop Positions to Russia
The latest strike comes after a pause of nearly two weeks in reported Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The last documented strikes on Russia’s oil sector targeted the Ryazan Oil Refinery on Oct. 15, followed by an attack on an industrial facility in Surgut on Oct. 16.
The pause came amid pressure from US President Donald Trump, who urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and energy infrastructure.
In the meantime, Ukraine appeared to redirect its drone campaign toward Russia’s metallurgical industry. According to Russian media outlets, Ukrainian forces had shifted their focus to steelmakers, targeting facilities belonging to major Russian industrial groups.
The latest attack on the Novokuybyshevsk refinery, however, suggests that Russian oil infrastructure may once again be back on Kyiv’s target list.
Ukrainian drones also hit Russian military food supplier
Separately, Ukrainian drones struck the Konservsushprod factory in the town of Starodub in Russia’s Bryansk region overnight on Oct. 30, according to photos and videos shared by local residents and analysed by ASTRA.
A large fire broke out at the facility following the strike.
The company describes itself as a historic supplier of canned food and individual food rations to Russian security forces and the armed forces. It also holds the rights to the “Russian Army” brand. The factory was previously targeted in 2023 and 2025.
Drone attacks force Moscow airports to close
Meanwhile, drone attacks prompted the closure of all four major Moscow airports overnight.
Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency imposed temporary restrictions on arrivals and departures at Domodedovo, Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo and Zhukovsky airports. Yaroslavl Airport was also closed.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that 862 drones had flown towards the Moscow region between the evening of Oct. 29 and 7 a.m. on Oct. 30.
Most were intercepted at a distance from the capital, he said, adding that 170 drones were shot down on the approaches to Moscow.

Bank of Japan says inflation hit 2 percent target after 13 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:21:21 UTC
15:21:21 KST

The Bank of Japan said on Oct. 30 inflation had hit its 2 percent target, more than 13 years after it adopted the goal in a bid to pull the economy out of deflation.
For decades successive governments struggled to pull the country out of a spiral of deflation, sustained falls in prices that are harmful for economic growth, and the 2 percent goal was set in 2013 as the BoJ launched massive monetary easing measures.
Although core consumer inflation at times topped the level in the early 2020s, Oct. 30 marked the first time that the BoJ confirmed the long-term price trend had been achieved.
"Underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally consistent with the price stability target of two percent, and is expected to remain at around that level," the central bank said on its website.
The BoJ also said in a statement that it had kept its key interest rate unchanged at 1.25 percent after an eight-to-one majority vote.
That decision came after the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank kept their policy rates unchanged earlier in the week.
However Japanese officials are expected to hike in December as inflationary pressure builds.
Japan's core inflation in September stood at 2.1 percent, sharply up from 1.7 percent in August, according to data released by the government last week.

Cryptocurrency platform Binance said it had fallen victim to a major hack that hit around $6.3 billion in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft.
The company, the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses."
The company later said on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion."
"We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far," it added.
That would be four times the amount impacted in what had been the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform, which was attributed to hackers affiliated with North Korea.
At about 0030 GMT on Oct. 30, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement."
"This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company said.
The company's statement on X said an initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorized party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," Binance said.
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.

Türkiye’s cotton output squeezed by rising costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:18:10 UTC
15:18:10 KST

Türkiye’s seed cotton production is expected to fall 38 percent as rising input costs and the war in the Middle East weigh on the sector, prompting farmers to switch to crops such as wheat and corn.
The new cotton harvest season has begun, but increasing production costs are putting the future of cotton fields at risk. Global cotton production is forecast to decline 2 percent in the 2026-2027 season, while Türkiye’s seed cotton output is projected to drop to 1.2 million tons.
ÇUKOBİRLİK announced a purchase price of 41.50 Turkish Liras per kilogram for first-grade white cotton with a ginning yield of 42 percent, while the price for spotted cotton was set at 40.5 liras per kilogram.
The Turkish Statistical Institute’s (TÜİK) second crop production estimate also predicts that seed cotton production will fall to 1.2 million tons, one of the lowest levels recorded in the past 35 years.
As cotton prices have failed to keep pace with rising costs, cultivation areas have contracted and farmers have increasingly turned to alternative crops such as wheat, corn and sunflower. Fertilizer, diesel, energy, seed and labor expenses, along with the impact of the war in the Middle East on input costs, are expected to shape the market during the new season.
Aydın accounts for 11.6 percent of Türkiye’s cotton production, followed by İzmir with 6.7 percent and Manisa with 3.4 percent.
Bülent Uçak, chair of the İzmir Commodity Exchange Assembly, said the area planted with cotton in the Aegean region had contracted 47 percent to 49,454 decares.
The region’s lint cotton production, which stood at 188,000 tons in the 2024-2025 season, is expected to decline to 93,700 tons in 2026-2027.
Seed cotton refers to the raw crop collected from fields, while lint cotton is the processed fiber ready for use.
In Şanlıurfa, which accounts for 41.7 percent of Türkiye’s cotton output, the cultivation area has fallen from 1.7 million decares to 800,000 decares.
Ahmet Eyyüpoğlu, a board member of the Union of Turkish Chambers of Agriculture and head of the Haliliye Chamber of Agriculture, said cotton prices had remained at the same level for three years.
“As input costs increased, farmers began to stop planting. Producers moving away from cotton have turned to wheat and corn,” Eyyüpoğlu said.
He said the cost of producing one kilogram of cotton had risen from 30 liras last year to approximately 40 liras this year, adding that the purchase price should be at least 50 liras per kilogram.
Number of cotton-growing villages falls sharply
Cotton cultivation areas in the Salihli district of Manisa have also declined by between 45 percent and 50 percent compared with last year.
Cem Yalvaç, head of the Salihli Chamber of Agriculture, said the cultivated area had fallen from 65,000-70,000 decares in 2012 to between 3,000 and 4,000 decares.
“The number of villages engaged in cotton farming has dropped from 12 or 13 to two. Producers have shifted to crops with lower costs, including corn, tobacco, peppers and watermelons,” Yalvaç said.
A report on agricultural product markets issued by Türkiye’s Agriculture and Forestry Ministry identified several factors expected to shape the global cotton market next season. These include the impact of geopolitical developments in the Middle East on input costs, the possible effect of drought on U.S. production, the influence of oil prices on cotton’s competitiveness against polyester and China’s production policies aimed at supporting higher yields.

====================================================================================================

The new time lord: Wei Koh on his first year as GPHG jury president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:16:13 UTC
15:16:13 KST

With just a week to go before the prestigious awards at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève, Euronews Culture caught up with one of watchmaking's most charismatic figures, Wei Koh, founder of media company Revolution and, for the first time, jury president of GPHG, the "Oscars of watchmaking".
White T-shirt, visible tattoos, large sunglasses, Wei Koh cuts through the crowd to greet us in the sweltering heat of the Geneva Watch Days pavilion, where dozens of fine watchmaking houses have gathered to show off their latest releases.
"Hey dude, what’s up?", he asks. Behind the infinitely laid-back energy, he's about to preside, for the first time, over the jury of the luxurious industry’s most prestigious competition, the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG).
This year, 84 nominated timepieces are competing for 19 prizes, including the coveted Aiguille d'Or, awarded every year since 2001 to the single most remarkable watch of the year. The 2026 awards ceremony will be held on 7 November in Geneva.
"The creativity is extraordinary this year. You've got watches that are executed at such a level of finesse that, as a watch lover, it makes you want to weep," promises the 54-year-old Singaporean.
What is the jury actually looking for?
The final list of 84 pieces in the running was published early September. Most are genuine feats of technical artistry, often produced in tiny numbers by confidential workshops most people outside the industry have never heard of.
So what makes a watch better than another? "I think singularity, right? Like a voice that's really unique," Koh says. "Remember the first time you listened to John Coltrane, or Miles Davis, or Tupac? Even if that person was relatively young, they were making a fundamental contribution to music. It's the same with watches."
He borrows a line from watchmaking legend François-Paul Journe, who once described the craft as one continuous wall. "If you want to enter this métier, your mission is to add at least one brick, a vital contribution," Koh explains. "That's what we're looking for."
Mechanical watchmaking know-how, sometimes billed as the 12th art, has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since December 2020.
Among this year's contenders, he quotes the first ever grand sonnerie able to play two different melodies for the quarter-hour chimes, a watch reviving a century-old balance-wheel technique thought lost to history, and a chronograph that reinvents how we physically interact with the complication altogether.
Behind closed doors
Choosing which timepiece deserves top honours is no small task. The 24-member jury will meet behind closed doors early November in Geneva, just days before the ceremony, to physically examine each of the 84 nominated pieces, to discuss and vote by secret ballot.
"We're kind of on an honour system, so we don't really talk much about what happens behind closed doors," Koh says, though he's quick to credit his predecessor, Nick Foulkes, for setting the tone: rigorous exchange, real disagreement, open dialogue.
"Nick has always believed in debate," Koh, who has been a jury member during the previous editions, remembers. "There are extraordinary moments where you're like, wow, I've just had a revelation. Someone explained it so well it completely changed my mind about a specific timepiece."
Wei Koh built his reputation the hard way. Back in 2005, he was handing out magazines at Baselworld. Some 21-years and a thriving media company later, he's one of the most recognisable names in the business, and the producer of Man of the Hour, one of the first documentary-style series dedicated to watchmaking.
"What I've learned over these years is that this industry is a meritocracy," he says. "If you strive for excellence, if you're consistent and honest in your efforts, you will succeed. But what this industry really rewards is when you try to contribute meaningfully to its survival, by protecting its principles."
The luxury watch market has hit historic highs over the past decade. The result of a careful balancing act between honouring heritage and pushing technical innovation. In the exhibition room of the Geneva Watch Days, centuries-old complications sit alongside breakthrough materials.
An industry in motion
This edition of the GPHG comes with real changes: the old "men's" and "women's" watch categories have been scrapped in favour of new categories built around technical criteria. On 7 October, adieu French, the ceremony will be held in English for the first time. A shift that echoes something Koh has spent two decades pushing for.
"The whole idea with Revolution was to uplift the founding ethics and principles of watchmaking while connecting it with a much bigger audience," he says. "For this craft, for this industry to survive, we have to keep growing the audience and bring in the next generation."
The renewed obsession with mechanical watches might seem surprising in the age of artificial intelligence. Koh states that they are more relevant than ever, and points to what he calls "tech and AI oligarchs, the people who built the hyper-digitised world we now live in, who have become huge watch collectors."
The most famous example is Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, who has been seen wearing high-end independent watchmakers such as Patek Philippe to F.P. Journe, H. Moser & Cie., and De Bethune.
"I think it's because a mechanical watch is the opposite of everything ephemeral. It outlives you. It only takes the energy you give it, by winding it or wearing it. There's something magical about that."
Wei Koh saves his best line for last: "Watchmaking gave me everything: a job, and my friendships, which are incredibly international. Because watchmaking transcends where you're from, your age, your religion, even your language. I find that to be this incredible force that binds us together." In the world we live in today, he suggests, that might matter more than it ever has.
The winners of the 2026 GPHG will be announced at the Bâtiment des Forces Motrices in Geneva on Saturday, 7 November and live on Euronews Culture and gphg.org.

Istanbul Airport handled an average of 1,491 arriving and departing flights a day during Oct. 19-25, making it Europe’s busiest airport, according to EUROCONTROL.
Amsterdam Schiphol followed with 1,371 daily flights, ahead of Paris Charles de Gaulle with 1,369, Frankfurt with 1,303 and Madrid Barajas with 1,299.
Flight numbers at Istanbul were 2 percent lower than the previous week and 3 percent below the same period last year. Antalya Airport also featured in the top 10, placing 10th with 875 daily flights.
The report was published on Oct. 29, the eighth anniversary of Istanbul Airport’s inauguration by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in 2018.
The airport has continued to expand its infrastructure, opening a fourth main runway on Sept. 18. The addition brought its total to six runways, including two backup runways.
The new runway is the airport’s first to run east-west. The Transport and Infrastructure Ministry said it was designed to shorten taxiing and flight times, particularly for domestic and eastbound services, while providing more options for operations in adverse weather.

AA photo.
Leaders of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) gathered in Ankara on Oct. 30 as Türkiye took over the group’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan, with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan calling for closer cooperation.
The 13th summit opened at the Presidential Complex under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.”

Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:12:55 UTC
15:12:55 KST

Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.
- Share:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk have completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station, marking another important step in a major upgrade to the orbiting laboratory's power system. The astronauts finished their work at 3:08 p.m. EDT.
During the spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed a new International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station's 2A electrical power channel. This is the seventh such array added to the station, providing additional electricity for essential operations, including the station's eventual safe and controlled deorbit.
Final Spacewalk Will Complete Solar Array Upgrade
The astronauts also performed several preliminary tasks to prepare for another spacewalk scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 5. During that mission, astronauts will install the eighth and final solar array on the station's 3B power channel. NASA plans to begin live coverage at 6:45 a.m., with information on how to watch available through the agency.
Once the final array is installed, the International Space Station's solar power expansion will be complete. Together, the eight new arrays will increase the station's available power by as much as 30%, raising its electricity generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.
A Milestone for Space Station Operations
The completed mission, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, marked Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. It was also the 285th spacewalk conducted to support the assembly, maintenance, and improvement of the International Space Station.

Turkish opposition backs voters to reject government ‘coercion’
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:12:09 CET
15:12:09 KST

By Huseyin Hayatsever
IZMIR, Turkey, Oct 30 (Reuters) - When Turkey’s opposition made big gains in local elections in March 2024, its leaders believed they had finally found a way to defeat long-serving President Tayyip Erdogan.
More than two years later, the opposition’s leading presidential challenger is in prison, its main party has been split by a court ruling and some of the opposition figures who were elected as mayors have defected to Erdogan’s AK Party.
The opposition remains defiant. It says it retains faith in democratic elections and that voters will reject what they see as a politically motivated legal crackdown on government opponents in the next national elections, due in 2028.
The opposition now faces a challenge to harness and sustain people’s anger until then over what they say is government coercion under Erdogan, who has been in power as prime minister and then president for 23 years.
“I do not believe this anger has disappeared,” said Seren Selvin Korkmaz, co-founder and co-director of the IstanPol Institute, an Istanbul-based think tank.
“However, unless this anger is channelled into political energy or organisational energy, it will fade away. It may evolve into disappointment, hopelessness or apathy.”
The government denies the legal cases against its opponents are politically motivated and says the judiciary operates independently.
IZMIR MAYOR’S DEFECTION
Few places capture the opposition’s challenges better than Izmir in western Turkey on the Aegean coast.
The AK Party has never managed to win Izmir, the country’s third-largest city with about 4.5 million residents, at the ballot box, but this month Mayor Cemil Tugay, who was elected on an opposition ticket in 2024, defected to Erdogan’s party.
Tugay’s defection represents a significant symbolic setback in what has long been regarded as the heartland of Turkey’s secular, social democratic opposition.
Tugay says he did so because it was “in the best interests of Izmir” and Erdogan has dismissed as slander opposition allegations that Tugay switched parties under pressure.
But the opposition New Party’s head in Izmir expressed confidence that voters in the city would show their opposition to Tugay’s move and what he depicted as government coercion when they vote in the next national elections.
“The government believes it can steer this process through coercion, but it will realise that it has made a grave miscalculation in the election,” Cagatay Guc, the New Party’s head in Izmir, told Reuters.
The New Party, which is led nationally by politician Ozgur Ozel, staged protests before Tugay’s defection and believes many local voters oppose his change of allegiance.
In interviews with Reuters, many Izmir residents criticised Tugay’s decision.
“It was Tugay who joined the AK Party, not the people of Izmir,” said a 50-year-old man who gave his name only as Koray for fear of recriminations. “The AK Party can never win over the people of Izmir.”
A 67-year-old woman who gave her name only as Halide said: “We have never voted for that side (the AK Party) anyway … and now we’ll vote for Ozgur Ozel.”
Some residents said they agreed with Tugay that Izmir, one of the largest industrial and trade centres of Turkey, might receive more municipal services under a mayor representing the governing party.
“As a resident of Izmir, I want to see more municipal services in our city… With the necessary support from government, this city will be rebuilt, I hope,” said a 46-year-old man, who gave his name only as Isa.
One resident suggested Tugay had “no other choice” than to switch parties.
“He would either end up in Silivri, or carry on by switching parties,” said 53-year-old Alpay, referring to a prison west of Istanbul where many opposition figures are jailed.
LOSING FAITH IN CHANGE?
Inmates at Silivri include Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, who is regarded as Erdogan’s chief rival. In the 2024 local elections, Imamoglu was elected mayor of Istanbul for a second term from the Republican People’s Party (CHP), which won 37.8% of the vote and also retained Ankara, Izmir and many other big cities.
Those successes encouraged the opposition to view control of Turkey’s biggest cities as a platform from which to challenge Erdogan nationally.
Dozens of mayors and hundreds of municipal officials are now in jail along with Imamoglu, who is awaiting trial on corruption charges which he denies.
The CHP has been split after a court ruling ousting Ozel as its leader and reinstating former leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu. Ozel, a close ally of Imamoglu, launched the New Party in response, hoping to sustain voter anger over the pressure on the opposition.
“If voters lose faith that change is possible, why would they bother to vote?” said Tanju Tosun, a political science professor at Ege University in Izmir. “Voter turnout in the general election may fall slightly, particularly amongst voters of the opposition parties.”
Turkey’s next presidential and parliamentary elections are scheduled for May 2028 but a presidential adviser said this month that the elections would probably be held slightly earlier than expected. Doing so would allow Erdogan to sidestep constitutional limits and run again for office.
(Additional reporting by Ali Kucukgocmen in Istanbul, Ali Dinc in Izmir and Mirac Eren Dereli, Editing by Daren Butler and Timothy Heritage)

US plans to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:12:08 CET
15:12:08 KST

By David Shepardson
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The United States plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds — a measure designed to prevent scam-related robocalls.
The US Federal Communications Commission said on Thursday that it will vote on November 19 on a proposal to ban China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers from direct access.
For telecom firms providing Voice over Internet Protocol — technology that converts voice into digital data and transmits it over broadband connections — direct access is a much cheaper option and makes it easier to offer advanced features.
“With this decision, the FCC will be strengthening our first line of defense against bad actors and illegal robocallers,” FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry said on Friday that it firmly opposes the likely US ban and accused Washington of overstretching the concept of national security and abusing state power to suppress Chinese enterprises.
“China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a daily press conference.
MORE BANS UNDER CONSIDERATION
The FCC also said on Thursday that it plans to bar IP-enabled service providers that use equipment from companies on the FCC’s list that pose national security risks, such as Huawei or ZTE.
The agency added that it would ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics in December 2028 and may also revoke direct number authorizations for Chinese companies that it deems to pose national security risks.
The FCC has previously barred China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from providing international telecommunications services to the United States.
Other measures under consideration include barring them from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centers in the US.
Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.
In late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers’ call records, US call data, and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms.
The FBI said this year that threats from Salt Typhoon are “still very much ongoing.”
In July, the FCC added California-based Digitalsystem Technology to a list of companies posing risks to US national security, citing links to Chinese telecom firms and its ownership by a Chinese national.
China has consistently denied any wrongdoing.
(Reporting by David Shepardson; Additional reporting by Ju-min Park in Beijing; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race tells BBC she put others at risk but backlash was traumatic
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:10:50 GMT
15:10:50 KST

'I made the wrong decision,' Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race tells BBC
- Published
An Australian athlete has admitted making the wrong decision and putting others at risk by continuing to race after soiling herself during an endurance sports event.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC ahead of her return to the sport, Joanna Wietrzyk suggested her determination to win the Hyrox race in Beijing in September had clouded her judgement: "It was my decision to continue racing so I take full responsibility for that."
Challenged over why she carried on, she said: "I didn't really think about those around me… the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect."
The 24-year-old said that the experience and subsequent backlash was "traumatic". She also said she had considered walking away from the sport, in which she holds a world record.
Hyrox sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, in northern Germany, and is now held across the world.
Roughly halfway through her event last month, Wietrzyk suffered a bout of diarrhoea. Images of faecal matter on parts of her body were then shared widely online.
Asked whether officials should have stopped her, she said no-one encouraged her to do so at the time.
Hyrox's co-founder, Moritz Fürste, has issued an apology saying it had been a mistake not to react immediately during the race.
New rules have now been introduced giving race directors the power to remove athletes if their vomit, urine or faeces pose a risk of contamination or threaten the welfare of themselves or others in a race that is primarily held indoors using shared equipment.
Although initially defiant in a now-deleted Instagram post, Wietrzyk apologised in the week after the Beijing event and said she would forfeit the win and retroactively withdraw from the race.
Due to compete in Hamburg on Friday, she said she was "nervous" about her return and hoped that the high-profile incident would not define her.
"I don't want it to become my identity," she said.
In her first interview since Beijing, Wietrzyk said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning but had gone into the race "feeling fresh, feeling really, really good".
"It was a very sudden experience," she told the BBC.
"It wasn't until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person… and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing.
"Obviously I did put other people at risk," she admitted.
Hyrox China has since reportedly refunded some competitors their entry fees.
Wietrzyk also said she regretted an initial social media post published after the race which included the words "Go hard or go home" and "a win is a win". She said she had been in "flight or fight mode" as she sought hospital treatment.
"I didn't really account for what the public would have seen that situation as."
Challenged over whether her apology could be seen as an effort at damage limitation, or too late, she said that she hadn't expected so much exposure from the incident.
"I needed those days to reflect on it and process it."
Speaking about the mentality of elite athletes, she said: "They're so hyper-vigilant on winning and doing the best that they can, putting their training to good use and showcasing their fitness to the world."
After reflecting over the past weeks, she said: "There is more to life… than just racing and just winning."
After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from future events.
Speaking about the comments and photo shares online Joanna Wietrzyk said there had both been support, to make sure she was OK, but that it had also shown social media can be a very "toxic place".
Wietrzyk told the BBC that it had been a "mentally and emotionally taxing period" and she had not expected the global scrutiny, saying her family had also received threats.
"[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who's 24, just out there racing.
"Yes, I did make the wrong decision but I don't believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online… At the end of the day I'm only human."
Wietrzyk said had been trying to stay offline and had sought to "isolate herself from the world" for a time: "I can't do that forever."
"I still have so much more I can achieve in this sport so I think, for me, my mental resilience is the key here where I can inspire others through what I've been through."

Israel faces coalition deadlock after inconclusive vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:08:51 UTC
15:08:51 KST

As part of his election campaign, Yashar Party leader and former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot holds a rally in Tel Aviv, Oct. 27.
Israel’s final election results have confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.
The results released early on Oct. 30 showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in the Oct. 27 election.
The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.
Difficult decisions lie ahead, with the main opposition parties facing a choice between partnering with Arab-led parties, despite the political sensitivity of such an alliance, or setting aside their campaign pledges to join Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government.
The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next week. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government.
That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.
If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.
In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20 of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.
The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas.
Reports also said Netanyahu might increase attacks on the Arab parties.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them.
Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.

Post Office suspends sending goods to the EU

Post Office suspends sending goods to the EU
- Published
The Isle of Man Post Office has stopped accepting goods for delivery to European Union countries until further notice.
It said third-party systems used to process international parcels were being updated ahead of changes to EU customs requirements, but were not yet ready.
Documents can still be sent to EU addresses, and goods can still be posted to the rest of the world, including the USA.
The Post Office said it had been preparing for the changes, but "an unexpected change in approach by one of our UK partners" meant further work was needed.
The suspension covers goods sent from Post Office counters and through its online postage, click & dispatch and franking services.
The Post Office said it was working with its suppliers to fix the problem and would give a further update when a solution was available.
Asked when the service would resume, the Post Office said it would be "as soon as possible but we are dependent on one of our UK partners for that".
It thanked customers "for your patience while we work to restore EU goods services".

"It was Tugay who joined the AK Party, not the people of Izmir," said a 50-year-old man who gave his name only as Koray for fear of recriminations. "The AK Party can never win over the people of Izmir."
A 67-year-old woman who gave her name only as Halide said: "We have never voted for that side (the AK Party) anyway ... and now we'll vote for Ozgur Ozel."
Some residents said they agreed with Tugay that Izmir, one of the largest industrial and trade centres of Turkey, might receive more municipal services under a mayor representing the governing party.
"As a resident of Izmir, I want to see more municipal services in our city... With the necessary support from government, this city will be rebuilt, I hope," said a 46-year-old man, who gave his name only as Isa.
One resident suggested Tugay had "no other choice" than to switch parties.
"He would either end up in Silivri, or carry on by switching parties," said 53-year-old Alpay, referring to a prison west of Istanbul where many opposition figures are jailed.
LOSING FAITH IN CHANGE?
Inmates at Silivri include Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, who is regarded as Erdogan's chief rival. In the 2024 local elections, Imamoglu was elected mayor of Istanbul for a second term from the Republican People's Party (CHP), which won 37.8% of the vote and also retained Ankara, Izmir and many other big cities.
Those successes encouraged the opposition to view control of Turkey's biggest cities as a platform from which to challenge Erdogan nationally.
Dozens of mayors and hundreds of municipal officials are now in jail along with Imamoglu, who is awaiting trial on corruption charges which he denies.
The CHP has been split after a court ruling ousting Ozel as its leader and reinstating former leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu. Ozel, a close ally of Imamoglu, launched the New Party in response, hoping to sustain voter anger over the pressure on the opposition.
"If voters lose faith that change is possible, why would they bother to vote?" said Tanju Tosun, a political science professor at Ege University in Izmir. "Voter turnout in the general election may fall slightly, particularly amongst voters of the opposition parties."
Turkey's next presidential and parliamentary elections are scheduled for May 2028 but a presidential adviser said this month that the elections would probably be held slightly earlier than expected. Doing so would allow Erdogan to sidestep constitutional limits and run again for office. REUTERS

The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) said in a statement that the eruption prompted the raising of the alert level.

It warned of danger from lava flows, rockfalls, and other volcanic hazards.
Mayon Volcano, also known as Mount Mayon, is an active stratovolcano in Albay province in Bicol region encompassing the southern part of Luzon Island and nearby island provinces of the Southeast Asian nation.

'Why would we want to leave?': Fiji islanders work on climate resilience to avoid relocation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:02:33 UTC
15:02:33 KST

Residents of Fiji's tiny Serua Island have rejected calls to relocate, instead opting to renovate flimsy coastal homes.
As the sun sets over Fiji's tiny Serua Island, its climate-threatened inhabitants soak in one of the reasons they have rejected attempts to relocate their village – the "100 million dollar views".
The island looks like a utopia from the mainland, two steep palm-covered knolls sandwiching its low-lying centre, flanked by coral reefs and rich fishing grounds.
But it is on the island itself that the risk from rising seas becomes clearer, with a concrete sea wall providing the only defence against waves that are already swamping homes.
"The stronger the air pressure, the higher the waves. So the waves wash through inside the village," says Serua Island resident Avenai Ranuku.
Dozens of homes are in harm's way when cyclones hit Fiji, as are vegetable crops and graves.
Water laps at the feet of concrete piles where homes and a hospital once stood on the island's eastern end, and two homes were also moved from the western side where land has been washed away.
Despite the risks, most residents say they would rather strengthen the island's defences than abandon their ancestral home.
'We love this island': Why residents are reluctant to leave Serua
Ranuku remembers when category five cyclone Winston hit as a child and the island's population moved up one of the island's peaks to take shelter.
"Terrifying," Ranuku says of that night.
"All of the villagers, when the chief mention it, we go up. No one left behind. We help everyone, carry everything from the house, food. This is our evacuation plan."
Safe on higher ground, Ranuku could hear "waves going around, and the roof of the houses being washed away".
From that same haven on the hill, Ranuku explains why the threat of cyclones and sea level rise doesn't deter people from living on the island.
"We love this island, you know. Fresh air, go out fishing every day, that's why they don't want to leave.
"Many people used to say, they go to that house on the hill to see the sunset, it's a 100 million dollar view."
Islanders work to reduce disaster risk from sea level rise and storms
Serua Village worked with Habitat for Humanity in 2025 to write a detailed disaster risk reduction plan, as most of the population rejected calls for it to relocate.
Instead residents wanted to protect their ancestral home and the culture linked to it.
The report found nearly 20 per cent of homes on the island were in critical condition, and just three houses were strong enough to withstand a cyclone.
"Serua Island experiences more frequent seawall overtopping during high tides and king tides, saline intrusion affecting soil fertility, and standing water after rainfall, elevating health risks," the report said.
"The assessment shows there is a lack of natural form of wave breakers on Serua Island, and it is constantly threatened by sea level rise and cyclones.
"More than 50 per cent of houses have a combination of unstable foundations and roofs, and weak joints, walls and bracing, making these homes most vulnerable to cyclones and severe weather events."
On receiving the report, the village wasted no time in working to strengthen its resilience.
During a visit in October, dozens of workers were renovating homes along the northern coastline.
Flimsy walls and corrugated iron roofing were being removed and taken by boat to the mainland. Some homes had already been raised to mitigate flood risk, and others would soon follow.
The report also recommended improving access to the island by building a more robust path. During low tide, it is possible to walk the 750 metres to the island, guided by a string of power lines protruding from the sea floor.
But at high tide the only access is by boat, and even then the report said work is needed to make docking on the island safer and easier.
It is work Ranuku says his village is committed to. "Why would we want to leave?", he says, looking across the water to Fiji's Coral Coast.

UK government’s obesity plan ‘doomed to fail’, MPs warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:01:45 UTC
15:01:45 KST

The UK government’s promise to reverse rising obesity rates in the next decade is “doomed to fail” without a major rethink and a new plan led directly by the prime minister, a cross-party committee of MPs has concluded.
The health and social care select committee said in a report that there are no signs the so-called “moonshot ambition on obesity”, set out in the 10-year health plan for England, will achieve anything significant.
More than a year after the promise to “end the obesity epidemic” within a decade was made, even the most basic questions – such as how progress will be measured and how a cross-departmental plan would work – remain unanswered, the MPs said.
The report said: “While the ambition to ‘end the obesity epidemic’ is a laudable one, we currently have no faith in the government’s commitment to this aim or ability to achieve it and predict that, unless they urgently reassess their approach, they are doomed to fail.
“The government will fail to tackle a challenge of this scale unless action is led from the top and delivery of the moonshot is made a clear, personal priority of the prime minister.”
It called for the creation of a dedicated cabinet committee on the obesity plan, chaired by the prime minister, to drive action and “to send a message that this government takes obesity seriously”.
According to the most recent official statistics, 30% of adults in England are living with obesity, with 66% either overweight or living with obesity. Close to a third of children are now estimated to be overweight or living with obesity. Obesity rates for adults and children have increased significantly since the 1990s and, while the trends have levelled off, there are no signs of a fall.
One of the major failings of the current strategy, the report said, is a lack of proper distinction between efforts to prevent future obesity, for example by cracking down on unhealthy foods, and those to support and treat people who already have obesity.
“Conflating these two things is in part responsible for the muddled thinking and lack of progress from successive governments to date,” the MPs said.
Any effective plan must be based on a clear definition of what the ambition to reduce obesity rates means in practical terms, along with interim progress markers that would allow MPs to hold ministers to account, they said.
The MPs also called for a “joined-up, cross-government action plan”, taking in the departments responsible, their planned actions and how these will be funded, covering prevention and treatment for adults and children.
Ministers should come to parliament within the next three months to set out the plan, the report said.
Leadership from No 10 was vital, said Layla Moran, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the committee. She added an effective plan “will mean standing up to the food industry on numerous points – regulating the constant presence of adverts and promotions for unhealthy food and drink that wallpaper our lives, simpler labelling on products, targets for supermarkets to sell more healthy foods and restricting fast food outside schools”.
She said: “This issue transcends government departments, and experience tells us that if the prime minister isn’t calling the shots on such a huge societal issue, the loose ends won’t join up and the moonshot will crash land.
“We urge him to take up this ambition and be the driver of change. In turn, the NHS, public health and the economy will reap the long-term benefits.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Obesity is one of the biggest challenges facing our health service, and this government is taking bold action to help drive the shift from sickness to prevention and give every child the best start in life.
“We have already restricted junk food advertising on television before 9pm and online, banned volume-price promotions on less healthy food and drink products, and given councils stronger powers to block new hot food takeaways near schools.
“Alongside our focus on prevention, we are supporting those already living with obesity by expanding access to weight management support, including NHS weight-loss drugs for those with the greatest clinical need.”

EU and Canada to seal new alliance in Montréal under Trump's shadow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

The EU-Canada summit in Montréal will expand cooperation across multiple areas, including trade, investment, supply chains, AI, climate, security and the Arctic, and advance Canada's integration into EU programmes.
The European Union and Canada have long been friends. But it was not until Donald Trump 2.0 that they realised just how inseparable they had become.
The two sides are set to bring their partnership to unprecedented depth and breadth at Friday's EU-Canada summit in Montréal, in the French-speaking province of Quebec.
"It has become clear that there's much more that we can do together," Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said in a speech at the C.D. Howe Institute peppered with Canadian references, from Emily Carr to Leonard Cohen.
"Canada and the European Union are two complementary systems."
The choice of venue is fitting: with its stately architecture and Baroque facades, Montréal has often been hailed as one of the most European-looking cities in North America.
The setting also reflects the bloc's ambition to make Canada its closest non-European ally, a title traditionally held by the United States.
But Trump's re-election flipped the picture on its head.
The US president's punishing tariffs, threats of annexation, affinity for Russia and relentless attacks on the multilateral system have left Europeans bruised, battered and increasingly distrustful of any policy with Washington's mark.
In Canada, the shock has been maximised by its entrenched reliance on the US economy. The search for alternative allies is now an existential imperative.
Trump's attempt to turn Canada into "the 51st state" has demolished a neighbourly bond that stretches back centuries and was believed to be immune to partisan shifts.
The shared sense of vulnerability has been on full display in the lead-up to the summit.
Von der Leyen invited Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to her State of the Union speech in September. The Commission chief stunned the audience when she proposed to make Canada the bloc's first-ever "associate member".
Carney delivered his own speech in Strasbourg to pitch an "alliance for the future" built on shared prosperity and security.
This alliance, Carney said ahead of the summit, should be "strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices" and "open enough that others can join", a not-so-subtle rebuke to Trump's "America First" maximalism.
The meeting is expected to expand cooperation across multiple areas, including trade, investment, supply chains, AI, climate, security and the Arctic, and advance Canada's integration into EU programmes, such as Horizon and Erasmus.
Critical raw materials and liquefied natural gas (LNG) – two strategic exports that Canada is ready to increase – are also high on the agenda.
The EU is seeking minerals to cut off its dependency on China, which Beijing has accused of weaponising, and new energy providers to bring down retail prices.
Another top-priority issue is support for Ukraine. The war-weary country is facing a €70 billion gap in its 2027 budget as Russia escalates its war of aggression, devastates the levers of the domestic economy and blockades the Black Sea routes.
The EU is willing to cover two-thirds of the shortfall, roughly €46 billion, and wants other allies, such as Canada, to take care of the remaining third. The assistance will have to be fresh and come on top of what has already been pledged, which means Canada's inclusion in the bloc's €90 billion support loan will not count.
Signalling the importance of the summit, von der Leyen is joined in Montréal by European Council President António Costa, High Representative Kaja Kallas and nine Commissioners.
The turnout reflects the institutional dimension of the new alliance. The plan envisions closer links between the governments, parliaments and courts on each side.
Brussels is considering holding a meeting between the entire College of Commissioners and the Canadian cabinet sometime next year.
This format, which is reserved for rare occasions of importance, was last used with India, another trading partner that Trump's disruption has brought closer to Europe.
"We're embarking on the start of a journey," a senior EU official said. "Let's be honest, this is a tiny bit of uncharted territory."
The summit was off to an awkward note: just hours before von der Leyen flew to Montréal, her native country, Germany, mounted a forceful push to remove all mention of "associate membership" from the final joint declaration.
Instead, the text speaks of a commitment to an "ever closer association".
Germany, it must be noted, introduced the label of "associate member" earlier this year in the context of Ukraine. Despite its mixed reviews, Berlin has never let go of the idea.
Von der Leyen, though, was undaunted by the setback. Speaking at the C.D. Howe Institute, she doubled down on her project to "open a new frontier together".
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession. But we can replace accession with a common ambition and vision," she said. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
Later, Carney backed her call, saying "we're in the process of forging a new alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member".

Opening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

Andy Burnham’s opening debate on whether Britain should rejoin the EU is divisive, painful and politically risky. That is why it should be welcomed. To jeopardise his popularity so soon after coming to office might seem reckless, but the issue is urgent and not going away. Brexit is continuing to damage the nation’s economy. The prime minister’s job is to challenge, if not reform it.
The Brexit decade has evoked a bizarre sense of guilt among Britons. Opinion polls show nearly 60% regard it as a mistake, with just a third still in favour. Almost a quarter of those who voted for Brexit now regret it. While early forecasts of economic disaster were proved wrong, the accumulated cost of cutting links with Britain’s biggest trading partner is estimated at 6-8% of GDP.
This is huge. It must rank as the greatest act of self-harm by a British government in modern times.
A year ago Keir Starmer began to ease some of the barriers, with modest deals on youth exchange and meat exports. Burnham wants to take this further, with negotiations resuming in Brussels next month. Yesterday in the Commons he cited damage to the car industry, while agriculture remains mired in dozens of pages of regulation. Fish rots in inspection sheds, and cars and passengers queue for hours at borders.
Yet if something must be done, the question remains: what? Burnham emphasises that he would not renege on Labour’s 2024 election pledge to honour the referendum in this parliament. But he certainly wants a revival of the debate and has a personal hope to see Brexit reversed one day. For now he seeks “an honest discussion … an open conversation” on where future negotiations might lead. He murmured the possibility of free movement of people for EU passport holders. The subject’s delicacy was demonstrated as Westminster Brexiters reacted like scalded cats. “Betrayal … catastrophe”, cried Reform UK’s Nigel Farage.
A reason for Burnham to proceed cautiously is that the public’s regret over Brexit is not matched by agreement on what should take its place. While 55% of all Britons would support rejoining the EU, that falls to 35% if the condition is surrendering the UK’s previous opt-outs – which would mean joining the euro and participating in the Schengen passport-free travel zone.
There could be a middle-ground Brexit model, including a bespoke place for Britain within a wider European economic area. But this in turn might be unacceptable to some existing EU countries. An alternative could include membership of the European Free Trade Association or a customs union.
The truth is Britain has always been ambivalent in its attitude to European unions. Ireland and Denmark had in the past reversed anti-EU referendums by negotiating opt-outs with Brussels. David Cameron attempted no such remedy in 2016. He simply resigned.
During the post-referendum Commons debates it was clear that many MPs would have favoured a “soft Brexit” option, its form as yet unclear. A responsible parliament at the time might have formed a coalition to pursue such an option. As it was, Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party preferred to exploit Theresa May’s internal divisions and leave the way open for Boris Johnson and his “hard Brexiters”. Manning Westminster’s party barricades took precedence over seeking a sensible compromise with Brussels.
Burnham must therefore tread with care. Westminster’s political culture slithers instinctively into conflict mode without thought for the message that this sends to the outside world. Plenty of Europeans remain sceptical of whether Britain truly wants to rejoin the EU, and will resist any demand for extensive opt-outs or concessions. But that is for another day. For now, Labour is committed to honour its referendum manifesto promise.
Burnham is right to open the conversation. But he must first detoxify Brexit and diminish its prominence – and that of the party whose existence depends on it, Reform. For the time being, as there is no question of rejoining the EU, there is no issue of British sovereignty. The negotiations should be boring, over regulations, conventions and protocols. These would inevitably involve compromise – but compromise that ensures both parties come away with something gained.
One solution would be to do what was not done after 2016: establish a strong cross-party Commons committee to monitor the November talks and take Burnham’s conversation forward. This should concentrate on reducing barriers to trade and growth, and promoting cultural and security relations with Europe. To put it mildly, Europe needs such concentration, and badly. On that, surely Westminster can agree.
- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Battle lines redrawn in Spain’s snap election after latest train disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

One of the most dependable cliches of contemporary Spanish politics is that it never pays to bet against Pedro Sánchez. Time and time again – as leader of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) and as prime minister – Sánchez has shown an almost preternatural ability to profit from adversity, and to confound expectations and wrongfoot his opponents.
But next month’s snap general election, called by Sánchez after rightwing and far-right parties voted down the housing reforms his coalition government had announced in response to angry protests, may suddenly not be the contest it once was.
Wednesday’s deadly rail collision, in which at least 69 people died, has, for the moment at least, subdued much of the vicious language and posturing that has come to characterise recent elections. The crash could sap Sánchez’s recently resurgent momentum and the issue of rail safety now threatens to overshadow his attempts to defend his record and remain in the Moncloa palace.
The poll the left had billed as a last chance to stop the conservative People’s party (PP) joining forces with the rightwing Vox party to roll back decades of social progress – and which the right had billed as an opportunity to end eight years of what it disdainfully calls sanchismo – will now take place in a country deep in shock and grief.
Not only has Spain’s extensive high-speed railway long been a source of national pride, it is also a transport network that millions of Spaniards depend on for work, holidays and family visits. This week’s crash, after another on the same line that killed 46 people in January, has left people angry, bewildered and worried.
Thursday’s headlines spoke for themselves. El Mundo’s front page lamented “Another massacre on the trains”; ABC’s noted “At least 68 dead nine months on”, while El País mourned the “Second high-speed catastrophe in less than a year.”
Even before Wednesday’s terrible events on the outskirts of Urda, Sánchez and his allies were facing a battle. As well as the housing protests, the prime minister has had to contend with a slew of corruption allegations surrounding his family and inner circle, while his government’s handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta over the summer had been fiercely criticised at home and abroad.
Pablo Simón, a political scientist at the Carlos III University of Madrid, stressed the delicacy of the moment, saying that people across Spain were still struggling to come to terms with what had happened this week.
“There are a lot of fronts [for the government] here, and I think this accident has a twofold impact,” he said. “First, it draws attention to the state of railway infrastructure, suggesting that the problem is structural, and pointing to a broader decline in public services in Spain, specifically regarding infrastructure.”
Simón said that Sánchez’s government, which has been in power since 2018, could not blame the state of things on its PP predecessor, which carried out austerity cuts. “That’s simply not credible,” he said.
“But there’s also a second issue: even before this, the government faced an uphill battle; it was already highly unlikely that they could secure the necessary support.”
Sánchez has said it is “unacceptable” for the country to experience two high-speed rail disasters in less than a year, and promised to strengthen safety measures “so that something like this never happens again”, but his opponents say that is simply not good enough.
The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on Thursday that any politician found to be responsible for the crash would be held to account, adding: “We can’t go on like this; this kind of management just can’t carry on.” According to the PP, Spaniards are not asking for “miracles; they’re just asking for a Spain where things work again”.
Vox, on the other hand, is going all out, accusing the government of “killing” the train crash victims and of systemic mismanagement and cronyism. It has also urged the supreme court to investigate Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, on suspicion of manslaughter and causing bodily harm through gross negligence. Puente has rejected allegations of mismanagement, insisting that Spain’s railway system is “safe and reliable”.
Simón said the contrasting reactions of the PP and Vox reflected splits on the right, as both parties compete to put an end to Sánchez’s government: “The question becomes what tone should one adopt: a more institutional one, which is what the PP is currently attempting, or a tougher, more aggressive one, which is what Vox is doing?”
He also suggested the sombre national mood could make it very hard for Sánchez to rally as many as 1.2 million “politically dormant” but PSOE-leaning voters, on whom he had been counting. The electoral event the prime minister had hoped to portray as a Manichean clash between progressives and reactionaries, fought over issues of housing and equality, has morphed into something else.
“An election campaign relies on high spirits and a sense of optimism,” Simón said. “But how can that exist when the entire country is in mourning over this tragedy?”

Helen Goh’s recipe for toffee apple hand pies | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

These plump and rustic little parcels are perfect for Bonfire Night: warming, portable and, wrapped in a napkin and held in one hand, easy to eat outdoors. Filled with gently spiced, toffee-glossed apples, they are deliberately more homely hand pies than anything overly neat or patisserie-like. The small amount of miso in the filling deepens the toffee flavour and rounds out the sweetness, without making it taste too savoury or funky.
Miso-toffee apple hand pies
Prep 10 min
 
Macerate 30 min
 
Cook 1 hr 15 min, plus chilling and cooling
 
Makes 8 
800g apples, ideally a mixture of granny smith and pink lady (about 3 of each), peeled, cored and cut into 1½-2cm pieces (650g net)
 
80g light brown sugar
  
2 tbsp apple cider vinegar
  
1 tsp ground cinnamon 
  
¼ tsp ground nutmeg
  
¼ tsp fine sea salt, plus a generous pinch for the egg wash
 
50g unsalted butter
  
20g white miso
  
1 tsp vanilla extract
  
1 small egg 
  
50g plain flour
  
2 320g packs shop-bought puff pastry 
  
1 tbsp demerara sugar
Put the apple pieces in a large bowl with the brown sugar, vinegar, cinnamon, nutmeg and salt, and toss to combine. Leave to macerate at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, tossing occasionally.
Strain the apples, reserving the liquid; you should have about 100ml. Melt the butter in a large, wide frying pan on a medium-high heat. Add the strained apples and cook, tossing occasionally, for four to five minutes, until they begin to soften. Pour in the reserved liquid and cook for a further three to four minutes, until the liquid reduces and a glossy caramel forms around the apples. Stir in the miso and vanilla until evenly incorporated, then take off the heat. Spread the filling over a tray or large plate, so it can cool quickly, then refrigerate until completely cold.
To assemble, lightly beat the egg with a generous pinch of salt and put the flour in a small dish. Unroll one sheet of pastry, leaving it on the baking paper it comes with, and cut into four equal rectangles. Keep the second sheet refrigerated while you assemble the first four pies.
Spoon about 60g filling on one half of each pastry rectangle, leaving a 1½cm border around three outer edges surrounding the filling, then brush these borders lightly with egg, keeping the egg wash just inside the cut edges (brushing it over the sides can seal the pastry layers and prevent them from rising properly). Fold the uncovered half of pastry over the filling and gently press the three edges together. Dip the tines of a fork in the flour, then use this to crimp all around the edges to seal.
Slide the four pies on their baking paper bases on to an oven tray and refrigerate while you repeat with the second pastry sheet and the rest of the filling on a second tray. Refrigerate both trays for 20-30 minutes, until the pies are cold and firm.
Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Brush the tops of the pies with the remaining egg wash and sprinkle with demerara sugar. Using the tip of a small, sharp knife, cut three slashes in the top of each pie, so the steam can escape, then bake for about 30 minutes, swapping the trays around halfway through cooking if necessary, until puffed and deeply golden. Leave the pies on the trays for 10 minutes, then transfer to a rack. Serve warm or at room temperature.
