Hitting the fan: London council angers residents with removal of 700 dog-waste bins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:46 UTC
15:00:46 KST

People in a west London borough fear it will become covered in dog poo after their cash-strapped council decided to remove 700 dog-waste bins to save money.
“People are worried there’s going to be dog shit everywhere,” said Daniel O’Neill, the chief road steward at Ruislip Residents’ Association.
Hillingdon’s pet dogs produce about 174 tonnes of faeces each year, which, until now, has been generally bagged up by their owners and deposited in dog-waste bins.
The Conservative-run council believes it will save £100,000 in waste collection costs by removing the bins. It hopes dog owners will use general litter bins instead, but O’Neill and many other people are unconvinced.
“Everybody’s going to have a Christmas tree of dog-shit baubles in their front garden because there’ll be nowhere else to put the bags of it,” O’Neill said. “I got one of those AI generators to make me a Christmas tree with dog-shit bags in different colours, to show what’s going to happen.”
Sital Punja who walks Marley, her springer-poodle, every day in Ruislip woods, said the “preposterousness” of the bin removals have dominated chat between dog walkers.
“People are really unhappy about it, it’s going to be dumped everywhere,” said Punja, who is an opposition Labour councillor. “The dog bins in the woods are already overflowing and there aren’t enough general bins. The dog bins have lids so the smell stays inside. General bins don’t, so they stink and can be got at by foxes.”
Hillingdon is not the first council to remove dog-waste bins to try to save money. Similar plans have prompted outrage in Cornwall, Kent, North Somerset and elsewhere.
Hillingdon borough’s large debts are increasing by £5.6m a year. Its schools grant deficit alone is £101.5m and the government has “serious concerns” about the borough’s finances, which could jeopardise its chances of continuing to rely on exceptional financial support grants from Whitehall.
At the same time, Hillingdon prides itself on having frozen council tax for years. This was the root of the problem, according to O’Neill, who said he had observed the last 150 council meetings.
“If they put the council taxes up, even to just the average in London, then they would bring in £26m,” he said, “but what they’re actually doing instead is not emptying the dog-shit bins to save £100,000.”
O’Neill said it was this issue that had really cut through with residents. “I tell people about the deficit, or about the audit problems, and nobody cares. When I tell them that their bins are going to get taken away, they go nuts.”
Comments on Ruislip’s residents’ association Facebook page appear to bear this out.
“What an absurd suggestion,” said one person. Another said it was “madness” and added: “Are they trying to completely alienate the residents? There are enough selfish dog owners who already don’t pick up after their dogs so they think removing the bins will improve that?”
One resident said: “Sadly this is probably a decision by someone who does not have a clue how much shit is created by dogs. As a dog owner there are not enough bins. This is shortsighted.”
Punja said Hillingdon had a lot of dog owners. “During Covid the rise of dog owners was astronomical. I was one of those Covid dog owners.”
She added: “This is just one of the council’s harebrained ideas they have come up with when they can’t balance the books … It probably would be simpler to put up council tax. I can only describe it as dog-shit, excuse my language – but to have to scramble to such a level where you have to take away dog bins; it’s desperate.”
A council report setting out the plan said it would save £160,000, of which £60,000 would be reinvested in street cleaning.
Wayne Bridges, the council’s cabinet member for residents’ services, said: “We do understand that some residents have concerns about these changes. We are simply changing how it is collected, making better use of the nearly 1,500 ordinary litter bins already available across Hillingdon.
“By allowing dog waste to be placed in ordinary public litter bins, which can already be used safely for this purpose, more than doubling existing capacity, we can bring collections into our existing street cleansing arrangements and remove the cost of running two separate services.
“Many councils across the country already allow dog waste to be disposed of through general waste arrangements.”

TUC leader expects wave of union recognition in private sector over coming year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:45 UTC
15:00:45 KST

The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, is predicting a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces come into force.
From Friday, as part of Labour’s Employment Rights Act, unions will have the right to enter workplaces or communicate with staff electronically. From January, employers will be obliged to inform workers of their right to join a union.
“I think it potentially could be transformative,” Nowak said. “This could open up large parts of … the private sector, where unions have been trying to get a foothold but have been hampered partly because of the legal framework. It gives us a real opportunity.”
He added: “My prediction would be that by this time next year, we’ll have signed hundreds, if not thousands of new recognition agreements with employers, taking that union voice into the private sector in particular.”
Polling carried out for the TUC by YouGov suggests 62% of workers would support a trade union negotiating on their behalf on pay and conditions, but 36% of those who are not members of a union say they would not know how to join one.
Nowak pointed to a flurry of recent deals, citing agreements between John Lewis and Usdaw and between the GMB and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as evidence that some employers are responding even before the rules have come into force.
“What we’re seeing is a whole range of employers, who have recognised that the legislation is changing, that the political climate is changed and are now reaching voluntary agreements with unions,” he said.
Just over a fifth of the UK’s workforce are trade union members, down from more than half in 1979, before Margaret Thatcher came to power.
Under the new rules, there will be a formal process to request access to a workplace if a union cannot agree with the employer, which will be overseen by the regulator, the Central Arbitration Committee.
Previously, unions trying to win the right to represent a workforce have sometimes had to do so from outside the building – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to win recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.
Nowak said Labour’s new approach “changes the mood, and I think it brings us much more into the European mainstream, which is that unions are part and parcel of the workplace”.
The access rights are the latest element of the government’s upgrade to workers’ rights to be implemented. Rights to sick pay have already been extended and further changes, including restrictions on zero hours contracts, are yet to come into force.
Some employers have complained about the potential costs of the new regime, but Nowak insisted good bosses need not worry.
“Genuinely, employers have got nothing to fear from this. They shouldn’t see their staff wanting an independent voice as somehow a negative verdict on them. You can work for a good, successful organisation and still want a strong, independent union voice.”

These are the world’s 20 most-visited museums – and five are in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

China dominated the list, claiming the number one spot with the Palace Museum in Beijing and having 12 entries in the top 20 overall.
From state museums covering a country’s history to archaeological sites that give a glimpse into the past, museums are a great introduction to a new destination.
In some cases, it’s the entire reason for the trip, and the most popular museums can rack up millions of visitors annually.
Now, the Themed Entertainment Association (TEA) has published its annual index looking back at visitor numbers for 2025, and five of the top 20 most-visited museums are in Europe.
China dominated the list overall with 12 entries, including the number one spot: Beijing’s Palace Museum, which saw 19 million people walk through its doors last year.
TEA attributed this to its large domestic audience as well as the fact that 91% of the country’s 7,188 registered museums offer free entry.
Of the remaining eight, there are two apiece in France, the UK, and South Korea, as well as one each in the US and Vatican City.
The top 20 most-visited museums worldwide
- Palace Museum, Beijing, China – 19,000,000
- Summer Palace, Beijing, China – 17,381,000

- Natural History Museum, London, UK – 7,117,000
- Vatican Museums, Vatican City – 6,934,000
- Opium War Museum, Dongguan, China – 6,929,000

- Nanjing Museum, Nanjing, China – 5,860,000
- Shenyang Palace Museum, Shenyang, China – 5,852,000
- China Science and Technology Museum, Beijing, China – 5,530,000
The most-visited museums in Europe in 2025
Unsurprisingly, given France is the most-visited country on the planet, the top museum in Europe is the Louvre in Paris, which saw nine million visitors over the course of 2025, placing it fourth overall.
Coming in fifth overall was another contender from France, the Palace of Versailles, with 8.4 million visitors.
Seventh place went to London’s Natural History Museum, with 7.1 million visitors, followed by the Vatican Museums, with 6.9 million people visiting.
The final European entrant is the British Museum in London, which came 13th overall thanks to its 6.44 million visitors.
Writing about museums in continental Europe, the report notes that “attendance remained at high and relatively stable levels as most major museums completed their post-pandemic recovery”.
Several museums in the UK saw major growth with the opening of new exhibitions or wings, like the Sainsbury Wing at the National Gallery, and Our Story with David Attenborough at the Natural History Museum.

LRT English Newsletter – October 30, 2026
It seems that passing the 2027 budget bill may not be as easy. Recall that the government’s proposal attempts to square the circle of maintaining massive military spending without cutting welfare – nay, even adding to it with an ambitious family support package. While Russia and low birth rates are the key existential threats to the nation, so are, apparently, any tax hikes – leaving borrowing as the only way to pay for everything (even the EU is growing reluctant to foot the bill for rearming its eastern flank).
The massive budget deficit has sent the centre-right opposition and liberal economists gasping about the sustainability of so much debt – the stress may have contributed to the hospitalisation of the finance minister this week – but even some within the ruling coalition are voicing dissent. Obviously, any suggestions of cutting military budgets are treated as traitorous blasphemy and social spending is poised to be popular with the electorate. The problem is that the Social Democrats will claim all the credit to the exclusion of their junior partners. So one of them, the Democrats “For Lithuania”, is demanding an earlier roll-out of new child benefits, while the other, the Farmers and Greens Union, is trying to peg their votes to a referendum on the definition of family, a culture war issue that has been so far successfully stifled by parliamentary proceduralism.
With calls for “cutting the deficit” and “giving more to the families” pulling the budget in opposite directions, this one may prove challenging to pass.
CROSSING BORDERS
The Lithuanian authorities said they received confirmation that two nationals were detained in Iran. They reportedly went there for travel purposes, but the reason for their detention is still unclear. There has been an increase in such cases, an Iran expert told LRT.lt, as people continue to travel to the country at war despite the risks, particularly to citizens of the countries allied with the United States and Israel.
BLOCKING BORDERS
Lithuania’s sports authorities continue to bar Belarusian and Russian athletes from entering the country, which has now led to the first real conflict with an international sporting organisation. Earlier this month, the International Modern Pentathlon Union withdrew the right for Kaunas to host a World Cup stage next year. Politicians and sporting officials maintain the country has no intention to change course, but if more sports organisations decide to admit Belarusians and Russians, this may force Lithuania and its athletes to make tough choices.
At the same time, LRT has confirmed it is not planning to boycott next year’s Eurovision even as more and more countries are withdrawing from the song contest over Israel’s participation.
YOU’RE IN THE ARMY SOON
The drive for rearmament now sees politicians calling for universal conscription. Having given up conscription in the 2000s, Lithuania partially reintroduced it in 2015 but has yet to reach its ideal of Israeli-style universal military service (minus the women). Curiously, it is the country’s armed forces that appear to be moderating politicians’ enthusiasm, noting they do not have enough instructors to train so many draftees or facilities to house them.
Impatient with the slow pace, the opposition conservatives presented a bill this week on having universal conscription by the end of the decade. The cabinet and the president, meanwhile, agreed to give it a little more time, until 2032.

Al-Jawad Pike refreshes Aesop store with terracotta-tiled counter evoking ancient Persia
Local studio Al-Jawad Pike has given skincare brand Aesop’s shop in London department store Harrods a revamp, centred on a terracotta-clad counter designed to have “the qualities of a miniature building”.
Aesop has had a counter in Harrods for over a decade. For this revamp, Al-Jawad Pike, which is a long-term collaborator of Aesop’s, aimed to take the design further than a regular beauty-brand counter.
“We were interested in giving the counter the qualities of a miniature building, with suggestions of apertures, openings and floor levels: something designed with the architectural ambition of a building but the care of a cabinet,” Al-Jawad Pike co-founder Jessam Al-Jawad told Dezeen.
“Through carved alcoves we also wanted to recall the architecture of ancient Persia – the highly literate civilisation that developed liquid perfumery.”
The studio drew on Harrods’ easily recognisable red brick facade when designing the central counter, which is clad in terracotta tiles from Italy that were chosen for their ability to hold scents.
“We chose glazed terracotta early on in the process because of its connection to traditional fragrance production, but also because of its strong association with Harrods’ iconic facade,” Al-Jawad explained.
The counter is decorated with an alchemist-style design piece, described by Aesop as an “olfactory sculpture.”
Glass vessels filled with fragrances hang from a copper stand, with copper cones that let visitors experience the different scents.
“The olfactory sculpture is something that Aesop has been independently developing in different forms across a number of their projects,” Al-Jawad Pike explained.
“Our take on this was to create a delicate but organised structure of copper piping and blown glass, through which fragrance-infused air is pushed to scent funnels for customers to interact with.”
The colour palette of the Aesop store complements the monolithic terracotta counter, with brushed copper brought in as a tactile contrast.
“The colour palette was chosen in collaboration with the team at Aesop for its intensity and richness, which we felt resonated with the olfactory experience of fragrance,” Al-Jawad said.
“We paired this with matte, brushed copper because of its connection to fragrance creation and distillation.”
Earlier this year, Aesop launched its first lighting collection at Milan design week. Previous Aesop stores featured on Dezeen include a Barcelona shop by Mesura that won the 2024 Dezeen Award for best interior.

SBS, ABC reject antisemitism envoy proposal for external ombudsman on Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:59:47 UTC
14:59:47 KST

In brief
- Australia's special envoy to combat antisemitism has released her latest roadmap.
- Recommendations include an external ombudsman to monitor SBS and ABC content on Israel and the Middle East.
SBS and the ABC could have an "external ombudsman" monitor their coverage of Israel and the Middle East to avoid perpetuating antisemitism, Australia's envoy to combat antisemitism has proposed.
Jillian Segal released, as part of a broader report, an updated proposal for the idea she first floated during hearings for the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. The broadcasters again rejected the idea and said their existing ombudsmen and complaints processes are sufficient.
Segal's report included other proposals such as bans on face coverings, and measures that would seek to combat language used throughout society which she said can lead to racist violence.
Key areas of focus include the introduction of codes of conduct in organisations across Australia, the stripping of public funding from institutions that "promote, facilitate or accept antisemitism", and reform of the education sector.
Australia's public broadcasters have previously been accused of "marking their own homework" by Segal, who suggested appointing an independent adjudicator to manage public complaints about coverage of Israel and the Middle East during antisemitism royal commission hearings in July.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The public broadcasters have independent but internally located ombudsmen. The Australian Communications and Media Authority also regulates media organisations in the country.
Segal spoke on the suggestion on ABC radio on Friday morning, saying that such oversight was neither sufficient nor satisfactorily independent.
"They should be subject to the same level of accountability and transparency in relation to where things might go wrong in terms of complaints as any other sector," she said.
Segal was appointed Australia's special envoy to combat antisemitism in 2024.
The government has thanked Segal for her "continued work to eradicate antisemitism in Australia" and said it will continue to work with her to strengthen social cohesion.
Independent ombudsman 'in the public interest'
Segal has called for all media outlets to "improve their practical understanding of antisemitism", with the "education of key management and editorial staff" a priority.
She has also requested greater transparency regarding the definitions of antisemitism public broadcasters draw from in their reporting.
Her report claims many in the Jewish community have become concerned over "disproportionate, misleading, or inaccurate" reporting on Israel and the conflict in the Middle East since Hamas' October 7 attacks on Israel in 2023 — which led to Israel's military campaign in Gaza.
Australians ought to receive "accurate, fair and impartial news", Segal's report continues, while making sure "editorial standards do not amplify antisemitic narratives".
"Given the extent and seriousness of concerns about subjective, inaccurate and disproportionate reporting in accordance with its own standards, it would be in the public interest for the public broadcasters’ coverage and approach to be the subject of more detailed analysis and independent review," she said.
Broadcasters defend their records
SBS and the ABC have defended their reporting on the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
In a statement, SBS said it "condemns antisemitism unequivocally and recognises the profound harm it causes Jewish Australians and Australia’s social cohesion."
SBS' editorial standards and independence are "essential to public trust", the statement said.
"SBS's existing complaints and accountability framework is robust and fit for purpose, including an independent Ombudsman and external oversight from the Australian Communications and Media Authority."
On Friday, the ABC said its complaints process was "the most robust and transparent in the Australian media".
"The ABC has the highest editorial standards and a comprehensive framework to ensure accountability, transparency and high editorial standards," it said in a statement.
"This framework is designed to balance accountability with editorial independence and robust journalism."
Jewish group rejects envoy's suggestion
Some members of the Jewish community have expressed fear they could be labelled antisemitic under the definitions presented in Segal's latest report.
Segal identified what she called "progressive" antisemitism as the most pervasive form facing the country.
"It takes the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes, and gives it a respectable face through the language of social justice and human rights," she wrote.
Bart Shteinman, executive officer at the Jewish Council of Australia, criticised the report, calling it "Orwellian" and saying it does not represent the views of all Jews.
"This updated report from the Special Envoy is so misguided, conspiratorial and frankly Orwellian that it's hard to know where to start," he said.
"The report does little to mask a right-wing ideology that will go to incredible lengths to silence those drawing attention to Israel's genocide in Gaza.
"The Australian Government would do well to remember that the special envoy does not speak for all Jews, many of whom could be classified as 'progressive antisemites' themselves under the ridiculous analysis Segal is promoting."
A United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry, which does not speak on behalf of the UN as a whole and has been sharply criticised by Israel, concluded last year that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.
Israel is separately defending a genocide case at the International Court of Justice, which has ordered provisional measures but has yet to issue a final ruling.
Israel has repeatedly denied committing genocide in Gaza, saying it has the right to defend itself.
Segal's report suggested "progressive antisemitism" could manifest as holding all Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government.
Segal stressed, however, that criticism of Israel similar to that levelled against any other country was not antisemitic.

Smart devices can be used for e-voting in Estonia's 2027 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:55:00 UTC
14:55:00 KST

Smart devices can be used for e-voting in Estonia's 2027 election
Voters will be able to cast a ballot electronically on a smart device in next year's Riigikogu elections, the National Electoral Committee has agreed.
It has been possible to vote online in Estonia's elections since 2005, but only using a computer, not a smart device, such as a mobile phone.
National Electoral Committee Chair Ingrid Kullerkann said in a statement issued Thursday that most members now find the risks "sufficiently mitigated" to allow voters to use smart devices when voting.
"Based on my current knowledge, voting using mobile devices does not involve greater risks than voting using a computer. Therefore, the time is ripe to take the next leap in the development of Estonia's digital state and enable voting on smart devices," she added.
Kullerkann cited "accessibility and crisis resilience of elections" as some of the reasons behind the development.
"It is possible to vote online even if a situation similar to the January 2005 storm should occur during the elections, if it is not advisable to leave home because of a drone warning, or if you live in a part of Estonia where the nearest polling station is several dozen kilometers away. Everyone who wants to vote should be able to do so," she explained.
A voting app will now be developed for smart devices running both iOS and Android operating systems. It will be available for download from the Google Play and Apple's App Store.
The electronic vote verification app will also be available from app stores and will allow voters to confirm that their vote has reached the electronic ballot box and correctly reflects their choice.
Head of the State Electoral Office Arne Koitmäe said: "The addition of new operating systems does not change the electronic voting system, but expands the number of devices from which people can cast their electronic votes."
E-voting is one of the most thoroughly audited and monitored systems in Estonia, undergoing load, recovery and security testing every year, he added.
"Every voter is free to choose whether they wish to vote on paper or electronically using a computer or mobile phone. All votes are securely protected and carry equal weight when the votes are counted," Koitmäe said.
The Riigikogu green-lit voting on smart devices in 2024.
In 2025, the State Electoral Office and the Information System Authority conducted a public test of electronic voting using smart devices, during which the casting, transmission, and receipt of votes were tested. The test found the application to be reliable and received positive feedback from users.

Bank of Japan says inflation hit 2% target after 13 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:46:32 UTC
14:46:32 KST

The Bank of Japan said on Friday inflation had hit its 2% target, more than 13 years after it adopted the goal in a bid to pull the economy out of deflation, but held off hiking interest rates for now.
Successive governments struggled for decades to pull the country out of a spiral of deflation - sustained falls in prices that are harmful for economic growth - and the 2% goal was set in 2013 as the BoJ launched massive monetary easing measures.
While core consumer inflation intermittently topped the level in the early 2020s, Friday marked the first time that the central bank confirmed the long-term price trend had been achieved.
"Underlying CPI (consumer price index) inflation is at a level that is generally consistent with the price stability target of two percent, and is expected to remain at around that level," the central bank said on its website.
Despite the central bank's view of sustainable inflation, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government has been more cautious about officially declaring victory over deflation.
"We're not there," Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said last week.
Takaichi is seen as prioritising economic stimulus measures over controlling inflation, at the risk of giving the impression of pressuring the BoJ to keep rates low.
The BoJ also said in a statement it had kept its key interest rate unchanged at 1.25% after an eight-to-one majority vote, following similar moves over the past two days by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.
However, Japanese officials are expected to hike in December as inflationary pressure builds.
Japan has faced sustained consumer price increases since spring 2022, and the BoJ began tightening rates in March 2024 after 10 years of ultra-loose monetary policy.
Core inflation in September stood at 2.1%, sharply up from 1.7% in August, according to data released by the government last week.
The BoJ warned Friday that the year-on-year rate of increase in CPI excluding fresh food "is likely to accelerate to a level clearly above two percent".
It said this was because of various factors including a rise in oil costs that "is expected to push up prices, mainly of energy and goods", and the rise in the price of semiconductors, reflecting the increase in global AI-related demand.
The depreciation of the yen is also a factor, it added.
Marcel Thieliant of Capital Economics said "further tightening looks very likely and we expect the policy rate to reach 2% by the middle of next year".
"If anything, the risks are tilted towards further tightening thereafter," he added.

Japan’s law to establish alternate capital as backup to Tokyo takes effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:42:21 UTC
14:42:21 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
A new Japanese law to establish an alternate capital as a backup to Tokyo took effect on Friday.
The law allows “eligible prefectures to apply for designation,” Kyodo News reported.
It allows for the continuity of national and social functions in case of a large-scale disaster, as well as the decentralization of economic activities away from the capital region of the world’s fourth-largest economy.
The law came to fruition as the ruling coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party, seeks to turn Osaka, its core base in western Japan, into a metropolis like Tokyo.
“The government is expected to announce in November its basic approach to second capital status and a timetable for its designation,” the report said.
Authorities will grant tax incentives to boost investment in areas designated as secondary capitals under the new law. It also allows the prime minister to designate a backup capital based on applications from prefectures.
“It does not limit the number of second capitals to one, leaving open the possibility that multiple prefectures could be designated,” the report added.
At least four prefectures — Hokkaido in the north, Aichi in central Japan, Osaka and Fukuoka in the southwest — are expected to apply for alternate capital status.
The government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi approved an ordinance last Tuesday setting requirements for gaining the status, including that a prefecture account for at least 2.1% of Japan's gross domestic product and contain a city with at least 1.2% of the country's population.

Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan hold technical talks on Kambarata-1 hydropower plant project
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have held technical negotiations on the implementation of the Kambarata-1 hydropower plant project, with the support of the World Bank, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy said, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The talks took place in Istanbul, Türkiye, bringing together representatives of all three nations to discuss the next steps in advancing the regional energy project.

Kazakhstan records one of its largest grain harvests in 15 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:39:51 UTC
14:39:51 KST

Kazakhstan records one of its largest grain harvests in 15 years
Kazakh farmers harvested 24.3 million tons of grain during the 2026 harvest season, marking one of the country's three highest grain harvests in the past 15 years, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Ministry of Agriculture.
According to the ministry, Kazakhstan has surpassed this year's grain harvest only twice in the past 15 years, both during exceptionally productive seasons.
The ministry also emphasized that this year's harvest stood out not only for its volume but also for the quality of the grain.
"According to preliminary data, around 72% of the soft wheat delivered to grain elevators meets Class 3 quality standards, while 48% of the samples tested have a gluten content exceeding 28%. In Akmola region, Class 3 wheat accounts for 90% of the total, with high-protein (Hi-Pro) wheat making up 70%," the ministry said.
Kazakhstan has also maintained positive momentum in grain exports.
"Over the past two marketing years, Kazakhstan exported 15.5 million and 16 million tons of grain and flour in grain equivalent, respectively, setting records for the country's years of independence. According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, grain exports reached 1.657 million tons between September 1 and October 19, 2026, an increase of 9%," the ministry noted.
Meanwhile, the use of mineral fertilizers has nearly tripled over the past three years, reaching 1.8 million tons in 2025. Farmers have already applied 2.1 million tons in 2026, approaching the annual target of 2.3 million tons.
The share of elite seeds has also risen to 12%, creating favorable conditions for further improvements in crop yields and agricultural product quality.
The ministry also highlighted the extensive use of agricultural machinery during this year's harvest.
"More than 130,000 tractors, 29,000 combine harvesters, 17,000 reapers, and approximately 130,000 other pieces of agricultural equipment were used during the 2026 harvest. Thanks to the steady modernization of the agricultural machinery fleet between 2023 and 2025, the proportion of worn-out equipment declined from 85% to 65%. The machinery renewal rate is expected to reach 8% by the end of 2026," the ministry added.
A preferential leasing program has also helped accelerate the modernization of Kazakhstan's agricultural machinery fleet.
Since the program was launched, farmers have purchased more than 12,700 tractors and 2,340 combine harvesters through the scheme. Equipment acquired under the program now accounts for approximately 10% of the country's total fleet of tractors and combine harvesters.
Earlier, Olzhas Bektenov instructed the Government to ensure the timely completion of the country’s harvesting campaign.

All votes have been counted in Israel’s parliamentary election, but neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition has secured enough seats to form a majority.

A majority in the Knesset, Israel’s 120-seat parliament, requires 61 seats.

Netanyahu’s bloc previously held 68 seats, meaning the election represents a substantial loss for the governing parties.
Netanyahu’s Likud remains the largest party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot’s Yashar party, established in 2025, with 21 seats.
Voter turnout reached 77.9 percent, the highest in decades, according to the Times of Israel.
Although counting finished overnight into Friday, the official results are not expected until Wednesday, following checks for errors and complaints.
President Isaac Herzog will then consult party leaders about who should form the next government.
A minority government is possible but would need parliamentary support from parties outside the governing coalition.
Opposition politicians have already begun exploring potential alliances.
Democrats leader Yair Golan said Thursday that he had met with Eisenkot and Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas.
“Israel’s survival is at stake,” Golan wrote on X following his meeting with Eisenkot.
Abbas said Tuesday that he hoped Ra’am could help the opposition secure a parliamentary majority.

Denmark introduces new GP payment system to improve care for patients with greater needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:38:34 UTC
14:38:34 KST

Patients in Denmark will be able to book different types of appointments with their general practitioners under a new four-year agreement aimed at improving access to medical care.
The agreement, announced Thursday, was negotiated between Praktiserende Lægers Organisation (PLO), the Danish organization representing general practitioners, and Regionernes Lønnings- og Takstnævn (RLTN), the regional body responsible for negotiating doctors’ pay and fees.
One of the main changes is a new payment system that takes patients’ medical needs into account.
Currently, clinics receive the same payment per patient regardless of whether patients are generally healthy or require extensive treatment.
Under the agreement, clinics treating patients with greater medical needs will receive higher payments.
The change is intended to improve financial conditions for practices in areas with fewer doctors, where patients with the greatest treatment needs are often found.
The agreement also introduces four appointment categories: short, regular, long and complex consultations.
These will allow doctors to address several medical concerns during a single appointment when necessary.
General practitioners will also receive separate payments for continuing education, helping them expand their skills and potentially reduce referrals to other medical services.
“It is a milestone that we now have an agreement on terms and frameworks for general practice that extends four years into the future,” PLO chairman Jørgen Skadborg said.
He added that the agreement would provide stability, allowing doctors to focus on patients and developing their clinics.
The agreement takes effect at the start of the new year, with 4.5 billion DKK allocated to general practice over four years.
By 2030, annual funding is expected to be 1.7 billion DKK higher than today.

Friday will begin with widespread clouds, haze and fog, although some areas could see the skies clear as the day progresses.
Northeastern Denmark, particularly Bornholm, is expected to enjoy the most sunshine, while the rest of the country may see only brief sunny spells.
Saturday will remain largely dry but cloudy, with patches of morning fog and haze across the country.

Sunday will also begin cloudy but mostly dry before a weak cold front brings rain into northwestern Denmark during the day.
The rain will gradually spread eastward through the afternoon and evening, eventually reaching much of the country.

The unsettled conditions are expected to continue overnight into Monday, with further rainfall possible in southeastern Denmark on Monday morning.
Despite the cloud cover and approaching rain, the weekend will remain relatively mild for late October, with little wind and no significant weather disturbances expected.

Nearly two million Danes register organ donation preferences as numbers surge
Nearly four in ten people aged over 15 in Denmark have registered their organ donation preferences, following a sharp increase over the past two years.
According to figures from the Danish Center for Organ Donation, 1,941,790 people had recorded their decision by the end of September, up from 1,404,297 in September 2024.
The increase follows changes to Denmark’s organ donation rules, under which all adults aged 18 and older are automatically registered as potential donors. However, individuals must confirm their registration on sundhed.dk to become active donors.
Helle Haubro Andersen, head of the Danish Center for Organ Donation, said direct communication encourages people to make a decision.
Following the rule changes, residents received notifications through e-Boks, Denmark’s digital mailbox service.
Most of those who responded granted full or partial consent, Andersen said.
Among people who have registered their preferences, 66 percent consented to donating all eligible organs, while 16 percent granted partial consent. Another 14 percent declined donation.
Residents can also indicate that they remain undecided.
Andersen explained that deceased organ donors generally must have suffered a severe brain injury, such as a major stroke or brain hemorrhage.
There is no upper age limit for donation. Denmark’s oldest organ donor was 92 in 2019, although kidneys and livers are generally more suitable for donation at advanced ages.
The figures come amid criticism of Rigshospitalet, which has rejected donor livers for children and adults because of capacity shortages.
Andersen declined to comment on the hospital’s situation but noted that organ transplants have increased nationally.
Last year, 455 patients received organ transplants, compared with 433 in 2024, 430 in 2023 and 338 in 2022.
Danish court rules citizenship denial to woman with disability was not discrimination
A Palestinian woman who was denied Danish citizenship because she could not meet the country’s self-support requirement has lost her discrimination case against the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court ruled Friday that the decision did not constitute unlawful indirect discrimination based on her disability, according to a statement published on the court’s website.
The woman arrived in Denmark in 1999 and was involved in a traffic accident 10 years later.
Following the accident, her reduced ability to work led to her being approved for a flexjob, a Danish employment arrangement for people with permanently reduced working capacity.
She subsequently received unemployment benefits for a period, preventing her from meeting the financial self-sufficiency requirement for Danish citizenship.
Her citizenship application was rejected in February 2023.
The woman and her lawyer argued that the refusal amounted to indirect discrimination and violated international conventions protecting people with disabilities and human rights.
However, the High Court rejected those arguments and ruled in favor of the ministry.
Her lawyer, Petra Alexandra Fokdal, argued that the rules create difficulties for people in flexjobs who become unemployed.
“Once you are referred to a flexjob, you cannot be in an unemployment fund. And if the employer no longer needs you, you receive unemployment benefits, but this makes it impossible to meet the requirement of self-support,” Fokdal said.
Because of its wider legal significance, the case was transferred directly from the district court to the High Court.
Fokdal said she intends to appeal the ruling to Denmark’s Supreme Court.
Parcels arriving from outside the EU to Denmark and other EU countries will face a new fee
Cheap goods from Chinese online shops are arriving in EU in huge numbers, raising concerns about product safety.
In 2025 alone, Danish customs registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Therefore, the European Union will introduce a permanent handling fee of 2 euros per line item in parcels arriving from outside the bloc starting Sunday, November 1, the Danish Customs Agency said Friday.
The fee, equivalent to about 15 Danish kroner, will apply regardless of a parcel’s total value. It will be added to the temporary customs duty introduced this summer on parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Items with the same commodity code count as one line item. Three cotton T-shirts, for example, would incur a handling fee of 2 euros. A cotton T-shirt and a pair of denim jeans would count as two line items, bringing the fee to 4 euros.
The existing customs duty is 3 euros per line item in parcels with a total value below 150 euros.
Christian Lützen, director of the Danish Customs Agency, said the number of low-value parcels sent to consumers from outside the EU had fallen since the customs duty took effect.
“With the handling fee, we are stepping up efforts even further to, among other things, strengthen member states’ opportunities to inspect the contents of parcels,” he said in the press release.
“There are still problems with many of the goods in relation to consumer safety, and as an authority at the border, we must take that seriously.”
When the customs duty was introduced this summer, Lützen said the agency had previously seen a sharp increase in goods arriving from Chinese online shops. He called it “a major problem across EU countries” and said the duty should help make shopping with Danish businesses more attractive.
In 2025, the agency registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros. A count showed that more than 90% of parcels entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Shein and Temu were among the 10 online shops most used by Danish consumers in the latest survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, a business organization.
The two platforms sell products ranging from clothing to kitchen equipment and have faced criticism over poor quality and illegal chemicals in their products.

Arctic sea ice survives summer with less melting than expected despite record-low winter
Arctic sea ice has retained more of its coverage than expected this summer, thanks to unusually cool weather conditions, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI).
In a statement Thursday, DMI reported that Arctic sea ice reached a record-low winter extent earlier this year but experienced relatively limited melting during the summer months.
A large low-pressure system over the Arctic helped keep temperatures cooler, slowing the melting process and allowing more ice to survive.
Gorm Dybkjær, a climate researcher at DMI, said the development was surprising but cautioned against interpreting it as a reversal of climate change.
“It is remarkable that the sea ice in the Arctic has retained so much of its winter ice after the winter’s record-low extent. But that does not mean that climate change has released its grip on the ice,” he said.
In September, when Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum, its extent ranked as the 16th-lowest since records began in 1978.
Despite this year’s relatively favorable conditions, scientists continue to observe a long-term decline in the thickness and volume of Arctic sea ice.
Since 2007, the Arctic’s total sea ice volume has fallen by an estimated 20 percent or more.
Dybkjær warned that thinner ice is increasingly vulnerable to changing weather and ocean conditions, which could trigger sudden, substantial losses.
Researchers also monitor sea ice because of its role in regulating Earth’s temperature through the albedo effect.
This refers to how much incoming sunlight is reflected into space.
Ice and clouds reflect substantial amounts of solar radiation, while darker ocean surfaces absorb more energy, contributing to warming.

Danish intelligence service warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
The Danish Security and Intelligence Service, known as PET, is warning Ukrainians in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them to carry out sabotage, potentially without their knowledge.
PET said in a press release that it is issuing information material in Ukrainian. The service has previously warned the wider Danish public about the threat.
Emil Græsholm, PET’s head of counterintelligence, said the warning also needs to be available in Ukrainian because Russian intelligence services may attempt to recruit Ukrainians living in Denmark.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making it appear that they are participating in Russian sabotage.
Russian intelligence services can hide their identities and recruit through intermediaries, leaving those carrying out assignments unaware of who they are working for.
Tasks may be presented as journalism, market research or general documentation, making them appear harmless, PET said.
Written Danish exam grades fall across Denmark’s upper secondary programs
Grades in written Danish have fallen across Denmark’s upper secondary education programs, according to the latest exam results released by the Education Ministry on Thursday.
At general upper secondary schools, known as stx, the average grade in A-level Danish, the highest subject level, fell from 6.8 in 2018 to 6.2 in 2026.
Across upper secondary programs, grades declined both compared with last year and over the longer term.
Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said the figures worried him and raised concerns about students’ use of artificial intelligence.
“Artificial intelligence has in a very short time changed the students’ everyday lives,” he said in a press release.
“And we cannot ignore what it can mean for their academic proficiency. Because if AI becomes a shortcut around the work of writing, analyzing, and expressing oneself, then we risk that the students learn less,” he said.
The figures follow a PISA international student assessment published in early September that showed declining performance in reading, mathematics and science among 15-year-olds, renewing debate about academic standards in Danish schools.

Her term was scheduled to expire in October 2027, when she would have completed eight years in the post.
The European Council, which brings together EU leaders, will appoint her successor.
European Council President António Costa said in a post on X that the search for the next ECB president was beginning that day.
Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.
Denmark among 36 countries confirmed for Eurovision 2027 as boycotts continue
Canada will make its Eurovision debut next year, while several European countries remain absent amid disagreements over Israel’s participation in the international song contest.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organizes Eurovision, announced that 36 countries, including Denmark and Israel, are registered for the 2027 competition.
Ireland and the Netherlands have withdrawn for the second consecutive year, citing Israel’s participation and concerns over the humanitarian situation in Gaza and restrictions on press freedom.
Spain, Iceland and Slovenia also boycotted this year’s contest over Israel’s involvement.
Iceland will remain absent in 2027, while Spain and Slovenia have until December to decide whether to participate.
“As the EBU acknowledges that the matter is complex, it has agreed to give both broadcasters a deadline until December,” Eurovision’s official website stated.
The Czech Republic has also withdrawn, with national broadcaster Česká televize citing budget adjustments.
North Macedonia, meanwhile, will return for the first time since 2022.
Next year’s competition will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, following Dara’s victory in Vienna with the song “Bangaranga.”
Denmark finished seventh this year with Søren Torpegaard Lund’s “Før vi går hjem,” its best result in 13 years.
The 2027 contest will feature semifinals on May 11 and 13, followed by the grand final on May 15, when 25 countries will compete.
Bulgaria, as the defending winner, qualifies automatically alongside the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy, which make the largest financial contributions to the competition.
Viewers and professional juries will determine the results of both semifinals and the final.
Five Danish municipalities agree to take additional Ukrainian refugees
Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.
“It is a shared task to ensure that the Ukrainians who come to Denmark also gain a proper foothold in our local communities,” Bødskov said.
The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.
Copenhagen Airport says tighter security checks and staffing shortfalls contributed to long queues
An order from the Danish Transport Authority led to additional baggage checks from October 8. Some passengers missed flights, and SAS reported rebooking 352 travelers.
Copenhagen Airport introduced additional security checks following an order from the Danish Transport Authority and underestimated staffing needs on some days in October, the airport said Wednesday after long queues caused passengers to miss flights.
The airport received the order on October 6 and introduced the measures two days later. The changes meant more passengers had their baggage checked manually, it said in a press release.
The airport did not explain why the authority issued the order or give details of its requirements.
There were periods of long waits on October 8, October 22 and October 23, the airport said. Passengers also faced waits of up to an hour early on Saturday, October 24.
Danish media have reported lengthy queues, particularly over the past five days, with some passengers reaching their flights too late to depart as booked.
The airport acknowledged that it had underestimated staffing needs on some days during October. It said “it is naturally not satisfactory” that some passengers had had “a bad experience”.
SAS said on October 23 that it had rebooked 352 passengers because of the long waits. Passengers were also urged to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time for security.
Norwegian also offered affected customers rebooking.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

A disagreement has emerged between Ukraine’s embassy in Copenhagen and independent Danish lawmaker Jacob Harris over attempts to arrange a meeting ahead of his planned talks with Russia’s ambassador.
In a written statement to Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency, the embassy said it had offered Harris two possible meeting dates but received no reply.
“We were surprised to hear these claims from Member of Parliament Jacob Harris,” the embassy said.
“After receiving an email from Jacob Harris requesting a meeting, we suggested two possible dates to him in the near future. However, we have not received any response.”
Harris maintains that he never received the embassy’s reply but said he was “glad that contact has been made”.
“Now I will write to them again with a view to arranging a meeting,” he said.
The embassy also stated that Harris had visited twice without an appointment, hoping to meet the ambassador.
On both occasions, the ambassador was attending previously scheduled events and was not at the embassy.
Harris confirmed the visits, saying he had hoped to arrange a meeting.
The disagreement follows Harris’ announcement Thursday that he plans to meet Russia’s ambassador in Copenhagen on November 10.
In a Facebook post, Harris called for “more diplomacy, more dialogue, and less war rhetoric”.
The planned meeting drew criticism from politicians across Denmark’s political spectrum.
Harris also wrote that he had repeatedly contacted Ukraine’s ambassador without receiving a response.
He now hopes to meet the Ukrainian ambassador before his scheduled meeting with Russia’s representative.
The Ukrainian embassy expressed appreciation for Danish political support and thanked the Danish public for its continued solidarity with Ukraine.
Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian envoy involved in negotiations over the war in Ukraine and an adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin on economic and international affairs, said Tuesday that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland.
