Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.

Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.

The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

Arctic sea ice survives summer with less melting than expected despite record-low winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:38:08 UTC
14:38:08 KST

Arctic sea ice has retained more of its coverage than expected this summer, thanks to unusually cool weather conditions, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI).
In a statement Thursday, DMI reported that Arctic sea ice reached a record-low winter extent earlier this year but experienced relatively limited melting during the summer months.
A large low-pressure system over the Arctic helped keep temperatures cooler, slowing the melting process and allowing more ice to survive.
Gorm Dybkjær, a climate researcher at DMI, said the development was surprising but cautioned against interpreting it as a reversal of climate change.
“It is remarkable that the sea ice in the Arctic has retained so much of its winter ice after the winter’s record-low extent. But that does not mean that climate change has released its grip on the ice,” he said.
In September, when Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum, its extent ranked as the 16th-lowest since records began in 1978.
Despite this year’s relatively favorable conditions, scientists continue to observe a long-term decline in the thickness and volume of Arctic sea ice.
Since 2007, the Arctic’s total sea ice volume has fallen by an estimated 20 percent or more.
Dybkjær warned that thinner ice is increasingly vulnerable to changing weather and ocean conditions, which could trigger sudden, substantial losses.
Researchers also monitor sea ice because of its role in regulating Earth’s temperature through the albedo effect.
This refers to how much incoming sunlight is reflected into space.
Ice and clouds reflect substantial amounts of solar radiation, while darker ocean surfaces absorb more energy, contributing to warming.

The new airport allows Ilulissat, a town in western Greenland, to receive larger aircraft and direct international flights.

The airport’s opening marks a change in how travelers can reach Ilulissat from Denmark and other international destinations.
Nearly two million Danes register organ donation preferences as numbers surge
Nearly four in ten people aged over 15 in Denmark have registered their organ donation preferences, following a sharp increase over the past two years.
According to figures from the Danish Center for Organ Donation, 1,941,790 people had recorded their decision by the end of September, up from 1,404,297 in September 2024.
The increase follows changes to Denmark’s organ donation rules, under which all adults aged 18 and older are automatically registered as potential donors. However, individuals must confirm their registration on sundhed.dk to become active donors.
Helle Haubro Andersen, head of the Danish Center for Organ Donation, said direct communication encourages people to make a decision.
Following the rule changes, residents received notifications through e-Boks, Denmark’s digital mailbox service.
Most of those who responded granted full or partial consent, Andersen said.
Among people who have registered their preferences, 66 percent consented to donating all eligible organs, while 16 percent granted partial consent. Another 14 percent declined donation.
Residents can also indicate that they remain undecided.
Andersen explained that deceased organ donors generally must have suffered a severe brain injury, such as a major stroke or brain hemorrhage.
There is no upper age limit for donation. Denmark’s oldest organ donor was 92 in 2019, although kidneys and livers are generally more suitable for donation at advanced ages.
The figures come amid criticism of Rigshospitalet, which has rejected donor livers for children and adults because of capacity shortages.
Andersen declined to comment on the hospital’s situation but noted that organ transplants have increased nationally.
Last year, 455 patients received organ transplants, compared with 433 in 2024, 430 in 2023 and 338 in 2022.
Danish court rules citizenship denial to woman with disability was not discrimination
A Palestinian woman who was denied Danish citizenship because she could not meet the country’s self-support requirement has lost her discrimination case against the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court ruled Friday that the decision did not constitute unlawful indirect discrimination based on her disability, according to a statement published on the court’s website.
The woman arrived in Denmark in 1999 and was involved in a traffic accident 10 years later.
Following the accident, her reduced ability to work led to her being approved for a flexjob, a Danish employment arrangement for people with permanently reduced working capacity.
She subsequently received unemployment benefits for a period, preventing her from meeting the financial self-sufficiency requirement for Danish citizenship.
Her citizenship application was rejected in February 2023.
The woman and her lawyer argued that the refusal amounted to indirect discrimination and violated international conventions protecting people with disabilities and human rights.
However, the High Court rejected those arguments and ruled in favor of the ministry.
Her lawyer, Petra Alexandra Fokdal, argued that the rules create difficulties for people in flexjobs who become unemployed.
“Once you are referred to a flexjob, you cannot be in an unemployment fund. And if the employer no longer needs you, you receive unemployment benefits, but this makes it impossible to meet the requirement of self-support,” Fokdal said.
Because of its wider legal significance, the case was transferred directly from the district court to the High Court.
Fokdal said she intends to appeal the ruling to Denmark’s Supreme Court.
Parcels arriving from outside the EU to Denmark and other EU countries will face a new fee
Cheap goods from Chinese online shops are arriving in EU in huge numbers, raising concerns about product safety.
In 2025 alone, Danish customs registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Therefore, the European Union will introduce a permanent handling fee of 2 euros per line item in parcels arriving from outside the bloc starting Sunday, November 1, the Danish Customs Agency said Friday.
The fee, equivalent to about 15 Danish kroner, will apply regardless of a parcel’s total value. It will be added to the temporary customs duty introduced this summer on parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Items with the same commodity code count as one line item. Three cotton T-shirts, for example, would incur a handling fee of 2 euros. A cotton T-shirt and a pair of denim jeans would count as two line items, bringing the fee to 4 euros.
The existing customs duty is 3 euros per line item in parcels with a total value below 150 euros.
Christian Lützen, director of the Danish Customs Agency, said the number of low-value parcels sent to consumers from outside the EU had fallen since the customs duty took effect.
“With the handling fee, we are stepping up efforts even further to, among other things, strengthen member states’ opportunities to inspect the contents of parcels,” he said in the press release.
“There are still problems with many of the goods in relation to consumer safety, and as an authority at the border, we must take that seriously.”
When the customs duty was introduced this summer, Lützen said the agency had previously seen a sharp increase in goods arriving from Chinese online shops. He called it “a major problem across EU countries” and said the duty should help make shopping with Danish businesses more attractive.
In 2025, the agency registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros. A count showed that more than 90% of parcels entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Shein and Temu were among the 10 online shops most used by Danish consumers in the latest survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, a business organization.
The two platforms sell products ranging from clothing to kitchen equipment and have faced criticism over poor quality and illegal chemicals in their products.

Denmark introduces new GP payment system to improve care for patients with greater needs
Patients in Denmark will be able to book different types of appointments with their general practitioners under a new four-year agreement aimed at improving access to medical care.
The agreement, announced Thursday, was negotiated between Praktiserende Lægers Organisation (PLO), the Danish organization representing general practitioners, and Regionernes Lønnings- og Takstnævn (RLTN), the regional body responsible for negotiating doctors’ pay and fees.
One of the main changes is a new payment system that takes patients’ medical needs into account.
Currently, clinics receive the same payment per patient regardless of whether patients are generally healthy or require extensive treatment.
Under the agreement, clinics treating patients with greater medical needs will receive higher payments.
The change is intended to improve financial conditions for practices in areas with fewer doctors, where patients with the greatest treatment needs are often found.
The agreement also introduces four appointment categories: short, regular, long and complex consultations.
These will allow doctors to address several medical concerns during a single appointment when necessary.
General practitioners will also receive separate payments for continuing education, helping them expand their skills and potentially reduce referrals to other medical services.
“It is a milestone that we now have an agreement on terms and frameworks for general practice that extends four years into the future,” PLO chairman Jørgen Skadborg said.
He added that the agreement would provide stability, allowing doctors to focus on patients and developing their clinics.
The agreement takes effect at the start of the new year, with 4.5 billion DKK allocated to general practice over four years.
By 2030, annual funding is expected to be 1.7 billion DKK higher than today.

Lars-Christian Brask, a member of Denmark’s parliament for Liberal Alliance, has been elected president of the Nordic Council, which brings together parliamentarians from the Nordic countries.
Brask was elected Thursday during the council’s session in Helsinki, Finland, according to a statement from Folketinget, Denmark’s parliament.

Arctic sea ice survives summer with less melting than expected despite record-low winter
Arctic sea ice has retained more of its coverage than expected this summer, thanks to unusually cool weather conditions, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI).
In a statement Thursday, DMI reported that Arctic sea ice reached a record-low winter extent earlier this year but experienced relatively limited melting during the summer months.
A large low-pressure system over the Arctic helped keep temperatures cooler, slowing the melting process and allowing more ice to survive.
Gorm Dybkjær, a climate researcher at DMI, said the development was surprising but cautioned against interpreting it as a reversal of climate change.
“It is remarkable that the sea ice in the Arctic has retained so much of its winter ice after the winter’s record-low extent. But that does not mean that climate change has released its grip on the ice,” he said.
In September, when Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum, its extent ranked as the 16th-lowest since records began in 1978.
Despite this year’s relatively favorable conditions, scientists continue to observe a long-term decline in the thickness and volume of Arctic sea ice.
Since 2007, the Arctic’s total sea ice volume has fallen by an estimated 20 percent or more.
Dybkjær warned that thinner ice is increasingly vulnerable to changing weather and ocean conditions, which could trigger sudden, substantial losses.
Researchers also monitor sea ice because of its role in regulating Earth’s temperature through the albedo effect.
This refers to how much incoming sunlight is reflected into space.
Ice and clouds reflect substantial amounts of solar radiation, while darker ocean surfaces absorb more energy, contributing to warming.

Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.
The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.
Veteran Venstre lawmaker expelled over party discipline dispute
Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.
“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.
Known for following his own conviction, he has previously gone against the party line. In 2021, he voted with eight members against launching an impeachment trial against Inger Støjberg, who ended up being convicted. The members were granted a free vote when they voted.
In the 2024 book “Ærlig talt – Borgen indefra”, he described that he was close to leaving Venstre because of Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s purchase of clothes with party money. The book also contains criticism of political conformism and the workflows at Christiansborg.
With Preben Bang Henriksen’s departure, Venstre loses another one of its vote-magnets, as he received the fifth-most votes in Venstre in the election in March 2026.
Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

Founded in 1945, Rambøll advises clients on construction, transport, the environment, energy and management. The Rambøll Foundation owns 98% of the company, with employees holding the remaining 2%.
Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft
Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.
University of Copenhagen rules out second cyberattack, but system disruptions continue
The University of Copenhagen says it was not hit by a second cyberattack Monday, reversing its initial assessment after shutting down several administrative systems.
Activity that appeared to signal another attack prompted the shutdown. By Monday evening, the university had determined that no new attack had occurred, it said on its website.
However, a controlled shutdown remains necessary as a precaution linked to the original breach, and some systems continue to experience disruptions.
The university disclosed the first attack Friday. Outsiders gained access to information about approximately 525,000 people, including details such as full names, CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers, telephone numbers and private email addresses.
The breach also compromised ID card PINs belonging to about 20,000 employees and students. The university temporarily restricted physical access to selected critical locations following a security assessment.
Those locations have reopened after all affected cardholders received new PINs.
The University of Copenhagen, the Technical University of Denmark and Aarhus University have all faced cyberattacks within a few weeks.
Christina Egelund, Denmark’s minister for research, higher education and digitalization, previously told Ritzau that leaders from the country’s eight universities had been summoned to a meeting Monday to discuss security.

Danes’ bank deposits fell for a second consecutive month in September, reaching 1,309.3 billion kroner, according to figures from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank.
That was down from 1,317.7 billion kroner in August and 1,323.2 billion kroner in July. The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.
The university confirmed the latest attack on its website, reporting disruptions to several administrative systems and difficulties accessing university websites on Monday evening.
The previous breach exposed personal information including full names, CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and private email addresses.
The university has not provided further details about Monday’s attack.
Denmark’s Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization, Christina Egelund of Moderaterne (the Moderates), expressed serious concern about the repeated incidents.
“It is the second time in a short period, and it does not become less serious that it comes in the wake of several attacks on our universities,” she told Ritzau.
Several Danish universities, including the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and Aarhus University, have also experienced cyberattacks in recent weeks.
Egelund said the incidents highlighted the seriousness of the security situation.
“It is an attack on our knowledge institutions, which are an absolutely crucial pillar of society in Denmark,” she said.
The minister summoned leaders from Denmark’s eight universities to a meeting Monday to discuss cybersecurity.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, explained that universities hold large amounts of personal and research data, making them attractive targets.
Their public visibility also increases their exposure to cyber threats.
“That makes us potential targets for both cybercriminals, foreign states, and activist groups,” he said in an Aarhus University press release.
New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.
Danish publisher bans AI tools for work on manuscripts
Danish publisher Lindhardt og Ringhof has prohibited employees and external partners from using artificial intelligence to complete work for the company.
The ban applies to proofreaders, editors, manuscript readers and consultants, according to a letter distributed by the publisher.
“It is not permitted for any purpose to use AI tools for tasks that one as an external partner solves for Lindhardt og Ringhof,” the letter states.
Manuscripts and other documents provided by the publisher must not be uploaded to AI systems under any circumstances.
The company said even apparently harmless uses, such as asking AI to summarize a manuscript, could create legal and copyright risks.
“Texts that are uploaded into AI tools can subsequently be copied and data mined, even if the provider claims otherwise,” the publisher said.
Literary director Sune de Souza Schmidt-Madsen told Danish public broadcaster DR that Lindhardt og Ringhof was not aware of external partners already using AI for its assignments.
However, he said the publisher expected the issue to emerge eventually and wanted to establish its rules in advance.
The restrictions also apply to the publisher’s own employees, Schmidt-Madsen said.

US plans to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers
- The US plans to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers. The FCC will vote on Nov 19, citing national security and scam robocall risks.
- The proposal targets China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom, plus other IP-enabled providers. It also seeks to block firms using Huawei or ZTE equipment and to bar Chinese labs from testing US electronics from December 2028.
- The move follows fears of spying and telecom data theft, including the Salt Typhoon cyber espionage case. China has denied wrongdoing, while the FCC says it is strengthening its “first line of defence".
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The United States plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds – a measure designed to prevent scam-related robocalls.
The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Oct 29 that it will vote on Nov 19 on a proposal to ban China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers from direct access.
For telecom firms providing Voice over Internet Protocol – technology that converts voice into digital data and transmits it over broadband connections – direct access is a cheaper option and makes it easier to offer advanced features.
“With this decision, the FCC will be strengthening our first line of defence against bad actors and illegal robocallers,” FCC chair Brendan Carr said in a statement.
China’s Foreign Ministry said on Oct 30 that it firmly opposes the likely US ban and accused Washington of overstretching the concept of national security and abusing state power to suppress Chinese enterprises.
“China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a daily press conference.
The FCC also said on Oct 29 that it plans to bar IP-enabled service providers that use equipment from companies on its list that pose national security risks, including Huawei or ZTE.
It added that it would ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics in December 2028 and may also revoke direct number authorisations for Chinese firms that it deems to pose national security risks. It has previously barred China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from providing international telecommunications services to the US.
Other measures under consideration include barring them from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centres in the United States.
Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.
In late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers’ call records, US call data and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms. The FBI said in 2026 that threats from Salt Typhoon are “still very much ongoing”.
In July, it added California-based Digitalsystem Technology to a list of companies posing risks to US national security, citing links to Chinese telecom firms and its ownership by a Chinese national.
China has consistently denied any wrongdoing. REUTERS

China unveils first Fengyun satellite AI models for extreme weather
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:30:23 CST
14:30:23 KST

CHANGSHA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- China released its first batch of Fengyun meteorological satellite extreme weather artificial intelligence (AI) models on Thursday at a users conference in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province.
The models, including an intelligent typhoon cloud imagery interpretation model and a severe convection nowcasting warning model, will effectively enhance the capability of Fengyun meteorological satellites in monitoring and warning against extreme weather, such as typhoons and severe convection, according to the China Meteorological Administration (CMA).
Nowcasting is a method used in meteorology for very short-range weather forecasts.
The intelligent typhoon cloud imagery interpretation model can automatically analyze the position, structure, intensity, and evolution of typhoons, while simultaneously generating standardized interpretation text and outputting visualized products, as a means of providing technical support for typhoon monitoring and forecasting.
At present, this model covers seven types of typhoon features, performs interpretation once every 15 minutes, and generates interpretation text within 27 seconds.
The severe convection nowcasting warning model uses continuous observations from the Fengyun-4 meteorological satellite over the past two hours to predict future cloud imagery evolution and identify potential severe convection areas, advancing the warning lead time to four hours.
Fengyun meteorological satellites are an important component of China's comprehensive meteorological observation system. With the rapid development of AI technology, quickly extracting key information from massive satellite data and further predicting weather evolution has become an important direction for their application.
To date, China has 10 Fengyun meteorological satellites in orbit, and their data is open to 141 countries and regions, according to the CMA. ■

====================================================================================================

The change vote turns: Why America's midterms could punish the party that promised it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:30:06 UTC
14:30:06 KST

Two years after riding a wave of discontent to total control of Washington, Donald Trump and the Republicans face the same message of change that brought them to power. This time, it's aimed squarely at them.
America's midterm elections are less than one week away. It's not a presidential election year, but the result could reverberate from the White House to Brussels. On the ballot are all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 seats in the Senate. Republicans currently hold a narrow 219-214 majority in the House and a 53-47 majority in the Senate. For President Trump, the stakes could hardly be higher. And the political winds that carried him back to the White House are now blowing hard in the other direction.
The change that brought them to power
Two years ago, inflation and the economy propelled Trump back to the White House and handed Republicans control of both chambers of Congress.
The message was simple: change. According to 2024 ABC News exit polling, 28% of voters said the ability to bring needed change was the most important quality in a candidate. Trump won those voters 74% to 24%. The economy was the top issue for 32% of voters, and Trump won them 81% to 18%, according to NBC News exit polls.
That message carried down the ballot. Republicans flipped four Senate seats — West Virginia, Montana, Ohio and Pennsylvania — to retake the chamber, ousting long-serving Democrats such as Sherrod Brown and Bob Casey.
Republicans went on the attack, and the Democrats never managed to mount a defence.
The incumbents now
This time, the Republicans are the incumbents. They face the same message of change that brought them to power, and it does not appear to be a message that will favour them.
The economy is in worse shape than when Trump regained power. Inflation is not only rising, it is higher than when he was elected: 2.7% in November 2024, against 3.7% this September, up from 3.4% in August and driven largely by soaring energy prices.
Voters have noticed. Trump left office in 2021 above water on the economy, 48% to 41%, and in 2024 voters trusted him over Kamala Harris to handle it by 53% to 46%, according to NBC News exit polls. Today, just 34% approve of his handling of the economy and 65% disapprove, according to the CNBC All-America Economic Survey — his lowest mark in either term, and a disapproval rating worse than Joe Biden's worst showing.
The once-unthinkable has happened: 37% of voters now say Democrats have the better approach on the economy, against 33% for Republicans, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, which puts Trump's approval at 32%.
The broken promise
The dismal reversal can be traced back to Trump's largest broken promise: no more wars.
He repeated it relentlessly in 2024, as did his surrogates and the podcasters who backed him. On Ukraine, CNN counted at least 53 occasions on which he promised to end the war within 24 hours or before even taking office.
Today, Russia's war on Ukraine grinds on, its latest "breakthrough" a local humanitarian ceasefire in the single occupied town of Oleshky. A year after Trump declared the war in Gaza over, few of the ceasefire's promises have been fulfilled.
And in February, Trump started a new war, joining Israel in launching strikes on Iran. Nearly eight months later, there is no end in sight. At a rally in Texas on Tuesday, Trump told supporters the war would end "whenever I want it to end."
It was unpopular from day one: 56% of Americans opposed it in the first week, according to a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. The opposition has only grown. Disapproval of Trump's handling of the war has risen from 61% in March to 65%, according to Pew Research, and in September a record share of more than 60% told Fox News it was the wrong decision.
The war has rattled the global economy, but Americans feel it most at the pump. Regular gasoline costs an average of $4.25 a gallon, up from $2.98 before the war, according to AAA, which says this is the first October that gas has averaged more than $4. Diesel has climbed from $3.76 to $6.35.
That hits everyone, but it hits Trump's rural base hardest: the farmers, ranchers and truckers who run on diesel.
'We're blowing it away'
Trump's response has been to insist that nothing is wrong. "Our first term, we had the greatest economy in the history of our country, and we're blowing it away," he told a rally in Tennessee this month. In March, as oil prices spiked, he went further: "When oil prices go up, we make a lot of money," he wrote on Truth Social.
But the impact on Americans is impossible to hide, or to blame on his opponents. Eight in ten rate the economy as fair or poor, according to CNBC.
Hitting home in the heartland
The war is not the only policy hurting Trump's most loyal voters. In late August, he paused certain beef tariffs for 90 days, opening the door to cheaper Brazilian beef. Cattle auction prices fell immediately.
Then there are the data centres, which have run straight into rural communities worried about their land, water and power bills. Half of Americans now oppose one within three miles of their home, up from 28% in January, according to a Politico poll. Farm bankruptcies are up 46% this year, according to the Nebraska Farmers Union, and 57% of rural voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, according to an AP-KFF poll cited by ABC Australia.
Cracks in the base
The cracks run through Trump's own movement. Marjorie Taylor Greene broke with him over the Epstein files, foreign wars and affordability, and resigned from Congress after Trump branded her a "traitor." Tucker Carlson broke with him over Iran and now says he regrets supporting him.
Joe Rogan, whose podcast helped deliver young men to Trump, put it bluntly: "He ran on no more wars... And then we have one that we can't even really clearly define why we did it."
Purging the conservatives
Rather than mend those fences, Trump spent primary season going after some of his party's most steadfast conservatives.
In Kentucky, Congressman Thomas Massie, a fiscal hawk with a lifetime Heritage Action score of 83%, lost his primary 55% to 45% to a Trump-endorsed challenger backed by many of the president's biggest donors, in a race that drew more than $32 million in advertising. His crime was not a lack of conservatism. It was a willingness to tell the president "no."
In Texas, Trump endorsed scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton late in his runoff against four-term Senator John Cornyn, who scored 96% with Heritage Action in the current Congress. Paxton won 64% to 36%.
Now Republicans could lose a seat they have held for more than three decades. Democratic rising star James Talarico leads Paxton in most recent polls, and Republicans further down the Texas ballot, once considered safe, are fighting for their political lives.
Follow the money
Across the country, the clearest evidence of Trump's drag on his party isn't in the polls. It's in where the money is going.
In April, the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC, unveiled a $342 million advertising plan across eight states. Texas, Kansas and Nebraska were not among them. Since 1 September, the group and its allies have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump won by double digits.
Meanwhile, the group has pulled most of its remaining ad money from North Carolina, cut reservations in Georgia, taken out a $5 million "insurance policy" in South Carolina and started spending in deeply conservative Mississippi.
"I don't think people had on their bingo card that we'd be talking about Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa," Marc Short, Trump's liaison to Congress in his first term, told USA Today. "I mean it's a direct reflection of the president's economic policies that that's where we're fighting right now."
Parties don't pour money into safe seats because the polls are wrong. They do it because their own data says the polls are right.
The House rout and the Senate fight
Six months ago, the House looked winnable for Democrats. Today, the Republican fight to hold it looks futile.
Democrats need to flip just three seats. Decision Desk HQ gives them an 80% chance of winning control and projects 238 Democratic seats, while Polymarket traders put their odds at 92%. The question is no longer whether Democrats win the House, but by how much.
The real battle is for the Senate, a long shot for Democrats as recently as last spring. They need a net gain of four seats, and Polymarket traders give them a 67% chance.
North Carolina looks likely to flip. Beyond that, the majority will be decided in races that are, statistically, dead heats:
· Texas: Talarico leads Paxton 48% to 46% (Emerson).
· Ohio: Sherrod Brown leads Senator Jon Husted 47% to 44% (Suffolk University).
· Alaska: Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan 49.1% to 47.5% (The Hill average).
· Iowa: Ashley Hinson and Josh Turek are deadlocked at 45.8% to 45.6% (The Hill average).
· Maine: Troy Jackson leads Senator Susan Collins 49% to 47% (Marist).
Best case, worst case
For Trump, the best realistic outcome is a split decision: a razor-thin 220-215 Democratic House and a Republican Senate that loses only North Carolina. Prediction markets give a Democratic House and Republican Senate a 27% chance.
The worst case is a rout. In a blowout, NBC News estimates Democrats could win as many as 263 House seats, the largest majority either party has held since 1990. In the Senate, a Democratic sweep of the remaining toss-ups on top of North Carolina would hand them 53 seats.
Either way, Trump would face two years of subpoenas, investigations and stalled legislation, and a Democratic House could launch impeachment proceedings.
A verdict on Trump II
If the worst comes to pass — or even a middle ground — it would be a heavy blow to Trump and a referendum on the first two years of his second term.
It would be Americans punishing a Republican Congress that rubber-stamped the White House as prices climbed and a new war began — and punishing Trump himself for the economy, inflation and broken promises.
And it would be a change vote that completely reverses the change vote of 2024. Two years ago, Americans voted for change and got a Republican Washington. Next Tuesday, they look set to vote for change again — this time, against them.

Nepal's public debt reaches over 19 bln USD
China
Unknown Publisher

13:30:02 CST
14:30:02 KST

KATHMANDU, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Nepal's public debt has surpassed 3 trillion Nepali rupees for the first time, reflecting a rapid increase in the country's debt burden over the past decade, the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) said.
The government's total outstanding debt reached 3.009 trillion Nepali rupees (about 19.77 billion U.S. dollars) by the end of the first quarter of the current fiscal year 2026-27 that began in mid-July, accounting for 45.59 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), according to the PDMO's latest statistics released on Thursday.
Of the total outstanding debt, foreign debt accounted for 53.13 percent, while domestic debt made up the remaining 46.87 percent.
Over the past decade, Nepal's public debt has risen rapidly as the country has increasingly relied on domestic and foreign borrowing to meet its financing needs, particularly following the devastating earthquake in 2015 and the COVID-19 pandemic.
In fiscal year 2016-17, Nepal's total public debt stood at just 697.68 billion Nepali rupees, equivalent to 26.84 percent of GDP at the time, according to the PDMO. As the country relied on public borrowing to finance post-earthquake reconstruction, its public debt crossed the 1 trillion rupee mark in fiscal year 2018-19 and continued to rise in subsequent years.
Public debt is expected to increase further in fiscal year 2026-27 as the government mobilizes additional resources for reconstruction and recovery following the devastating floods on Aug. 26, the Asian Development Bank said in its Asian Development Outlook 2026, released in September.
"Despite higher financing needs, Nepal remains at low risk of debt distress," the report said. ■

London’s Oxford Street Opens Its First Traffic-Free Phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

In 2016, Mayor of London Sadiq Khan first expressed the intention to pedestrianize Oxford Street, located in the City of Westminster in central London. The original plan was to complete the project in 2020, but after two public consultations, the project was blocked in 2018. Resumed in 2024, it was followed by two public consultations that showed majority support among respondents. Final approval was granted in February 2026, and on Monday, October 26, almost a kilometer, from Orchard Street to Great Portland Street, became traffic-free. This milestone marks the first phase of the program: the section is now closed to private motorized vehicles, buses, taxis and private hire vehicles, cycles, scooters and pedicabs.
The project is led by landscape and urban design practice East, based in East London. The team of subconsultants includes Gehl, the global urban strategy and design consultancy; research and urban design practice Publica; landscape architects J&L Gibbons; sustainability and low-energy building consultants Etude; and transport consultants NRP. Working in parallel with East, architecture practice Hawkins\Brown is developing a long-term design vision for the entire project, extending from Marble Arch to Tottenham Court Road. To oversee the project, the Mayor created the Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC), a Mayoral Development Corporation with the ability to take over planning powers from Westminster City Council.
This urban transformation is the latest chapter in a long history of change on one of London's busiest and most famous streets. The East team has drawn on descriptions of the street by Henry James and Virginia Woolf, which capture its spectacle and historic image. The team's objective is to give Oxford Street "a distinct character and a richer, more varied life." The street's wide variety of shops will be accompanied by new workplaces, leisure facilities, and cultural and hospitality destinations. During this transition period, works will remove road markings and add new seating, planting and signage. A textured stone surfacing will guide movement down the street, while larger pavers will mark north-south street crossings.
Related Article
Designed for Walking: 6 Unbuilt Projects for Pedestrian Movement from the ArchDaily Community
Street furniture is a key part of the transition phase, combining timber and steel benches in areas where they do not obstruct circulation. Seating placed at regular intervals aims to facilitate not only sitting but also meeting, eating and resting. Timber seats and tables are located in areas marked by distinct surface textures that indicate stopping points. During the transition period, East will test furniture configurations to ensure they are usable, welcoming and suitable. The project's landscape design includes tree planting intended to mitigate the urban heat island effect, capture carbon, intercept rainwater and increase biodiversity. Trees will be grown in large pots until they are ready to be lowered into the ground permanently. Later phases will include two new public squares marked with a new surface dressing, one close to Holles Street and the other close to Duke Street.
The transition phase serves as a trial period for the project. The OSDC and East will assess real-time insights into how the space is used and collect feedback from residents, accessibility groups, businesses, workers, transport partners and other Londoners to inform later phases. Sensors built into the furniture will monitor the flow of people and duration of use, and this data will inform the design of the permanent scheme. Public use of the traffic-free section will provide information on current needs to guide the design of public spaces. Construction of the permanent scheme for the section between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is expected to begin later in 2027, with completion anticipated in 2028.
In other news about public space design, Stefano Boeri Architetti was recently selected to transform a former locomotive factory into a new green neighborhood in Tbilisi, Georgia. The preliminary design integrates the industrial heritage with contemporary design, public spaces and community recreation hubs. Portuguese architecture and urbanism practice OODA has released new images of an urban design project in Prague, Czech Republic. The design transforms an existing building block into a permeable site with municipal social housing, commercial units and a landscaped central plaza.

More greens, higher testosterone? What a Finnish study found
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:27:07 UTC
14:27:07 KST

Research involving more than 2,500 men found contrasting associations between animal and plant protein intake — but does not show that changing diets boosts testosterone.
Sport, smoking and alcohol are often discussed as factors that can affect men’s testosterone levels. But diet — and whether protein comes from plants or animals — could also play a role, according to new research from Finland.
A study of 2,546 men found that those with the highest intake of animal protein had lower testosterone concentrations than those who consumed the least, while the opposite was true for men with the highest intake of plant protein.
Testosterone is a key male sex hormone, involved in sexual function, muscle development and bone health. Its levels vary with age, body weight and other factors, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of any single part of a person’s diet.
Higher dairy-protein intake was associated with lower total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations. Meat-protein intake, meanwhile, was associated with lower sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations but not with total testosterone.
Higher intake of plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products was associated with higher total testosterone.
Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland analysed data from men aged 42 to 60 living in eastern Finland. Their diets were recorded over four days between 1984 and 1989, and their blood samples were used to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin, a protein that influences testosterone concentrations in the blood.
Men in the highest animal-protein intake group had average total testosterone concentrations that were 1.2 nanomoles per litre lower than those in the lowest-intake group. For plant protein, the association ran in the opposite direction: men in the highest-intake group had concentrations 1.1 nanomoles per litre higher than those in the lowest-intake group.
The researchers adjusted their analyses for age, body mass index and several other dietary, lifestyle and health-related factors.
The Finnish study does not establish that animal protein lowers testosterone or that switching to a plant-based diet raises it.
The research was cross-sectional, meaning it examined associations rather than demonstrating cause and effect.
“Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small,” Miika Wynne-Ellis, a doctoral researcher at the University of Eastern Finland, said in the university’s announcement of the findings.

Aid convoy sets off for Russian-held town of Oleshky in Ukraine, Izvestia says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:23:10 CET
14:23:10 KST

By Dan Peleschuk
KYIV, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Starving and exhausted residents of a Russian-held town in southern Ukraine were evacuated by bus on Friday as part of a joint relief operation by the opposing sides, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.
Under a local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, an aid convoy arrived in the town of Oleshky to distribute food and medicine.
Those wishing to leave - some for Russia, some for Ukraine - were taken initially to Russian-annexed Crimea in 25 buses and nine ambulances, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said, before splitting into separate convoys.
Senior Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamia said those heading for Ukraine would be taken from there to Anapa in southern Russia before flying to Belarus and finally crossing back into Ukraine by bus - a route of more than 1,000 miles.
Although it was a striking example of cooperation between the warring sides, a spokesman for Russian President Vladimir Putin described it as “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for peace.
Attacks continued elsewhere, with Russian strikes overnight targeting seven regions of Ukraine, the capital Kyiv and the southeastern city of Dnipro, officials said. On Thursday, a Russian drone killed at least 15 people on a rail platform in Dnipro.
Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries despite a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before midterm legislative elections next week. There was no comment from Ukraine.
SOME RESIDENTS STAY BEHIND
It was not clear how many people had chosen to stay behind in Oleshky, which has suffered extensive war damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the Kakhovka dam upstream from the town in 2023.
Residents have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads - one known as the “road of death” - to get food and water. Some say they have survived on little more than a cup of rice or buckwheat a day.
“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with Lantratova.
“I’ve been told that it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”
In another video clip, he embraced a woman who gave her name as Anna, and asked if she was packed and ready to leave.
“Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine,” she said.
BOTH SIDES KEEN TO PLACATE TRUMP
Both sides have praised the US first lady for brokering the deal, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo. Kyiv and Moscow have reasons to ensure its success to avoid antagonising the US president before the midterm elections, with US-mediated peace talks due to resume in November after a nine-month gap.
For Russia, which seized Oleshky in the first days of the war in 2022, the operation also provides a PR opportunity. Russian state TV has shown aid boxes destined for Oleshky, decorated with the Russian flag, being loaded by people wearing T-shirts reading “Putin’s Team - The People’s Front”.
Russia’s Lantratova said food, hygiene products, medical supplies and fuel were being delivered. Ukraine’s Lubinets said everyone in need of help would get it.
Relations between the pair were cordial - something not seen between Russian and Ukrainian officials since the start of the war - as they appeared side by side to address reporters.
They later spoke together to residents, some of whom were in tears. One woman switched hesitantly between Russian and Ukrainian, a moment that seemed to symbolise the plight of fearful people caught up in a war.
MOST EXTENSIVE CEASEFIRE OF ITS KIND
The ceasefire came into force in Oleshky and the Kherson region on Tuesday. Lubinets said that in terms of the front line, it was the most durable and extensive of the war, in which the two sides have intensified long-range airstrikes this year while battlefield front lines remain largely static.
The aid convoy’s arrival was preceded by demining operations in which Lantratova said a Russian sapper and one other person were killed.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there was a “high degree of coordination” between Lantratova and Lubinets.
But when a state TV reporter asked if this showed it was possible for Russia and Ukraine to agree on other issues, he replied: “This is an isolated situation, which is difficult to extrapolate to the entire settlement process at this stage.”
(Reporting by Dan Peleschuk in Kyiv, Jekaterina Golubkova in Tokyo and Moscow bureau; writing by Mark Trevelyan; Editing by Kevin Liffey)
