Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3 billion security breach
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:23:10 CET
14:23:10 KST

By Lawrence Delevingne, Summer Zhen and Elizabeth Howcroft
BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets.
The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company’s total user assets and public reserves.
Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.
Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a “complex attack” that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, “making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.”
The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called “hot” wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
“Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust,” Teng wrote.
‘LARGEST KNOWN THEFT’
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
“This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.
The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, which makes this a national security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM, said.
Binance is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Secret Service (USSS), a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.
The FBI said it was “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps.”
The USSS said in a statement that its investigators “are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday.”
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”. Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised. Bitcoin last stood at $77,355 and ether at $2,229. Binance’s BNB token was down 6.74% over the past 24 hours at $698.
SECURITY IMPLICATIONS
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin’s most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to “deliver” on ensuring no customers suffered losses. “Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient,” he wrote on Friday.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
(Reporting by Tom Westbrook, Ankur Banerjee and Rae Wee in Singapore, Summer Zhen in Hong Kong, Rocky Swift in Tokyo, Vallari Srivastava and Anusha Shah in Bengaluru and Mrinmay Dey in Mexico City, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris, Tom Wilson in London, AJ Vicens in Detroit and Lawrence Delevingne in Boston; Writing by Lawrence Delevingne, Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook. Editing by Stephen Coates, Mark Potter, Elisa Martinuzzi, Tommy Reggiori Wilkes and David Gaffen)

Exclusive-Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:22:46 CET
14:22:46 KST

By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas
Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the comments that have drawn US officials’ attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
EUROPE SHOULD AVOID “POKING” RUSSIA
The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.
One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no “poking” directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was “cornered like a rat” as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a “rat in a corner” in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon’s recent private messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE’S RESOLVE
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon’s advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO’s mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.
The Pentagon messages to NATO officials come at a fraught time for European security.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration’s push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin’s continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington’s force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in America’s troop presence on the continent.
US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.
(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell)

Erin Patterson began the day with hope. Now Australia’s mushroom murderer knows she’s likely to die in jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:12:14 UTC
14:12:14 KST

Erin Patterson raised her chin and stared out on the brilliant blue promise of a mid-spring morning.
To the east, Victoria’s grandest court room was filled with people she had brought together, yet she was there only on a screen.
Patterson watched on, clad in prison-issued blue, from the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre.
Soon, three justices of the court of appeal would enter the Banco court, and Patterson would learn whether she would walk under that sky again as a free woman.
Patterson, 52, was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
Anyone who sat through her appeal hearings in August considered her prospects to be slim.
She argued on seven grounds that her conviction should be set aside, but there was little thrust to her arguments, little sense that the justices were for turning.
Indeed, they appeared more receptive to an appeal by the director of public prosecutions that Patterson’s non-parole period of 33 years was manifestly inadequate.
Even if the status quo remained, with Patterson’s appeal against her conviction failing and the DPP’s bid for her sentence to be increased also falling short, there was little to look forward to – she would be in her early 80s before she could apply for parole.
It took only 15 minutes for Justice Stephen McLeish to stifle even that breath of hope.
McLeish said the court dismissed all but two grounds of Patterson’s appeal, granted leave to appeal on the final two but dismissed those too, and agreed with the DPP that Patterson should be resentenced.
It was not just that her non-parole period was too short, McLeish said: it was that she should not have any prospect of ever being released.
McLeish said Patterson sustained an intent to murder all four people for three weeks, from the time they were invited to the lunch, during the meal, and during the “protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted”.
The offending was “carefully planned and deliberate”, he said, and involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” – including claims that she had cancer, denying she had foraged mushrooms, and lying about the source of the mushrooms.
In the plain language of the courts, McLeish said that under the sentencing act he and his fellow justices had found that the nature of Patterson’s crimes meant that fixing any non-parole period was inappropriate.
“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest possible terms,” McLeish said.
There was a sense in the court at this point of time standing still, of the import of the decision lingering, its weight being felt on the shoulders and in the balls of the feet.
But it was hard too not to think back to the day in Ian Wilkinson’s church when Patterson invited her in-laws to lunch, to them sitting at her table less than a fortnight later, and saying grace.
To the individual beef wellingtons in front of them, her own plate a different colour to theirs. To her sitting with them, watching them eat what she hoped would be their last meals.
And then the frantic search for answers when they fell unwell, and Patterson appearing dumbfounded, denying she had foraged, suggesting Asian grocers in far-flung suburbs as the source of the mushrooms, her lies mounting as her victims slipped ever closer to death.
As she stared blankly at the camera in front of her, there was no sense of how Patterson felt. She maintains the beef wellingtons were accidentally laced with death cap mushrooms, that she too fell sick after eating them, that her lies after the lunch were caused by panic.
Patterson may see the inside of a court room again – she has 28 days to seek leave to appeal to the high court.
Should fresh and compelling evidence emerge – a high bar rarely cleared – she could also seek a fresh court of appeal hearing.
Even should she do so, there remains little prospect that a question at the heart of the case will ever be resolved.
It is a question that has not been answered by the millions of words spoken and written and broadcast about murders covered perhaps more ghoulishly than any other in Australian history.
That question is why Erin Patterson murdered people who loved her and showed her kindness, who loved her children, who she invited into her home and looked in the eye as they ate the meal that killed them.
When McLeish finished speaking and the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, turned her back on the window and that brilliant blue, and walked off-screen.

Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3 billion security breach

Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3 billion security breach
Oct 29 - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said a security breach had resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact that analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist ever and might make investors rethink the risks of owning digital assets.
Binance said it had worked with partners to freeze the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover "all hacking losses".
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday.
Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.
The incident could be the world's biggest crypto heist, according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts.
"It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic OTC business.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report.
"User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement. "As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners."
BINANCE HAS SECURE ASSET FUND
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.
"It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.
"My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.
INCIDENT ADDS TO STRING OF CRYPTO THEFTS
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance by an unknown actor.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.
Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.
In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders. REUTERS

Sustainable Makeup Entrepreneur Laney Crowell on Making Small Starts Toward Big Change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:09:42 UTC
14:09:42 KST

As the CEO and first-time female founder of Saie, one of the fastest growing beauty brands, Laney Crowell has shown how to build a business with social impact and purpose. Saie bridges a gap between high performance makeup formulas, non-toxic natural ingredients, and sustainable business practices. What started as a wellness blog that hosted conversations around clean beauty alternatives has turned into a viral business. On Thursday night in New York, Crowell, a 2025 TIME100 Next Honoree, received TIME’s 2026 Earth Award.
The award was presented by fashion designer and 2024 TIME Earth Award Honoree Gabriela Hearst.
Past recipients of TIME Earth Awards include marine biologist Ayana Elizabeth Johnson, former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, former U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry, U.N. Secretary General António Guterres, and actor and activist Jane Fonda.
Saie, beyond gaining cult popularity and surpassing $100 million in product sales, has implemented many climate commitments into its business, including plastic reduction and responsibly sourced packaging.
In her acceptance speech for the honor, Crowell stressed the importance of taking action. “I’m an entrepreneur. And entrepreneurs have a particular kind of superpower: we can take a teeny-tiny idea, believe it becomes something, and move it forward, until it’s bigger than we ever imagined,” she said. “We built Saie around that belief, and it has grown into a global powerhouse. But my instinct to take action didn’t start in beauty—and it doesn’t end there.”
She recalls picking up litter on trails when, as a child, she went hiking with her family. Now she’s taking those small lessons on leaving places better than she found them and applying them to making a difference in the massive beauty industry, which she said creates an estimated 120 billion units of plastic packaging waste every year.
Since Saie started in 2019, Crowell’s company has committed one percent of sales to environmental causes and partnered with rePurpose Global to collect twice as much plastic as they produce. Over five years, Crowell said Saie has recovered 200,000 pounds of waste.
While her contributions sometimes seemed small in the face of the staggering amount of new waste generated daily, Crowell realized that she didn’t have to do this alone. In 2025, Saie launched Planet Beautiful with Sephora and rePurpose Global, funding the recovery of more than 1 million pounds of plastic waste from nature in its first year. The number of brands that are joining have only been growing, she says, turning into greater amounts of waste collected.
“In climate, we talk a lot about the enormity of the problem—and we should. But we also need to talk about the power of beginning. That is how individual action becomes a collective movement,” Crowell said. “My goal is for Saie to help recover 100 million pounds of plastic waste from nature. And I hope that one day soon, even that number feels small.”
The TIME100 Next Gala was presented by Rolex, Toyota, American Airlines, Danantara, Project Management Institute, and Target.

Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
Oct 30 - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations."
Among the comments that have drawn US officials' attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
EUROPE SHOULD AVOID "POKING" RUSSIA
The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.
One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was "cornered like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a "rat in a corner" in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
"We are helping you. The Americans are there," said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon's recent private messaging. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise."
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE'S RESOLVE
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon's advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO's mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.
The Pentagon messages to NATO officials come at a fraught time for European security.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin's continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington's force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in America's troop presence on the continent.
US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia. REUTERS

Crypto platform Binance confirms major hack with more than $2.5bn frozen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:05:50 UTC
14:05:50 KST

Cryptocurrency platform Binance said on Thursday it had fallen victim to a major hack that hit around $6.3 billion (€5.5bn) in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft.
The company - the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes - posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses".
Binance later said on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3bn (€5.5bn)".
"We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~ $3bn (€2.6bn) frozen on-chain so far," it added.
That would be more than four times the amount involved in what had been the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5bn (€1.3bn) taken in February 2025 from the Bybit platform.
The Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said on Thursday it had "high confidence" that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing "robust on and off-chain intelligence".
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group - which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview", a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Fund freeze
At about 0030 GMT (0230 CEST) on Friday, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement".
"This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company said.
The company's statement on X said an initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer", allowing the unauthorised party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," Binance said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether - a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT - said his firm had frozen about $1.6bn (€1.4bn) "related to a potential Binance exchange hack".
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800m (€696m) in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins", or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Crypto prices tumble
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, with the exception of stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
At about 0400 GMT (0600 CEST), bitcoin and Ethereum were down 0.8%, recovering after plunges of nearly 5% and nearly 6%, respectively. BNB, Binance's native cryptocurrency, was up 2.7% after tumbling nearly 10%.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express concerns that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

What Women in Indonesia and Malaysia Want From Research on Climate and Health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:05:00 UTC
14:05:00 KST

Women are 14 times more likely to die than men during a climate and extreme weather event. Their limited mobility, access to information and decision-making, and limited access to healthcare and services are to blame. On closer inspection, studies show that during a disaster or an extreme climate event, women face surging rates of gender-based violence, high psychological distress, sexual and reproductive health issues (including maternal mortality), pregnancy complications, high exposure to and risk of death from vector-borne diseases, particularly among pregnant women, and compromised menstrual and sexual health.
These impacts are particularly severe in low-and-middle income countries, where the climate crisis intersects with low resource health systems and other external factors (e.g., humanitarian crises, poverty). Across Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia and Malaysia, women are living through the realities of climate change every day. For example, in Indonesia, unsafe water sources, especially in rural and hazardous coastal areas, are linked to a larger share of deaths among women (29 percent) compared to men (25 percent). Yet despite being among those most affected by climate-related health risks, women remain underrepresented in the research and policy processes that shape responses to these challenges.
Our studies conducted with women in Indonesia and Malaysia offer a different perspective. Rather than asking what researchers or policymakers believe should be prioritized, the research explored which climate and health issues matter most to women themselves and how they would like to be involved in future climate-health research. To explore this question more deeply, we added an intersectional lens by speaking with Indigenous women (Orang Asal) in Malaysia and Indonesia, women experiencing or caring for people with disabilities, religious minority women, low-income women, and outdoor working women, etc. The findings reveal both a distinct set of priorities and a strong willingness among women to contribute beyond their role as research participants.
Women involved in our research consistently described climate change through its effects and its everyday impact on health, caregiving, food, water, livelihoods, and community wellbeing. Their concerns were rooted in everyday experience rather than abstract or grand environmental concepts.
Many participants highlighted their responsibilities for securing food and water, supporting unwell family members, juggling childcare and elderly care during climate-related disasters, and helping households recover after climate-related events. These roles often place women at the center of climate-related health impacts.
The research also found that these experiences are shaped by broader social inequalities and gender biases. Patriarchal norms restrict decision-making and prescribe household expectations and caregiving responsibilities, creating unequal recognition and access to resources that influence both women’s vulnerability to climate-related health risks and their opportunities to participate in decision-making processes.
Women Identified Different Climate-Health Priorities
In Indonesia, women ranked air pollution as their top priority followed by water and food security and environmental degradation. Respondents highlighted these issues well before the forest and peatland fires that affected almost the entire Indonesian archipelago — with haze even spreading to Malaysia — toward the end of 2026. This indicates that these priorities are not merely temporary or seasonal concerns, but rather the result of the long-standing experiences of Indonesian women. Participants expressed concerns about respiratory illness, food affordability, water contamination, industrial pollution, and the loss of ecosystems that support health and well-being. Female taxi (Grab) drivers described how the environment affects their health.
In Malaysia, women ranked extreme heat as their top priority, followed by severe weather events and air pollution. Women reported concerns about heat stress, dehydration, impacts on work and caregiving responsibilities, flooding, storms, impacts on their menstrual health and hygiene, other reproductive and sexual health complications, disrupted livelihoods, and mental health effects associated with climate-related events. Indigenous women, especially, described food and water security as a concern.
These findings show that climate-health priorities vary across Southeast Asia. Women’s concerns reflected local environmental conditions, household responsibilities, and their lived experiences across diverse social and geographical contexts.
The research further highlighted how climate-health risks affect women differently across the life course, affecting adolescent girls and women of reproductive age, women experiencing menopause, and older women.
Caregiving emerged as a particularly important lens for understanding climate impacts. Their experiences suggest that climate-health policies must consider not only individual health outcomes but also the broader caregiving responsibilities that shape women’s lives.
The studies also examined how women perceived their potential role in climate and health research. Women in our study believed they could play important roles across the research cycle. These included helping to formulate research questions, validating methodologies, collecting data, interpreting findings, communicating research outputs, engaging policymakers, and contributing to community outreach and capacity-building activities.
Many participants regarded lived experience, local knowledge, and community networks as important forms of expertise. Indigenous women highlighted their ability to identify cultural inaccuracies and provide insights into environmental change that might otherwise be overlooked. Other participants emphasized their understanding and their role in collective climate action, addressing community health challenges, gender-based violence, and decision-making about household realities and local priorities as valuable contributions to future research.
The findings suggest that women’s knowledge and perspectives can strengthen the relevance and contextual grounding of climate-health research and policy action.
Participants consistently emphasized the importance of safe, supportive environments. Women preferred women-only spaces where they could speak openly, with the option to bring children if needed, flexible scheduling, and research activities accessible within local communities.
Caregiving responsibilities emerged as a major challenge. Some women reported needing permission from husbands or male family members to participate in activities outside the home, while others highlighted concerns about conflict or gender-based violence if they acted independently. These barriers were particularly evident in settings where traditional gender norms remain influential.
The findings indicate that meaningful involvement requires more than an invitation to participate. It requires attention to the social, cultural, and practical realities that shape women’s lives and opportunities.
Trust Matters
Across both countries, trust emerged as a key factor shaping participation. Participants emphasized the importance of working through trusted intermediaries, including religious leaders, village chiefs, community organizations, teachers, and local coordinators. These individuals were seen as vital bridges between researchers and communities.
Women also highlighted the value of relationship-building activities, such as sharing meals, spending time in communities, and creating informal opportunities for discussion. Many participants felt that trust must be established before meaningful participation and dialogue can occur.
The findings from Indonesia and Malaysia point to an important opportunity for researchers, funders, and policymakers.
Women identified priorities that may not always receive sufficient attention in climate-health planning, including air pollution, extreme heat, food and water security, environmental degradation, caregiving burdens, and community resilience.
They also demonstrated a willingness to contribute to climate-health research when appropriate support systems are in place such as childcare, women only safe spaces. Participants highlighted the value of local knowledge, lived experience, cultural understanding, and community networks as resources for future research and policy development.
As climate change intensifies across Southeast Asia, ensuring that women’s perspectives inform research agendas and policy discussions is not simply a matter of representation. Our work suggests that women offer valuable insights into the health consequences of climate change and the practical realities of adaptation within households and communities.
Researchers, funders, and policymakers need to prepare to create the conditions that let those perspectives shape future climate and health research and action.
The authors wish to acknowledge the women and NGOs from Indonesia and Malaysia who contributed to our workshops: the Monash Climate Communication Research Hub team members Dr. Azliyana Azhari (based in Malaysia), Dessy Rosalina (based in Indonesia), Savyna Selvarajan (based in Malaysia), and Nadira Chairani (based in Indonesia). Finally, we wish to thank the WHO Climate and Ethics team.

The White House Farm massacre phone calls: could a single disputed digit set Jeremy Bamber free?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

On 7 August 1985, five people were found dead at White House Farm in Essex, England: 28-year-old Sheila Caffell (known to her family as Bambi); her six-year-old twin sons, Daniel and Nicholas; and her 61-year-old adoptive parents, June and Nevill Bamber. All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s 24-year-old brother, Jeremy Bamber, who was also adopted, had called to alert Essex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – and had been outside with the police for four hours before the bodies were discovered. Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised with schizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chin and a bloodied Bible by her side.
The case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later, Bamber was arrested after relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him; his former girlfriend Julie Mugford then told police he had made a confession to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s convictions. It was later discovered that Mugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamber was convicted. Essex police and crown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her for burglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness” against Bamber.
Bamber was found guilty of the murders and has now been in prison for 41 years, but questions have always been asked about the safety of his conviction. These have grown recently. The proper body to examine these is the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), but it has already taken the CCRC four years to consider less than half the evidence that Bamber has submitted to them. In July 2025, it concluded that the first four of 10 points did not meet the high evidentiary threshold needed to refer the case back to the court of appeal.
In the third piece in our series considering discrete pieces of evidence, we analyse discrepancies in timelines recorded by Essex police that could prove Bamber’s innocence.
“Imagine how stupid I’d have to be to put myself in the frame for murdering my family by telling the police I’d received a phone call when I hadn’t,” Jeremy Bamber says. “Like most people, I assumed the police would have been able to trace the call. If it turned out Dad hadn’t called me, I’d have basically been handing myself in.”
Bamber is writing to me from Wakefield prison. For the past 41 years, he has been locked up for the murder of five members of his family, while always protesting his innocence.
In his letter, he is referring to a phone call he made to Essex police from his cottage in the middle of the night on 7 August 1985. Bamber, now 65, told the police his father, Nevill, had just called him to say Bamber’s sister, Sheila Caffell, had “gone crazy” at the family home, White House Farm, and got hold of one of Nevill’s guns. Bamber said the line had then gone dead. His call to Essex police has never been disputed. What has been disputed is his claim that Nevill called him.
At Bamber’s trial, the prosecution claimed he had made up the call to provide himself with a false alibi. They argued that he had killed the five members of his family at White House Farm between 12am and 3am, before cycling back to his cottage and calling the police himself.
This is a story about telephone calls, technology and timings. It is also a story about a single disputed digit in police logs, which could prove Bamber’s innocence. A digit that, at the time of the trial in 1986, neither the jury nor Bamber’s defence team could possibly have understood was so significant. It was only 25 years later, when 347,000 documents relating to the case were released, that its importance became clear.
The digit relates to the time Bamber called the police. At trial, there was confusion about whether it was 3.26am or 3.36am. The presiding judge, Sir Maurice Drake, told the jury to accept a timing of 3.26am. But a series of police logs and statements that were not disclosed at trial suggest Bamber made the call at 3.36am.
It appeared to be an obscure time-keeping argument in court, of little real significance. But it seems there is evidence that the jury was misled and that the differing times in fact refer to two different calls – the first made by Nevill and the second by Jeremy Bamber. And if Nevill did call the police to report his daughter had gone “berserk” with a gun, his son should not be in prison.
The trial
Chelmsford crown court, October 1986. PC Michael James West, who took Bamber’s call at Chelmsford police station in the early hours of 7 August 1985, takes the stand to give evidence for the prosecution. He explains that he works in the control room, a radio and telephone hub for the Chelmsford division, where the unit’s calls are received and officers are allocated their tasks. PC West says he filled out an event log, called a C1, as the conversation took place with Bamber, and that the practice is to log the time at the beginning of the conversation. Surprisingly, that C1 call log is not available to the jury. West tells Anthony Arlidge, the QC for the prosecution, that he recorded the time of 3.36am using the digital clock on the wall in the control room.
Arlidge doesn’t mention the time again. It is only when Geoffrey Rivlin, counsel for the defence, cross-examines West that he is challenged about the purported inconsistencies in his record-keeping.
In his first statement, made two days after the murder, West said he received the call from Jeremy Bamber at 3.26am. In a more detailed statement a month later, the time had changed to 3.36am. Rivlin suggested in court that West had got the time wrong when he changed it and that the call was made, as he had said in his first statement, at 3.26am.
Rivlin: I would like to ask you about times first, if I may. The time you have recorded was 03.36.
West: That is correct.
Rivlin: Is it right that you may have misread the clock and the time may have been 03.26?
West: I was informed I actually spoke to the information room at a time prior to the one that I have recorded so I can only assume that I have wrote – I actually recorded the wrong time, as it were.
But then West, it seems, becomes defensive. He is reluctant to say he made a mistake or that the clock was inaccurate.
Rivlin: The situation is, you looked at the clock and recorded 03.36. You were told subsequently that was almost certainly wrong and you said you may have misread the clock.
West: Well, there is a dispute over the times. I don’t know whose time is right and whose time is wrong.
Rivlin: Let me ask you this question. As regards the clock in the control room at the police station, is that accurate?
West:. Yes, it is.
Rivlin: Are you sure about that?
West: It has on occasion been inaccurate, but on very few occasions.
Rivlin: Would you agree with this, that the control room wall clock rarely shows an accurate time?
West: I would have to disagree with that.
Rivlin: You disagree?
West: Yes.
Rivlin: At all events, perhaps we need take it no further than this, that you did subsequently agree you may have misread the clock?
West: It is possible, although certainly there is a variance in times, yes.
This exchange must have been baffling for the jury. West appeared unwilling to concede that he got the time wrong. Rivlin seemed to suggest the difference between 3.26am and 3.36am was highly significant, but never explained why. He was determined that 3.26am should be recognised as the correct time, but the jury was given no explanation for his insistence.
The reason Rivlin was adamant that the call was made at 3.26am is simply because he thought it looked better for the man he was defending. Bamber had said he received the call from his father at about 3.15am, then rang his girlfriend, Julie Mugford, before calling the police. What kind of man waits 20 minutes and speaks to his girlfriend before contacting the police in such an emergency? Ten minutes, Rivlin thought, would seem more acceptable to a jury.
But Bamber says that is looking at it with the benefit of hindsight: “The last thing I thought when Dad called me was that this was going to end up with my whole family killed.” There had been previous incidents with Caffell, who had a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder and had been hospitalised after a psychotic episode five months before the murders. But none had ended in disaster.
The evening before the killings, Bamber had been at White House Farm and had taken out his father’s .22 rifle, to try to shoot rabbits. When he returned to the farmhouse, he had removed the magazine and the bullet in the breech of the rifle and left those items, and the gun itself, on a bench in the annexe of his parents’ kitchen.
He didn’t fear for the worst when he got the phone call from Nevill, he tells me, because he knew the gun was unloaded. “I assumed my dad, who was 6ft 4in and a strong man, would take the gun off Sheila and that she would calm down.”
As for waiting 20 minutes before calling the police, Bamber has always claimed his father was cut off in the middle of their conversation and that he tried a number of times to call him back, but kept getting the engaged tone. He says he then called Mugford at 3.30am and asked her what she thought he should do. Mugford – who told police a month after the murders, just after Bamber ended their relationship, that he had confessed the killings to her – advised him to “go back to bed”.
He ignored her and at 3.36am, he says, he called the police. “If I’d made up the call from Dad, why on earth would I have said I took 20 minutes to call the police? I would have said I called the police immediately.” Bamber is telling me this in letters sent a few months ago, before the prison banned him from discussing his case with journalists.
But the 3.26am timing of the call appeared to be supported by a rolling log made by a civilian phone operator, Malcolm Bonnett. He was situated at Essex police HQ, a building roughly a mile away from Chelmsford police station, where West was stationed.
Bonnett’s job was to log radio messages and send help from the police and other emergency services. Emergency 999 calls came in to Bonnett, but he also took phone calls from local police stations and officers such as West.
The Bonnett log was shown to the jury at the trial – exhibit 29. It was presented to the court as his record of a call West made to him about the phone call he had received from a Mr Bamber. The jury was told that the Mr Bamber in question was Jeremy. Bonnett’s rolling log starts with an entry at 3.26am. The subject line for this call is “Daughter gone berserk”. This is the only document the jury were shown in regard to the time of the call. It was never explained why West’s C1 log of the phone call was not included in the bundle given to the jury. They had no idea why West had logged the time as 3.36am or why the confusion in court when it was suggested he had got it wrong.
Something didn’t add up. At the trial, it was unclear whether West or Bonnett actually sent out the police cars. Both appear to claim to have done so. West said he radioed the officers asking them to attend the scene, but Bonnett also said that after receiving the call from West about the incident he sent the first police car, CA7, to White House Farm at 03.35am, followed by another car, CA5, at 03.36am. These timings only made sense if West had taken the call from Bamber at 3.26am.
After West and Bonnett’s evidence, the time of Bamber’s call played no part in the trial until the summing up, in which Drake stated that the clocks in the information room were later checked and found to be correct. He advised the jury to accept the true time of Bamber’s call as 3.26am. “You would, in effect, be giving the defence case the benefit of a doubt, and I will suggest that you may – although it is always a matter for you – work on the timing of 03.26 as the time when the phone call was made to Chelmsford police station, and accept that Police Constable West quite simply made a mistake when reading the clock, or writing down 03.36.”
In fact, though, insisting that the call was made at 3.26am gave Bamber anything but the benefit of the doubt. Instead, it put him in the time frame for the murder, because the chronology now made sense: Bamber called West at 3.26am, and West called local officers, who set off for White House Farm at 3.35am.
After a month-long trial, the jury came back with a 10-2 majority on 28 October 1986. Bamber was convicted of one of the most notorious crimes in British history and sentenced to life with a recommended minimum of 25 years. This was later extended to a whole-life tariff by the then home secretary Douglas Hurd in 1988, although Bamber was not made aware of this until 1994.
Fast-forward 25 years. It’s 2011 and Bamber now spends most of his life in prison searching for exculpatory evidence. There is also a campaign team working on his behalf to try to get his conviction overturned. He belatedly receives 347,000 pages of documents, initially withheld by Essex police, after public interest immunity laws are amended in favour of greater disclosure.
This is when Bamber’s team becomes convinced it has found the smoking gun. Amid the myriad documents is the C1 form that West filled in as he was speaking to Bamber on 7 August 1985. Astonishingly, this log wasn’t even included in the exhibit list, which includes every document that can potentially be shown to the jury. The time recorded on it is 3.36am, as he stated at trial. At the top, it clearly states who has made the call and from what address – Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger. The subject is “Distress call”.
When West’s C1 log is compared with Bonnett’s log, important differences, apart from the times of the call, become obvious. In West’s C1 log of Bamber’s call, it says: “Father phoned (aged 62). Please come over your sister has gone crazy and has the gun. Phone went dead. Sister Sheila Bamber age 27 has history of mental illness.” This is clearly Bamber relating the call from his father – hence the reference to father and sister.
By contrast, the opening of Bonnett’s rolling log, which begins at 3.26am, is told from a wholly different perspective. For a start, it refers to Caffell as “daughter” rather than “sister”. The subject of the log is “Daughter gone berserk” and it says “Daughter Sheila Bamber aged 26 yrs has got hold of one of my guns”. The guns at White House Farm belonged to Nevill. In West’s C1 log it refers to the gun. Both logs get Caffell’s age wrong. Bonnett’s says she is 26, West’s 27. In fact, she had celebrated her 28th birthday a couple of weeks earlier. In West’s log, Bamber has mistakenly added an extra year to his father’s age. In Bonnett’s log, no age is given.
Then there is the different way in which the caller’s name and address is logged. The convention in police logs is to start with the informant’s name and address, because it immediately establishes who is providing the information, and it means they are traceable if contact is lost. Bonnett’s log of West’s call refers to “Mr Bamber, White House Farm, Tollshunt D’Arcy”. West’s log refers to “Mr Bamber, 9 Head Street, Goldhanger”. Next to the address for White House Farm is the phone number. Bonnett’s rolling log doesn’t have a number for the farm till 03.56am, when the police confirm that the phone is off the hook.
In addition, Bonnett’s 3.26am log makes no mention of Caffell’s history of mental health problems, a crucial fact that any officers dispatched to the scene should have been informed of. The differences in perspective and facts between Bonnett’s log and West’s log would surely have been spelled out by Rivlin for the defence if both had been available.
There is a line space in Bonnett’s log after the initial paragraph, and then it states: “Message passed on to CD [Control Chelmsford, the code used to refer to the central radio control room where West was stationed] by the son of Mr Bamber after the phone went dead”. The line space suggests it could be a new entry.
When Bamber’s team came across West’s C1 form, they were convinced that this explained the confusion between 3.26am and 3.36am and why the first police car had been dispatched before Bamber’s call: there had been two distinct calls. They believed that the first section of Bonnett’s log referred to a call from Bamber’s father, Nevill, and that this was the information the police appeared to have responded to. This would finally explain how a car had been sent to White House Farm before West said he took Bamber’s call. And, crucially, it would prove Bamber’s innocence.
“At the trial, I had no idea why they were making such a fuss about whether I’d made my call at 03.26am or 03.36am,” Bamber writes. “It was only when we finally saw the log from West 25 years after I was first jailed that it became obvious there must have been two calls. The language is different, the perspective’s different, the information provided is different. It can only be two different people reporting the same incident as they see it.”
In 2016, a documents expert, Dr Chris Davies, studied the new evidence and concluded that the most likely reason for the inconsistencies was that there were two phone calls. “I consider that this would be my preferred explanation for them,” he said. If Nevill called the police at 3.26am to say his daughter had “gone berserk” and had the gun, it puts Bamber in the clear.
If there was an earlier call from Nevill Bamber, there are various theories about who may have taken it, including Malcolm Bonnett (who died in 2023) and officers who were in the control room with PC West (there were at least two others).
Bamber’s team felt that the 3.26am and 3.36am logs finally enabled them to make sense of a mystery from the original investigation: why had the police devoted so much energy to trying to prove that Bamber could have cycled from White House Farm back home to Goldhanger in 10 minutes, before finally concluding that it was impossible? This early police theory appears to have allowed for two calls – one from White House Farm at 3.26am and the other from Goldhanger at 3.36am, both made by Bamber.
Fifteen years on from the disclosure of West’s C1 log, Bamber’s team are still scouring the 347,000 documents that were released to them. In 2020, they came across “pocket book no.49”, belonging to DC Stephen Myall, one of the three officers originally radioed, alongside PS Bews and PC Saxby, asking them to attend the incident at 3.30am, six minutes before West stated on his C1 log that he received the call from Bamber. At the time, they were on an undercover foot patrol of an industrial estate after a spate of burglaries.
In his pocketbook, Myall wrote that he, Bews and Saxby immediately returned to Witham police station when, at “03.37am approx”, they received a phone call from West about the incident at White House Farm. “The Officer (PC West) at CD Control was on the phone and told us that he was relating information to us and still had the informant (Jeremy Bamber) on the other telephone.” Myall wrote that Bamber had told West that his father had said “words to the effect of ‘Come quick, your sister’s gone berserk. She’s got a gun’. The telephone had then gone dead.”
Bamber’s team believes it is now clear that Bews, Saxby and Myall were contacted by radio at 03.30am, as a result of a call from Nevill at 03.26am. The police officers were not at Witham police station at that point, but immediately returned from the nearby industrial estate to collect the police car, which they hadn’t taken with them on the undercover job. West then contacted Witham police station, by telephone, at 3.37am, having spoken to Bamber for a minute, from 03.36am.
The CCRC, the body that investigates alleged miscarriages of justice, has examined Bamber’s convictions three times. In 2002, it sent the case back to the court of appeal, but the judges concluded: “The more we examined the detail of the case, the more likely we thought it to be that the jury were right.”
In 2011, the CCRC refused to refer the case, stating that the evidence did not raise a real possibility that the court would find Bamber’s convictions unsafe. In 2021, his legal team made a new submission, consisting of 10 points. The CCRC has been widely criticised in recent years for its tardiness and its poor referral rate. In 2024/25, only 2% of cases – 31 out of 1,541 applications – were referred back to the court of appeal. (This rate has improved considerably since Dame Vera Baird became interim chair in June 2025.) By July 2025, the CCRC had examined four of the 10 points in Bamber’s submission and declared that, on the basis of these four points, it would not be referring the case back, although it would continue to explore the remaining six points.
One of the four points that was dismissed was the discrepancy between 3.26am and 3.36am being recorded as the time of Bamber’s call to the police. The CCRC remains adamant that the different timings are a result of police error and that there was only one call, from Bamber, at 3.26am. This is despite the C1 log from West stating it was at 3.36am and despite Myall’s record stating that West had Bamber on the phone at 3.37am.
The CCRC also claims that the issue of the call timings “had been dealt with at trial”. This is plain wrong. At trial, and at his 2002 appeal, Bamber’s team had no idea that there were two logs suggesting two calls to police about the same incident.
Since the 2021 submission to the CCRC, more valuable evidence has been uncovered. After the trial, Drake ordered the Dickinson review, an internal inquiry by Essex police into what the Times called the “blunders, omissions and ineptitude” of the force’s early investigation into the murders. The review would examine, for example, why the crime scene was grossly contaminated; the destruction and mismanagement of vital evidence; and the timeline and call-log inconsistencies.
The findings of the inquiry have never been made fully public. However, some documents from the review were released to Bamber’s lawyers in 2011 after a legal challenge. His defence team only recently discovered that the Dickinson review supports the 3.36am timing of Bamber’s call in its timeline of events on the day. It states that Bamber called West at 3.36am and, at 3.37am, “PS Bews, PC Myall & Saxby [were] at Witham. Receive telephone message from PC West. Despatched to White House Farm.” All these references are consistent with the first call to the police having been made by Nevill at 3.26am, officers being asked to attend White House Farm, then West taking a second call from Bamber at 3.36am.
Today, West works for the Masons. I contact him to suggest that his original log, which stated that Bamber called the police at 3.36am, was in fact accurate and consistent with the statements provided by other officers. He tells me he cannot recall the details, 41 years on, without seeing the specific documents and suggests that we meet face to face.
After this conversation, West does not respond to my calls. I text him with an explanation of why I believe his initial record of 3.36am was correct and suggest that a separate call may have been made at 3.26am. But he is having none of it: “Simon, I have nothing to add to anything that has been said and absolutely no comment on any of your rather ridiculous postulations. Jeremy Bamber was found guilty and remains a convicted felon. No one seems to ask: ‘What if that was the correct decision?’”
Meanwhile, Bamber’s team continue to try to piece together the missing pieces of the jigsaw. A few months ago, they re-examined PC West’s trial transcript and came across an astonishing exchange between him and defence council Geoffrey Rivlin.
Rivlin: You made it clear to him [Bamber] that police officers would be sent to the house.
West: Police officers had already been sent when I spoke to him, yes.
Here, PC West states that police officers had already been sent when he was speaking to Bamber. But if the police only received one call alerting them to the incident and the time of it was 3.26am, as the CCRC and Essex Police now insist, that would mean the first car had left before then. Yet the earliest mention of a radio call to officers is 03.30am and officers leaving is 03.35am. On the other hand if we stick with the 03.36am timing on West’s log, it only makes sense if there had been an earlier call because of the radio call to local officers at 03.30am and the leaving time of 03.35am.
This was the closest the jury ever came to hearing that the police appeared to have received two different calls about the incident. Unfortunately, neither the defence nor the jury picked up on West’s answer that officers had already been sent to White House Farm when he spoke to Jeremy Bamber.
When asked to comment about the failure to disclose evidence and inconsistencies in officers’ logs, a spokesperson for Essex Police said: “In August 1985, the lives of five people, including two children, were needlessly, tragically and callously cut short when they were murdered in their own home by Jeremy Bamber. In the years that followed, this case has been the subject of several appeals and reviews by the court of appeal and the Criminal Cases Review Commission – all of these processes have never found anything other than Bamber is the person responsible for killing his adoptive parents Nevill and June, sister Sheila Caffell and her two sons Nicholas and Daniel.”
A CCRC spokesperson said: “Mr Bamber has made three applications to the CCRC. The first application led to a referral to the Court of Appeal in 2001. His conviction was subsequently upheld. The second application to the CCRC in 2004 did not result in a referral. A third application received in 2021 is currently under review. A provisional decision on part of this latest application was issued to his legal representatives, and they responded to us in January this year. Work now continues to consider additional matters which were raised in Mr Bamber’s application. It would be inappropriate for us to discuss the case or make any further comment while the application is being reviewed.”
Those convinced of Bamber’s guilt maintain that Nevill Bamber’s calls to his son and the police never happened. Which takes us back to the first statements Bamber made when he was arrested. At the end of an aggressive 11-hour interrogation by Essex Police on 10 September 1985, Bamber is getting frustrated with all the questioning about the phone call he claims to have received from his father. He suggests there is one easy way of settling the issue. Get hold of British Telecom’s records. Bamber is apparently convinced this will provide him with an alibi and prove that he is telling the truth. If his father never called him, this is a kamikaze defence. All Essex Police need do is check BT’s records, and if there isn’t a call from White House Farm, he has implicated himself.
Bamber: Telecom must be able to tell you the times of phone calls on my parents’ phone.
Officer: What d’you mean by that?
Bamber: It would be proof that I received a phone call from my father.
Officer: If I tell you that Telecom can’t give such details then your theory can’t be checked.
Bamber: I thought Telecom could.
But it couldn’t. Or at least that’s what he was told. Despite an extensive advertising campaign in Essex stating that phone records were being digitised at the time, Essex Police said that calls in the area could not yet be itemised and bills still relied on an anonymised meter system. Years later, documents emerged showing that Telecom did indeed have itemised bills of earlier calls made from Bamber’s home phone number, though these were long-distance calls.
One aspect of the Bamber case that must have shocked the judge was how much evidence was destroyed on the day of the murders. At the time, the police believed it to be an open-and-shut murder-suicide. But that can never excuse the destruction of bloodied mattresses and bed linen.
However, in 1996, 11 years after the murders, an even more shocking obliteration of evidence took place. Although it was known that Bamber was preparing an appeal for the Home Office (which was subsequently inherited by the newly formed CCRC, in 1997), Essex police unilaterally destroyed vital evidence. Among the list of exhibits that were destroyed are bullets, blood samples and swabs, all of which may have provided exculpatory evidence for Bamber as DNA testing became ever more sophisticated. It was particularly alarming that Essex Police destroyed Sheila Caffell’s heavily bloodstained night dress, which may have shown her to have been in contact with the other victims, who were also very bloodied.
As so often in Bamber’s case, the document listing the evidentiary material and whether it was to be filed or destroyed is incomplete. Here it starts at number 167 and finishes at 661. At numbers 598 and 599, it says “British Telecom extract of calls”, citing the telephone numbers for Bamber’s home and White House Farm. By the side of both entries, it says “Destroy”.
