Operation Rummy: Franco-British Nuclear Cooperation Strengthens European Deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Operation Rummy: Franco-British Nuclear Cooperation Strengthens European Deterrence
Operation Rummy, the first joint Franco-British nuclear air exercise, deepens bilateral deterrence and offers a template for wider European nuclear cooperation.
On 20–21 October, the Royal Air Force and France’s Strategic Air Forces (Forces aériennes stratégiques, or FAS) conducted a joint nuclear exercise, marking a noteworthy advance in Franco-British cooperation on nuclear deterrence. The mission – dubbed Operation Rummy – saw British Eurofighter Typhoons escort French Rafales from the Saint-Dizier airbase in northeastern France to the Mediterranean Sea for a simulated long-range nuclear strike mission. The exercise was a step forward in the operationalisation of the 2025 Northwood Declaration, under which France and the UK committed to closer nuclear cooperation and coordination. It has also had the benefit of allowing the UK and France to signal their respective and joint commitments to European nuclear deterrence more broadly – which has thus far posed some challenges. The next step will be figuring out how to bring the various nuclear cooperation efforts underway in Europe together, so as to maximise their effectiveness and clarity.
Benefits to Bilateral Nuclear Cooperation
Operation Rummy follows earlier attendance by British officials at France’s Operation Poker nuclear exercise in December 2025. The active participation of British aircraft this time around is a valuable – and much awaited among the expert community – demonstration of the French and British intent to use the Northwood Declaration for meaningful engagement, not just political signalling.
The joint exercise reinforces a sense of shared British and French threat perception and signals – to adversaries as well as allies – a progressively advanced level of strategic and operational coordination on nuclear matters between the two countries. In a real-world scenario, escorting a French nuclear strike would implicate the UK as a key enabler for the attack, thereby making it a target for retaliation. By playing out such a contribution in training, London has therefore demonstrated an ability – as well as a potential willingness – to serve in such an enabler role and to bear the associated risks. In fact, British Typhoons could make an important contribution to a French nuclear operation in what the French call an épaulement (conventional support) role, given their particular suitability to Defensive Counter Air operations.
Considering that France holds sacred the independence and self-sufficiency of its nuclear deterrent, it remains unclear to what extent the FAS would be willing to rely on foreign enablers for a real-world nuclear mission, or just how far Paris would be willing to take cooperation in practice. However, Operation Rummy is an encouraging indicator of a broader willingness in both Paris and London to think ambitiously about possible avenues for a further expansion of Franco-British nuclear collaboration and cooperation. This could – in theory – take a variety of forms, including more complex joint exercises or even eventual joint nuclear planning and targeting (though the latter remains a remote prospect for the time being).
A desire to avoid the perception that forward deterrence might compete with US extended deterrence by replicating NATO-style nuclear coordination outside of NATO structures will also limit France’s ability to bring the various bilateral conversations together, limiting the effectiveness and ambitions of the initiative
For the UK, closer engagement between the RAF and the FAS also presents valuable learning opportunities as the RAF gets ready to return to a nuclear role with NATO’s DCA (dual-capable aircraft) mission. Unlike the FAS – which carry sovereign French nuclear weapons – the RAF would be delivering American B61 bombs as part of a wider NATO mission, commanded by SACEUR (Supreme Allied Commander Europe). As such, the two air forces’ nuclear roles will be very different. Nevertheless, there is room for meaningful exchange on a range of matters, including effective force management to account for both conventional and nuclear mission requirements, as well as considerations relating to personnel training and broader cultural aspects necessary for effective nuclear mission delivery. Should the UK decide to eventually consider a return to a sovereign air-launched capability (for now, still an academic discussion), experience gained through engagement with the FAS will become even more relevant.
The Bigger European Picture
More broadly, Operation Rummy – and any future joint Franco-British nuclear exercises – point to new opportunities for both France and the UK to strengthen their contributions to European nuclear deterrence.
In the last several months, France has held a number of bilateral nuclear steering groups with partners who have joined its ‘forward deterrence’ initiative. The initiative – announced by President Macron in March – is aimed at making more tangible the ‘European dimension’ of France’s ‘vital interests’, which guide the Élysée’s nuclear decision-making. However, thus far, French engagement with allies has largely been limited to bilateral meetings – with the exception of a joint drill flown by the FAS and the German Luftwaffe over Germany in July. Germany was also due to take part in Operation Poker in the autumn, though there has been no public reporting of German involvement in the latest iteration of the exercise in September.
Certain aspects of French nuclear posture – including the sanctity of the independence of the French nuclear deterrent and France’s absence from NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group (NPG) – complicate efforts at closer practical collaboration with partners. A desire to avoid the perception that forward deterrence might compete with US extended deterrence by replicating NATO-style nuclear coordination outside of NATO structures will also limit France’s ability to bring the various bilateral conversations together, limiting the effectiveness and ambitions of the initiative. These and other challenges risk leaving French forward deterrence partners increasingly frustrated over the lack of meaningful engagement and risk creating a disjointed and confused approach to nuclear deterrence in Europe.
Critically, it also demonstrates the UK’s capacity to engage in meaningful nuclear cooperation – at both a strategic and operational level – with NATO Allies, independent of its relationship with the US
The UK faces a different set of challenges when it comes to clearly and credibly signposting the role of its nuclear deterrent in the security of European allies. First, the UK’s nuclear deterrent is closely linked to that of the US, as the Trident D5 missiles that carry the UK’s nuclear warheads are leased from a shared UK–US pool. This has led to concerns by some over potential vulnerabilities that could arise in the credibility of the UK deterrent should the US’ relationship with the UK or NATO sour further. Furthermore, the UK’s nuclear forces – unlike those of France – are assigned to the defence of NATO, which remains the primary venue for UK engagement with allies on nuclear issues. In a shifting European security environment, that may no longer be sufficient. However, bilateral engagements on nuclear matters outside of the NATO architecture could introduce confusion into alliance signalling or planning, if not managed carefully. Finally, SSBNs (nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines) are simply not as well suited as a fleet of Rafales – or any other aircraft, for that matter – for clear alliance signalling. While the latter can be forward-deployed or engage in highly visible joint exercises, the effectiveness of SSBNs is predicated first and foremost on their stealth, making it somewhat more challenging (though certainly not impossible) to use them for nuclear signalling to allies or adversaries.
Franco-British nuclear cooperation – particularly through joint exercises – presents opportunities for both France and the UK to overcome some of these challenges. For France, Operation Rummy – alongside earlier British attendance at Operation Poker and the joint FAS–Luftwaffe sortie – serves as an example of what is possible with other partners under forward deterrence, and helps demonstrate France’s commitment to meaningfully operationalising the initiative with partners. For the UK, participation in joint nuclear air exercises with France allows it to signal British commitment to European nuclear deterrence more easily than would otherwise be possible with SSBNs. Critically, it also demonstrates the UK’s capacity to engage in meaningful nuclear cooperation – at both a strategic and operational level – with NATO Allies, independent of its relationship with the US. At the same time, the UK is currently uniquely positioned – as a nuclear peer and having flown in a simulated nuclear strike mission with the FAS – to serve as a conduit between French and NATO nuclear planning. France is highly unlikely to join the NPG or to take part in Steadfast Noon (NATO’s nuclear training exercise) anytime soon; however, the UK – and hopefully other allies in the future – can use their experience of flying in French nuclear exercises to inform NATO’s nuclear planning and training, and vice versa.
Next Play
The challenge now will be to maintain momentum when it comes to meaningful nuclear cooperation under the Northwood Declaration and, for France, its forward deterrence initiative. As perhaps the most obvious next step, France could consider involving the RAF in Operation Poker, which would facilitate a more expansive exchange on strategic and operational matters. At the same time, looking for opportunities to get more forward deterrence partners flying with the FAS – initially in conventional, and hopefully eventually in nuclear, training missions – should also be (and likely already is) a priority.
One way to maximise the effectiveness of any future joint training missions would be to conduct these operations on a trilateral, rather than a bilateral, basis – with France, the UK and non-nuclear allies taking part together. This could include, for example, simultaneously involving Germany and the UK in a future iteration of Operation Poker. Such an approach would have the benefit of ensuring greater coherence in efforts to strengthen European nuclear deterrence and in British, French and broader European nuclear signalling, while still remaining conscious of concerns over duplication with NATO nuclear deterrence arrangements. Combining allies’ participation in joint training missions would also allow the leveraging of a more diverse set of capabilities in a single exercise. It would likely also be less resource intensive than a series of bilateral engagements. Aligning the timings of Steadfast Noon with one of these bilateral/trilateral exercises (where allies’ resources allow) with Operation Poker – as has been suggested elsewhere – could further reinforce the ability to coordinate NATO and French nuclear operations, while maintaining the clear independence and self-sufficiency of multiple decision-making centres.
Operation Rummy was a welcome public display of the progress being made behind closed doors on strengthened Franco-British nuclear cooperation. It is also a clear demonstration of how bilateral cooperation between Europe’s two nuclear powers strengthens the credibility of their respective deterrents, as well as of European nuclear deterrence in the round. Finding ways of maintaining momentum on these efforts – and bringing them together, where possible – will be key to making clear both to allies and to adversaries that French and British nuclear commitments to Europe are anything but a bluff.

Samsung's Q3 net profit surges sixfold on booming AI chip demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Samsung's Q3 net profit surges sixfold on booming AI chip demand
South Korean technology giant Samsung Electronics reported a more than sixfold increase in third-quarter net profit, driven by robust demand for semiconductors used in artificial intelligence infrastructure, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Yonhap.
According to the company's regulatory filing released Thursday, net earnings reached 75.13 trillion won (US$56.2 billion) in the July–September period, marking a 514.6% increase from 12.22 trillion won recorded a year earlier.
Samsung's operating profit climbed 783.1% year-on-year to 107.44 trillion won, while consolidated revenue advanced 126.9% to 195.25 trillion won.
The results made Samsung the first technology company worldwide to surpass 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit. The South Korean chipmaker also extended its record-breaking streak, reporting all-time-high quarterly revenue and operating earnings for the fourth consecutive quarter.
The semiconductor division was the main contributor to the company's performance, generating 106.5 trillion won in operating profit, equivalent to approximately 99.1% of Samsung's overall operating earnings.
The company attributed the division's strong results to increased shipments of sixth-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM4) chips and growing demand from AI data centers and server manufacturers.
Samsung, the world's largest memory chip producer, has benefited considerably from expanding global investment in AI infrastructure. The company was also the first in the industry to launch mass production and commercial shipments of HBM4 memory.
Looking ahead, Samsung anticipates continued growth in memory chip demand during the final quarter of 2026, supported by ongoing investment in artificial intelligence technologies.
The company also expects favorable conditions in the semiconductor market to persist into 2027, citing strong AI-related capital expenditure and constraints on chip supply.
However, performance across Samsung's other businesses was less favorable.
Its Device Experience division, which includes smartphones and consumer electronics, recorded an operating loss of 800 billion won, marking a second straight quarter in negative territory.
Despite the loss, the division registered higher sales compared with the previous year, supported partly by the introduction of premium smartphones, including the Galaxy Z Fold8. Rising component prices and difficult market conditions continued to weigh on profitability.
Separately, Samsung announced a quarterly cash dividend of 4,601 won per common and preferred share.
The company estimates that total shareholder returns in 2026 could reach between 90 trillion and 110 trillion won. With approximately 35 trillion won already distributed or committed, an additional 55 trillion to 75 trillion won may be returned through dividends, share repurchases and share cancellations.
Samsung's announcement followed another record-breaking earnings report from domestic rival SK hynix, which unveiled a shareholder return initiative exceeding 100 trillion won for 2026.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Samsung had forecast a nearly 1,800% year-on-year surge in second-quarter operating profit, driven by booming demand for AI memory chips.

DOJ escalates Alaska Senate lawsuit over dueling Sullivan candidacies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:55:09 UTC
08:55:09 KST

The Department of Justice on Thursday escalated its lawsuit targeting potential certification of the result of Alaska's Senate election, which it argues could be tainted by the candidacy of a man with the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The DOJ filed an amended version of its original complaint to add a new legal claim and details from Wednesday's New York Times article detailing alleged efforts by the people in the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola to recruit a retired schoolteacher named Dan J. Sullivan into the race.
The amended complaint in Anchorage federal court suggests that Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee misled Judge Sharon Gleason by saying in recent court filings they lacked knowledge about why the retiree Sullivan entered the race earlier this year.
The amended suit also notes that Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, late Wednesday ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged recruitment of the retired teacher violated criminal or civil laws. Dunleavy cited the Times' report as the reason for that probe.
"The New York Times has reported that Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC were well aware of the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy: they orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected," the DOJ said in its amended complaint.
The DOJ, in a separate filing Thursday, said that the filing of the amended complaint with the new claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution means that motions to dismiss the case by the state, Peltola's campaign, the DSCC and others are now moot. The DOJ cited precedent in the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals for that argument.
Gleason had given the DOJ until 5 p.m. Alaska Time Thursday to respond to the motions to dismiss, which have asked her to toss out the DOJ's original complaint before Election Day, Nov. 3.
The judge has yet to rule whether the dismissal motions are now moot.
Later Thursday, Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher and other state election boards blasted the DOJ in a motion asking Gleason to expedite consideration of a motion to dismiss the amended complaint.
"Rather than filing a substantive opposition to the Division's motion to dismiss, the United States has filed an amended complaint adding a second—but equally meritless— count (relying on the same underlying legal theory) and then opposed the Division's motion on the ground that it has been mooted by the amended complaint," the motion said.
"In the context of these expedited proceedings, the Court should not tolerate this gamesmanship," the motion said.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, in a subsequent motion to dismiss late Thursday, scoffed at the DOJ's new complaint and claim that it misled Gleason.
"In the portion of the proposed answer DOJ cites, Alaskans for Mary and DSCC stated that they did not have knowledge or information sufficient to admit or deny an allegation about Daniel J. Sullivan's mental state — whether he filed to run 'with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality,' " the campaign and DSCC said in the motion.
"The only one who could possibly know Daniel J. Sullivan's true reasons for filing as a candidate is Daniel J. Sullivan, and Alaskans for Mary and DSCC's statement that they could not admit or deny that allegation was entirely proper."
"The Court should dismiss the Amended Complaint, with prejudice, before election
day," the motion said. 
"DOJ's choice to file the Amended Complaint, which adds nothing of substance to the original complaint, is a transparent attempt to keep this case alive for a few more days to cast a pall over the upcoming election and let the federal government continue to interfere in Alaska's elections."
The DOJ's lawsuit, originally filed on Oct. 23, seeks to block the state from immediately certifying any Senate election result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ to file the suit.
The political stakes in the Alaska Senate race are potentially momentous. The winner could determine the power balance in the Senate, where Republicans hold a six-vote majority.
The new DOJ filings came as NBC News reported that the department "has issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests" to Peltola's campaign offices and those of the former schoolteacher Sullivan.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, which have previously denied involvement in the retiree Sullivan's campaign to CNBC, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the amended DOJ suit.
Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on Thursday in response to Dunleavy's announcement, said, "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any politician will keep her away from that fight."
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," the campaign said.
Trump, before flying to South Carolina for a campaign rally Thursday morning, was asked by a reporter whether Senate Republicans should try to block Peltola from taking the seat in January if she wins Tuesday's election.
"Well, you're going to have to see what happens," Trump said.
"It's hard to believe that she can even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run," the president said.
Trump said the retired teacher Sullivan "was just put there as a fraud."
"But people aren't going to know that, so nobody's going to know what to do," Trump said.
Both Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have argued that Trump and other Republicans are being hypocritical in their claims about the Senate race.
"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns — including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," a DSCC spokesperson said Wednesday.
The DSCC pointed to instances of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.
Alaska election officials in a court filing have said the Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
The retired teacher's name on the ballot is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.
Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as "Sullivan, Dan. S." with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.
Alaska election officials said in their court filing that "the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate."

France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:52:30 UTC
08:52:30 KST

France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
Authorities vow firm action against violence as yellow vest and student movements announce widespread demonstrations.
France’s interior minister has announced the deployment of 70,000 police officers across the country in preparation for planned protests on Saturday, coinciding with Halloween.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Thursday that security measures, including the use of armoured vehicles and water cannon introduced last week, will be strengthened.
Nationwide protests over the rising cost of living have rocked France, with some degenerating into large-scale looting and riots.
“The day of October 31 presents a very high risk of public disorder,” Nunez said at a news conference.
About 70,000 police officers and gendarmes will be mobilised, matching the number deployed at last week’s protests, he said, calling the move an “exceptional measure”.
Demonstrations last Saturday drew about 410,000 protesters nationwide, according to the interior ministry, though unions put the figure at roughly double that. The ministry said more than 2,700 people were arrested a week earlier.
Warning on Halloween masking
The “yellow vest” movement and student unions have called for a new day of protests on Saturday.
Nunez warned demonstrators against using Halloween as “a legitimate reason to hide one’s face” to cause disturbances in public areas.
He told reporters demonstrations would be allowed, but “not in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.
The interior minister issued a warning to far-right groups that clashed with left-wing protesters at rallies in about 15 French cities.
“We will tolerate no excesses,” he said, and pledged an “extremely firm” response.
Nunez accused the “ultra-left” movement and some yellow vest activists of circulating messages on social media promoting demonstrations on Halloween evening that called for a “revolution”.
“These gatherings will be banned,” he said.
The yellow vest movement has already announced a “third act” of its protests on Halloween and called for demonstrations outside the National Assembly and all town halls in the country.

Israel election results unaffected by foreign interference probe, committee says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:48:35 UTC
08:48:35 KST

Israel's Central Elections Committee said early Friday that the Shin Bet security agency's investigation into suspected election bribery and foreign interference would not affect the final results of Tuesday's parliamentary election. 
In a recorded statement released overnight, acting committee director general Dean Livne also stressed that the investigation does not concern any particular community and dismissed reports circulated throughout Thursday as entirely unfounded. Livne said the statement was issued with the approval of committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg.
"Yesterday, the head of the Shin Bet presented classified intelligence to the committee chairman, which led to the opening of the investigation," Livne said. "With the chairman's approval, the main points were also presented to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, opposition leader Yair Lapid and Yashar! party chairman Gadi Eisenkot."
Livne emphasized that access to the intelligence was extremely restricted because of its high security classification. "No further details can be disclosed, but reports published throughout the day are entirely unfounded," he said.
"The investigation is taking place alongside the Central Elections Committee's ongoing work and will not affect the final results submitted to the president. Nor does it concern any particular community," Livne added. Once the investigation is completed, its findings will be submitted to Sohlberg, who will assess their scope and implications. The committee will update the public as quickly as possible, subject to the necessary restrictions.
Final election results confirmed
In a separate statement, the Central Elections Committee confirmed the final vote count for Israel's 26th Knesset, as announced earlier Thursday evening. Likud won 27 seats, Yashar! 21, Together 12, the Joint List 11, the Democrats 8, Ra'am 8, Yisrael Beiteinu 7, Otzma Yehudit 7, United Torah Judaism 7, Shas 6 and Religious Zionism 6.
The committee said the final voter turnout was 77.9%, with 5,716,665 votes counted. Of those, 5,690,778 were valid and 25,887 were invalid. The electoral threshold, set at 3.25% of valid votes, was 184,947 votes.
The committee stressed that the results remain subject to minor corrections over the coming days as part of its routine verification process, which includes reexamining a substantial number of polling stations, correcting data entry or transcription errors and reviewing complaints submitted by the public and candidate lists. "Subject to minor corrections, as in every election, these are the results that will be submitted to the president of the State of Israel on Wednesday, November 4," the committee said.
The Shin Bet issued its own statement Thursday concerning the investigation into suspected violations of election integrity, emphasizing that the inquiry was limited in scope and did not implicate any entire community. "An investigation of this kind is focused and limited, and does not cast suspicion on or accuse an entire community that exercised its democratic and legal right to vote," the agency said. "Only those who acted unlawfully will be dealt with."
The controversy began after Sohlberg sent a letter to Shin Bet chief David Zini instructing him to investigate suspicions involving foreign actors. According to reports, the intelligence concerns suspected transfers of money from Qatar, allegations Doha has categorically denied. Turkey has also rejected allegations of involvement.
"The integrity of elections is at the heart of democracy," Sohlberg wrote to Zini. Although he stressed that he could not assess the substance of the allegations, he said their reported connection to foreign actors made a thorough investigation essential. Such an inquiry, he wrote, was necessary to protect the integrity of Knesset elections and prevent unlawful activity intended to undermine democratic institutions or engage in subversion.
In its statement Thursday evening, the Shin Bet clarified that the intelligence underlying the investigation came from information gathered by the agency as part of its legal responsibility to detect foreign influence. It did not originate from any political party or political figure on either side of Israel's political spectrum. The agency also said that, apart from Sohlberg, no one outside the Shin Bet had access to the information before the elections concluded.
The Shin Bet stressed that the investigation was ongoing and cautioned against speculation about the nature of the allegations. "Any statement concerning the content or substance of the suspicions does not reflect the Shin Bet's position and should have been avoided," the agency said. The findings will be presented to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee, who is authorized to make decisions on the matter.
The agency said all relevant information would be submitted to election officials in full, transparently and without interpretation once the investigation was completed. It also confirmed that, at Sohlberg's request and with his approval, Zini had personally briefed Netanyahu, Eisenkot and Lapid over the preceding 24 hours on the main allegations being investigated. The Shin Bet emphasized that it is a state institution whose actions are carried out solely under its legal mandate, with oversight from its professional and legal officials.

SBU detains driver suspected of directing Russian attacks on Kyiv' regions thermal power plants
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
According to the SBU, one of the enemy's main targets was thermal power plants in the Kyiv region that were being brought back online after previous attacks.
"Under the guise of work-related trips, the suspect drove around the perimeters of power plants to assess the current state of energy infrastructure and photographed their exteriors with his phone. He then returned home, compiled the images, pinned their locations on Google Maps and added his own comments before preparing the files to send to his FSB handler," the SBU said.
SBU officers documented the suspect using a truck to scout the progress of restoration work on a power unit at a local thermal power plant. He was detained while preparing a report for the enemy, the agency said.
The investigation found that the driver had come to the attention of Russian intelligence after posting anti-Ukrainian comments in Telegram channels. After being recruited, he communicated with an FSB operative through a specially created chatbot, the SBU said.
According to investigators, he also monitored the locations of repair bases used by Ukraine's Defense Forces.
During searches, officers seized two mobile phones from the man. One of the phones had been damaged in an apparent attempt to destroy evidence of his cooperation with Russia, the SBU said.
SBU investigators notified the suspect that he was charged under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Amazon on Thursday reported that its third-quarter net sales rose 12 percent year on year to 201.94 billion U.S. dollars, driven in part by strong growth in its cloud computing business, while net income declined 2.4 percent.
According to the U.S. e-commerce and technology giant's financial results for the quarter ended Sept. 30, net income fell to 20.69 billion dollars from 21.19 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share decreased to 1.89 dollars from 1.95 dollars.
Amazon attributed the decline in net income primarily to the impact of pretax gains of 9.5 billion dollars in the third quarter of 2025 from its investment in artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic.
Amazon Web Services (AWS), the company's cloud computing division, reported net sales of 45.98 billion dollars, up 39.3 percent year on year, marking its fastest growth in nearly five years. AWS operating income rose 55 percent to 17.77 billion dollars from 11.43 billion dollars a year earlier.
Net sales from advertising services increased 11 percent year on year to 19.64 billion dollars.
The company's free cash flow turned negative in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, recording an outflow of 42.4 billion dollars, compared with an inflow of 14.8 billion dollars a year earlier, primarily reflecting increased investment in AI infrastructure.
Looking ahead, the company expects fourth-quarter net sales to range from 240 billion to 247 billion dollars, representing year-on-year growth of 12 percent to 16 percent. Operating income is projected to reach 28.5 billion to 33.5 billion dollars, up from 25 billion dollars a year earlier. ■

According to the company's financial results for the quarter ended Sept. 26, net income attributable to Intel fell to 3.32 billion dollars from 4.06 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share decreased to 0.6 dollars from 0.9 dollars.
The company's gross margin increased to 43 percent from 38.2 percent a year earlier. On a non-GAAP basis, diluted earnings per share rose to 0.52 dollars from 0.23 dollars.
Revenue from Intel's Data Center and AI segment jumped 78 percent year on year to 7.3 billion dollars, marking the company's strongest data center revenue growth in 15 years.
Revenue from its Client Computing and Physical AI Group declined 5 percent to 8.1 billion dollars, reflecting continued challenges in the personal computer market.
Intel Foundry, the company's semiconductor manufacturing business, reported revenue of 6.7 billion dollars, up 58 percent year on year. The figure includes transactions with other Intel business units.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said demand for the company's central processing units remained robust despite near-term headwinds in the PC industry, adding that increasing supply to meet demand for Xeon server processors was an immediate priority.
Looking ahead, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of between 15 billion and 16 billion dollars. The company forecasts diluted earnings per share attributable to Intel of 0.10 dollars under GAAP and 0.25 dollars on a non-GAAP basis.
Intel also projects a GAAP gross margin of 37.1 percent for the fourth quarter, down from 43 percent in the third quarter. ■

Trump cancels weekend rallies, plans to phone in to other midterm campaign events
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Maryland – US President Donald Trump on Oct 29 cancelled planned weekend campaign stops in Kansas and Iowa, and his allies said he would instead join rallies nationwide by phone after four weeks of travel to boost Republicans’ election chances.
Trump told reporters that he did not “feel like I have to go to Kansas”, a Midwestern state where Senator Roger Marshall, a fellow Republican, is in an unexpectedly competitive race against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton.
“He is doing very well,” Trump said of Marshall. “We are going to have a strong Tuesday night.”
Later on Oct 29, the Republican National Committee said in a statement that it would also cancel a planned rally in Iowa, which is home to several competitive congressional races.
The cancelled in-person rallies were set for Salina, Kansas, on Oct 31, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Nov 1.
Since Oct 1, Trump has hosted 25 rallies in 19 states, often speaking for his party in rural areas of Republican-friendly states.
The Nov 3 midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain their narrow control of the US Senate and House of Representatives.
MAGA, a campaign funding group aligned with Trump, said on Oct 29 that it would host a series of “tele-rallies” with the President in at least 19 states, including Kansas and Iowa, before election day.
Trump is still expected to travel to rallies in several states before the Nov 3 election, including in Florida on Oct 30.
Trump has noted that his recent series of more than hour-long campaign speeches has been challenging. Sounding hoarse in Mississippi on Oct 26, he said: “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”
On Oct 29, after campaigning for Senator Darline Graham in South Carolina, Trump ridiculed a Reuters reporter who asked how he felt after weeks of rallies and whether he was sick of travelling.
“You’ve been following me for two weeks,” Trump said before boarding his motorcade back to the White House. “I feel perfect.” REUTERS

Manosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:30:37 UTC
08:30:37 KST

The manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by the government as a public health issue, in the same way as obesity or smoking, experts have said.
Writing in the Lancet, the authors of a new report argue that a coordinated response is needed, involving governments, schools, health services and community organisations, similar to the public-health response to tobacco use and ultra-processed food.
“Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions, and masculine identity is commodified through products and paid content that normalise and reinforce health-harming and performance-oriented masculinities,” the authors write.
The report defines the manosphere as “a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation”.
It goes on to outline how the manosphere has evolved into a highly lucrative online industry that makes money by promoting “the most extreme expressions of misogyny and aggrieved masculinity”.
Prof Kent Buse, a co-author of the paper and co-founder of the social justice thinktank Global 50/50, said: “This is a business model, not a fringe. Outrage and grievance are good for business, so the system rewards the most extreme content. Expect the playbook that served tobacco so well: blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom. Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it.”
He added: “Boys and men are not the problem. The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”
The authors also point to growing disengagement from education among boys around the world, as well as loneliness, money worries and social exclusion, which can leave young men searching for a sense of belonging. These problems, they say, can make them more vulnerable to online communities that offer simple explanations for their difficulties and often encourage them to blame women and feminism.
Prof Sarah Hawkes, the report’s other author, said: “The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard.
“Those needs are real. A response that only removes the manosphere, without offering something credible in its place, will fail. We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid.”
Mark Brooks, the policy and communications director at the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys, welcomed the report’s position that it was a public health issue and that men, boys, women and girls were all victims of this content.
“Far too often, the manosphere discussion has positioned all men and boys as a problem and not taken into account the broader economic, educational and cultural challenges that drive their engagement,” he said.
“Not all men and boys engage with this content equally. We are currently working on research to identify who is most at risk.”
Jake Richards, minister for men and boys, said: “This report lays bare the impact of toxic online influences and why action is needed now. It’s not just an issue for men and boys – it is a wider societal challenge. As the first minister for men and boys, I’m determined to drive this issue up the national agenda, dismantle the manosphere, and give young men the opportunities and role models they need to thrive.

A Russian Passport Can Reportedly Get You Banned From Claude, Even Abroad
Anthropic’s Claude AI service has begun requiring users to verify their identities and reportedly blocking accounts after they submit Russian passports, including those with active paid subscriptions.
This was reported by The Moscow Times on October 29, citing Russian technology outlet VC.ru and complaints from affected users.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The service reportedly suspends access until users complete know-your-customer (KYC) verification, requiring identification documents and facial recognition. Some accounts have been permanently blocked after verification, and subscription payments have been refunded.
Anthropic conducts identity checks through Persona, a verification platform that requires users to upload a passport or another identification document and complete a facial scan.
One user in the Telegram community, "Sioloshnaia," reported being banned "within a minute" of submitting a Russian international passport. Other users claimed they successfully completed verification using Russian driver's licenses while selecting another country.
One Russian national living in New Zealand on a four-year visa reported losing access to Claude Code after submitting his Russian passport. The account was blocked despite New Zealand being among the countries where Claude officially operates.
The user had renewed his subscription just two days earlier. Another user reported on X that Claude stopped accepting requests after passport verification and that an appeal against the suspension was unsuccessful.
Digital platforms have also become a tool of the war inside Russia itself, where security services have been impersonating the ATESH partisan movement to track down people trying to assist the resistance.
Fake accounts posing as the group have appeared in chat groups of other movements, including Freedom of Russia, urging users to contact an automated bot that mimics the partisans' real handle with a slight misspelling.
The campaign follows an October 21 sabotage operation against military communications around IXcellerate, one of Moscow's largest commercial data centers, allegedly used for air-defense command traffic.

US military movements don't signal decision to strike: Israel prepares, waits on Trump again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:28:07 UTC
08:28:07 KST

Is the United States preparing to resume its war against Iran? When could another attack take place, and what would its objectives be? A series of military movements observed in recent weeks has raised these questions, but there is still no clear indication that President Donald Trump has decided to order renewed strikes. 
Israel's defense establishment is preparing for the possibility of another conflict, both offensively and defensively, while security officials stress that the developments remain preliminary and are intended, at least in part, to give the president military options should he decide to act.
One of the most significant developments involves the deployment of U.S. forces in the Arabian Sea, near Iran's coast. Twelve American destroyers have been operating in the area in recent weeks, up from approximately eight to 10 previously. Some may be involved in the naval blockade, but the increased presence is also being examined in the context of preparations for a possible military campaign. Two U.S. aircraft carriers are also stationed in the region, while a third is expected to complete its deployment near Japan. Washington will then have to decide whether to send it to the Arabian Sea as reinforcements or use it to replace one of the carriers already there.
Is overthrowing Iran's regime back on the table?
Alongside the naval buildup, preliminary indications of increased American air activity have also emerged. According to an analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), aircraft tracking data cautiously suggests that the United States is rebuilding its aerial refueling network in Europe, potentially providing a staging point for moving additional forces into the area covered by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Between Wednesday and Thursday, an American RC-135 reconnaissance aircraft flew from the United States to Britain, while eight C-17 military transport aircraft landed in southern Israel. The assessment is that the aircraft were carrying air defense equipment and logistical supplies, potentially indicating preparations to reinforce defensive systems and offensive capabilities. The IDF has not commented on reports of the landings.
Security officials emphasize that the movements do not necessarily indicate a decision to attack. Trump could still pursue a diplomatic solution, and the scale of the preparations primarily reflects Washington's desire to keep the military option available. "The Americans are preparing options for the president, if and when he decides to launch an attack," a security official said.
The central question is what the objectives of another military campaign would be if one were launched. During Operation Rising Lion, Israel struck Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States joining the campaign toward its conclusion by attacking the Fordow nuclear facility. During Operation Roaring Lion, which lasted 42 days, nuclear targets were largely avoided. Instead, the campaign focused on weapons manufacturing facilities, military and national infrastructure, Iran's navy and missile systems, alongside more limited strikes against symbols of the regime and the Basij paramilitary forces affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Another factor is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's declaration ahead of Israel's elections that he had instructed the country's security agencies to advance a plan to overthrow the Iranian regime in cooperation with Trump. Netanyahu intensified his rhetoric on the issue in the days leading up to the vote and on Election Day itself. The IDF's Military Intelligence Directorate and Israeli Air Force are continuing to update their target lists, divided into categories including infrastructure, nuclear facilities, military buildup and missile capabilities. Any effort to overthrow the Iranian regime would also require a comprehensive operational plan developed by the Mossad intelligence agency in coordination with other Israeli security bodies.
Israeli defense officials are also considering the possibility that Iran could launch an attack of its own, driven by mounting economic distress and fears of another American-Israeli operation after having been caught off guard by major opening strikes on two previous occasions.
"In systems like the American military, preparing the available options takes time," a senior security official explained. "We are talking about weeks, certainly when it comes to a broad military campaign rather than a limited operation, even if it is a short one, as foreign media reports have suggested." The official said it remains difficult to predict Trump's decision. Even if the president authorizes renewed fighting, an attack would not necessarily follow immediately. Israel would prefer a short, intensive campaign, particularly after Operation Roaring Lion stretched to 42 days, considerably longer than initially planned.
Hezbollah prepares for possible confrontation
Military preparations are unfolding alongside diplomatic efforts. According to reports in recent days, U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a figure considered close to Mojtaba Khamenei, to explore the possibility of renewing negotiations between Washington and Tehran. American officials said the initiative was undertaken with Trump's knowledge and at his direction. At the same time, the president continues to threaten a return to military action, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections. The simultaneous diplomatic contacts and military movements leave open the possibility that Washington is seeking to increase pressure on Tehran while preparing for potential military action.
Another concern is Israel's northern front. Israeli defense officials are preparing for the possibility that renewed fighting against Iran could expand into a confrontation with Hezbollah in Lebanon. During the past month, Israeli interceptor missiles have been launched near the Lebanese border. The IDF has not disclosed the targets of those interceptions, but Israeli assessments suggest that at least some may have involved Hezbollah reconnaissance drones attempting to gather intelligence on Israeli troop deployments. Hezbollah has also been moving weapons and preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting with the IDF.
Israel's Northern Command is working to reinforce defensive lines held by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon, establish positions offering greater control through observation and firepower, and prepare plans for capturing additional Hezbollah strongholds.
A renewed conflict could also affect Israel's political situation, with uncertainty continuing over the formation of a governing coalition following the elections. Another war against Iran could reshape the public agenda, alter the balance of power among political parties and place national security and relations with Washington back at the center of political debate. For now, Israel continues updating its military plans while Washington maintains both diplomatic contacts and threats of renewed action. Whether the preparations will lead to another military campaign, and what its objectives might be, remains uncertain.

All Moscow airports shut amid drone attack on Russian capital

Source: Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya); Russian media outlet Astra; Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson to spend rest of life in prison after losing appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:25:26 UTC
08:25:26 KST

in brief
- The Victorian Court of Appeal has resentenced Patterson to life without parole.
- Patterson had already been serving a life sentence for the murders of three family members she poisoned with death cap mushrooms.
Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson will likely die in prison after Victoria's Court of Appeal dismissed her conviction challenge and upheld a prosecution bid to impose a whole-of-life sentence without parole.
Delivering judgment from Melbourne's Supreme Court on Friday morning, justice Stephen McLeish confirmed the jury's guilty verdicts before setting aside the 33-year non-parole period imposed by the trial judge as inadequate for what he termed "shocking criminality".
McLeish said Patterson had calculated murdering all four of her lunch guests for nearly three weeks before the incident and that the sentence should reflect that.
"It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of the applicant's extended family," he said.
"In re-sentencing, it is necessary that the sentence vindicates unequivocally the primary value that our society places on each individual human life."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In its written judgment, the court described the offending as "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and said it "stands to be denounced in the strongest terms".
The court's ruling marks the latest chapter in a case that shocked the nation following a home-cooked family lunch in regional Victoria in July 2023.
Patterson was found guilty last year of murdering her former parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, 66, after deliberately serving them beef Wellington laced with lethal death cap mushrooms at her Leongatha home.
Heather's husband, church pastor Ian Wilkinson, spent nearly two months in hospital with critical organ damage before eventually recovering. Patterson was found guilty of attempted murder alongside the three murder convictions.
Patterson, 52, was not in the courtroom when Friday's judgment was handed down.
She watched via video link from Dame Phyllis Frost Centre in Ravenhall as the bench stripped any prospect of future release, delivering one of the harshest penalties in Victorian legal history.
Defence challenge dismissed
Following a nearly three-month trial, Supreme Court Justice Christopher Beale sentenced Patterson in September 2025 to life imprisonment with a 33-year non-parole period.
However, Patterson's appeal barristers argued that significant issues at trial invalidated her convictions.
Primarily, her defence said the jury was insufficiently sequestered during deliberations, as it emerged that jurors were accommodated in the same hotel as the Crown's primary police investigator and two prosecutors.
However, McLeish dismissed the challenge, noting that the jury keeper had verified there was no communication between the parties.
"As against that assurance, there was only conjecture, guesswork, or surmise," McLeish said, ruling there was "no objective basis for a fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function."
They also argued that the Crown's five-day cross-examination of Patterson was needlessly aggressive and that the prosecution incorrectly changed its case by suggesting a fresh motive during closing remarks.
Whole-of-life sentence imposed
At the same time, chief crown prosecutor Brendan Kissane argued that the court should impose a harsher sentence and strip Patterson of her right to parole.
The prosecution maintained that the killings involved calculated premeditation, exacerbated by her failure to tell medical staff about the death caps her victims had consumed while doctors were still trying to save them.
McLeish agreed with the prosecution's argument, saying that a 33-year minimum term did not capture the calculating nature of her crimes.
"The applicant's intent to murder all four victims was sustained for nearly three weeks, from when she invited them to lunch, through to preparing and serving the poisonous meal, and then throughout the protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted," McLeish said.
The bench highlighted an "elaborate series of deceptions", including Patterson's fabricated cancer claims used to explain why her children were absent from the lunch, persistent lies about where the mushrooms came from, and the deliberate destruction of evidence.
"This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms," McLeish said.
"In all the circumstances, after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period."
Active suppression orders remain strictly enforced for the media and the public.
Patterson's children and their schools cannot be named while rebroadcasting, photographing, or replicating any part of the court's live stream is a criminal offence.
Legal experts say her only remaining legal avenue is an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court of Australia.

Tributes Pour In for Patrick Stewart, Who Has Died at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:21:50 UTC
08:21:50 KST

Tributes have poured in following the death of British actor Patrick Stewart, known for his decades of Shakespearean stage performances and his leading roles in the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises.
Stewart, 86, died at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday in the company of his wife, Sunny, after a “brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer's and dementia, according to a statement posted Stewart's official Instagram account announcing his death on Thursday.
“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement read. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”
Stewart's long and celebrated career spanned mediums and genres over more than six decades—from his first roles with the Royal Shakespeare Company to a variety of performances in television and film. He is set to make his final on-screen appearance in “Avengers: Doomsday,” which premiers in December, reprising his role as the X-Men’s Professor Charles Xavier.
In an interview with TV Insider in June, Stewart said that he couldn’t “imagine ever officially ‘retiring.’”
“I’ll always and forever be an actor,” he said at the time.
Patrick Stewart’s career took him from Shakespeare to ‘Star Trek,’ and beyond
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in the West Yorkshire town of Mirfield in England’s coal-mining country, where he later recalled growing up in poverty and a home marked by domestic violence. He described acting as a “safe space” and a “refuge from real life” that he discovered after a teacher first introduced him to Shakespeare.
Years before he made his big-screen debut, Stewart trained in classical theater and took on his first professional roles on the British stage in the 1950s and 1960s. He joined the esteemed Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966, going from smaller supporting roles to storied leading parts over the course of more than 15 years as a regular member of the company.
Beginning in the 1970s, Stewart appeared in television series including “Fall of Eagles” (1974), “I, Claudius” (1976), and “Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.”
He reached a new level of international stardom with his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series, which he played from 1987 to1994. In 2000, Stewart took on another career-defining part, that of Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” movies.
Throughout his career, Stewart received various accolades, including two Laurence Olivier Awards, recognized as the highest honor in British theater, and a Grammy for his recording of “Peter and the Wolf,”; as well as garnering nominations for the Golden Globes, Emmys, and a Tony. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for his service to drama in 2010.
Outpourings of praise and remembrance
The news of Stewart’s death quickly drew tributes from many within the “Star Trek” and Marvel worlds where he inhabited two of his most recognizable roles.
“We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days,” wrote the actor Hugh Jackman, who starred as Wolverine in the “X-Men” films alongside Stewart.
Marvel Studios also paid tribute to Stewart on Thursday.
“Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from ‘X-Men’ to ‘Logan’ to ‘Avengers: Doomsday.’ He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman,” Marvel wrote in a statement shared on social media.
The studio's president, Kevin Feige, said in a statement to Variety that “after years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas.”
Feige added that “away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor.”
The “Star Trek” franchise remembered Stewart in a post on its official Instagram page as “a voice. A presence. A captain unlike any other.”
“Sir Patrick Stewart gave generations of fans an icon who inspired us to look toward the stars,” the post read. “Today, we celebrate an extraordinary life and an enduring legacy. Thank you, Sir Patrick.”
William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk in the “Star Trek” franchise, said in a post on X that Stewart was “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”
George Takei, who played Lt. Hikaru Sulu in the original “Star Trek” series, called Stewart on threads “a true and irreplaceable legend.”
“He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,” Takei said.
Stewart’s “Star Trek: The Next Generation” co-stars Wil Wheaton, who played Wesley Crusher on the series, and Jonathan Scott Frakes, who played William Riker, also shared tributes to the late actor.
“Godspeed, Captain,” Wheaton wrote in a message on Instagram, alongside a photo of himself with Stewart.
“Rest in peace, my friend,” Frakes wrote.
Rebecca Romijn, who like Stewart has played roles in both the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises said in a video posted on social media: “I feel so grateful to have known him for the last 25 years, and to have been in his orbit … both as a fellow mutant and as a fellow member of Starfleet.”
“He was positively delicious, hilarious, naughty, incredible sense of humor, and that booming voice of his that always spoke to the very back of the room, as every classically trained Shakespearean great needs to master, has always been an inspiration,” she said. “I send my condolences to his family, and I’ll miss my friend dearly. Rest in peace, Patrick.”
Cary Elwes, who starred alongside Stewart in “Lady Jane” and “Robin Hood: Men in Tights,” recalled that he “first met Patrick on the set of Lady Jane back in 1984 and fell in love with him immediately.”
"Not only was amiable and kind with a great sense of humor, he was incredible to work with. His command of the screen with his sheer presence and that unmistakable voice was a sight to behold," Elwes wrote in a post on Instagram.

ASEAN Special Envoy Concludes Humanitarian Mission to Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:17:00 UTC
08:17:00 KST

Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro yesterday wrapped up a two-day humanitarian mission in Myanmar, potentially her last as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s special envoy to the country.
According to the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Lazaro began her mission with a visit to the city of Taunggyi in a military-controlled region of Shan State, to oversee the distribution of aid through the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance.
She then traveled yesterday to the capital Naypyidaw, where she met with Myanmar’s Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe. The two officials discussed “the humanitarian situation and hard-to-reach communities, as well as the overall implementation of the Five-Point Consensus,” ASEAN’s plan for managing the Myanmar conflict, the DFA said in a statement.
While in Naypyidaw, Lazaro also visited a school and monastery in Pyinmana Township that were granted Philippine humanitarian assistance after the devastating earthquake of March 2025. The DFA added that she concluded her mission in Yangon, where she held “consultations with ASEAN Embassies.”
Unsurprisingly, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry characterized yesterday’s meeting between Lazaro and Tin Maung Swe differently, stating that the two envoys “held substantive discussions on ways to restore Myanmar’s original role and rights within ASEAN.” The Myanmar foreign minister informed Lazaro of the government’s efforts to promote peace and stability, address “terrorism,” and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and “underscored Myanmar’s full cooperation under the ASEAN framework.”
The Five-Point Consensus, promulgated by ASEAN two months after the military coup, calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to Myanmar’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid. However, the military’s failure to implement the most important terms of the Consensus prompted ASEAN to exclude Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings in late 2021.
Since taking office in April, the new military-backed administration headed by coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has pushed hard for normalization with ASEAN. Five ASEAN member states – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
At the same time, it has explicitly rejected the Five-Point Consensus and denounced ASEAN for its “discrimination.” While the Myanmar Foreign Ministry stated that Tin Maung Swe “highlighted the Government’s constructive cooperation towards implementing the ASEAN Five-Point Statement” – it now refuses to refer to it as a “Consensus” – he added that it would do so “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives,” some of which directly contradict the ASEAN plan.
It is thus unsurprising that Naypyidaw would seek to characterize Lazaro’s visit as a step on the road toward the current Myanmar regime’s relegitimization. Indeed, as one observer noted today on X, allowing Lazaro to preside over the distribution of humanitarian aid in Taunggyi, far from most of the active conflict zones in Shan State, allows the Philippines to claim progress on the Five-Point Consensus.
Notably, though perhaps not surprisingly, Lazaro, whose position as special envoy will end when Singapore takes over ASEAN’s chairmanship in 2027, concluded her mission without meeting detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
The 81-year-old has been in custody since the coup, but the military-backed government has loosened the terms of her detention somewhat over the last six months, in pursuit of its goal of regional normalization. After announcing her move from prison to house arrest in April, it has released photos of her meeting with a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross. This month, it also allowed her to receive two books and a diplomatic package from Britain’s King Charles III and to hold a phone call with her son, Kim Aris.
As ASEAN chair in 2026, the Philippines has pressed Naypyidaw for access to the Nobel laureate. It made its first request for “brief access” after she was moved to house arrest in April and again in August after she was allowed to meet with the ICRC representative. The Myanmar administration refused both.
While Myanmar is keen to use Aung San Suu Kyi to extract concessions from its key partners, it is clear that this will stop short of recognizing her as a legitimate political interlocutor. Moreover, having rejected the need for an ASEAN special envoy at all back in August, the outcome of Lazaro’s mission is a sign that Naypyidaw will use ASEAN’s special envoys not to advance the Five-Point Consensus, but to support its chosen pursuit of political consolidation at home and diplomatic normalization abroad.

The US and Israel launched attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US targets across the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled over disagreements related to the waterway’s security.
The latest reported military deployments come amid renewed concerns over a possible escalation between the US and Iran.

Russian President Vladimir Putin says he welcomed the rare phone call from the leaders of Finland and Norway, adding that Moscow has always supported efforts to normalize relations with European countries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store spoke with Putin on Tuesday, breaking with the longstanding practice among European leaders of avoiding direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. The initiative drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who questioned its effectiveness and said it was not coordinated with European partners.
At a press conference in the Kremlin on Thursday, Putin said he welcomes dialogue with Western countries despite their military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia.
“I believe it was the right thing to do. After all, there are people in Europe who, unlike some others, do not want to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia but instead want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” he stated.
He added that Russia will support “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations” with European countries, whether through the EU or on a bilateral basis.
Putin reiterated that Russia is not seeking a broader conflict with the EU or NATO. “We do not want any war with Europe. If some of them want one, let them prepare. But they have not achieved their goal of inflicting a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia, and it is unlikely that this will be possible by 2030,” he said.
And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.
The leaders of Norway and Finland said they sought to convey messages directly to Putin “regarding future negotiations to help to end the war,” ahead of US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the near future. They described the conversation as a follow-up to their meeting with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on October 20.
Norway and the Kremlin disputed a report by the Financial Times claiming that Putin spent much of the call lecturing his counterparts on Russian and Slavic history.
Stubb has cultivated a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, with whom he has frequently discussed the Ukraine conflict, earning him the nickname ‘the Trump whisperer’ in the media.
The Finnish leader noted his country’s long experience of dealing with Russia. Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer border with its eastern neighbor and maintained peaceful, if sometimes uneasy, relations with Moscow throughout the Cold War.
The call came amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and subsequently waived additional restrictions following Zelensky’s refusal to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Trump blamed for soaring fuel prices.

Analysis-Bukele’s gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:07:31 CET
08:07:31 KST

By Sarah Morland
Oct 28 (Reuters) - El Salvador’s deployment of thousands of troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force went missing in a gang ambush, is the first major overseas test of President Nayib Bukele’s anti-gang tactics.
Around 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were in Haiti as of Wednesday night, a security official told Reuters. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said these would for now be capped at 2,500. Yet authorities have not clarified the troops’ command, or rules of engagement, fueling concerns of more risks to civilians in a country with a long history of harmful foreign interventions.
Bukele billed the deployments as a rescue mission for four aircraft technicians who were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. They have been missing since they jumped from a burning vehicle during the ambush in a gang-controlled area on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.
Haitian and Salvadoran authorities have said the troops’ main mission is to rescue the missing technicians. But the deployment’s size - matching in 10 days what the UN-backed force struggled to deploy over more than a year - has prompted questions over whether the soldiers could be part of a broader and longer-term operation.
On Thursday, Bukele said the deployments were nearly finished and his government was covering 90% of the costs.
Bukele, in office since 2019, won huge popularity at home with tough-on-crime policies, including a gang crackdown that relied heavily on mass incarceration. Other governments have sought to replicate his approach, despite rights activists’ warnings over due process and innocent deaths.
Bukele would, however, likely encounter a profoundly different security environment in Haiti, analysts warned, as institutions have been whittled down by corruption and faltering funds, prisons are vastly overcrowded, the judiciary paralyzed and many gang recruits are underage.
“This could help increase support for Bukele if this helps his narrative of being an anti-gang force in the region and delivering results,” said Maria Fernanda Arocha, an analyst at conflict monitoring group ACLED.
“We don’t know if this will bring the results he is expecting.”
A CID Gallup poll on Wednesday showed 86% of Salvadorans approved of the Haiti mission, though 82% also expressed concern for their countrymen.
In El Salvador, security analysts said they were cautious of a risky mission without a formal agreement, UN backing, or support from the Shield of the Americas - a US-led anti-crime coalition the Trump administration launched earlier this year.
POINTS TO ESCALATION
Haiti’s unelected leaders have since 2022 called for international forces to help fight heavily-armed gangs that have expanded their influence beyond the capital and are responsible for massacres, gang rapes and widespread extortion.
But successive UN-backed missions were slow to deploy, leaving a fractured security response. Haiti hired a private military company run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince to fight the gangs, which nonetheless continued to make gains.
Sam Vigersky, a policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he believed the UN-backed mission - renewed for just six months in September - was under pressure to produce results but the Salvadorans’ arrival signaled more chaos.
“The overall security picture is not pointing towards one of stabilization, it’s pointing towards one of escalation,” he said.
Since the October 18 ambush, the area has been the site of continuous armed clashes. A security official said operations there were largely run by Haitian police.
Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a security expert at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said residents were skeptical of yet another foreign intervention and had reported heavy gunfire, drone strikes and possible civilian deaths.
He said he was not aware of humanitarian corridors to help people escape: “The gang leaders do not want people to leave the area because they probably want to use them as shields and make sure the population actually slows operations against them.”
Washington has not publicly supported the mission but a US military official said Pentagon C-130s helped it deploy.
Irwin Stotzky, a rights expert at the University of Miami, said the US administration, which ended immigration protections for about 350,000 Haitians, has reasons to be invested.
“We’ve got to make it appear as if it’s safe to send 350,000 people back to Haiti, when they actually are in great fear of their lives,” he said.
(Reporting by Sarah Morland in Mexico City, Harold Isaac in Port-au-Prince, Gerardo Arbaiza in San Salvador; Additional reporting by Simon Lewis in Washington; editing by Cassandra Garrison and Sanjeev Miglani)
