Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:16:51 UTC
07:16:51 KST

Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data
An Icelandic web company, FlokiNET, has defended the data’s publication as satisfying a ‘legitimate’ public interest.
The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has asked an Icelandic web hosting company to take down a site with information about tens of thousands of its employees.
On Thursday, the Icelandic company FlokiNET posted a letter it received from the cybersecurity firm ZeroFox, on behalf of DHS.
The letter accused FlokiNET of violating its terms of service by publishing a “stolen” employee dataset and asked it to “remove or disable” the information.
“The content is live and places more than 40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking, and physical harm,” the letter said.
FlokiNET said the letter concerned one domain, icepi.cx, which has compiled information about employees from a range of DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Those agencies have come under intense scrutiny since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign in 2025.
But the Trump administration has often refused to identify DHS agents involved in specific operations, citing safety risks.
Though FlokiNET said it refused to comply with DHS’s request, it noted that the website’s registrar ultimately suspended the domain. The employee information has since moved to a different domain.
In a statement posted online, FlokiNET defended its decision not to remove the site.
“Federal officers carrying out an enforcement programme are not private individuals while they are carrying it out,” the company said. “The public has a legitimate interest in knowing who is doing that work, under whose authority, and in which office.”
The database was first posted online on Wednesday by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a group that showcases leaked government data.
In the past, DDoSecrets has released emails from convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, as well as information from the Israeli Ministry of Justice and police departments in the US.
A hacker group calling itself the “Department of Peace” has claimed responsibility for obtaining and sharing the DHS data.
Since the database was first published, other groups have spread the information elsewhere, including on sites like icepi.cx. As a result, the information is unlikely to be entirely scrubbed from the internet.
The Trump administration, however, has taken an aggressive approach to online platforms purporting to contain information about ICE employees and other agents involved in immigration operations.
Last year, for instance, the US Department of Justice pressured tech giants like Apple to remove apps that track ICE agents, including one called ICEBlock.
The move sparked backlash from Democrats and free-speech advocates, who argued that the public has a right to report on ICE’s movements.
“Blocking access to these apps at the request of the federal government raises the distinct possibility that Apple is working with government to violate its customers’ First Amendment right to record and report on the activities of their government,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin wrote in a letter last year, asking Apple to review its decision.
Immigration agents, meanwhile, have taken several steps to conceal their identities during operations, including wearing face masks or street clothes.
That lack of transparency has spurred criticism from human rights groups and immigration advocates, who argue that they have little recourse to pursue allegations of excessive force or impropriety during ICE raids.
Since Trump was sworn in for a second term, at least 25 people have faced gunfire from immigration agents. Six of the shootings have resulted in deaths.
Other cases have involved alleged violations of civil liberties – including unlawful arrests and racial profiling – as well as controversial tactics like car ramming and tackling.

Classrooms in Sumy Oblast are moving underground due to Russian shelling: 13 such schools are already operating, nine are under construction, and another 14 are at the design stage. Russian attacks have damaged 165 schools in Sumy Oblast since the start of the full-scale invasion.

The mission aims to bring aid to civilians and facilitate their safe departure.
Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge. The bridges are of critical importance. About 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro River in Kyiv every day.
Russia may not give Oleshky evacuees a free choice to return to Ukraine, ISW warns, after Putin called the town a “Russian settlement”. Those who choose Ukraine will likely have to travel through Russia first, with no public guarantees that they will be let go.

Ankara tells Washington it’s ready to help revive Ukraine-Russia talks—but names no date or venue. Moscow claims a contact is near but that talk of Abu Dhabi is premature while it is still preparing. Kyiv wants that round before a summit without Ukraine.

Ukraine wants its Abu Dhabi talks with Russia before a proposed Trump-Putin-Xi summit. Tusk pointed to a first Abu Dhabi round after 4 November. Kyiv says the meeting now depends on Washington.

Nations said to be undermining science at UN nature talks
Political tensions are mounting in the final days of the United Nations biodiversity talks with a handful of countries accused of trying to weaken the science that underpins global nature policy.
The growing feud over the role of science has alarmed veteran negotiators and follows recent efforts by fossil fuel-reliant nations to delay reports by the IPCC, the global authority on climate change.
“The same thing is happening here as what is taking place with the IPCC,” said a French government delegate at the COP17 summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
He said four countries – Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil – were frustrating progress.
Brazil’s Bolsonaro isolated, ridiculed after self-exile
In a viral wave of mockery, Brazilian popstar Anitta declared herself free of cellulite, one influencer declared himself the “true president” of Twitter, and another social media user proclaimed himself the winner of the next lottery.
The target of the taunts was Flavio Bolsonaro, who – after fleeing to the United States following his election defeat – proclaimed himself the leader of Brazil on Oct 28 in a confusing series of revised statements.
The moves by the 45-year-old senator have been met in Brazil with a mixture of derision, disbelief, and disapproval, even from within his own camp.
2 dead as ‘fairy chimney’ rock spires collapse in Turkey
A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkey’s Cappadocia tourist region on Oct 29, killing at least two people, the local governor said.
Turkey’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.
“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
Ex-factory worker crowned China’s richest woman, again
A factory worker-turned-entrepreneur who made her fortune producing glass screens for Apple’s iPhones has reclaimed the title of China’s richest woman on the back of her foray into high-end manufacturing.
Zhou Qunfei, 56, founder and chairman of Lens Technology, is worth 127 billion yuan (S$24.4 billion) today. This is up 15% from a year ago, according to the Hurun Richest Women in China 2026 list released on Oct 28.
She overtook Zhong Huijuan, founder of drugmaker Hansoh Pharmaceutical, whose estimated wealth stands at 124 billion yuan, to take the top spot for the second time. Zhou was first crowned China’s richest woman in 2015.
Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies at 86
Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV’s Star Trek: The Next Generation and the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.
“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” it said.

Putin says Moscow seeks better European ties, conflict will produce no winners
MOSCOW – Russia supports any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, President Vladimir Putin said late on Oct 29, adding the outbreak of any conflict would leave a situation with no winners.
Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin said Russia was prepared for a potential war with Europe, though it did not want one.
“We support any steps... we support any actions aimed at restoring full-fledged and complete relations with European countries,” Putin told reporters after hosting a summit with African leaders.
“First of all, we are ready, but we want no war with Europe. And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal – to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.”
Putin said Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere had been right to make the call despite criticism from some European capitals that the two were breaking ranks by initiating contact with Moscow.
He said Russia wanted no impediments to navigation in the Baltic Sea and added that restricting communication could lead to a situation similar to that in the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the US-Iranian conflict in February.
“Does someone want the same situation in the Baltic as in the Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz?” Putin said.
“I don’t know. We don’t want that, but we will respond to any challenge.” REUTERS

Philadelphia appoints new rat control manager

Philadelphia appoints new rat control manager
Philadelphia has appointed a new Rat Abatement Manager to tackle its rodent problem, following approximately 4,000 rat-related complaints each year, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the city’s Department of Public Health, Adrian Jordan will lead a team of health inspectors conducting door-to-door visits in neighborhoods most affected by rat infestations. The team will assess the scale of the problem, carry out control measures and advise residents on preventing further infestations.
According to the department, Philadelphia receives around 4,000 complaints about suspected rat activity annually. Inspections confirm approximately 2,000 cases, prompting treatment and follow-up prevention efforts.
Jordan will also coordinate efforts between five municipal agencies, including the Water Department, Sanitation Department and Streets Department, to address problems that require cooperation across city services.
The city has a long history of battling rodents. In the early 1900s, Philadelphia’s health authorities paid residents five cents for every dead rat delivered to a designated collection station.
Today, officials emphasize prevention rather than financial incentives. Residents are advised to store garbage in tightly sealed metal containers, remove potential rodent hiding places and seal openings larger than half an inch (1.27 cm) around their homes.
The department also encourages residents to report rat sightings so inspectors can investigate and take appropriate action.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency explained how rodents can spread plague.

The identity and location of seven Russian tankers transporting 288,000 metric tons of diesel to the U.S. were announced by Greenpeace Ukraine on Oct. 29.
Following U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian oil exports, a live tracker map developed by Greenpeace, an international environmental organization, shows Russian tankers currently moving across the Atlantic Ocean, with one vessel approaching the U.S. East Coast.
“Every shipment of Russian diesel comes at a human cost," Polina Kolodiazhna, energy campaigner at Greenpeace Ukraine, said in a statement. "Every dollar flowing into Russia risks fueling more attacks, more destruction and more deaths. These shipments also undermine the international sanctions regime and send a dangerous message that business with Russia can continue as usual, even as its war against Ukraine rages on."
Greenpeace Ukraine identified the tankers as the Taurus, Pvt Azura, Agioi Fanendes, Talisman, Leruo, Iblea, and Primorye. Three of these vessels, the Talisman, Leruo, and Primorye, are currently sanctioned by multiple countries as part of Russia's "shadow fleet" illegally exporting oil, according to Ukraine's war sanctions portal. The Talisman has been under U.S. sanctions since January 2025.
The ships are expected to arrive in the U.S. in early November, though it is not known at which ports they will arrive.
Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Sept. 28 restricting access to data on the country's oil refineries and energy exports amid Ukrainian campaigns against Russia's oil infrastructure. The decree added another layer of secrecy to Russian exports, helping shadow fleet vessels evade sanctions.

On Oct. 9, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that he was temporarily allowing the sale of Russian diesel in the country in an attempt to lower oil costs heightened by the war with Iran. The move spurred international backlash from Ukraine and its allies, as well as lawmakers in the U.S.
U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, issued a warning on Oct. 28 to a shipping company transporting the Russian diesel to the United States: turn back, or risk violating U.S. sanctions law.
Blumenthal says that diesel shipments are banned under the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, signed into law by former President Joe Biden following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Trump's diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin does not "supersede clear, unambiguous law," Blumenthal argued.

Make no mistake: Trump's diesel deal with Putin is corrupt and illegal, and I am evaluating options to stop it from arriving at a port in New Jersey.”

Attack of the clones: Alaska has a ‘black PR’ moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:05:29 UTC
07:05:29 KST

Attack of the clones: Alaska has a ‘black PR’ moment
US President Donald Trump has accused Democrats of fraud over an alleged plot to field a namesake candidate in Alaska’s Senate race.
An electoral trick familiar to Russians who remember the political free-for-all of the 1990s, the tactic involves recruiting a candidate whose name matches that of an established politician in the hope of confusing voters and siphoning off votes.
In Russia, such contenders became known as “clone candidates” and were a hallmark of the country’s notoriously ruthless election campaigns, forming part of the political “black PR” playbook.
In Alaska, Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan now faces a namesake challenger, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher who is also running in the November 3 election.
According to a New York Times investigation, operatives linked to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee allegedly helped recruit the namesake candidate as part of a broader effort to undermine the incumbent. The newspaper cited interviews, text messages and documents detailing the operation, which reportedly began in 2025. Both Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic committee have denied involvement.
Following the report, Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, ordered an investigation into whether any laws had been broken and whether criminal charges or civil action was warranted. Trump has branded the alleged scheme “voter fraud at the highest level” and called for Peltola and the namesake candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.
@Odinsraven66 @StephenM To be precise, there is no indication what party "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.” might be affiliated with on the Alaska bingo card. https://t.co/TWjsD2dWtT
— DougS (@doug_swartout) October 24, 2026
US black PR that came to Russia
Russians know the playbook. During the 1998 elections to the St. Petersburg Legislative Assembly, namesake candidates appeared in multiple constituencies. At least two challengers sharing the surname Mironov ran against Sergey Mironov, then acting speaker of the regional parliament. He nevertheless secured a decisive victory with around 70% of the vote.
In a 2000 State Duma by-election in Sverdlovsk Region, Yekaterinburg police chief Nikolay Ovchinnikov faced Vladimir Ovchinnikov, who appeared above him on the alphabetically arranged ballot. The namesake reportedly secured more than 5% of the vote, although the police chief ultimately won.
An isolated example of the practice surfaced in St. Petersburg as recently as 2021, when opposition politician Boris Vishnevsky faced two rivals who had legally changed their names to Boris Vishnevsky, adopting similar hairstyles and beards for their election portraits.
This is not the first time the practice has appeared in the US. In the 2020 Florida state Senate race, a little-known candidate named Alex Rodriguez received more than 6,000 votes, while Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodríguez lost to Republican Ileana Garcia by just 32 votes.
The namesake candidate subsequently pleaded guilty to campaign-finance offenses connected with the scheme, which involved a former Republican state senator.

PROFILE - Patrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men star, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:03:24 UTC
07:03:24 KST

Sir Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British actor who achieved worldwide fame as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films after decades on the Shakespearean stage, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles following an illness involving Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, his spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, confirmed Thursday to the Hollywood Reporter.
He spent his final hours surrounded by family and friends, including his wife, singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell, according to a statement released by his representatives.
His death marked the end of a career spanning more than six decades across theater, television, and film, becoming one of the world's most internationally recognized actors.
From Yorkshire to Shakespeare
Born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, Stewart grew up in a working-class household with limited financial means.
His father, a British Army veteran of World War II, struggled with the psychological effects of his military service and was physically abusive toward Stewart's mother, an experience the actor would later discuss publicly.
Stewart discovered acting while still at school and briefly worked as a newspaper reporter before pursuing the stage professionally.
He trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and spent his early career performing in regional theaters across Britain.
In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, beginning an association that would establish him as a leading classical actor.
Over the following decades, he appeared in productions of Macbeth, Hamlet, King Lear, Antony and Cleopatra, and numerous other works by Shakespeare.
He also performed on the London stage and Broadway, earning recognition for his commanding voice, disciplined performances, and ability to portray complex characters.
From the stage to global stardom
Despite his established reputation in British theater, Stewart's international breakthrough came in 1987 when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.
The series, which ran until 1994, introduced a new generation of audiences to the science fiction franchise.
Stewart's portrayal of Picard, a thoughtful and diplomatic Starfleet commander who often relied on reason and negotiation rather than force, became one of the franchise's defining performances.
He reprised the role in several Star Trek feature films before returning decades later in the television series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 to 2023.
His popularity grew further in 2000 when he took on the role of Charles Xavier, the powerful telepathic leader of Marvel’s X-Men superhero team, a role many fans saw him as perfectly suited for.
As Professor X, as the character is also known, Stewart appeared in multiple installments alongside fellow British actor Ian McKellen, who portrayed Xavier's adversary and frenemy Magneto.
His performance in the critically acclaimed 2017 film Logan brought another major chapter of the character's story to a close.
He also appeared in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness in 2022 and is expected to appear posthumously in the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday.
Beyond his dramatic roles, Stewart demonstrated his comedic abilities through appearances in television productions including Extras and voice work on the animated series American Dad.
Theater, honors, and advocacy
Despite his Hollywood success, Stewart remained closely connected to theater throughout his career.
He frequently performed a one-man adaptation of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol and appeared alongside McKellen in acclaimed productions of Waiting for Godot and No Man's Land.
His performances earned him two Laurence Olivier Awards, a Grammy Award, and nominations for several Emmy and Golden Globe Awards.
In 2010, Queen Elizabeth II knighted him for services to drama.
Stewart also became an outspoken advocate for survivors of domestic violence and military veterans experiencing mental health difficulties.
Drawing on his own childhood experiences, he supported organizations including Refuge, which assists domestic abuse survivors, and Combat Stress, which works with veterans.
In his 2023 autobiography, Making It So: A Memoir, Stewart reflected on his upbringing, career, relationships, and the lasting impact of witnessing violence in his childhood home.
The book traced his journey from a modest Yorkshire household to international stardom and explored the personal challenges behind his public success.
Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, whom he married in 2013, and two children from his first marriage.
His career leaves a legacy spanning classical theater and popular entertainment, with his portrayals of Picard and Professor Xavier remaining among the most recognizable characters in modern science fiction.

Hegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:01:56 UTC
07:01:56 KST

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has reportedly dismissed Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking army strategist serving on the Pentagon’s joint staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public.
The Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had referred an alleged information leak case for criminal investigation, maintaining that the removal of the senior general was essential “to protect sensitive information”, the Washington Post reported.
Sylvia had served as the director for strategy, plans and policy on the joint staff.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell acknowledged the dismissal in a statement on social media, though he did not mention Sylvia by name.
“Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information,” Parnell wrote. “To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action.”
“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” he added.
A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said in a statement that it “has ongoing investigations related to possible leaks of classified information”.
“We work closely with our government partners, which includes the Department of War,” the spokesperson added, using the Trump administration’s name for the Pentagon.
Sylvia’s removal represents one of the most significant actions so far in Hegseth’s extensive campaign to identify officials suspected of sharing information with journalists, as the unpopular US war on Iran moves into its ninth month.
In July, Hegseth announced that the Pentagon and the US Department of Justice had created a joint taskforce “to identify and prosecute” what he called the “unauthorized disclosure of sensitive” information to the press.
Last year, Hegseth implemented new restrictions governing media access that prompted legal concerns from press organizations.
Dozens of journalists surrendered their press badges rather than agree to the new media policies, which have been subject to legal challenges.
A senior Pentagon official told Reuters that Sylvia failed three separate polygraph tests, in which he was asked whether he had disclosed classified material.
“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said, according to Reuters.
However, a colleague of Sylvia told the Washington Post that the general had consistently rejected accusations that he leaked classified information, while also acknowledging that he had previously communicated with members of the press.
In August, three journalists fired by the Pentagon from the US government-funded news outlet Stars and Stripes sued the department in federal court, arguing their dismissals were illegal and violated their first amendment rights to free speech.

Netanyahu wants new election, but opposition can block it, says Arab Party leader Ahmad Tibi

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:00:12 UTC
07:00:12 KST

Ahmad Tibi, head of the Joint Arab List's parliamentary bloc in Israel's Knesset, has alleged that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking another election to cling to power, urging opposition parties to thwart his plans by forming a government led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot.
In an exclusive interview with Turkish news agency Anadolu, Tibi said he believes Netanyahu intends to remain at the helm of a caretaker government while preparing to launch another war against Iran in coordination with US President Donald Trump.
"I think Netanyahu wants another election. For now, he wants to remain prime minister of the caretaker government," he said.
"Netanyahu wants to launch a war against Iran in cooperation and coordination with Donald Trump after the US midterm elections, then hold another election," he added.
Tibi urged opposition parties to move swiftly and decisively to prevent Netanyahu from carrying out that scenario.
"The opposition must block Netanyahu by announcing that a government will be formed under Eisenkot as prime minister. We, as the Joint Arab List, are ready to help," he said.
He stressed that the Joint Arab List does not intend to join a new government but is prepared to facilitate its formation through understandings with opposition parties.
"We in the Joint Arab List do not want to enter a government. We have spoken about providing a safety net for our community and making it possible to bring down Netanyahu’s government and establish an alternative government through understandings with the opposition," he said.
Tibi said Arab lawmakers would seek commitments addressing the needs of their communities in exchange for providing parliamentary support.
"The most important thing for us now is to bring down this government," he added.
He expressed hope that opposition leaders would overcome their differences and end internal disputes following Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.
Arab turnout 'blocked Netanyahu's plans'
Tibi described the high turnout among Arab voters as a major political achievement that prevented Netanyahu from securing another parliamentary majority.
"Netanyahu is deeply disturbed by the high turnout among Arab voters because it blocked and disrupted his plan to form another government under his leadership," he said.
"Netanyahu cannot form a government. Itamar Ben-Gvir will never be police minister again," he added.
Tibi said the participation of Arab voters had also prevented far-right politicians, including Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, from returning to power.
"This is an achievement for our politically aware Arab public, which acted with great political wisdom and responsibility," he said.
He urged Arab lawmakers to use their electoral gains to help establish an alternative government.
"We all want to use this trust, these votes and these seats to contribute to bringing down Netanyahu’s government and making way for another, less harmful alternative government," he said.
Rejects allegations of election fraud
Tibi accused Netanyahu and his political allies of conducting a campaign against Palestinian-Israeli voters following the election.
"Netanyahu is conducting an open campaign against Arab voters for all to see," he said.
He rejected allegations from Netanyahu’s political camp that Palestinian-Israeli voters had engaged in election fraud.
"The only address for thieves is Netanyahu’s Prime Minister’s Office. Benjamin Netanyahu is the last person who can lecture us on honesty and integrity," Tibi said.
He pointed to the corruption charges against Netanyahu and criminal investigations involving other government officials.
Tibi said Palestinian-Israeli voters had participated in large numbers despite physical difficulties, citing elderly people and people with disabilities who made their way to polling stations.
He accused Netanyahu’s political camp of seeking to discourage Palestinian-Israeli participation to remain in power.
"They want Arabs not to vote so they can continue governing. Our votes brought down their plans," he said.
Tibi also alleged that the campaign was intended to delay the publication of official election results and prevent the replacement of Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
He said he was reassured by the Central Elections Committee’s position that the allegations would not affect the publication of the results.
Responds to Netanyahu over Qatar visit
Asked about a social media post in which Netanyahu questioned why he had traveled to Qatar two days before the elections, Tibi dismissed the criticism.
"Netanyahu posted a tweet asking why Ahmad Tibi traveled to Qatar and published a picture of me at Al Jazeera," he said.
"It is clear to everyone that I gave an interview watched by millions on Al Jazeera and returned quickly. If I am invited again, I will go and participate. Anyone who does not like that can deal with it."
He reiterated that Netanyahu was "the last person" qualified to lecture others about honesty and integrity.
Open to coordination with other Arab parties
Tibi said the Joint Arab List was open to coordinating with the United Arab List (Ra’am) led by Mansour Abbas to facilitate the formation of an alternative government.
"We have a common goal: bringing down this government. Of course, there is nothing wrong with coordinating with our brothers in the United Arab List," he said.
He also dismissed the possibility that Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, would abandon the opposition bloc.
"I don’t think so, but this is always Lieberman’s behaviour after elections. He is trying to pressure Eisenkot and the change bloc to secure a period as prime minister," Tibi said.
He criticised Lieberman’s apparent distancing from the opposition following the election as irresponsible.
"I heard him say he does not want to sit with Bibi (Netanyahu) or Tibi. I say that’s right, because I don’t want to sit with Lieberman either," he added.
Election leaves blocs short of majority

Amazon's cloud-computing unit reported more rapid third-quarter growth than analysts had projected.

"Our core compute and storage revenue grew at their fastest rates in several years," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with analysts. The AWS growth rate was the highest since the fourth quarter of 2021.
Amazon remains the top cloud by revenue, but growth has also sped up at rivals Alphabet and Microsoft. On Wednesday Alphabet said the Google Cloud business, which contains infrastructure and Google Workspace subscriptions, more than doubled in the third quarter.
All the major clouds have been racing to build data centers that can accommodate high artificial intelligence demand. During the quarter, AWS announced plans to expand its portfolio of Nvidia graphics processing units that can handle AI workloads.
AWS also acquired data analysis startup DuckLabs and signed deals with Meta and OpenAI, according to the statement.
The AWS segment generated $17.77 billion in third-quarter operating income, up 55% and more than the $16.97 billion StreetAccount consensus.
The unit now accounts for almost 23% of Amazon's revenue, a record.
On Wednesday, Microsoft published its first earnings report that contained revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars. Azure is 72% the size of AWS, up from 58% two years ago.
AWS came before Azure and the Google Cloud Platform, with its first services appearing in 2006.
"With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we're adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028, and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years," Jassy said.
Google has been pumping up its cloud revenue by making its tensor processing units for AI available outside its own facilities. Now Amazon will adopt the strategy with its Trainium chips for training models, starting in late 2027.
"With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027," Jassy said.

Five more Ukrainians evacuated from temporarily occupied territories – Lubinets
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets announced this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
"Today, five Ukrainian citizens who had been in temporarily occupied territories returned to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government. All of them needed assistance from others during the transfer because of serious health conditions and limited mobility," Lubinets said.
He stressed that this was a separate mission from the humanitarian operation in Oleshky.
Those evacuated included a married couple.
"On September 11, 2026, they were going to buy food in the temporarily occupied territory. Their car hit a mine, and both sustained multiple injuries and shrapnel wounds. After the explosion, a passerby helped them get home, covering about three kilometers together with them," Lubinets said.
"Because of the difficult security situation, the ambulance crew they called never arrived. There was virtually no possibility of getting help from other residents, as the village had been deserted. The route to nearby Hola Prystan ran through a dangerous area in the immediate vicinity of the combat zone," Lubinets said.
According to the ombudsman, the injured couple went without medical assistance for 12 days.
"The couple remained at home without adequate medical care, suffering from serious injuries under occupation and in constant danger. They were finally taken to a hospital on September 23 – 12 days later," Lubinets said.
According to him, "the couple's condition was deteriorating. The husband had lost his sight and had multiple shrapnel wounds. His wife needed urgent skin graft surgery. Her diabetes complicated the course of treatment. Time was working against them."
The couple's son contacted the ombudsman for help and asked him to save his parents.
"Returning people with serious injuries and limited mobility is an extremely difficult task. It requires careful coordination and individual planning, as the transfer must take into account each person's health, the need for medical supervision and subsequent treatment," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman expressed his gratitude to everyone involved in the operation, particularly the International Committee of the Red Cross in Ukraine.
On October 29, a Ukrainian delegation led by Lubinets set off toward temporarily occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region to monitor the humanitarian operation.

Most of private equity in health went to west &amp; south: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:56:06 UTC
06:56:06 KST

A study found that private equity investment in India’s healthcare sector is concentrated in urban hospitals in southern and western states, leaving rural and underserved regions largely overlooked. (AI-generated image)
A mapping of private equity investments in India’s health sector over past 18 years has revealed investments are overwhelmingly in multispecialty hospitals in the urbanised southern and western states, while vast rural and underserved regions attracted little or no investment at all.In the study by Brown University’s School of Public Health and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, which identified 70 private equity (PE) backed acquisitions between Jan 2007 and May 2025, over 73% of the investment was in 45 hospital groups, including 187 multispecialty hospitals and several single ones. Among 16 outpatient care providers targeted, ophthalmology and fertility/reproductive care were the most common ones.According to the study, the investments accelerated after 2020 and peaked in 2023, which witnessed 18 deals. “This timing mirrors global post-pandemic trends, where healthcare emerged as an attractive investment sector amid favourable financial conditions. During the pandemic, low interest rates and large amounts of available capital (“dry powder”) made financing inexpensive and widely available, while healthcare’s relatively stable revenues made it more attractive than other economic sectors,” stated the study published in BMC Health Services Research, an open source journal.
Karnataka recorded 13 deals, the highest number, followed by 10 each in Maharashtra and Telangana. Gujarat had six deals while Keralam and Haryana saw five each. Northern and eastern states saw minimal or no investment.Four hospital groups that together accounted for one-third of the total deals were Manipal Health Enterprises and Health Care Global Enterprises, both headquartered in Karnataka; and CARE Hospitals and ASG Eye Hospitals.Of the total number of acquisitions, 47 (67.1%) were financed solely by foreign PE firms, including those based in US, Singapore, and Mauritius, while 18 were backed exclusively by Indian investors.Among the 25 observed PE exits, secondary sales to other PE firms were most common (64%) exit strategy. Average holding period among those that exited was 5.1 years, with hospital platforms accounting for over half of these exits.
Forty-five hospital groups (64.3%) remained under their original PE ownership.Several of the PE-backed platform deals were initially structured as minority stakes, with ownership expanding gradually over time, a staged pattern of engagement consistent with more cautious, multi-step investment approaches observed elsewhere in Brics markets, noted the study.

EU trade measures threaten UK auto recovery: SMMT
China
Unknown Publisher

05:54:25 CST
06:54:25 KST

LONDON, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- European Union (EU) trade measures threaten a projected recovery in British vehicle production next year, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) warned Thursday.
An independent industry outlook forecasts that annual vehicle production will decline this year before rising to 752,000 units in 2027 as new models, mostly electric vehicles (EVs), enter production, the SMMT said.
The SMMT identified three major threats to the industry's competitiveness, including two related to Britain's trading relationship with the EU.
The European Commission's "Made in EU" proposals could, in their current form, effectively exclude British-built vehicles from the EU, their largest export market, it said.
The SMMT also warned that tougher rules of origin taking effect in 2027 under the Trade Cooperation Agreement could result in tariffs totaling 1.4 billion pounds (about 1.9 billion U.S. dollars) annually on two-way EV trade.
Exports accounted for more than three-quarters of British vehicle production in September, with the EU receiving 57.5 percent of those exports, SMMT data showed.
The SMMT said both measures would damage the automotive industry on both sides and called the forthcoming EU-UK Summit "a vital opportunity to agree pragmatic solutions and safeguard an 80-billion-euro (about 90 billion dollars) trading relationship."
The society also warned that what it described as unrealistic domestic EV sales targets was putting manufacturers under acute pressure, eroding profitability, diverting resources and undermining the attractiveness of the UK as a place to invest. ■

Erin Patterson to learn fate as appeal handed down in mushroom murders case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:51:35 UTC
06:51:35 KST

in brief
- Victoria's Court of Appeal will today deliver its judgment on Erin Patterson's murder convictions.
- Judges must also rule on the prosecution's challenge seeking a life sentence without parole.
Erin Patterson faces legal reckoning as Victoria's highest court hands down its decision on the deadly mushroom poisoning case that captivated and shocked the public.
Three Court of Appeal judges will deliver their rulings on two competing legal challenges at 10am on Friday.
The 52-year-old Leongatha woman is fighting to overturn her jury convictions for the triple murder of her former in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, as well as the attempted murder of local pastor Ian Wilkinson.
All four fell critically ill after eating beef Wellingtons laced with lethal death cap mushrooms during a family lunch at Patterson's regional home in July 2023. Only Ian survived.
Patterson is expected to watch the proceedings remotely from Dame Phyllis Frost Centre in Ravenhall in Melbourne's west, where she is serving a life sentence.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Victoria's director of public prosecutions is appealing Patterson's sentence, calling for her non-parole period of 33 years to be stripped to ensure she spends the rest of her life behind bars.
Why Erin Patterson is appealing her triple muder convictions
Patterson's legal team launched an appeal following her 2025 trial in the regional Victorian town of Morwell, arguing that multiple procedural errors resulted in a serious miscarriage of justice.
At the heart of the appeal, argued over two days in August this year, was the overlapping accommodation used during the jury's final deliberations.
Patterson's barristers revealed that sequestered jurors were lodged in the same hotel as the prosecution's lead police investigator and two Crown team members.
They argued that sharing a building created an "unacceptable risk" of jury contamination, saying even catching sight of the Crown's team through windows or hotel corridors threatened a fair trial.
Her legal team also challenged the Crown's courtroom approach, labelling the five-day cross-examination by senior prosecutor Dr Nanette Rogers as needlessly aggressive, oppressive, and unfair. They argued the hostile questioning risked leading the jury.
Finally, the defence also claimed the Crown altered its fundamental theory during closing addresses by introducing suggestions of a motive after previously telling the jury in opening remarks no motive could be established.
Prosecution pushing for whole life sentence
While Patterson is attempting to overturn her convictions, the Crown is seeking a harsher penalty.
In September last year, Supreme Court Justice Christopher Beale sentenced Patterson to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years — meaning she would not be eligible for release until she was in her mid-80s.
Crown prosecutor Brendan Kissane argued the sentence was wholly inadequate, given the killings involved calculated premeditation, exacerbated by her failure to tell medical staff about the death caps her victims had consumed while doctors were still trying to save them.
The Crown also challenged the decision to discount her sentence due to the difficult protective custody she had to endure. Her extreme notoriety meant Patterson needed years of strict segregation so as not to influence her trial.
However prosecutors said her conditions in maximum security — including gym access, library resources, crocheting materials, and video calls with her children — did not justify leniency, given the serious nature of her crimes.
What could the court decide?
Under Victorian law, the appellate bench first has to decide if Patterson's case meets the threshold to be granted leave to appeal before determining the final order.
The Court of Appeal has four options:
- Refuse leave of appeal: They find grounds for appeal insufficient and dismiss her legal challenge, meaning she will remain behind bars.
- Grant leave, but dismiss appeal: Judges acknowledge the merits of the case but determine no substantial miscarriage of justice occurred.
- Grant leave, uphold appeal, call a retrial: The court overturns the guilty verdict due to issues with the trial and orders a new trial with a new jury.
- Grant leave, uphold appeal, enter an acquittal: The court overturns the convictions entirely and acquits Patterson, meaning she will be set free.
If the appellate bench upholds Patterson's appeal, the prosecution's challenge against her sentence will automatically be dismissed.
What happens next?
If the Court of Appeal dismisses Patterson's conviction challenge, the judges will immediately decide on the Crown's sentencing appeal.
The bench will choose between upholding Beale's original 33-year non-parole order or re-sentencing Patterson to an indefinite life term without parole.
Given the major international interest in the case, the decision is being heard in the Supreme Court's trial division building, rather than the appellate building. A public live stream will also be running.

Europe’s coffin-makers warn Chinese imports could be death knell for industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:50:16 UTC
06:50:16 KST

Europe’s coffin-makers warn Chinese imports could be death knell for industry
A new coalition is preparing an anti-dumping complaint, arguing that cheap imports and alleged customs loopholes are putting European producers at risk.
BRUSSELS — European coffin manufacturers are joining forces to ask Brussels to investigate Chinese imports, warning that low prices and potential customs loopholes are threatening an industry built around one of the continent’s most predictable markets: death.
A group of manufacturers — which until now had no dedicated lobby representation — has formed a coalition and met with European Commission officials, including from its trade department, the initiative’s organizers told POLITICO. The group is preparing an anti-dumping complaint — a request for the EU to investigate whether Chinese coffin makers are selling their products in Europe at unfairly low prices.
The industry says the damage is already being felt. Over the past five years roughly a quarter of European coffin manufacturers have shut down, their numbers falling from about 120 to 90, according to Folco Ciulli, a consultant helping coordinate the complaint.
Advertisement
“Smaller companies were unable to withstand competition from non-European importers,” Ciulli said, adding those that survived have absorbed only half the production previously handled by the businesses that closed.
The push follows an appeal by a group of EU lawmakers to Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič last year. The MEPs raised concerns about Chinese competition, and were told the industry could submit a formal trade complaint.
“The EU takes robust action to protect its industries from unfairly traded imports and at present has over 200 measures in place,” a Commission spokesperson said. They declined to confirm meetings with the manufacturers, saying contacts with industry over potential trade defense complaints are confidential.
The price of death
At the heart of the industry’s case is a stark price difference.
According to manufacturers’ estimates, producing a coffin in China costs roughly one-third as much as an equivalent product in Italy, even when the same type of wood is used.
The coalition — which has yet to agree on a name for itself — flags several factors it believes give Chinese producers an advantage, including state subsidies, export-related tax benefits, lower labor costs and cheaper timber. It also argues that Chinese manufacturers benefit from preferential raw-material supply chains, and that higher U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods have helped redirect production toward Europe.
Advertisement
But cheap prices alone don’t constitute dumping under EU trade rules.
To secure anti-dumping duties, European manufacturers must provide evidence that Chinese producers are selling coffins in the EU below their established normal value, that the EU industry is suffering material injury, and that dumped imports are responsible for that injury.
The coalition is therefore collecting detailed information on production costs, raw materials, labor and factory-gate prices to compare equivalent coffins manufactured in China and Europe.
Not adding up?
European coffin manufacturers are also examining a hypothesis that some coffins entering the EU from China are not being categorized as such by customs authorities.
Emiliano Inguscio, a mathematician hired by the industry to analyze trade and production data, said his calculations had identified an unexplained discrepancy equivalent to around 30,000 coffins a year in Italy.
“In theory, the number of coffins available for consumption should broadly correspond to domestic production plus imports, minus exports and adjusted for changes in inventories,” Inguscio explained.
Advertisement
Because demand for coffins is relatively predictable and closely linked to mortality, he argues, significant discrepancies could indicate that some imports are not being properly recorded.
The coalition is concerned that such shipments could escape accurate recording in import statistics, obscuring the true extent of Chinese competition.
This has led to a hypothesis that manufacturers have dubbed the “IKEA loophole,” by which some Chinese coffins arrive in Europe flat-packed, with their components declared to customs as wooden parts rather than finished funeral products. Once inside the EU, the pieces are assembled and sold as coffins, the theory goes.
The Commission confirmed that unassembled goods can still be classified as finished products under international customs rules, provided they retain the essential characteristics of the completed item. That means a flat-packed coffin cannot necessarily be treated simply as wooden components for customs purposes.
The industry has also raised a second hypothetical loophole: coffins being imported as packaging for other merchandise, rather than declared as commercial products in their own right.
A widening trade battle
The coffin-makers’ campaign reflects a broader shift in Europe’s trade disputes with China, as complaints about low-cost competition spread beyond strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, steel and chemicals to more traditional manufactured goods.
Advertisement
According to the Commission’s latest annual trade defense report, published in September, the EU launched 32 new trade defense investigations in 2025, nearly matching the previous year’s record.
Coffin-makers would not be the first relatively small, traditional European industry to win protection.
In January, the Commission imposed anti-dumping duties of between 56% and 60% on Chinese candles following an investigation into damage to an EU industry employing around 9,000 people across 80 companies.

Several hours earlier, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that new intelligence indicated Russia was preparing further ballistic missile strikes.
The latest strike followed earlier daytime attacks that left 20 people dead and at least 109 injured.
Store partially destroyed in Dnyprovskyi district
In the neighboring Dniprovskyi district, missile debris fell near a residential complex and caught fire in its courtyard, Klitschko said. The debris partially destroyed a store building, setting it on fire, though the blaze was later contained.
At two separate, undisclosed locations, blast waves blew out windows in residential buildings, damaging private vehicles parked in one of the courtyards.
Emergency services were dispatched to the affected sites as authorities assessed the extent of the damage.
Missiles launched from the north
The Ukrainian Air Force warned of a ballistic missile threat from the north at 10:40 p.m. Kyiv time, reporting a missile over Chernihiv region heading toward Kyiv.
Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
Within minutes, it said at least two ballistic missiles were flying toward the capital, followed by more. The threat was declared over at 11:23 p.m.
Russian jet-powered attack drones were also active over the region throughout the evening.
One flew toward eastern Kyiv via Brovary, while another, tracked later in the night, headed west toward Fastiv in the Kyiv region, according to the Air Force.

Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro isolated, ridiculed after self-exile
- Flavio Bolsonaro fled to the United States after defeat and called himself Brazil’s “true president”, then “leader”, triggering ridicule and anger across the country.
- Brazilian media and politicians rejected his claim, while allies like Tarcisio de Freitas said “the election result is sovereign” and must be respected.
- Analysts say the move may keep Bolsonaro influence alive in the right, but his exile and the party’s strong Congress majority may limit his power.
AI generated
RIO DE JANEIRO - In a viral wave of mockery, Brazilian popstar Anitta declared herself free of cellulite, one influencer declared himself the “true president” of Twitter, and another social media user proclaimed himself the winner of the next lottery.
The target of the taunts was Flavio Bolsonaro, who – after fleeing to the United States following his election defeat – proclaimed himself the leader of Brazil on Oct 28 in a confusing series of revised statements.
The moves by the 45-year-old senator have been met in Brazil with a mixture of derision, disbelief, and disapproval, even from within his own camp.
The eldest son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro was blindsided by his election defeat to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Oct 25, after leading a first-round vote earlier this month.
In a cloak-and-dagger operation he sneaked out of Brazil via Argentina and Ecuador, after being ordered to surrender his passports due to several ongoing investigations against him.
Hours after his arrival in Florida, he posted a statement on social media declaring himself the “true president” of Brazil, before revising the wording a few minutes later to describe himself as the “leader” of the country.
A Bolsonaro ally who published an earlier version of the statement bearing Brazil’s old coat of arms, abandoned in the sixties, said it had been a ChatGPT error.
‘Lunatic asylum Napoleon’
The letter was met with outrage in Brazilian media, which described its tone as “coup-mongering,” while politicians from across the spectrum called for the election results to be respected.
A column in the O Globo daily likened Flavio Bolsonaro to a “lunatic asylum Napoleon,” while the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper slammed the statement as “pathetic.”
On the right, the powerful governor of Sao Paulo, Tarcisio de Freitas, quickly distanced himself.
De Freitas was a former minister under Jair Bolsonaro who had been tipped as the main candidate for the right before the former president chose his son
“We are democrats. The election result is sovereign. What we have seen is the will of the majority of the population, which must be respected,” De Freitas said in an interview with the Estadao daily.
As speculation switched almost immediately to who would lead the right with Flavio out of the country, the governor – a favourite in business circles – said a 2030 run was “a possibility”.
Rogerio Marinho, who co-ordinated Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign, said there was “no evidence” of electoral fraud, as claimed by the defeated candidate.
Electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by Jair Bolsonaro, issued a statement to highlight the “secure electoral process.”
‘No one approves’
Flavio Bolsonaro also said he would lead the opposition from abroad.
His self-proclamation as Brazil’s leader in exile “is not a misstep, it is a calculated move” intended to maintain his influence over the conservative camp in Brazil, said Geraldo Monteiro, a political scientist at the State University of Rio de Janeiro.
The stakes are high: despite their election defeat, the right scored a strong majority in Congress.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) will hold the largest number of seats from February.
“I do not believe he has the means to lead the opposition from afar, as the newly elected officials have already secured their seats and no longer need him,” Monteiro told AFP.
He said Flavio Bolsonaro’s letter has “drawn a red line” between those who choose “extreme loyalty” and those who “prefer not to embark on another putschist adventure.”
Monteiro said Flavio was following in the footsteps of his father, who was sentenced to 27 years for plotting a coup after his 2022 election loss to Lula.
On Oct 29, PL leader Valdemar Costa Neto visited Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving his sentence under house arrest.
“No one approves” of the letter, Neto said as he left the meeting, adding that the party needed to “move forward.” REUTERS

Amazon mining boss wanted by Brazil for sheltering Jair Bolsonaro’s spy chief has businesses, properties in Florida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:43:47 UTC

BRAZIL
Amazon mining boss wanted by Brazil for sheltering Jair Bolsonaro’s spy chief has businesses, properties in Florida
Bolsonaro’s son Flávio landed in Florida yesterday after he lost Brazil’s presidential election, claiming himself the legitimate winner.
A Brazilian gold miner wanted for allegedly helping former President Jair Bolsonaro’s spy chief flee to Florida has built a network of companies and properties in the Sunshine State, ICIJ media partner Agência Pública reports.
Rodrigo Martins de Mello and his family are under investigation by Brazil’s Federal Police for helping Alexandre Ramagem, the former director of the country’s intelligence agency, escape Brazil and sheltering him in Miami, ICIJ and Agência Pública reported on Oct. 22.
De Mello, known as Rodrigo Cataratas, is a strong Bolsonaro supporter. Convicted of leading illegal gold mining on Yanomami Indigenous land, De Mello champions Brazil’s informal miners to his more than 43,000 Instagram followers, attacks the leftist government and calls for amnesty for Bolsonaro, Agência Pública reported. That campaign suffered a blow Oct. 25, when President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva came from behind to defeat Bolsonaro’s son Flávio in the presidential runoff. Three days after the election, Flávio, under investigation in Brazil for alleged money laundering, also fled to Florida.
De Mello himself is now a fugitive. In an order previously under seal that became public this month, Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered his arrest for his alleged role in Ramagem’s escape in December 2025. On Oct. 19, the court rejected De Mello’s request to overturn the order, noting that police have been unable to locate him, the Brazilian news site Amado Mundo reported, and Agência Pública confirmed.
In Brazil, De Mello kept an active social media presence. He posted a photo in March 2025 welcoming Ramagem to Boa Vista, the capital of the Brazilian northern state of Roraima, where De Mello built his mining business.
But in recent months, his accounts have gone silent.
“He vanished off the map,” a former business partner in the United States told Agência Pública.
De Mello has been far more discreet about another aspect of his life: his businesses and properties in the U.S., a country he has frequented since the 1990s. He registered to vote in Florida in 1997, a step that requires attesting to U.S. citizenship, according to Miami-Dade County records obtained by ICIJ. An official from the Department of Elections told ICIJ that internal records show he has never voted, and his registration is inactive. Corporate records reviewed by ICIJ and Agência Pública link De Mello to at least three Florida companies since 1998 and to several addresses in the state since 1997, including a house with a pool in Boca Raton that he once co-owned.
One of the companies, X One Charters LLC, was founded in July 2023 and registered at the Sole Mia apartment where Ramagem would later stay. Founding documents list De Mello as its owner. A month after his arrest was ordered, in January 2026, he left the company, and Marcos Felix Ribeiro became its director. Yet the WhatsApp number on the company’s website is a phone number that belongs to De Mello, Agência Pública found. X One Charters rents out a yacht of the same name for cruises on Miami’s waters.
Ribeiro told Agência Pública that he had done business with De Mello in a mining venture in Guyana and that he received the yacht as payment for an excavator he left there, a trade worth about $100,000, the outlet reported.
A freight company also tied to the Sole Mia apartment lists as a director a pilot whom federal prosecutors accuse of flying for De Mello’s mining operation, according to Agência Pública. The pilot, who denied any business ties to De Mello, stayed in the Miami apartment months before Ramagem.
In August, De Mello was charged in a separate case with laundering more than 200 million reais, about $37 million, in gold and tin ore from Yanomami land between 2021 and 2023, Agência Pública reported. X One Charters was founded in July 2023, as the alleged scheme was underway.
De Mello did not respond to ICIJ and Agência Pública’s requests for comment.

The Verkhovna Rada has strengthened fire protection for critical enterprises
Kyiv • UNN
Bill No. 15102 allows critical enterprises to receive firefighting equipment from partners during martial law and thereafter. The document also defines requirements for the targeted use of humanitarian aid.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a whole Draft Law No. 15102, which strengthens fire safety protection for critically important enterprises. The Ministry of Internal Affairs reports this, UNN informs.
Details
According to Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Bohdan Drapiatyi, the document provides for the possibility of receiving firefighting and rescue equipment from international partners for enterprises in the energy, oil and gas, chemical, and metallurgical industries, as well as the defense industry.
According to Bohdan Drapiatyi, enterprises will be able to receive assistance during martial law and for 12 months after its termination or cancellation. The equipment will be used for fire safety protection of facilities by units of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine.
These legislative changes are of particular importance, as they create additional opportunities to strengthen fire safety protection at the relevant facilities
The law also defines requirements for the targeted use of humanitarian aid. The procedure for its receipt and distribution will be established by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine.
Previously
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada voted as a whole for a draft law on the safety and health of workers at work. The document is intended to regulate occupational safety issues in line with European approaches.
