A Tired Debate, a Clear Divide: Why Sunday’s Runoff Is About Bulgaria’s Place in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:37:58 UTC
06:37:58 KST

In Thursday night’s debate on the Bulgarian National Television, the only one before Sunday’s runoff, Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov were asked about the war next door. “Peace can only be achieved through negotiations,” Yotova said. “Russia cannot be excluded from this process.” For the Black Sea, where drones have hit five merchant ships in Bulgaria’s economic zone this month, she proposed a meeting of the six littoral states, Russia among them, to agree a moratorium on hostilities. Gyurov’s reply was shorter. “A moratorium, expressed merely as a wish, does not constitute a defense strategy. Silence is not defense.” He asked her to call the aggressor state by its name and then: “Did you call Putin to ask him to stop the war?”
That exchange captured what Sunday’s runoff has become. Presidential elections in Bulgaria are usually fought over domestic grievances, above all corruption and the cost of living. This one started that way. By its final week, Rumen Radev’s government had told voters the runoff was a choice “between peace and war,” refused to name Russia over the Black Sea strikes and hinted that Romania had invited further attacks by doing so. On Thursday, the two candidates gave opposite answers to the question Radev had posed.
What the Debate Showed
It was not a memorable night for either candidate. Both looked tired, with Yotova on the attack for most of the two hours and Gyurov on the defensive, replying with reasoned but brief and low-energy answers, as if Gyurov were the incumbent and Yotova the ambitious opposition figure. Neither landed a knockout blow. The substance, though, was unusually clear.
Yotova filled out her position with history and diplomacy. She argued that sending more weapons to Ukraine only adds to the casualties, that the war began in 2013 and 2014 and not in 2022, and that Russia cannot be brought to the table through ultimatums. Gyurov said the Black Sea “has become more insecure than the Persian Gulf,” the result of “a policy of appeasement,” and that an aggressor stops only “when the cost of an attack becomes prohibitively high.” On Bulgaria’s place in Europe he put it more bluntly still: “If you aren’t at the table, you’re on the menu.”
The debate also exposed where each candidate stands toward the government. Asked by moderator Poli Zlatareva whether she would uphold the policies of the government and Progressive Bulgaria from the presidency, Yotova would not answer, suggesting the question was a talking point of “the people who nominated Gyurov.” Gyurov said he was “an independent candidate” with “no connection” to the parties supporting him. The claim is generous to himself, since he co-founded Yes, Bulgaria, chaired We Continue the Change’s parliamentary group and runs with the backing of PP, DB and the DSB. But he answered the question, and she did not, and it matters because of what an aligned presidency would be aligned with.
Her other answers suggested what that alignment would look like. She said she would sign the government's next budget "even if, through some very unfortunate turn of events, you were to win," which is accurate, since her current term runs until January 2027. She called for scrapping the restricted list of caretaker prime ministers, echoing a proposal Radev's government announced in August. Asked about a deputy prime minister who divides the press into "good" and "bad" media while the government's press office campaigns for her, she replied that freedom of the media means freedom of opinion "for the Deputy Prime Minister, for the Prime Minister, and for everyone else."
Several of her claims do not survive a check. She said the deal with Turkey's Botas came about because "Kiril Petkov and Asen Vassilev cut off Russian gas supplies to Bulgaria overnight." In fact Gazprom halted deliveries in April 2022 after Sofia refused to pay in rubles, and the Botas agreement was signed in January 2023 by the caretaker government of Galab Donev, whom Radev appointed. Bulgaria has since come to owe Botas hundreds of millions of dollars. She presented Gyurov's security agreement with Ukraine as a commitment to send Bulgarian soldiers as peacekeepers, but Radev himself told parliament that the agreement contains no commitment to specific actions and his government has not terminated it. And when Gyurov argued that Bulgaria should shape EU decisions instead of waiting to veto them, Yotova said she could not recall a single Bulgarian veto, although Sofia blocked the start of North Macedonia's EU accession talks from late 2020, with Radev's backing, the very dispute the two argued over minutes later.
Gyurov was not immune either. His suggestion that the arrests of DPS mayors were the result of a broken deal between Progressive Bulgaria and DPS is speculation for which he offered no evidence. Yotova, in turn, accused him of describing the arrests as a new "Revival Process," the communist-era campaign against Bulgarian Turks, which he denied ever saying, and she cited no source. Former prime minister Kiril Petkov, whose government Yotova attacked over the French proposal on North Macedonia, responded after the debate that it was his cabinet that turned the veto into the French proposal backed by the whole EU, that his trip to Skopje with Yotova had been for the opening of a friendship club, unrelated to the negotiations, and that it was Russia that cut off gas supplies. Petkov is a partisan voice, but on Gazprom the record bears him out.
If the government wants this vote to be about where Bulgaria stands in the world, voters are entitled to take the question seriously. The answer the evidence points to is that Bulgaria's security lies with its allies in the European Union and NATO and that the presidency should be held by someone willing to say so clearly.
How the Governing Camp Reframed the Vote
The shift began the morning after the first round, when Yotova's 20-point poll lead had shrunk to 2.8 points in the actual count. Speaking at the Sofia Economic Forum on October 26, Radev framed the runoff as a choice between peace and war and urged voters to "send the 'assembly' to oblivion," his term for the coalition of GERB, DPS and PP-DB that preceded his government. He accused Andrey Gyurov of entering the race to protect Delyan Peevski and the official page of Progressive Bulgaria has since claimed that Gyurov met Peevski, which Gyurov calls a lie and for which no evidence has been offered.
The message went out through the Council of Ministers' official channels. When Gyurov's team complained to the Central Election Commission, the government's press office responded by instructing media to report the prime minister's words accurately, prompting the Association of European Journalists in Bulgaria to warn of conditions for censorship. A government that uses the state's machinery to tell voters that one candidate means war has no grounds to complain when the vote is read as a referendum on its foreign policy.
The online campaign has followed the same pattern. A Sensika Technologies report on the campaign's social media found coordinated, artificially amplified activity on both sides: a network of Facebook groups with about 320,000 members, built around Nikolay Barekov and the BNews site, was renamed to back Yotova at the end of August, while anonymous TikTok "resistance" accounts posted 544 videos praising Gyurov. In neither case did the researchers find a direct link to the official campaigns. The report also found the Russian network Rybar presenting Radev and Yotova as a "stability factor" and identical texts circulating between Revival-linked Telegram groups and channels tied to Russian networks, though it cautions that timing alone does not prove coordination.
Who Has Lined Up Behind Whom
The endorsements of the past four days tell their own story. Behind Yotova stand Progressive Bulgaria, the Bulgarian Socialist Party and Georgi Parvanov's ABV. On October 28 Ivelin Mihaylov of Greatness, who finished fifth with 57,643 votes, called on his supporters to vote for her, describing it as a step toward "a change in governance" and insisting it was no choice of the lesser evil.
Revival's Kostadin Kostadinov has stopped short of a formal endorsement, but he ruled out Gyurov entirely, promising that "Andrey Gyurov will not receive a single vote from Revival" and predicting that his voters would split between Yotova, abstention and the "I do not support anyone" box. In the same briefing he complained that the European Council had blamed Russia for the Black Sea attacks without evidence, and after the latest strike he suggested the targeted ship had "probably carried weapons," again without evidence. He told BGNES that Revival voters might have acted differently had Yotova formally asked for their support, and in the same remarks announced that he would travel to Moscow for a BRICS-related meeting where he is due to meet Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chair of Russia's Security Council, once again. The Party of European Socialists has endorsed Yotova, which led Ivaylo Mirchev of Yes, Bulgaria to ask how she squares that with tacit backing from a party that sits alongside Germany's AfD in the European Parliament.
Gyurov has the support of We Continue the Change, Democratic Bulgaria and the DSB, and a deputy chair of the Union of Democratic Forces has called for a vote for him. MECH's Radostin Vassilev has not formally endorsed Gyurov either, though on election night he told his voters that they should vote "under no circumstances for Iliana Yotova," adding: "In other words, they either vote for Andrey Gyurov or stay home." GERB and DPS have said nothing. Political analyst Berkay Chokdzhan argued on Bulgarian National Radio that both kept their voters at home in the first round to measure their electoral weight, and he doubts the arrests of DPS mayors were the main reason for the boycott.
A candidate is not responsible for everyone who votes for them. Still, a camp that now gathers the parties most reluctant to name Russia as the aggressor in the Black Sea has defined itself, whether Yotova intended it or not.
The Black Sea Paradox
Nothing captures the governing camp's position better than Radev's remark about Romania. At the same forum on October 26 he said that Romania had pointed to Russia as the force behind the drone strikes and that new attacks on ships in Romanian waters had followed. Damyana Veleva of Svobodna Tochka summed up the logic with a schoolyard image: you point at the bully, and your neighbor scolds you for causing the next fight because you did not keep quiet. In Romania, the reaction ranged from former interim prime minister Cătălin Predoiu's call for "consistency, logic and mutual solidarity" to commentator Cosmin Prelipceanu's verdict on Digi24 that the remark was "pure delirium."
The paradox is plain. Romania, where ships were sunk and sailors died off Constanța, is cast as partly responsible for naming the aggressor, while the aggressor goes unnamed. If accusing Russia provokes Russia, then Sofia already knows who is behind the attacks and has chosen not to say so. Radev has instead cited Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who, by his account, assured him she had no information that the drones were Russian.
The policy has not even bought Bulgaria the quiet it implies. On October 28 the container ship Contship Jet, bound for Constanța, was hit by three sea drones about 17 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra, the fifth attack in Bulgaria's own economic zone this month. A French patrol aircraft spotted it. Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov said the drones could not be intercepted because the attack took place outside Bulgarian territorial waters. Romania, meanwhile, has used F-16s to shoot down drones over its territory and summoned Russia's ambassador, and its new foreign minister, Dan Neculaescu, called the strikes a deliberate escalation in violation of international law. Sofia has asked allies for patrol aircraft, and that help is welcome, but it still will not name the threat that Bucharest has named.
The pattern extends onshore. On October 9, eight of the 18 antennas at a Starlink ground station near Sofia that supports Ukraine's defense were set on fire. Two 19-year-old German citizens were arrested in Duisburg on October 23, and Lithuanian prosecutors, who have charged them over a similar attempt in Vilnius, are examining possible links to Russia. Ivaylo Mirchev of Yes, Bulgaria says a partner intelligence service warned Sofia at least a week in advance, a claim the government has not confirmed. Radev chose to brief journalists instead of answering in parliament.
The Case for Yotova and Its Limits
Yotova's supporters have a case, and it deserves a fair hearing. Bulgaria is a small country next to a war and caution has real value. Insisting on evidence before blaming a nuclear power is defensible diplomacy, and a president who promises that no Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine speaks to a fear that many voters genuinely hold. After five years of political chaos, there is also something to be said for a head of state who works with the government instead of against it.
The trouble is that caution has become an excuse for passivity. The pledge on soldiers addresses a decision that belongs to parliament, which already ruled out participation in the fighting in February 2025, so it protects voters from a danger nobody proposed. The demand for proof has hardened into a refusal to draw the conclusion that Bulgaria's own allies, including the European Council and the government in Bucharest, have already drawn. And the language of peace has done nothing to stop ships burning off Kaliakra. Bulgaria's security in the Black Sea depends on Romanian coordination, French aircraft and NATO assets, and every hint that the victims brought the attacks on themselves makes that help harder to keep.
Gyurov's Answer
Gyurov's reply came in a video address this week. "While those in power frighten us with war, it is precisely their inaction that allows the war to reach our shores," he said. "The government cannot, does not know how to and fails to protect its citizens." He accused Radev and Yotova of acting as observers who "do not inform the population, hide and refuse to take clear action," and dismissed Progressive Bulgaria's claim about a meeting with Peevski as "desperate lies."
Not every line was measured. Comparing the government's use of the word "warmongers" to the vocabulary of Goebbels and Stalin is the kind of escalation his campaign should leave to others. The substance, though, has been consistent. After the October 13 strikes he called for consultations under Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which means talks among allies and no military commitment. He has argued for working with Romania and Turkey and for using EU and NATO mechanisms to protect shipping, and on Ukraine he speaks of support for a lasting peace backed by security guarantees. A fabricated quote claiming he would send Bulgarian troops to Ukraine was debunked by Factcheck.bg.
His central promise is modest and that is its strength. A president from outside the governing majority, he argues, would check a government that already controls parliament and the cabinet, without trying to bring it down.
What Sunday Decides
Bulgaria will remain a member of the European Union and NATO whoever wins on Sunday and no honest reading of the race turns it into a literal choice between Brussels and Moscow. The decision is narrower and still important. Voters are choosing whether the one institution outside the government's control should echo a cabinet that hesitates to name Russia and lectures its neighbors for doing so, or stand apart from it and insist that Bulgaria acts with the allies it depends on.
Radev asked voters to choose between peace and war. On the evidence of this month, peace in the Black Sea is better served by a president who stands with Romania, NATO and the EU than by one who waits for Moscow's ambassador to confirm what everyone else has already concluded. On Thursday night, Yotova was asked whether she would be the government's president and declined to answer. Voters can answer for her on Sunday.
This is an opinion piece. It reflects the author's views and was not commissioned or paid for by any candidate, party or initiative committee.

NEW DELHI: BJP is banking on twin planks of combativeness and persuasion directed at the opposition and the masses, respectively, as it looks to step up its nationwide mobilisation of people in the coming days, with top organisational functionaries and Union ministers Thursday giving shape to the party’s strategy ahead of INDIA bloc’s rally on Nov 1.“If they (opposition), for the sake of showing power, can gather 15,000 people at one place, we can gather much bigger crowds in many places the same day. Nabin expressed confidence that BJP’s rivals will bite the dust. “BJP’s ideology has found so much acceptance that even those who do not vote for it acknowledge that only PM can lead the nation in the right direction,” he said.
While BJP has zeroed in on seven outreach modes, including press conferences and interactions involving eminent citizens and the youth in nearly 800 places across country, mobilisation of a large number of people through “padyatra” (foot marches) in cities is its key instrument to blunt the opposition’s move to raise the heat on Election Commission and govt through its similar measures and rallies.

US conservatives charged over burqa voting stunt (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:36:41 UTC
06:36:41 KST

US conservatives charged over burqa voting stunt (VIDEO)
Conservative US influencers James O’Keefe and Cam Higby are facing felony charges over a video on Minnesota voting practices that allow one to “vouch” for eight others from the same precinct, while not having to show any ID.
Titled ‘I Wore Burqa To EXPOSE Election FRAUD In Minneapolis’, the stunt was shot during the Minnesota primary election in August. It features Higby posing as a Muslim woman dressed up in a full-face veil, with O’Keefe also wearing mock Muslim attire and speaking in a thick accent.
US President Donald Trump has for years alleged that Democrats have committed voter fraud, including by allegedly allowing non-citizens to participate in elections. The Republican has long advocated a standardized photo ID verification for voting.
On Wednesday, the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office announced that O’Keefe and Higby had been charged with unlawful voting and identity theft. According to Attorney Mary Moriarty, the pair had “visited multiple precincts… and misrepresented their identities by giving election judges names of registered voters in the precinct without those voters’ knowledge or permission.”
Speaking during a press conference, Moriarty said that summonses had been issued in both men’s names. Should O’Keefe and Higby fail to appear in court, an arrest warrant will follow, the official clarified.
While the Hennepin County attorney conceded that neither man signed an oath for ‘vouching’, she insisted that they still intentionally misrepresented “their identity to election judges in applying for a ballot.”
The conservative influencers availed themselves of a procedure which allows a registered voter in Minnesota to vouch for up to eight other voters from the same precinct, permitting the latter to cast their ballots without any further verification. Under Minnesota law, a person vouching for someone else must sign an oath and could face charges of perjury if it turns out that they lied on it.
Commenting on the charges filed against him in the Democratic-run state, Higby wrote on X that he was “not afraid of Minnesota.”
In their video, the conservative influencers specifically state they are “not actually going to vote… [and] touch any ballots,” with no intention to “break the law [or] to commit voter fraud.”
The idea was rather to “point out the vulnerabilities in the system and how easily exploitable it is,” O’Keefe and Higby explain.
Having visited three polling stations in different precincts, the pair concluded that “any person who has the address and name of another person can walk into a Minnesota… polling station and vote in that person’s name without ID.”
Additionally, poll workers “were going to allow me to vouch for eight other people so that they could vote the same day, also without verifying their ID,” Higby says in the video.
Late last year, Minnesota was thrust into the national spotlight after the federal authorities launched an investigation into an unrelated alleged fraud scheme involving multiple childcare centers run by locals of Somali background that appeared to be non-operational fronts.
The probe followed an expose by YouTuber Nick Shirley who claimed that the alleged fraudsters had received more than $110 million in state funds for non-existent services.

Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash

Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash
- Published
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of a deadly train crash that killed 69 people near Urda in central Spain on Wednesday morning.
The crash, between a high-speed Renfe train and a stationary Iryo train on the same track, also injured more than 100 people, many seriously.
The impact caused carriages to derail, and there are fears the death toll could still rise, with reports of family members searching for missing relatives in hospitals across the region.
The bodies of those killed have been taken to the main forensics institute in Toledo, where families have been giving DNA samples to help identify them.
The crash is the second rail disaster in Spain this year, and the worst in the country's history since 2013.
Who are the victims?
Julieta Gallego
Julieta Gallego, 24, was a Spanish long jumper who competed for Madrid athletics club, AD Sprint.
"The entire club is heartbroken," it wrote on Instagram.
The Royal Spanish Athletics Federation (RFEF) announced her death, external, expressing its condolences to her family, friends and teammates.
Gallego regularly competed in Spanish club championships, local media outlet ABC reported, external, and had a best jump of 5.9m (19ft 3in).
Raúl Chapado, president of RFEF, told the outlet that her death is a "blow that strikes at the very heart of the athletics family."
"Today, the sport mourns the passing of Julieta, a life ahead of her that has been unjustly extinguished".
Fátima Báñez
The death of former employment minister Fátima Báñez, 59, was confirmed by the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE), which she chaired.
"Her warmth, generosity, and commitment leave an indelible mark on businesses and the entire CEOE team," it said in a statement.
Báñez served in the government under former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy from 2011 until 2018, and was the first woman to hold the role. In 2012, she introduced controversial labour reforms that made it easier for companies to fire people, sparking mass protests across the country.
Following news of her death, Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso paid tribute to her, saying she would be "deeply missed".
"Spain loses a great political figure," she said.
José Manuel Chacón
The Civil Guard confirmed the death, external of its officer José Manuel Chacón, 31, in a statement expressing its "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
Antonio Montero Domínguez
Finance and tax lawyer, Antonio Montero Domínguez, was remembered as a "meticulous professional" and "tireless worker" by legal news website, El Derecho, external.
His death was confirmed by Spain's tax authority, external, where he had been an inspector between 2012-2016.
Additional reporting by Sarah Rainsford, Madeleine Lake and Tom McArthur

IN BRIEF: Putin hails Russia-Africa Summit, outlines prospects for cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:31:46 UTC
06:31:46 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The Third Russias-Africa Summit was a success and will give a strong impetus to the development of ties between Moscow and the African continent, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a press conference following the summit.
The head of state highlighted the significant potential for the further development of relations between Russia and African countries, noting that Moscow welcomed the continent's aspiration to play a greater role in international decision-making. He also outlined his views on global security, dialogue with Europe and the lessons of world wars.
TASS has compiled the key takeaways from the Russian president’s statements.
Summit’s success
The Third Russia-Africa Summit was a success and "will undoubtedly give a powerful impetus to the development of Russia-Africa cooperation."
"I would like to point out that this is the third Russia-Africa Summit. Holding such large-scale events has become a good tradition, which clearly indicates the determination of both Russia and African nations to continue boosting and strengthening multipolar ties in the spirit of true partnership and mutual respect for the sake of common growth and prosperity."
The motto of the Moscow-hosted summit was "For Peace, Security and Development," which set the tone and defined the topics of discussions.
"It is certainly satisfactory that the Moscow summit brought together 21 leaders of African nations, along with high-level delegations from most countries of the continent, and the heads of almost all leading African integration structures."
Russia and African countries adopted the 2027-2029 action plan for the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum: "The joint action plan through 2029 that we approved today contains an extensive list of specific goals aimed at developing Russia’s ties with the countries of the continent in the economic, trade, social and humanitarian spheres, as well as at implementing the decisions made at this summit."
As for economic goals, the action plan calls for increasing the volume of mutual imports and exports and improving their structure: "We are confident that the current level of the Russian-African trade turnover, which stands at $27 billion, is far from the limit. It’s safe to say that we are just starting out. However, if we look at our investment, it has reached billions of dollars, so we will definitely be able to increase trade."
The results of productive work at the Russia-Africa Summit are reflected in the Moscow Declaration: "This comprehensive document, designed for the long haul, reaffirms the commitment of all our countries to establishing a fair and democratic multipolar world order based on generally recognized principles of international law and the United Nations Charter."
It has been decided to continue holding Russia-Africa summits on a regular basis: "It’s important that all leaders have unanimously agreed to continue the practice of regular Russia-Africa summits."
The dates and venue of the next Russia-Africa sumit "will be agreed on in due course."
Prospects for cooperation
"It has become clear that the positions that Russia and Africa hold on most global and regional issues are not only very close but often coincide."
"Russia sincerely seeks to build a truly strategic, multifaceted partnership with Africa. And it’s important for us that we see the same constructive approach on behalf of our African friends to work together, hand in hand."
Russia has never been a colonial power, so the question about African territory potentially being used as an area for competition with other powers should not be directed to Moscow: "Throughout history, Russia has always viewed African countries only as friends. We have never pursued colonial policies; on the contrary, we helped African nations to break free from colonial dependence."
Russia and African countries "are natural allies in building a new, fairer multipolar world order."
"Of course, African countries seek to play a greater role in international decision-making, and we support that."
The African continent should definitely be represented on the UN Security Council: "Our African friends should figure out the way Africa will be represented there, either as a single voice, or African countries will rotate on the UN Security Council."
The UN needs reform but the process requires broad consensus: "The only question is that these decisions should be made on the basis of, as we say, broad consensus, and that we should not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Not to destroy universal international instruments, such as the United Nations, which are perhaps rightly criticized today, but are singularly unique."
Russia values the trust of African nations and seeks to take a careful approach to problems facing the region, including by "holding consultations with all parties involved in a conflict."
"Africa needs development and, as my colleagues have said, asks for nothing, only makes proposals and offers cooperation options. We are ready to boost our traditionally friendly relations on a completely new, modern soil."
At the meetings in the Kremlin, the African leaders supported the idea of "expanding the network of branches of Russian universities in their countries and creating new educational centers that promote the Russian language, science and culture: Several colleagues talked about opening Russian cultural centers."
Russia will increase the number of students from African countries enrolled in its universities, "including on a free basis."
Training African students is beneficial for Russia because later they will become the people Moscow can rely on in Africa: "I want to say that we in Russia need and benefit from such work [of educating African students]. Why? Because the people who worked with us, studied, received knowledge, acquired this knowledge, later use it in their countries. And, of course, they are guided by their partners in the Russian Federation. These are, relatively speaking, the people we rely on in these countries."
Russia will continue to supply grain to Africa, "we will do this as before, both contractually and free of charge."
Russia will easily adapt agricultural technologies to other climatic conditions, and then Africa will be able not only to produce but also to export its products: "Everything can be transformed, and Africa will not only be a food producer, it will not only fully cover its needs, but will also be able to export to foreign markets."
Russia and African countries intend to deepen their health protection partnership. In particular, joint exercises are planned to combat outbreaks of infections: "We will increase the supply of effective medicines, transfer mobile laboratories, and conduct joint exercises to respond to outbreaks of infections.
"I will mention, in particular, the decision taken to extend the Russian program of assistance to African countries to combat infections until 2029."
Advantages of cooperation with Russia
Back in the early 2000s, Russia was only a buyer of grain, "and now we top the world as a grain exporter."
The experience of Moscow medicine should not only be implemented in other regions of Russia but also offered for export: "We still have many healthcare problems in Russia. This is clear, and we must spread what is happening in Moscow to other regions of the Russian Federation. But why not offer the same to our friends in other countries, including Africa?"
Russia is one of the few countries in the world that can boast full digital sovereignty. Its IT companies successfully compete in foreign markets: "Russia, along with the United States, the People's Republic of China, is one of the few countries that has full sovereignty in digital technologies. Our platform solutions are very interesting and good. All this is developing not only on the territory of the Russian Federation. Our companies successfully compete in foreign markets.
"Our partners have great interest in small nuclear power plants. Our international competitors, almost everyone, are talking about their readiness to build low-power nuclear power plants, but so far no one has done anything. Only Russia has created such small nuclear power plants, which are working, even in the north they are working. Now we are actually completing two more nuclear power plants."
Of the 32 nuclear power units that are being built by third countries abroad, 28 are being built by the Russian company Rosatom: "The investments are significant. We are investing almost $25 billion in just one power plant in Egypt. There are other such examples. And we are ready to continue working in Africa."
Lessons of world wars and readiness for dialogue with Europe
Russia remembers all the tragic pages of history well, including the lessons of both world wars, and for its part does its best to ensure that nothing like this happens to humanity again: "We in Russia remember all this well, including the lessons of WWI and WWII. And we are doing everything to ensure that nothing like this happens on a global scale."
The West has not achieved its goal of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia: "Many people are talking about preparing for war by 2030. Is this right or wrong? First of all, we are ready, but we don't want any war with Europe."
If it comes to a war between Russia and Europe, "there will be no winners. No one should forget about this."
Russia supports any steps to restore full-fledged relations with European countries: "Either with all of them together in the form of the well-known EU organization, or bilaterally. OK, we don't care, whatever they want."
"Regarding the telephone conversation with the representatives, or rather, with the leaders of the EU countries, with Finland and with Norway. They immediately stressed at the beginning of the conversation that they do not represent the EU as an organization, they are calling me in a national capacity, as they say."
The telephone conversation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store was initiated by them: "The conversation took place on their initiative, indeed.
"I know that there was criticism of them later, but it's not our business to assess whether it was correct or incorrect. I think it's right [that Stubb and Store called]. After all, there are the people in Europe who do not want to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia, as some do, but rather want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue."
Russia does not want a situation similar to the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf one to develop in the Baltic Sea. The issue of security in the Baltic was raised during the telephone conversation with Stubb and Store, who hope that all participants in international communication will comply with international maritime law: "We support this approach. Can it be different? Otherwise, there will be a situation similar to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. Does anyone want the same situation to develop in the Baltic Sea as in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz? I don't know. We don't want that."
Moscow is ready to respond to any challenge in the Baltic Sea but does not want to create tension there: "We do not want this. But we will respond to any challenge."

Can Canada, UK and Australia grasp chance offered by US-China rivalry?
As the US shifts away from its commitment to global primacy, these Anglosphere nations have the potential to be a pivotal force for global stability
As middle powers, Australia, Britain and Canada can do more than most other nations to influence global peace in the face of a new great power rivalry between China and the United States. These three nations owe their citizens, and perhaps the wider world, an earnest effort to rise to the challenge of being peacemakers.
They have three attributes in common that give them unique potential to be a pivotal force. First is their own shared histories as members of the Anglosphere and therefore close allies of the US. Second is the recent US impetuousness and erratic behaviour towards the three of them, which demands greater independence and balance in their international relationships. Third is their shared middle power status, affording them enough diplomatic, military and trade significance to have great influence.
Today, though, Australia’s, Britain’s and Canada’s results as agents for global stability are mixed.

Steinmeier urges China to use its influence on Russia to end war against Ukraine
He made the statement during a speech at Peking University on Thursday, Ukrinform reports.
"China is a permanent member of the Security Council and has close ties with Russia, so let us work together to persuade Russia to cease its attacks and engage in serious negotiations," Steinmeier said.
He stressed that Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is an attack on one of the fundamental principles of the international order: that borders must not be changed by force and that states must not be deprived of their freedom and independence.
"The people of Ukraine must be able to choose their own path to the future – just like the Chinese, the Germans and people of other nationalities want to do," Steinmeier said.
He stressed that Russia's war threatens not only Ukraine but also peace throughout Europe. Steinmeier also recalled that, for decades after the Cold War, Germany had sought to build a stable and reliable security architecture with Russia, but Moscow had chosen confrontation.
He noted that several months ago, an airport in central Germany had been targeted by drones, and evidence of those responsible led to Russia.
Addressing his Chinese audience, Steinmeier stressed that a prolonged war also runs counter to China's own economic interests, as it threatens international trade routes, supply chains, and energy and food security.
"After almost five years of war, longer than the First World War, after hundreds of thousands of deaths, after daily attacks on heat, water and electricity, especially now as winter looms, people long for an end to the suffering. They rightfully expect us to use the different means available to us, but to work together to bring this about," the German president said.

Starbucks sales miss expectations, but its U.S. turnaround is gaining steam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:29:59 UTC
06:29:59 KST

Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.
However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026.
"We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website.
Starbucks is ahead of schedule to meet the fiscal 2028 targets laid out at its investor day in January, he said on the company's earnings conference call.
For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%.
Starbucks is projecting North American same-store sales growth of 4% for the fiscal year.
The company's earnings and revenue outlook includes an additional week and the effects of the shift in its China business to a joint venture business model. Starbucks is also projecting slight deflation in coffee prices and slowing net new North American cafe openings, which will both weigh on its full-year revenue, according to CFO Cathy Smith.
Here's what the company reported for the quarter ended Sept. 27 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 80 cents adjusted vs. 72 cents expected
- Revenue: $9.14 billion vs. $9.23 billion expected
Starbucks reported fiscal fourth-quarter net income attributable to the company of $677.2 million, or 59 cents per share, up from $133.1 million, or 12 cents per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring and impairment costs and other items, the company reported earnings per share of 80 cents.
Net revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, reflecting the joint venture deal in China.
The company's global same-store sales increased 7.2%, fueled by growth in average ticket, and beating Wall Street estimates of 6%, according to StreetAccount. Transactions grew 1.8% in the quarter.
Starbucks' U.S. cafes reported same-store sales growth of 7.7%, topping StreetAccount estimates of a 6.5% increase.
Under Niccol's "Back to Starbucks" strategy, the company has focused on improving service, making its cafes more welcoming and sharpening its marketing. The changes have helped to win back customers.
"Starbucks brand affinity is at near record levels as our menu innovation, marketing and merchandise continue to create moments that drive culture and bring people into our coffee houses," Niccol told analysts.
The company said its North American rollout of its fall menu, which includes the iconic pumpkin spice latte, was the company's strongest ever autumn launch day. And matcha is now a $1 billion drink for Starbucks.
Outside of North America, the company's international comparable sales ticked up 0.9%, as traffic declines offset an increase to average ticket. That growth fell short of analyst estimates of a 3.2% increase, according to StreetAccount.
After its China business transitioned to a joint venture, Starbucks has shifted most of its international business to a licensed model, allowing local operators to take charge. The company is also exploring selling a majority stake in its Japan business, Reuters reported in September.
Starbucks opened 303 net new cafes during the quarter. In September, the company announced it would close about 1% of its North American footprint, or about 250 locations, as part of its turnaround.
By the end of its fiscal year, across the U.S. and Canada, the company also completed more than 1,700 cafe uplifts, meant to make its stores more welcoming to customers. The company has said locations that receive a makeover, with tweaks like increased seating and softer lighting, see higher transactions in the aftermath.

Exclusive-Greek PM calls Turkey-Libya maritime deal ‘void;’ calls for global truce after Black Sea attacks
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:25:57 CET
06:25:57 KST

By Antoni Slodkowski
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said on Thursday that the recently signed maritime deal between Libya’s eastern parliament and Turkey was “blatantly illegal, null and void,” adding that it “completely disregards the geography.”
Mitsotakis, speaking to Reuters as Greece ends its UN Security Council presidency, also called for an urgent “international truce” to protect shipping in the Black Sea after the sinking of a Greek-owned container vessel on Wednesday.
Libya’s eastern parliament last week approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey, drawing condemnation from Athens, but also Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, as a threat to regional security and international legal order.
“It completely disregards the geography, the reality that there are Greek islands — they seem to completely disappear in the thinking of Turkey and Libya,” Mitsotakis said, accusing them of attempting to create a “fait accompli” that ignores the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has said that reactions from the EU and others to the approval of the agreement, originally agreed in 2019, had no legitimate basis, defending Ankara’s policy in the eastern Mediterranean.
Since the 2019 Libya-Turkey deal, Greece has awarded a license to a consortium led by Chevron to look for gas off the island of Crete and has sought a separate agreement with Libya on demarcating their maritime zones.
Mitsotakis assured “there’s no risk that these explorations will be in any way challenged.”
Referring to Libya and Greece as “natural neighbors,” Mitsotakis, who first became prime minister in 2019 and is in his second term, urged the African country to negotiate directly with Athens and take the discussions “very, very seriously.”
ATTACKS ON SHIPS IN THE BLACK SEA
Mitsotakis, 58, spoke to Reuters after chairing a council debate on maritime security, only hours after a Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria in the latest strike on ships in the western Black Sea this month.
Greek-operated ships are among the world’s largest fleets of tankers and are pivotal for trade across the Black Sea region, whose waters are shared by Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania and Turkey, as well as warring Russia and Ukraine, which Moscow invaded in February 2022.
“We do need some sort of international truce when it comes to the freedom of navigation,” said Mitsotakis, adding that it was of “utmost priority” to allow for exports of grain from the region into the world through the Black Sea.
“Greek shipowners would be the first to resume trading in the Black Sea, also from Ukraine, assuming a safe passage is guaranteed,” he said, stressing the rising costs of shipping as chartering and insurance expenses have “gone through the roof.”
It was not immediately clear who had carried out the attack, which added to growing concerns about the impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine on commercial shipping in the area.
Mitsotakis said that Ukraine was financially dependent on exports of its products: “They had a bumper harvest, but the grain is now sitting in silos, in danger of rotting.”
“Unfortunately, for the moment, Russia doesn’t seem to be interested in engaging in a substantive discussion,” he said.
RED SEA SECURITY, RUSSIA
Mitsotakis also called on the European Union to bolster its naval mission to protect shipping in the Red Sea called Aspides, which was launched in 2024 to protect from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Intensifying hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
“My argument is simple: the European Union has an interest in having a concrete presence with hard assets in this part of the world, and we need more countries to participate in Aspides,” Mitsotakis told Reuters.
He said Greece, Italy and France have deployed “assets” as part of the mission and that was “clearly not enough.” Diplomats told Reuters as of late September there were six warships operating as part of the operation.
The Houthis said this week they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route.
“If we really want to send the message also to the Gulf countries that we take their security seriously, but we also protect the critical arteries and waterways that are absolutely indispensable for European trade, we should be willing to deploy more assets to this part of the world,” Mitsotakis said.
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s move earlier this month to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, Mitsotakis reaffirmed Greek support for sanctions on Moscow.
“We believe that we need to put economic pressure and impose more financial pain on Russia to send a very clear signal that as long as they prolong this war, they will suffer very specific economic consequences,” he said.
(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

álvaro urbano brings casa cueva’s botanical memories to life at museo jumex in mexico city
in an exclusive interview, the spanish artist discusses helen fowler o’gorman’s overlooked legacy, the possibilities of architectural fiction, and why a sculpted leaf can have an attitude.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ÁLVARO URBANO REVISITS CASA CUEVA AT MUSEO JUMEX
An architectural history can begin with the person tending the garden. In Helen, at Museo Jumex in Mexico City, Álvaro Urbano approaches Casa Cueva through the botanical imagination of Helen Fowler O’Gorman, the artist who shared the house with her husband, artist and architect Juan O’Gorman. Built in the mid-20th century in Pedregal de San Ángel, the home brought architecture into close contact with the surrounding terrain and vegetation. Urbano draws its histories into an installation where sculpted plants, geological references, and architectural memories occupy the same uncertain present. Curated by Rosela del Bosque and Carolina Estrada García, the exhibition runs from October 16, 2026, to February 7, 2027, placing Helen’s work and her relationship with Mexico’s flora at the center of the story.
Urbano’s introduction to Helen came through conversations with Mexican friends, whose stories about Casa Cueva prompted him to investigate her practice. ‘In spaces built by their own inhabitants, architectural decisions are closely tied to a way of living,’ he tells designboom in an exclusive interview. For the artist, the house was itself a sculpture, its relationship with the landscape inseparable from the routines of those who lived there. ‘The house opened onto the landscape, or rather surrendered itself to it, incorporating the conditions of the terrain and the presence of plants.’ The garden Helen planted and maintained belonged to that same conception of space. Following her through the house shifts attention toward the daily acts of observation, cultivation, and care that helped give the architecture its character.
HELEN FOWLER O’GORMAN’S BOTANICAL WORLD TAKES SHAPE
Inside her studio at Casa Cueva, Helen spent fifteen years working on the book published in 1961 as Mexican Flowering Trees and Plants. Its scope extended beyond her garden into the wider Mexican landscape, which she explored alongside Juan. While he searched for differently colored minerals for his petro-murals, she collected flowers and plants. ‘There is something beautiful about that shared search for color: he found it in minerals; she found it in flowers and plants,’ Urbano reflects. The parallel gives the exhibition an intimate point of departure: two practices looking at the same terrain, gathering different elements, and bringing them back into a shared domestic world.
With Helen’s original watercolors lost, Urbano turned to the book’s printed reproductions, translating their botanical imagery into three-dimensional forms through metal and paint. ‘I conceived these sculptures as small monuments to her way of observing Mexico’s flora, to her affections and the attention she devoted to it,’ he explains. That passage from watercolor to printed page to sculpture makes the distance from the originals part of the work. Helen’s plants enter another material life, carrying traces of her looking alongside the decisions of the artist interpreting them. Within the installation, they coexist with references to the Pedregal’s geological landscape, Juan’s petro-murals, and the later alterations made by Mexican artist Helen Escobedo, who subsequently occupied Casa Cueva.
ARCHITECTURAL FICTION ALLOWS DIFFERENT TIMES TO COEXIST
Those successive lives remain deliberately unresolved. ‘We do not know whether the petro-murals are being covered or uncovered,’ Urbano says of the installation. ‘Rather than fixing an original state of the house, I wanted its different times to coexist.’ Testimonies, photographs, and material remnants offer access to Casa Cueva while leaving gaps and occasionally contradicting one another. Urbano gives those inconsistencies room within the exhibition, allowing the house to emerge through the experiences of its inhabitants. A visitor encounters a place whose transformations resist a single definitive account, with Helen’s botanical work providing a way into memories that architectural histories can leave at the margins.
This interest in unfinished stories extends across Urbano’s practice, which frequently returns to interrupted projects and places where something remains pending. Fiction lets him change the coordinates: continue an abandoned possibility or bring together moments that never coincided. ‘Architecture thus becomes a character with its own voice, capable of recounting its changes, triumphs, and failures,’ he explains. The question ‘what if?’ opens a building to possibilities beyond its documented past. It also prompts a closer look at the construction of that record: whose version survives, which experiences disappear, and what might still be told through the gaps. In Helen, that freedom allows the house’s botanical, geological, and domestic histories to share a stage.
SCULPTED PLANTS AND THE ART OF BELIEVABLE ILLUSION
Theater and cinema inform how Urbano builds these encounters, giving apparently ordinary objects the ability to suggest events beyond the visitor’s view. Describing his installations, he points to cigarette butts that imply someone has just been there, or dry leaves that suggest a gust of wind has crossed a room. ‘Illusion allows me to show the life of an object,’ he says. ‘More than replicating its appearance, I seek to imitate its life and transport it into a setting where it can tell a story.’ Such details invite viewers to assemble their own account of what happened. Urbano connects this process to memory itself: fragmentary, blurred, and liable to absorb things that never occurred.
The illusion also rewards close inspection. Urbano sculpts the works in his Berlin studio without taking molds from the original objects, making each bend and inclination a deliberate gesture. ‘The tilt of a leaf or the orientation of a flower gives them an attitude,’ he explains. ‘I am interested in how the object looks at you, what relationship it establishes with you.’ Approaching the sculptures reveals their materials and the traces of their making, adding another encounter to the one suggested from a distance. For Urbano, discovering how the scene has been constructed leaves its emotional possibilities intact: ‘As in theater, recognizing the artifice does not prevent us from entering the fiction or establishing an emotional connection with what happens.’

On Oct. 20, European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno declared a hunger strike in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky.

CCPA penalises Justdial, Sunrise Foods for safety, misleading product claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:22:14 UTC
06:22:14 KST

File photo: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)
NEW DELHI: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed penalties on online business directory Justdial and Sunrise Foods for violations involving consumer safety and misleading product claims.While it slapped a Rs 10 lakh penalty on Justdial for allowing listings of ammonium nitrate, a regulated explosive substance, on its platform without adequate safeguards, a Rs 1 lakh penalty was imposed on Sunrise Foods for marketing its bread as “100% Whole Wheat Bread” without disclosing its actual whole-wheat content.In an order on Wednesday, CCPA held that Justdial’s platform carried listings of ammonium nitrate without adequate disclosure of sellers’ valid licences issued by Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), verification of buyers’ eligibility and mechanisms to ensure transaction traceability. The listings also lacked appropriate warnings about legal restrictions on the possession and use of the substance.Justdial argued that it was an online directory and information-listing service, not a trading platform and that the listings were old and sourced from public-domain information or user submissions. However, CCPA held that reliance on vendor representations and removal of listings only after complaints or regulatory intervention was insufficient.
It directed the company to immediately discontinue listings, advertising and facilitation of access to the product.In a separate order, CCPA penalised Sunrise Foods for its “Everyday 100% Whole Wheat Bread”. The authority found the product contained only 64% whole wheat, below the prescribed 75% threshold for using the nomenclature “whole-wheat bread”. The packaging did not disclose the proportion of whole wheat, potentially misleading consumers about the product’s composition.
Sunrise Foods argued that the “100%” claim referred to the wheat flour component being entirely whole-wheat flour rather than refined flour. However, CCPA said the representation created a misleading impression about the product’s composition. It directed the company to discontinue the claim across print, electronic and social media with immediate effect.It directed the company to immediately discontinue misleading advertisements across media and submit a compliance report within 15 days.

Why Does Spain Keep Having Deadly Rail Accidents?

Why Does Spain Keep Having Deadly Rail Accidents?

====================================================================================================

Everything that went wrong with Spain’s high-speed railways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:21:13 UTC
06:21:13 KST

Everything that went wrong with Spain’s high-speed railways
Spain’s high-speed rail network once embodied the country’s rise as a modern European power. Deadly crashes are raising fresh questions over safety, maintenance and years of investment choices.
For decades, Spain’s high-speed rail network had been a source of national pride, symbolizing the country’s rapid modernization and its rise among Europe’s leading economies.
But Wednesday’s deadly train disaster — following another mass-casualty rail crash in January — is turning that legacy into a political liability and putting the state of the railways at the center of the campaign ahead of the Nov. 29 snap election.
“The deaths of more than 100 people in two train accidents in the span of eight months raise serious questions about the integrity of the railway system,” opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said Thursday, adding that Spaniards “deserve answers.”
Advertisement
Those answers are hard to find. Experts point to human error, maintenance issues, austerity and EU-level rail safety reform as all having played their part in the deaths of at least 69 people near Toledo on Wednesday.
Spain’s transport ministry says the preliminary investigation points to a chain of failures. After a computer malfunction knocked out the German-made signaling system installed in 1992, railway network officials took control and authorized a train to proceed along a track where another had stopped, causing the deadly collision.
Jaime Tamarit, a former director of a European railway-signaling certification laboratory who helped oversee the development of the pan-European system meant to prevent railway accidents, said the system failure revealed the grave state of Spain’s high-speed rail network.
“The whole point of a train-protection system is to guard against human error,” he said, adding that the failure of such a critical mechanism suggested, “the infrastructure is in a terrible state.”
Between 2018 and 2022, Spain allocated an average of €1.5 billion a year to high-speed rail —more than France or Germany — but most of that money went toward new infrastructure. Maintenance, renewals and upgrades accounted for about 16% of Spain’s high-speed rail spending, compared with 34% to 39% in France, Germany and Italy, according to European Commission data.
“If you have more train lines, you need more staff, and to spend more on maintenance,” Tamarit said.
Advertisement
The safety expert attributed the apparent lack of investment to political prioritization that values flashy new construction over maintaining existing infrastructure. “Maintenance is vital — but also politically invisible,” he lamented.
Adif, Spain’s railway infrastructure manager, has repeatedly defended the adequacy of its maintenance regime and insists it has always complied with safety requirements. The state-owned company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Unanswered questions
Ana Miranda, a European Parliament lawmaker from Galicia’s nationalist BNG party, accused Spanish authorities of failing to learn from past rail disasters, drawing parallels between Wednesday’s crash near Toledo and the 2013 Angrois disaster in Galicia, which killed 80 people and injured 152.
“The Angrois accident is happening again,” she said, arguing that the government of then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy had focused on human error while failing to adequately address the technical and systemic issues that may have contributed to the disaster.
“In the Angrois case they singled out the driver, and now they’re trying to do the same with the control workers,” Miranda said. “We need to get to the root of the causes, and that requires investigations.”
The EU Agency for Railways reached a similar conclusion in 2016, when it issued a report finding the investigation into the Angrois disaster had not met the required standards of independence and recommended a new inquiry. The European Commission subsequently launched infringement proceedings over wider shortcomings in Spain’s railway safety oversight.
Advertisement
Miranda said authorities had also failed to conduct a sufficiently rigorous inquiry into January’s Adamuz crash, which killed 46 people. An independent technical investigator assisting the probe has alleged that Adif altered accident reports, while questions have also emerged over documentation relating to inspections of track welds on the stretch where the crash occurred.
Adif denies wrongdoing and says it has cooperated with the judicial investigation.
For Miranda, the repeated controversies point to a failure spanning successive governments. She accused the country’s two dominant parties — the center-right People’s Party, which was in power at the time of the Angrois crash, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's center-left Socialists, who have governed Spain since 2018 — of maintaining a “pact of silence on high-speed rail.”
“They had enough time to implement rules,” she said. “How easy is it to blame the worker when nothing has been done to change things?”
Europe’s slow transition to safer railways
Wednesday’s crash highlights a wider European challenge: replacing fragmented national signaling systems with modern technology while maintaining aging infrastructure.
The trains involved in the deadly collision in Toledo were not using ERTMS, the European Union’s standard rail-signaling system, which can automatically brake trains that exceed permitted speeds or fail to obey signals.
Spain’s post-pandemic recovery plan included investments to modernize railway signaling and traffic control, including the deployment of ERTMS. The Madrid–Seville line was also due to be equipped with the system under a separate signaling-renewal project authorized in 2020, but the upgrade remains incomplete.
Advertisement
Investigators have yet to determine whether ERTMS would have made a difference in Wednesday’s crash.
Deployment of the latest railway safety technology across Europe remains far behind schedule. By the end of 2024, European Train Control System technology — the core signaling component of ERTMS — was operational on only about 12,400 kilometers of track, roughly 10% of the EU’s trans-European transport network, according to the European Union Agency for Railways.
National plans aim to expand coverage to 40,000 kilometers by 2030, out of roughly 63,000 kilometers the EU wants equipped across the bloc. But an EU official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, said they doubted that target would be met on time.
Politics has been part of the problem, the official said, with countries having “different reasons for not adopting the system” and Brussels allowing national systems to remain in place for years. “It was only in 2024 when we actually said ERTMS is going to be the single European system,” the official added.
The EU aims to have ERTMS installed on 57% of its main rail corridors by 2030 — but that target increasingly seems out of reach.
Rail lobbies in Brussels say funding for signaling and network upgrades is insufficient. But these concerns have only sharpened after the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU proposed cutting the Connecting Europe Facility by 14% from the Commission’s original proposal in its latest negotiating document for the bloc's next seven-year budget.
Advertisement
Further safety improvements could be undermined by cuts to EU research programs. Indeed, a draft of the new Horizon Europe structure under the next long-term budget, seen by POLITICO, could cut rail research entirely — even though that research is what underpins the ERTMS blueprints the industry will have to adopt.
The official added that companies won’t expand production without knowing that “there are contracts for next year.”
Despite the obstacles, the European Commission is trying to accelerate the rollout of the safety mechanisms.
Last September, industry and policymakers gathered in Brussels to discuss an “ERTMS Deal” aimed at standardizing technical requirements, speeding up approvals and encouraging deployment through EU funding.
But the technical blueprint underpinning the plan is still being developed, with an initial batch of results expected by the end of 2027 and some elements requiring further testing and validation.
That leaves little time before the EU’s 2030 deployment targets. For an industry seeking to expand production, the official said, the uncertainty itself is an obstacle for companies that ultimately need to know “there are contracts for next year.”
Delays in improving rail safety remain a challenge across Europe. The deadly crash on the line between Madrid and Seville is a stark reminder that the stakes of getting those improvements right are measured in human lives.

Stephen Curry ties LeBron James for most 40-point games at age 35 or older
Stephen Curry has tied LeBron James for the most NBA games with at least 40 points after turning 35, according to a post published on the Golden State Warriors’ official Instagram account, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The 38-year-old scored a season-high 44 points in Golden State’s 119-114 road victory over the Minnesota Timberwolves at Target Center in Minneapolis on Wednesday, October 28. It marked his 15th 40-point game since turning 35, matching James’ record. Michael Jordan ranks third with 12.
Curry finished with eight rebounds and six assists, shooting 11 of 27 from the field, including six 3-pointers, and making all 16 of his free throws. Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg contributed 26 points as the Warriors earned their second straight victory after opening the season with three losses.
Golden State led by as many as 24 points before Minnesota mounted a late comeback. The Timberwolves were playing without Anthony Edwards following surgery on his right knee.
Curry is a four-time NBA champion, two-time league MVP and the NBA’s all-time leader in made 3-pointers. In 2016, he became the first unanimous MVP in league history after helping Golden State finish the regular season with a record 73 wins and nine losses. That season, he also set the NBA record with 402 3-pointers.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that LeBron James had joined the Philadelphia 76ers after eight seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers. The move took the four-time NBA champion to Philadelphia ahead of his 24th NBA season.

Fang said the Committee for the Protection of Journalists still considered Sarraj a legitimate journalist, and the ABC did too.
Henderson then claimed that the IDF had a Hamas ID card which belonged to Sarraj.
In a statement provided to the ABC today, she admitted she was wrong.
"While the IDF concluded Mr Al-Sarraj was a Hamas military operative, I incorrectly said he held a Hamas ID card rather than the two Al Jazeera journalists I referenced in the hearing who had Hamas military ID numbers,” Henderson said in a statement.
Labor MP warns of international student 'overcorrection'
Friend of the blog Clare Armstrong is reporting this morning that Labor is recalibrating its international student crackdown to make sure the tough rules do not deter quality applicants from Australia.
The review will focus on international student coming from South Asia, over concerns that high refusal rates are dissuading genuine applicants and damaging Australia's education sector.
Visa rejections have soared in the two years since a ministerial direction was introduced to strengthen assessments of whether education is the primary purpose behind a student's application.
Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill has defended the reforms in a speech in Sydney today as necessary for restoring integrity, but has warned against an "overcorrection".

Spender warns CGT changes 'not fair' as bill heads to Senate
Community Strong MP Allegra Spender says the government's changes to the capital gains tax system are wrong and need to be fixed.
The changes would see the existing 50 per cent capital gains tax discount for individuals, trusts, and partnerships replaced with cost base indexation.
The bill passed the House of Representatives this week and will now come before the Senate.
Spender has told News 24 says while she supports change, the legislation in its current form would discourage investment.
"You take a lot of risk starting a business and it's not the same as getting wages, it's a different level of risk," she says.
Spender is pushing for the CGT concession to change from 50 per cent to 40 per cent, applied to all businesses and shares.
Fast-track inquiry launched into new anti-drone laws
A very quick parliamentary inquiry has been launched into new legislation handing Defence new powers to manage drones flying over its bases.
Drones are a rapidly growing problem for Defence, which yesterday told Estimates it is seeing hundreds of incidents each year where drones are flown into, or over, sensitive bases.
A series of incidents at one of the Air Force's most sensitive bases caused alarm earlier this year, when drones were seen flying over Williamtown, near Newcastle, which houses much of Australia's fleet of f-35 fighter jets.
Reports that staff on the base were instructed to close the blinds prompted questions over whether the ADF was capable of, or even allowed to, take down drones flying over its bases.
Legislation introduced to parliament this week aims to remedy that, giving the ADF the legal authority to "conduct counter-measures"—that is, take down—drones if it needs to.
Hearings are already underway this morning, with Defence officials up first, and companies like DroneShield up later on.
Trucking sector calls for renewed fuel tax relief
Australia's peak trucking and road freight bodies are urging the government to reinstate fuel tax relief.
This week's September inflation figures came in hotter than expected, with soaring fuel prices contributing to the rise.
The treasurer has so far ruled out repeating the temporary cuts to the fuel excise and heavy vehicle road user charge, which were implemented earlier this year.
But NatRoad CEO Warren Clark says the government should bring the road user charge down to zero until the end of January.
"What it does is give small businesses the cash flow injection, the cash flow help that it needs to actually remain in business through that really difficult and challenging time," Clark tells AM.
The Australian Trucking Association's Mathew Munro agrees, saying that with diesel prices once again on the rise, targeted relief must be back on the table for the industry.
"While the government can't do anything about the war in Iran, they certainly can do something about the taxation measures that they apply," the CEO says.
"We think that given the circumstances now are comparable to what they were early on in this crisis, we think that relief is now warranted again."
Man charged with threatening a federal politician
A Cairns man has been charged with threatening a federal parliamentarian on social media, marking the latest crackdown by federal authorities on digital abuse aimed at public figures.
The arrest comes just over a week after an alleged attack on Independent MP Helen Haines shocked the nation and highlighted the volatile environment facing Australia's elected representatives.
An Australian Federal Police statement said one of their National Security Investigations (NSI) teams executed a search warrant at the 53-year-old's Earlville home.
He was served a Notice to Appear in court for using a carriage service to menace, harass, or cause offence under section 474.17(1) of the Commonwealth Criminal Code.
The charge carries a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment.
The man is scheduled to appear in the Cairns Magistrates Court on December 3.
Reliability, diversification on agenda for Australia Post inquiry
Labor MP Susan Templeman, chair of the communications, arts and sport committee, says the probe into Australia Post announced today will have a broad remit to look at the role the service plays in communities across the country.
Templeman said the committee would examine its ongoing sustainability and accessibility in both metropolitan and regional Australia.
"It's an absolutely vital part of all our communities … vital for business, and vital for our economy," she said.
The committee will consider growing competition from other parcel carriers and what that means for Australia Post's long-term future, while also considering how the service can diversify and what additional offerings it could provide.
It will also look at the reliability of postal services, particularly for small businesses that rely on the network to reach customers.

CSIRO job cuts help keep science skills 'current'
The CSIRO has told a Senate estimates hearing that job losses are a part of the organisation's efforts to stay "contemporary and modern".
The science agency has slashed hundreds of jobs in recent years and says it is consulting on changes that could affect another 86 full-time jobs in its biosecurity and technology research units.
CEO Doug Hilton said the units could potentially be merged or transferred to make room for reinvestment in other research areas.
"There are opportunities to invest in areas that we think could generate more impact for the community," he said.
The reinvestment process could create 150 new roles, but Mr Hilton said it was not always possible to transfer staff between units.

Parliamentary probe into future of Australia Post
The Albanese government is launching a parliamentary inquiry in a bid to shore up the long-term viability of Australia Post.
The 217-year-old institution has faced challenges in recent times, with falling foot traffic at some post offices and a drop in letters.
Last financial year, there were about 1.42 billion letters sent through Australia post — but that was down 14.7 per cent from the year before.
Communications Minister Anika Wells says changing consumer behaviour and commercial conditions posed significant challenges to the sustainability of Australia Post.
"That's why I've asked the House committee to explore how we can better support a sustainable and accessible postal service that delivers for all Australians," she said.
An Australia Post spokesperson said it looked forward to engaging constructively in the inquiry.
"For several years, we have highlighted the growing challenges facing Australia Post, which are shared by postal organisations around the world," they said.
"We welcome the government's action to address these challenges and support our long-term sustainability."
The inquiry is due to report back by the middle of next year.

Classrooms in Sumy Oblast are moving underground due to Russian shelling: 13 such schools are already operating, nine are under construction, and another 14 are at the design stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:20:12 UTC
06:20:12 KST

Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Russian forces have damaged 165 schools in Sumy Oblast and destroyed 21 beyond repair, according to the head of the regional administration. The administration’s answer is to move classrooms underground. Design documentation for 14 new underground schools has already been prepared, Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Oblast Military Administration, said in an interview with Ukrinform published on 28 October 2026. In addition, 13 such schools are already operating in Sumy region, while nine more are under construction, the media outlet reported.
Sumy region is one of the areas regularly shelled by the Russian military, making it dangerous to hold classes in above-ground school buildings. Of the region’s 280 schools, 225 have shelters, mostly basic ones, while more than 70 have radiation-protective shelters, Hryhorov noted.
“The process is ongoing and is being scaled up as much as possible,” he said, adding that the region is bringing in partners.
Underground classrooms provide a safer learning environment in Sumy Oblast
The construction of new underground schools is primarily focused on the larger cities of Sumy Oblast, where most schoolchildren are concentrated, Hryhorov explained.
The learning process at such a school differs from the usual format. This was explained by Oleksandr Vaniushenko, the principal of one of the first underground schools in Sumy, Suspilne reported on 23 December 2025.
“We have the first shift—entirely younger children, and fifth- and sixth-graders also go out to the open locations. The second shift brings in just as many more children. The total number studying per day is 360–370,” Vaniushenko noted.
The shelter has backup power supplies, allowing children to continue their lessons during air raid alerts and power outages, according to the project, media reported.
Currently, 22 schools operate entirely in person, while 193 use a hybrid learning format, the head of the regional administration said. A total of 75,000 children are currently attending school in Sumy Oblast, he noted.
A Russian bomb hit a Sumy school during lessons in September
On 29 September, Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram aerial bomb while children in grades 1 to 4 were there, Serhii Kryvosheienko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration, reported. He said the Russians aimed the bomb at the school on purpose. About 40 students were in the school’s shelter when the bomb hit, a school employee told Suspilne.
"With no pity or compassion whatsoever, they strike at children? There is nothing human in the enemy! He is not fighting on the battlefield—he is destroying a nation," Kryvosheienko said.
