Palestinians face growing bans from Al-Aqsa as Israel tightens control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:16:26 UTC
06:16:26 KST

Palestinians face growing bans from Al-Aqsa as Israel tightens control
As Israel renews a ban on Al-Aqsa imam, Islamic Waqf officials warn of shrinking authority at Muslim holy site.
For more than two years, Sheikh Ekrima Sabri has been barred from occupied East Jerusalem’s Al-Aqsa Mosque, unable to pray or deliver sermons at the holy site.
And with his latest exclusion order extending the ban until April 2027, the Palestinian preacher – the head of the Higher Islamic Council in Jerusalem – is among those facing Israeli restrictions at the site – the third holiest in Islam and a Palestinian national symbol.
Sabri has faced repeated exclusion orders since August 2024. The latest order, issued on October 20, prevents Sabri from praying or delivering sermons at Al-Aqsa until April 2027.
At the same time, far-right Jewish religious activists have increasingly been allowed to pray at the site under Israeli police protection, going against a longstanding status quo and opposition from ultra-Orthodox Jewish religious authorities.
The restrictions began after Israeli police detained Sabri in August 2024 over a sermon in which he mourned the Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh, who was assassinated by Israel.
Sabri, one of the most prominent Palestinians in East Jerusalem, has faced repeated Israeli interrogations.
Palestinians say this is part of a campaign against them at Al-Aqsa. The Wadi Hilweh Information Center, a Palestinian human rights monitoring group, says Israeli authorities have issued more than 1,000 exclusion orders barring Palestinians from Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Old City since the beginning of 2026, including against religious figures and Islamic Waqf employees.
The centre reported an increase in exclusion orders ahead of Jewish holidays, documenting more than 40 issued over five days in early September.
Sabri told Al Jazeera that the latest extension was the fifth time Israeli authorities have issued an exclusion order against him.
He described the decision as unjust, illegal, inhumane and uncivilised, saying it was intended to silence those speaking out about Al-Aqsa.
Sabri said that he would continue defending Al-Aqsa despite the restrictions, describing the mosque as an integral part of his Islamic faith.
“These measures are aimed at diminishing the Palestinian presence at the mosque, while simultaneously allowing settlers to carry out incursions in large numbers,” Sabri said. “Such actions represent an aggressive policy targeting the Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Islamic presence within it.”
Prohibited activities
Ibrahim al-Natsheh was released by Israeli police earlier this month after spending a week in detention after he was arrested while attending funeral prayers for his cousin at Al-Aqsa Mosque.
He told Al Jazeera that officers took him to a police room and handed him a six-month exclusion order barring him from East Jerusalem’s Old City. He said no specific charge was brought against him.
According to al-Natsheh, the order warns that he could face arrest and further penalties, including a fine or imprisonment, if he enters the prohibited area.
Al-Natsheh said he has received so many exclusion orders that he has lost count. He said the restrictions began about nine years ago, following an Israeli crackdown on Islamic study circles at the mosque.
Palestinian students, teachers and activists associated with the activities have faced arrests and exclusion orders.
“The orders banning us from the mosque provide no specific reason; they simply cite ‘disturbing the peace’, even though we are there solely to pray,” al-Natsheh told Al Jazeera. “Ahead of the Jewish holidays, they sent a message to me and a group of other worshippers, warning us not to approach the mosque or else we will be arrested.”
Even when he is not subject to a formal exclusion order, al-Natsheh said, Israeli police have prevented him from entering Al-Aqsa. He also alleged that officers have repeatedly arrested him at Al-Aqsa’s gates and severely beaten him while in detention.
“The path to the mosque has become incredibly difficult; it is swarming with soldiers and settlers,” he said. “We are denied the ability to reach it with any ease, and if we try, we face arrest and beatings with batons. It is deeply painful to witness what is happening to Al-Aqsa now.”
Al Jazeera has reached out to Israeli authorities for comment, but has yet to receive a response.
Diminishing Waqf role
Al-Aqsa Mosque has seen an escalation in Israeli restrictions and violations throughout 2026.
After the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28, Israeli authorities closed Al-Aqsa to most worshippers for 40 days, reopening the compound on April 9.
Meanwhile, according to the Palestinian Authority’s Jerusalem Governorate, almost 28,000 visits by Israeli settlers were recorded at Al-Aqsa between July and September.
Ma’rouf al-Rifai, an adviser to the Jerusalem Governorate, told Al Jazeera that during recent Jewish holidays, Israeli restrictions on Muslim worshippers had intensified.
These measures included closing the mosque for periods of time, preventing noon prayers on at least one occasion, and restricting access for residents of the Old City during visits to the site by Israeli settlers and Jewish religious activists.
Al-Rifai said the Islamic Waqf Department faces mounting constraints on its role in managing the mosque’s affairs.
He said Israeli police have prevented Waqf officials from accompanying Jewish groups when they entered the site, curtailed the authority of mosque guards, and arrested or barred several employees from the compound.
As a result, he said, fewer than 15 guards are now on duty during the morning shift, compared with approximately 50 previously.
He pointed out that the closure of the mosque for 40 days during the war with Iran took place without consulting the Waqf or providing prior notification, which he said demonstrated the Waqf’s diminishing role in the mosque’s administration.
“Settler incursions have undergone a shift over the past three years; they now include Jewish prayers and religious rituals, the raising of Israeli flags, and attempts to bring in sacrificial offerings,” al-Rifai said.
These changes have undermined longstanding arrangements at the compound, under which the Waqf manages Muslim religious affairs while Israeli police oversee security and access.
According to al-Rifai, Israeli authorities have prevented the Waqf from carrying out restoration work at the Bab al-Rahma prayer hall and restricted maintenance of the compound’s trees and gardens. He said the committee responsible for restoration work at Al-Aqsa has been unable to carry out its duties for years.
He warned of efforts to alter the status quo at Al-Aqsa Mosque, pointing to several proposals and developments, including demands to allow Jewish visitors into the compound on Saturdays, plans advanced by Israeli politicians to divide access to parts of the site between Muslims and Jews, and an Israeli police recruitment drive for volunteers tasked with escorting Israeli incursions at the site.
Al-Rifai said these developments represented a further erosion of the Waqf’s authority and warned that they could eventually transform the arrangements governing worship and access at the holy site.

Bar bodies foiled plan to rope in ex-judges: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:15:06 UTC
06:15:06 KST

SC lamented that its 2021 judgment to re-engage retired judges as ad hoc high court judges under Article 224A remains on paper due to resistance from bar associations
NEW DELHI: With case pendency exceeding 65 lakh in high courts, Supreme Court Thursday lamented that its 2021 judgement for re-engaging retired judges as ad hoc high court judges under Article 224A to speed up case disposal remained on paper, despite having been diluted, because of resistance from bar associations.Dealing with a case related to pension of judges, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the attempt to avail services of some retired judges with impeccable integrity to speed up disposal of cases in HCs has not fructified as bar associations are passing resolutions against such appointments.
“Retired high court judges have established lucrative practices in Supreme Court or are enjoying better gains in conducting arbitration proceedings or in writing opinions. They are reluctant to become ad hoc judges,” said Justice Bagchi.In 2021, the apex court had activated the dormant Article 224A of Constitution and issued general guidelines for re-engagement of retired judges as ad hoc judges of HCs to help clear backlog of cases, many of them more than 15 years old. In Allahabad HC, there are more than 12 lakh cases pending.
On Jan 30 last year, a bench of Justices Sanjiv Khanna, B R Gavai and Surya Kant had diluted certain tough conditions recorded in the 2021 judgment and had said a maximum of five retired HC judges could be reappointed to an HC but their number would not exceed 10% of that HC’s sanctioned judge strength.
Two important conditions in the 2021 judgement that were kept in abeyance in Jan 2025 were ad hoc judges can be appointed only when there is less than 20% vacancy in an HC; and if 10% of the pending cases were more than five years old.Till 1970, some retired SC judges were reappointed as ad hoc judges in the apex court. But it was rarely the practice in HCs, with retired judges being appointed only for specific purposes – Justice Suraj Bhan to Madhya Pradesh HC in Nov 1972 for disposal of election petitions; Justice P Venugopal for two years in Madras HC in Aug 1983; and Justice O P Srivastava to Allahabad HC in 2007, as he was part of the special bench hearing Ayodhya suits.

The portraits of dead friends are coming off the walls. After 29 years, Russia’s independent Novaya Gazeta newspaper is being forced out of its Moscow newsroom.
Novaya Gazeta will be evicted from its office on Potapovsky Lane in central Moscow, where it has been based for 29 years, the news outlet Ekho reported. Ekho cited a letter to readers from editor-in-chief Sergey Sokolov and journalist Irina Gordiyenko.

Novaya Gazeta stopped publishing its print edition in 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia’s Basmanny Court revoked its media license that same year.
In September 2026, Novaya Gazeta was designated a “foreign agent.”

Students rally against police repression in Paris despite protest ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:03:54 UTC
06:03:54 KST

Umit Donmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Students and activists gathered Thursday in Paris to protest police and judicial measures against social movements, despite a court-ordered ban on a planned march toward the La Sante prison.
The gathering, organized by the Ile-de-France Regional Student Coordination, took place at Paris Cite University's Grands Moulins campus in the 13th arrondissement, under heavy police surveillance.
Organizers set up an "anti-repression village" featuring information stands, workshops and speeches between noon and 3 pm local time (1100GMT and 1400GMT).
Participants demanded that charges against demonstrators be dropped, that those imprisoned in connection with protests be released, and that the right to peaceful assembly be protected.
The Paris police prefecture had prohibited a march scheduled to leave the campus at 3 pm for the La Sante prison, citing risks to public order following violence during previous demonstrations.
The Paris Administrative Court upheld the restriction, according to the Revolution Permanente outlet.
Dozens of officers, including riot police equipped with helmets and shields, were deployed around the campus, alongside police vehicles and motorcycles.
The gathering followed nationwide protests on Oct. 24 that drew 410,000 participants, according to the Interior Ministry. The CGT trade union estimated attendance at 800,000.

First Guardian investors dealt another 'utterly devastating' blow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:00:29 UTC
06:00:29 KST

Liquidator deals First Guardian investors another blow, signals little can be recovered
In short:
First Guardian investors are devastated to learn they may not recover millions of dollars.
Out of nearly half a billion lost in the collapse, liquidators have recovered about $8 million.
The corporate regulator ASIC is taking legal action.
Thousands of First Guardian investors have received the devastating news that they may not be able to recover the millions of dollars they invested in the scheme that later collapsed.
Out of nearly half a billion lost in the collapse, liquidators have been able to recover about $8 million, but some $7 million has already gone in liquidation fees.
Corporate regulator ASIC is taking legal action against several players involved in marketing and running the schemes.
The liquidators of Falcon Capital, Ross Blakeley and Paul Harlon of FTI Consulting, said they still could not tell 6,000 First Guardian investors how much, if anything, they will get back from asset sales.
That is because most of the funds appear to have been channelled offshore.
They expect to give a firmer picture after a series of court hearings involving some of the major players in November and December this year.
The directors valued the fund's investments at $512.8 million.
So far the liquidators said they have recovered $8.02 million, or just 1.56 per cent.
'Utterly devastating'
First Guardian investor Melinda Kee, who also runs the group Save our Super, felt broken after hearing the news.
In November 2023, Ms Kee was given financial advice to switch her super from a retail fund into First Guardian and she lost $400,000 of her retirement savings.
She is one of 11,800 investors who collectively lost more than $1 billion in retirement savings after moving their super into First Guardian and the Shield-managed investment schemes, both of which later collapsed.
"It is utterly devastating that after 18 months, just $8 million has been recovered from more than $512 million in investments, while almost $7 million has already been absorbed by liquidation costs," Ms Kee told ABC News.
"Behind these shocking figures are real Australians whose life savings, retirement dreams and financial security have been shattered,"
she said.
"People living with unimaginable stress and uncertainty, watching their futures slip away while they continue to wait for answers, justice and accountability."
First Guardian investors still at a loss
In December, under a deal with the corporate regulator, Netwealth reimbursed about $100 million to about 1,000 First Guardian investors who invested through its platform.
The settlement raised suggestions two other financial services groups, Diversa and Equity Trustees, through which clients invested in First Guardian, would also do a similar deal with the regulator.
But ASIC is pursuing both Diversa and Equity Trustees in court, and they have said they will defend the lawsuits.
Some First Guardian investors are considering a class action to try to recover their money.
Others can apply through what is known as the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, but that is capped at $150,000 and some investors lost far more than that.
Money channelled into 'speculative' investments
In their report, liquidators FTI Consulting, sort the investments into three main groups.
These include "written off" or "settled" investments worth about $117.6 million.
Of these, only $3.49 million, about 3 per cent, has come back, and the liquidators do not expect much more, since several of the companies involved are themselves in liquidation.
The second category includes "further recoveries expected" based on investments totalling $50.75 million.
So far $4.53 million (or 8.9 per cent) has come back, but the liquidators said they do not expect to recover the full value.
The third category the liquidators list falls under "uncertain" recoveries worth about $344.5 million.
In this case, nothing has been recovered so far and may never be, as they are mostly investments that the fund's operators channelled into overseas property and "speculative technology start-ups".
FTI Consulting also reports the value of the fees it is taking in the process—payments were about $6.96 million. The biggest items were their legal fees ($3.33 million) and liquidators' remuneration ($3.23 million).
Regulator 'considering all options' to disrupt InterPrac sale
On Thursday, ASIC told Senate Estimates that the corporate regulator is considering all options to disrupt the sale of InterPrac Financial Planning to Bellbird Australia.
Loading...
Of the more than 11,000 investors who pumped about $1 billion of their retirement savings into the First Guardian and Shield schemes, more than 6,000 were clients of advisers under InterPrac, which is owned by publicly listed company Sequoia.
These 6,000 clients put $680 million into the two funds on the advice of their financial planners who were licensed under InterPrac, and worry that the sale could shrink the pool of money available to compensate them.
ASIC chair Sarah Court told Senate Estimates that the regulator was "considering all options" on whether it could stop InterPrac's attempted sale of its business to Bellbird Australia.

'Lunatic asylum Napoleon' — Flavio Bolsonaro's 'leader of Brazil' declaration draws wave of mockery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:00:10 UTC
06:00:10 KST

In a viral wave of mockery, one influencer declared himself the "true president" of Twitter, and another social media user proclaimed himself the winner of the next lottery.
The target of the taunts was Flavio Bolsonaro, who — after fleeing to the United States following his election defeat — proclaimed himself the leader of Brazil on Wednesday in a confusing series of revised statements.
The moves by the 45-year-old senator have been met in Brazil with a mixture of derision, disbelief, and disapproval, even from within his own camp.
The eldest son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro was blindsided by his election defeat to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, after leading a first-round vote earlier this month.
In a cloak-and-dagger operation he sneaked out of Brazil via Argentina and Ecuador, after being ordered to surrender his passports due to several ongoing investigations against him.
Hours after his arrival in Florida, he posted a statement on social media declaring himself the "true president" of Brazil, before revising the wording a few minutes later to describe himself as the "leader" of the country.
A Bolsonaro ally who published an earlier version of the statement bearing Brazil's old coat of arms, abandoned in the sixties, said it had been a ChatGPT error.
'Coup-mongering'
The letter was met with outrage in Brazilian media, which described its tone as "coup-mongering," while politicians from across the spectrum called for the election results to be respected.
A column in the O Globo daily likened Flavio Bolsonaro to a "lunatic asylum Napoleon," while the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper slammed the statement as "pathetic."
On the right, the powerful governor of Sao Paulo, Tarcisio de Freitas, quickly distanced himself.
De Freitas was a former minister under Jair Bolsonaro who had been tipped as the main candidate for the right before the former president chose his son
"We are democrats. The election result is sovereign. What we have seen is the will of the majority of the population, which must be respected," De Freitas said in an interview with the Estadao daily.
As speculation switched almost immediately to who would lead the right with Flavio out of the country, the governor — a favourite in business circles — said a 2030 run was "a possibility."
Rogerio Marinho, who co-ordinated Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign, said there was "no evidence" of electoral fraud, as claimed by the defeated candidate.
Electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by Jair Bolsonaro, issued a statement to highlight the "secure electoral process."
'No one approves'
Flavio Bolsonaro also said he would lead the opposition from abroad.
His self-proclamation as Brazil's leader in exile "is not a misstep, it is a calculated move" intended to maintain his influence over the conservative camp in Brazil, said Geraldo Monteiro, a political scientist at the State University of Rio de Janeiro.
The stakes are high: despite their election defeat, the right scored a strong majority in Congress.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) will hold the largest number of seats from February.
"I do not believe he has the means to lead the opposition from afar, as the newly elected officials have already secured their seats and no longer need him," Monteiro told AFP.
He said Flavio Bolsonaro's letter has "drawn a red line" between those who choose "extreme loyalty" and those who "prefer not to embark on another putschist adventure."
Monteiro said Flavio was following in the footsteps of his father, who was sentenced to 27 years for plotting a coup after his 2022 election loss to Lula.
On Thursday, PL leader Valdemar Costa Neto visited Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving his sentence under house arrest.
"No one approves" of the letter, Neto said as he left the meeting, adding that the party needed to "move forward."

Henry Holland creates wallpaper and fabric collection with a "language developed through ceramics"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Henry Holland creates wallpaper and fabric collection with a “language developed through ceramics”
Designer Henry Holland‘s textual fabric and textile collection for luxury interior furnishings company Harlequin was informed by his work as a ceramicist, he tells Dezeen in this interview.
Simply named Harlequin x Henry Holland, the collection of wallpapers and fabrics was heavily influenced by both the extensive archive of Harlequin’s parent company Sanderson and Holland’s love of the Japanese pottery technique nerikomi.
“The starting point for the collection was our ceramic work,” Holland told Dezeen. “We used the organic patterns and forms created in our handbuilt work as the starting point, and then similarly we built the colour palettes around the clays that we use to create our pieces.”
“To add further depth and range to the collection, we also delved into the incredibly rich archive that the Sanderson group have across all of their brands and reinterpreted some archive prints that felt like the right additions to the collection.”
The collection features four distinct fabrics that translate ceramic patterns and colours into materials that can transform interior spaces.
For Holland, this transformation of scale, from a hand-held object to entire rooms and interiors, was the most exciting part of the collaboration.
“For me, the collection is really about taking the language we have developed through ceramics and allowing it to live on a completely different scale,” he said.
“At the studio we make objects that sit within a room, whereas with Harlequin we suddenly had the opportunity to take those patterns, colours and textures and make them become the room,” he added.
“There is something really exciting about that shift in perspective. Our work has always been about balancing the graphic with the organic, and I think that really comes through in the collection. There are moments that feel bold and energetic and others that are much softer and quieter.”
Holland worked closely with the Harlequin team to understand which elements of the nerikomi technique could be translated and upscaled to fabric. He found clear similarities in methodology between the technique and the process of making textile fabrics.
“With nerikomi, the pattern isn’t something that is applied to the surface afterwards – it is created through the material itself by layering, compressing, slicing and rebuilding different coloured clays,” he said. “There is always this balance between control and chance, which is something I love about the process.”
“Working with the Harlequin team and looking at those surfaces and identifying elements within them that could become a wallpaper or a fabric was fascinating,” he continued.
“We were able to isolate gestures, enlarge details and play with scale in ways I wouldn’t necessarily have considered. Some tiny detail from a ceramic piece can suddenly become this huge, immersive pattern across a wall.”
Holland has a personal connection to each of the four fabrics developed for the collection – Southborough, Elsworthy, Great Hey and Blenets Check Mini – and each was named after one of his and his partner’s former homes.
“We created a really autobiographical narrative by naming the patterns and pieces in the collection after homes that my husband and I have lived in through our lives,” he said.
While the patterning on the fabrics, which ranges from checkerboard in Blenets Check Mini to moiré-style in Elsworthy and chevrons in Southborough, was informed by ceramics, so too were the colours selected.
Pastel tones of chocolate and moss were informed by unglazed pottery, while Holland looked to glazed earthenware for the collection’s bolder colours.
“We were able to split the palette into more subdued, almost pastel tones, taking our lead from our unglazed ceramics, and then a bolder level of colour where we used our glazed pieces as the reference,” explained Holland.
“It was really important to me that, even though we were translating the work into completely different materials and applications, everything still felt very rooted in the studio and recognisably ours.”
Although the fabrics and wallpapers in the collection each have a distinct aesthetic and feel, Holland believes the pieces form a coherent collection because they come from a shared creative thought process.
“They share a common DNA because ultimately they all come back to the same source material, which is the ceramics,” he said.
“Within my ceramic work there has always been a contrast between very precise pattern and much looser, more organic pattern. Some pieces can be incredibly controlled and almost mathematical, while others are much more fluid. I didn’t want to lose that contrast when translating the work into print,” he continued.
“What brings everything together is colour, movement and the sense that everything has been touched by hand. Even when the patterns are quite different, there is a shared irregularity and energy to them. Nothing feels too perfect or overly digital, and that was really important to me.”
Holland hopes designers will use the collection’s fabrics in a wide variety of interiors, working out how to combine and layer pieces to create unique and interesting spaces.
“I don’t think there should be too many rules around how it is used,” he said. “One of the things we really wanted was for the collection to have enough cohesion that you could layer different elements together without everything having to match perfectly.”
“The colour stories run throughout the collection, so you can pick up a tone from one of the more expressive wallpapers and echo it through a fabric or a quieter pattern elsewhere in the room,” continued Holland. “I think interiors are much more interesting when there is that kind of tension.”
Overall, Holland hopes people will enjoy using the fabrics and wallpapers and enjoy the spaces that are created.
“Ultimately, I want people to have fun with it,” he said. “I like interiors that feel collected and personal rather than overly prescribed.”
“Hopefully the collection gives designers and customers the tools to create spaces that have personality, warmth and a real sense of individuality,” he continued.
The collection is the result of a deep collaboration between Holland and Harlequin, which has resulted in its success.
“It was a very genuine back-and-forth process,” said Holland. “I didn’t want to simply hand over some ceramic patterns and say, ‘turn these into wallpaper’.”
“The interesting part was bringing together what we know about ceramics and pattern at Henry Holland Studio with Harlequin’s incredible knowledge of textiles, wallpaper, colour and interiors,” he continued.
“We started with the ceramics and the archive of patterns and colour combinations we have developed at the studio, and from there the Harlequin team began exploring scale, repeats, textures and different interpretations. We would respond to those, push certain things further, pull other things back and keep refining the palette.”
Holland believes this close collaboration is key to the collection’s success.
“I think the best collaborations happen when both sides bring something to the project that the other couldn’t necessarily achieve alone,” he said.
“There are things in this collection that feel Henry Holland Studio completely, but they have been transformed through Harlequin’s expertise into something entirely new. That’s what made the whole process so rewarding.”

3rd Russia-Africa Summit adopts declaration calling for multipolar world order, expanded cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:58:26 CST
05:58:26 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The third Russia-Africa Summit on Thursday adopted a declaration calling for a more multipolar world order, greater African representation in global governance and expanded cooperation in trade, energy, security and technology, the Kremlin said.
The declaration emphasizes national sovereignty, non-interference in internal affairs and respect for the UN Charter. It calls for reforms to international institutions, including greater African representation on the UN Security Council, and opposes unilateral coercive measures and the unlawful seizure of sovereign assets.
On economic ties, the document calls for diversifying trade, reducing trade barriers and boosting investment and industrialization in Africa. It highlights cooperation in energy, including nuclear power and natural gas, as well as agriculture, fertilizer supplies, critical minerals processing and transport infrastructure.
The declaration also calls for closer security cooperation to combat terrorism, violent extremism and maritime piracy. It proposes establishing a permanent high-level Russia-Africa dialogue on counterterrorism, food security and information security.
Other priorities include cooperation in artificial intelligence, digital technologies, science, education, healthcare and cultural exchanges. The document also calls for greater recognition of the enduring consequences of colonialism, efforts to promote historical justice and the return of cultural property.
Held in Moscow on Oct. 28-29, the summit brought together representatives from 48 African countries, including 22 represented by their heads of state, according to the Kremlin. ■

OSLO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A new international airport opened Thursday in Ilulissat, western Greenland, after receiving approval from Danish aviation authorities, airport operator Greenland Airports said.
The airport's 2,200-meter runway can accommodate large passenger aircraft, enabling direct international connections to Greenland's third-largest town and improving access to Disko Bay and northern Greenland.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority said final approval was granted overnight following months of inspections and testing, including a test flight.
An Air Greenland Airbus A330neo arrived from Copenhagen on Thursday to mark the launch of the direct route. Regular winter services will begin in November, initially operated by Jettime using Boeing 737-800 aircraft. Flights will operate primarily once a week on Wednesdays, with additional Monday departures during selected periods.
Greenland Airports said operations would expand gradually, with the aim of reaching full operation by the summer 2027 season.
The opening completed a three-airport development program, following the opening of new airports in Nuuk in November 2024 and Qaqortoq in April 2026. The operator said the new facilities would improve transport links and create opportunities for tourism, cargo and regional business.
Ilulissat is known for its icebergs and the nearby Ilulissat Icefjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. ■

Israel requires airlines to report crew details 48 hrs before departure

Unknown Publisher

04:58:23 CST
05:58:23 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Airlines operating flights to Israel will be required to submit crew information at least 48 hours before scheduled departure, as part of new measures to strengthen Israel's civil aviation security, authorities said Thursday.
The new measures were announced in a statement by Israel's National Center for Passenger Information Analysis. The move followed Israel's decision to tighten aviation security requirements after an attempted attack aboard a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv on Sept. 30, carried out by a co-pilot from Oman.
Under the new guidelines, airlines must submit an initial crew list at least 48 hours before departure, update the information to reflect any changes two hours prior, and provide a final crew list at departure.
The statement said the new requirements would give relevant Israeli authorities more preparation time than is customary internationally and are expected to improve Israel's aviation security response.
Until now, crew information was often reported shortly before departure or even after takeoff. ■

Canada unveils first national security strategy in over 20 years
China
Unknown Publisher

04:58:20 CST
05:58:20 KST

OTTAWA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday launched "The Plan for a Stronger Canada," the country's first national security strategy in over two decades aimed at countering evolving security threats and safeguarding national sovereignty.
The prime minister's office said in a news release that the rules-based international order is eroding and the line between economic security and national security has disappeared, noting that national security now relies not only on defense and resource capabilities, but also on the strength of the economy, the resilience of institutions, and the partnerships with allies.
According to the release, the strategy outlines five main priorities: strengthening economic security and resilience by transforming strategic industries and securing supply chains; advancing a disciplined foreign policy to diversify partnerships; rebuilding and strengthening the Canadian Armed Forces; enhancing public safety against foreign interference, espionage, violent extremism, and transnational organized crime; and modernizing intelligence capabilities to anticipate and counter emerging threats.
Carney said in the release that in a rapidly changing and more dangerous world, Canada must have the capacity to defend its sovereignty and the resilience to withstand emerging threats.
The Canadian government will update the strategy at least every four years. ■

BERLIN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- German sportswear giant Adidas reported a 13 percent year-on-year increase in third-quarter revenue in China, extending its run of sales growth in the country to 14 consecutive quarters, the company told Xinhua on Thursday.
Revenue in China reached 1.138 billion euros (1.27 billion U.S. dollars) in the third quarter, bringing the total for the first nine months of 2026 to 3.227 billion euros (3.6 billion dollars), up 15 percent year-on-year.
Adidas described China as one of its most important strategic markets and attributed the sustained growth to product innovation and locally developed designs.
Globally, revenue rose 7 percent from a year earlier on a currency-neutral basis to a quarterly record of 7.25 billion euros (8.1 billion dollars), while operating profit climbed 37 percent to a quarterly record of 1 billion euros (1.12 billion dollars), the results showed.
Europe was the only market where revenue declined in the third quarter, with revenue down 4 percent year-on-year, the figures showed. Adidas expected sales in the region to return to growth in the fourth quarter, supported by delayed wholesale shipments and higher sales ahead of the year-end shopping season.
For the full year, the company raised its operating profit forecast to 2.5 billion euros (2.8 billion dollars), up from its previous projection of 2.3 billion euros (2.6 billion dollars). ■

BRUSSELS, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- European Union (EU) member states have pledged to accelerate the release of 42.6 million barrels of strategic oil reserves over the coming months, nearly half of which will be diesel, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said Thursday.
EU energy ministers met in Luxembourg to discuss energy security ahead of the winter, energy prices and measures to stabilize diesel supplies.
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Jorgensen said relevant EU member states had reaffirmed their commitment to accelerating the release of 42.6 million barrels from strategic reserves.

Global energy markets remain under pressure amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East. In its October Oil Market Report, the IEA said global diesel markets remained tight, with prolonged disruptions to supplies from the Middle East and Russia contributing to declining inventories, while diesel prices in Europe and other regions remained elevated. ■

Unknown Publisher

05:57:20 KST

The man who lobbed gasoline bombs at a pro-Israel rally in Colorado last year, injuring several people, including a woman who later died, pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal hate-crime charges, the US Department of Justice said.
Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 47, an Egyptian national, is already serving a life sentence for his guilty plea in May to more than 100 state charges, including first-degree murder.
Soliman pleaded guilty to nine counts of hate-crime offenses and three explosives charges in federal court in Denver, according to the DOJ. The charges are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty.
The plea deal asks that Soliman be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years. Soliman will be sentenced on January 7.
"The defendant admitted that he committed the attack because of the actual or perceived Jewish religion and Israeli national origin of the group he targeted," the DOJ said in a statement.
David Kraut, a federal public defender listed as Soliman's lawyer, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Soliman admits to tossing Molotov cocktails
Soliman has admitted tossing two Molotov cocktails at people taking part in a rally in downtown Boulder on June 1, 2025, held in solidarity with hostages seized by Hamas terrorists who stormed Israeli villages from the Palestinian enclave of Gaza on October 7, 2023.
Prosecutors said Soliman yelled "Free Palestine" as the gasoline bombs he lobbed at the crowd burst into flames outside a municipal courthouse in the heart of Boulder's popular Pearl Street shopping district.
Admitting his guilt in state court nearly six months ago, Soliman denounced his own crimes as contrary to "the teachings of Islam" and insisted he bore no ill will toward Jewish people. He went on to lament the "thousands of families who have lost their families in Palestine and Gaza," and said the "enemy is Zionism."
Authorities in Colorado identified 29 victims from the attack, including 14 who were burned or injured while fleeing and 15 who were close enough to be considered targets of attempted murder. One victim, 82-year-old Karen Diamond, died of her injuries later that month. Her husband suffered severe burns and survived.
The firebombing came amid heightened tensions over the 2023 Hamas raid and Israel's military assault in Gaza, which sparked a surge in anti-Jewish and anti-Muslim hate crimes across the US and a wave of pro-Palestinian protests that many Israel supporters branded as antisemitic. Pro-Palestinian protesters reject accusations that their support of Gazans amounts to antisemitism.
Family's immigration detention
According to affidavits filed in court by prosecutors, Soliman told investigators after his arrest that he had planned his attack for a year, but delayed going through with it until after his daughter had graduated from high school.
Soliman, who had lived with his wife and five children in Colorado Springs, also has asserted that his family members were unaware of his intentions beforehand.
The family was taken into immigration custody in June 2025 after his arrest and transported to a detention facility in Texas. They were held until a court-ordered release on April 23, 2026, more than 10 months later.
The children and their mother, who subsequently divorced Soliman, were rearrested on April 25 of this year just after returning to Colorado. They were freed again when attorneys intervened a day later, according to court documents.
Court records entered at about the time that Soliman reached a plea deal with federal prosecutors earlier this month showed that he had withdrawn motions seeking to preclude any further attempts at removing his family.

Gasoline prices will fall by 42 agorot per liter at midnight between Saturday and Sunday, the Energy and Infrastructure Ministry's Fuel and Gas Administration announced on Thursday, defying earlier forecasts of a sharp increase to near-record levels.

The maximum price of a liter of self-service, unleaded 95-octane gasoline, including VAT, will fall to NIS 7.35, compared with the current NIS 7.77. The additional charge for full-service fueling will remain unchanged at 26 agorot per liter.
The announcement came as a surprise to Israeli drivers. Earlier on Thursday, sources in the energy market estimated that prices at gas stations would rise by approximately 30 agorot, reaching around NIS 8.30 per liter.
Those forecasts were based on a combination of rising global oil prices amid expectations of a regional escalation involving Iran and the strengthening of the US dollar following the election results.
However, the Fuel and Gas Administration's calculations produced a positive turnaround, delivering a significant price reduction that will provide immediate financial relief to millions of vehicle owners across Israel.
Despite the welcome news at gas stations, drivers will need to closely monitor developments at the Finance Ministry in the coming days.
Consumers currently benefit from a reduction in the excise tax on gasoline amounting to NIS 1 per liter. The measure, introduced by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich for a limited period, carries a budgetary cost of approximately NIS 326 million per month.
The current temporary order is set to expire on November 3.
The Energy and Infrastructure Ministry has already issued a warning: "If the excise tax order is not updated, the temporary provision concerning the excise tax order will expire overnight between November 4 and 5, meaning that from November 5, the maximum price will stand at NIS 8.35 per liter."
To prevent the dramatic NIS 1-per-liter increase on November 5, the finance minister must sign an extension of the tax benefit for another month.
Such a move would bring the total budgetary cost of the excise tax subsidy over the past three months to approximately NIS 800 million.

Longtime associates of Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich founded a paid consular appointment service, investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:57:01 UTC
05:57:01 KST

A company that charges Russians abroad to find available appointments at Russian consulates has ties to people in Roman Abramovich’s circle, Verstka reported.
Konsul Prime operates as an official partner under an agreement with Russia’s Foreign Ministry, offering help with paperwork and priority access to appointments.
The company always has appointments available, even though people usually wait weeks to book one. Konsul Prime began operating in late 2022. Russian emigrants say in group chats and online forums that getting a consular appointment has become even harder since the service launched.
Konsul Prime’s main legal entity, Tsentr Servis LLC, was established in December 2022 by Yefim Malkin. Malkin began working with Abramovich in the 1990s at Sibneft, according to Verstka. He was later linked to Millhouse entities that managed assets belonging to Abramovich and his partner, Yevgeny Shvidler.
In September 2022, Mikhail Livergand, another Abramovich associate who had previously worked in investment and real estate and served as Malkin’s assistant, took ownership of Konsul Prime. In August of that year, Livergand founded Tsentr Servis Digital, which owns the rights to Konsul Prime’s software platform.
Meduza found that Konsul Prime’s clients in Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, France, and Switzerland sign contracts with legal entities registered in the United Arab Emirates: Docs Management L.L.C. and Konsul Prime DMCC. That information comes from the company’s privacy policy.
The owner of Docs Management L.L.C. is unknown, but Comfort Care Travel L.L.C. is registered at the same address in Dubai. It is the Dubai representative office of Malkin’s Russian company, Tekhnologii Meditsinskogo Turizma.
Konsul Prime DMCC is owned by Tsentr Servis, according to Tsentr Servis’ financial statements.
Since July 2023, Darya Zhurova, 53, has held 49% stakes in both Tsentr Servis and Tsentr Servis Digital, becoming another co-founder of both companies, according to Verstka. Livergand retained controlling stakes in both companies. Zhurova is the first co-owner with no ties to Abramovich, Verstka’s journalists wrote, suggesting that she may be a nominee owner.
Tsentr Servis founded most of Konsul Prime’s legal entities abroad, Verstka reported. Another company responsible for Konsul Prime’s branches, Konsul Tsentr, operates on behalf of Russia’s Foreign Ministry. Since 2024, Livergand and Zhurova’s Tsentr Servis has owned 90% of Konsul Tsentr, with just 10% belonging to an administrative office under the ministry.
In February 2026, Russia’s Unified State Register of Legal Entities stopped disclosing information about the founders of Konsul Prime’s Russian legal entities. But even the information still publicly available makes clear that Konsul Prime is not a state company at all, nor is it even formally dependent on the state. It has more ties to Roman Abramovich than to Russia’s Foreign Ministry. Yet the service still presents itself as the ministry’s sole partner, collects Russians’ data, and charges for exclusive access to consular services.
Tsentr Servis Digital’s business is currently valued at 1.17 billion rubles, according to its financial statements, which Meduza reviewed.

What a British think tank gets wrong about Russia’s ultimate weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:55:09 UTC
05:55:09 KST

What a British think tank gets wrong about Russia’s ultimate weapons
A few days ago, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) released a report titled ‘Russia’s Nuclear Deterrent and Its Weapons Procurement’. The report examines the development of Russia’s nuclear triad amid stringent financial constraints and the rising threat of a potential US non-nuclear counterforce strike.
The author of the report, Sidharth Kaushal, makes conclusions based on the publications of Russian military experts in the journal ‘Voennaya Mysl’ (Military Thought), as well as established Western practices for analyzing Russia’s nuclear capabilities.
A British diagnosis of Russia’s nuclear future
Here are the key takeaways from the report:
- Paradigm shift: Russia is being compelled to shift its focus from a posture of “assured retaliation” (increasing the survivability of mobile missile systems and submarine-launched ballistic forces to effectively counter a first strike) to a Launch on Warning (LOW) posture (employing its arsenal early against an enemy attack).
- Vulnerability of mobile forces: Advancements in US space reconnaissance make the concealment of mobile ground-based systems increasingly ineffective.
- Greater reliance on silo-based launchers, which are viewed as more secure bases for strategic missiles. Silo-based systems will comprise a greater proportion of throw weight, particularly since RS-28 Sarmat heavy intercontinental ballistic missiles are silo-launched to ensure instant readiness.
- Economic challenges: According to the report, modern Russia cannot pursue a large-scale quantitative increase in its missile arsenal due to the enormous costs associated with developing and maintaining the conventional armed forces amidst the ongoing military operation in Ukraine.
- Due to cost parity, the domestic production costs of strategic missile systems compete with conventional weaponry – for example, producing one Yars missile is equivalent to the cost of 15 T-72 tanks.
- A labor shortage in the nuclear and missile industries is unavoidable in the current conditions and necessitates a significant increase in wages.
The author also provides interesting assessments of specific weapons systems:
- RS-28 Sarmat: The report projects no quantitative increase in the deployment of these missiles. Emphasis is placed on a short boost phase and a high payload capacity for overcoming missile defense systems.
- The medium-range Oreshnik missile is seen as a priority in the European theater of operations and as a tool for preemptively neutralizing US Dark Eagle systems in Europe. Given manufacturing shortages, it is expected to be deployed primarily in its nuclear variant.
- The long-range KH-BD air-launched cruise missile (with a range up to 6,500 km) is designed to be carried by Tu-95 and Tu-160 bombers, in light of the lack of progress on the PAK DA next-generation stealth strategic bomber.
- Burevestnik and Poseidon programs are considered technically unfeasible by the author of the report; due to the high costs, they are perceived primarily as methods of psychological intimidation
- Space-based warfare: The report highlights the jamming of US missile defense systems as a major priority for Russia. It predicts the launch of nuclear electronic warfare satellites into orbit and the eventual deployment of full-scale space-based nuclear weapons to create massive plasma fields in the ionosphere.
How can we assess this report? Generally, the picture is more complex than described. Like in the Indian parable about the blind men and the elephant, the author of the report sees certain aspects of the ‘elephant’ but fails to see the general picture, which may be quite different. Let’s take a closer look.
The logic behind Russia’s nuclear shield
Regarding the structure of the strategic nuclear forces and the shifting balance between mobile and stationary systems, the distinctive feature of the Soviet, and now Russian, approach lies in balancing mobile and stationary strategic missile systems. Despite advances in satellite reconnaissance, mobile missile systems hold certain advantages: for example, hundreds of them are deployed over vast territories. Moreover, several Peresvet laser weapon systems have already been deployed; these can blind potential adversaries’ optical reconnaissance systems at a critical moment. While reliance on space-based systems is understandable, it’s important to note that these technologies are also vulnerable to various factors, as we have seen recently.
Stationary missile systems come with a significant drawback: it’s relatively easy to spot their location. However, they offer a high level of protection against non-nuclear strikes and maintain relatively high (though not absolute) survivability in the event of a nuclear exchange. Russia’s strategy combines hard-to-detect mobile missile systems with stationary systems that can be employed in response to a nuclear attack. This combination allows for greater flexibility and multiple operational scenarios. Considering this strategy, it’s likely that a large inventory of Sarmat missiles isn’t necessary – two regiments with 50+ missile silos might suffice. This doesn’t indicate a shift in priorities but rather reaffirms a conservative and justified traditional approach.
We must also note the naval component, which ensures reliable retaliatory capability. Both Russian and Western analysts have grown accustomed to the fact that the Bulava submarine-launched solid-fuel missile has been deployed and will eventually replace other ballistic missiles in the Russian Navy. However, that’s not entirely true. Project 667BDRM DELTA-IV submarines equipped with liquid-fueled R-29RM missiles remain on duty. These missiles are among the most effective strategic systems in terms of their energy-mass efficiency. Judging by statements from 2022, it seems that Russia may very well renew its interest in liquid-fueled sea-based missiles. Maintaining two centers for naval missile production is more expensive than having just one, but if it results in a higher number of warheads with fewer missiles, financial concerns could be overlooked.
Lastly, the demonization of the Oreshnik missile in the West is understandable and, overall, justified. Its minimal flight time presents a significant threat. There’s also the option for hybrid use – deploying it with non-nuclear payloads to signal intentions or for use in low-intensity conflicts. The existence of such a missile system increases the range of potential scenarios for employing strategic forces and provides substantial flexibility.
Even a few launch facilities would suffice for these purposes, which raises questions about the costly deployment of multiple brigades. Most likely, we’re talking about the deployment of divisions with 3-4 TELs instead of full brigades consisting of 12 TELs. This strategy also allows to increase the number of deployed missiles, should the need arise.
Beyond the bluff: Weapons built for retaliation
The assessment of the aviation component of the strategic nuclear forces seems fairly accurate, but it’s necessary to note that several other weapon programs are also being developed alongside the KH-BD missiles. Russian defense contractors consistently work on multiple projects, regardless of the current financial climate. It’s reasonable to assume they’re developing air-launched hypersonic missile systems for both tactical and strategic aviation, as well as various types of cruise missiles for strategic use. Additionally, it’s highly likely that a range of tactical munitions for front-line aviation is also under development. Similarly, work on the new PAK DA strategic bomber is probably ongoing, even if the urgent need for this expensive project has diminished.
I’d like to highlight the assessments regarding the Burevestnik nuclear-powered cruise missile and the Poseidon nuclear-powered UUV. Both systems boast practically unlimited range and the ability to remain airborne/underwater for extended periods of time. There’s a lot of speculation and publicity surrounding these projects, and it makes sense to leverage such groundbreaking initiatives for propaganda purposes. However, this doesn’t negate their real military significance or the seriousness of intentions regarding their deployment.
Infrastructure for these projects wouldn’t be carried out solely for PR purposes. At least one major base with several launch systems is being constructed for Burevestnik missiles, and for the Poseidon UUV, basing facilities are being built in the Pacific Ocean, and it is set to be deployed to the Northern Fleet.
Experts monitor progress and construction through satellite imagery. Tracking testing activities is more complex, but there are signs that work continues in this direction as well. Most importantly, these combat systems possess an unknown yet potentially immense retaliatory capability, which is difficult to evaluate due to the absence of analogues. What’s certain is that their potential is significant. Poseidon UUVs may not be able to target naval fleets, but their true purpose is to ensure guaranteed retaliatory strikes capable of causing total destruction along an adversary’s coastline.
In summary, despite economic and financial challenges, Russia will undoubtedly find the resources necessary to maintain and advance its nuclear triad, or even the more powerful new strategic nuclear forces.

Justice for Maya women in Guatemala, girls back in school in India, restored land in Mali: The UN has named its 2026 SDG Action Award winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:53:00 UTC
05:53:00 KST

UN honors grassroots heroes in Rome
October 29, 2026
A legal aid group for Indigenous women in Guatemala, a movement of village mothers in rural India, and a Malian entrepreneur who restores farmland have won this year's UN SDG Action Awards.
The winners were announced at the ninth Heroes of Tomorrow awards ceremony in Rome, Italy, run by the UN SDG Action Campaign. They were chosen from more than 7,000 entries from 190 countries.
Nine finalists were shortlisted for three categories: resilience, creativity and changemaker.
Justice for Maya women
The Resilience Award went to the Women's Justice Initiative. Many indigenous women in Guatemala face high rates of violence, poverty and discrimination, made worse by language barriers and a lack of access to information. The initiative helps women and girls get access to justice and lead change in their communities. According to the organization, more than 16,000 women and girls have participated.
"I accept the UN SDG Action Award in the honour of the Maya Kaqchikel women and girls in Guatemala who are building a more just future for their communities. Ending violence against women requires all of us. Only together, we can build a future where every woman and girl lives with dignity and realizes her full potential," said Viviana Patal, the initiative's legal director.
Keeping girls in school in India
The Creativity Award was given to Mothers of Courage, a grassroots campaign that aims to keep girls in education in rural India. Its organizers say more than 1.2 million people have joined and pledged to keep their daughters in education and to prevent early marriage.
"This award today belongs to all the mothers in those villages, all the women leaders, who are working hard to change the destinies of their daughters and their daughters-in-law," said Khushboo Awasthi, Mothers of Courage's chief curator.
"Together, let's create a world where no girl ever has to negotiate for her right to dream and to aspire and to thrive."
Trees and livelihoods in Mali
The Changemaker Award when to Malian entrepreneur Rokiatou Traore. Her organization, Herou Alliance, helps women and small farmers bring worn-out land back to life by planting trees alongside their crops. The trees also help farmers generate extra revenue, allowing them to sell products from moringa and other valuable trees.
"Receiving this award means a lot to me. It is a reminder of why I started this journey," said Traore. "I invite you all to join us, to plant more trees, to empower more women, and above all, to create a future full of opportunities for communities for today and for future generations."
The UN Trust Fund to End Violence against Women and Girls received an honorable mention. Speaking about the award, President of the Organization of Women's Freedom in Iraq Jannat Al Ghezi paid a tearful tribute to its founder Yanar Mohammed, who was assassinated outside her home in Baghdad in March.
'Be that change'
UN Assistant Secretary-General Michelle Muschett said the finalists "remind us that the future is something we create together and that each of us has the power to help shape it and open doors for the next generations."
"When they tell you that one person cannot make a difference, prove them wrong," UN SDG Action Campaign Director Marina Ponti told the audience. "Change has always begun with people who refused to accept that the world could not be different. So be courageous. Be persistent. Be that change."
How are the awards organized?
A panel of 20 judges from UN leadership, government, civil society, the arts, business and youth activism chose the winners. They included UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo, Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar, and Otto Group Vice President Tobias Wollermann.
The awards are run by the UN SDG Action Campaign, a special initiative of the UN Secretary-General. The campaign supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals, 17 targets adopted by member states that cover areas including poverty, hunger, education, gender equality and climate protection.
The awards are supported by Italy's Foreign Ministry and Germany's Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Editor's Note: DW Director General Barbara Massing was a member of the 20-person jury panel.

Ukraine has received a new shipment of humanitarian energy assistance from Azerbaijan valued at over $1.47 million.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian officials confirmed that since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, energy hubs have processed 159 aid deliveries from Azerbaijan totaling more than 2,432.4 metric tons of specialized gear, including power transformers, transformer substations, power generators, and electrical cables.

International supplies of Patriot interceptors are severely constrained, leaving Kyiv scrambling alongside European allies to secure hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles before the cold sets in.
With Ukrainian air defense intercepting only a fraction of incoming ballistic missiles, experts and officials warn that the upcoming winter threatens to bring severe energy disruptions and critical infrastructure challenges across the country.

In Finland, police have launched an investigation into Google over forest clearing for data centers
Kyiv • UNN
Finnish police are investigating Tuike Finland Oy over possible environmental pollution during preparations for a data center. The case is expected to be concluded in 2027.
The Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation against Tuike Finland Oy, a Google subsidiary, over the clearing of forests for data centers. This is reported by the Finnish police, according to UNN.
Details
This week, a criminal investigation was launched based on a request for an investigation from the Licensing and Supervisory Agency. The case is being investigated under the article on "environmental pollution." Five requests for an investigation related to the data center construction project in Muhos were submitted to the Oulu Police Department, and all of them are being handled as part of a single criminal investigation
The case is being investigated under the article on "environmental pollution," which also covers possible less serious offenses related to the case. Other possible offenses will be clarified later during the preliminary investigation.
According to preliminary information, ambiguities and deficiencies were identified in the drainage and water management processes at the construction site of Tuike Finland Oy’s data center project. Among other things, the preliminary investigation is establishing the circumstances related to these issues.
Given the scale of the case, the preliminary investigation is expected to take a long time and is planned to be completed during 2027.
To remind you
Google was ordered to temporarily suspend work at two sites for the construction of data centers in Finland because the company had not carried out the required environmental impact assessment.

Patrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men star, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:52:16 UTC
05:52:16 KST

Gizem Nisa Çebi Demir
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
British actor Patrick Stewart, best known for playing Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles at the age of 86, according to a report.
"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Kelly Bush Novak, longtime spokesperson for Stewart, said in a statement Thursday on Instagram.
Born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, England, Stewart overcame a difficult childhood to become a celebrated Shakespearean actor before achieving international fame in middle age, The New York Times reported.
According to the daily, he debuted as Picard in 1987 in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," which ran for seven seasons and won 18 Emmy Awards and a Peabody Award.
His character became known for the commands "Engage!" and "Make it so." Stewart later reprised the role in four feature films and the television series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons from 2020.
Beyond "Star Trek," Stewart played Gurney Halleck in David Lynch's 1984 film "Dune" and Professor Charles Xavier in five "X-Men" films, including "Logan" (2017). Several of the films featured his close friend Ian McKellen. 
Before Hollywood
Before his Hollywood success, Stewart had established himself as a leading British stage actor, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He won Olivier Awards for his performances in "Antony and Cleopatra" (1979) and "Hamlet" (2009), and received the London Fringe Theatre best actor award in 1986 for "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?"
Despite criticism from some theater colleagues over his move to Hollywood, Stewart defended his work in popular entertainment.
"They used to ask me 'Why, why, why?' as if I was somehow slumming it," he told The Independent in 2003.
"What snobbery!" he said, adding: "For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that's fine. I really believe we created an admirable individual."
Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British Army regimental sergeant major, and Gladys (Barrowclough) Stewart, a textile factory worker. Known for his commanding baritone voice, he built a career spanning classical theater and major science-fiction franchises, earning acclaim across generations.

Berlin's Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Berlin's Left leader Elif Eralp under fire over Der Spiegel interview
October 29, 2026
Elif Eralp, the candidate on course to become the next mayor of Berlin, sparked controversy on Thursday after having unintentionally aired personal security fears that appeared to be linked to pro-Palestinian activists in the city.
The controversy came about based on internal remarks that were part of her interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel.
Eralp, whose Left Party (Die Linke) came out on top in local elections in Berlin last month, appeared to suggest in remarks made during an internal authorization process for an interview that she gave to Der Spiegel that she couldn't make references to a particular pro-Palestinian activist out of fear for her own safety.
"I can't put myself and my family in danger for Der Spiegel," the magazine cites her as having written in a Word Document edit, which was inadvertently sent back to the reporters.
"What do we do now? Cancel the whole interview?" she is cited as having asked her press officer and other party colleagues, while stating in another remark, "I should never have agreed to this interview."
Elif Eralp under pressure to clearly label out threats she sees
In the Der Spiegel interview, which was conducted on Monday in Eralp's office in Berlin's House of Representatives, the 45-year-old was asked about allegations of antisemitism that have been leveled at members of her socialist party.
Those accusations came about after at least two instances where people with questionable backgrounds showed up to celebrate after Eralp's party won elections in the city state last month.
For instance, the Left Party election celebration in the Berlin district of Neukölln was attended by a controversial pro-Palestinian activist associated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is classified as a terrorist organization by the European Union.
In the past, Ibrahim Ibrahim has described Yahya Sinwar, the former head of Hamas in Gaza, widely regarded as the mastermind behind the deadly terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as a "martyr" and a "hero." He has since rejected accusations of antisemitism and of supporting terrorism or Hamas.
Asked by Der Spiegel whether she was referring to the Ibrahim incident, Eralp initially responded with a "yes." But she later returned the interview transcript to the magazine with the question crossed out and the comment regarding her and her family's safety.
In Germany, it is standard practice for an interviewee to review and approve direct quotations with media outlets before the interview is published.
In notes included in the approved version of the transcript, which Der Spiegel believes were left in by accident, Eralp wrote that Berlin police had previously advised her not to comment on specific individuals.
Der Spiegel on why it published the notes
That Eralp chose to conceal her concerns publicly led some politicians to ask whether she was the right person to be the mayor of Berlin.
Der Spiegel wrote in its story:
"There were reasons not to publish – Eralp's security concerns first and foremost," the magazine wrote. "But the political importance of her notes outweighed them. Der Spiegel believes that the public should know."
It added that the story begs the question: "Can a woman who is too scared to name a terrorist sympathizer in an interview be responsible for the security of all Berliners?"
SPD, Greens also weigh in
Rival politicians weighed in, including from the Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens, with whom the Left Party is due to conduct coalition talks in Berlin next month.
"I would advise my party to distance itself from an alliance with the Left Party," said the SPD's Karl Lauterbach, who rose to prominence as Germany's health minister during the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Further talks about a coalition with this party should be out of the question for any social democrat," added SPD internal affairs spokesman Sebastian Fiedler.
Katharina Dröge, the leader of the Green Party's parliamentary grouping, asked in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, "Will [Eralp] continue to let herself be influenced by those in her own ranks who are close to criminal groups and who tolerate threats and intimidation towards their own lead candidate? Or will she manage to give a clear and tough response?"
The chairman of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, warned: "The SPD and the Greens have a duty not to hand governmental responsibility for Berlin and for the security of the Jewish community to the Left Party" and claimed the story showed that "the Left Party is incapable of distancing itself from terrorist sympathizers and antisemites."
Eralp issues tough response, hits out at critics
Eralp hit back later on Thursday, slamming a "truly toxic debate," vowing not to be intimidated and promising a tough stance "against organized crime, against organizations that glorify violence, against violence, against terror."
She said she wouldn't comment on the specifics of the Der Spiegel story but insisted that she would "ensure the security of all Berliners."
Eralp also received backing from the vice-president of the German parliament and veteran Left Party colleague Bodo Ramelow, who criticized the Der Spiegel story as "more than questionable."
He said the reporting "targeted a person who feels vulnerable and made them even more vulnerable." He said internal communications had been used to depict the "anachronistic cliché" of a "weak woman."

Zaporizhzhia experienced a record number of Russian FPV drone attacks on 29 October, injuring 14 people, including a 14-year-old boy, regional authorities said.
Russian forces used FPV drones and multiple-launch rocket systems to attack civilian infrastructure, targeting municipal transport and damaging residential buildings, warehouses, and cars, prosecutors said.
Zaporizhzhia reports record FPV drone attacks
Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration head Mykhailo Semikin said Zaporizhzhia had experienced a record number of FPV drone attacks on Thursday. After meeting with military officials, he said the authorities were aware of the situation and relevant services and Ukrainian defenders were responding.
He said Russian forces had “changed their tactics and modified their drones,” adding that Ukrainian military personnel were working on countermeasures to address the new threats.
Semikin urged residents to remain calm, heed air raid alerts, and exercise particular caution.
Russian drones target municipal transport
The attacks included strikes on a municipal bus, a minibus, and a trolleybus, according to Semikin.
In the morning, a Russian FPV drone struck a municipal bus, injuring four people.
In a separate attack, Russian forces struck 15 vehicles, a warehouse building, and a power line, sparking a fire and damaging a nearby apartment building. Two men, aged 41 and 66, were injured.
At around midday, another FPV drone hit a minibus in central Zaporizhzhia, injuring one person.
Later, a Russian drone struck a municipal trolleybus, critically injuring a 56-year-old woman and lightly injuring two other women, aged 71 and 66.
Zaporizhzhia’s proximity to the front line
Zaporizhzhia lies relatively close to the front line in southern Ukraine, leaving the city exposed to Russian attacks with weapons that can be used at shorter ranges, including FPV drones and multiple-launch rocket systems.
The proximity allows Russian forces to threaten civilian infrastructure more easily without relying solely on long-range missiles or drones.
Prosecutors investigate suspected war crime
The Zaporizhzhia Regional Prosecutor’s Office said it had opened a war crimes investigation. Investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine’s regional directorate are conducting the pretrial investigation.
The casualty count and damage reports were preliminary, and authorities said information was still being updated as the attacks continued.
Russian attacks kill civilians in several Ukrainian cities
Zaporizhzhia was not the only major city hit by Russian attacks on 29 October. In Dnipro, a Russian strike on the railway station killed at least 14 people.
In Chernihiv, two teenage girls were killed and 23 people injured, including four children. In Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, three people were killed and 15 injured, including three children.
The attacks damaged residential buildings and civilian infrastructure in all three cities.

Latvian Border Guards Will Be Allowed to Use Weapons to Protect Infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:47:34 UTC
05:47:34 KST

Latvian border guards will be allowed to use weapons to repel attacks on border infrastructure facilities.
This is provided for by amendments to the Law on the State Border Guard of Latvia, adopted by the country’s Saeima. LSM+ reports on this.
Border guards will be able to use weapons without warning if, under specific circumstances, it is impossible to prevent an attack by other means.
The amendments also stipulate that if the use of weapons results in injury or death, the border guard service must immediately, but no later than within 24 hours, notify the prosecutor’s office.
Raimondas Bergmanis, Chair of the Defense Committee, previously noted that the inviolability of the state border and the protection of infrastructure in the context of hybrid warfare are important components of Latvia’s territorial integrity.
“The amendments to the law have expanded the border guards’ capabilities to immediately stop violations,” the statement reads.
In early October, armed and masked men, who were accompanying a group of intruders from Belarus and behaving aggressively, attempted to smuggle them across the border into Latvia.
At that time, servicemen of the Latvian National Armed Forces thwarted this attempt.
Recently, another provocation took place, one that was particularly blatant and aggressive.
Armed escorts threatened Latvian servicemen while actively pushing a group of migrants toward the border.
Later, a previously little-known group called Melnie rusi (Black Rus) claimed responsibility for this incident on the Latvian-Belarusian border.
In October, a group of unknown masked individuals infiltrated Latvia from Belarus and damaged border surveillance infrastructure.
