What to Know About China’s Top-Secret Spaceplane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:45:36 UTC
05:45:36 KST

A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.
The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.
The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.
Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the Defense Intelligence Agency assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified DIA assessment of threats to the United States in space.
Catch and Release
The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.
The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.
Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.
The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing.
Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.
A Fleeting Glance
The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation.
The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).
NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.
The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.
Pew-Pew With DEWs
The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite. One potential use for lasers in space would be to dazzle a sensor on an adversary’s satellite.
“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
The DIA noted China’s testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles and the country’s historic demonstration last year of satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit, a regime some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, something no other country has achieved above LEO. China has also tested a robotic arm that could snag a spacecraft out of orbit, and now operates a growing fleet of satellites called TJS that routinely approach foreign spacecraft.
The US Space Force also has a constellation of inspector satellites in geosynchronous orbit and recently procured more that could be refueled, overcoming maneuverability limitations. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed last month that the Pentagon has fielded weapons in space, making the United States the first nation to acknowledge possession of orbital weapons.
Russia is pursuing its own orbital combat program, which includes an ambition to deploy a nuclear weapon in space, according to US intelligence officials.
A more conventional Russian weapons system, known as Nivelir, is designed to fire projectiles from one satellite to smash into another. The Russian military simulated an attack using the Nivelir system in 2020. In April, Russia launched a fleet of small satellites into an orbit close to a commercial radar remote sensing satellite owned by ICEYE that provides reconnaissance imagery to Ukraine. One of the Russian satellites moved within “tens of meters” of the ICEYE satellite earlier this month before backing away, US officials said.
This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

Foster + Partners unveils replacement for landmark San Siro stadium in Milan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:45:00 UTC
05:45:00 KST

Foster + Partners unveils replacement for landmark San Siro stadium in Milan
British architecture studio Foster + Partners and US studio Manica have unveiled their design for Generali Stadium, a new football stadium for clubs AC Milan and Inter Milan, set to replace Italy’s iconic San Siro.
Planned to be built alongside the 99-year-old San Siro stadium, which will later be torn down, the 71,500-seat replacement will be defined by a structural facade composed of elongated X-framed concrete supports.
Foster + Partners‘ founder Norman Foster told Dezeen the overarching goal is “to create a new home for two storied football clubs, which captures the unique energy of the city and its distinctive architectural and structural traditions”.
“The Generali Stadium celebrates the enduring connection between the football clubs – FC Internazionale Milano (Inter Milan) and AC Milan – and the city of Milano and will drive this shared heritage into the future,” he explained.
The design reveal follows the sale of the iconic stadium to the two rival football teams, which was approved by Milan’s city council in October 2025. It is being developed by Foster’s firm with the US practice Manica, and the naming rights belong to insurance giant Generali.
AC Milan and Inter Milan will continue to share the existing San Siro venue until the 2032 European Championship, co-hosted by Italy, for which the new stadium is scheduled to be completed. San Siro will then be demolished, according to the BBC.
Generali Stadium’s defining feature is its pre-cast structural facade, which will support the stadium bowl and double-curved roof. This will also frame and naturally ventilate a series of lofty loggia-like spaces on its upper levels, intended to feel open and welcoming.
“The structural facade is the defining architectural concept of the stadium: a holistic and monumental piece of infrastructure rising approximately 60 metres in height, composed of interlocking low-carbon precast concrete segments connected through expressed structural joints,” Foster said.
“It is a celebration of Milanese and Italian engineering tradition, where architecture and structure become one,” Foster explained.
Another distinctive element will be “two curvas” – the curved north and south stands, designed to bring spectators near to the pitch, with opposing fans closely facing each other.
“That relationship of two opposing walls of supporters, each tied to one of the city’s great clubs, is unique to Milan and found in no other stadium in the world,” said Manica founder David Manica.
“The whole seating bowl is built around it,” he told Dezeen. “Rather than starting with an image or an icon, we began with the experience of the fans. The architecture is a result of that guiding principle.”
According to Foster, this design also draws on San Siro’s distinctive structure.
“Its seating bowl is inspired by the San Siro itself, with its distinctive ‘curvas’, but with greater proximity to the pitch,” Foster explained.
“The external shape is driven by the curvas behind the goals. Here, the north and south ends rise on a 37-degree pitch to house 11,700 at each end – north for Internazionale and south for AC Milan.”
The stadium is planned to be all-electric and carbon-neutral in operation, targeting LEED Gold Certification. The roof will incorporate 27,500 square metres of photovoltaic panels, while a “low-carbon precast concrete system” will be utilised to minimise waste and construction time.
The bowl’s geometry will be engineered to “amplify the roar of crowds within the stadium, enhancing the atmosphere during events while significantly reducing acoustic spillover and noise pollution”, Foster said.
“San Siro is famous for its noise, and the best way to honour that legacy was to capture that atmosphere – and amplify it,” added David Manica.
“We treated acoustics as a primary design driver from the very first sketches,” he said. “The result is a stadium where the chanting and singing build on themselves, taking the atmosphere Milanese supporters love and making it even more powerful.”
The project forms part of a wider 281,000-square-metre masterplan that will combine public spaces with green areas and leisure and retail zones.
Designed by architect Ulisse Stacchini, San Siro, otherwise known as Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, was built in 1925. It has been modified several times over its lifetime, but has remained unchanged since the 1990 World Cup.
The possibility of its demolition emerged in 2019, when AC Milan and Inter Milan announced they were exploring plans to build a replacement venue for San Siro.
The clubs later selected a design by architecture studio Populous, called the Cathedral, but the Regional Commission for the Cultural Heritage of Lombardy blocked its development in 2023 because of the existing building’s cultural significance.
Demolition was made possible by the building’s sale, which was approved after an overnight debate that took place for nearly 12 hours.
At the time, mayor Giuseppe Sala suggested the sale would prevent Milan from being left “with the burden of an abandoned arena”, as the two clubs had begun exploring plans to build two separate stadiums on the city’s outskirts.
Reflecting on the project, Foster said the Generali Stadium’s design draws on his “great personal connection with the city”.
“As a student of architecture, I spent many hours walking through and sketching its heroic public spaces – the urban route of the historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II and individual structures such as the Torre Velasca and Pirelli Tower – and studying the pioneering work of Pier Luigi Nervi,” he explained.
“The verticality and rhythm of the Duomo, the civic generosity of the city’s porticos, and the spatial experience of the city’s great public plazas have all been inspirational and inseparable as a background to the design of the Generali Stadium, which will be a new civic monument for Milano.”
Elsewhere, Foster + Partners is also developing its design for Manchester United’s new 100,000-seat stadium in the UK.
The stadium, which is designed with a giant tent-like structure, was described by Foster as “one of the most exciting projects in the world”.

Putin Says Nordic Leaders Were Right to Call Him, Despite EU Criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:40:52 UTC
05:40:52 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin defended Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre over their Oct. 27 telephone call with him, saying they were right to reach out despite criticism from other European leaders.
Speaking at a press conference after the Russia-Africa summit on Thursday, Oct. 29, Putin confirmed that the conversation took place at the initiative of the Nordic leaders and covered a wide range of issues.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I know that criticism was later directed at them, but it is not for us to judge whether this [the call] is right or wrong. I believe it is right,” Putin said, according to Interfax-Ru.
“After all, there are people in Europe who do not want to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia, as some do, but want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” he added.
The remarks came on the same day that the Kremlin ruled out European participation in the next month’s Abu Dhabi negotiations with Ukraine and the US.
Dialogue offer paired with a warning
Moscow, according to the Russian president, backs any effort to rebuild relations with Europe, whether with the EU as a bloc or individual countries.
Russia has always supported steps toward restoring “full-format and full-fledged relations” with European states, he added.
However, during the same remarks, Putin warned that a war between Russia and Europe would have “no winners,” claiming that the West had failed in its goal of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia and was unlikely to achieve it by 2030, Russian-state owned media TASS reported.
Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
The warning comes as European governments step up preparations for a possible confrontation.
Germany’s elite KSK special forces began training for a role in conventional warfare with Russia, shifting away from its traditional focus on hostage rescue and counterterrorism, Brig. Gen. Andreas Kuhne told Germany’s BILD earlier this week.
European countries are also facing a rise in hybrid warfare threats, including sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and frequent drone incursions into their airspace.
While some European leaders have described the situation as already amounting to a war, as the line between hybrid tactics and direct conflict continues to blur, others have been more cautious, refraining from such labels to avoid escalating tensions with Moscow.
Mixed reaction from European leaders
The abrupt discussion drew a mixed response from Ukraine’s European allies, particularly from other Nordic countries, who said the call was not coordinated with them in advance.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” Euronews reported, adding that Russia’s ongoing escalation against Ukraine remains evidence that “Moscow is not serious about diplomacy.”
“We have previously emphasised, with clear backing from the rest of Europe, that when others have gone solo and, for example, travelled to Moscow, it is crucial that we, Europeans, stand together,” she continued, in a reference to former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orbán who flew to Russia to meet with Putin at the time of his tenure.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson reiterated that she also has “pretty low expectations for this kind of [direct] talk.”
Støre defended the call by saying Europe needs to speak with Russia, instead of only relying on messages mediated by the US administration, which has a different take on the war.
The content of the call had also become a point of dispute.
On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Financial Times reported that Putin spent much of their 90-minute conversation discussing medieval history, while an immediate ceasefire was barely raised.
Støre rejected the FT’s report, asking the newspaper to correct it. “That he gave a lecture on Slavic history is simply not correct,” he said, adding that the time was distributed relatively evenly between the participants. The newspaper has refused to issue a correction.
The call came after a week of diplomacy involving the two Nordic leaders.
On Oct. 20, they hosted a meeting between President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in Oslo, with US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joining remotely.
Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg for a direct meeting with Putin on Oct. 21, where he urged Putin to consider resuming trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US, bringing documents outlining approaches to ending the war.
The Kremlin reiterated that a just and lasting peace in Ukraine was possible only if Russia’s interests were taken into account.

Palestinians injured, arrested in Israeli raids across West Bank

Palestinians injured, arrested in Israeli raids across West Bank
This comes as more than 3,300 Palestinians are forced from homes in Hebron in Israeli military offensive.
Israeli forces and settlers have escalated pogroms and raids across the occupied West Bank, attacking and injuring Palestinians, restricting their movement, carrying out arrests and demolishing homes.
This comes as a military offensive and siege on the Hebron governorate entered its seventh day – an operation that has displaced or besieged hundreds of Palestinian families and kept tens of thousands of students out of classrooms.
In the Qalandiya refugee camp just north of occupied East Jerusalem, Israeli forces carried out a raid that triggered clashes on Thursday. Two children were wounded, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said.
It said its teams treated a 15-year-old boy who was shot with live ammunition in both legs, and a child, aged 12, who was injured by live-bullet fragments. Both were taken to hospital.
In a separate incident, Israeli soldiers and settlers beat disabled Palestinian Mohammad Ahmad Ayesh Thawabta in the village of al-Maniya, southeast of Bethlehem, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces detained 13 Palestinians, including three brothers, in raids before dawn on Thursday, the Palestinian Prisoners Media Office and local sources said. Most of the raids were in the Nablus governorate, where soldiers searched homes and harassed families.
Hebron offensive
In Hebron, Israeli forces continued raids and closures that began last week after two Israeli soldiers were killed in a gun attack. Both Palestinian suspects were also killed.
Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said on Thursday that 537 families, comprising 3,361 people, have been forced from their homes, Wafa reported.
They include 232 infants, 326 older people, 147 pregnant or breastfeeding women and 213 people with chronic illnesses. Municipal figures put the total number affected, including those under siege, at about 5,000 people from 780 families.
Dudin said the offensive has disrupted education for about 262,000 students across 589 schools in the governorate this week, forcing schools to move to remote learning. Officials estimated daily economic losses at 10 million to 12 million shekels ($3.2m to $3.9m).
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society said Israeli forces detained 110 Palestinians in the governorate from Friday to Wednesday. Soldiers beat two men in Dura and Wad al-Saman and arrested two brothers while they were ploughing their land east of Yatta, it said. Israeli forces also raided homes in Taffuh and Halhul, and settlers attacked vehicles at the city’s closed northern entrance, it added.
Memorials demolished
In nearby Masafer Yatta, armed settlers attacked US journalist Jasper Nathaniel and two activists in the village of Umm al-Khair on Wednesday. Russian activist Adele Shoko said on X that the settlers beat and threatened them and stole their equipment and Nathaniel was pepper-sprayed and arrested.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Israeli forces are still operating in Hebron, blocking access and imposing tight restrictions on movement across the governorate.
They are “disrupting Palestinians’ access to livelihoods, education and healthcare. Most displaced families are staying with relatives,” OCHA said, calling for the prevention of further forced displacements and demolitions.
Israeli forces also demolished memorials to Palestinians in several parts of the Hebron governorate on Thursday. In Dura, south of Hebron city, soldiers fired a heavy barrage of tear gas before bulldozing a mural bearing the images of several of the town’s dead, including Bajis Abu Atwan, who was killed in the 1970s.
The targeting of memorials “appears to be a new pattern recently adopted by Israeli forces across all West Bank governorates – though at a higher rate here in Hebron”, Al Jazeera’s Muntasir Nassar said, reporting from Dura.
Israeli military and settler attacks across the West Bank have intensified since Israel’s war on Gaza began in October 2023.

US chipmaker Intel posts 21% revenue jump in Q3 on data center demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:39:55 UTC
05:39:55 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
US semiconductor producer Intel reported a 21% year-on-year increase in third-quarter revenue to $16.5 billion on Thursday, driven by robust demand for its data center and artificial intelligence processors.  
Revenue rose from $13.7 billion in the third quarter of 2025, topping company guidance, according to its financial results statement.
The Data Center and AI group led the performance with revenue surging 78% year-on-year to $7.3 billion, delivering the segment's fastest growth rate in 15 years.
Intel Foundry revenue climbed 58% year-on-year to $6.7 billion during the quarter.
In contrast, revenue in the Client Computing and Physical AI Group fell 5% to $8.1 billion, reflecting persistent weakness across the personal computer market.
Under generally accepted accounting principles, net income attributable to Intel declined 18% to $3.3 billion, or $0.60 per diluted share, down from $4.1 billion, or $0.90 per share, a year earlier.
On an adjusted basis, non-GAAP net income surged 169% to $2.8 billion, or $0.52 per diluted share, compared with $1.0 billion, or $0.23 per share, in the third quarter of 2025.
Gross margin improved to 43% from 38.2% a year earlier, while the operating margin expanded to 15.3% from 5%.
"Our Q3 results demonstrate improving execution, meaningful progress expanding supply and continued advancement of our process technology," said Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel.
"Despite near-term headwinds across the PC industry, demand for our CPUs remains robust, reinforcing our confidence in the long-term growth opportunities for our business," Tan added.
David Zinsner, chief financial officer of Intel, warned that the slowdown in personal computer demand is expected to continue through at least the first half of 2027.
During the quarter, the company completed a $23 billion public equity offering to strengthen its balance sheet and announced plans to acquire quantum software platform Classiq.
For the fourth quarter of 2026, Intel expects revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion, with diluted earnings per share projected at $0.10 on a GAAP basis and $0.25 on a non-GAAP basis.

Australia's Cape Town desperation evident on another pulsating Test day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:39:18 UTC
05:39:18 KST

If there was any doubt how much the Cape Town Test matters to Pat Cummins's Australian team, one only needed to clock the cooing pack of them careening towards Cameron Green and Mitchell Starc an hour into the evening session of day three at Newlands.
Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, set fair on 62 and attacking everything Australia threw at him, had tried to limbo away from a Starc bouncer that followed him like a heat-seeking missile. Not quite agile enough with his Matrix manoeuvre, Ackerman faintly edged the ball flush into his faceguard, from which it ballooned into the cordon.
Unsure of the deflection and with his ears still ringing from the ding on his grill, Ackerman walked over to his skipper Temba Bavuma to discuss a review of the umpire's call, perhaps as surprised as the Australians when Travis Head arrived on the scene to inquire after his health.
But, in all the chaos and confusion, the crucial 15 seconds had passed before Ackerman could signal for a review. He had to depart.
Loading Twitter content
It has been that sort of series, really; so many periods of ascendancy abruptly terminated by moments of genius, madness and confusion, and so many subversions of the pattern recognition Test cricket followers can normally rely on to impose a sense of order on what they're looking at.
Earlier, in the latter stages of its first innings of 429, Australia probably let an extra 100 runs go begging. It sets up a perfect scenario even for those Australian fans who are not normally night owls: a thrilling finish on Friday night into Saturday morning.
On a pulsating day that produced 243 runs and 10 wickets, there was a second Test century for the recalled Josh Inglis and 80 for Alex Carey, both of whom fell to the off-spin of Simon Harmer.
An obscurity to most Australians before this series, and tipped to be dropped after the first Test, Harmer was in the thick of everything again with four wickets, two catches, a busted finger and plenty of chatter.
Youngster Cooper Connolly, looking entirely at home at Test level, made a patient 29 from 83 deliveries and might have kicked on further with better support from Australia's tail; the loss of 6-59 to finish off Australia's first innings was, as Pat Cummins often phrases such things, not ideal.
Yet it was still a 100-run lead, and early in South Africa's second innings you got the sense the game was about to break right open for an early finish.
In quick succession, Aiden Markram, who has been a thorn in Australia's side, lazily slapped a loose one from Starc into the clutches of Head at mid-off, and David Bedingham, seemingly rattled by a Starc bouncer that cannoned into his chest, holed out with another inexplicable hook.
The Proteas were 2-31, still 69 runs behind, and the hyenas were circling.
Via the counter-attack of Ackerman, then in a slow and steady partnership between Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke, South Africa began its rally. Yet there was one last twist in store with barely 15 minutes left in the day's play.
Having tortured Bavuma for a few hours with his sharp turn out of the footmarks, Nathan Lyon removed the Proteas skipper again, this time a dipping off break that snuck between bat and pad to castle the lunging batsman. Bavuma is not quite to Lyon what Daryll Cullinan once was to Shane Warne, but he is not far off.
On the matter of hoodoos, much has been made in recent days of Cummins's record-breaking streak without a wicket.
It continued today, despite periods in which the Aussie skipper bowled with genuine pace and guile, although his desperation to break his drought was made clear by one ill-advised review. Even when it is 1.6 metre Bavuma in the firing line, it is always difficult to get an LBW call when it hits above the batsman's knee roll.
In truth, the odd brain fade was perfectly excusable due to the ratcheting up of the atmosphere as this game progressed.
Some testiness and conflict in this series was inevitable, but it has manifested in curious ways. Each team's most vocal player — Marnus Labuschagne for Australia, Matthew Breetzke for the Proteas — has been its worst performed.
Breetzke, in fact, finally started to come good late on day three, and will resume tomorrow believing he is the man to turn the game for his country.
Given the way these two teams have echoed each other's efforts in the past few weeks, perhaps that suggests one last tantalising and slightly mad prospect in the Australian chase: how about Marnus Labuschagne as the last-minute hero?

Amazon net sales surge 12% to $202B in Q3 as cloud unit accelerates
Unknown

2026-10-29
20:38:26 UTC
05:38:26 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
US e-commerce and technology giant Amazon reported a 12% year-on-year increase in net sales to $201.9 billion for the third quarter of 2026, driven by accelerating growth in its cloud computing division, the company announced on Thursday.
Net sales rose from $180.2 billion in the same period of 2025, or 13% excluding an unfavorable foreign exchange impact of $900 million.
Operating income jumped 61% to $28.1 billion in the July-September period from $17.4 billion a year earlier, lifting the operating margin to a record 13.9%.
Amazon Web Services net sales surged 39.3% year-on-year to $46 billion, marking its fastest growth pace in nearly five years and pushing its annualized revenue run rate to $184 billion.
AWS operating income climbed 55% to $17.8 billion from $11.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025.
In the retail business, North America segment sales grew 6% year-on-year to $112.9 billion, while international sales increased 5% to $43.1 billion, or 8% excluding currency fluctuations.
Net income slipped 2% to $20.7 billion, or $1.89 per diluted share, compared with $21.2 billion, or $1.95 per diluted share, a year earlier, primarily reflecting a $9.5 billion pre-tax gain from investments in AI firm Anthropic recorded in the third quarter of 2025.
"Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working, with over 39% year-over-year revenue growth in Q3 and projected revenue growth rates of over 40% both in 2027 and in 2028," said Andy Jassy, president and chief executive of Amazon.
"There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years," Jassy added.
For the fourth quarter of 2026, Amazon expects net sales between $240 billion and $247 billion, representing year-on-year growth of 12% to 16%.
Operating income in the final quarter of the year is projected between $28.5 billion and $33.5 billion, compared with $25 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025.
The company reiterated that it expects cash capital expenditures for full-year 2026 to reach approximately $220 billion, driven primarily by investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Gulf War Air Campaign Map Featured in New Smithsonian Exhibit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:37:31 UTC
05:37:31 KST

A map pinned to the wall in a basement 36 years ago will go on display in November at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.
The map, used to identify strategic targets across Iraq in the fall of 1990, was used in the planning of Operation Desert Storm, and will be included in the museum’s new “Modern Military Aviation” gallery in Washington D.C., tracing advances in airpower from the Korean War to the present.
The exhibit seeks to expose visitors to the advances that changed the nature of warfare.
The map is one of two created at the time by now-retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. Deptula was the principal air attack planner for Operation Desert Storm—identifying strategic targets across Iraq and developing the blueprint for the coalition air campaign.
Two Gulf War maps remain in Deptula’s possession, and both are on display at AFA’s headquarters in Arlington: one depicting Baghdad hangs in AFA’s Heritage Hall, while a larger map of Iraq hangs in Deptula’s office, surrounded by other mementos and artifacts from throughout his career.
A reproduction of the map will be displayed as a large-format graphic panel at the Smithsonian. Dr. Michael Hankins, the Smithsonian’s Curator of U.S. Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps post-World War II Aviation, learned about the maps during a chance conversation with the Mitchell Institute’s Executive Director Doug Birkey. Hankins was aware the maps had existed, but did not know they had been carried back from Saudi Arabia after the war.
Hankins immediately recognized the narrative the maps could tell and saw them as a perfect bridge for the exhibit he was creating, one that could help tell the story of the evolution from conventional airpower to the age of stealth and precision bombing that has defined military strike operations ever since.
Given the map’s fragility and size, Hankins decided a reproduction would be more accessible to visitors at the Smithsonian.
“As we were planning the layouts for some of these different labels, we had an opportunity, particularly in that section, to have a large-scale photo as an introduction to the Desert Storm section of the gallery,” Hankins said. “What better visual image to use than this to speak to that? … [It shows] how the thought process of using military aviation was different in 1991 than it might have been in previous conflicts.”
The Map, Deptula, and the Black Hole
While the map tells the story of Operation Desert Storm, it is also a pivotal artifact in the career of the officer who led the planning of that operation over countless 20-hour days in a basement room in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, that came to be known as “the Black Hole.” On Aug. 2, 1990, Iraqi forces under dictator Saddam Hussein invaded neighboring Kuwait and conquered the country within days. In response, a coalition led by the United States was formed to eject Saddam’s forces from Kuwait.
Deptula, then a lieutenant colonel working in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, was pulled into a Pentagon strategic planning cell known as “Checkmate,” led by Col. John Warden III. The Checkmate team had been developing a new strategic air doctrine for the post-Cold War era when it was tasked to create an operational concept for countering Iraq’s invasion with airpower. They dubbed their plan “Instant Thunder.” After briefing Army Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf, who as commander of U.S. Central Command would oversee the operation, as well as Gen. Colin Powell, then the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Warden, Deptula and a couple of others flew to Saudi Arabia to brief Gen. Chuck Horner, the top air commander for the theater, on the plan.
Horner, unconvinced of Warden’s ability to lead the actual planning, accepted Warden’s concept, but sent Warden back to Washington, while retaining the others. Among them, only Deptula stayed long term, becoming the principal target planner for the entire campaign.
Based in the Royal Saudi Air Force headquarters basement, their “Black Hole” office was defined by secrecy, the sensitive political nature of American forces planning offensive operations on Saudi soil, and the punishing hours demanded of its occupants—and, Deptula recalled, once “someone was allowed to come into it, they were never allowed to go out.”
Here Deptula created his map and the Master Air Attack Plan that would ultimately orchestrate every strike of the campaign. On the map, Deptula and his team pinpointed strategic targets, coded by category: air defense, leadership, military bases, Scud ballistic missile launchers, command and control systems, and electricity and telecommunications networks.
The map helped planners to identify relationships between targets, coordinate force packages across multiple objectives simultaneously, and find gaps in Iraqi defenses that a list of coordinates alone could not reveal. For example, the map revealed a gap in Iraqi border monitoring stations that allowed Deptula to safely route F-15E attack aircraft to strike Scud launchers in western Iraq before they could fire on Israel. “It wasn’t just a pretty map that hung on the wall in our planning cell,” Deptula said. “That’s what the visualization of a map does that a bunch of target coordinates and names doesn’t.”
Underlying the Instant Thunder concept was the conviction that airpower could systematically dismantle Iraq’s war-making ability. Each mark aimed to take a specific capability off the table. It was a deliberate break from what Deptula called “an attritional, intelligence-based philosophy” that had defined air campaigns in Vietnam, where success was measured by the percentage of damage inflicted rather than by what capability had actually been removed.
Using the F-117 Nighthawk’s stealth capability to lead the attack, and precision munitions to ensure rapid success, coalition air forces disabled Iraq’s command and control almost instantly, and took away other war-making capabilities within weeks—all while greatly minimizing overall infrastructure damage across the country.
By targeting electrical transformer yards, rather than power plants, planners saw they could shut down the electrical grid while keeping reconstruction manageable. In some cases, Deptula recalled, Iraqi power plant managers switched off their facilities, and the coalition chose not to strike them.
“By the third night of the war, there hadn’t been an electron flowing in the Iraqi power grid,” said Deptula. “So that’s the objective.” For Hankins, the map illustrated the evolution of airpower in a way no other artifact could. He said, “I think the map shows that in an interesting way, because you can see who’s targeting what, what kinds of things they are able to target, what kinds of things they were successful at. It’s different than something you would see in the sections on the Korean War or the Vietnam War.”
Serving as the visual introduction, the map opens the gallery’s Desert Storm section, which focuses on the new technologies that defined the conflict: a scale model of an F-117 stealth fighter and an interactive display explaining how stealth technology works and why it proved so decisive.
Separately, the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center near Dulles Airport received an original F-117 in October, so Washington visitors can see the real thing up close.
The Desert Storm section will also serve as a bridge to the conflicts of the Global War on Terror that the United States has fought over the past three decades, including the Predator drone Deptula would later help pioneer as an armed platform. After the September 11 attacks, Deptula was directing the Combined Air Operations Center for the opening of the Afghanistan campaign when the United States fired a Hellfire missile from an RQ-1 Predator at al-Qaeda targets, the first combat use of an armed remotely piloted aircraft.
For Deptula, the map’s display at the Smithsonian represents an acknowledgment of a turning point in how America wages war and as validation of the campaign itself. “I think it’s recognition of the significance of the operation,” Deptula said. “It was the birth of how we conceive air operations.”
For Hankins, the map’s greatest value may be what it teaches visitors who know nothing about the Gulf War. “It’s not just let’s launch a bunch of airplanes and go drop a bunch of weapons,” he said. “It’s much more careful than that. It takes a lot of people a lot of time.”
The Modern Military Aviation gallery, the final chapter of the Smithsonian’s eight-year renovation, is scheduled to open to the public on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, 2026.

Greek PM calls Turkey-Libya maritime deal 'void;' calls for global truce after Black Sea attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:36:23 UTC
05:36:23 KST

Greek PM calls Turkey-Libya maritime deal 'void;' calls for global truce after Black Sea attacks
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 29 - Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said on Thursday that the recently signed maritime deal between Libya's eastern parliament and Turkey was "blatantly illegal, null and void," adding that it "completely disregards the geography."
Mitsotakis, speaking to Reuters as Greece ends its UN Security Council presidency, also called for an urgent "international truce" to protect shipping in the Black Sea after the sinking of a Greek-owned container vessel on Wednesday.
Libya's eastern parliament last week approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey, drawing condemnation from Athens, but also Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, as a threat to regional security and international legal order.
"It completely disregards the geography, the reality that there are Greek islands -- they seem to completely disappear in the thinking of Turkey and Libya," Mitsotakis said, accusing them of attempting to create a "fait accompli" that ignores the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has said that reactions from the EU and others to the approval of the agreement, originally agreed in 2019, had no legitimate basis, defending Ankara's policy in the eastern Mediterranean.
Since the 2019 Libya-Turkey deal, Greece has awarded a license to a consortium led by Chevron to look for gas off the island of Crete and has sought a separate agreement with Libya on demarcating their maritime zones.
Mitsotakis assured "there's no risk that these explorations will be in any way challenged."
Referring to Libya and Greece as "natural neighbors," Mitsotakis, who first became prime minister in 2019 and is in his second term, urged the African country to negotiate directly with Athens and take the discussions "very, very seriously."
ATTACKS ON SHIPS IN THE BLACK SEA
Mitsotakis, 58, spoke to Reuters after chairing a council debate on maritime security, only hours after a Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria in the latest strike on ships in the western Black Sea this month.
Greek-operated ships are among the world's largest fleets of tankers and are pivotal for trade across the Black Sea region, whose waters are shared by Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania and Turkey, as well as warring Russia and Ukraine, which Moscow invaded in February 2022.
"We do need some sort of international truce when it comes to the freedom of navigation," said Mitsotakis, adding that it was of "utmost priority" to allow for exports of grain from the region into the world through the Black Sea.
"Greek shipowners would be the first to resume trading in the Black Sea, also from Ukraine, assuming a safe passage is guaranteed," he said, stressing the rising costs of shipping as chartering and insurance expenses have "gone through the roof."
It was not immediately clear who had carried out the attack, which added to growing concerns about the impact of Russia's war in Ukraine on commercial shipping in the area.
Mitsotakis said that Ukraine was financially dependent on exports of its products: "They had a bumper harvest, but the grain is now sitting in silos, in danger of rotting."
"Unfortunately, for the moment, Russia doesn't seem to be interested in engaging in a substantive discussion," he said.
RED SEA SECURITY, RUSSIA
Mitsotakis also called on the European Union to bolster its naval mission to protect shipping in the Red Sea called Aspides, which was launched in 2024 to protect from attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
Intensifying hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
"My argument is simple: the European Union has an interest in having a concrete presence with hard assets in this part of the world, and we need more countries to participate in Aspides," Mitsotakis told Reuters.
He said Greece, Italy and France have deployed "assets" as part of the mission and that was "clearly not enough." Diplomats told Reuters as of late September there were six warships operating as part of the operation.
The Houthis said this week they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route.
"If we really want to send the message also to the Gulf countries that we take their security seriously, but we also protect the critical arteries and waterways that are absolutely indispensable for European trade, we should be willing to deploy more assets to this part of the world," Mitsotakis said.
Asked about US President Donald Trump's move earlier this month to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, Mitsotakis reaffirmed Greek support for sanctions on Moscow.
"We believe that we need to put economic pressure and impose more financial pain on Russia to send a very clear signal that as long as they prolong this war, they will suffer very specific economic consequences," he said. REUTERS

TEL AVIV, October 29. /TASS/. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won the majority of votes in the October 27 parliamentary election, with all ballots counted, according to preliminary figures released by the Central Elections Committee (CEC).
Likud is projected to win 27 seats in the 120-member Knesset, Israel’s parliament, followed by Yashar, led by Netanyahu’s main opposition rival Gadi Eisenkot, with 21.
The bloc comprising Likud and the far-right and Orthodox parties that support Netanyahu and make up the current governing coalition also retains its lead. It is set to secure 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition. Arab parties are projected to win 19 seats, although neither Likud nor the opposition is expected to be willing to form a coalition with them.
The official final results are expected no later than November 4, once appeals are reviewed. President Isaac Herzog will then consult representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset before tasking one of its members with forming a new governing coalition.
A coalition needs at least 61 Knesset seats to form a government, a threshold no political bloc has reached. The leader of the party with the most seats usually becomes the candidate for prime minister. However, the president may also task a politician whose party did not win the majority of votes with forming a government if that politician can assemble a coalition.
The first candidate will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible two-week extension. If that attempt fails, the president will give another lawmaker two weeks to form a coalition, without the possibility of an extension.
If no lawmaker succeeds in forming a stable coalition, new elections will be called after 90 days. Netanyahu will continue to lead Israel’s government until a new cabinet is sworn in.

Iraq: Life sentences for 3 French 'Islamic State' suspects
October 29, 2026
Three French nationals on Thursday received sentences of life imprisonment in Iraq after being convicted of joining the so-called "Islamic State" terror group.
The criminal court in Baghdad sentence Charly S., Kamal M, and Amir A. to life terms in prison which amounts to 20 years of imprisonment in Iraq.
What more do we know?
The trio were found guilty of "the crime of joining the terrorist Islamic State organisation and of having contributed, together with members of the group, to spreading terror," an AFP correspondent said.
Tuesday saw another six French nationals from the same group sentenced to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years for belonging to the Islamist militant group.
All of the French nationals sentenced thus far belong to a group of 47 French nationals who were transferred from detention in Syria last year.
The 'Islamic State's' years of terror in Syria and Iraq
The militant group carried out a campaign of terror as it sought to establish a self-proclaimed caliphate in Iraq and Syria from 2014 under its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.
Thousands of foreign nationals from across the world joined the group, which carried out mass executions and other atrocities, many of them filmed and shared on social media platforms.
Among its most heinous crimes was the capture and killing of thousands of Yazidis in Iraq’s northern Sinjar region. Many Yazidi women and children were forced into sexual slavery and other forms of enslavement.
In 2014, IS also captured and killed hundreds of Iraqi military cadets at Camp Speicher in Iraq's Tikrit in 2014, much of the massacre filmed and shared on social media.
The terror group also carried out a series of executions of Western journalists and aid workers in highly choreographed videos as part of its media campaign.
Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over IS in 2017, and along with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces would go on to ultimately defeat the group territorially in Syria two years later.
The remaining fighters were eventually cornered and defeated in Baghouz in Syria's eastern Deir Ezzor, near the Iraqi border in March, 2019.

When Will US Transfer Operational Control to South Korea? Debate Rages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:31:25 UTC
05:31:25 KST

For years, U.S. and South Korean officials have said they want to reach an arrangement where, should war break out on the peninsula, Seoul’s military commanders would have operational control of American forces there.
Such a setup would be unprecedented in modern times, and what it would mean for U.S. Airmen, Guardians, and other troops remains to be seen. But recent comments from U.S. and Korean leaders underscore just how complex and even controversial the idea remains.
Since World War II, the U.S. has been the ultimate authority for all its combined forces’ wartime operations. But South Korea—officially called the Republic of Korea—has been pressing to finalize the transfer of wartime operational control, or OPCON. Since taking office last year, President Lee Jae Myung has publicly stated his goal is to reach OPCON before his term ends in 2030, and likely earlier.
But the commander of U.S. Forces Korea, Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, sounded far more cautious at a Center for Strategic and International Studies summit on Oct. 14. Evolving security concerns, such as recent ballistic missile launches, have created “new standards” that must be met before OPCON can be transferred, Brunson said.
Brunson said the transfer must be “conditions-based” and not follow a political timeline.
His comments spurred immediate backlash from Korean officials, including Defense Minister Kan Shin-chul and National Security Advisor Wi Sung-lac, who claim that Brunson’s remarks about new conditions amount to shifting the goalposts and will make the planned transfer impossible.
On Oct. 29, Sung-lac said during a parliamentary audit that the government had been consulting with Washington to complete the transfer by or before 2030. But a planned Security Consultative Meeting scheduled for December in Washington to discuss various alliance and security concerns has been postponed to next year.
A U.S. Pacific Command spokesperson declined to respond to specific questions regarding the conditions required for transfer but did provide a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” Navy Lt. Cmdr. Chloe Morgan wrote. “Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs. We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.”
While the OPCON process continues and Korean leaders push to move forward, not all American experts agree that it’s a good idea. During an Oct. 27 symposium hosted by the Institute for Korean-American Studies, former USFK commanders Walter Sharp and Paul LaCamera, both Army four-stars, critiqued the weakening of the U.S.-Korea alliance, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
“That whole combined nature goes away and … [I] really do see it as a doorway to greatly reducing the alliance, greatly reducing our work with Korea,” Sharp said.
LaCamera was even more pointed.
“It will be suboptimal when the fighting starts, and then we will quickly get to optimization because it is adapt or perish,” he said.
As the debate continues, South Korea is leading combined missions during a two-week, biannual, air-focused Freedom Flag exercise.
The top ROK air commander, Col. Lee Seung-hwan, emphasized his airmen’s role and its ultimate goal.
“While using this as an opportunity to build teamwork among South Korean and U.S. pilots and polish combat skills, we will also cultivate capabilities in preparation for the OPCON transfer,” Seung-hwan said.
To Transfer or Not
The idea behind transferring OPCON to South Korea dates back to the 1980s when President Roh Tae-woo made it a campaign promise in 1987, driven by a desire to strengthen South Korean sovereignty. The United States didn’t transfer peacetime control to Seoul until 1994. Wartime control was expected to soon follow but was derailed during the 1993-1994 North Korean nuclear crisis.
The South Korean push renewed under President Roh Moo-hyun in 2003. Then-U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld championed the idea, calling it “pushing on an open door” to free up U.S. forces on the peninsula and give the Pentagon more strategic flexibility.
The pair formalized an agreement in 2006 to begin the wartime OPCON transfer.
But getting to the point where the transfer makes sense for both sides isn’t so simple, multiple retired commanders with deep experience on the peninsula told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“Conditions should determine the timeline,” retired U.S. Army Special Forces Col. David S. Maxwell told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The timeline should never determine the conditions.”
Maxwell explained that target dates help drive budgets, procurement, training, and accountability, but can’t substitute for demonstrated combat capability.
“If political leaders want to accelerate transition, they must accelerate the fielding of equipment, development of personnel, and combined exercises required to meet the agreed conditions,” Maxwell said. “Political authority cannot manufacture readiness.”
Retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also emphasized the importance of not rushing the transfer.
“My principal concern would be any arrangement that sacrifices combat effectiveness to satisfy an arbitrary political timeline or the symbolism of transferring command,” Deptula said. “We cannot afford to discover deficiencies in command and control after a conflict begins.”
Still, Maxwell, now vice president of the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy, said changing conditions “cannot become an unexplained justification for indefinite delay.”
“Both allies must identify what has changed, which operational requirements it affects, and what capabilities will close the resulting gaps. We should distinguish the agreed conditions from the evolving military capabilities required to satisfy them,” Maxwell said. “The objective is a successful transition that strengthens deterrence and combined defense. Most importantly, political leaders cannot base decisions on threat assessments from five, 10, or 20 years ago.”
Maxwell and Deptula highlight several critical conditions before OPCON transfer should go through:
- South Korea should demonstrate the capability to lead a combined defense and coordinate offensive actions at scale.
- There should be comprehensive alliance capabilities to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats.
- A stable security environment
- Integrated architecture for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and early warning for near-real-time actionable data
- Integrated air and missile defenses across U.S. and ROK forces
- Secure, resilient command and control in the face of cyber and electronic attacks.
- Sufficient munitions, logistics, infrastructure protection, and sustainment capabilities.
- Certified initial operational capability, full operational capability, and full mission capability assessment results for readiness.
While wartime control of the entire combined U.S.-ROK force is in question, more complex considerations apply to the use of the 7th Air Force, USFK’s air component based at Kunsan and Osan Air Bases in South Korea.
The Air Side
If conflict were to break out today, U.S. and ROK forces would be controlled by a Combined Forces Command that has existed since 1978. The commander of U.S. Forces Korea is dual-hatted as the head of the CFC and has a Korean deputy.
Once the OPCON transfer occurs, that arrangement would flip: a South Korean four-star commander with a U.S. four-star deputy. But even with that combined arrangement, the Pentagon doesn’t cede control of its forces entirely, and it does not give the Korean commander authority over U.S. aircraft in the Pacific.
Retired Lt. Gen. Jeffrey A. Remington, who commanded the 7th Air Force from 2008 to 2012, explained that under the new arrangement, the 7th Air Force commander would still oversee the air component for the Korean general in charge, informing the general on the status of air forces, personnel, and wartime options.
“[The 7th Air Force commander] would continue to be the air component commander, not a Korean, … a U.S. Air Force three-star general,” Remington said.
The commander would then come to the Korean four-star and say, ““Here’s the options, here’s what I can do for you. Here’s the implications of those options,’ and we’ll come to an agreement,” he said.
Even in that arrangement, Remington said Washington likely wouldn’t be involved directly in any major decision involving U.S. forces, especially major airpower assets.
Deptula stressed that in hammering out the details of this arrangement, “the issue is not whether a South Korean general is capable of commanding American airpower. It’s whether the command structure provides the authority, experience, capabilities, and operational flexibility necessary to employ airpower effectively.”
The ROK military is highly professional and capable and a solid U.S. ally in the region, Deptula added. But such a transfer requires more.
“Commanding a modern, integrated air campaign involving hundreds of aircraft, sophisticated intelligence and surveillance capabilities, electronic warfare, space-based systems, and long-range strike assets requires far more than flying airplanes or managing individual missions,” Deptula said.
Day-to-day operations running an Air Operations Center and delivering air tasking orders already happen in a combined way through the AOC at Osan Air Base, Deptula said.
“The real issue is creating a master air attack plan,” he said. “That is the mechanism through which an air campaign translates strategic and operational objectives into coordinated tactical actions. It integrates offensive counterair, defensive counterair, strategic attack, interdiction, close air support, intelligence collection, electronic warfare, air refueling, and other capabilities into a coherent campaign.”
While the U.S. has participated in combined forces operations in World War II and with NATO in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it has never been in a combined force operation without being the ultimate authority for wartime OPCON.
Most U.S. operations during the Global War on Terror and since have been in coalitions. Those typically operate with separate militaries covering different areas, such as the British contribution to the invasion of and early stages of the Iraq War, where their forces were concentrated near Basra and controlled the southeastern section of the war effort near Kuwait.
Combined warfare is different.
“Combined warfare means you’re there together. You’re executing together. You’re mixed and making things happen,” Remington said. “Whereas in a coalition it’s not all that combined, especially from a command-and-control perspective.”
In a very technical sense, for U.S. aviators that might mean being controlled through another nation’s airborne early warning or air battle management systems.
That has been somewhat common with NATO combined forces arrangements in past operations and exercises and with South Korea via their ROKAF Master Control and Reporting Centers. Those two MCRCs serve as nerve centers for all air ops on the peninsula and have operated since the mid-1980s, preceded by a Tactical Air Control Center that ran from the early 1980s until the advent of MCRC.
One MCRC, call sign Watchman, is at Osan. The other, call sign Acacia, is at Daegu Air Base and serves as a reserve aerospace operations center.
Beyond the Peninsula
While 7th Air Force is the USFK air component with primary duties to defend South Korea, it also relies on Pacific Air Forces for support and contributes to PACAF’s needs to support U.S. Pacific Command. U.S. Forces Korea are not on a proverbial island, focused solely on local security concerns.
Should a conflict with China or other regional problems erupt, USAF may need to draw upon 7th Air Force.
“The U.S. military is operating with declining force structure and must meet growing global requirements,” Deptula said. “Aircraft, aircrews, munitions, tankers, intelligence platforms, and other assets cannot be committed to two different campaigns simultaneously without accepting significant operational risk.”
That fact means that contingency planning, force allocation, and command relationships take on even more significance when looking to transfer operational control, Deptula said
“Both nations must understand in advance what capabilities are committed, what reinforcements may be available, and under what circumstances U.S. forces might be required elsewhere,” he said.
Any such transfer “must preserve” U.S. commanders’ ability to employ their capabilities where they can achieve the greatest strategic effect, he said.
“Any future defense of South Korea must begin with an appreciation for the fact that air superiority provides the freedom to attack and the freedom from attack,” Deptula said. “It enables all other military operations. The campaign must be designed to achieve the degree of air superiority necessary to permit the joint force to operate effectively, rather than simply contest the airspace.”

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russia and African countries consider reform of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Trade Organization and the World Bank necessary, according to the Declaration of the Third Russia-Africa Summit.
The parties agreed to advocate comprehensive reform of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in order to ensure that the institutions operate based on the principles of depoliticization, equality and respect for the interests of all parties. They also called for greater African representation in the IMF and World Bank leadership, as well as a greater role for African countries in decision-making.
Russia and African nations also agreed to promote reform of the World Trade Organization to ensure an open, transparent, inclusive, non-discriminatory and rules-based trading system.
The parties emphasized the need to preserve the central role of the World Trade Organization and uphold fundamental principles, including consensus-based decision-making, most-favoured-nation treatment, and special and differential treatment for developing and least-developed countries.

The US justice department on Thursday is reported to have issued subpoenas in response to a report that the Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign collaborated with party operatives to get a challenger with the same name as the Republican senator Dan Sullivan on the midterm ballot.
ABC News and the Associated Press reported the subpoenas, citing sources familiar with the matter. The federal investigation comes a day after the New York Times found that the effort to recruit a second candidate named Dan Sullivan in the Senate race set to be decided on Tuesday was led by Peltola’s campaign, which had for months denied involvement.
Earlier on Thursday, Alaska’s Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, announced a criminal inquiry into the effort, which the Times reports was intended to confuse Alaskans who wanted to support the Republican incumbent.
Last week, Trump said he had ordered the justice department to file a lawsuit to block the certification of the Senate election if Sullivan does not win. That suit is pending.
The subpoenas are the latest aggressive move by the justice department amid a politically sensitive matter in the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections. The department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions against candidates in the weeks before an election, or other public steps that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Election law experts said they were unaware of what federal law would justify the investigation.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DoJ would have jurisdiction over,” said Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under Joe Biden. “Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
The information came to light the same day that the justice department issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration. Earlier Thursday, a federal judge in California appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. That action came less than 24 hours after the judge rejected the justice department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified, a ruling the department immediately appealed.
For months, the justice department has been looking into allegations that Dan J Sullivan Jr entered the race to mislead voters and help Peltola’s campaign. The potential targets of the justice department’s investigation are unclear, but Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Peltola defeat the Republican senator Dan S Sullivan.

Patrick Stewart, Shakespearean actor turned ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ star, dies at 86
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:29:43 CET
05:29:43 KST

By Will Dunham
Oct 29 (Reuters) - Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV’s “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” movies, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.
“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” it said.
Stewart became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for “Star Trek: The Next Generation” — a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s “Star Trek” — that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.
“Make it so,” his character Picard often said, instructing a subordinate to carry out a command, or sometimes deploying the similar catchphrase, “Engage.”
It was a role he had debated even taking after his longtime friend and fellow Shakespearean Ian McKellen advised him to spurn “Star Trek” and remain in theater. Stewart did take the role and became both a fan favorite and an indispensable part of a lucrative sci-fi franchise, playing Picard not only in 176 episodes over seven seasons of that series but also in several “Star Trek” films and in the later streaming series “Star Trek: Picard” that began airing in 2020 when he was 79.
“As the seven seasons of TNG (“The Next Generation”) went by, the distinction between Jean-Luc Picard and Patrick Stewart became thinner and thinner, until it was impossible for me to know where he left off and I began. So much of what I believed and felt went into that show,” Stewart told the Guardian newspaper in 2022.
Stewart also initially balked at being cast as the wheelchair-using mutant Professor X in the “X-Men” movies, based on the popular Marvel comic book character.
“I said, ‘Look, I know this isn’t science fiction, but it’s fantasy, and I’ve done that.’ But they persuaded me that it wouldn’t be like ‘Star Trek,’ so I did it. And yet again I was proved wrong,” Stewart told the Guardian.
He became a critical part of another big-money franchise, starting with the first entry “X-Men” in 2000 and followed by several more, including the 2002 Marvel movie “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.” He appeared alongside McKellen, who played the villain Magneto, in some of the “X-Men” films.
Stewart, playing Charles Xavier, took part in the filming of the highly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday” and will appear in the Marvel film that is due to hit theaters in December. Marvel Studios paid tribute to Stewart on Thursday in a statement, calling him “a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman.”
ACTING WAS SAFE SPACE
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in the English town of Mirfield in Yorkshire. He was raised in poverty, with a father who he said returned from World War Two an alcoholic who suffered from post-traumatic stress syndrome and physically abused Stewart’s mother. Stewart recalled putting his body between his father and mother to try to protect her.
As a child, Stewart said, acting became a “safe space” after a schoolteacher introduced him to Shakespeare — specifically “The Merchant of Venice” — during a class when he was 12. He started losing his hair at age 17 and was bald by 19. He was embarrassed at the time, but eventually embraced it.
“Star Trek,” created by Gene Roddenberry, presented a hopeful vision of the future, with humankind venturing into the cosmos in spaceships exceeding the speed of light and encountering alien races. The enduring popularity of the original series and the success of spinoff films prompted Roddenberry to create “The Next Generation” sequel series.
The Picard character was the opposite of the swashbuckling and sometimes unintentionally buffoonish Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner, of the original series — envisioned as more cerebral and disciplined, though sometimes coming across as stuffy, humorless, or self-important.
Stewart recalled being a little bit too serious toward his cast mates early on.
“I tell the story of calling a meeting of my principal fellow cast members and telling them that I thought we were not disciplined enough, that we should not be fooling about on the set as much as we were but taking everything seriously,” Stewart told the New Yorker in 2023.
“And one of the cast members said, ‘Oh, come on, Patrick, we’ve got to have some fun.’ And I thumped the chair and said, ‘We are not here to have fun’ — which they have never let me forget. They taught me so much about loosening up and being freer,” Stewart added.
Stewart also felt the series improved as it went along, faulting his own portrayal of Picard in the first two seasons.
“I found it lacking intimacy. It was very authoritative, but there were few other qualities in him,” Stewart said, adding that his work got better in subsequent seasons.
In fact, the finest work for the entire cast may have been the two-part, time-bending series finale.
He became Sir Patrick Stewart when he was knighted by the queen at Buckingham Palace in 2010. He told reporters that his heroes were British actors Laurence Olivier, John Gielgud and Alec Guinness, who also had been knighted, adding that being “in that company is the grandest thing that has professionally happened to me.”
Stewart was married three times and had two children. His third marriage, in 2013, was to American musician Sunny Ozell.
(Reporting by Will Dunham in Washington; Additional reporting by Ryan Patrick Jones and Christian Martinez; Editing by Diane Craft and Rosalba O’Brien)

SAO PAULO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - A close ally of Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Thursday said AI chatbot ChatGPT was responsible for language in a letter briefly posted on social media by the right-wing lawmaker describing himself as Brazil’s rightful “president-elect,” while insisting the mistake did not alter Bolsonaro’s view that the election was illegitimate.
Bolsonaro stunned Brazil’s political establishment on Wednesday by making the claim and alleging without evidence that Sunday’s runoff election, which he lost to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than 4 million votes, had been marred by fraud.
Roughly an hour after sharing the document, the senator deleted it from his accounts and published a revised version, replacing the term “president-elect” with “leader of Brazil.”
As Brazilian media and political observers speculated about the abrupt change, one of Bolsonaro’s closest allies suggested that the explanation for the mistake was not political, but technological: the use of OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
Right-wing influencer and podcast host Paulo Figueiredo, who serves as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States and first shared the letter with journalists, said the document had gone through several drafts and incorporated contributions from multiple people.
Figueiredo said that Bolsonaro’s younger brother, former Congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, sought ChatGPT’s help to finalize the letter. According to Figueiredo, the chatbot inserted an outdated version of Brazil’s coat of arms and used a previous draft of the letter.
“When generating the document, AI ended up including an earlier version of the text, in which Flavio presented himself as the true ‘president-elect’,” Figueiredo wrote on X, adding the mistakes were noticed only after he distributed the letter to the press.
According to him, Bolsonaro ultimately opted for the term “leader” for legal and moral reasons. He added that those involved found the mistake “hilarious” and described tweaking the letter as “nothing major.”
OpenAI and Bolsonaro’s press officers did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
“In the end, the essential is expressed precisely by Flavio: these elections were illegitimate, he does not recognize the result, and he will continue fighting to restore democracy in Brazil,” Figueiredo said.
The senator arrived in Miami on Wednesday after leaving Brazil, where he refused to comply with a Supreme Court order to turn in his passports as part of a probe into alleged money laundering, in which he denies wrongdoing.
Bolsonaro’s decision to declare himself the country’s rightful “leader” has failed to garner support from key figures in his political camp, leaving him increasingly isolated.
Lula’s victory has been recognized by Brazil’s federal electoral court, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party.
(Reporting by Fernando Cardoso, additional reporting by Luciana Magalhaes; Editing by Aurora Ellis)

Germany records highest number of suicide deaths in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

05:24:08 KST

Germany records highest number of suicide deaths in 2025
Germany recorded 11,334 suicide deaths in 2025, up 9.3% from the previous year, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office, the total was the highest in the published series covering 2012-2025. It also exceeded the average for the past ten years by 15.6%.
Annual suicide deaths have increased each year since 2019, when Germany recorded 9,041 deaths. The figure reached 10,119 in 2022, 10,304 in 2023 and 10,372 in 2024.
Men accounted for 7,846 deaths in 2025, or 69.2% of the total. Women accounted for 3,488 deaths, or 30.8%.
The overall distribution between men and women remained relatively stable. However, suicide deaths among women have risen faster since 2023. The increase reached 17.9% among women, compared with 5.8% among men.
Suicides accounted for 1.1% of all deaths in Germany, similar to previous years.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Japan plans to fund local child suicide prevention efforts from April 2027.
