Eisenkot faces coalition trap as Netanyahu keeps unity question open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:23:50 UTC
05:23:50 KST

With Israel's vote count officially complete, attention has shifted to the next political battle: forming a government. Political figures in both rival blocs expect Yashar! party leader Gadi Eisenkot to receive the first opportunity to assemble a coalition, but the election results have left him with few realistic options.
The uncertainty has already prompted preliminary contacts and private discussions among party leaders, even as it remains unclear who will ultimately succeed in forming a government. Next week, President Isaac Herzog is expected to summon representatives of the political parties to his official residence for consultations before deciding whom to task with forming a coalition.
In Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, there has been an unusual silence in the day following the election. Breaking with his usual practice, Netanyahu did not immediately call his political allies after the television exit polls were released, waiting nearly 24 hours before reaching out.
He spoke with Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich on Wednesday evening and met Smotrich, chairman of the Religious Zionist Party, in person on Thursday. Netanyahu is also expected to speak with the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Some members of Netanyahu's bloc have questioned his approach, wondering why he has not moved more quickly to consolidate support following the election. Others believe he is concentrating primarily on the results and on efforts to prevent the replacement of the Knesset speaker, a move that could take place in two weeks.
Meanwhile, parties in the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu are coming to terms with election results that fell somewhat short of their expectations. Eisenkot met Thursday with Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats, and with Naftali Bennett. Golan also met Yair Lapid, although a meeting between Golan and Bennett has yet to be arranged.
Avigdor Lieberman, chairman of Yisrael Beytenu, is keeping his distance from the political maneuvering for now, waiting for the situation to become clearer before deciding his next steps.
Lieberman told members of his party and local branch leaders Thursday that his campaign commitments not to join a government with ultra-Orthodox or Arab parties remain firmly in place. His position is expected to complicate Eisenkot's efforts to build a governing coalition.
Who will blink first?
Ultra-Orthodox parties signaled Thursday that they would be willing to negotiate joining a government led by Eisenkot. But a major obstacle stands between them: their demand for legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service.
Such a law would undermine any potential partnership with other members of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, whose parties pledged during the election campaign not to form a government with ultra-Orthodox parties and to address the contentious issue of military conscription.
Despite these difficulties, political figures in both blocs believe Eisenkot will be the first to receive a mandate from the president to try to form a government.
Eisenkot told supporters Thursday that he would work to establish "a new government that is good for Israel," but offered no details about how he intended to accomplish that goal.
He is expected to conduct extensive discussions with leaders across his political bloc, as well as with ultra-Orthodox parties, to determine whether any common ground can be found.
Behind the scenes, figures in both camps have also begun discussing the possibility of a national unity government.
Sources in the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu say that for such an arrangement to become possible, Netanyahu would need to demonstrate a greater willingness to compromise than he has in the past. They also believe influential figures would have to push the sides toward an agreement.
Among those mentioned are U.S. President Donald Trump and President Herzog, who has repeatedly pledged in recent weeks to do everything possible to prevent Israel from holding another election.
Some politicians in the anti-Netanyahu bloc believe the prime minister has little interest in forming a unity government. In their assessment, Netanyahu would prefer another election rather than make significant concessions or dismantle his traditional political alliance.
Netanyahu, however, has yet to reveal his intentions. He has not discussed the possibility of a unity government with his political partners or close associates within Likud, leaving one of the most consequential questions of the post-election negotiations unanswered.

It was a substantive meeting, and we count on further steps regarding air defense for Ukraine as well," Zelensky concluded.

Israel election result shows no overall majority as vote count complete
Opposition explores options to form coalition as no party secures the 61 seats required for parliamentary majority.
Vote counting is complete in Israel’s elections with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition winning a majority in parliament, Israeli media have said.
As the provisional results were being published on Thursday, opposition politicians met to explore options for a coalition.
With more than 99 percent of Tuesday’s ballots tallied, Netanyahu’s bloc held 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot secured 48 seats, Israeli outlet Haaretz reported. The Arab list parties, meanwhile, held a combined 19 seats, it added.
Both Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition parties fell short of securing the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
The final results of the Knesset elections will be certified and announced by Wednesday. Until that date, the results are subject to change.
Tuesday’s elections – the first since the October 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – were widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s premiership.
Coalition options
On Thursday, Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, met former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together party, to discuss ways to form a new government “as quickly as possible”, according to a statement reported by Israel’s Ynet News outlet.
Eisenkot also met Democrats party chairman Yair Golan, the only member of the opposition alliance to support forming a coalition with parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, while all other political groups have rejected any such union.
Golan met separately with Mansour Abbas, who leads the United Arab list, or Ra’am, which is projected to win eight of the 19 Arab party seats.
“This is a time for action. Our responsibility is not to miss the opportunity for change and the salvation of Israel,” Golan said in a post on X after his meeting with Abbas.
Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh noted that “Eisenkot has an uphill battle ahead of him.”
The former military leader-turned-politician has pledged “not to ally himself or get into a partnership with the Palestinian Israeli parties”, Odeh said, reporting from the occupied West Bank because Al Jazeera is banned from Israel.
But given the fact that no political bloc has a majority, the Eisenkot-led opposition bloc cannot form a governing coalition without the support of Arab-led parties, she added.
Netanyahu ‘using state institutions for his personal needs’
Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s Likud party has continued to amplify unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance – claims that have been rejected.
The head of the Central Elections Committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought to him in a letter to the Shin Bet security agency. Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims, but given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of working to delegitimise the election results with his allegations.
In a video posted on his X account, Eisenkot said: “The days of Netanyahu using state institutions against Israeli interests for his personal needs are over,” adding that no “spin” can change voters rejecting his government at the polls.
“Benjamin Netanyahu is not satisfied with the results, no matter how much he has been saying that he won,” political analyst Xavier Abu Eid told Al Jazeera.
He added that while it seems unlikely the opposition could take advantage by overcoming differences with the Arab-led groups, there could be an understanding to replace the current speaker of the Knesset, who is close to Netanyahu.
“If there is a new speaker in the Knesset, … Netanyahu loses an important ally,” Abu Eid said, adding that this might give an opening for the opposition to “actually start passing legislation” against him.
Odeh said the next steps would involve negotiations between political groups after the Central Elections Committee announces and certifies the election results by Wednesday.

Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86

Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86
Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his work in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises and his prolific award-winning stage career, has died at 86 years old, his spokesperson confirmed.
Stewart died at home on Wednesday, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement. His death followed "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Novak said.
"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Novak said.
Stewart began his acting career doing stage plays in the United Kingdom, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.
Stewart's most recognizable role began in 1987, when he started playing Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The show ran for seven seasons and also spawned four "Star Trek" films featuring Stewart as Picard and the rest of the "Next Generation" cast. Stewart later reprised the role for Paramount+ series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons.
In a 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart said "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry initially turned him away.
"He was talked into employing me by the other producers," Stewart said.
Fellow "Star Trek" legend William Shatner posted: "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."
George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original "Star Trek" series, said on Threads that "Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."
Stewart also played "X-Men" leader Charles Xavier in over half a dozen films in the "X-Men" franchise. He reprised the role for the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released in December 2026. Marvel Studios said on social media that it was "deeply saddened" by Stewart's passing, calling him a "singular talent" who defined the character "for generations of fans."
"X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said in a social media post "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
Stewart appeared in dozens of other film and television roles, including voice work on Seth MacFarlane's animated shows "Family Guy" and "American Dad."
"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us," MacFarlane wrote on social media Thursday. "... He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come ... We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."
The bulk of Stewart's work was on the stage: He was a frequent presence on Broadway and in London's West End, where he played characters from Shakespearean villains to Charles Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge. He appeared with "X-Men" co-star Ian McKellen in "Waiting for Godot" in London in 2010, then again in New York City in 2013. He also performed his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol" frequently over the decades.
Stewart appeared in over 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions. The company named him an "Honorary Associate Artist" to celebrate his contributions to their work. He has also been awarded three Olivier Awards for his London stage performances and received one Tony nomination for his work on Broadway.
Stewart was nominated for multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG awards for his on-screen roles. He won a Grammy Award in 1995 for "Best Spoken Word Album for Children."
In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. In 2010, Stewart received a knighthood, again from Elizabeth II, for his services to drama.
In 2023, Stewart published the memoir "Making It So." The book landed him on the New York Times' best-sellers list. He also recorded a companion audiobook.
Stewart was actively working until 2026. In addition to his role in "Avengers: Doomsday," he recorded an audiobook where he narrated and commented on all 154 of William Shakespeare's sonnets. He also had a voice role in the animated comedy "The Sheep Detectives."
Stewart was married three times. He wed Sheila Falconer in 1966. The pair had two children — Daniel and Sophia — before divorcing in 1990. From 2000 to 2003, he was married to producer Wendy Neuss. In 2008, he began dating singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell. The two married in 2013 and were wed until his death. Novak said Ozell was at Stewart's side when he died.
In that 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart reflected on what he believed made a successful relationship.
"I think it's being open and a good listener and to make connection," he said. "You don't have to be exactly the same but it's necessary that you can share – I think very important. So sharing and respecting."
Stewart was also "a fierce advocate for causes he strongly believed in," his spokesperson said. Those causes included social justice, women's rights, domestic abuse advocacy, veterans' rights, the refugee crisis, animal rights and political reform.
"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," Novak said. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. … He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life."

The survey found that 61% of voters for Eisnekot’s Yashar, Naftali Bennett’s B'Yachad, Yair Golan’s Democrats, and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu favored forming a government with Mansour Abbas’ Ra'am, making it the most popular option among supporters of the parties seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The findings come amid uncertainty over the formation of Israel's next government, after Tuesday's election left neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the change bloc with the 61 Knesset seats required for a parliamentary majority without support from Arab parties.
The possibility of cooperation with Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, has become a central issue in coalition discussions. The four opposition parties had agreed to coordinate their election efforts ahead of the vote, although questions remained over the composition of a future government and the selection of its leader.
An earlier Israel Democracy Institute survey, published before the election, found that Eisenkot was the most broadly acceptable candidate for prime minister among both Jewish and Arab respondents. That survey also examined public preferences for new elections and alternative government arrangements in the event of a political deadlock.

====================================================================================================

Broken promises or new elections? Netanyahu, Eisenkot face coalition dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:19:17 UTC
05:19:17 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his opponent Gadi Eisenkot will have to break their promises to their constituents if they want to form and lead Israel’s next government.
Their potential political allies will have to do the same.
Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar party both garnered more votes than any of the other nine parties that met the threshold to join the next parliament.
Netanyahu and the bloc of parties that ideologically align with him, however, secured only 53 of the 61 seats needed for a governing majority in the 120-seat Knesset. The Eisenkot bloc won 48.
For Eisenkot, three divisive issues are likely to dominate the debate and force some politicians to renege on campaign pledges: aligning with Arab parties, mandatory military service for Haredi men and a unity government with Netanyahu.
Support from the Arab parties
Eisenkot’s bloc includes four Jewish Israeli parties, referred to as Zionist parties: his own party Yashar, B’Yachad led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Israel Beytenu led by Avigdor Liberman, and the Democrats led by Yair Golan.
Eisenkot could easily become prime minister with a 67-seat coalition if he added the Arab parties, Ra’am with 8 seats and the Joint List with 11. But that is far from straightforward. Three of the bloc’s four parties — Yashar, B’Yachad and Israel Beytenu — explicitly pledged not to form a government with the Arab parties. And relying on their support would face an additional legitimacy hurdle given Netanyahu’s advantage among Jewish voters.
Eisenkot himself has repeatedly and unequivocally said he does not intend to form a government with the Arab parties. During the campaign, he set four conditions for joining his government, including a commitment to Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and to the values of the Declaration of Independence, mandatory military or national service, and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization.
In an interview with Channel 12 News in late September, Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff, said the Arab parties did not meet his conditions and therefore would not be part of the government.
On election night and since then, he has continued to speak of a coalition with Jewish Zionist parties.
Naftali Bennett, the former prime minister who relied on the support of the Ra’am party in 2021, when he and Lapid formed their coalition, also ruled out sitting in a government with the Arab parties. Liberman, whose party won seven seats, said he would form a coalition made up of “Zionist parties only.” Only Golan spoke prior to the election of sitting with Arab parties and has since the election called on the other three parties in his bloc to do so.
One attempt to circumvent the issue would be for Eisenkot to form a minority government that would depend on votes from Ra’am and the Joint List from outside the coalition. A more solid version of that game plan would be a coalition that included Ra’am but relied on the Joint List from outside the government. However, this option is also likely to face significant political and public opposition.
The Joint List stated in an official declaration following the election that it was willing to engage in “political cooperation to bring down Netanyahu’s government,” but it did not publicly clarify whether, and under what conditions, it would support a government led by Gadi Eisenkot. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas said in an interview with Channel 12 News on the eve of the election: “I will know how to bring a government to the Knesset.”
The draft issue
Without the Arab parties’ support, the change bloc could theoretically turn to the 13 seats held by the ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, to form a government.
All four parties in the bloc made ending the ultra-Orthodox exemption from military service a central campaign issue. Cooperation with those parties would amount to breaking an explicit campaign promise.
Shas and UTJ have similarly promised their Haredi constituents that they would not allow for forced conscription.
A unity government with Netanyahu
With the path to a government that excludes Netanyahu looking tenuous at best, the change bloc’s alternative would be to join Netanyahu in a national unity government.
But that, too, would represent a flagrant breach of its campaign pledges. The one clear binding principle of these four parties is their goal of unseating Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, whom they have said poses an existential threat to the country.
In a late-October radio interview, Eisenkot said, “I unequivocally commit that I will not sit under Netanyahu, not even in a rotation,” in which he and Netanyahu would share the prime ministership. Bennett said in a radio interview, “I am not going to sit under him because he is the person destroying the State of Israel.” Liberman wrote on X two weeks ago, “With Netanyahu — even if the world turns upside down, we will not sit with him under any circumstances.” Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, said, “We will not sit with Netanyahu and his partners. Period.”
The challenge for Netanyahu
On the other side, Netanyahu also has no clear path to forming a government. The parties in his coalition defied expectations by winning 53 seats, but securing the eight additional seats needed for a majority appears out of reach. Netanyahu deployed the prospect of the Arab parties in the coalition as a cudgel to bash the opposition during the campaign. In a speech on the eve of the election, Netanyahu called cooperation with those parties “a disgrace.”
That may not stop him from trying to form a government with one of the Arab parties, particularly Ra’am, whose leader Mansour Abbas told Channel 12 on election night that he was speaking with politicians from both blocs.
Netanyahu during the 2022 election held talks with Abbas about forming a government.
Even if Netanyahu were to do the unthinkable and cooperate with the Arab parties, however, he would be unlikely to secure a majority. His ultra-nationalist partners, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, made clear during the campaign that such cooperation was out of the question for them.
With all apparent paths to a government blocked, forming a coalition in Israel may require a fundamental breach of campaign promises that would shake up the entire political system. The alternative is another election, which would be held if no side succeeds in forming a government.

Shin Bet probes foreign election interference, warns against blaming Arab voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:19:04 UTC
05:19:04 KST

The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) said Thursday its investigation into suspected foreign interference in Israel’s election was based on intelligence it collected itself and not information supplied by a political party.
The inquiry should not be a reason to cast suspicion on all Arab voters, it added.
Its statement followed a day of competing allegations over Tuesday’s election, after Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg’s instruction to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery became public.
Money from abroad, perhaps from Qatar and Turkey, allegedly was used to influence voting in Arab communities, Israeli media outlets reported.
Likud cited the allegations to argue that Arab parties had “stolen” the election, and other parties must not rely on their votes to form a government or replace the Knesset speaker.
Arab party leaders denied wrongdoing, while opposition figures accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of using an unfinished investigation to undermine the legitimacy of the results.
The dispute has extended beyond suspected offenses to the role of Arab parties in the next Knesset. The Shin Bet’s statement did not announce findings establishing foreign interference, and overturning election results would require a separate court proceeding.
The Shin Bet said its investigation remained unfinished, and statements about the substance or nature of the suspicions did not represent its position. The inquiry was focused and limited, it said, adding that it should not be used to discredit a community that voted democratically and lawfully.
The Central Elections Committee also rejected claims of systematic election misconduct. In a response issued with Sohlberg’s approval, acting Director-General Dean Livne said the election had been conducted lawfully, and as far as the committee knew, allegations of systematic harm to election integrity were unfounded.
The inquiry would not delay publication of the final results or prevent President Isaac Herzog from selecting a party leader to begin the coalition-building process, a committee source told The Jerusalem Post.
Asked whether the investigation could lead to another election, the source said it was “far too early for such a question.”
“First, we need to examine whether there was any impact and whether it affects the distribution of Knesset seats at all,” he said.
In a letter dated Wednesday and made public on Thursday, Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet Director David Zini to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery.
He described serious suspicions but expressly said he could not assess their merits. He directed Zini to obtain evidence to substantiate or refute them and requested any available findings during the coming week, citing the timetable for election appeals.
The sequence is important: The Shin Bet was in possession of intelligence before Tuesday’s vote; Sohlberg’s written directive and Zini’s meeting with Netanyahu followed on Wednesday; and the inquiry became public on Thursday. The precise date the investigation began, and when Sohlberg first received the information, remain unclear.
Neither Sohlberg’s letter nor the Shin Bet’s subsequent statement identified countries, political parties, or funding routes. Encouraging voter participation is not, by itself, evidence of election bribery.
The Shin Bet said no one outside the agency, apart from Sohlberg, had been exposed to the intelligence before the election ended. On Election Day, Zini publicly described voting as secure and properly supervised.
The Shin Bet said Zini had personally briefed Netanyahu, Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot, and opposition leader Yair Lapid during the preceding 24 hours at Sohlberg’s request and with his approval. Zini initiated the Wednesday evening meeting with Netanyahu.
Meanwhile, four more suspects had been arrested on suspicion of election bribery and were being questioned by Lahav 433 – The National Crime Unit, the Israel Police said Thursday.
Three residents of the South were arrested Tuesday morning, and the case was later transferred to Lahav 433.
The police reported finding cash and Ra’am voting slips during searches. That case remains separate from the election-fraud investigation.
Police dismiss Likud claims
There had been relatively few election-integrity incidents of Election Day, and there was no investigative or intelligence support for Likud’s broader allegations of a stolen election, the police said Thursday.
On Wednesday, Likud said Arab parties had stolen the election through bribery, intimidation, fraud, and other offenses, adding that it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to the authorities. The party intends to seek the invalidation of results at polling stations where it suspects irregularities, a Likud lawyer told the Post.
Ra’am chairman Mansour Abbas welcomed Sohlberg’s instruction to investigate, denied that Ra’am had any connection to the affair or other cases, and pledged full cooperation with law enforcement. He accused Netanyahu of inciting against Arab citizens and seeking to delegitimize them.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said Qatar had not interfered in the election or funded activities intended to influence its outcome. He accused Israeli politicians and their media contacts of drawing Qatar into domestic political disputes through disinformation.
Turkey also denied interfering in the election, and the presidency’s Center for Combating Disinformation said the allegations were baseless.
The Joint List accused Netanyahu of trying to steal the election and described the allegations as a campaign to undermine the legitimacy of Arab votes. It urged opposition leaders to reject the accusations and act on the election results.
Eisenkot, speaking after meeting Zini and Sohlberg, said it was too early to understand what had happened, “or whether anything happened at all,” and called for an investigation free of political interference.
He accused Netanyahu and Likud of an organized campaign to delegitimize the results and vowed to oppose any departure from the scheduled Knesset swearing-in.
Eisenkot said his teams were preparing bills on conscription and service, a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre, and budget allocations, which he intended to bring to a vote when the Knesset convenes.
The Democrats chairman Yair Golan called for genuine suspicions to be investigated. He accused Netanyahu of trying to delegitimize the electorate’s decision, particularly Arab voters.
The Democrats MK Naama Lazimi compared Likud’s campaign to the January 6 storming of the US Capitol.
Section 86
Knesset Elections Law Section 86 provides a court procedure for challenging election results. No automatic cancellation is triggered by suspicions or unlawful funding. Challenges may concern elections conducted unlawfully, incorrect allocation of votes or seats, or votes obtained illegally. A central requirement is that the alleged irregularity could have affected the results.
Eligible challengers include participating candidate lists and their candidates, MKs, factions of the newly elected Knesset, Central and Regional Election Committee members, and the attorney-general.
An appeal must be filed with the Jerusalem District Court, sitting as an administrative court, within 14 days of publication of the results. A three-judge panel hears the case, and the deadline may be extended in special circumstances.
The court can order a new election nationwide or at a particular polling station, correct the allocation of votes, or determine that one candidate was elected instead of another.
A further appeal on a legal question generally requires permission from the Supreme Court president. If the election is annulled nationwide, those eligible to challenge the results can appeal before five Supreme Court judges or a larger odd-numbered panel.
An election appeal does not suspend the Knesset’s work or invalidate decisions it has already taken.
Amichai Stein and Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Legendary X-Men, Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart dies at 86
Unknown

05:18:37 KST

Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV's "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" movies, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.
"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," it said.
Stewart became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for "Star Trek: The Next Generation" - a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s "Star Trek" - that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.
"Make it so," his character Picard often said, instructing a subordinate to carry out a command, or sometimes deploying the similar catch phrase, "Engage."
Patrick Stewart's rise to fame as Captain Jean-Luc Picard
It was a role he had debated even taking after his longtime friend and fellow Shakespearen Ian McKellen advised him to spurn "Star Trek" and remain in theater. Stewart did take the role and became both a fan favorite and an indispensable part of a lucrative sci-fi franchise, playing Picard not only in 176 episodes over seven seasons of that series but also in several "Star Trek" films and in the later streaming series "Star Trek: Picard" that began airing in 2020 when he was 79.
"As the seven seasons of TNG ("The Next Generation") went by, the distinction between Jean-Luc Picard and Patrick Stewart became thinner and thinner, until it was impossible for me to know where he left off and I began. So much of what I believed and felt went into that show," Stewart told the Guardian newspaper in 2022.
Stewart also initially balked at being cast as the wheelchair-using mutant Professor X in the "X-Men" movies, based on the popular Marvel comic book character.
"I said, 'Look, I know this isn't science fiction, but it's fantasy, and I've done that.' But they persuaded me that it wouldn't be like 'Star Trek,' so I did it. And yet again I was proved wrong," Stewart told the Guardian.
He became a critical part of another big-money franchise starting with the first entry "X-Men" in 2000 and followed by several more.
Patrick Stewart's childhood marked by poverty and domestic abuse
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in the English town of Mirfield in Yorkshire. He was raised in poverty, with a father who he said returned from World War Two an alcoholic who suffered from post-traumatic stress syndrome and physically abused Stewart's mother. Stewart recalled putting his body between his father and mother to try to protect her.
As a child, Stewart said, acting became a "safe space" after a schoolteacher introduced him to Shakespeare - specifically "The Merchant of Venice" - during a class when he was 12. He started losing his hair at age 17 and was bald by 19. He was embarrassed at the time, but eventually embraced it.
"Star Trek," created by Gene Roddenberry, presented a hopeful vision of the future, with humankind venturing into the cosmos in spaceships exceeding the speed of light and encountering alien races. The original series' enduring popularity and the success of spinoff films prompted Roddenberry to create the sequel series, "The Next Generation."
Jean-Luc Picard's cerebral leadership contrasted with Captain Kirk
The Picard character was the opposite of the swashbuckling and sometimes unintentionally buffoonish Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner, of the original series - envisioned as more cerebral and disciplined, though sometimes coming across as stuffy, humorless, or self-important.
Stewart recalled being a little too serious with his castmates early on.
"I tell the story of calling a meeting of my principal fellow cast members and telling them that I thought we were not disciplined enough, that we should not be fooling about on the set as much as we were but taking everything seriously," Stewart told the New Yorker in 2023.
"And one of the cast members said, 'Oh, come on, Patrick, we've got to have some fun.' And I thumped the chair and said, 'We are not here to have fun' - which they have never let me forget. They taught me so much about loosening up and being freer," Stewart added.
Stewart also felt the series improved over time, faulting his own portrayal of Picard in the first two seasons.
"I found it lacking intimacy. It was very authoritative, but there were few other qualities in him," Stewart said, adding that his work got better in subsequent seasons.
In fact, the finest work for the entire cast may have been the two-part, time-bending series finale.
He became Sir Patrick Stewart when he was knighted by the Queen at Buckingham Palace in 2010. He told reporters that his heroes were British actors Laurence Olivier, John Gielgud, and Alec Guinness, who were also knighted, adding that being "in that company is the grandest thing that has professionally happened to me."
Stewart was married three times and had two children. He married American musician Sunny Ozell in 2013.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s renowned independent newspaper whose editor Dmitry Muratov recently received the joint Nobel Peace Prize, is being evicted from its historic Moscow headquarters after nearly three decades. The eviction announcement was originally reported by RBC and Echo; Mediazona also has a copy of the letter.
According to a letter sent to readers on October 28 by editor-in-chief Sergey Sokolov, the editorial team has been given until November 9 to vacate their Potapovsky Lane office. The staff was given minimal time to pack, and a new location has not yet been secured.
The sudden eviction forces the closure of the newspaper’s internal museum dedicated to Anna Politkovskaya, its investigative journalist who was assassinated in 2006. “Portraits of our fallen friends are being taken down from the walls,” Sokolov wrote to readers.

Just two weeks prior to the eviction notice,Russian security forces raided Sokolov’s home. The search was linked to a criminal case against Novaya Gazeta investigative reporter Oleg Roldugin, who is currently under house arrest on charges of illegally using personal data.
Founded in 1993 with the financial backing of former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya Gazeta has long been renowned for its investigative journalism about corruption and human rights abuses. Six of its journalists and contributors have been murdered in connection with their work.

Russia’s anti-LGBT crackdown is punishing homophobes, too. Mediazona documents five cases of people penalized for posts that weren’t meant to promote LGBTQ rights.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:16:54 UTC
05:16:54 KST

Russia’s anti-LGBT crackdown is punishing homophobes, too. Mediazona documents five cases of people penalized for posts that weren’t meant to promote LGBTQ rights.
Nearly three years ago, Russia’s Supreme Court banned the nonexistent “international LGBT movement” as extremist. Since then, “LGBT extremism” has become grounds for at least 14 criminal investigations and hundreds of citations for administrative offenses. Because the system often doesn’t look into the context in which a rainbow flag appears on social media, even homophobes end up being targeted. Mediazona has compiled cases in which opponents of same-sex relationships have been punished for “promoting” them.
How Russia passed laws targeting the queer community
In 2013, Russia passed a law banning the promotion of “nontraditional sexual relationships” to minors.
In December 2022, the authorities extended the ban on “gay propaganda” to people of all ages. They also amended the Code of Administrative Offenses to prohibit “promotion of pedophilia” and the distribution of information “capable of making minors want to change their sex.”
In November 2023, the Supreme Court outlawed the “international LGBT public movement” by declaring it an “extremist organization.”
- Vera Makeyeva, a retiree from Kurgan who welcomed Russia’s ban on the “LGBT movement,” was fined under that ban six months later — 1,500 rubles for old reposts of homophobic content featuring a rainbow flag. “It’s my own fault. I hadn’t cleaned up my photo albums in 13 years. Some people were interested enough to go through them,” Makeyeva told Mediazona.
- Pyatigorsk resident Pyotr Voronin was jailed for one day for an image showing the presidents of Ukraine and France alongside a swastika and a rainbow flag (both are considered extremist symbols in Russia). Voronin had intended to mock Ukraine and France — and was outraged that “the FSB’s AI decided I was spreading propaganda.” “I asked [in court], ‘So maybe I should officially apologize to Zelensky?’ Basically, the AI that reads our messages online is a complete idiot, and we mean nothing to it,” Voronin concluded.
- Vladimir Sugakov, a retiree from the Kemerovo region, was fined 100,000 rubles for “LGBT propaganda” in homophobic posts. Among the posts that caught law enforcement’s attention was a slideshow of photographs from Pride events set to Sergei Trofimov’s song “Petushki” (“Little Roosters,” Russian prison slang for gay men). Sugakov said the video criticized the LGBTQ community, but the police and the court didn’t bother to look into it. He decided against appealing the fine, saying he wasn’t an “idiot” who would “take on the system.”
- In Moscow, a video titled “Nazi Initiation” led to a 100,000-ruble fine. In it, a young man shaves his head, puts on clothes popular with neo-Nazi skinheads, and has sex with two similar-looking men. The video ends with an image of a swastika and the message “Join our ranks!!!” The Moscow resident who posted the video said he had done so “as a joke.” The court saw “LGBT propaganda” rather than humor.
- Father Grigory (Grzegorz Zwoliński), a Polish Catholic priest who lived in Kirov, had long criticized Archbishop Paolo Pezzi, who heads the Catholic Archdiocese of Moscow, for supporting the LGBTQ community. Father Grigory added a rainbow flag to one of his posts about Pezzi “to draw attention.” He was fined 1,000 rubles for it. The fine, in turn, led to the revocation of his Russian residence permit and a ban on re-entry. After 24 years in Russia, the priest returned to Poland, where he now writes that the “rainbow church” took revenge on him.

Actor Patrick Stewart, star of 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men', dies aged 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:08:45 UTC
05:08:45 KST

The 86 year old acclaimed Shakespearean British actor died in Los Angeles on Wednesday following "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease.
The legendary British actor Patrick Stewart has died. He was 86.
Best known to millions around the world for portraying Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films and Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the sci-fi television series Star Trek: The Next Generation and subsequent films, Stewart spent much of his early career on stage.
A post on the actor's official Instagram and X accounts said: "We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."
"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all."
A career spanning seven decades
Stewart's career on stage and screen spanned nearly seven decades. It began in Mirfield, northern England, before he trained as an actor and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company.
His theatrical roles ranged from Claudius to Macbeth. He also frequently performed a one-man adaptation of A Christmas Carol and appeared alongside his longtime friend Ian McKellen in West End and Broadway productions of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land and Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot.
Stewart received numerous honours throughout his career, including a Grammy and two Laurence Olivier Awards, as well as Emmy, Golden Globe and Tony nominations. He was also honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010.
As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Stewart appeared throughout the seven-season run of Star Trek: The Next Generation between 1987 and 1994. He also starred in four Star Trek films before returning to the role on the small screen in Star Trek: Picard from 2020 to 2023.
Tributes paid to the internationally acclaimed actor
In a post on Instagram, actor George Takei, who also starred in the Star Trek franchise, wrote: "As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the Starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity."
"Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."
Actor Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside Stewart in the X-Men films, described him as a "tremendous friend and man". In a post on Instagram, he wrote: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."
"I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
Marvel Studios also paid tribute to Stewart, saying he brought Charles Xavier to life with "extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday."
The post continued: "He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art."
William Shatner, who starred alongside Stewart in Star Trek Generations, also paid tribute to him on X. He wrote "Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also honoured Stewart. In a post on X, he wrote: "He never forgot his roots, nor did he shy away from using his voice to stand up for others, particularly those affected by domestic violence."
He was also a prominent campaigner against domestic violence, speaking publicly about his childhood experiences of witnessing his father abuse his mother and supporting organisations working with survivors.
Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, and his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.

Ukrainian Neptune strike destroys two Russian Su-34 bombers used to attack frontline cities, Ukraine’s Navy says
Unknown

20:07:56 UTC
05:07:56 KST

Ukraine’s Navy said on 29 October that it destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers in a Neptune missile strike on Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd Oblast.
The reported strike targets aircraft Russia uses to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, military positions, and frontline communities. Destroying the two jets would reduce Russia’s capacity to carry out these attacks.
Neptune strike hits Russian military airfield
According to the Ukrainian Navy, its units struck the site where Russian aircraft were stationed at Marinovka airfield using a Neptune coastal missile system.
The Navy said the strike destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers belonging to Russia’s 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment, based near the settlement of Oktyabrsky in Volgograd Oblast. The regiment is part of the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia’s 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army.
The Ukrainian Navy did not provide further details about the strike.
Su-34s are key to Russia’s guided bomb attacks
Russia uses Su-34 fighter-bombers to launch guided aerial bombs, known as KABs, against Ukrainian military positions and settlements, particularly in frontline areas. These attacks threaten both Ukrainian troops and civilians in communities near the front.
According to Ukrinform, Russia’s Aerospace Forces had approximately 140 Su-34 aircraft of various modifications in service as of 22 October.
The Ukrainian Navy said it would continue striking Russian military targets to weaken Moscow’s ability to wage war against Ukraine.

European energy giants declare record profits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:07:11 UTC
05:07:11 KST

European energy giants declare record profits
As European households struggled to pay their energy bills, the continent’s oil companies more than doubled their profits over the last quarter, reaping the benefits of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Eight months to the day since American and Israeli forces began bombarding Iran, Brent crude prices sat at $115 on Thursday, up from $72 pre-war. Dated Brent, the actual on-the-spot price that purchasers are paying for Brent cargoes in the North Sea, was even higher, at $120.
This price spike has driven the cost of petrol, diesel, and heating oil to record highs across Europe. However, it’s been a windfall for Europe’s largest oil companies, according to quarterly profit statements compiled by Germany’s Der Spiegel on Thursday.
British oil and gas giant Shell recorded a profit of $12.1 billion between July and September, a more than twofold increase on the previous quarter, and on the same quarter last year. Between July and September 2025, Shell made $5.43 billion in profit.
France’s TotalEnergies increased profits by 127% to $9.1 billion in the same period, while Spain’s Repsol recorded an almost fivefold increase, from $640.7 million to $3.1 billion. Austria’s OMV, meanwhile, increased profits by 68% to $2.36 billion.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil and his counterparts in Austria, Italy, Poland, Portugal, and Spain, have called for an EU-wide windfall tax on the oil giants, similar to the “solidarity levy” imposed by Brussels after the escalation of the Russia/Ukraine conflict in 2022.
“The Commission has been very reserved on this issue, although several member states have been calling for models to be presented for a long time,” Klingbeil said after a meeting of EU finance ministers in Ireland last month. “This must happen by the next [finance ministers’] meeting in October at the latest,” he added.
The European Commission shot down Klingbeil’s proposal, and October passed with no action from Brussels. “It is in the hands of member states,” EU Economic Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters. “Member states can go ahead and take those decisions on the taxing of windfall profits.”
Despite Gulf exports reportedly recovering to 80% of pre-war levels, Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities and shipping, the threat of naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and warnings of an “intense” new US military campaign against Iran have all played a role in keeping oil prices nearly twice as high as they were at the beginning of February.

'Extremist right-wing ideologies' an increasing threat in France & 'across much of democratic world'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:06:36 UTC
05:06:36 KST

'Extremist right-wing ideologies' an increasing threat in France & 'across much of democratic world'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Dr Joseph Downing, Senior Lecturer in International Relations and Politics at Aston University. He reacts to last week's deadly shooting in the Paris suburbs, which was allegedly motivated by racist and anti-Muslim hostility.
In modern France, Downing notes, the politics of insecurity increasingly extends beyond questions of crime and public order to encompass deeper struggles over national identity, disappearance of the political centre and erosion of democratic values.
The emergence of far-right extremist violence, alongside the persistent stigmatisation of ethnically diverse working-class suburbs, raises urgent questions about the relationship between fiery and divisive political rhetoric and far-right radicalisation.
Downing examines these interrelated challenges against the backdrop of a deadly shooting in the Paris suburbs, allegedly motivated by racist and anti-Muslim hostility.
For Downing, the attack illustrates a broader shift in Europe's extremist landscape, in which the rise of far-right political violence demands greater public and institutional attention: "This is really one of the first and one of the most serious right-wing nationalist, nativist-inspired terror attacks that you see in France."
Read moreParis shooting suspect admitted to targeting Muslims and Africans, prosecutor says
Yet Downing's analysis reaches beyond the horrific attack. He challenges the political representation of France's working-class suburbs as centres of Islamist radicalism, describing such portrayals as a divisive rhetorical strategy that stigmatises communities whose residents are overwhelmingly engaged in ordinary civic and economic life.
His central political concern is the weakening of the democratic centre. Amid rising living costs, social insecurity and the circulation of polarising identity narratives through digital media, he argues that political movements on the ideological fringes gain an advantage by offering apparently simplistic, and often divisive solutions, to deeply complex problems. "The centre of politics in France, as in many other democracies, is struggling to hold."
Perhaps most revealingly, Downing identifies the deliberate or careless conflation of racial identity, migration status and religious extremism as a particularly damaging feature of contemporary political discourse. By treating French citizens of African or Arab heritage as perpetual outsiders, political commentators risk reinforcing the very divisions that undermine national cohesion.
The interview therefore opens onto a wider question at the heart of contemporary democratic politics: what happens when narratives of national insecurity become more politically influential than the social realities they claim to describe?
Downing's reflections illuminate not only the challenges facing France but also the wider vulnerabilities of democratic societies confronting political polarisation, economic anxiety and the normalisation of exclusionary rhetoric.

'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
- Published
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost despite warnings of public finance shortfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:02:16 UTC
05:02:16 KST

John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.
Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions.
In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.
Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.
“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.
The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”
He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”
However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”
Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits.
Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.
With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.
But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”
Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”
The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.
The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.
Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.
“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”
Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.
The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”
As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.
The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.
Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.

Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French citizen with Congolese heritage, was killed in the attack.

====================================================================================================

Social media use ranks among the top predictors of depression in a study of 183,000 adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:00:03 UTC
05:00:03 KST

An analysis of more than 183,000 American adults surveyed over an 11-year span indicates that higher daily social media use is consistently linked to an elevated likelihood of reporting depression. Using machine learning models to evaluate demographic and media habits from 2014 through 2024, researchers found that social media use ranked among the strongest predictors of self-reported depression, with its contribution to predicted risk rising once use exceeded about two and a half hours per day. The findings, published in npj Mental Health Research, suggest that the connection between heavy social media use and self-reported depression is not limited to teenagers and has remained stable across a decade of shifting digital trends.
Social media encompasses online platforms built for interpersonal communication, content sharing, and public commentary on community life, services, or products. Over the past decade, the rapid adoption of platforms such as Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok has reshaped how people socialize, express themselves, and compare their lives to the lives of others. Alongside this expansion, public health experts have raised questions about whether heavy engagement with these apps contributes to depression, a mood condition characterized by persistent sadness, low energy, and a reduced interest in everyday activities.
Some early studies suggested that heavy use of social platforms might take an emotional toll. In a 2016 experiment involving 1,095 adults in Denmark, participants who took a one-week break from Facebook reported higher life satisfaction and more positive emotions than those who kept using the site, particularly if they were heavy users or prone to envying others online. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2018 found that teenagers who spent more free time on screen-based activities reported lower happiness than peers who spent more time on in-person activities, with the happiest teens using digital media for less than an hour a day.
Other studies complicated this picture by questioning whether social media actually triggers mental distress or whether people who are already struggling simply turn to their screens more often. For instance, a 2018 study of university students tracked 125 undergraduates seven times a day for two weeks and found that feeling lonely or tired predicted more passive scrolling later on, whereas scrolling did not predict subsequent increases in depression symptoms or stress.
Meanwhile, some researchers analyzing large time-use diaries argued that overall screen time had little negative impact on youth well-being, while critics countered that combining television, gaming, and social media into a single screen-time measure can hide risks specific to interactive social platforms, particularly among women and girls.
Most of the debate surrounding digital media and mental health has centered on teenagers and young adults or relied on data from a single point in time. That narrow focus has left open whether the association between social media time and depression extends across the broader adult lifespan and whether it has held steady as smartphone habits evolved. Martin Block of Northwestern University, Vikram Suresh and Hans Breiter of the University of Cincinnati, and their colleagues examined 11 years of national survey data from American adults aged 18 to 70, building on Block’s earlier analysis of the 2014 survey data, which linked media use to depression.
The researchers analyzed data from the Media Behavior and Influence Study, an annual survey conducted each January and February from 2014 through 2024 by the market research firm Prosper Analytics. Participants were recruited through corporate customer databases, social media, and direct mail, with each yearly sample balanced to match U.S. Census benchmarks for age and gender. After screening out incomplete responses and people who finished the questionnaire in under two minutes, the analytic sample included 183,300 adults across the 11 annual waves, with between 15,410 and 17,869 participants surveyed each year.
To measure self-reported depression, the survey presented participants with a list of 31 health conditions and asked them to indicate with a yes-or-no answer which conditions they experienced. Participants also estimated the likelihood, from 0 to 100 percent, that they engaged in different media activities during each hour of a typical weekday and weekend day. From these hourly ratings, the authors calculated each person’s average daily minutes spent on social media, general internet browsing, television viewing, video gaming, email, and news consumption.
The team first used logistic regression, a statistical technique that estimates how strongly each type of media use relates to the odds of reporting depression while holding demographic factors constant. They then trained machine learning models known as balanced random forests for each survey year, combining 15 demographic and media-use variables: personal income, age range, gender, ethnicity, marital status, education level, occupation, household size, number of children under 18, and daily minutes spent on social media, internet use, television, gaming, email, and news.
A balanced random forest builds many decision trees using equal-sized samples of depressed and non-depressed individuals, which keeps the larger non-depressed group from overwhelming the computer’s predictions. To understand how the models reached their classifications, the researchers calculated Shapley Additive Explanations, a method grounded in economic game theory that measures how much each individual variable pushes a person’s predicted probability of depression up or down.
Across the 11-year study period, both daily social media time and the share of adults reporting depression climbed steadily. The proportion of respondents reporting depression rose from 15.1 percent in 2014 to 22.0 percent in 2024, following an upward trajectory both before and after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After adjusting for demographic characteristics, every additional minute of daily social media use was associated with a 0.26 percent increase in the odds of reporting depression, which translates to roughly 17 percent higher odds (not the same as a 17 percent higher chance) for each additional hour spent on social media per day.
Comparable positive links emerged across all 11 years for daily time spent playing video games, browsing the internet, watching television, and using email, with gaming and internet use showing per-minute associations as strong as or slightly stronger than social media, whereas news consumption showed a weak relationship in only two of the 11 survey waves.
In the machine learning analyses, the balanced random forest models showed moderate ability to distinguish adults with and without self-reported depression. On a standard measure of this ability, where 0.5 reflects chance and 1.0 reflects perfect sorting, scores ranged from 0.66 to 0.74 across the 11 annual datasets, and the models correctly flagged roughly 40 to 53 percent of adults who reported depression. To test whether patterns learned in earlier years remained relevant later on, the researchers trained a model exclusively on surveys from 2014 through 2018 and used it to predict depression in the 2019 through 2024 datasets. The model performed similarly in those later years, with scores of 0.68 to 0.72, indicating that the relationship between media habits, demographics, and depression remained stable over time.
Additional sensitivity tests showed that removing the 2020 and 2021 survey waves or accounting for the COVID-19 pandemic as a separate factor did not alter the link between social media use and depression. When the authors ranked the 15 predictors across three different importance measures over the entire decade, personal income had the strongest overall influence on predicted depression, followed by social media use, general internet use, and age range.
Social media use grew more prominent as a predictor over the course of the decade, rising from ninth place in the game-theory rankings in 2014 to consistently place among the top four predictors from 2019 through 2024. While social media use is a daily habit that people can change more easily than demographic traits like income or age, the authors caution that high importance rankings can reflect how much a behavior varies across a population rather than showing that changing the behavior will reduce depression.
Examining how different amounts of daily social media time affected the machine learning predictions pointed to a consistent pattern across multiple survey years. Below roughly 150 minutes per day, time spent on social media had a nearly neutral effect on whether the model classified a participant as depressed, but beyond two and a half hours per day, additional social media time increasingly pushed predicted depression risk upward. The authors describe this 150-minute mark as a hypothesis for future studies to test rather than an established safe limit.
Subgroup analyses also highlighted notable demographic patterns. Among young adults aged 18 to 25, self-reported depression prevalence ranged between 24 percent and 40 percent for women across the decade compared to between 15 percent and 25 percent for men, while the machine learning models performed better among adults aged 45 and older than among the youngest age group.
The link between heavier social media engagement and depression aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2019, which tracked symptom severity longitudinally in adolescents rather than self-reported depression across the adult lifespan and similarly found that higher social media and television use predicted more severe depression symptoms over four years, although video gaming was not linked to depression in that teen sample. The results also echo a meta-analysis covered by PsyPost earlier in 2026, which examined longitudinal data in children and teens rather than repeated surveys of adults and found that higher social media use was consistently linked to increased depression and anxiety.
At the same time, the new findings stand in tension with a longitudinal study covered by PsyPost in 2020, which tracked individual adolescents over an eight-year period into young adulthood rather than analyzing population-level data in adults aged 18 to 70 and found that increases in daily social media time were not associated with increases in depression or anxiety. They also contrast with a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which used objective smartphone screen-time tracking in a small sample of mostly young adults rather than self-reported usage across a broad adult population and found no meaningful association between social media use and depression.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study relied on repeated cross-sectional surveys that sampled a new group of adults each year rather than following the same individuals over time, the analysis cannot establish whether heavy social media use causes depression. It is possible that adults who are already experiencing depressive symptoms spend more time online seeking distraction, social connection, or relief from low mood when in-person interactions feel difficult. The relationship could also work in both directions, with heavy social media exposure contributing to distress through social comparison or disrupted sleep while depressive feelings simultaneously encourage more time online.
Depression was assessed through a single self-reported yes-or-no question rather than a clinical interview or a multi-item diagnostic scale. That approach may overlook milder symptoms or include inaccurate self-diagnoses. Daily media time was also estimated from self-reported hourly probabilities collected exclusively in January and February. The sample also came from a commercial survey panel recruited through company customer lists, social media, and direct mail rather than a random national sample, and it was balanced only on age and gender, so it may not fully represent American adults.
In addition, the survey did not separate passive scrolling from active interactions such as messaging friends or sharing original posts, leaving open which specific online habits account for the link with depression. The authors suggest that future longitudinal and experimental studies should track individuals over time, incorporate psychological measures of how people weigh rewards and negative experiences, and test whether keeping daily social media use below the 150-minute mark offers a meaningful benefit for mental health. Recruiting partly through social media could also tilt the sample toward heavier users.
The study, “Social media use and depression across 11 years of U.S. adult data,” was authored by Martin Block, Vikram Suresh, Johnathan Avant, Sumra Bari, Nicole Vike, Felix Zhan, and Hans Breiter.
