Powderfinger announce more shows, discuss split and joyful reunion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Powderfinger's joyful reunion was inspired by their kids and Cold Chisel
When Powderfinger broke up in 2010, their farewell tour sold 220,000 tickets.
Sixteen years later, their reunion tour has become Australia's hottest ticket. All 300,000 tickets for the Brisbane band's initial 26 shows sold out in six days.
"The response was genuinely overwhelming," guitarist Darren Middleton tells the ABC's Zan Rowe.
"As soon as tickets went on sale, we were like: 'Holy shit!'
Today, they've added nine more dates, including stops in Hobart and Canberra, to supply the intense demand.
Ticket requests have come from some unlikely places.
"It was pretty nuts," frontman Bernard Fanning says. "Not just the public response but privately.
"Like, plumbers that fixed a drain 15 years ago and still have my phone number."
Among the most beloved and best-selling Australian acts of the 90s and 2000s, Powderfinger's return was kept under wraps over 18 months of "white lies" and clandestine meetings.
In May last year, Fanning, Middleton, guitarist Ian Haug, bassist John "JC" Collins, drummer Jon Coghill and long-time manager Paul Piticco conferred to "seriously" discuss the prospect fans had longed for since the group's 2010 split.
"We got together and said, 'Let's think about if we want to do it. Is this the right time for everyone?" Middleton says.
"One idea put around was: 'No-one in the band owes Powderfinger anything.' If someone doesn't want to be a part of it, we don't do it. That's OK."
After a month away to deliberate their reasons for reuniting, they reconvened. "We got on the Zoom [call] and went, let's do it!"
Why now? Family and falling in love with the band
One of Fanning's "main reasons" for getting back together was "for my kids".
"Because they haven't seen [us perform], they'd love to be part of it … and every one of us said exactly the same thing."
"We're never very cool in our kids' eyes," Middleton adds.
Each member has taken a different path over 16 years: from raising families to pursuing solo projects, politics and other careers.
"We've all gone through different experiences, learned to stand on our own two feet again and discover who we are," Middleton reflects.
"And actually fall in love with music and with the band again."
Fanning says time apart has deepened the bonds of their friendship.
"By the end of the band, there was tension, which is natural after 21 years [together].
"But now, all those petty differences have completely disappeared in a sea of nappies and teenage angst and whatever else.
"In the last 16 years, we've had time to think about how much fun and joy there was … try and bring that into the equation again."
It's a rare opportunity whose significance isn't lost on Middleton.
"We're still alive," he enthuses. "It sounds silly, but I've lost friends in the music industry … their bands no longer have the chance to do what they did. We're super lucky."
Cold Chisel, community and nostalgia
Powderfinger's choice to headline concerts outdoors under stadium-sized tents was inspired by attending Cold Chisel's "Big Five-O" anniversary shows.
"It feels like a festival but it's indoors, it's the best of both worlds," says Fanning, who never saw Chisel the first time round, but was thrilled when he got the chance to see them reunite.
That people feel the same way about Powderfinger "makes sense," he reasons.
The group's chart-topping, award-hoovering anthems were the soundtrack to people's lives in the pre-streaming era, ruled by CDs, TV and radio, not algorithms.
"There's a warmth of feeling for that time when Powderfinger was doing well [and] people want to recapture that a little bit," Fanning acknowledges.
"I think nostalgia gets a bad rap. Because it generates good feelings amongst people, which are seriously lacking in our society at the moment.
At a time of "so much difficulty and division in the world", harnessing live music's power to foster community was a driving force for the reunion.
A multi-generational moment
Powderfinger's cross-generational popularity was evidenced by last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, where the majority of voters (aged 18–29) voted in three songs.
"It's crazy," Middleton remarks.
"My 25-year-old daughter, her friends are pumped about coming. It makes me feel young again.
"People coming to see us are parents with kids who are teenagers or above. What a great experience! 'Dad, take me to see that band that you used to love …'"
Since the band bowed out in 2010, "society has devalued music incredibly", Fanning says.
Particularly Australian music, with homegrown music accounting for just 8.4 per cent of local streaming, according to a recent APRA AMCOS report.
In response to increasing festival cancellations, venue closures and declining live attendance, the frontman says there needs to be a "concentration on the arts and how important it is for our stories to be told by us".
"And that comes from musicians, from artists, authors, journalists, from whoever. It's really important to encourage that Australian storytelling to continue."
To that end, Powderfinger are committing to an all-Australian line-up of support acts for their tour, including partnering with triple j Unearthed to give emerging acts a platform to perform for tens of thousands of people. Stay tuned for details.
Will there be new music?
All five members always voted on every major career and creative decision.
Is Powderfinger still a democracy in 2026?
"Yes, unfortunately," Fanning deadpans to hearty laughter.
"It has to be. We wouldn't be able to function any other way.
"It's part of [our] DNA … sometimes there's some late-night lobbying" with JC serving as "the whip", he continues.
Beginning rehearsals in December, each member will have a say on figuring out which tunes will make the cut.
Fanning experimented with writing a set list "of what I thought were essentials".
"There were 22 songs, which is too long."
Don't expect epic four-hour long shows.
"No way. I want the quality to be really high the whole way through," Fanning says.
Middleton counters: "We'll craft a few different set lists [that] we'll revolve."
And the burning question: Will These Days and My Happiness find new company?
"I'll happily accept criticism that it's a nostalgia tour, because we're not making new music," Fanning says.
"The one thing Jimmy Barnes said to me: 'If you ever get the band back together do not make a record.'"
That said, "the chemistry of the five of us being together is very unique … [we're] never closed off to the idea of a new song, from anybody," Fanning says.
"That's what I'm excited about again. That chemistry you cannot manufacture."
But the reunion marks a new adventure.
"All of us are approaching it with so much excitement," Fanning says.
"We know it's different now, the way that we relate to each other is different.
"We obviously have to step up to a really high level or else we will disappoint a lot of people."
But Powderfinger are intent on putting in the hard work. For them, it's about proving some chemistry, between band members, between artists and audiences, between generations, is irreplaceable. And sharing that with 300,000 people and counting.
"I don't want to anticipate how it's going to feel," Middleton says.
"All I know is it's going to be an amazing end to 2027."

Zelensky: Intelligence reports Russia preparing new ballistic missile strikes
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in his nightly video address, Ukrinform reports.

He instructed the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry to accelerate this work with partners.

Zelensky recalled that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes that destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers and also hit an Iskander missile launcher.
"Thank you, guys, for the result! Glory to Ukraine!" the president said.

Russia, Ukraine complete demining for humanitarian mission to Oleshky

Russia and Ukraine have completed demining along routes designated for a humanitarian mission to Oleshky, a Russian-controlled city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, the two countries’ human rights commissioners said on Thursday.
Russian commissioner Yana Lantratova and Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets announced in separate Telegram statements that the humanitarian convoy was ready to depart for the city’s central district hospital.
The officials said residents wishing to leave Oleshky would have the opportunity to do so until 2 pm local time (1200 GMT), while humanitarian aid distribution would begin after 2.30 pm.
“All necessary security measures will be in place,” the commissioners said, according to their statements.
Officials thank Melania Trump for mediation
Lantratova and Lubinets both thanked US first lady Melania Trump for her “personal involvement, mediation, and coordination”, which they said had helped make the humanitarian agreements possible.
The completion of demining marks a key step towards enabling the planned aid delivery and providing civilians with an opportunity to leave the city safely during the agreed ceasefire.
Temporary ceasefire enables aid and evacuations
A ceasefire brokered by US President Donald Trump between Russia and Ukraine in Oleshky took effect at 0100 GMT on Tuesday.
The arrangement is intended to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations in the city, which Moscow took control of in 2022.
The ceasefire is scheduled to remain in force until 1059 pm GMT on Sunday, giving humanitarian operations a limited window to proceed.

Quick hits: Marnus caught in ugly exchange after all-time send off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:18 UTC
04:54:18 KST

Marnus Labuschagne was involved in an ugly moment of DRS drama after giving a retaliatory send-off, as Temba Bavuma threw his wicket away in the shadows of stumps.
Here are the quick hits from day three of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. DRS drama and Labuschagne's ugly exchange
It was one of the most contentious moments of the series when, midway through the evening session, with South Africa 2-95 and still five runs behind, Mitchell Starc collected Marques Ackerman with a steepling, searing bouncer.
The South African lost his balance as the ball thudded into what looked to be a mixture of helmet and bat before flying to Cam Green behind the wicket.
The Australians went up and so did the umpire's finger.
Undoubtedly dazed from the contact, the batter regained his composure and met with partner Temba Bavuma.
Eventually, a referral was called for, but only as the DRS timer ticked to zero.
It was touch and go, but the officials deemed Ackerman had taken too long, despite the severity of the hit.
With the South Africans pleading their case to the umpires, the ever-vocal Marnus Labuschagne could be heard giving his own opinion over the stump mic.
"The timer's up, oh no, see you buddy!" Labuschagne said from his position at the other end of the wicket.
Meanwhile, Travis Head had made his way over to the South African camp.
"Heady, what are you doing mate? He's off!" Labuschagne could be heard saying.
Head, hands outstretched towards batter and umpire in what appeared to be a peace offering, turned back towards his team and replied.
"I'm just checking if he's alright," Head said.
Reluctantly, Ackerman made his from the middle, but spent some time at the boundary in the futile hope of being called back.
Thankfully, the replays showed the ball had collected a thick edge before crashing into visor, meaning Ackerman was doomed to be out for 62 even if the review had been permitted.
2. Bloodied Harmer keeps South Africa in the game
With an advantage to press home at the beginning of day three, the set Australian pair of Alex Carey and Josh Inglis would have been hoping for at least another full session of batting.
The conditions were perfect, the pitch was flat, and things looked very promising as Inglis reverse-swept his way to a hugely impressive second Test century.
However, neither wicketkeeper-batter would see the other side of the first drinks break, with off spinner Simon Harmer once again doing the damage.
Only moments after ripping a nail and bloodying his fingers while attempting a low catch with his non-bowling hand, Harmer had Inglis caught behind for 102.
It was a brilliant delivery; drifting away, spinning in and kissing the outside edge of the Western Australian's blade.
Four overs later, a similarly exquisite off break had Carey (80) nudging to Aiden Markram at slip, and Harmer, a fingernail down, had dragged his side back into the game.
Australia's tail proceeded to eke out a 100-run first-innings lead, eventually dismissed for 429.
3. Marnus gives it to Bedingham
Labuschagne was in quite a mood on day three.
Before the DRS drama in the evening session, the Queenslander took quite some pleasure in giving it back to Proteas batter David Bedingham.
On day two, Matthew Breetzke had joyously celebrated Labuschagne's five-ball duck by leaping over the pitch and shouting directly at the Australian.
And when Bedingham holed out to Josh Hazlewood during the middle session on day three, Labuschagne responded in similar fashion.
The Queenslander had his chest puffed out as he ran towards the South African, face red and fist pumping, screaming what you can only imagine was something entirely considered and reasonable.
Loading Twitter content
Bedingham was out for 11 and South Africa's second innings was already beginning to teeter at 2-31.
4. A strange moment on the hill
It was a strange morning on the hill.
During the first session, the broadcast cameras found a man holding a sign that read: "Ryan Rickelton, is your mum single?"
The middle-aged gentleman received a good amount of screen time, which he used to blow kisses and adjust his sunglasses in a performance that probably wouldn't have endeared him to anyone in the Rickelton family.
Loading Twitter content
Rickelton, South Africa's wicketkeeper-batter, was stony-faced in response, before pursing his lips and shaking his head solemnly.
The commentators were lost for words at what was an uncomfortable moment for everyone involved — and especially, you'd imagine, for Ryan Rickelton's mother.
5. Bavuma throws it away in the shadows of stumps
Stumps were in sight for Bavuma and Breetzke.
The South African pair had so diligently rebuilt South Africa's innings after Ackerman's dismissal, and had just eight more balls to survive.
But with shadows lengthening at Newlands and with the pitch offering more and more for the slower bowlers, Nathan Lyon conjured a little bit of magic.
It was the perfect off spinner's delivery; drifting, turning sharply and bowling a swinging Bavuma clean through the gate.
However, it was a wildly inappropriate shot from the usually so-considered Bavuma, and the South African captain couldn't quite believe what had happened.
He grimaced and shook his head as he made is way from the middle for 35, with South Africa finishing the day on 4-140 and just 40 runs in front.

California, feds continue election war after courts rebuke challenge to 20,000 ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:53:07 UTC
04:53:07 KST

California, feds continue election war after courts rebuke challenge to 20,000 ballots
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Courts have twice rejected the Trump administration’s bid to block the counting of 20,000 ballots that it says may be from noncitizens; the Justice Department is appealing.
- The ongoing battle is part of a multifront election battle between the administration and the state that has also seen L.A. County officials subpoenaed.
- Gov. Gavin Newsom says California is deploying election lawyers to protect voting, while county officials have rebuffed Justice Department threats.
Soon after a federal judge in Los Angeles sharply rejected a Trump administration effort to block 20,000 California ballots from voters it alleged may be noncitizens, the U.S. Justice Department appealed — leaving attorneys on both sides preparing Thursday for yet another court battle.
That was despite the lower court judge calling the request an unlawful threat to eligible voters in Tuesday’s midterm election and to free and fair American elections moving forward, and the same appellate court having already rejected the plan days before.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” wrote First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead prosecutor in L.A.
Early Thursday, Gov. Gavin Newsom swiped back at the Trump administration, writing, “A warning to Donald Trump: I’m deploying election lawyers to key battleground districts in California to protect every vote. And I just made it a FELONY to illegally seize ballots.”
With just days to go until polls close, the heated election war between California and the Trump administration is showing no signs of slowing down despite multiple court orders rejecting the administration’s central effort to interfere in the midterms by accusing state and county officials of willfully turning a blind eye to voter fraud.
That’s in part because lawyers within the U.S. Justice Department have been unrelenting in their pursuit of such control, both through court orders and threats to state and county officials — including through criminal grand jury subpoenas issued to at least three officials in Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan’s office.
The subpoenas, reviewed by The Times, demand that the officials appear before prosecutors the day after the election with a slew of internal documents and testify as to how their office handled the Justice Department’s demands to set aside the ballots.
It’s also because those same state and county officials have refused to yield, denouncing the threats as unconvincing and illegal in recent letters back to the Justice Department.
“Be aware that we consider DOJ’s efforts to threaten California election officials with criminal sanctions for following federal and state law to be an effort to unlawfully intimidate both election officials and California voters, which can undermine voters’ faith in the election process,” Susan K. Blitch, counsel for Monterey County, wrote in one.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter ruled that the administration’s allegations were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws.
Several election experts warned that Trump administration officials are trying to sow confusion and suspicion about an election in which the Republican Party is poised to lose ground, in part so they can reject the outcome. But they also said the courts have consistently rebuffed the Trump administration and will continue to do so through Nov. 3 and after — with the recent rulings over the 20,000 flagged ballots a perfect example.
“The federal government lost in every way it could possibly lose. It lost on the law, and it lost on the facts, and it lost on the equities — [or] weighing the harms to the various parties,” said Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law.
Appeal, rebuke, appeal
Last week, Trump administration attorneys decided that U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was not ruling quickly enough on their emergency request for a temporary restraining order to block California, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Logan from counting the 20,000 ballots the administration asserted were from “likely noncitizens” — so they appealed to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
On Monday, a three-judge panel there — including two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — denied the appeal for a lack of jurisdiction, because Carter hadn’t weighed in yet. However, two of the judges — Mark J. Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote separately to make clear that they also would have denied the administration’s request for being likely unconstitutional and in violation of federal law.
On Wednesday, Carter, an appointee of President Clinton, ruled that the administration’s allegations about noncitizen voters were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws, sow chaos in the ongoing midterm election, likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections.
“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If [the Trump administration’s] last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.”
Carter wrote that never in American history “has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”
The ruling — forceful, unequivocal and based on several of the same arguments made by Bennett and Sanchez — was cheered by state officials and voting rights groups. Election experts said it squared directly with their understanding of the law and was appropriate in the face of the Trump administration’s unprecedented, legally baseless effort to intervene in an ongoing state-run election.
Justice Department lawyers filed a sparse appeal back to the 9th Circuit on Thursday, arguing the ongoing counting of ballots constitutes an emergency the court must intervene to stop, and asking it to do so by Friday. The same panel that previously rejected the request took the case back up, and gave the state, L.A. County and several voting rights groups until Friday morning to respond.
War of words
On Wednesday night, Newsom appeared on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and predicted Trump will take sweeping steps to “literally suppress the vote, to set the conditions where he will then express doubt in the electoral outcome, and suggest that it was rigged.” But he also said California is fighting back and prepared.
“Right now, I am focused on getting over 1,000 poll workers, folks out there to monitor the DOJ monitors that Trump’s gonna send to try to steal this election,” Newsom said. “We have been running tabletop exercises. We have 1,000 volunteers. We have 134 election law attorneys that we’re sending out.”
On Thursday, Essayli replied to the latter deployment, writing, “You’re going to protect every legal or illegal vote? What about California citizens whose votes are being diluted by ineligible voters. Do their constitutional rights matter.”
Everything you need to know about how to vote in the 2026 California general election, including how to register, where to vote and how to check the status of your ballot.
Trump, meanwhile, asserted with no evidence that “there are hundreds of thousands of bad ballots, bad votes, in California. Millions, in my opinion.” He said that California has “very corrupt elections,” and that if it had honest ones, he “would have won it by a lot.”
The remarks were just the latest in a swirling and highly public war of words between state and federal officials.
Federal prosecutors have issued three grand jury subpoenas to officials in Logan’s office. One dated Saturday and addressed to the office’s records custodian seeks internal emails, text messages, guidance and discussions related to the Trump administration’s demands that Logan’s office investigate alleged noncitizen voters. It orders the custodian to appear in Santa Ana on Wednesday, the day after the election, or provide the records and a signed certification beforehand.
Prosecutors are also seeking records describing how the county screens for unlawful voting, prevents noncitizen ballots from being counted and handles evidence that noncitizens voted in federal elections or that others helped them to do so.
A Justice Department spokesperson said it doesn’t comment on grand jury subpoenas, but noted Carter had “explained that voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure.”
Carter did say that a “clear remedy” to the administration’s concerns already existed, in that prosecutors could criminally charge individuals committing voter fraud. But he also explicitly denounced what he called the administration’s “threat” to charge election officials, writing that “these threats must stop.”
Logan, in a statement, said Carter’s “admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated. At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”
In Carter’s courtroom Tuesday, Essayli claimed the federal government has maintained a collaborative “tone” since it first demanded the state set aside ballots, and said he was surprised at how “adversarial” state election officials had been. But Essayli and other Justice Department officials have been engaged for weeks in an aggressive back and forth with California officials online — which is highly unusual for prosecutors actively litigating related cases.
When Newsom’s office recently wrote that “Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted — and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” Essayli shot back, “Hey Fraud King,” with a crown emoji. “We’re not waiting for them to vote.”
Also unusual have been the threats Justice Department attorneys have been sending to county election officials in California, including in a series of letters Friday in which they asserted varying numbers of “likely aliens” per county, set a 48-hour deadline for the counties to cooperate with federal authorities to prove those voters are citizens.
In one letter to Kristin Connelly, head of the Contra Costa County registrar’s office, U.S. Atty. Craig Missakian flagged 407 potential noncitizens in the county and said he was writing “to make unmistakably clear the legal implications” of processing any ballots from those voters.
On Wednesday, Thomas L. Geiger, Contra Costa County counsel, responded with his own letter, questioning the accuracy of the noncitizen claims and saying it would be “legally unsound” for Connelly to “disregard both California and federal law” in order to comply with Missakian’s demands.
Other California officials have signaled a willingness to work with federal authorities. San Luis Obispo County District Atty. Dan Dow said Thursday that his office is investigating “63 federally identified suspect registrations” off a list also provided to the county clerk-recorder.

Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.
A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market’s website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.
On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appeared to have been affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but the company said it will refund impacted traders.
The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company’s newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries.
This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced security woes. In June 2026, Polymarket experienced another breach, which resulted in over $2 million in losses for impacted traders.
The company has been a lightning rod for controversy since its 2020 launch. In the past few years, it has been the center of several high-profile alleged insider trading incidents resulting in arrests. One case involved a Special Forces soldier accused of wagering on the capture of Venezuela’s former leader; another involved a Google employee who allegedly used confidential information to make millions. In both cases, the suspects have pleaded not guilty.
Polymarket recently raised $1 billion in August 2026, with a fundraising round led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. It is now valued at $21 billion.

Shelters, postponements, and new requirements: how the Cabinet of Ministers plans to change the way businesses operate during an air raid alert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:49:34 EET
04:49:34 KST

Shelters, postponements, and new requirements: how the Cabinet of Ministers plans to change the way businesses operate during an air raid alert
Kyiv • UNN
The government plans to extend the transition period and allow neighboring shelters. Protection-capacity requirements will depend on the number of people.
The Cabinet of Ministers is preparing changes to the rules under which Ukrainian businesses may continue operating during a yellow-level air raid alert. Businesses are promised more time to equip shelters, will be allowed to use nearby protective structures, and the requirements will be linked to the number of people at the site. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the changes on October 29 after presenting the proposals to business associations. UNN explains which rules are already in effect and what entrepreneurs should prepare for.
What the “yellow” level of an air raid alert means
The government introduced the division of air threats into yellow and red levels in September 2026 by Resolution No. 1092. The yellow level means a drone threat, while the red level is declared in the event of a missile, missile-and-drone, or massive drone threat. These are different response regimes for attacks. The yellow-level signal lasts 30 seconds and may be issued separately for individual districts. If the nature of the threat changes, the notification must be updated.
During a yellow-level alert, businesses may continue operating if they ensure the conditions for protecting employees and visitors prescribed by law. During a red-level alert, work must be stopped and people must be organized to move to a shelter. If a drone threat escalates into a missile threat, the business must respond to the new signal without waiting for a separate all-clear.
It should be understood that the yellow color of an air raid alert does not guarantee complete safety: drones and their debris remain dangerous and can maim or kill. Therefore, a visitor has the right to decide independently whether to remain at an establishment during a yellow alert, but staff are obliged to report the threat and available shelter options.
Why the government decided to review the requirements
The division of alerts was intended to prevent the shutdown of trade, production, and services during prolonged drone threats, preserve jobs, and maintain citizens’ access to essential establishments. However, according to the head of government, a significant number of businesses have not even begun fulfilling the basic requirements for people’s safety. The government did not specify how many such sites there are.
The priority, as before, is people’s safety
A café with a few tables and a large shopping and entertainment center have different capabilities. Some businesses operate in rented premises without basements and cannot carry out construction work independently. Therefore, the government is proposing more flexible conditions.
Extension: how much time entrepreneurs will receive
The current Resolution No. 1092, which entered into force on September 4, provides a three-month transition period for sites without shelters. During this period, they may operate during a yellow-level alert with the approval of the workforce. The initial deadline is December 4, 2026.
On October 29, the government proposed extending the period.
An extension does not mean the requirements are being canceled
By March 4, 2027, military administrations are to collect data on compliance with the requirements. After that, the Cabinet of Ministers will make further decisions. At the same time, we emphasize that as of October 29, the current version of Resolution No. 1092 contains the previous three-month period. Therefore, March 4 cannot automatically be considered a new legally established date for every entrepreneur. It is necessary to wait for the official publication of the relevant amendments.
New requirements for businesses: how many people must the shelter accommodate
The second area of changes is the differentiation of requirements depending on the number of employees and visitors simultaneously present on the premises. When determining the required capacity, the plan is to take into account not only the company’s staff but also the actual load on the site. Thus, a hair salon may have several people present at the same time, while a supermarket or shopping and entertainment center may have hundreds. Accordingly, the required number of spaces and the organization of the move to a shelter will differ.
The government has not yet published specific population thresholds, formulas for calculating capacity, or possible exceptions. The details are to be announced by the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Therefore, it is still too early to say that a particular type of shelter is sufficient for a specific number of people.
Is a business required to have its own shelter
The government does not require a separate protective structure to be built on the premises of every store or office. The current rules provide for several options:
-  a protective structure; 
-  a temporary or permanent shelter; 
-  a dual-purpose structure; 
-  a safe space in the building. 
The government also proposes explicitly allowing the use of a shelter outside the business premises if it is located nearby and has sufficient capacity. For a store, for example, this could mean access to an underground shelter nearby. However, an address on a sign is not enough if the shelter is locked, overcrowded, or impossible to reach without obstruction.
It should be noted that a "safe space" is not the same as a full-fledged shelter. The resolution defines it as a protected area of a building equipped with consideration for calculations of blast impact. Simply calling a corridor or storage room such a space is not sufficient.
How the Cabinet of Ministers’ new decisions will affect stores, cafés, and shopping centers
For stores, beauty salons, coffee shops, and workshops, the new rules may make it possible to avoid expensive construction if an accessible shelter is available nearby. At the same time, employees must know how to act when the threat intensifies.
For supermarkets and shopping and entertainment centers, the issue is more complicated: dozens of tenants operate in one building, while the number of shoppers changes throughout the day. Therefore, it would be advisable for the property owner and tenants to agree on who is responsible for alerts, signs, access to the shelter, and the organized movement of visitors.
Cafés and restaurants should establish procedures for kitchen staff and waiters to follow during a red alert. Customers need clear information about the route to the shelter.
Who will monitor compliance with the requirements
By March 4, 2027, according to the government, military administrations must collect information on how businesses ensure the protection of people. This is primarily a stage for assessing businesses’ readiness.
The proposals announced on October 29 contain no separate new inspection procedure, list of inspectors, or special fines specifically for failure to comply with the requirements of the yellow regime. It is also not yet known what unified form the administrations will use to collect information or whether this will involve on-site inspections.
Violations of the rules governing access to facilities in the protective-structure fund or their maintenance may result in sanctions provided for by law.
What entrepreneurs need to do now
First, it is worth calculating the maximum number of employees and visitors present at the same time and, for a shared shelter, also taking neighboring establishments into account. After that, its capacity should be checked.
Next, the route to the shelter should be tested in practice: whether it is open, whether there are any obstacles, and whether people with limited mobility will be able to use it. If the premises are rented, it is necessary to agree with the building owner who will ensure access, information, and maintenance of shared areas. It is advisable to record the arrangements in writing.
The next step is to establish an alert system. Current regulations require the alert signal to be communicated to employees and visitors, the procedure for staff to follow to be determined, and an information sign measuring 100 by 60 centimeters to be placed at the facility indicating the presence or absence of a shelter or safe space. Employees should be briefed and the action algorithm for yellow and red levels checked for clarity. It is useful to appoint those responsible for alerts, opening passageways, and assisting visitors who require support.
It is also necessary to monitor amendments to Resolution No. 1092 and explanations from the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Any possible postponement should be used to arrange protection.
Reminder
Earlier, we explained whether employers would be able to force employees to work during a "yellow" alert.

Ukraine war latest: 'Russia's mass murder' — Deadly Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
Key developments on Oct. 28:
- 'Russia's mass murder:' Drone strike on Dnipro station kills 14 amid deadly daytime attacks on Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
- Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
- Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine's ombudsman says
- Ukraine strikes Russian 'drone port' in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says
- UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
- Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher
Russian forces struck a train platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 more, authorities said.
A passenger train was preparing to depart the platform for Zaporizhzhia when the station was attacked by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media.
The brazen daytime attack was followed in close succession by deadly strikes against civilians in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.
The strikes on civilians come not only in the middle of a scheduled local ceasefire in Kherson Oblast, agreed to by Kyiv and Moscow to help evacuate and deliver aid to the residents of the occupied city of Oleshky, but also ahead of the first trilateral "peace negotiations" mediated by the United States since February this year.
According to Ukraine's Air Force, Dnipro was attacked around 11:00 a.m. by four Russian jet-powered drones, three of which were downed by Ukrainian air defense before reaching their targets.
Despite the air raid alert and announcements of a heightened threat, people remained on the platform, Ukrainian Railways said.
Passengers were told to evacuate from the stationary train around ten minutes before the strike, with station and train staff checking each train car one by one.
At 11:29 a.m., Dnipropetrovsk Oblast governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported that medics were already at the scene of the attack, providing first aid.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. "The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
"How many such terrorist attacks has Russia carried out on our people after lifting sanctions on some Russian oligarchs and energy companies instead of de-escalating."
Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze described the attack on Dnipro as "mass murder."
Following the Russian attack on Dnipro, 25,000 people in the city and surrounding Oblast were left without electricity, Hanzha said in the afternoon.
Later in the day, Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov reported that a Russian drone struck the dormitory of a vocational school in Dnipro, setting the entire fifth floor on fire. There were no injuries, Filatov said, as the students had managed to reach the shelter before the strike.
Throughout the day, Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured four more people, including a 15-year-old girl, Hanzha said in an evening statement.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, the cities of Chernihiv and Kremenchuk were also targeted by daytime Russian attacks.
Around noon, Russian forces struck the center of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
At least 25 more people were injured in the attack, including four children, the youngest one 10-months-old, Chaus later said.
Meanwhile, in the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, at least three people were killed and 32 injured, including six children and two people still in critical condition, after Russian drones struck an apartment building in a residential area, according to local authorities. Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Poltava Oblast.

Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
Ukraine's Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets in a strike against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast, using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported on Oct. 29.
The aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia's 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment near the settlement of Oktyabrsky, according to the Navy. The regiment belongs to the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia's 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army. The Navy did not provide any visual confirmation of the strike. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Later on Oct. 29, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the destruction of the two Su-34 jets, adding that Ukrainian forces had also hit a Russian Iskander missile launcher.
The Su-34 is one of Russia's main aircraft used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, frontline settlements, and military positions. Strikes against these aircraft could weaken Russia's ability to carry out such attacks, while replacing the losses requires significant time and resources.
Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service as of Oct. 22, including the modernized Su-34M, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) reported on Oct. 29.
According to the agency, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed and another seven damaged since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Such losses are quite significant for the aggressor's aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation," HUR said.
The agency estimated that Russia can manufacture approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually, meaning the number of destroyed aircraft is equivalent to roughly 2.5–3 years of production.

Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine's ombudsman says
Demining of designated routes in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has been completed, and a humanitarian convoy is ready to depart, Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets announced on Oct. 29.
The convoy is expected to arrive at the city's central hospital, where humanitarian assistance will be provided to residents, Lubinets said.
Residents wishing to leave the city will be able to do so until 2:00 p.m. local time, with security measures arranged for their evacuation. Humanitarian aid distribution is scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., according to the ombudsman.
Delegations from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States have gathered to coordinate the next steps of the mission, with journalists from all three countries also present, Lubinets said.
The mission is being carried out jointly with Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova, with mediation and coordination by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
"Our shared goal is to deliver humanitarian aid to civilians and facilitate the safe departure of everyone who wishes to leave the city," Lubinets said.
The operation follows a temporary ceasefire in and around Oleshky, announced by the White House on Oct. 23 and subsequently confirmed by Ukraine and Russia. The pause in fighting, which began on Oct. 27, is expected to remain in effect until Nov. 1 to allow aid deliveries, mine clearance, and civilian evacuations.

Ukraine strikes Russian 'drone port' in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says
Ukrainian forces have struck a Russian military facility used to launch long-range attack drones at Ukraine, the General Staff said on Oct. 29.
The overnight attack targeted the Russian drone base near Navlya in Bryansk Oblast, around 70 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
According to the General Staff, the strikes damaged a storage facility for Russian long-range Geran-type drones, as well as fuel and lubricant storage facilities and the 'drone port' itself.
Ukrainian media and open-source intelligence (OSINT) groups have tracked Russia's building of several large 'airfields' designed for unmanned systems and built across Russia's western border areas.
The building of these new 'drone ports' reflects Moscow's growing investment in long-range attack drones as a long-term strategic tool, which can be used both against Ukraine or against countries on NATO's eastern flank.
The Oct. 29 attack was the second strike on the Navlya facility, with the first being on Aug. 3, also targeting launch and storage facilities.

UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
The United Nations has appointed a Russian diplomat to a senior position overseeing mine action, drawing criticism from Ukraine as the country continues to clear hundreds of thousands of explosive devices left behind by Russia's war.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres announced the appointment of Gleb Desyatnikov as assistant secretary-general for mine action and police in the Department of Peace Operations on Oct. 27.
Desyatnikov has served as Russia's ambassador to Jordan since 2018, including throughout Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to the U.N., he has more than 35 years of experience in international relations and security affairs, including previous positions at Russia's Foreign Ministry.
"Moscow has mined the United Nations," Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X on Oct. 29, criticizing the decision.
"Entrusting this responsibility to a representative of the aggressor state is deeply troubling and undermines trust in the United Nations," he added.
The appointment comes as Ukraine faces one of the world's largest demining challenges, with Russian mines and unexploded ordnance threatening civilians and complicating the recovery of agricultural land and infrastructure.
In southern Kherson Oblast, demining teams have neutralized 300,691 explosive devices on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank since the start of clearance operations, according to the regional military administration.
Between Oct. 22 and 28 alone, specialists surveyed 602.8 hectares (1,490 acres) and neutralized 471 explosive devices, the administration reported on Oct. 29. Authorities said 74.5% of the territory designated for clearance on the region's right bank has now been cleared.

Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher
A Russian lieutenant general has been charged in absentia with ordering the strike on the Kharkiv Oblast museum dedicated to 18th-century philosopher Hryhorii Skovoroda, the Prosecutor General reported on Oct. 29.
On May 6, 2022, a Russian missile struck the museum, located in the village of Skovorodynivka, some 55 kilometers (about 35 miles) from the regional capital. The strike did not completely destroy the museum, but left it in serious disrepair.
According to the Prosecutor General, the Russian lieutenant general who ordered the attack is originally from the village of Chuhuiv in Kharkiv Oblast and commands Russia's 6th Guards Air and Air Defense Forces Army.
"The (lieutenant) general knew for certain that he was attacking not a military target but a monument of Ukrainian culture. Despite this, he gave the combat order to destroy it," the Prosecutor General wrote.
Skovoroda is considered one of the most influential philosophers in Ukrainian intellectual history. His written works are vital contributions to the Ukrainian Baroque and Enlightenment traditions. The building that housed the museum was once the estate where Skovoroda spent his final years and died in 1794.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's cultural heritage since the start of the full-scale war. As of September 2026, 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions in Ukraine had been damaged or destroyed, according to data collected by the Culture Ministry.

Spain train crash survivor recalls scenes of devastation as accident unfolded
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:38:15 CET
04:38:15 KST

By Jaime Lopez
MADRID, Oct 29 (Reuters) - When his train drew to a halt, Sebastian Herrero thought the stoppage was due to a fallen overhead line, a problem that has increasingly beset Spain’s high-speed railway network in recent years.
But concerns about arriving late at his destination were suddenly interrupted when he found himself flying through the air and landing face-first on the seat opposite as another train slammed into the back of his.
Herrero, 46, was on his way on Wednesday to Seville from Madrid on an early-morning train operated by Iryo when a train operated by state-owned Renfe ploughed into it, sending its final three carriages careering down a raised embankment in a crash that killed 69 people.
Herrero and others in his carriage escaped by scrambling down the embankment and crossing a fence into a field. Looking back, he realised the extent of the accident for the first time.
“The scene was devastating. You saw carriages completely burnt out, as if they’d exploded. What you see coming out were people in a very bad way, and others who start pulling out the bodies of the deceased and placing them right there next to where we were,” Herrero said in an interview in Seville.
Herrero, who said he feels “born again” after surviving the disaster, was fortunate that his carriage was near the front of the train, but the impact still left many passengers with broken arms or noses.
DILEMMA AFTER JANUARY CRASH
The crash followed another accident that killed dozens in January and involved the same rail companies on the same line near the town of Adamuz. It has revived a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, Europe’s longest and — until recently — a source of pride for Spaniards.
Herrero remembers people asking him after the Adamuz accident whether he felt safe taking the train.
“I remember when the Adamuz thing happened because I spent a month and a half thinking about lots of things, as I had to drive there and the roads aren’t exactly in the best condition either,” he said.
“Petrol isn’t at its cheapest right now, far from it, and flying isn’t an option. So for many of us who have that connection between Seville and Madrid and whose lives depend on it, you can’t see any other solution.”
For many of the people of different nationalities and backgrounds involved in Wednesday’s accident, the prevailing feeling was one of indignation.
“It is high time for whoever is responsible to take responsibility,” Herrero said.
“I don’t know whether it is up to the courts to say so, or whether it is up to politicians, or whether it is for the Spanish people to decide, but what is clear is that it is unacceptable for this to happen and it is inconceivable that it could ever happen again,” he added.

EU pressure on Antigua’s ‘golden passport’ trade threatens budget cushion
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:38:07 CET
04:38:07 KST

By Sarah Peter
CASTRIES, St Lucia, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Antigua and Barbuda’s likely move to end its citizenship-by-investment program under European Union pressure threatens a vital revenue stream for the island nation and could test the future of Caribbean “golden passport” schemes, analysts said.
The issue exposes a vulnerability across the Caribbean, where several small economies have built government revenues and luxury developments around demand for passports valued partly for the access to Europe they provide.
Prime Minister Gaston Browne said this month Antigua would “very likely” commit to phasing out its citizenship-by-investment program after the EU gave Antigua and four other Eastern Caribbean nations until November 12 to agree to close their schemes by June 1, 2028.
The EU says the programs pose security risks by allowing foreigners with few ties to a country to obtain citizenship and visa-free entry to the Schengen area, a key selling point for passport buyers. Countries that keep the schemes risk losing that access.
The EU had initially requested the June 2028 phase-out in letters sent to Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis and Saint Lucia in June. Under a revised EU visa-suspension mechanism, operating an investor-citizenship program can itself provide grounds for suspending visa-free access, though the suspension is not automatic.
The programs, which require investments starting at $200,000, grant foreign applicants citizenship and a passport, rather than temporary residency, typically in exchange for contributions to state funds or investments in approved projects.
Buyers have included nationals of China, Russia and Middle Eastern countries who would normally need visas to enter the EU, and applicants generally have not been required to live in the Caribbean to obtain citizenship. Demand from Americans has grown since 2020, according to Kristin Surak, a London School of Economics professor who researches investment migration.
Citizenship-by-investment inflows in 2023 equaled about a fifth of the combined GDP of the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union, a group of eight Caribbean economies that share a currency and central bank, according to a 2025 International Monetary Fund paper.
The IMF estimated in a paper published in 2025 that direct investment in projects tied to the passport programs was so large that it represented between 100% to 170% of all foreign direct investment officially recorded across the five countries with such schemes.
‘EXISTENTIAL FISCAL QUESTION’
Schengen access has traditionally been an important attraction for buyers of Caribbean citizenship-by-investment passports, and losing it could reduce their value while affecting ordinary citizens too, said Surak.
A suspension could force hotels and other developments financed through passport sales to seek fresh capital, delay construction or abandon projects altogether, analysts said.
The immediate stakes are high for Antigua, where citizenship sales are the government’s largest source of non-tax revenue, according to C. Justin Robinson, director of the University of the West Indies Five Islands Campus.
The government collected about $58 million from the program in 2025 and budgeted $44.4 million for 2026, or roughly 7% to 11% of recurrent revenue, he said.
Ending the program would erase more than half of Antigua’s projected primary surplus this year, Robinson estimated.
The consequences could be even greater elsewhere.
In St Kitts and Nevis and Dominica, where such inflows have at times exceeded 10% of GDP, suspension could pose what Robinson called an “existential fiscal question.”
Antigua’s experience could also test how aggressively Brussels is prepared to use access to Europe as leverage over citizenship policies beyond its borders. The EU also withdrew Vanuatu’s visa-free access in 2024 over concerns surrounding its investor-citizenship scheme.
(Reporting by Sarah Peter in Castries, editing by Cassandra Garrison and Deepa Babington)

Analysis-Brazil’s Lula to reap gains from Bolsonaro family flight
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:37:39 CET
04:37:39 KST

By Lisandra Paraguassu and Oliver Griffin
BRASILIA/SAO PAULO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Flavio Bolsonaro did leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a huge favor by fleeing his legal problems in Brazil to declare himself Brazil’s rightful “leader” from his new home in the United States, analysts and Brazilian officials said.
Bolsonaro’s departure, which came after he refused to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, weakens an emboldened conservative opposition in Brazil’s Congress and lends credibility to Lula’s accusations of US meddling to help the Bolsonaro family, they said.
Bolsonaro says he was a victim of an electoral coup, but has not provided evidence for electoral fraud.
While Lula faces a groaning inbox of challenges, from taming growing debt to grooming a credible leftist successor, he now has one less Bolsonaro to worry about, allowing him to build a more transactional relationship with leaderless congressional opponents, they added.
“Considering the local dynamics, Lula benefits from Flavio’s escape to the US,” said Rodrigo Russo, a São Paulo-based partner at consultancy firm Control Risks.
BOLSONARISMO WEAKENED
Lula’s victory has been recognized by Brazil’s federal electoral court, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party, which did not back Bolsonaro’s claims of electoral fraud.
On Thursday, the day after Flavio moved to the United States, his political allies sought to distance themselves from his claims of being Brazil’s legitimate “leader.”
Bolsonaro’s exit is likely to spark a power vacuum over who will now lead Brazil’s right that Lula may be able to exploit.
“There’s generally more willingness to engage with an administration that has secured a new term,” Rafael Cortez, a political scientist and partner at Tendencias Consultoria, said. “An opening for dialogue emerges.”
Flavio’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, is currently serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a 2022 coup, while his brother, former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, is also based in the United States and unlikely to return to Brazil.
Jair Bolsonaro’s three other children are not currently seen as credible torchbearers of Bolsonarismo.
Michelle Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s wife and a prominent evangelical who appeals to millions of Brazil’s faithful, is taking her first steps in Congress after being elected senator this month.
On Tuesday, the head of Flavio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, posted a photo on X of him smiling alongside her, saying they had discussed “the future of our party and the challenges we face ahead.”
Flavio’s exit has weakened Bolsonarismo, a Lula aide told Reuters.
The adviser said that the right-wing opposition that remains in Brazil will likely deal with Lula more pragmatically. “It creates space for the emergence of a more democratic right, something we’ve seen the country is clearly missing,” the aide said.
US-BRAZIL TIES MAY BECOME STRAINED
Bolsonaro’s flight to the United States lends credibility to Lula’s claims of improper US support to bolster his candidacy, analysts said, while complicating relations between the two most populous nations in the Americas.
In July 2025, Washington announced a series of measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices’ visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the alleged “persecution” of Jair Bolsonaro for putting him on trial.
So far, US President Donald Trump has criticized Brazil’s election but skirted around questions over which candidate won, which experts interpret as him wanting to maintain a working relationship with Brazil, home to the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths after China.
Bolsonaro’s departure “complicates the relationship with the US government, which will have stakeholders pushing for sanctions and tariffs,” Russo said.
The Lula adviser said Trump is likely to be more concerned about weak polls ahead of next week’s midterms than about ties with Brazil.
The US will not want to pay a high price for backing Bolsonaro, especially as it tries to limit Chinese influence in the region, including around issues like rare earths, said Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE.
“It’s a pragmatic view because Brazil is a key piece in the chess game the United States is playing as it seeks to expand its influence in the Americas,” Braga said.
(Reporting by Lisandra Paraguassu and Oliver Griffin; Editing by Gabriel Stargardter and Aurora Ellis)

US files lawsuit claiming Google wouldn’t give employee new job following military leave

US files lawsuit claiming Google wouldn’t give employee new job following military leave
- The US sued Google, saying it broke USERRA by not giving reservist Mark Davisson his old or a similar job after one year of military leave.
- Davisson kept his pay and title, but Google allegedly blocked customer account work, limiting advancement. It later moved him and fired him after more military leave.
- The lawsuit seeks lost wages, benefits, and damages, and wants Google to improve USERRA training and keep a non-discriminatory workplace.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The US filed a lawsuit accusing Google of failing to give an employee his old job back or find him a similar job after he took one year of military leave as a US Army reservist.
The Oct 29 case in Manhattan federal court is a rare instance of the US government suing a private employer for violating the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 (USERRA), which protects the civilian employment of military personnel called to active duty.
According to a complaint filed in Manhattan federal court, Mark Davisson had spent 2½ years as a Google key account executive, handling cloud services accounts for asset manager BlackRock and hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and managing the US business of the former Credit Suisse.
Upon Davisson’s return from leave in May 2023, Google allegedly refused to let Davisson handle any customer accounts, depriving him of career advancement though he kept his pay and title.
Employee fired after further military leave
The complaint said Google assigned Davisson in January 2024 to a cloud solutions position that also involved no management of customer accounts, and fired him seven months later following another military leave and as part of a broader workforce reduction.
Davisson, a Bronze Star and Meritorious Service Medal recipient, has a home in Charlotte, North Carolina, but lived and worked in Manhattan while Google employed him, the complaint said. Google’s parent Alphabet is based in Mountain View, California.
“We disagree with the claims in this complaint,” Google spokesman Atle Erlingsson said in an e-mail.
“Google takes compliance with employment laws, including USERRA, seriously and investigates allegations of workplace wrongdoing.”
Lost wages and benefits
The lawsuit was brought by the civil rights unit of the US Attorney’s office in Manhattan, with backing from Assistant Attorney-General Harmeet Dhillon, the Trump administration’s top civil rights enforcer.
It seeks to recoup lost wages and benefits as well as additional damages for Davisson, and requires Google to ensure a non-discriminatory workplace including by improving training regarding USERRA.
“Federal law ensures that our brave soldiers, who sacrifice so much to keep us safe, are not punished by employers when they return to the civilian workforce after completing their military service,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald in Manhattan said in a statement. REUTERS

Kazakhstan and four other countries to work on QR payment integration by year-end
The central banks of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan have agreed to work out a mechanism for integrating their national QR payment systems by the end of 2026. This will allow citizens to pay for purchases abroad using their familiar banking apps, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The agreement was reached at the fourth regional meeting of representatives of the central banks of the five countries, held in Tajikistan on October 22-23, a statement from the National Bank of Kazakhstan reads.
Participants discussed the development of national payment platforms, instant payment systems, cashless transactions and remote customer identification.
The Kazakh delegation presented the progress made in developing the National Digital Financial Infrastructure, including the digital tenge, open banking, biometric identification platforms and the National Anti-Fraud Center.
Special attention was given to the Interbank Mobile Payment System, which enables users to make transfers using phone numbers and pay for goods and services via QR codes.
The participants supported Kazakhstan’s proposed approaches to integrating national QR payment systems.
In the future, citizens of the five countries will be able to pay for goods and services while travelling abroad using their banks’ mobile apps, as well as send and receive money transfers in real time.
Kazakhstan also proposed joint measures for information sharing and the regulation of digital assets.
The parties then discussed protecting payment infrastructure against cyberattacks, combating fraud, and applying artificial intelligence in the supervision of payment systems.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan plans to set up a National Cryptocurrency Analytics Center to monitor transactions involving digital assets.

Russian attack on humanitarian mission bus in Zaporizhzhia region kills woman, injures three
Yevhen Kaplin, head of the Proliska humanitarian mission, announced this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
"Today, at around 14:30, a Russian FPV drone attacked a social bus operated by the Proliska humanitarian mission in the village of Bilenke, Zaporizhzhia region. The bus was transporting residents of a frontline settlement to the city of Zaporizhzhia," Kaplin said.
According to him, "preliminary information indicates that it was a drone lying in wait. The attack took place in the center of the settlement, on a stretch of road protected by anti-drone netting. The bus was clearly marked with the Proliska humanitarian mission's insignia on the hood and roof, as well as the words 'social bus.'"
Kaplin said: "This social bus was the only means of transport serving the settlement. Our team launched the service at the request of the regional and local authorities because, after commercial transport operators stopped running, village residents had no way to reach the regional center to access administrative, medical, banking and other essential services, buy food and medicines, or receive pension payments and winter assistance under government and humanitarian organization programs."
According to Kaplin, more than 1,600 people live in Bilenke.
"At the time of the strike, there were 23 passengers and the driver on board. Most of them were elderly people. The drone struck the roof of the vehicle. A female passenger born in 1952 was killed. The bus driver sustained serious injuries and was evacuated to a medical facility. Another passenger, a man born in 1947, sustained multiple shrapnel wounds and was also evacuated to a medical facility. Another woman was injured by broken glass. The other passengers suffered acoustic and blast injuries," Kaplin said.
The injured were evacuated by specialized National Police units and military personnel, accompanied by aerial cover teams because of the threat of further drone attacks.
Kaplin stressed that since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, this was the 121st attack on the mission's staff and volunteers while they were providing assistance, as well as on its vehicles, offices and warehouse facilities.

Weimar Triangle Deputy Ministers for European Affairs meet in Giżycko
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:29:35 CET
04:29:35 KST

Weimar Triangle Deputy Ministers for European Affairs meet in Giżycko
26.10.2026
On 25-26 October, MFA Undersecretary of State Ignacy Niemczycki met in Giżycko with French Minister Delegate for Europe Benjamin Haddad and German Minister of State for Europe Gunther Krichbaum. The talks within the framework of the Weimar Triangle focused on European security, the EU budget for 2028-2034, the competitiveness of the European economy, and the EU enlargement.
Deputy ministers from Poland, France, and Germany discussed Ukraine’s difficult situation in the light of the ongoing Russian aggression and the approaching winter. They shared the opinion that Russia does not show that it is ready to engage in constructive peace talks and reaffirmed the need to continue and strengthen European support for Ukraine, to tighten sanctions against Russia, and to accelerate the disbursement of tranches from the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan (USL). They also highlighted the need for Europe’s representatives to take part in any possible peace negotiations.
In the context of regional security, the partners emphasised that Russian attacks on grain export route across the Black Sea are aimed not only at depriving Ukraine of its sources of income, but also at triggering a global food crisis and increasing migratory pressure on the EU.
The meeting, held as partof the Weimar Triangle, provided an opportunity to exchange views on the EU’s future Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028–2034, on the eve of the decisive phase of the budget negotiations. The talks centred on the importance of the future EU budget for the implementation of common European priorities and for addressing the challenges facing the EU member states and their regions. French and German ministers also familiarised themselves with the characteristics and challenges of the Warmińsko-Mazurskie Province as an eastern border region.
The discussions focused as well on the need to simplify EU regulations and reduce the administrative burden on businesses and farmers. The deputy foreign ministers of Poland, France, and Germany highlighted the excessive reporting obligations, the number of delegated acts, and the need to match requirements to the size of entities and their actual impact on the environment. They also emphasised the importance of improving the lawmaking process in the EU and providing an environment for European businesses that is conducive to competitiveness and single market access.
When discussing climate transition, the deputy ministers found it necessary to align environmental objectives with protecting the competitiveness of European economy and maintaining its industrial potential. They also talked about the differences of approach to the implementation of climate solutions, in particular the ETS.
The EU’s economic security in its external dimension was another item on the agenda. The deputy ministers emphasised that solutions must be put in place to bring together the Union’s economic sovereignty, decarbonisation, and competitiveness, while ensuring level playing ground in regard to international partners. Also discussed was the state of play on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). Moreover, the ministers agreed that the EU’s economic policy instruments should be put to a more effective use in the relations with external partners and that favourable conditions should be created for the growth of industrial production in Europe.
The Weimar Triangle’s deputy foreign ministers talked about current challenges concerning the EU enlargement policy. They welcomed the latest developments, namely the opening of Clusters 2 and 3 with Ukraine and Moldova and the closing of further negotiating chapters with Montenegro and Albania. The deputy ministers emphasised that the enlargement is a geopolitical necessity but pointed out that the process remains merit-based and requires concrete measures to be taken by the candidate countries.
The meeting saw the adoption of a joint declaration whereby the participants reaffirmed readiness to continue to work together in the Weimar Triangle for a strong and safe Europe. The declaration put an emphasis on the commitment to strengthening NATO’s and the EU’s eastern flank as well as Europe’s defence capabilities and defence industry.
The meeting in Giżycko was an opportunity to familiarise the French and German partners with the specific character of a border region of the European Union that has been faced with serious security and economic challenges due to Russia’s hostile policy.

In a statement through his lawyers earlier this month, Ibrahim said he was not a member of the Left Party and said he rejected antisemitism. “I categorically reject the accusation of supporting terrorism,” his statement said.
In another private comment on the Ibrahim Ibrahim question, Eralp referred to an unidentified man by his first name, saying he “does not want to name specific individuals, neither does my husband, nor do I. He is afraid of these people, and so am I.” Der Spiegel did not identify the unknown man or explain his relationship to Eralp.
The CDU’s mayoral candidate, Stefan Evers, who placed second in the vote, said the remarks exposed a contradiction between Eralp’s concerns and her party’s position. The Left Party has called for reducing police numbers, while Evers alleged that members were working with the people Eralp feared.
“If the woman who is supposed to govern Berlin in the future is so afraid for herself and her family that she hesitates to publicly name terrorist sympathizers, while parts of her own party are working hand in hand with those very circles, then reasonable voices within the Greens and [Social Democrats] must finally pull the emergency brake,” Evers told POLITICO.
Former Berlin Mayor Michael Müller, a Social Democrat, warned that Eralp could be vulnerable to blackmail.
Eralp said Thursday she still wants to become Berlin’s mayor. Asked about the report, she told journalists: “I will not comment because private, internal information has been published. But what I can say very clearly is that, as governing mayor, I will ensure the safety of all Berliners.”

On the evening of October 28, the Italian Embassy in Brasília hosted the charity gala organized to mark the 40th anniversary of Abrace (Brazilian Association for Assistance to Families of Children with Oncological and Hematological Diseases), one of Brazil’s leading philanthropic organizations dedicated to supporting children and adolescents with serious oncological and hematological diseases and their families. The event brought together figures from the local political scene, representatives of the diplomatic corps, leaders from civil society and the Brazilian and Italian business communities, as well as journalists and prominent figures from the cultural scene of the federal capital. It is a symbol of the historic and deep bond between Italy and Brazil, capable of bringing together institutions, businesses, and civil society to support causes of fundamental human and social importance.”
   In 2025, ABRACE carried out over 180,000 assistance interventions, reaffirming its commitment to supporting more than 900 families with children and adolescents suffering from serious oncological diseases. Among the achievements were 26,295 donations of goods, 6,259 deliveries of medications and hospital supplies, and 9.50 metric tons of food distributed to the families receiving assistance.
