EU governments helpless as energy prices soar to four-year highs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:00:41 UTC
04:00:41 KST

LUXEMBOURG — Europe’s energy ministers are running out of ideas to protect citizens from surging energy prices as winter approaches.
But at a summit in Luxembourg on Thursday, they were clear on one thing: Demanding voters cut back on power use is not an option.
European gas prices soared above €100 per megawatt-hour on Wednesday for the first time since 2022, as last-minute panic-buying to fill European gas reserves added to supply pressures linked to the war in the Middle East.
Advertisement
But at the Thursday summit, EU energy ministers broadly acknowledged that both Brussels and national capitals had run out of ideas to contain price pressures.
“We’ve exhausted most of our short-term options,” said one senior European energy official, granted anonymity to offer a candid perspective. “What’s left is really crisis management.”
For the past year, government attempts to cushion price rises with renewables schemes, windfall taxes and costly fuel subsidies have ultimately failed to contain anxieties that have since boiled over into widespread protests across the continent.
“The EU and member states don't have a magic wand to make the price increases go away,” Irish Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, told reporters. “There's a lot of measures that have been taken already in the short term. What today is about is actually seeing how we can move to more sustainable measures.”
But even crisis management is proving politically difficult. Despite calls by EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen earlier this year to encourage consumers and businesses to cut energy use, European ministers are reluctant to make such a move official policy.
“I don't want to see that we will limit people,” said Mika Nykänen, the state secretary to Finland's energy ministry. Instead, he called for policy designed to “change behavior” and reduce energy consumption less painfully. “Industry does it naturally. Normal households, normal families — they sometimes need encouragement,” he said. “For instance, subsidies to invest in the energy efficiency of houses, windows.”
Advertisement
Demand reduction “has an impact on industry, it has an impact on business, and in a difficult situation, it could be the way to do that. But it does not … solve the long-term,” Polish Secretary of State for Energy Wojciech Wrochna told reporters.
High prices “will regulate demand by itself,” Swedish Energy Minister Ebba Busch told reporters.
Fossil fuel subsidies
Such was the opposition to demand reduction measures on Thursday, Jørgensen — who was at the summit warning of a "difficult" winter of soaring fuel prices ahead — gave up even proposing it, focusing instead on subsidies. He reluctantly accepted that such subsidies could include fossil fuels as well as clean alternatives, but urged that they be "targeted and temporary."
Since the war started, governments have paid €18 billion for tax relief on fossil fuel products, including a controversial move by Rome earlier this month to reduce the impact of gas prices on electricity costs.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned national leaders against this tendency, urging them at a summit this month to keep policies temporary and targeted to avoid inadvertently increasing fossil fuel demand and distorting the EU single market, according to two EU diplomats familiar with her comments.
That remains a point of contention among EU leaders, with some, including Greece, calling for greater fiscal space to increase energy subsidies while others warn of the dangers of subsidizing fossil fuels.
Advertisement
“Our concern is to make sure that we don't create conditions where different member states go very far in different national decision-making,” said Lithuanian Energy Minister Lukas Savickas in a separate interview.
Jørgensen did not respond to POLITICO's question at a subsequent press conference when asked whether new fiscal flexibilities were being considered.
Other ideas have gone by the wayside. Von der Leyen rejected calls by countries to establish an EU-wide tax on windfall profits of oil and gas companies at this month’s summit, the diplomats cited above said even as European oil companies like Shell, TotalEnergies and Repsol rake in their biggest profits since 2022.
Member countries also questioned the value of a Commission proposal to coordinate the purchase of energy supplies. Such a scheme would work in theory but be hard to implement for “big players” with established supply chains, Wrochna said.
Neither has the EU’s commitment to hastening the release of strategic crude oil and diesel reserves earlier this month — in response to what EU officials described as U.S. “blackmail” — done much to ease fuel costs.
Even so, the EU's commitment will now include over 40 million barrels on top of the 10 million pledged by Paris, France's economy minister Roland Lescure told reporters on Thursday.
Advertisement
A parallel push to delay methane monitoring requirements — a plank of the EU's 2024 Green Deal that industry argued was poorly designed and would disrupt supplies — also had no impact on prices.
Slow pay-off
To be sure, measures designed to lower electricity prices and encourage consumers to switch away from imported fossil fuels are starting to work, with soaring sales of heat pumps and electric vehicles in Europe this year. "There's no silver bullet, but when you add all of these things up, it can actually matter," said Jørgensen.
But even longer-term efforts to encourage the switch to cleaner energy are facing backlash as countries resist ceding power to Brussels.
One example is a Commission proposal to make electricity bills more affordable and speed up electrification, including by ensuring electricity is not taxed more heavily than natural gas. Member countries pushed back against the proposal’s taxation provisions on Thursday, arguing that Brussels is overstepping EU treaties requiring that tax changes be approved unanimously, risking higher costs for households and industry.
Busch, the Swedish energy minister, said the proposal’s taxation provisions went too far, warning it would face “a lot of pushback” from countries concerned about EU interference in national tax policy.
Germany and Poland also raised concerns about the proposal’s potential impact on industry and national tax systems, while Italy warned that changing tax rates could make energy more expensive rather than encourage electrification.

Oldest known Mars rock is a ‘Rosetta stone’ for the Red Planet’s watery past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:59:44 UTC
03:59:44 KST

In 2022 a group of nomadic meteorite hunters discovered a strange stone in the Sahara Desert. Called Teghaza 001, initial analysis by experts showed it was a meteorite from Mars. Now new research reveals it’s the oldest ever found, and it’s revealing more about the Red Planet’s complex history.
Scientists fortunate enough to get their hands on samples of the space rock have been analyzing tiny pieces of Teghaza for years to better understand exactly what it is and when it formed. The new paper, published today in Science, identifies it as a piece of Mars’s crust that’s at least 4.1 billion years old, from a time when that world was warmer, wetter and more Earth-like.
“We’re holding a piece of a rock that’s dated even before the oldest Earth rock—a piece of Mars that’s so ancient, it existed when life had just started on Earth,” says Yang Liu, lead author of the study and a planetary scientist at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Several hundred Martian meteorites are known. All of them got here by giant impacts that have pelted Mars for eons, occasionally blasting bits of the planet into space, some of which by chance fall to Earth. Most are relatively young, each revealing little more than a snapshot from the most recent 600 million years or so of Mars’s 4.5-billion-year history. The only other known intact ancient sample, a meteorite discovered in Antarctica in the 1980s, is just 10 million years younger than Teghaza.
When Liu received a piece of the rock from the team at the University of New Mexico that initially analyzed it, she was tasked with studying its manganese, an element that can help scientists discern whether an ancient rock was ever exposed to water and oxidation. But soon she noticed the presence of zircons in the meteorite—tough crystalline minerals that can endure in rock for billions of years and contain radioactive isotopes that can be used for ultraprecise dating. The zircons, Liu realized, made Teghaza very special. In the exhaustive work that followed, she and her team isolated zircons and other minerals from small scraps of their precious samples, pinning down the meteorite’s chemical composition and dating its elements to the early days of Mars’s history.
Teghaza, they found, is an igneous rock that formed from slowly-cooled magma and was once a piece of the planet’s crust. Comparing ratios of certain elements in the meteorite to those measured by orbiters for larger swaths of the planet’s surface, Liu and her team found the closest matches within the rugged, crater-pocked terrain in Mars’s southern highlands, a region thought to be among the world’s most ancient.
Pinpointing the possible sites where Teghaza was launched by a giant impact on its fateful journey to Earth is a feat all its own, but the meteorite’s chemical composition shows something even more enlightening.
As detailed in work from Liu’s team published earlier this year, some of the minerals in the meteorite have been aqueously altered—a sign that liquid water once percolated through Mars’s ancient mantle and crust. And careful analysis of remnant hydrogen trapped inside Teghaza shows that even when the rock formed, more than 4.1 billion years ago, the planet was already well on its way to losing most of its atmosphere, growing cold and transitioning to its current freeze-dried state. Taken together with the results in today’s paper, Liu says, all this reinforces how Mars’s mantle is likely more heterogeneous and complex than many planetary scientists have long assumed.
Liu’s research on Teghaza is ongoing; her team “has only scratched the surface,” she says, of the insights the meteorite might hold.
A clearer understanding of Mars’s deep past can also inform our own. Mars and Earth formed in similar ways, with giant magma oceans that cooled into cores, mantles and crusts. Because of its tectonic activity that continuously buries, melts and recycles the planet’s crust across geological time, Earth’s surface does not preserve many (if any) samples from its primordial youth—but Mars is different, as its geophysical tumults ebbed long ago.
One reviewer of the paper called this meteorite “the Rosetta stone of Mars,” Liu says, because it may be able to tell the stories of planets across the solar system.
“We’re hoping to start using Mars to compare and contrast and to understand what makes a planet habitable for life,” she adds.
There’s much still to learn about this meteorite’s mysteries, says Arya Udry, a planetary scientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who was not involved with the Science study. But truly understanding the full story of Mars requires more than gathering additional impact-imported fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth; what’s necessary is more visits to the world itself.
“Mars is a complex planet, and this meteorite is really cool, but we don’t know exactly where it came from, so this is really another example of why we need to bring back samples,” she says.

AFRL Plans to Award $30M for Cislunar Project Starting Next Spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:57:37 UTC
03:57:37 KST

The Air Force Research Laboratory plans to launch its latest technology challenge next month—a project meant to speed up development of systems that can operate beyond geosynchronous orbit.
SpaceWERX is leading the effort, dubbed Cislunar Prime. The space innovation hub is looking for commercial capabilities that could put the Space Force on a faster path toward cislunar operations in three focus areas:
- space domain awareness
- cislunar communications
- positioning, navigation, and timing
The tentative plan, according to an AFRL spokesperson, is to officially announce Cislunar Prime in December, solicit proposals in January, and begin awarding contracts next spring. The program has $30 million to fund 15 direct-to-phase-two Small Business Innovation Research contracts worth $2 million each.
The Space Force defines cislunar as the region of space past GEO and extending to the moon and beyond, hundreds of thousands of kilometers in distance and 1,728 times the volume of space complained within GEO. Conditions there present challenges for satellite operations like PNT and SDA, given its distance from the Earth and its unstable trajectories.
Speaking Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s Space Industry Days conference, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Advanced Programs Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy said because of these dynamics, the Space Force needs a better understanding of how to operate in cislunar space.
“Space is often described as hard and difficult and a fight that we’re not seeing,” he said. “But I would characterize cislunar as even harder and more difficult, and we really don’t see what’s going on in that arena.”
The Space Force has a handful of active projects exploring cislunar operations, including AFRL’s Oracle program, which plans to launch its first satellite in December—a pathfinder for efficient cislunar mobility, navigation, and space domain awareness. Over the past year, the service has signaled it plans to ramp up cislunar research and development activities, driven in part by China’s plans to establish a presence beyond GEO and on the moon.
Purdy said the Pentagon’s posture toward cislunar operations and planning has shifted significantly over the past year. He cited President Donald Trump’s December 2025 executive order that emphasized the importance of cislunar operations, as well as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine’s acknowledgement of cislunar as a “warfighting domain” during AFA’s Air, Space, and Cyber Conference in September.
Now, the service is looking to quickly fund satellites and software that could be ready for operations as soon as 2029, Purdy said. Beyond Cislunar Prime, the Space Force and its newly established Cislunar Coordination Office have two forthcoming requests for information—the first focused on existing cislunar hardware and software that could fly in the next two to three years, and the second for AI and autonomous processing capabilities.
“We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-developmental solutions, hardware with actual relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and ground systems,” Purdy said. “This isn’t a four- or five-year science project. This is about getting capability out soon.”

Germany and Ukraine test armed ground robot for frontline deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:56:57 UTC
03:56:57 KST

Remote-controlled and heading for the front lines. ARX Robotics and the Ukrainian company ROBONEERS report completion of the first major system tests.
A German and a Ukrainian defence company have tested an armed ground robot for use by Ukrainian forces, with the first systems due to be integrated and delivered by the end of 2026.
The cooperation agreement was signed in early October during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's state visit to Kyiv, in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Before the end of 2026, the first robotic vehicles fitted with the new weapons modules are expected to be ready for deployment and delivered in line with the needs of Ukraine's armed forces.
How the new system works
It's known as GEREON. Built by ARX Robotics, the unmanned vehicle provides mobility and power and can carry out reconnaissance using cameras and sensors.
It can be fitted with the SABER weapons module, built by Ukrainian company ROBONEERS, which is mounted on top and provides remotely operated fire support for attack and defence capabilities. The companies say this allows soldiers to operate the system from a safer distance.
Unarmed versions of GEREON are already being used for a range of tasks in Ukraine. They can transport supplies, evacuate wounded personnel, support electronic warfare, carry out reconnaissance and counter drones. The platform can also be adapted for combat missions.
The companies say the aim is to create one flexible robotic system that can be quickly adapted for different frontline missions.
The SABER weapons module is also customisable, allowing soldiers to fit different weapons depending on the mission, from rifles to grenade launchers.
ARX says GEREON is the largest fleet of Western-built unmanned ground vehicles currently being used in Ukraine.
Maximilian Wied, CFO and co-founder of ARX Robotics, said: "Modern land forces need combat platforms that can be quickly adapted to different missions, integrate new technologies and work seamlessly with existing systems."
ROBONEERS says its robotic systems have already been used in more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014.
The two companies are already cooperating in other areas. They have set up a joint venture to expand production of another unmanned ground vehicle, the Rys Pro, in Germany and Ukraine. The companies are targeting production of more than 1,000 units in its first year.
German defence minister to visit tech company Helsing
Artificial intelligence is also a focus for German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, who is visiting defence technology company Helsing at its headquarters in Munich.
The visit will focus on the company's latest products and AI capabilities, alongside meetings with management, employees and the works council.
Helsing was founded in 2021 and has grown rapidly into one of Europe's most prominent defence technology companies.
It develops artificial intelligence and software for military systems, including technology designed to add AI capabilities to existing platforms such as tanks, submarines and fighter jets.

Kazakhstan sets out $14 billion development plan to drive economic growth
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:56:34 EET
03:56:34 KST

ASTANA, October 29 – Kazakhstan has announced a nationwide investment and construction programme worth approximately $14.27 billion, setting out plans to modernise infrastructure, expand industrial production, attract foreign investment and strengthen its position as an economic and transport centre connecting Europe and Asia.
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev presented the programme during his State of the Nation Address on October 28, outlining a development strategy that places infrastructure, technological innovation and economic diversification at the centre of Kazakhstan’s ambitions for the coming decade.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The initiative, known as Halyqtyq Qurylys, or People’s Construction, will draw approximately 6.5 trillion tenge from the country’s National Fund by the end of 2029. It represents the largest infrastructure programme announced in Kazakhstan’s history.
Tokayev also proposed declaring 2027 the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction, with investment reaching cities, towns and rural communities throughout the country.
The announcement comes as Kazakhstan celebrates 35 years of independence and begins implementing a Constitution that entered into force on July 1, following its adoption in March.
According to the President, the country has reached a stage where its financial resources, industrial capacity and technological development provide a foundation for further economic expansion.
“Strong cities create strong regions, and strong regions create a strong country,” Tokayev said in his address.
The programme aims to translate Kazakhstan’s accumulated financial resources into infrastructure, employment and economic opportunities.
The government’s initial construction plans include approximately 70 healthcare facilities and 50 educational, sporting and cultural institutions. Investment will also support housing, transport networks, utilities and improved access to natural gas and drinking water.
Around 1.5 trillion tenge will be earmarked for social infrastructure projects during 2026 and the first two months of 2027.
The government has until the end of this year to prepare a list of projects covering every region.
Kazakhstan’s economic indicators provide context for the investment programme. Citing projections from the International Monetary Fund, Tokayev said the country’s gross domestic product is expected to approach $400 billion in 2026, with GDP per capita exceeding $19,000.
The President said Kazakhstan is expected to rank 47th globally by economic size, while manufacturing now accounts for more than 14 per cent of GDP.
The combined value of Kazakhstan’s gold and foreign exchange reserves and National Fund assets has exceeded $130 billion.
These resources give the government financial capacity to pursue infrastructure development while maintaining its focus on investment and economic stability.
Tokayev stressed that public expenditure must attract private investment rather than replace it. He also instructed the government to involve domestic companies in construction and industrial projects.
The programme is expected to generate employment opportunities for hundreds of thousands of people, while increasing demand for locally produced construction materials, metal structures and engineering equipment.
“The use of National Fund resources to finance imports must not be permitted,” Tokayev said.
The requirement is intended to ensure that infrastructure spending supports domestic production, employment and industrial development.
Kazakhstan’s transport sector forms another part of the government’s economic strategy.
Situated between China, Russia, Europe and the Caspian region, Kazakhstan occupies a geographical position along trade routes linking Asian manufacturing centres with European markets.
Tokayev said approximately 85 per cent of freight transported from China to the European continent passes through Kazakhstan.
The government intends to expand the country’s role beyond providing transit routes by developing logistics operators, distribution centres, manufacturing facilities and trading hubs.
The Bakhty–Ayagoz railway, scheduled to enter service in 2027, is expected to increase freight capacity on routes towards China by 20 million tonnes.
Construction of the Aral–Caspian transport corridor began in August 2026. The project is designed to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by approximately 1,000 kilometres and reduce delivery times by up to three days.
The government also plans to complete the reconstruction of all road border crossings in 2027 and strengthen oversight of road construction across the country.
A new airport in Astana is scheduled to begin construction next year in partnership with an international company.
Meanwhile, restoration work at Arkalyk Airport has been completed, and airports at Zaysan, Katon-Karagay and Kenderli are expected to enter service.
Tokayev also called for investment in air cargo infrastructure and the digitalisation of international freight documentation.
The measures form part of Kazakhstan’s ambition to become a Eurasian logistics centre, generating revenue from transport, distribution and related industries.
Energy development is another priority.
Kazakhstan currently generates approximately 123 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, but increasing industrial demand and the expansion of digital infrastructure have placed pressure on the national power system.
Tokayev instructed the government to achieve a sustained electricity surplus by 2029.
The strategy includes constructing generating facilities, modernising power stations and transmission networks, developing cleaner coal generation and expanding renewable energy, particularly solar power.
The government will also update the country’s long-term energy balance through 2035 to account for electricity demand from industry, artificial intelligence and data centres.
Nuclear energy occupies a place in these plans.
Tokayev said construction of the Balkhash nuclear power plant might begin in 2027 and called for a cooperation agreement to advance the proposed Moyynkum nuclear power plant.
He also proposed examining the establishment of a strategic uranium reserve capable of meeting Kazakhstan’s nuclear fuel requirements for the next century.
The President said cooperation with foreign nuclear technology partners should include training for Kazakh specialists, technology transfer and the development of domestic industries.
Such arrangements would link investment in electricity generation with the expansion of Kazakhstan’s engineering and technological capabilities.
The government is pursuing a parallel strategy to develop the digital economy.
Under the Digital Qazaqstan programme, Kazakhstan has commissioned two supercomputers, with a third scheduled to enter service before the end of 2026.
Construction of a fibre-optic connection across the Caspian seabed has also been completed, while additional data centres are under development.
Tokayev called for the commercial application of artificial intelligence, blockchain technologies and asset tokenisation across the economy.
The government intends to establish a simplified legal framework for digital employment by the end of this year.
In 2027, authorities and private companies will begin pilot projects to help rural producers reach customers through digital marketplaces, supported by financial services and logistics networks.
The initiative seeks to extend the benefits of digital technology beyond major cities and provide businesses in rural communities with access to markets.
Kazakhstan also intends to introduce artificial intelligence into public administration, including expenditure monitoring, financial management and infrastructure planning.
Digital models of urban infrastructure will support planning and resource management in cities.
Tokayev said the objective is to create an economy in which technology supports employment, entrepreneurship and productivity.
The President also identified investment reform as a condition for achieving Kazakhstan’s economic targets.
Small and medium-sized enterprises currently generate approximately 40 per cent of GDP and account for almost 70 per cent of investment in fixed capital.
The government has been instructed to prepare a development plan for medium-sized businesses, focusing on long-term financing, technological modernisation and closer cooperation with major enterprises.
Tokayev proposed discussing a three-year moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses beginning on January 1, 2027.
The proposal follows a similar moratorium implemented between 2020 and 2023.
The government will also examine measures to reduce regulatory barriers, improve competition and increase access to public procurement for smaller companies.
For international investors, Kazakhstan plans to strengthen investment coordination and develop legal institutions designed to support commercial activity.
Tokayev proposed giving Baiterek Holding a greater role in coordinating investment policy alongside the relevant government ministries.
In Alatau City, the government plans to establish an Investment Court based on the English common law model.
The court would handle commercial disputes, while a separate Civil Court would deal with other matters under the city’s special legal regime.
The government must submit the necessary legislative amendments by the end of January 2027.
The initiative aims to provide investors with a legal framework for commercial activity and dispute resolution.
Kazakhstan’s mineral resources also feature in its plans for industrial development.
Tokayev instructed the government to modernise geological exploration, expand access to geological data and attract private investment into mineral development.
The government will prepare proposals for a national system to manage critical mineral reserves, including financing mechanisms and agreements to purchase production from domestic companies.
Kazakhstan also intends to strengthen partnerships with international companies to develop processing facilities and participate in global manufacturing supply chains.
The strategy places emphasis on increasing the value of products manufactured within Kazakhstan rather than relying solely on raw material exports.
Agriculture offers another area for expansion.
According to figures presented in the address, Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector grew by almost 6 per cent in 2025, while agro-industrial output reached 15 trillion tenge.
Baiterek Holding has identified food-industry investment projects worth more than 500 billion tenge.
The government plans to improve access to long-term financing, expand domestic agricultural machinery production and support investment in food processing and storage facilities.
Artificial intelligence is also expected to play a role in agricultural modernisation.
Tokayev referred to a visit to Astana by NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang, during which the introduction of artificial intelligence into Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector was discussed.
The President endorsed the proposal and called for its implementation.
Water management will accompany agricultural expansion.
The government has been instructed to reduce losses in water distribution networks, improve monitoring of consumption and complete the National Water Resources Information System.
Tokayev said irrigation projects should incorporate water-saving technologies, while investment in processing and logistics should increase the economic value of agricultural production.
Alongside industrial and infrastructure development, the government announced measures aimed at raising household incomes and improving public services.
From January 1, 2027, Kazakhstan’s monthly minimum wage will increase from 85,000 tenge to 110,000 tenge, an increase of approximately 29 per cent.
The measure is expected to raise incomes for nearly 1.8 million people, including more than 370,000 public sector employees.
The government will also increase remuneration for district-level primary healthcare specialists by up to 40 per cent, depending on continuous length of service.
More than 77,000 healthcare professionals are expected to benefit.
Healthcare investment under the People’s Construction programme includes eight perinatal centres and seven multidisciplinary children’s hospitals.
The hospitals will serve Atyrau, Aktobe, Almaty, Shymkent, Kaskelen, Semey and Aktau, while Astana will receive two additional medical facilities.
The government intends to involve private investors and public-private partnerships in developing healthcare infrastructure.
Education will also receive attention.
Kazakhstan has nearly seven million children, representing approximately 34 per cent of its population, with more than 330,000 births annually.
More than 237,000 children have special educational needs.
Tokayev instructed the government to expand inclusive education facilities, improve early identification of additional needs and increase the availability of specialists.
He also called for a reduction in teachers’ administrative duties to allow them to concentrate on education.
The President linked these investments to Kazakhstan’s long-term economic development, arguing that modern infrastructure and education must advance together.
Macroeconomic stability remains part of the government’s programme.
Tokayev identified inflation control and rising real incomes as priorities requiring cooperation between the government and the National Bank.
Kazakhstan’s banking sector holds assets exceeding 75 trillion tenge, while deposits have reached 52 trillion tenge.
The President called for more long-term lending to productive industries and closer cooperation between commercial banks, development institutions and international financial organisations.
He also instructed authorities to develop a unified financial market strategy involving the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange, the Astana International Financial Centre and Alatau City.
Tax reform is expected to accompany these measures.
The government will prepare amendments to the Tax Code to address provisions that create uncertainty or place excessive burdens on businesses.
Tokayev also proposed discussing higher taxation for individuals with substantial wealth, while maintaining constitutional protection for lawfully acquired property.
A new Civil Code, designed to reflect changes in technology and commercial activity, is expected to reach adoption by the end of 2027.
The economic programme coincides with reforms to Kazakhstan’s political and administrative institutions following the introduction of the new Constitution.
The Presidential Administration has been instructed to submit a comprehensive public administration reform plan by June 1, 2027.
The plan will cover government institutions from central ministries to rural administrations, with an emphasis on administrative efficiency, digital technology and professional standards.
A separate long-term development strategy will be prepared within one year by the Presidential Administration, the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms and research institutions.
Tokayev placed particular emphasis on the role of young people in Kazakhstan’s future, linking the country’s development ambitions to education, science and technological competence.
“Our country will always need outstanding scientists, highly skilled engineers, wise teachers and qualified doctors,” he said.
The President also called for national unity, respect for the law and public responsibility as Kazakhstan enters its next phase of development.
“I see Kazakhstan as a just and progressive state, a united country offering equal opportunities to everyone,” Tokayev said.
“I place great hopes in patriotic young people who will lead our nation forward.”

Wallabies star Charlie Cale proud as brother Jack represents Australian Deaf Rugby
For as long as he can remember, Wallabies back-rower Charlie Cale has always been able to rely on his older brother Jack.
Growing up in Sydney's northern suburbs, they would often team up together against the eldest of the Cale boys, Sam, in fierce backyard rugby battles.
Even when it came to studying during their school years, Charlie knew Jack was in his corner.
"He helped me with a lot of my schoolwork," Charlie fondly tells ABC Sport.
"There's been a few exams … he's helped me in a lot of ways, actually.
"That's the best thing about Jack. He's always been there for me and anyone else that has needed him.
"He's one of a kind."
Jack's encouragement is repaid by the support he receives from Charlie and Sam, who both keenly follow his career with the Australian Deaf Rugby (ADR) men's squad.
Last Tuesday night in Sydney, Charlie proudly presented Jack, Australia's vice-captain, with his official team tie ahead of the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which begin in Tokyo this weekend.
Australia's men's and women's squads are among the favourites to emerge triumphant once the tournament concludes on November 3.
Jack is grateful to have Charlie and Sam's backing as he juggles rugby commitments with his job as a lawyer.
"It's always been really helpful having two brothers to go through a rugby career with," says Jack, who has played for Eastwood (Shute Shield) and Mosman (Subbies) at club level.
"We're always checking in with each other, trying to watch each other's games.
"Charlie, even with the limited time he gets outside of training with Brumbies and Wallabies squads, is always trying to watch our games as well."
On the international stage
Jack's introduction to deaf rugby came out of the blue.
"In late 2022, I got a phone call from an old coach of mine on a Saturday morning," says Jack, who had played colts and grade rugby in Sydney by this stage.
"He gave me a call and said, 'Mate, there's this deaf rugby trial happening down at Hunters Hill.'
"Of course, I didn't know what he was talking about as I hadn't really heard anything before.
"I went down there and ran around in a bit of a sevens trial, for maybe 20 or 25 minutes.
"I didn't think I'd actually played that well. I didn't touch the ball that much.
"I came off the field and I wasn't sure what to expect."
A letter arrived in the mail a few months later in early 2023, informing Jack he was selected in the ADR men's squad for the World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship, which were being held in Córdoba, Argentina in April of that year.
There was one small problem, though.
Jack found out about his selection during the club rugby off-season, meaning he was not exactly at peak fitness.
"I had to get myself fit pretty quickly without any rugby training, which was a bit of a struggle," Jack laughs.
Jack worked his way back into shape and seamlessly joined the Australian line-up, which he helped lead in his vice-captaincy role.
They made the final, gallantly losing 20-5 to Wales, while Australia finished third overall in the women's competition.
In Tokyo, the men's squad faces England, Japan, Hong Kong China and Italy in the pool stage, with the top three advancing to the knockout rounds of the tournament.
Australia is one of six teams in the women's draw, where it plays Fiji, England, Wales, New Zealand and a combined Barbarians team in a single pool.
Each will progress, with the two top-ranked teams moving directly to the semifinals.
Having avoided Wales in the men's round-robin matches, Jack considers England to be Australia's main threat in the preliminary phase.
"You've obviously got to go match by match," Jack says.
"It's important to get through the pool stage as well as we can and then the mindset obviously shifts to the knockout stages.
"I'd consider us in the better pool for the opportunity to do that."
Embracing challenges
To participate in World Deaf Rugby tournaments, players must have an average bilateral hearing loss across both ears of at least 40 decibels.
The level of hearing loss varies from player to player in the Australian teams, which illustrates to Jack the importance of non-verbal communication during matches.
"I stepped into this environment where nothing was said on a rugby field," he says.
"It was a bit of a challenge to get used to that.
"But I also really enjoyed that challenge, being able to communicate with some of those guys whose hearing is a lot more affected than mine is."
As much as Jack loves playing alongside his Australian teammates, he also gets a kick out of facing them in club rugby.
On one such occasion last year, he and Australian captain Tim Anstey opposed each other when Mosman met Newport in the NSW Subbies competition.
"It's pretty awesome playing against someone like that, who you now travel with on international tours," Jack says.
"But it's also surreal finding out that someone you might have been playing rugby against is also partially deaf and had the same struggles as you growing up, and you're now representing your country with them.
"It's pretty cool."
While Jack relishes every chance to represent Australia, spreading the message of inclusivity is just as important to him and everyone involved in deaf rugby.
ADR states its goal is to give every deaf and hard-of-hearing athlete the opportunity to play the game, regardless of their experience level.
"We want to find as many deaf or hard-of-hearing rugby players as we can," Jack says.
"It's really just word of mouth within deaf and hard-of-hearing communities."
Jack's family is also firmly behind the cause.
"I've got a lot of respect for this [ADR] program," says Charlie, who has played six Tests for the Wallabies.
"It gives these guys a platform and opportunity they may have lacked growing up.
"We know how much it means to Jack and therefore it means a lot to us."
Family support
Charlie got up early in the morning to watch Jack play at the world titles in Córdoba three years ago.
But a friendlier time zone will make it easier for him to follow his brother's progress in Tokyo.
"I don't think I've missed a game," Charlie says.
"I've woken up at 2am or 3am. I love watching him play."
As he did in Córdoba, Jack will have his devoted mum and dad, Sue and Tim, barracking from the sidelines in Tokyo.
The Cale parents do everything possible to watch their three sons play rugby.
"I don't think our mother has missed a rugby game of ours in God knows how many years," Jack says.
"Dad is always on the phone, straight after games, checking in with us and seeing how we've gone."
Just as he helped Charlie all those years ago with his schoolwork, Jack knows he can also depend on the support of his family.
"We're incredibly proud of him," Charlie says.

Putin says Russia is ready for war with Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:50:20 UTC
03:50:20 KST

- Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is ready for war with Europe but does not want one, warning there would be no winners.
- He spoke in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, responding to European plans to be ready to repel a Russian attack by 2030.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is “ready” for a war with Europe but does not want one, and warned that a conflict between them would leave no winners, responding to European warnings that Moscow could be able to attack NATO by the end of the decade.
Putin made the remarks at a press conference in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, held jointly with the African Union’s chairman, Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, The Moscow Times reported, citing Interfax. He was asked about his recent phone calls with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and said Russia supports any steps to restore full relations with European countries, either with the European Union as a whole or one by one.
“Many are talking about preparing for war by 2030. First of all, we are ready, but we do not want any war with Europe. If they want to prepare, let them prepare,” said Putin.
He added that Europe had not managed to inflict a “strategic defeat” on Russia and was unlikely to do so by 2030, according to TV Rain.
“If things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that,” Putin said.
Putin also referred to tensions in the Baltic Sea, asking whether anyone wanted the region to end up like the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, and said Russia did not want that but would respond to any challenge. He did not name any country or describe what kind of response he meant.
The 2030 date Putin cited matches the timeline European governments have set for rearmament. EU states aim to be able to repel a Russian attack by 2030, and several European officials have warned that Russia could rebuild enough military strength to strike a NATO member before then. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and the head of Germany’s armed forces, Gen. Carsten Breuer, have said Russia could be capable of a large-scale conventional attack on NATO territory by 2029, and a classified German intelligence and military analysis reported in 2025 said Moscow was preparing the conditions for a conventional war against NATO, with the Baltic states a possible target. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said Europe should be prepared for a possible major conflict with Russia as early as 2027.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected those warnings, and Putin has long said Russia has no plans to attack NATO countries. In December 2025, he said that if Europe “suddenly wants to wage a war with us and starts it, we are ready right away,” Fox News reported, while also saying Moscow did not seek war with Europe. European leaders, for their part, say Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, shows why they need to rearm.
Putin’s latest comments came two days after his calls with Stubb and Støre, which European officials have not described in detail. Neither Finland nor Norway, both NATO members that border Russia, had publicly responded to Putin’s remarks by Thursday evening.

EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit

Unknown Publisher

EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
October 29, 2026
European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.
"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.
But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
What's on the agenda for the summit?
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

Trains in Europe are getting safer despite recent tragedies in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:49:16 UTC
03:49:16 KST

Europe's trains are actually getting safer, despite recent tragedies in Spain
Spain was once regarded as a world leader in rail systems, but after suffering two of its deadliest train incidents in over a decade this year alone, questions have emerged.
The country has commenced three days of mourning after at least 69 people died, and dozens more were injured, after two high-speed trains collided just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday.
A computer system failure saw six trains stopped on just over 60km of track between Madrid and Seville, while another was manually given clearance to move, according to Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
What are the recent incidents in Spain?
Spain's high-speed rail network, operated by state-owned RENFE, is among the largest in the world, second only to China.
In January, 46 people died on the same rail network after two high-speed trains carrying around 400 passengers collided.
It was the first fatal incident along Spain's dedicated high-speed rail lines since its opening in 1992.
According to European Union data, rail fatality rates in Europe have decreased over the last decade, and last year recorded no fatalities or major accidents.
However, a series of accidents in 2023 saw a spike in those numbers.
Between 2022 and 2024, Spain recorded some of the lowest fatalities per million train kilometres in Europe.
University of Sydney's Rico Merkert, who specialises in European transport systems, said isolated incidents shifted people's perception around safety.
"There are so many trains, including high-speed trains, operated or run each and every day in Europe. There are millions of people travelling on those trains," Professor Merkert said.
"One incident is catastrophic and really not good and very tragic in terms of the number of fatalities.
"But statistically speaking, it's still safe due to the large volumes of passengers using trains and high-speed trains every single day in Europe."
He added that the European Train Control System (ETCS) prevented trains from reaching excessive speeds and could recognise when there was potential for a collision.
"The problem with the accident that happened [this week] is that there was a signalling sort of failure,"
he said.
"There was a system issue, so it broke down, and it's not quite clear whether that ETCS system was actually operating at all or partially unavailable. It looks like that system failure caused manual operations or signalling."
How does train safety in Europe compare?
A report into railway safety from the European Union found Australia, South Korea and the EU were among the safest railway systems between 2020 and 2024.
It also looked into passenger fatalities and found Japan was the safest, with no fatalities recorded.
Professor Merkert said it was difficult to compare Australia's rail system to Europe, because it does not have high-speed trains.
"[It] is not comparing apples with apples … high-speed trains are between 250 and 300 kilometres an hour, and you simply don't have those trains operating here in Australia," he said.
The report into railway safety said the gap in passenger fatality rates between Europe and Japan would be difficult to close in the medium term.
Professor Merkert said that was due to Japan's long tradition of running high-speed rail safely and efficiently.
"Similarly, China, they had a few incidents themselves, but overall again, the number of trains that they're operating and the number of people using those trains without having any accidents is quite remarkable," he said.
He said overall railway systems were safe, but once automated, additional safety procedures were required.
"There needs to be manual safeguards and governance structure in place that prevent things like what has happened [this week], and that simply seems to not have occurred,"
he said.

Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:48:14 UTC
03:48:14 KST

Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is stirring up trouble at home during a controversial trip to Montreal, turning what should have been a straightforward trade mission into a petty argument over Canada’s fictional “membership” in the bloc.
The EU mandarin traveled to Montreal for the 21st annual EU-Canada summit on Thursday, with her tail between her legs. A month after unilaterally promising Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney “associate member” status of the bloc, she was reportedly forced to scrub all mentions of the term and downgrade her offer to one of an “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada.
When the summit closes on Friday, both sides will issue a revised joint statement that reads: “We will create an even closer association between Canada and the EU... and work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” according to a draft seen by Policito.
Why was the text changed?
Von der Leyen reportedly gave neither the EU’s vast bureaucracy, nor its members’ wary leaders, any warning before she told Carney in front of the European Parliament that she “would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union.”
Unilateral decisions and boundary-overstepping are von der Leyen’s calling cards, as her fellow Eurocrats have repeatedly complained to the press. “Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” an unnamed diplomat told The Guardian on Wednesday. The widespread anonymous briefing to various mainstream European media made it clear that France, Germany, Greece and Italy had forced von der Leyen to adopt the new, watered-down terminology.
Ursula goes rogue
In her first speech in Montreal on Thursday, von der Leyen refused to adopt the new, sanitized wording. After noting that “Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography,” she insisted that “we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union. Our idea is simple: it is an ‘association without accession’.”
Whatever form Friday’s communique will take, von der Leyen has evidently chosen to disregard the concerns of the EU’s largest member states for the sake of her own personal project. However, the difference between both statements is purely rhetorical.
What does ‘associate member’ mean anyway?
Neither “Associate member” nor “ever closer association” are defined anywhere in EU law.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz attempted to define “associate membership” in May when he suggested that it be granted to Ukraine. Under his proposal, Ukraine would participate in European Council meetings without voting rights, send representatives to the European Parliament, receive more EU funding, and become party to the EU’s mutual defense clause.
The proposal was rejected by Kiev, with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky arguing that this kind of ‘membership-lite’ would leave his country “present in the European Union, but voiceless.”
“Ever closer association” is an even more meaningless term, lifted straight from ‘Ever Closer Union’, a hagiography on EU integration by the bloc’s court historian, Desmond Dinan. Writing in 1994, Dinan argued that “European integration is a good thing,” and the phrases he used – “ever closer union” and “pooling sovereignty,” for example – have since become staples of EU speeches and press releases.
US President Donald Trump ridiculed von der Leyen’s word games last month, calling the concept of associate membership “laughable,” and threatening to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if the EU-Canada proto-alliance ever harmed US interests.
Carney – who plainly insisted last month that Canada is “not looking to become a member of the European Union” – responded diplomatically to the intra-EU squabbling. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” he said ahead of the summit. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
However, Von der Leyen’s “membership” promise and the subsequent retraction has undermined Carney in front of his opponents. In a social media post on Thursday, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre described the concept of “associate membership” as “theater,” and dismissed the summit as “yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more."
How long will this theatre go on? While Canadians can’t afford food and homes, Mr. Carney has distracted for months with big talk about “Associate Membership” with Europe. Now, Europe has rejected it. For the next two days, we will be distracted again from the cost-of-living crisis with wall-to-wall media coverage on yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more. No one’s mortgage or grocery bill will come down. We already have a free trade deal with Europe, Mr. Carney. Get the 9 countries who have not ratified it to do so. And get EU countries to let our beef into the continent and cancel their planned carbon tariff on Canada. Otherwise stop wasting your time and our money. Both are running out.
— Pierre Poilievre (@PierrePoilievre) October 29, 2026
What does von der Leyen actually want?
Von der Leyen has far more riding on this summit than Carney. While the EU needs energy, minerals, and Canada’s geographic clout in the Arctic, Canada only needs to diversify some of its trade away from the US – which accounts for around 72% of its exports and 46% of its imports – in order to hedge against Trump’s tariffs and trade restrictions. At present, the EU accounts for less than 6% of Canada’s exports and 12% of its imports.
🛬 Touchdown in Montréal 🇨🇦 Rarely have I looked forward to a Summit this much. An ocean separates Europe and Canada. Yet we have never felt closer. We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as Associate Member of the EU. And we want to take our unique partnership even further. With an Alliance for the Future, we will stand together and respond to a world of growing rivalries. Montréal, we’re about to write a new chapter in our shared history.
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 28, 2026
Although the agenda is wrapped up in the language of “shared values” and “respect for the rules-based international order,” Brussels’ priorities in Montreal are clear: the energy-starved EU needs access to Canada’s resources.
According to Euronews, the latest draft of the joint declaration includes a promise to “assess opportunities for long-term energy connectivity,” including the supply of Canadian liquefied natural gas to the EU. Remember that in July 2025 von der Leyen personally pledged to Trump that bloc members would buy $750 billion worth of US energy by the end of 2028, in a trade deal that was widely seen as one-sided.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne has also announced that Ottawa and Brussels intend to sign an agreement on the supply of critical minerals including lithium, nickel, and cobalt. The EU currently controls less than 4% of the world’s supply of these minerals, which are vital in the production of electric vehicles and missiles – both of which the EU intends to increase.
The Europeans also intend to sign defense production and technology-sharing deals, to squeeze cash out of Canada for the bloc’s increasingly stretched €90 billion loan package for Ukraine, and deepen involvement in the Arctic, according to the summit agenda. As the EU set out in its updated Arctic Strategy’ earlier this month, Brussels intends to increase its military presence to challenge Russia in the north, and plans to literally redraw the map of the region to increase its meager Arctic claims, and to pursue closer ties “with like-minded partners,” including Canada.
To challenge Russia in the Arctic, the EU likely has its eyes on Canada’s polar-trained military and its 20-strong icebreaker fleet, compared to the ten such vessels spread across the 27-member bloc. None of these icebreakers are nuclear powered, and even if they were to operate on joint Arctic missions, they would be outnumbered and outclassed by Russia’s fleet of 43, eight of which are nuclear powered
However, any hope von der Leyen may have had of securing preferential single market-style trade deals with Carney have apparently been dashed. According to AFP, the “associate member” version of the joint statement included an “explicit goal of deeper financial market integration.” The new, “ever closer association” communique has replaced this with a promise by both sides to “limit potential negative effects on each other.”
Von der Leyen’s unforced error
Whether von der Leyen will, by virtue of repetition and against the will of four EU member states, invent an “associate membership” is immaterial. The concept is a legal fiction, and by insisting on the word “membership,” the European Commission president set herself up for an entirely avoidable clash with the French, Germans, Greeks, and Italians.
It’s very interesting to see the Commission president goes so defiantly against the position of Germany — the biggest member state and her home country — on an issue that, as of now, remains strictly theoretical.
— Jorge Liboreiro (@JorgeLiboreiro) October 29, 2026
The argument over the statement’s wording has overshadowed the summit, but the geopolitical reality remains unchanged: the EU needs Canada’s energy supplies to keep its economy afloat, Canada’s money to prop up its Ukraine project, and Canada’s geography to legitimize its Arctic expansion. For these, it doesn’t matter how the deal is dressed up.

Lubinets travels to occupied Oleshky

He said he wanted to be on the ground to see the situation firsthand and report on the mission’s progress. Lubinets also asked the public to rely on official sources and wait until he returned before raising further questions about the negotiations.
The Ukrainian ombudsman said the negotiations had been difficult and lengthy, adding that the mission had reached only the halfway point toward its goals.
“If I had to go for the sake of one person, I would go again,” Lubinets said, describing the mission as his duty to help Ukrainians in need.
US-mediated ceasefire enables humanitarian operation
The mission is being conducted jointly by Lubinets and Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, with mediation and coordination by Melania Trump.
The localized ceasefire took effect on 27 October to allow mine clearance, humanitarian deliveries, and civilian evacuations.
Oleshky, on the east bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, has been under Russian occupation since 2022. Russian occupation and restrictions on access to the city have left civilians facing severe shortages of food, medicine, and other essential supplies, while access to medical care has become increasingly difficult. The humanitarian mission aims to deliver urgently needed aid and help residents who want to leave reach safety.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
Lubinets thanked Melania Trump and the Ukrainians and US citizens who helped bring attention to the situation in Oleshky and support the negotiations. He said the mission’s priority remained delivering assistance and helping civilians leave safely.

'They know exactly what they're doing' — What Russia gains from a ceasefire in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:47:26 UTC
03:47:26 KST

Why did Russia agree to the Oleshky ceasefire?
An aerial view of Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, Ukraine in a photo published on Sept.16, 2026. (Dmytro Lubinets / Telegram)
Moscow's consent to a temporary ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky seems like a long-overdue and welcome concession from a country that has repeatedly rejected or violated ceasefire proposals during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
So why is the Kremlin so on board with Oleshky? Experts, as well as information from Oleshky itself, suggest Russia's motives go far beyond addressing the humanitarian catastrophe it created itself.
Instead, the highly publicized ceasefire brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump presents several opportunities for Moscow to manipulate facts on the ground, an international audience, and — crucially — the White House, all as it positions itself ahead of a new round of peace talks.
"They know exactly what they're doing," John Foreman, a former U.K. defense attache in both Kyiv and Moscow, told the Kyiv Independent.
The propaganda opportunity
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 29 accused Ukraine of "creating a humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky, despite the fact that Russian forces have been in control of the city since 2022.
Military analyst Vasyl Pehno said on Oct. 27 that Russia had created the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and is now presenting itself as "heroically rescuing civilians."
The evacuation of residents from Oleshky provides the Kremlin with the opportunity to convince the world that Ukrainians under occupation would rather live in Russia than go back to Ukraine.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents will have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
But a source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."
Footage broadcast by Russian state media channel TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
read also
The political gains
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XIV, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
The first lady facilitated the ceasefire arrangement after she learned about the crisis during the United Nations General Assembly week, her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 28.
He added that her involvement in the Oleshky ceasefire was "wanted very much" by Putin, something Foreman said betrays obvious political motives.
"Allowing Melania to take the credit bolsters (Russia's) credentials to the MAGA base as peacemakers before the midterms," he said.
Foreman argued that the temporary truce could help Putin placate Trump as he continues to blame Ukraine for blocking the peace process.
"(It's the) same Kremlin approach for the diesel deal, agreeing to three-way talks, and releasing a hostage in return for pausing new sanctions," he said, adding that each time Russia has gained something substantial without "conceding anything significant."
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow wants to give Trump another opportunity to claim he has helped stop a war.
Russia is unlikely to violate the ceasefire this time, he said, not out of concern for civilians, but because the Kremlin would not want to jeopardize its relationship with Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Despite this, the Beckman is adamant that Russia is acting in good faith.
"It's my understanding and my belief in being very close to all of these negotiations and knowing all of the parties for a long time, that everybody, the Russians included, is working in good faith," Beckman said.
"It's understood that this is a humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and these elderly people need to be saved."
read also
Crisis beyond Oleshky
While the Kremlin agreed to the Oleshky ceasefire, it remains silent about the dire humanitarian situation across other occupied territories.
Daria Rabinovitsch, co-executive director at Helping to Leave, a charity that helps civilians leave the occupied territories, told the Kyiv Independent that calculating how many settlements are isolated is nearly impossible due to broken communications and missing internet access, but at least three other areas are known to be suffering from isolation.
These include the Kinburn Spit, settlements in the Polohy District of Zaporizhzhia Oblast where drivers refuse to go, and Enerhodar, where access has become hazardous due to intense air attacks along transport routes.
Such enclaves frequently appear when the front line shifts and Russia gains more territory, Rabinovitsch said. In some places, Russian military personnel relocate residents from active combat zones deeper into occupied lands, she added.
While the ceasefire might facilitate temporary relief efforts in Oleshky, it leaves systemic problems facing Ukrainians under Russian control unaddressed.
Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.
"Oleshky is not the only community on the temporarily occupied territories that is experiencing a humanitarian catastrophe, and while we are happy and hopeful for the people there, we know that this evacuation will not resolve the systemic problems facing Ukrainians in the Russian occupation," Rabinovitsch said.
According to Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, the initial 30 hours of the ceasefire proceeded without incident. While Kherson Oblast had a brief chance for respite, Russian forces continued striking other Ukrainian regions and killing civilians.
As Lubinets headed to Oleshky on the morning of Oct. 29, Russian troops attacked the railway station in Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, with a jet-powered drone, killing at least 13 people.

Bluebottle drones that never sleep level playing field in Pacific drug war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:47:12 UTC
03:47:12 KST

Australian-made Bluebottle drones to patrol Fiji's waters for drug traffickers
Fiji's hundreds of islands and vast maritime territory make it difficult to detect drug traffickers.
Intent on accessing lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand, smugglers from the Americas use the island nation as a Pacific transit point.
"Our biggest challenge is our waters are too big," Fiji's Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua said.
"We don't even have eyes on it, let alone have the capability to affect anything on it."
But a new fleet of uncrewed maritime surface drones could help level the playing field.
The 7.4-metre-long Australian-made Bluebottles can remain at sea for up to six months, while using artificial intelligence to identify suspicious activity.
Powered by a retractable solar sail that can harness the sun and wind, they also have an underwater flipper that converts the boat's rocking in the waves into forward motion.
Mr Tikoduadua said the Bluebottles would help Fiji capitalise on its limited resources.
Traffickers are known to use yachts, fishing vessels, freight ships and even semi-submersibles, known as narco-subs.
Fiji's navy, meanwhile, operates just two large patrol boats, RFNS Savenaca and RFNS Timo, both Australian-donated Guardian-class vessels.
The RFNS Timo replaced a previous vessel, the RFNS Puamau, which ran aground during its maiden voyage in 2024.
'Virtually impossible to detect'
Australia is donating the drones and training as part of a $600 million package for the Pacific-wide Waqa Moana maritime security initiative to counter illicit drug trafficking.
The money will also fund new Australian Federal Police programs and regional surveillance support.
Fiji's first drones are expected to start arriving next year, but the total number has not been made public, with Mr Tikoduadua saying they wanted to "keep drug dealers guessing".
Australian Minister for Defence Industry and Pacific Island Affairs Pat Conroy earlier this month said the Australian Navy had 15 Bluebottles, most of which monitored the country's northern coastline, with orders in for another 40.
"They are virtually impossible to detect unless you get very close to them," he said.
An Australian company, Ocius Technology, designed the Bluebottles and operates them from a military base in Darwin.
Ocius chief growth and market development officer Rob Brezniak said the vessels could be fitted with high-tech surveillance sensors, including infrared cameras, radar and sonar to detect submarines.
He said they relayed intelligence to a team of human operators via satellite, with AI helping to filter the data and flag potential threats for a faster response.
"A government can then task an asset like a crewed vessel to approach," he said.
Mr Brezniak did not expand on how the AI technology made its assessments, saying "a combination of things helped it make an informed decision".
He also declined to disclose the individual cost of the drones, however the Australian government said its contract with Ocius to deliver the 40 drones was worth $176 million.
In Fiji's case, Mr Tikoduadua said Fijian personnel would control the Bluebottles and configure them to monitor surface vessels, with a detection range of up to 30 nautical miles (55.5km).
He said intelligence would be transmitted to human operators at the Vuvale Maritime Essential Services Centre (MESC), an Australian-funded security hub near Fiji's capital Suva which houses Fijian agencies including the navy, police and fisheries.
Mr Tikoduadua said the gathered information could be shared with partner countries and organisations if a vessel left Fiji's jurisdiction.
"If we need partner navies to come take a look, or a commercial vessel to take a look, it gives us that flexibility," he said.
Levelling the playing field
Mr Tikoduadua has seen the Bluebottles in action.
New Zealand recently deployed two to Fiji during a four-week joint operation.
Associate Professor Jose Sousa-Santos, convenor of the Pacific Regional Security Hub at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, said officials reported the unmanned drones detected more than 100 illegal fishing vessels, many of which had switched off their transponders.
"They did exactly what they were supposed to do," he said.
"They were supported by the New Zealand Air Force and when they identified vessels that raised red flags, they were able to contact the RNZAF to provide further surveillance coverage."
Mr Sousa-Santos said the Bluebottles had the potential to disrupt trafficking operations if they were positioned in zones smugglers regularly operated in.
"It would force them to move to other trafficking routes which might not be as safe or profitable," he said.
A new frontier
Steve Symon, who chaired New Zealand's Ministerial Advisory Group on Transnational, Serious and Organised Crime, said the Bluebottles were a valuable tool.
But he feared the region's size meant they could only be effective if deployed in large numbers.
He added the crime syndicates would probably adapt.
In the short term, Mr Symon said traffickers could rely more heavily on cargo ships and corruption within ports if surveillance drones made their operations more difficult.
But it might only be a matter of time before traffickers started using similar drones, he said.
Criminal syndicates had a powerful incentive to adapt because of the huge demand for illicit drugs in Australia and New Zealand, he said.
"The reason why these [Bluebottle] drones are so good is because they are solar-powered and you can send them out for months at a time.
"But we'd be naive to think organised crime isn't going to be ready adopters of the same technology."
Sharing with Australia
Mr Tikoduadua said data the Bluebottles collected would be shared with partners, including Australia.
Mr Conroy said Australia needed to work with Fiji to stamp out the illicit drug trade, which meant "working together in a coordinated way in terms of intelligence gathering, intelligence sharing and interdiction".
Australian officials did not say whether the Bluebottles in Fiji would be used for anything beyond detecting drug traffickers and illegal fishing, such as monitoring foreign military vessels.
Jennifer Parker, an adjunct professor of defence and security at the University of Western Australia, said she did not believe the drones would have wider strategic implications for Australia's defence.
"Fiji and Australia have a significant defence partnership and we would already share significant information about what is happening in our maritime domains," she said.
"So the employment of Bluebottles to support collection of that kind of information would not be any different to, I suspect, what's already in place."

It also builds on the broader NATO-Ukraine cooperation across their innovation ecosystems, which has developed significantly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine," the press release notes.
